Brasil encara Argentina em segundo amistoso antes do Mundial Feminino
Após vencer o primeiro confronto, seleções voltam a campo na Arena de Pernambuco em preparação para a Copa do Mundo de 2027
A Seleção Brasileira Feminina enfrenta a Argentina nesta terça-feira (13), às 20h30 (de Brasília), na Arena de Pernambuco, em Recife. O amistoso é o segundo confronto entre as equipes e serve como preparação para a Copa do Mundo Feminina de 2027, que será disputada no Brasil.
No primeiro duelo, realizado no último sábado (10) no Beira-Rio, em Porto Alegre, a equipe brasileira venceu por 3 a 1.
Luany, Geyse e Angelina marcaram os gols do Brasil, enquanto Maricel Pereyra descontou para a Argentina.
Para a partida desta terça-feira (13), o técnico Arthur Elias terá que lidar com desfalques importantes. A volante Angelina, uma das artilheiras do último jogo, fraturou o nariz durante o confronto e foi cortada da convocação.
A lateral Bruninha também está fora, após romper o ligamento cruzado anterior (LCA) do joelho direito, necessitando de cirurgia.
Reforços e possível escalação
Em contrapartida, a Seleção Brasileira terá o retorno de três atletas que cumpriram suspensão no primeiro amistoso: a zagueira Tarciane e as atacantes Kerolin e Bia Zaneratto. O próprio técnico Arthur Elias também estará de volta à área técnica, após cumprir suspensão no último sábado.
Com essas opções, Arthur Elias pode promover mudanças na escalação e dar minutos a jogadoras que não atuaram ou tiveram pouca oportunidade no confronto anterior. Uma possível formação do Brasil inclui Lorena; Isabela, Mariza, Tarciane e Raíssa Bahia; Duda Sampaio, Maiara e Kerolin; Tainá Maranhão, Bia Zaneratto (Jhonson) e Geyse.
Histórico do confronto e próximos jogos
Brasil e Argentina já se enfrentaram 22 vezes na história do futebol feminino, considerando o primeiro amistoso deste mês.
Os dados do Fifa Data Centre mostram a superioridade brasileira, com 19 vitórias, um empate e apenas duas derrotas contra as rivais.
Este duelo será o último compromisso da Seleção Brasileira em território nacional em 2026. A equipe de Arthur Elias já tem agendados dois amistosos contra o Japão na próxima Data Fifa: em 29 de novembro, em Hiroshima, e em 5 de dezembro, em Okayama.

artigo.texto: Gil Torquato, Abranet: É difícil pensar na regulamentação do Redata ainda este ano Para o presidente da Abranet, a renovação do Congresso Nacional e a própria eleição presidencial deve provocar um delay. "É ruim, mas é o momento que estamos vivendo". Ele também defendeu o adiamento da Reforma Tributária. O presidente da Associação Brasileira de Internet (Abranet), Gil Torquato, defendeu ao participar de um painel na Futurecom 2026 que a regulação da Inteligência Artificial tem de ser “o mais cirúrgica possível e cobrir setores específicos para não inibir a inovação”. Segundo ele, quanto menos regulação será melhor para a IA, uma vez que é necessário estimular e não inibir o mercado. Em entrevista, Gil Torquato disse que as regulamentações têm de dar respaldo e segurança jurídica para assegurar os investimentos. Sinalizou ainda que uma agência para IA tem de ajudar nas diretrizes, mas não teria de ter uma visão punitiva. Gil Torquato é descrente da possibilidade de o Marco Legal de IA ser aprovado ainda este ano. “Houve uma renovação do Congresso e o tema tem de ser mais discutido”, pontuou. O presidente da Abranet falou também sobre o Redata. Ele também acha difícil ter a regulamentação ainda este ano – ela está com o poder executivo – diante das eleições presidenciais. “O Redata é muito importante, gostaria que saísse, mas acho que teremos um delay”, admite. E ao ser questionado sobre a Reforma Tributária, Gil Torquato lembrou que as empresas não estão preparadas e o próprio governo está atrasado. Ele defendeu o adiamento da vigência do novo regime. “É um tema sensível. Afeta todas as empresas e é preciso rediscutir as alíquotas”. Assista a íntegra da entrevista com o presidente da Abranet, Gil Torquato.

artigo.texto: A expansão dos data centers voltados à inteligência artificial e o uso da fibra e dos lasers nos drones, em especial na guerra da Ucrânia, provocou uma busca acima da demanda de componentes e uma crise igual a vivida na pandemia da covid no supply chain, revela o CEO da PadTec, Carlos Raimar. A empresa, multinacional brasileira que tem como objetivo dar vida a conexões de alta capacidade, está negociando com os seus fornecedores. “A fotônica está entrando nos data centers. São dezenas e dezenas de semanas de espera. Tem de se programar por um a dois anos à frente com nossos fornecedores. E, infelizmente, não há cenário dessa crise terminar tão cedo. O que temos de fazer é tentar desenvolver fornecedores e tecnologia local”, observa o CEO da PadTec, em entrevista à CDTV, do portal Convergência Digital. No mercado brasileiro, a PadTec está abrindo uma unidade fabril em Manaus. E a escolha está ligada aos custos e à segurança de manter os benefícios até 2070. A empresa tem uma fábrica em Campinas e uma sala limpa, dentro do CPQD, também em Campinas. “A Lei de Informática vai até 2029 e não sabemos que irá acontecer com ela. Nossos planos são de longo prazo. E Manaus tem acordos com Zonas Francas da América Latina, o que expande muito o nosso mercado”, observa o executivo. A unidade em Manaus vai produzir toda a linha de valor agregado, mas não produzirá amplificadores, que são muito sensíveis e exigem uma mão de obra muito especializada. Raimar diz que na América Latina, o ano foi de expansão. Mas no Brasil, o cenário foi de aperto. “Muitos projetos engavetados e redes estão no limite. Acredito que no ano que vem, os investimentos voltem”. Um dos recados da PadTec é que a empresa está indo além da fotônica e quer ser a fornecedora de infraestrutura crítica digital. “Nós preparamos o barco para avançarmos muito. E vamos crescer no mercado de cabos submarinos. Estamos negociando contratos maiores”, detalha. Sobre o Redata, Raimar diz que vai beneficiar porque data centers virão para o Brasil e há uma ‘certa’ proteção à indústria nacional. Mas ele diz que a indústria terá de ser criativa para fazer soluções de cloud e inteligência artificial para o ambiente digital. Uma situação incomoda muito: o mercado dos Estados Unidos perdido para o tarifaço. “O mercado americano ficou impossível com o tarifaço e investimos muito na homologação e nos testes para atender a demanda local. Hoje o que vendemos é o que nossos concorrentes não entregam”. Assistam a íntegra da entrevista com o CEO da PadTec, Carlos Raimar.

artigo.texto:
Energy infrastructure AI platform Karman (formerly known as Utilidata) has partnered with French industrial group Legrand to integrate Karman into its data center power distribution product lines.
According to the companies, this will include Legrand's intelligent AC rack PDUs and DC power shelves, which it claims are designed for high-density AI data centers.
Karman’s platform utilizes AI to provide real-time visibility for grid operators and data center firms. It works by identifying and managing distributed energy resources, which it claims enhances resiliency and offsets the need for future infrastructure investments. The platform can integrate with smart meters, providing AI solutions for utility companies and their customers.
The company developed the platform using a custom version of the Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, which it claims provides 100 times the processing power of other meter-based solutions. The platform can connect to millions of endpoints and coordinate them to monitor and react to real-time conditions.
According to the partners, the deployment could allow Legrand’s data center customers to power more compute and generate 50 percent or more AI tokens using the same provisioned power.
"By partnering with Karman, Legrand continues to demonstrate its technological leadership and innovation by delivering additional value to data center operators,” said Swen Anderson, CTO of Legrand's data, power, and control division.
“We’re providing data centers with the tools to unlock stranded power and deliver measurable competitive advantages and increased revenue.”
“Power continues to be the primary limiting factor to data center capacity expansion. Yet, a large portion of provisioned power in data centers goes untapped,” added Josh Brumberger, CEO of Karman. “This partnership with Legrand changes that. By embedding Karman into Legrand’s power distribution products, data center operators can now utilize that power to expand capacity immediately, while reducing the price per GPU hour.”
Karman was rebranded earlier this month, formerly operating under the name Utilidata.
In June, the firm raised $60.3 million in Series C funding to scale its platform, led by Renown Capital Partners, with participation from Quanta, Nvidia, and existing investor Keyframe Capital.

Why AI Data Center Cooling Needs to Get Smarter AI is pushing data center cooling to its limits, so the real advantage comes from integrating smart sensing, motor control, and power management into a single responsive, failure-anticipating system. The job of a data center cooling system is simple in concept: absorb heat where it isn’t wanted and move it where it can be released safely. AI is making that job much harder, pushing rack power past 100 kW, with some AI clusters expected to exceed 1 megawatt within the next few years. Operators racing to add AI capacity must deploy quickly while protecting uptime, managing energy use, and safeguarding valuable hardware. There is no single way to cool an AI data center. The right architecture depends on rack power, workloads, and facility requirements. Engineers typically reserve the most advanced liquid cooling for AI racks, while other approaches serve standard workloads and facilities without existing water infrastructure. Liquid cooling is becoming increasingly important, but this mix of approaches adds complexity: mitigating leak risk, supporting multiple architectures at once, and ensuring that cooling responds precisely as thermal demands change. Moving heat more efficiently is no longer enough. The next step is to make cooling systems more intelligent through real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management. Together, these technologies can make cooling more responsive, reduce energy consumption, and maximize uptime while laying the foundation for AI-enabled predictive maintenance. Why Smarter Control Matters Consider what happens when a liquid-cooled rack develops a leak. Many of today’s rack installations use on-off valves that stop the coolant when a sensor detects a leak, shutting down the entire rack until technicians can locate and fix the leak source. With a whole rack at stake, detection must be reliable. Yet the most common leak sensors, moisture-sensitive resistive ropes, can be limited in both accuracy and response time. A more intelligent approach could detect leaks faster and control coolant flow at the server-tray level, helping keep unaffected parts of the rack running. That points to three capabilities working together: real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management. Real-Time Motor Control Keeps Coolant Moving Inside the coolant distribution unit (CDU), pumps and fans form the mechanical heart of the cooling loop. Reliability is the top priority. Depending on the CDU placement, a single pump failure can take an entire rack – or worse, an entire row – of AI computing equipment offline. Real-time motor control helps keep that system stable. Microcontrollers process sensor data and adjust performance accordingly, while motor drivers run pumps and fans efficiently. Motor control also extends to the server tray. Valves at the CDU typically open or close, but linear valves at the tray level can regulate coolant flow much more precisely. As power density inside the tray continues to rise, that level of precision becomes more important. Precision Flow Sensing Tracks Coolant at the Tray Precise flow control requires precise flow measurement, so linear valves at the tray work alongside accurate flow sensors. Together, they enable more granular control of GPU and CPU die temperatures. How the sensor is installed matters, too. Conventional flow sensors are inserted into the coolant line, creating an additional potential leak point. Non-invasive ultrasonic sensing can avoid that risk while also making installation easier and faster. Moisture-sensitive resistive ropes are still commonly used for leak detection. Still, concerns about accuracy and response time are pushing engineers to evaluate alternatives such as humidity sensors, capacitive sensors, and negative-pressure CDU designs. Flow readings also contribute to a broader operating picture. Combined with temperature, humidity, and pressure sensors, they can help detect changes that any single sensor might miss. High-Efficiency Power Management Keeps Cooling Lean The pumps and fans cooling AI racks consume power themselves, so their efficiency matters. Power management and motor control meet in the pump drive, where gallium nitride (GaN) power devices can improve overall pump-system efficiency by up to 2% compared with traditional silicon while enabling a smaller form factor. In server trays that still combine air and liquid cooling, fans remain critical, and many are shifting from 12 V to 48 V to reduce power consumption and improve efficiency. Power delivery is evolving as well. CDU pumps already operate on input voltages ranging from 48 V DC to 380 V AC. As 800 V high-voltage DC (HVDC) distribution gains traction in parts of the industry, operators will need pumps designed to support it. Edge AI Lays the Groundwork for Predictive Maintenance Sensing can also become predictive. Edge AI can process data from a cooling system’s full sensor array, an approach known as “sensor fusion,” enabling faster response times and lower latency. That matters for leak detection, which remains a bottleneck for reliable liquid cooling. Sensor fusion can improve detection speed and accuracy. It also opens the door to predictive maintenance for pumps and other critical mechanical components. Combined with tray-level flow control, edge AI and sensor fusion point toward cooling systems that sense changing conditions, anticipate problems, and adjust automatically. Building Intelligence into Every Architecture No single cooling design fits every AI data center, and mixed architectures are likely to serve the industry for years. But every architecture, from rear-door heat exchangers to immersion tanks, shares many of the same building blocks: sensors to measure conditions; motor control to drive pumps, fans, and valves; power management to supply them

artigo.texto: How Chiplets Could Transform Server Design – And Data Centers Chiplets are reshaping CPU design, enabling data centers to do more without increasing space or power consumption. Since the advent of microprocessors more than 50 years ago, CPUs have typically been built as single pieces of silicon. As a result, servers and the data centers that house them have largely been designed around that model. However, that is beginning to change. The growing adoption of chiplets – small modular dies that can be combined in a single processor package – is giving chipmakers a new way to build CPUs. By improving manufacturing flexibility and enabling more specialized processor designs, chiplets could reshape not just server architecture but also how data centers approach compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning. What Are Chiplets? A chiplet is a small integrated circuit designed to perform a specific function within a larger processing package. Depending on the design, chiplets may handle compute, input/output (I/O), cache, memory connectivity, or workload-specific acceleration, such as AI acceleration. When combined, chiplets can provide the same overall capabilities as a traditional CPU. The key difference is that, instead of manufacturing a processor as one large monolithic die, chipmakers can build it from multiple smaller dies assembled in a single package. The chiplet concept has existed for decades, and related multi-die approaches are not entirely new. But adoption accelerated in the late 2010s as chipmakers sought more efficient ways to improve processor performance, manage manufacturing complexity, and scale designs across different workloads. The Benefits of Chiplets A chiplet-based approach to CPU design offers several potential advantages. Reduced manufacturing costs. Smaller dies are often easier to manufacture with higher yields than a single large, complex die. If a single die has a defect, the loss is usually less significant than losing an entire monolithic processor. It can also be easier to engineer and optimize a smaller die for a specific function than to design one large chip that must handle multiple functions at once. Design freedom. By separating functions such as compute and I/O into different dies, chipmakers can tailor processor designs more efficiently for different types of workloads and product segments. Potentially higher compute density. In some cases, chiplets allow chipmakers to pack more processing capability into a single processor package, helping to enable more powerful servers without necessarily increasing physical server size. Supply chain flexibility. Because smaller dies are often easier and faster to manufacture than very large monolithic chips, chiplet-based designs may reduce some production constraints. That said, they do not eliminate supply chain risk altogether, because advanced packaging and integration can create bottlenecks on their own. In short, chiplets can make it easier for chipmakers to scale processor designs, improve yields, and optimize hardware for growing demand. What Do Chiplets Mean for Data Centers? Although chiplets directly affect processor design, their impact could extend well beyond the chip itself. One important implication is the potential for increased compute density inside data centers. If chiplets allow server vendors to deliver more processing power within a single server platform, operators may be able to support heavier workloads without expanding physical footprints at the same pace. Historically, higher compute density has often meant higher power draw and greater cooling requirements. Chiplets do not automatically solve that problem. However, if they enable more efficient processor designs or better performance per watt, they could help offset some of the infrastructure strain that typically comes with denser compute environments. A key result of greater chiplet adoption, then, could be data centers that support higher IT loads without requiring proportionally more space or power. In that scenario, existing facilities could become more valuable because operators would be able to do more with the infrastructure they already have. Chiplets may also help reduce the risk of server procurement delays by giving manufacturers more flexibility in how processors are designed and produced. This does not remove supply chain challenges altogether, but it could make sourcing CPUs and servers somewhat easier over time. In the longer term, chiplets could also encourage more specialized server designs. As chipmakers gain flexibility to mix and match dies optimized for different functions, server platforms may become increasingly tailored for workloads such as AI, analytics, storage, or high-performance computing. That would give data center operators more options, but it could also make infrastructure planning more workload-specific than it is today. A Shift Worth Watching Chiplets are no longer a futuristic concept. They are already becoming an important part of modern processor design, especially as chipmakers look for new ways to improve performance and efficiency. For data centers, the biggest impact may not come from chiplets themselves, but from the servers they enable. If chiplet-based designs continue to improve compute density, efficiency, and workload specialization, they could play a major role in shaping the next generation of data center infrastructure.

artigo.texto: AI Data Center Land Buying Hits $6B as Power Premiums Rise US data center land spending hit roughly $6 billion in the first half of 2026, as power access now drives land value and pricing more than location alone. US purchases of land for future data centers reached about $6 billion in the first half of 2026, up 79% from a year earlier, according to Avison Young. The spending reflects demand for large AI campuses, as hyperscalers, neocloud providers, energy-first developers and investors compete to secure sites for new computing capacity, according to the Q2 2026 Data Center Market report. For data center operators, the stakes are both operational and financial. Delayed power can push back capacity delivery, complicate customer commitments and leave expensive buildings waiting to enter service. “The biggest thing right now is speed to power,” John Andril, manager of market intelligence at Avison Young, told TechTarget in an interview. In Northern Virginia, entitled land without power can sell for roughly $4 million an acre, compared with at least $6 million an acre for powered land, Andril said. Entitlements, infrastructure and other site characteristics also affect prices, so the comparison does not isolate the value of electricity alone. “The premium is increasingly payment for uncertainty removed, not just for megawatts nearby,” said Neil Osnato, an industry analyst who has examined data center land transactions. Committed Power Drives Land Value An Altus Group analysis of 80 verified data center land transactions in August found committed utility load was the strongest predictor of land pricing. Sites associated with 230-kilovolt or 500-kV infrastructure traded at roughly 2.4 times the pricing of sites associated with 138-kV or lower infrastructure, according to the analysis. Transmission access can reduce the upgrades required to serve a project. In some cases, existing infrastructure can also shorten the regulatory process and save about a year, Andril said. However, proximity to a transmission line doesn’t guarantee that a utility can deliver the required capacity on schedule. “If you don’t have power until the early to mid-2030s, you’re probably not going to get a lot of interest,” Andril said. Andril said a genuinely power-ready property generally needs electrical infrastructure deliverable within about 18 months, roughly matching the time needed to prepare a building for its initial load. Developers also need clarity on the equipment required for a substation and who will fund and build it. For campus planning, developers generally use about 0.5 to 1 acre per megawatt as a rule of thumb, Andril said, although land-constrained markets can support higher densities. A large project, therefore, requires both enough land and a credible plan for delivering its electricity. A Texas Deal Puts a Value on Power A transaction involving Plug Power and Stream Data Centers illustrates how power capacity can affect a project’s economics. Plug agreed to sell its Graham, Texas, project to Stream for $50 million, with up to $26.5 million in additional consideration tied to the electrical load capacity ultimately established for the project. The agreement used a 164-megawatt (MW) reference capacity. Plug had an interconnection request with Oncor and had deposited $6.5 million with the utility to secure a requested 164 MW of load. It also posted a $7.75 million letter of credit under the ERCOT Batch Zero agreement. The project includes about 66 acres, development rights and grid-interconnection assets. The transaction was later restructured. Stream acquired high-voltage electrical infrastructure for $40 million in August, while the land and remaining interconnection assets remained subject to closing conditions. The original agreement shouldn’t be described as a completed $76.5 million land sale. Its significance is that additional consideration depended on the capacity ultimately established, putting a price on the uncertainty surrounding the project’s power supply. Northern Virginia Shows the Stakes Loudoun County records show SDC Twin Creeks Parent LLC, a data center developer, paid $615.05 million for 97.15 acres in November 2025, or about $6.33 million an acre. The property is part of the Twin Creeks data center development in Leesburg, Va. Dominion Energy separately paid $45 million for about 14 acres associated with the development. The transactions don’t isolate electricity’s contribution to the land prices. Entitlements, development rights, site assembly and market conditions also influence valuations. They illustrate the scale of investment in data center sites in one of the country’s most competitive markets. Andril said the effect can be pronounced in lower-cost markets, too. Land that might sell for roughly $10,000 an acre without a viable data center power path can become worth six figures per acre after developers establish the infrastructure and utility relationships needed for a large project. Utilities Want Proof Developers Are Serious Utilities face a planning problem of their own. They must prepare for large new loads without spending billions of dollars on projects that never materialize. Developers, meanwhile, want confidence in power delivery before committing substantial capital to a site. Andril described the problem as a “chicken-and-egg” situation. Letters of credit, take-or-pay agreements and stricter interconnection-queue requirements can help utilities separate serious projects from speculative requests. Andril said established developers and end users can support those measures because removing speculative projects makes legitimate demand easier to evaluate. Onsite generation offers another option. Developers can use it to support initial operations while waiting for utility infrastructure, Andril said. Whether that approach makes financial sense depends on generation costs and the project’s economics. For data center operators, those factors belong in site selection

artigo.texto: Brazil’s Data Center Growth Pushes Beyond São Paulo Brazil’s data center growth is spreading beyond São Paulo to Rio, Fortaleza, and the south, but power grid delays and lengthy permitting will decide which markets actually succeed. Brazil’s data center market is beginning to expand beyond its longtime base in São Paulo as hyperscale and AI-driven projects draw attention to Rio de Janeiro, Fortaleza, and southern Brazil. The shift reflects growing demand for capacity, but it also highlights a harder question for developers: whether Brazil’s energy and connectivity advantages can be translated into sites with dependable power and workable construction timelines. São Paulo still accounts for 76% of Brazil’s live data center capacity, according to DC Byte’s August market analysis. The city continues to benefit from its concentration of customers, network density, and established operator presence. That ecosystem gives the market a depth that emerging regions cannot quickly replicate. However, São Paulo faces a shrinking supply of powered land and slow transmission upgrades. At the same time, newly enacted federal tax incentives could improve project economics in other parts of the country, even as environmental licensing and electricity infrastructure remain potential constraints. São Paulo Still Dominates Capacity Brazil’s existing market is still driven principally by hyperscale cloud demand and enterprise deployments, even as large AI projects begin to influence development plans. “Demand continues to be driven predominantly by hyperscale cloud providers, which remain the largest consumers of data center capacity in the country,” Rodrigo Gomez, senior Latin America analyst at DC Byte, told Data Center Knowledge. São Paulo’s advantage comes from more than scale alone. The market combines demand from Brazil’s largest metropolitan economy with dense fiber connectivity and access to international networks, reinforcing its position as the country’s primary cloud and interconnection hub. Operators including Ascenty, Elea, and Scala have built substantial footprints in Brazil. DC Byte also points to investments by Microsoft and Equinix as evidence of growing international interest. Gomez said the maturity of that ecosystem remains central to Brazil’s appeal. Investors can enter a market with established customers and infrastructure while also pursuing opportunities in less developed locations. “At the same time, Brazil is beginning to see greater investment in facilities designed to support AI workloads, reflecting the global shift toward high-density computing and next-generation digital infrastructure,” he said. This leaves Brazil serving two overlapping tracks of demand: continued growth in cloud and enterprise capacity, and the development of larger, higher-density facilities designed for AI and other intensive computing workloads. Power and Permitting Remain the Main Constraints Power availability remains the central variable in how quickly new capacity can be delivered. Brazil’s access to renewable electricity strengthens the country’s long-term investment case, but generation does not necessarily mean a site can be connected on schedule. Gomez identified the pace of electrical infrastructure development as the market’s main challenge. Generation, transmission, and broader grid expansion all take time, making delivery schedules for new substations and transmission capacity critical for developers. Bruno Porto, manager for industrial, logistics, and data centers in Brazil at real estate services firm JLL, told Data Center Knowledge that some locations will require transmission reinforcement before additional data center load can be supported. “Environmental licensing in Brazil is also critical, with this phase alone potentially taking up to 18 months depending on the region and the scale of the project,” Porto noted. Those factors can stretch project timelines even where land, capital, and customer demand are available. For developers looking outside São Paulo, the key question is not just whether a market looks attractive on paper, but whether permits and power delivery can align with construction schedules. Porto said he expects growth through 2027 to depend heavily on projects already negotiated during 2026. He added that the volume of facilities now under construction should allow providers to bring new capacity online within the next 12 months. That outlook applies to projects that have already advanced through the development process, not to every large campus proposal in the national pipeline. Longer-range projects still depend on securing infrastructure and approvals before they can move into execution. “Environmental licensing in Brazil is also critical, with this phase alone potentially taking up to 18 months depending on the region and the scale of the project.” – Bruno Porto, manager for industrial, logistics, and data centers in Brazil, JLL Regional Hubs Offer Different Advantages Outside São Paulo, Brazil’s emerging markets offer different combinations of customer access, connectivity, and development potential. Rio de Janeiro is positioned to support both domestic and international traffic, with Gomez describing it as an important gateway for digital services serving eastern Brazil. Its development pipeline includes both more conventional colocation projects and larger AI-oriented ambitions. Those figures represent long-term development ambitions rather than operational capacity. Fortaleza’s competitive strength is more directly tied to international connectivity. artigo.texto: How to Secure Data Centers During the Construction Phase Before operations begin, layered defenses at the site and in the supply chain help prevent theft, vandalism, counterfeit gear, and covert endpoints. As data center build-outs accelerate, most conversations about physical security focus on operational facilities, with threats ranging from mundane events, such as break-ins, to novel threats like drone attacks. Yet the period of greatest exposure is often earlier: during construction. Sites are porous, contractor populations are large and fluid, and high-value materials and preinstalled equipment can be targeted or tampered with. Protecting the build phase should be a core pillar of any data center’s broader physical security strategy. Construction-Phase Risks to Data Centers Physical intrusions during construction come in many forms: Material theft. Theft of construction materials is common on open or lightly controlled construction sites. Copper, cabling, generators, and networking gear are all attractive targets, leading to financial losses and construction delays. Vandalism and sabotage. In some markets, community opposition to data center expansion can increase the likelihood of on-site disruption or damage. Deployment of spy devices. More covertly, malicious actors may attempt to plant devices – such as rogue wireless access points, small network switches, or hidden sensors – during construction to enable remote backdoor access once the facility is operational. Supply chain tampering. Risks also extend into supply chains: tampering with shipments, swapping components, or introducing counterfeit or compromised gear can create backdoors or degrade reliability before the facility ever goes live. Aerial reconnaissance or nuisance activity. Hobbyist drones can expose site layouts and procedures or create safety hazards. Practical Strategies to Secure Data Center Construction Sites While the overarching goal is simple – prevent unauthorized access to construction sites and their supply chains – executing this amid complex projects and large contractor populations is challenging. The following layered controls help reduce risk while maintaining construction speed. Establish a strong perimeter and active monitoring. Build robust physical barriers, ensure all ingress/egress routes are controlled, and funnel all foot and vehicle traffic through staffed gates. Pair this with temporary but professional-grade surveillance cameras covering the perimeter, material laydown yards, and sensitive areas; lighting designed with Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design principles; and motion or thermal sensors where feasible. Verify and control who enters the construction site. Vet contractors and delivery personnel before granting access, consistent with local laws and company policy. Require visible badges and use zoned access so workers can enter only the areas relevant to their tasks. This is no guarantee that bad actors won’t find their way in, but it’s one way to reduce risk. Grant access in phases. Bringing contractors on-site in smaller groups (e.g., having electricians complete their work before allowing HVAC workers to begin) reduces crowding and makes anomalous activity more visible. The trade-off is that this may slow construction by reducing the amount of work contractors can perform in parallel. Rope off construction areas. In addition to establishing a strong perimeter around the data center site, roping off or caging high-value storage (e.g., copper, cabling, generators, and networking equipment) provides another layer of defense against theft and sabotage. Harden the supply chain and track custody. Vet vendors for chain-of-custody controls, tamper-evident packaging, and secure transit practices. Upon receipt, record serial numbers and MAC addresses of networked devices, use barcodes or RFID to track movement, and keep sensitive equipment in controlled cages until deployment. Prepare for drone threats. Use drone detection where appropriate for visibility into potential aerial activity. Many forms of active drone interdiction are illegal, so coordinate with local authorities and legal teams, emphasizing deterrence, detection, and evidence capture rather than unlawful countermeasures. Validate what’s installed before commissioning. Another way to detect supply chain abuse is to compare installed assets against purchase orders and approved bills of materials. Conduct technical sweeps for unauthorized wireless signals or unexpected network endpoints to identify situations where someone installed a device that isn’t supposed to be included. Balancing Speed and Security Complete eradication of construction-phase physical security risks isn’t realistic, just as fully preventing cyberattacks isn’t. However, a multilayered defense strategy based on practices like those described above goes a long way toward reducing the likelihood and impact of intrusions, while improving your chances of detecting and remediating those that do occur.

artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems. In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parc

artigo.texto: A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira, 13 de outubro, o requerimento de urgência do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3.716/2026, que propõe retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias como reserva de capacidade. Com a decisão, a proposta poderá ser votada diretamente pelo plenário, sem precisar passar pelas comissões. O requerimento de urgência foi apresentado pelo deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE). Já o projeto é de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). O PL revoga o parágrafo 6º do artigo 3º-A da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que determina que os custos das contratações de reserva de capacidade com baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Com a revogação, passaria a valer para as baterias a regra geral da lei, que prevê o rateio dos custos da reserva de capacidade entre os consumidores, assim como acontece copm as demais tecnologias contratadas nessa modalidade. Apoio das associações A aprovação da urgência ocorre após seis associações do setor elétrico divulgarem, em 7 de outubro, uma nota conjunta em defesa do projeto. As entidades argumentam que a regra atual estabelece tratamento diferente para as baterias em relação às demais tecnologias contratadas nos leilões de reserva de capacidade. O posicionamento foi assinado pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica), Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (Abiape), Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (Abihv), Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) e Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). Segundo as entidades, a cobrança exclusiva dos geradores pode elevar os custos da energia elétrica para os consumidores, uma vez que os valores podem ser repassados às tarifas no mercado regulado e aos preços dos contratos no mercado livre. As associações também argumentam que os sistemas de armazenamento podem reduzir outros custos do setor elétrico. A nota cita estudo da Volt Robotics que estima economia superior a R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano para os consumidores, por meio da redução da volatilidade do Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças (PLD) e do acionamento de usinas termelétricas. As entidades defendem que os custos da reserva de capacidade sejam distribuídos conforme os benefícios proporcionados ao sistema e que baterias recebam tratamento equivalente ao das demais tecnologias que oferecem potência e flexibilidade.

artigo.texto: Você sabe carregar seu celular corretamente? Confira dicas para preservar a vida útil da bateria Conectar primeiro o carregador ou o celular? Onde deixar o aparelho? Usar o celular durante a carga tem problema? Veja alguns cuidados básicos Por O Globo Atualizado Há hábitos diários que repetimos sem nem nos dar conta. E, com certeza, carregar o celular é um deles. Tem quem demore até a bateria ficar no vermelho, outros preferem se precaver e, na primeiro oportunidade, dar aquela carga a mais por garantia. Apesar da duração das baterias poder variar entre as marcas e modelos, há alguns protocolos que merecem ser respeitados para prolongar na vida útil do aparelho, segundo especialistas. - Você é um dos 83 milhões de brasileiros endividados? Ferramenta do GLOBO ajuda a organizar suas contas; confira - Fim da escala 6x1: você trabalha mais ou menos do que a média no Brasil? E no mundo? Confira Pequenos cuidados podem ajudar a evitar, por exemplo, microdescargas causadas por flutuações de tensão. Aquela "escorregada" vez ou outra não compromete o aparelho, o problema está na recorrência de maus hábitos, em que, sucessivamente, vai mitigando o funcionamento. Mesmo nessa tarefa simples de carregar o celular, a ordem impacta no aparelho. Idealmente, você deve primeiro conectar o carregador à tomada, e só então conectar o cabo ao celular, dando início à recarga. Isso acontece porque o circuito interno precisa de alguns instantes para estabilizar o fluxo de energia. Na hora de desconectá-lo deve ser feito o caminho inverso, à fim de proteger os componentes, primeiro desconectando o celular do cabo do carregador, e só depois retirá-lo da tomada. Às vezes pode ser difícil ficar longe do celular, deixando-o recarregar sem uso. Responder uma notificação rápida, até vai, mas ações como jogar videogames ou assistir a vídeos em alta resolução geram um aumento de temperatura que afeta sua vida útil. Outro risco é tensionar ou dobrar o cabo durante esse manuseio, o que pode causar fissuras e rupturas comprometendo o carregamento e até estragando-o. Também está diretamente relacionado à temperatura do aparelho a superfície em que ele é mantido apoiado durante o carregamento. Materiais que ajudem a dissipar o calor, pois facilita o resfriamento durante o processo, dispondo o celular sobre móveis, como mesa ou escrivaninha, ou pedra, como mármore ou granito. Isto deve ser combinado a uma área bem ventilada e uma superfície seca. Deixar o aparelho sobre cobertores, travesseiros ou plástico deve ser evitado. O recomendado é escolher ambientes com pouca umidade, por isso, é importante evitar cômodos como banheiros e cozinhas, ainda para evitar risco de choque elétrico. Deixar o celular no chão também não é uma boa opção devido às chances de entrada de sujeira na porta de carregamento. Outros fatores que merecem atenção é o uso de carregadores de baixa qualidade, que causa tensões instáveis que danificam tanto a bateria quanto seus circuitos internos. O uso do acessório original ou de um certificado pelo fabricante garante a transferência segura de energia para o equipamento. E deixar o dispositivo conectado à tomada durante a noite é desnecessário para baterias modernas.

artigo.texto: The Nozu Project adds to Trina Storage's growing track record in Japan's utility-scale energy storage market. As deployment of grid-scale battery storage expands in the country, Trina Storage has established local capabilities to support projects from system configuration and technical consultation through delivery coordination and after-sales service. Through its team in Japan, Trina Storage works closely with customers and project partners to address local technical and project requirements, providing support throughout the project lifecycle. This local capability is complemented by Trina Storage's global experience in battery cell technology, system integration and utility-scale energy storage deployment. Dr. Leo Zhao, Head of Energy Storage (APAC), Trina Storage, said, "We are pleased to support Japan's growing renewable energy portfolio through the AEJ Nozu Battery Energy Storage System project. With Trinasolar's longstanding experience in solar and Trina Storage's growing presence in utility-scale energy storage, we see significant opportunities to support Japan's evolving energy needs. For Nozu and other projects in Japan, our focus is on combining advanced technology with strong local capabilities." Trina Storage is also supplying a 160MWh utility-scale BESS project in the Kyushu region, adding to its growing project track record in Japan. In September, it also signed an MoU with AMP-lify for approximately 1GWh of grid-connected BESS projects in Japan, featuring the latest Elementa 3 series. The MoU agreement, together with projects like Nozu, reflects Trina Storage's continued expansion in Japan as demand for utility-scale energy storage grows.

Dr. Leo Zhao, Head of Energy Storage (APAC), Trina Storage, said, "We are pleased to support Japan's growing renewable energy portfolio through the AEJ Nozu Battery Energy Storage System project. With Trinasolar's longstanding experience in solar and Trina Storage's growing presence in utility-scale energy storage, we see significant opportunities to support Japan's evolving energy needs. For Nozu and other projects in Japan, our focus is on combining advanced technology with strong local capabilities." Trina Storage is also supplying a 160MWh utility-scale BESS project in the Kyushu region, adding to its growing project track record in Japan. In September, it also signed an MoU with AMP-lify for approximately 1GWh of grid-connected BESS projects in Japan, featuring the latest Elementa 3 series. The MoU agreement, together with projects like Nozu, reflects Trina Storage's continued expansion in Japan as demand for utility-scale energy storage grows.

artigo.texto: The Andhra Pradesh Power Coordination Committee (APPCC), acting on behalf of Andhra Pradesh’s distribution companies (APDISCOMs), has invited proposals for developing 1,250 MW / 5,000 MWh of standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) across three locations in the state. The projects will be developed under the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model through tariff-based competitive bidding, allowing selected developers to build, own and operate the storage facilities. The initiative aims to strengthen energy storage infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh and support the integration and management of renewable energy. The proposed projects will be located at the Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant (RTPP), Talaricheruvu Renewable Energy (RE) Project and NP Kunta RE Project. The tender provides an opportunity for battery energy storage developers to participate in large-scale standalone storage projects under a competitive procurement framework. The total planned capacity comprises three separate projects. The first project involves the development of a 500 MW / 2,000 MWh Battery Energy Storage System at the Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant. The second project covers 250 MW / 1,000 MWh of storage capacity at the Talaricheruvu RE Project. The third project involves another 500 MW / 2,000 MWh installation at the NP Kunta RE Project. Together, these installations will provide 1,250 MW of power capacity and 5,000 MWh of energy storage capacity. The projects are structured to provide standalone battery storage facilities at designated locations, with developers responsible for implementing and operating the systems under the BOO arrangement. To facilitate project development, land will be provided to selected developers on a Right-of-Use (RoU) basis. The annual land lease charge has been set at a nominal rate of INR 1 per acre. This arrangement is intended to provide developers with access to the required land for establishing the battery storage installations at the identified project sites. APPCC issued the request for selection (RfS) document on October 7, 2026. The pre-bid meeting is scheduled for October 22, 2026, at 11:00 hours. Interested bidders must submit their pre-bid queries by 17:00 hours on the same day. The last date and time for submitting bids is November 23, 2026, at 17:00 hours. The technical bids will be opened on November 24, 2026, at 15:00 hours. Prospective bidders will need to follow the tender schedule and submit the required documentation within the specified deadlines. The cost of the RfS document is INR 3 lakh, plus 18% Goods and Services Tax (GST). The tender fee is non-refundable. Bidders must also submit an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of INR 5 lakh per MW of their quoted capacity. Permitted EMD instruments include a Demand Draft, Bank Guarantee, Payment on Order Instrument (POI) or Insurance Surety Bond. Additionally, selected developers will be required to provide a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of INR 10 lakh per MW of contracted capacity before signing the Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). Through this procurement, APPCC is seeking developers to establish large-scale battery storage infrastructure across three strategic locations in Andhra Pradesh. The tender outlines the project capacities, land-use arrangements, financial requirements and bidding timeline for interested participants. artigo.texto: SINEXCEL Completes PCS Shipment for 100MW/400MWh Energy Storage Project in Chile VALLENAR, Chile, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SINEXCEL (300693.SZ) has shipped all StellaON 1250K power conversion systems for RelyEZ Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd.'s 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage project in Chile. The four-hour system in Atacama will charge during lower-demand periods and discharge at peak times, supporting grid flexibility and project returns. On-Schedule Delivery Supports Project Execution Large-scale overseas projects require production, inspection, and shipment schedules to remain closely aligned with on-site construction. SINEXCEL completed the full PCS order on schedule, helping RelyEZ Energy protect the timetable for transport, installation, commissioning, and grid connection. For a project of this scale, delays in a single batch can narrow the construction window. Coordinated delivery reduces uncertainty and helps local teams plan the next stages. StellaON 1250K PCS Built for Atacama's Demanding Conditions Energy equipment in Atacama must operate in an environment that can include high temperatures, dust, and sand. The StellaON 1250K PCS has a maximum efficiency of 99% and a rated-power efficiency of 98.5%. It supports operation from -40°C to 60°C, maintains full power output at 55°C, and has an IP65 protection rating. Maintaining rated output in high temperatures can reduce power derating and the need for additional capacity. Higher conversion efficiency also limits energy losses across repeated charge-discharge cycles, supporting stable operation and long-term returns. Strengthening Local Service Capabilities Across the Americas Following shipment, the project will move into on-site installation and commissioning. SINEXCEL has a dedicated after-sales team in Latin America and seven service centres across the Americas. Technical requests can receive a response within 30 minutes, backed by round-the-clock support and a seven-day spare-parts guarantee. SINEXCEL has deployed more than 17GW of energy storage capacity across over 5,000 projects and works with more than 600 partners in 60+ countries and regions. Following shipment, the Chilean project moves into its on-site delivery phase. SINEXCEL will continue to expand its local operations across Latin America, providing customers with support throughout the project lifecycle. About SINEXCEL Founded in 2007, SINEXCEL is a pioneer in energy storage, EV charging, and power quality solutions. With 17 GW of installed storage, 200,000 EV DC chargers, and nearly 20 million amperes of Active Harmonic Filters deployed, SINEXCEL partners with industry leaders to empower energy freedom. artigo.texto: The City of Madison’s moratorium on data centers will expire in January 2027, leaving citizens to enact framework amidst company planning. Madison enacted the moratorium to moderate the development of potentially harmful facilities in January 2026. The regulation was set to last one year and expires on Jan. 24, 2027. To prepare, the City is establishing zoning regulations that allow for data center construction and specify potential facility locations. A Wisconsin State Journal map shows potential data center sites fall in Districts 3, 14, 15, 16 and 17. These districts are also largely on Madison’s east side and in overall lower-income, less populated areas. For Derek Field, District 3 alder and member of the Plan Commission, land use is central to the data center debate. He told The Daily Cardinal his east Madison district contains land not yet developed that is “intended to grow in the form of neighborhoods and mixed-use areas that meet residents' needs.” Several small data centers, Field points out, already exist in Madison, since the moratorium did not include properties under 10,000 square feet. There are currently 15 of these centers throughout the Madison area. Field said he has not heard concerns from citizens about these smaller centers. However, he believes an increase in size or location coverage could influence public response. “We need to make sure large-scale data centers or clusters of data centers cannot locate in Madison [or] take up too much land that we've planned for neighborhoods,” Field said. Michael Zhang, founder and CEO of WiscAI, a Madison-based AI consulting firm, told the Cardinal he believes the outcome of local data centers is in resident hands. “I don't think it's a simple net positive or negative,” Zhang said. “It depends on the terms: who pays for the extra power, how much water it uses and what the community gets back in jobs and taxes.” University of Wisconsin-Madison freshman Neha Pesaramelli is dubious about these positive effects of potential data centers. “When we consider how much environmental impact data centers have, as well as how they impact water and different resources people need, I feel really disappointed that our government and the people that are supposed to be looking out for us aren’t weighing the lives and wellbeing of Madison residents over profit,” Pesaramelli told the Cardinal. Although the proposed data center locations are far from central Madison, Pesaramelli hesitated about their proximity to an urban setting in general. “I think it is privileged to say that [companies] should push data centers out of cities into more rural areas,” Pesaramelli said. “But I also think there has to be other alternatives to our energy needs that aren’t putting citizens at risk like this so close to where people are living.” Oscar Bertram, another UW-Madison student, told the Cardinal he agrees. “It still is harming those communities and making it harder for them to get out of [their situation],” Bertram said. Apart from data center location, Field acknowledges the city may not have as much control as many citizens believe. Entities like the Wisconsin Public Service Commission are often the sole decision-makers for rules about eco-friendliness and water consumption, according to Field. “The City's scope of regulations will be pretty limited, which I think is going to be frustrating to many community members,” Field said. As the discussion of data center zoning in Madison develops, a public information meeting through the Department of Planning and Community and Economic Development will take place on Oct. 27. The meeting is meant to bring public opinion into future data center regulation and framework.

artigo.texto: O Brasil está vivenciando uma expansão acelerada de data centers, centros de dados digitais que movem a economia. A busca por energia estável e segurança levou esses empreendimentos para cidades do interior, como Varginha, em Minas Gerais. A previsão é de que o setor atraia até R$ 100 bilhões em aportes até 2030, redesenhando o mapa tecnológico do país. O Brasil está vivendo um grande crescimento na construção de data centers, que são estruturas essenciais para guardar e processar os dados da internet. Essa expansão, que pode atrair até R$ 100 bilhões de investimentos até 2030, está levando esses empreendimentos para fora das grandes capitais e para o interior do país. Muitas pessoas não percebem, mas toda a nossa vida digital depende de uma infraestrutura física enorme. A busca por energia elétrica estável e segurança está fazendo com que empresas de tecnologia instalem seus servidores em cidades menores, mudando a cara da infraestrutura digital do Brasil. - O setor de data centers no Brasil deve receber entre R$ 60 bilhões e R$ 100 bilhões em investimentos até 2030. - Varginha, em Minas Gerais, recebeu em setembro de 2025 o primeiro data center do Sul de Minas, com previsão de R$ 23 milhões em aportes. - O Brasil conta com cerca de 200 data centers, ocupando a 12ª posição no mundo e liderando a América Latina. - A energia é o fator mais importante: a demanda por conexão de grandes cargas deve somar 54,2 GW até 2038. - Construir um data center exige planejamento rigoroso de energia, refrigeração e conectividade antes mesmo de comprar os servidores. Como funciona a estrutura por trás da internet Segundo Henrique Reis, especialista em infraestrutura digital e fundador da Sourei, construir um data center não começa com a compra de computadores ou servidores. O primeiro passo é entender se a região tem energia elétrica estável e suficiente. É necessário verificar se há rotas diferentes de fibra óptica para conexão, se o sistema de refrigeração é adequado e se existe segurança para manter a estrutura funcionando 24 horas por dia, sem pausas. Uma decisão errada nessa fase inicial de planejamento pode atrapalhar toda a operação no futuro. A redundância, ou seja, a existência de fontes alternativas de energia e internet, é o ponto central. Se a eletricidade ou a internet falharem em uma única fonte, serviços de bancos, comércio online e empresas podem parar de funcionar. Henrique explica: Quando o usuário acessa um sistema, ele não vê o que existe por trás daquela aplicação. Há servidores, energia, refrigeração, fibra óptica e equipamentos trabalhando continuamente. O data center é justamente a estrutura que mantém essa operação disponível mesmo quando ocorre uma falha em algum componente. Energia define onde a tecnologia vai crescer A disponibilidade de energia elétrica é o principal fator que decide onde novos data centers podem ser construídos. Em São Paulo, por exemplo, estudos indicam que serão necessários cerca de R$ 1,6 bilhão em investimentos na rede de transmissão de energia para liberar espaço para novas conexões. Outras obras planejadas para 2026 devem aumentar ainda mais essa capacidade. Para o especialista, não basta apenas olhar a quantidade de energia disponível. É preciso garantir que ela seja estável e que haja espaço para expandir a capacidade futura. Como os servidores geram muito calor constantemente, a quantidade de energia e de sistemas de ar condicionado (refrigeração) precisa ser calculada com precisão. Um servidor trabalhando gera calor continuamente. Quanto maior a capacidade computacional instalada, maior também a necessidade de energia e refrigeração. Por isso, essas decisões precisam ser feitas em conjunto. Não adianta ter espaço físico se a região não consegue sustentar tecnicamente a operação, aponta Henrique. O interior entra no mapa tecnológico Com as grandes cidades ficando mais caras e complexas, a busca por novas áreas abriu espaço para cidades médias. Varginha, por exemplo, está localizada estrategicamente entre São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e Belo Horizonte. A cidade possui acesso a redes de comunicação, aeroporto e uma atividade empresarial que exige serviços digitais. No entanto, trazer um data center para o interior não é apenas uma questão de encontrar terreno mais barato. É preciso analisar as rotas das fibras ópticas, a segurança do local, a distância dos principais pontos de conexão da internet no país e se há profissionais técnicos qualificados na região. O interior pode ter vantagens importantes, mas não basta disponibilizar uma área. É preciso saber por onde chegam as fibras, quais são as alternativas em caso de falha, como está a oferta de energia e se existe capacidade de expansão. Data center é uma decisão técnica antes de ser geográfica, afirma Henrique. O data center instalado em Varginha foi projetado para oferecer serviços como armazenamento de dados, cópias de segurança (backup) e processamento, conectando-se diretamente ao grande eixo econômico do Sudeste. Infraestrutura é a base da economia digital Sistemas bancários, plataformas de compra online, serviços em nuvem, filmes de streaming e ferramentas de inteligência artificial dependem de capacidade física para processar informações. É por isso que a discussão sobre data centers deixou de ser apenas assunto de técnicos de TI e passou a fazer parte das decisões sobre investimento e desenvolvimento regional. Henrique ressalta que o software apenas funciona porque existe hardware sustentando a operação. A economia digital depende de hardware, conectividade, energia e disponibilidade. Quanto maior a digitalização das empresas e dos serviços, maior será a necessidade de capacidade instalada. Na avaliação do empresário, cidades fora dos grandes polos de tecnologia podem se tornar importantes para o país. O interior não precisa ser apenas consumidor de tecnologia. artigo.texto: Recently, the strategic cooperation signing ceremony between Rockcheck New Energy Group and Suzhou Qingde Hydrogen Energy Technology Co., Ltd. was held in Tianjin. Relying on the Sunan Institute of Molecular Engineering at Peking University, the two parties will focus on the field of hydrogen agriculture to jointly develop and promote hydrogen molecular fertilizers, while deepening cooperation in hydrogen beauty and health and hydrogen industry sectors, working together to open up new tracks for diversified hydrogen energy applications. Peking University professor and doctoral supervisor Li Xingguo, Qingde Hydrogen Energy General Manager Xie Lei, and Rockcheck Group Director, Vice President, and Rockcheck New Energy Group Chairman Zhang Lihua attended the ceremony. Hydrogen energy industry enters a new era of multi-scenario large-scale application Currently, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the Ministry of Finance, and the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) have approved five major urban clusters including Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei to carry out comprehensive hydrogen energy application pilot projects. China's hydrogen energy industry has officially moved from single-point breakthroughs in fuel cell vehicles into a period of multi-scenario large-scale application. The strategic cooperation between Rockcheck New Energy and Qingde Hydrogen Energy is an important initiative by the two enterprises to actively implement the national hydrogen energy pilot deployment, which will continue to broaden the boundaries of hydrogen energy applications and build a diversified hydrogen energy industry ecosystem. Strong alliance between technology R&D and scenario operations This cooperation achieves a strong alliance and complementary advantages between technology R&D and scenario operations. Rockcheck New Energy is a benchmark enterprise in the commercial and large-scale implementation of hydrogen energy, positioned as an integrated solution provider for the hydrogen energy industry. It has built an entire industry chain layout covering "production, storage, transportation, refueling, application, research, and equipment manufacturing," and created a "one core, two poles" development model centered on a digital and intelligent big data platform, with the "hydrogen +" economy and "vehicle +" economy as the two poles. To date, it hascumulatively put into operation 1,255 hydrogen fuel cell heavy trucks and 17 hydrogen refueling stations, with mature project implementation capabilities, rich multi-scenario operation experience, and a complete industrial supporting system. Qingde Hydrogen Energy is a hydrogen energy technology innovation enterprise relying on the Sunan Institute of Molecular Engineering at Peking University. The company has developed efficient and safe nano-hydrolysis hydrogen production materials, which are widely used in hydrogen molecular biomedicine and hydrogen agriculture. It holds multiple independent intellectual property rights and has carried out project cooperation with multiple industry leaders, demonstrating outstanding strength in technological innovation and commercialization of research outcomes. Industrial layout implemented across three major tracks According to the agreement, the two parties will implement industrial layout across three major tracks: first, jointly promote the civilian application, productization, and scenario-based implementation of hydrogen health technologies, creating a new sector in the hydrogen beauty and health industry; second, use hydrogen-enriched technology to empower the transformation of modern agriculture,jointly develop and promote hydrogen molecular fertilizers, and explore a new model of green, efficient, and low-carbon smart hydrogen agriculture; third, tap into the value of hydrogen energy storage, promote the large-scale application of hydrogen energy in scenarios such as renewable energy consumption and power grid peak shaving, and cultivate new growth poles for the hydrogen energy industry. The two parties will establish a special working group, build an industry-academia-research collaboration mechanism, and jointly carry out technical research, demonstration project construction, and market expansion, promoting the extension of hydrogen energy applications from transportation and logistics to diversified scenarios such as public health, modern agriculture, and new-type industry.

artigo.texto: SWI arrecada US$ 894 milhões para reestruturar a antiga mineradora de bitcoin da FTX, Genesis Digital, para IA O Grupo SWI afirmou que utilizará os recursos provenientes de uma captação de fundos de 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) para transformar a Genesis Digital Assets, adquirida da falência da FTX, de um minerador de bitcoin para um data center focado em IA. - O Grupo SWI levantou 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) de investidores institucionais, avaliando a empresa em 6,1 bilhões de euros, para expandir projetos de inteligência artificial e data centers na Europa e nos Estados Unidos. - A empresa planeja reutilizar as instalações nos EUA e na Suécia da Genesis Digital Assets, a mineradora de bitcoin anteriormente apoiada pela FTX que agora controla como SWI Digital, para cargas de trabalho de IA, enquanto vende os locais da unidade no Cazaquistão. - A estratégia da SWI reflete uma mudança mais ampla na indústria, à medida que os mineradores de bitcoin transformam conexões de energia e capacidade de data center em receita de IA e computação de alto desempenho. SWI Group (SWICH), que controla a mineradora de bitcoin Genesis Digital Assets, anteriormente pertencente à FTX, afirmou ter levantado 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) junto a investidores institucionais para expandir seus projetos de data center e de computação em inteligência artificial (IA) na Europa e nos Estados Unidos. A empresa listada na Euronext Amsterdã, uma firma de investimentos focada em infraestrutura digital, anunciou o aumento de capital avalia-o em 6,1 bilhões de euros. Anunciou a aquisição de cerca de 40% da Genesis Digital em junho por 500 milhões de dólares, concluindo o aquisição em agosto com 70% dos direitos de voto e renomeando a unidade para SWI Digital. A estratégia da empresa ilustra o que se tornou uma operação conhecida para as empresas de mineração de bitcoin. Seu ativo mais valioso não são mais suas máquinas de mineração, mas as conexões de energia e os locais dos data centers que podem ser reaproveitados para clientes de IA. Mineradores de bitcoin assinaram mais de US$ 70 bilhões em contratos de IA e computação de alto desempenho, à medida que buscam uma receita mais estável do que a mineração de bitcoin atualmente oferece. A mudança do foco da mineração de criptomoedas para o processamento de computações de IA coloca a empresa na mesma corrida que os mineradores listados como a TeraWulf e Core Scientific , que estão convertendo o acesso à energia e a capacidade de data centers em negócios de hospedagem de IA. O CEO da SWI, Max-Hervé George, disse ao Wall Street Journal que ele “"juros zero” na mineração de bitcoin. A empresa está vendendo os sites da Genesis Digital Assets no Cazaquistão e pretende utilizar suas instalações nos EUA e na Suécia para cargas de trabalho de IA em vez disso. Alameda Research, a empresa de negociação de criptomoedas pertencente ao ex-CEO da FTX, Sam Bankman-Fried, investiu mais de US$ 1 bilhão na Genesis Digital Assets desde 2021 e detinha cerca de 20% da mineradora, informou o WSJ. FTX declarou falência em novembro de 2022, deixando esse investimento entre os muitos ativos analisados pelo espólio.
