artigo.texto: CATL remains the world’s largest electric vehicle battery supplier in 2026, ahead of BYD and LG Energy Solution. However, the competition extends beyond market share: battery prices, manufacturing efficiency, customer diversification and regional demand are determining which suppliers can grow profitably. Global battery installations reached 844.2 gigawatt-hours from January through August 2026, increasing 19.7 percent year on year. The figures cover batteries installed in registered battery-electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hybrid electric vehicles, rather than total battery production. For automakers, supplier selection connects vehicle affordability with dependable delivery, charging performance and long-term warranty support. CATL and BYD together supplied approximately 460.9 GWh, accounting for roughly 54.6 percent of installations. Seven Chinese suppliers held a combined 73.3 percent share. Growth varied sharply: CATL increased installations 25.2 percent, Gotion 47.1 percent, EVE 53.9 percent and REPT 126.3 percent. BYD grew 6.2 percent, while SK On declined 14.5 percent. These are eight-month results, not full-year rankings from Insight -SNE Research. CATL Combines Market Leadership With Financial Strength CATL’s 2025 annual results, released in March 2026, reported revenue of RMB 423.7 billion, up 17 percent, and net profit attributable to shareholders of RMB 72.2 billion, up 42 percent. Lithium-ion battery sales reached 661 GWh, increasing 39 percent. These sales include applications beyond electric vehicles and therefore differ from SNE’s automotive installation figures. CATL reported 772 GWh of production capacity, with another 321 GWh under construction at year-end. Research and development spending reached RMB 22.1 billion, approximately 5.2 percent of revenue. The company also processed 210,000 tonnes of spent batteries and regenerated 24,000 tonnes of lithium salts. The combination of earnings, research spending and manufacturing scale gives CATL resources to develop products and expand internationally. Its challenge is to bring additional capacity online at a pace that matches commercially viable demand. BYD’s Integrated Model Creates a Different Advantage BYD combines battery manufacturing with vehicle production, allowing battery design and vehicle engineering to develop within the same group. Its Blade Battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry. LFP avoids nickel and cobalt in the cathode and is widely used where cost, durability and thermal stability are priorities. BYD’s structure can simplify coordination between vehicle platforms and battery supply. However, it also means battery deployment is closely linked to the performance of its own automotive business. For buyers comparing BYD with independent suppliers, the relevant questions extend beyond installation volumes. External supply availability, platform compatibility, commercial terms and production location determine whether a battery offering fits an automaker’s requirements. LG Energy Solution, Panasonic and SK On Face Different Demand Exposure LG Energy Solution and Panasonic recorded installation growth below the overall market, while SK On’s volumes contracted. These suppliers remain important because of their established vehicle programmes and manufacturing relationships. Their results illustrate how customer concentration and regional exposure can influence performance even when worldwide battery demand rises. The International Energy Agency notes that Tesla continues sourcing most of its EV batteries from established suppliers including Panasonic, LG Energy Solution and CATL, despite developing its own manufacturing capabilities. For suppliers, winning a vehicle programme creates an opportunity rather than a guaranteed production volume. Actual demand depends on vehicle sales, launch schedules and the customer’s decisions about battery sourcing. Battery Prices Show Why Chemistry Matters BloombergNEF’s 2025 battery price survey provides a cost benchmark for evaluating the market in 2026. Average lithium-ion pack prices fell 8 percent to $108 per kilowatt-hour. Battery-electric vehicle packs averaged $99/kWh, while chemistry averages across applications were $81/kWh for LFP and $128/kWh for nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries. Using those chemistry averages, an illustrative 60 kWh pack would cost approximately $4,860 with LFP or $7,680 with NMC—a difference of $2,820. This calculation is not a supplier quotation or a comparison of otherwise identical packs. China’s regional average was $84/kWh. North American and European prices were 44 percent and 56 percent higher, respectively, implying approximately $121/kWh and $131/kWh. Stationary-storage packs averaged $70/kWh, down 45 percent, demonstrating why automotive and storage battery prices should be compared separately. Lower Battery Costs Do Not Automatically Mean Cheaper Cars Battery purchasing costs influence vehicle economics, but retail prices also reflect manufacturing, electronics, distribution, taxes and financing. For an illustrative 75 kWh vehicle, a $10/kWh reduction in pack cost represents $750 in potential manufacturing savings. An automaker could use that saving to lower prices, improve margins or fund additional features. Likewise, a lower-priced chemistry is not automatically the best choice for every model. Energy density, pack size, charging behaviour and vehicle weight affect the final design. Suppliers that offer several suitable products can address more vehicle categories, while automakers must evaluate the complete battery system rather than the cell price alone. Manufacturing Capacity Exceeds 4 TWh The IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 battery analysis reports that global lithium-ion nameplate manufacturing capacity exceeded 4 terawatt-hours at the end of 2025, up approximately 30 percent. artigo.texto: A well-known local engineer said he's completely reimagined the concept of data centers — and he said it addresses just about every concern communities have expressed. Opposition to data centers has exploded almost as quickly as the industry itself. Channing Blackwell believes he's got the solution. Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. “We're not putting off any pollution, we're not putting off any noise,” he said. Blackwell is a professional engineer, and whether or not you know his name, you know his work. His firm designed several monuments in D.C., including the National Museum of African American History and Culture. His father's company helped design the underground Metro system. When it came to looking at data centers, Blackwell said the solution was as easy as turning the problem upside down. “Once I put it underground, then I started really pushing on optimizing the building,” he said. He calls it “The Renaissance System.” Northern Virginia Northern Virginia news, events and updates “For 12 months, they've worked quietly fixated on three core principles: community security, environmental security, national security. That work gave birth to The Renaissance System,” a corporate video described the project. Buried below the ground, crowned by a berm adorned with solar panels, the subterranean data center concept would be powered by geothermal energy, relying on zero fossil fuel. At hyperscale, it would span 30 acres, cost less than half of the current hyperscale data center and be nearly as powerful as the largest data center currently operating in the U.S. — not to mention that Blackwell said it wouldn't need to plug into the electric grid. “People that are 20 miles down the road that are protesting the power lines — Are they really needed if you get rid of the above-ground data centers that are obsolete technology and go to something that we've designed?” he said. Just last week the U.S. Department of Energy released a report suggesting geothermal technology could solve one of the largest issues current data center design creates: heating and cooling. Blackwell explained that above ground, data centers struggle to keep the thermostat at a comfortable level for their servers, and it costs a lot of money to do it. Underground cooling comes naturally and requires zero community water. Blackwell said mother nature will work for us — all she requires is that we listen to her. “If you're sloppy with your design, she can't close it for you. But, if you're mindful, it's there,” he said. As Blackwell launches his Renaissance System, he's not the only game in town. Other companies around the country are working on similar projects. In fact, a company based in Texas just inked a deal with Google to provide geothermal energy to a data center out west. While the future of this technology has yet to be proven, one thing is certain: There are people hearing the concerns about the data center industry, and they are working on solutions. This Saturday, the Piedmont Environmental Council is hosting a march in Leesburg, calling for a statewide data center moratorium. News4 asked a council spokesperson about using geothermal energy to power data centers. The spokesperson was unfamiliar with the Renaissance System but said they hope it works.

artigo.texto: Diagnóstico de 90 dias vai mapear a infraestrutura do estado para disputar a instalação de empresas de tecnologia e data centers junto ao resto do Nordeste por Cynara Maíra Publicado em 12/10/2026, às 12h26 - Atualizado às 12h51 Estudo encomendado: Governo de Pernambuco e LIDE contrataram a Deloitte para fazer um raio-x da infraestrutura digital do estado em 90 dias. Financiamento privado: Os custos do levantamento são pagos pelas empresas Cavalcanti Petribu, Estratégica Engenharia e Dislub Equador. Secretarias envolvidas: Participam do projeto as pastas de Administração, Ciência e Tecnologia e Desenvolvimento Econômico. Objetivo: O documento vai apontar gargalos e orientar ações do governo para atrair empresas de tecnologia e investimentos privados. Lançamento: O encontro de apresentação ocorre nesta quarta-feira (14), às 10h30, na sede da Secti, no Bairro do Recife. O Governo de Pernambuco e o LIDE Pernambuco iniciam nesta semana a elaboração do Estudo Estratégico do Ecossistema de Infraestrutura Digital do estado. O levantamento, conduzido pela consultoria Deloitte com prazo de conclusão de 90 dias, vai traçar um diagnóstico técnico para orientar políticas públicas e atrair investimentos privados voltados à conectividade, inteligência artificial e centros de processamento de dados (Data Centers) no estado. A ideia é que o anúncio do início dos trabalhos ocorra nesta semana, na quarta-feira (14), como a primeira entrega formal da parceria entre o Governo do Estado e o Lide, após o início do acordo de cooperação técnica firmado em julho de 2026. A ideia é que o grupo de cooperação continue pelos próximos quatro anos. Na parte do Executivo, participarão as secretarias de Administração; Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação e a pasta de Desenvolvimento Econômico. No lado privado, bancarão os custos o Grupo Cavalcanti Petribu, a Estratégia Engenharia e o Grupo Dislub Equador. A partir das conclusões da Deloitte, a gestão estadual pretende definir prioridades para modernizar a rede, ampliar a conectividade e aumentar a competitividade econômica local. Quando o relatório for entregue, os dados ficarão disponíveis para consulta pública. A apresentação oficial do estudo acontece nesta quarta-feira (14), às 10h30, no auditório da Secti, no Bairro do Recife. O encontro reúne as titulares das secretarias envolvidas, lideranças do LIDE e dirigentes das empresas que patrocinam o projeto. O Lide Pernambuco é uma organização empresarial que reúne diversas empresas do estado que defendem o fortalecimento do ambiente de negócios e o desenvolvimento econômico do estado. Parte do acordo de cooperação técnica com o estado já previa o incentivo a projetos nas áreas de conectividade, data centers sustentáveis, atração de investimentos e desenvolvimento da economia digital no estado.

artigo.texto: Virginia’s New Data Center Bargain: Power, Permits and the Right to Build Key Highlights - Virginia is reshaping data center development through new executive directives, utility policies and proposed regulatory reforms addressing infrastructure costs, environmental impacts and community concerns. - New utility-rate commitments, infrastructure cost-allocation rules and a statewide electricity consumption tax are increasing the financial stakes for large data center projects. - Prince William County has sharply reduced its by-right development district, while Loudoun County is considering further restrictions on permitting and project approvals. - Established development approvals and legally vested rights are becoming increasingly valuable competitive assets as zoning requirements tighten and grandfathering protections face scrutiny. - Data center development continues across Virginia, but projects face growing pressure to demonstrate financial readiness, infrastructure accountability and tangible community benefits. In Loudoun County, Virginia, the changing rules of data center development came into unusually sharp focus during an October 6 Board of Supervisors meeting. County officials warned that rescinding grandfathering protections for certain previously filed data center projects could expose Loudoun to roughly $60 million in potential litigation costs. At the same meeting, officials explained why Amazon could not proceed by right with plans for more than 800,000 square feet of data centers on the former George Washington University campus in Ashburn. The two disputes highlighted opposite sides of the same increasingly consequential question: What development rights does a data center project actually possess, and how secure are those rights as local governments reconsider the rules? That question is taking on new urgency across Virginia, where Gov. Abigail Spanberger's September 18 Data Center Accountability Framework is signaling a broad change in the Commonwealth's relationship with the industry that made Northern Virginia the world's largest data center market. Accompanied by Executive Order 22 and reinforced by the administration's October 1 Virginia Energy Plan, the framework seeks to shift more responsibility for energy infrastructure, environmental impacts and community costs toward the developers and operators whose projects create those demands. Some changes are already underway. Others remain proposals for legislation or future regulation. Meanwhile, existing utility-rate reforms, a new statewide electricity consumption tax and increasingly restrictive local zoning decisions are already altering the economics of development. The result is not a retreat from data centers in Virginia. The Commonwealth remains deeply invested in the industry's continued growth, with an established ecosystem of operators, contractors, network infrastructure and development expertise that competing markets cannot easily replicate. But the conditions for participating in that market are changing. For developers, the implications extend well beyond additional permitting requirements. Land entitlement, utility commitments, project financing, infrastructure cost allocation and community acceptance are becoming increasingly interconnected. A project that once might have advanced through those stages sequentially may now face pressure to resolve more of them before construction becomes financially or politically viable. Virginia's next phase of data center growth may therefore depend less on how many prospective sites developers can assemble than on how convincingly they can demonstrate that those sites can actually be powered, permitted, financed and operated under a more demanding set of expectations. What Took Effect—and What Still Requires Legislation Spanberger laid out the administration's rationale in announcing the framework: “In the years before I took office, data centers came to Virginia and the Commonwealth did not have a clear or coordinated plan to address their impacts on Virginians — on their electric bills, their water, their land, their air, or their quality of life. That changes today. I have said many times that Virginia should be leading the nation in setting the highest standards for this industry. And now, I believe we are doing just that.” The distinction between what Virginia has already implemented and what the administration intends to pursue is consequential. Executive Order 22 establishes immediate directives for state agencies, while significant portions of the broader Data Center Accountability Framework remain proposals for the 2027 General Assembly or future regulatory action. Among the immediate changes, executive-branch agencies are prohibited from entering into or enforcing new nondisclosure agreements that conceal material information about proposed commercial data centers, public incentives, resource demands or community impacts. Existing contractual commitments are preserved, with limited exceptions contemplated for extraordinary circumstances, including national security. The prohibition does not yet extend automatically to local governments. The order also excludes new data center projects with anticipated peak electrical demand of 25 MW or greater from the Virginia Business Ready Sites Program and similar discretionary state site-readiness and expedited-review assistance. A separate, potentially more consequential proposal would eliminate by-right development approval for data centers using more than 25 MW, requiring local approval even for projects with prior authorizations. That provision has not been enacted statewide and could introduce significant legal questions concerning established development rights. The administration is also accelerating environmental oversight. artigo.texto: Websites down and bots disabled: The unexpected consequences of bombing data centers The militaries of Ukraine, Russia and Iran have launched several waves of attacks on these facilities, causing billions of dollars in losses and, in some cases, the permanent destruction of data Ukraine has struck a major blow to Russia’s digital infrastructure. Since last Thursday, Ukrainian drones have carried out a series of attacks that destroyed three large data centers belonging to Yandex — known as “the Kremlin’s Google”— on the outskirts of Moscow. The Yandex Taxi ride-hailing app and the group’s payments service, Yandex Pay, have been temporarily taken offline. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy even said the bombings disabled Russian bots. This is not the first time a regular army has targeted data centers. According to repeated complaints by Kyiv, Moscow has been doing so since March. And before Russia, Iran did it as well. On February 28, after coming under attack from the U.S. and Israel in the bombings that marked the start of the war, Tehran used drones to destroy three commercial Amazon Web Services (AWS) data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. The attack disrupted regional cloud services and affected payment systems across the Persian Gulf. It also triggered a cascading effect that was felt across several AWS availability zones, including in various countries in the Americas and along the U.S. East Coast. The fact that Russia and Ukraine are destroying each other’s data infrastructure, and that Iran chose to strike these facilities as soon as the war began (there have also been reports of bombings in the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia), shows that data centers are increasingly in the crosshairs. “Data centers are secondary targets, right after the obvious military sites,” Matt McCrann, a former executive at counter-drone firm DroneShield with experience in the United States and the Middle East, told Forbes. It also illustrates another point in Iran’s case: in the modern era, not even a distance of 7,000 miles guarantees immunity from retaliation. “The attacks showed that physical distance from a conflict zone is no guarantee of insulation from the impacts of kinetic warfare,” says Tomáš Foltýn, an analyst at the cybersecurity company ESET. The Iranian strike on the three AWS data centers did more than disrupt services in the Middle East and elsewhere, including the United States, where platforms such as Snowflake, Anthropic’s Claude, and some financial applications experienced outages or degraded performance. The drones also permanently destroyed some of the data stored in those facilities, something that does not appear to have occurred in the case of the Russian data centers. The attack served as a reminder that so-called cloud computing is ultimately just a metaphor. Far from being ethereal, it relies on physical infrastructure. And when that infrastructure fails, everything can be lost. A new military target Data centers are the guts of the cloud: highly sophisticated facilities resembling industrial warehouses, packed with racks of servers, essentially computers as tall as wardrobes. These processors run software remotely, including streaming services, and store data such as files saved online. This infrastructure is essential to the functioning of online services, from email and word-processing applications to banking platforms. If data centers did not store files and run software remotely, all of that computing power and storage would have to reside on users’ devices themselves. Smartphones would be incapable of doing nearly as much as they do today, and we would likely have to carry portable hard drives wherever we went. In recent years, data centers have taken on a third role in addition to running software and storing data: training and operating artificial intelligence models, which requires equipping facilities with far more powerful microprocessors that also consume much more energy. That helps explain why academic Eliezer Yudkowsky, concerned that AI systems could one day rebel against humanity, has suggested humanity “be willing to destroy a rogue data center by airstrike” in countries that refuse to limit the computing power available to such systems. Because they are highly technology-intensive facilities that also require an uninterrupted power supply, data centers are among the most expensive pieces of infrastructure in existence. And that makes them an attractive target. “Attacking them makes a lot of sense from an Iranian military perspective. They are multibillion-dollar investments that emerged after Trump’s visit early in his term and are tied to other personal business interests of Trump and his family in the region,” says Colonel Ángel Gómez de Ágreda, author of Un mundo falaz. El nuevo orden global en la era de los algoritmos y la manipulación (A False World: The New Global Order in the Age of Algorithms and Manipulation). Gómez de Ágreda agrees that data centers are already among military targets. “One could also argue that data centers are legitimate [noncivil] targets, since they provide support to military operations,” he says. Permanent data loss Any company can rent server space from a cloud provider to store its data. AWS is the global market leader, with a 28% share, followed by Microsoft Azure (21%) and Google Cloud (14%), according to data from Synergy Research Group. Companies generally choose data centers located as close as possible to the markets they serve in order to reduce latency, the time it takes for data to travel from a device to a server and back. One of the keys to Netflix’s expansion, for example, was signing long-term agreements with AWS, allowing it to rely on the company’s global infrastructure so that its streaming service performed reliably in virtually every country. Both AWS and its competitors typically build data centers in groups of three, known as an availability zone: three nearly identical faciliti

artigo.texto: Once upon a time in the high-stakes world of clean energy procurement, a project team sat around a conference table, staring at a massive, complex document: the Energy Storage Contract Alliance (ESCA) Model Supply and Purchase Agreement. To the untrained eye, a utility-scale battery contract looks like a dry maze of legal jargon.But to the lead developer and the chief technical officer, this wasn't just paper. It was the superhero blueprint that turned a chaotic market into an accessible, bulletproof project. This is the problem that is sought to be solved with a model BESS contract from ESCA. Buyers representing 40 GWh of utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) projects have launched the Energy Storage Contract Alliance (ESCA) and published an open model contract for buying utility-scale BESS. The contract is meant as a common reference for developers, EPCs, independent power producers, asset owners, and battery manufacturers and integrators. ESCA's twenty-two members are utilities, independent power producers, project developers and asset owners with projects worldwide, including Goldbeck Solar, Neoen, ILOS, Pacifico Energy and Eiffage. Anyone, buyer or supplier, can read the core contract free of charge. Members get the full agreement and its technical appendices. The market is growing fast. Global BESS shipments rose about 75% to around 420 GWh in 2025, and InfoLink Consulting expects around 600 GWh in 2026. Contract terms have not kept up. Many projects still start from a blank page or from one party's own template, and topics such as cell traceability, serial defects, inspection sampling and cybersecurity are handled unevenly. A common reference draft can cut drafting time and transaction costs for both sides and make offers easier to compare. A public baseline also lets suppliers respond to tenders against known requirements, and lets smaller developers negotiate on the same footing as large utilities. "Every BESS project works through the same technical and contractual questions, and most of the answers are not project-specific," said Arthur Claire, Secretary General of ESCA. "Those answers used to stay in each company's drawer. ESCA puts a complete baseline in the open, so any developer, utility or manufacturer can take it, use the parts that fit and ignore the rest." The model contract covers technical specifications, factory and site acceptance testing, commissioning, warranties, payment and price-adjustment mechanisms, and cybersecurity. More than fifteen technical appendices set out requirements at system, rack, pack and cell level. The contract sets no prices, price levels or discounts. These remain entirely for each buyer and supplier to negotiate. Sinovoltaics, ESCA's technical secretariat, drafted the first version as a baseline for members to build on. Users can adopt it in full, in part or not at all, and can change any clause. Members can comment on each clause, and the Steering Committee decides on revisions. The Steering Committee includes MN8 Energy, Neoen, Fortum and Munich RE. "As the energy storage sector is witnessing increasingly large procurement processes that often focus on the lowest possible costs, this race-to-the-bottom approach may undercut vital contractual and procurement-related practices and threaten the viability of a BESS project," commented Naim El Chami, Battery Technical Expert at Neoen and a member of the ESCA Steering Committee. Here is how the ESCA model agreement turns confusing legal hurdles into pure peace of mind for energy buyers. For the full contract, see end of story. Act I: The Shield of Traceability and Quality In years past, buying a massive battery system meant placing an order and praying that the manufacturer didn’t swap out high-grade components for cheaper alternatives halfway through production. Enter Clause 4.3 (The Designated Cell) and Clause 4.5 (Traceability Requirements). The contract acts as a digital ledger that locks down the exact cell chemistry, model, and physical factory site down to the individual serial number. When the CTO's team wants to know where their hardware came from, they don’t get vague promises but a transparent, machine-readable as-built register linking every single container directly to its manufacturing batch. Even better, Clause 4.4 (Change Control) guarantees that the supplier can’t change so much as a line of firmware or a bracket on the enclosure without the buyer’s written blessing. For buyers, this turns what used to be a nerve-wracking "black box" into a crystal-clear glass house. Act II: The Gift of Total Data Visibility (Or, How Buyers Can Stop Worrying and Love the Telemetry) Fast forward to Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT). Normally, a buyer receives a summary PDF signed by the factory manager saying, "Trust us, it passed." Not under this agreement. Clause 5.1.8 and Clause 6.6 (Data Monitoring) hand the keys to the kingdom over to the buyer. The contract mandates 1-second interval raw data streams covering voltage, current, and temperature for every single cell during testing and operation. Through Clause 6.5 (Battery Analytics Solutions), independent software monitors the battery's health in real time. The contract explicitly states that the buyer owns all generated data, can access it without paying hidden subscription fees, and never has to rely on the vendor's cloud servers just to check if their asset is running safely. It makes world-class quality control as accessible and simple as checking a smartphone app. Act III: The Guarantee That Keeps on Giving (Or, The 15-Year Safety Net) As the project approaches commercial operation, the financial team usually asks the scariest question of all: "What happens five or ten years from now when these cells degrade or a component breaks?" This is where the ESCA agreement shows its true beauty through a stacked defense of buyer-friendly guarantees: - The Single Point of Responsibility (Clause 7.1.4): The seller can’t point fingers

artigo.texto: Resumo O Governo Federal trabalha para expandir o modelo de desenvolvimento de data centers implementado no Ceará para todos os estados da Região Nordeste. Siga o canal de Economia no WhatsApp para ficar bem informado A informação foi divulgada pelo ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Siqueira, no último sábado, dia 10, ressaltando o potencial do Nordeste para se consolidar como um hub digital de alcance global. Segundo o ministro, a Região reúne as condições centrais buscadas por investidores internacionais para a instalação de grandes centros de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial. O movimento apoia-se em três pilares estratégicos identificados no ecossistema cearense: Confira os assuntos econômicos no Ceará, no Brasil e no Mundo Estudos da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV) citados pelo titular das Comunicações apontam que a implantação de um único data center focado em inteligência artificial no Complexo do Pecém tem potencial de mobilizar até R$ 25 bilhões em investimentos. O impacto econômico prevê a geração de 12,5 mil empregos durante a fase de construção e a criação de 1.860 postos de trabalho permanentes na operação do empreendimento. A iniciativa citada pelo ministério insere-se no contexto de investimentos de grande porte atracados no Ceará. O empreendimento em desenvolvimento no Pecém é o primeiro de um conjunto de cinco data centers autorizados a operar na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Ceará. Acompanhe mais notícias de Economia no Linkedin do O POVO No total, o projeto global está avaliado em R$ 200 bilhões e tem como cliente final a gigante chinesa ByteDance, controladora do TikTok. Desenvolvido pela Omnia, o primeiro centro de dados contará, apenas em sua fase inicial, com uma capacidade instalada de processamento de 200 megawatts (MW). O volume é expressivo quando comparado ao cenário nacional atual: somados, todos os data centers em operação no Brasil possuem cerca de 700 MW de capacidade. Veja dicas rápidas sobre Educação Financeira no Dei Valor Assim, a entrada em operação do primeiro módulo no Pecém representará, sozinha, um incremento de 28,5% na infraestrutura de processamento de dados de todo o País. Já o projeto do data center da Voltalia no Pecém, em Caucaia, está com a licença prévia em análise pela Superintendência Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Semace) e priorizará a utilização de água de reúso. A informação foi divulgada pela Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) em agosto. Operado pela multinacional francesa, o empreendimento ocupará 62 hectares na região, o que equivale a 87 campos de futebol. O investimento total previsto é de R$ 181,7 bilhões em quatro anos, com uma geração de 2.300 empregos diretos na construção e 400 durante a operação. Além disso, conforme a ZPE, a estrutura exigirá expansão de usinas eólicas e solares. Demais informações, entretanto, não puderam ser divulgadas, devido ao “estrito cumprimento às normas de compliance e à legislação vigente”. “A ZPE Ceará esclarece que, em estrito cumprimento às normas de compliance e à legislação vigente, está legalmente impedida de divulgar dados comerciais, operacionais ou financeiros de empresas instaladas ou em processo de instalação na ZPE”, informou.

artigo.texto: Global law firm Dentons has advised PPF banka a.s. in connection with the financing of the construction and development of the 72 MW BESS Frasinet 1 battery energy storage system project in Romania. With this transaction, PPF banka a.s. has financed a third BESS project of the RSJ PE SF Batteries fund, a joint platform of RSJ Investments and Second Foundation that is building a broader portfolio of battery energy storage assets across the EU. Dentons advised on the drafting and negotiation of the financing and security documentation, reviewed key project contracts, and supported the transaction through to signing and completion, including the issuance of a legal opinion and management of conditions precedent. The cross-border Dentons team included Daniel Hurych, Partner and Co-Head of the Banking and Finance group in Prague, Martin Fiala, Senior Associate, Jan Kořistka, Associate, and Tomáš Husička, Junior Associate, together with Petr Zákoucký, Partner and Head of the Energy practice in Prague. Romanian law advice was provided by a Bucharest-based team comprising Simona Marin, Partner, Stefi Ionescu, Counsel, and Maria Brinza, Associate, all in the Banking and Finance group; Angelica Pintilie, Counsel, Alin Dimache and Carolina Mitea, Associates, all in the Energy group; and Luiza Onofrei, Counsel, and Alice Neagu, Associate, both in the Real Estate group. Dentons said this mandate highlights its capabilities in cross-border project finance and energy infrastructure, combining Czech and Romanian financing, security, real estate, and energy advice to support the development of battery energy storage capacity in Romania.

artigo.texto: Ucrânia ataca maior data center russo e põe em risco avanço de Moscou em IA Ataque contra instalação do Sberbank amplia ofensiva contra infraestrutura tecnológica russa; sanções ocidentais dificultam a substituição de equipamentos usados no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial Drones ucranianos atingiram nesta quarta-feira (14) o maior data center da Rússia, em uma série de ataques que parecem ter como alvo as ambições de Moscou de desenvolver capacidades de inteligência artificial (IA) comparáveis às dos Estados Unidos e da China. - Leia também: - Ucrânia diz que SpaceX restringiu uso do Starlink em meio a tensões com os EUA - Ataques da Rússia matam três e danificam instalações de energia na Ucrânia O ataque ao data center de Balakovo, pertencente ao Sberbank, maior banco e empresa de tecnologia da Rússia, ocorreu após três ataques realizados na última semana contra data centers do grupo russo de tecnologia Yandex. "Confirmamos que o centro de processamento de dados foi atacado. Ao mesmo tempo, todos os sistemas e serviços do Sberbank estão funcionando normalmente, sem interrupções", afirmou a jornalistas Alexander Vedyakhin, primeiro vice-presidente executivo do Sberbank. O presidente Vladimir Putin realizou nesta quarta-feira uma reunião não anunciada previamente com autoridades de alto escalão para discutir "segurança da informação", da qual participou o presidente executivo do Sberbank, German Gref. O Kremlin afirmou que o encontro não estava relacionado aos ataques contra os data centers. A agência estatal russa RIA Novosti informou, em 2024, que o centro do Sberbank atingido nesta quarta-feira abrigaria o maior supercomputador da Rússia, com entrada em operação prevista para 2027. Os data centers da Yandex atingidos anteriormente abrigavam os três supercomputadores em funcionamento da empresa. Nem a Yandex nem o Sberbank informaram se os supercomputadores, utilizados para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial, foram danificados nos ataques ucranianos. Ao lado da Yandex, sua principal concorrente no mercado doméstico, o Sberbank é um dos líderes russos no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial. O mercado interno é dividido entre o modelo GigaChat, do Sberbank, e o YandexGPT. Dificuldades para comprar chips As duas empresas investiram pesadamente no desenvolvimento de seus modelos, mas estão até nove meses atrás das líderes globais dos EUA e da China, segundo estimativas do próprio Sberbank. Parte dessa defasagem se deve às sanções ocidentais, que dificultam o acesso da Rússia aos equipamentos mais avançados. "Está claro quais dificuldades enfrentamos para comprar unidades modernas de processamento gráfico. Tanto nós quanto a Yandex sofremos com isso", afirmou Gref em 29 de setembro, apontando o problema como a principal razão para o atraso da Rússia em relação a Washington e a Pequim no setor de IA. O Sberbank está negociando a compra de chips de fabricantes chineses, mas, em entrevista à Reuters em 3 de junho, Vedyakhin afirmou que o monopólio da fabricante americana de chips Nvidia sobre sua plataforma de software CUDA, que se tornou um padrão na indústria de inteligência artificial, representa um problema ainda maior. A Yandex informou anteriormente que seus supercomputadores utilizavam chips Nvidia A100, modelo lançado em 2020 e posteriormente sucedido pelos chips H100, mais avançados. O Sberbank possui dois supercomputadores em funcionamento. O mais avançado deles, chamado Christofari Neo, ocupa a 167ª posição na lista Top 500 dos supercomputadores mais poderosos do mundo. Localizado em Moscou, o equipamento utiliza chips Nvidia A100. O supercomputador mais avançado da Yandex, chamado Chervonenkis, ocupa a 101ª posição na mesma lista. O especialista em tecnologia da informação Mikhail Klimarev disse à Reuters que a substituição dos chips pode levar muito tempo devido às sanções ocidentais, enquanto eventuais danos aos supercomputadores poderiam atrasar ainda mais o setor russo de inteligência artificial, já prejudicado pelas restrições. "Os equipamentos estão sendo importados, mas a um custo elevado, por rotas indiretas. Primeiro, é preciso negociar para encontrar alguém disposto a vendê-los e que não tenha medo das sanções", afirmou. Proteção dos ativos Alguns comentaristas compararam a ausência de interrupções relatadas pelo Sberbank, controlado pelo Estado, com a situação da Yandex, cujas operações de transporte por aplicativo e entrega de alimentos registraram problemas. De acordo com eles, isso demonstra que os data centers do Sberbank estão mais bem protegidos. "Este é um ótimo exemplo do que um empresário pode fazer para proteger seus ativos", escreveu o blogueiro militar Alexander Kots. De acordo com um decreto assinado por Putin em agosto, o Estado pode assumir a gestão de instalações que não estejam adequadamente protegidas. O complexo do Sberbank fica próximo à usina nuclear de Balakovo, utilizada como fonte de energia pelo data center, e à usina hidrelétrica de Saratov. Não houve relatos de danos a nenhuma das duas usinas em decorrência do ataque. A Ucrânia afirma que está respondendo aos ataques russos contra suas próprias instalações de dados. Os dois países também têm atacado refinarias, usinas de energia, portos e empresas de comércio eletrônico um do outro. O Ministério do Desenvolvimento Digital da Rússia informou nesta semana que está em negociações com os militares para reforçar a proteção dos data centers, enquanto alguns parlamentares defenderam que essas instalações sejam transferidas para estruturas subterrâneas, onde os equipamentos ficariam fora do alcance dos drones. "Precisamos de uma espécie de bunker de dados para o fim do mundo", afirmou Valery Yermakov, vice-presidente executivo da Rostelecom, empresa controlada pelo Estado e outra grande operadora de data centers, durante uma conferência em Moscou.

artigo.texto: Danville has added more than 100 housing units to its market since 2023, with over 200 more in construction. In Pittsylvania, a master-planned community will soon add more than 1,800 units to the county’s housing stock. It’s still not enough, local officials say. Danville and Pittsylvania County are experiencing unprecedented levels of growth, for which the housing market wasn’t prepared. Job creation in the region, which is driving the increase in demand for housing, has picked up rapidly in recent years, after decades of job losses tied to the declining tobacco and textile industries. Large facilities locating at industrial parks in the region are expected to create thousands of jobs in the coming years. The Berry Hill megasite, the largest industrial site in the state, will soon be home to lithium-ion battery separator manufacturer Microporous. Microporous has promised to create about 2,000 new jobs. And data center developer Stack Infrastructure is promising about 2,500 permanent jobs at an AI data center facility that is also expected to come to the Berry Hill site, though there has been no formal announcement. Close to 1,000 new housing units are needed to support the Microporous project alone, according to the Danville Housing Navigator. The workers will need places to live, said Linda Green, executive director of the Southern Virginia Regional Alliance, a regional economic development group. That’s why local development group Southside Investing is building a massive master-planned community development in Axton, nine miles from the megasite. Tony Salah, with Southside Investing, said the group “has been actively preparing to meet the housing demand of future jobs.” The 590-acre development, called Sugar Tree Living, will create more than 1,800 units across all housing types — single-family, apartments, townhomes and senior living. Salah joined other developers, along with real estate professionals, builders, bankers and economic development officials in Danville on Thursday for the fifth annual Southern Virginia Regional Housing Summit. At the event, Green said that housing demand in the region has increased even since 2022, when a study identified a pent-up demand for about 600 single-family homes and 700 apartment units in Danville. “Housing has been built, new projects have been announced and our economic development pipeline has changed substantially,” she said. “But the projections for tomorrow change even faster and more drastically.” Since the study was released, the city has built 112 rental units and 16 for-sale units, with 233 more units in construction. Despite this, the demand has continued to grow, according to a 2025 update to the study. Pent-up demand in the city now calls for nearly 4,000 rental units and 1,300 owned units, said Susan McCulloch, Danville’s director of housing and development. Housing is now seen as a key part of economic development, Green said. Companies always ask about housing when considering whether to locate in an area, she said. “They’re going to ask the housing question, and if you don’t have a solution for it, you can’t win the project,” Green said. “That’s why we increasingly view housing as workforce and economic development infrastructure. You no longer see a division between the departments.” Salah echoed this sentiment, calling the housing deficit “the overwhelming regional refrain of need.” The Pittsylvania County Board of Supervisors approved the Sugar Tree Living project in 2023, over a year before the Microporous announcement, anticipating that a major housing development would be needed to support eventual jobs at the megasite. On top of 1,800 housing units, the development will also offer amenities like healthcare, childcare, retail, dining, hospitality and recreation, and services like on-site fire and rescue. When it was approved, the master-planned community drew some pushback from residents about traffic, loss of agricultural land and the natural beauty of the county, and the possibility that the development could kickstart a chain of similar developments. Microporous locating at the megasite “validated our time and energy and dollars into this area,” Salah said in a 2024 interview after the company’s announcement. “We want to be the supply solution for a portion of the housing demand,” he said then. After Thursday’s housing summit, Salah added that Southside Investing is feeling “more and more confident that an abundant wave of well-paying, good jobs are closer than ever.” A second tenant at the megasite — and thousands of additional jobs — is on the horizon, with data center developer Stack Infrastructure planning to build an AI data center campus on nearly 3,000 acres at the site. A local performance agreement for the project outlines Stack’s promise of $1.3 billion in investment and more than 2,000 permanent jobs. “The housing implication is clear,” Green said. “We must prepare for both permanent employment growth and the workforce needed to construct and equip these growing facilities.” Information about the region’s housing needs, current projects and available sites can be found on the Danville Housing Navigator website.

The global Compressed Air Energy Storage (CAES) market is entering a transformative phase as power systems worldwide pivot toward deep decarbonization and grapple with the intermittency of rapidly expanding wind and solar capacity. Unlike short-duration battery storage, CAES offers multi-hour to multi-day discharge capabilities, making it a compelling solution for long-duration energy storage (LDES) requirements that are increasingly critical for grid reliability. The technology landscape is diversifying beyond traditional diabatic designs, with advanced adiabatic (AA-CAES), isothermal, and liquid air energy storage (LAES) variants attracting significant research and development investment. These next-generation systems aim to eliminate fossil fuel dependence, improve round-trip efficiency, and reduce geographic constraints related to geological storage. Policy support, including investment tax credits and capacity market mechanisms in key regions, is bolstering project economics. The market is also witnessing a shift from isolated demonstration projects to commercial-scale deployments, supported by declining component costs and growing expertise in system integration. This report provides a data-driven analysis of the CAES market from 2026 to 2035, covering technology segments, end-use applications, regional dynamics, and competitive strategies. It serves as a strategic resource for utilities, technology providers, investors, and policymakers navigating the evolving energy storage landscape. The baseline scenario for the global CAES market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust expansion, underpinned by the accelerating global transition to renewable energy and the corresponding need for long-duration storage. As variable renewable energy sources account for a growing share of electricity generation, grid operators face mounting challenges in balancing supply and demand, managing curtailment, and ensuring reliability. CAES, with its ability to store energy for extended periods and provide synchronous inertia, is well-positioned to address these challenges. The market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.2% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 420 (2025=100) by 2035. This growth will be driven by a wave of new project announcements, particularly in regions with favorable geology for underground storage and supportive policy frameworks. Advanced adiabatic and isothermal CAES systems are projected to capture an increasing share of new capacity additions, as they offer higher efficiency and zero-emission operation. However, the market will continue to face competition from lithium-ion battery storage, which benefits from established supply chains and declining costs, as well as from other LDES technologies such as pumped hydro and hydrogen. Nevertheless, CAES's unique combination of scale, duration, and operational flexibility is expected to secure a distinct niche in the future energy mix. The forecast period will also see a growing emphasis on hybrid systems that integrate CAES with renewable generation and other storage assets to maximize value. Grid-scale energy storage represents the largest and fastest-growing application for CAES systems. As utilities and independent power producers integrate increasing shares of wind and solar generation, the need for multi-hour to multi-day storage becomes critical to avoid curtailment and maintain grid stability. CAES plants can absorb excess renewable energy during periods of low demand and discharge it during peak hours, effectively shifting energy across time. The demand-side indicators include the volume of renewable capacity additions, the frequency of negative pricing events, and the implementation of capacity remuneration mechanisms that value long-duration storage. Through 2035, the segment will be driven by the retirement of coal and nuclear baseload plants, which creates a gap in dispatchable capacity that CAES can fill. Additionally, the growing adoption of corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs) for renewable energy will necessitate storage solutions to ensure reliable delivery. Major projects in the pipeline, such as those in Australia, the United States, and Europe, highlight the increasing bankability of CAES for grid-scale applications. Representative participants: Siemens Energy, General Electric, Mitsubishi Power, Highview Power, and Hydrostor. CAES systems can store excess renewable energy during periods of high output and low demand, then release it when generation is low or demand is high, effectively firming renewable power. artigo.texto: Africa shifts from carbon market potential to delivery as Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026 opens in Kigali Africa must move beyond carbon market potential towards delivery, building high-integrity, investable markets that attract long-term capital while protecting national climate priorities and ensuring greater value reaches African countries and communities. That was the central message from the opening keynote sessions of the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026 in Kigali, Rwanda, where policymakers, investors, project developers, development finance institutions and international climate organisations gathered to accelerate Africa’s participation in global carbon markets. Representatives from 45 countries, including 21 African nations, are participating in the summit, where discussions have shifted decisively from market readiness to implementation, investment and transactions. Officially opening the summit, Hon. Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, Rwanda’s Minister of Environment, said Africa’s carbon markets must be shaped by African priorities and deliver tangible benefits for the continent. “The question before us is therefore no longer simply whether Africa is ready. It is whether we can deliver at scale, with integrity and with innovation.” Minister Arakwiye said progress is already evident as African countries establish carbon market frameworks, grant authorisations, sign bilateral agreements and develop projects. However, she cautioned that carbon finance remains concentrated in a relatively narrow range of project types. She called for diversification into renewable energy, electric mobility, sustainable waste management, industrial decarbonisation, agriculture and landscape-scale nature-based solutions. Minister Arakwiye identified three priorities for scaling Africa’s carbon markets: accessible methodologies suited to African contexts; project preparation and readiness finance; and long-term demand at fair value. “Trust is the currency of this market,” she said. “To our buyers and investors, I say: look closely at these efforts. Reward them with long-term demand, fair prices and patient capital.” From potential to execution The call for delivery was echoed by Hon. Hamad Yusuf Masauni, Tanzania’s Minister of State in the Vice President’s Office responsible for Union Affairs and Environment, who said the continent now has an opportunity to reposition itself in global carbon markets. “For too long, Africa has been spoken about as a continent of potential. At the Carbon Markets Africa Summit, we declare that the era of potential is giving way to the era of execution.” Minister Masauni stressed the importance of moving high-quality, bankable projects through to issuance and offtake rather than focusing solely on the size of project pipelines. “Credibility is built one verified tonne, one closed deal and one community that sees real benefit at a time.” The importance of ensuring value reaches communities was also central to remarks from Maxwell Gomera, UNDP Resident Representative in South Africa and Director of the Africa Sustainable Finance Hub. Gomera called for market infrastructure capable of carrying value “from the buyer all the way to the farmer”, backed by strong community rights, enforceable benefit-sharing, early-stage finance and partnerships focused on delivery. Africa urged to compete on integrity, not price Speakers also stressed that Africa’s competitive advantage should be the quality and integrity of its carbon assets rather than simply offering the lowest-priced credits. Perumal Arumugam, Manager of Markets and Non-Markets and Stakeholder Interaction at UN Climate Change (UNFCCC), said Africa should move beyond asking how it can participate in carbon markets and instead consider how carbon markets can advance African priorities. “Africa should not compete simply by offering the cheapest tonnes. Africa should compete by offering credible and creditable tonnes, a sustainable tonne, and a tonne that the world can trust.” He said success should ultimately be measured not only in credits issued, but in investment mobilised, mitigation unlocked, value reaching communities, stronger economies and African countries retaining control over their climate transitions. Speaking on behalf of AUDA-NEPAD, Esterine Fotabong similarly called for African countries to scale carbon markets on their own terms, supported by predictable authorisations, functioning registries and credible monitoring, reporting and verification systems. She also highlighted the need to build greater African capacity in validation and verification and expand access to carbon finance in sectors such as agriculture. Global demand will reward quality Representing the European Commission, Lukas Visek, Deputy Head of the Directorate-General for Climate Action Task Force for Carbon Pricing and Carbon Markets, signaled future European demand for international carbon credits while stressing that quality requirements would be stringent. “Additionality and permanence are not negotiable,” he said. “Quality, however, will be rewarded.” The message to developers was clear: projects being developed for future international demand will need robust data, genuine additionality, strong community participation and demonstrable alignment with national and global climate goals. Turning carbon projects into investable assets The summit’s opening programme then moved directly from policy to capital and deal flow, with leaders from the African Development Bank (AfDB), Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) and Kigali International Financial Centre (KIFC) examining the practical barriers preventing more investment from reaching African projects. Policy certainty, early-stage project preparation, bankable pipelines, robust governance and appropriate financial risk-sharing were identified as critical to accelerating capital flows. artigo.texto: Key Capture Energy NY1 at Luther Forest in Saratoga County was the first utility-scale battery energy storage system in New York. It is located in Stillwater and broke ground in 2018. HUDSON— The Common Council’s legal committee recommended a six-month pause on battery energy storage systems in the city at a meeting Thursday. The move means the full council will vote on the proposal at its next meeting. The energy storage systems store power, typically from renewable sources, in rechargeable batteries for later use. Common Council President Margaret Morris said the moratorium recommendation began after developers reached out about building the facilities in Hudson. “Our code enforcement officer (Nick Fox) reached out to me, and he had had a couple of inquiries from, I think, two companies inquiring about what Hudson has in its code in relation to large-scale battery operations,” Morris said. One company is eyeing the site of the former Overhead Door garage building on Hudson Avenue, Morris said. Because Hudson has nothing in its code regarding the facilities, Fox suggested the council take some action. The council should be careful not to regulate an opportunity to bring revenue to the city, support the electrical grid, and help the environment, 3rd Ward Councilmember Jason Foster said. Morris countered that battery storage systems are mostly large-scale operations, not compatible with a two-square-mile city like Hudson, and compared them to artificial-intelligence data centers. Morris also cited the risk of large battery fires that can last for weeks, a concern that has led to moratoriums throughout the Twin Counties, including in neighboring Claverack. “There is benefit to these if they didn't catch on fire and didn't explode,” Foster said. “That is always possible. But they are balancing out the grid… I'm just trying to think about ways to help our budget and discuss it further rather than going straight to ixnay.” While the fire risk is concerning, the area does need to be developed, 4th Ward Councilmember Jennifer Belton said. “I would frankly rather see some other kind of small industry come in and do something in that same space,” Belton said. The Columbia Economic Development Corporation has made multiple attempts to get the current owners to sell the property, Morris said. With so much uncertainty, the smartest move would be to pass a moratorium on facilities while city lawmakers reach an agreement on next steps, Common Council attorney Ken Dow said. “If there's not a consensus about just prohibiting them or limiting places where they could go, I think it would be prudent to do a local law, instituting a moratorium for 3 to 6 months,” Dow said. “That way nothing gets in there that you regret. You can then figure out in more detail other places (for the facilities), learn more about these things, the size of them, put together something over the next few months and then modify the code.” Morris said Hudson would use moratoria from other municipalities to shape its moratorium. Foster also asked for an informational presentation on the battery energy storage systems.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 13 de outubro de 2026, às 18:06 Na matéria publicada anteriormente, o nome por extenso do NIL foi grafado de forma errada. O correto é Nature Investment Lab. Também houve erro na grafia do Climate Ventures. Segue a versão corrigida: Apontada como um dos principais entraves para que projetos de reflorestamento e de Redução das Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal (Redd+) consigam acessar linhas de financiamento, a modelagem dos contratos passará a ter um padrão, que está em desenvolvimento pelo Natural Investment Lab (NIL). A minuta desse contrato modelo foi apresentada publicamente durante a Semana do Clima que aconteceu recentemente em Nova York e, para elaborá-la, o NIL conversou com 25 importantes instituições. Entre elas, Itaú BBA, Regia Capital, Systemica, Petrobras e Regreen. No próximo passo, o rascunho do contrato modelo será colocado em audiência pública e deve ganhar destaque durante a COP31, que acontecerá entre os dias 9 e 20 de novembro na Turquia. A meta é concluir o trabalho até o final deste ano. O NIL aposta no processo de amadurecimento desse mercado, que já vem durando mais de 20 anos e que deverá elevar o carbono ao status de commodity, com possibilidade de ser negociado internacionalmente. “A ideia é preparar os desenvolvedores dos projetos de produção de carbono para que consigam lidar com todas as exigências com as quais vão se deparar quando tentarem acessar recursos”, explica Fabiana Philipi, gerente de projetos da Climate Venture, organização que lidera o NIL. Ela pondera, no entanto, que o documento de referência poderá ajudar os outros players desse mercado, como os compradores e financiadores do mercado de carbono. Segundo Philipi, as propostas de produção de carbono bem elaboradas têm forte demanda e o objetivo é ajudar desenvolvedores de todos os portes, desde empresas já consagradas como Re.Green e Mombak, até aquelas que estão dando os primeiros passos. As maiores compradoras dos créditos de carbono brasileiros, atualmente, são as big techs, principalmente a Microsoft. A minuta apresentada em Nova York refere-se a contratos offtake – compra mínima garantida – que são acordos jurídicos firmados entre comprador e vendedor de uma mercadoria, antes dela entrar em produção. O documento apresenta cláusulas referentes à estrutura comercial, como preço, pagamento e financiamento, garantias, recebíveis e financiadores, ciclo de vida dos créditos, entrega e titularidade, falha de entrega, entre outros. O NIL é um laboratório de investimentos criado a partir de uma iniciativa que reúne o Banco do Brasil, o Instituto Itaúsa, o Instituto Clima e Sociedade (iCS), o Banco Nacional do Desenvolvimento (BNDES) e a internacional Gfanz. O seu objetivo é atrair e estruturar financiamentos, além de promover inovação financeira, para ampliar a chamada economia de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN). artigo.texto: SPARTANBURG —A former cryptocurrency mining facility in the Tiger River Industrial Park is being converted into a data center. The company hopes it’s operational by the end of 2027. BV Power Alpha previously received a fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement for its crypto mining facility that started up in 2022. The company, owned by Jerry Tang, is now called AIB Data Centers. In February, Tang abandoned efforts to build a new data center in the Tyger River Industrial Park after Spartanburg County Council declined to offer tax incentives in the wake of community criticism over the project. Since then, county council passed a data center moratorium that could prevent new data centers that have an IT electrical load of 65 megawatts or more. Council voted to include the caveat after lobbying from William Crawford, president of Pacolet Milliken, and Bryan Stone, president of Pacolet Milliken subsidiary Lockhart Power, who argued that small data centers create revenue that helps keep costs down for ratepayers. Pacolet Milliken developed the Tyger River Industrial Park and Lockhart supplies much of the power there. The new AIB data center will have an electrical load of only 50 megawatts, falling below that 65-megawatt threshold, according to the company. It will buy power from a utility instead of producing it, meaning it won’t create the type of air pollution that the NorthMark data center will generate. Company spokesperson Pierre DuBois said in an email that the planned data center would exist on the same land footprint as the bitcoin mining facility. “Essentially, the same equipment moves inside the walls, with other equipment added within those walls,” he added. DuBois also said the water use in the data center would be a fraction of what the crypto mining facility used. “Since the site began operating, it has used about 14,000 gallons a day,” said DuBois. “We estimate the data center will use about 165 gallons a day.” For comparison, the NorthMark data center projects to use more than 1 million gallons a day. In an email, DuBois said the new data center wouldn’t be a “hyperscale mega-project,” and that the company “offered to give up incentives awarded to the crypto mining facility in 2022, which would otherwise have carried over to the data center. The county accepted.” According to a news release, AIB has already signed a 12-year agreement with Dutch AI company Nebius. It includes two potential five-year renewal periods.

artigo.texto: CATL and SERES Group signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement on October 10, 2026, in Chongqing, China, covering battery manufacturing, charging services and international expansion. CATL, a Chinese battery technology company, supplies batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage applications, while SERES Group operates in the automotive sector through brands including AITO. Under the agreement, AITO will continue using CATL batteries across its vehicle lineup, following cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million vehicles. The companies plan to accelerate Phase 2 of their Plant in Plant project at the SERES Super Factory, targeting 10–12 GWh of annual battery production capacity. Once both phases are completed, their combined annual production capacity is expected to exceed 20 GWh. The partnership also covers supercharging networks, battery lifecycle services and manufacturing coordination. CATL and SERES will additionally explore opportunities in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia. artigo.texto: Mercado global de sensores de umidade por condutividade térmica: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de sensores de umidade por condutividade térmica até 2035, impulsionado pela demanda de data centers e da indústria Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de sensores de umidade por condutividade térmica, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de sensores de umidade por condutividade térmica entra em uma fase de expansão sustentada, apoiada pela crescente demanda por medição de umidade precisa e durável em data centers, automação industrial, sistemas de climatização automotiva e equipamentos médicos. Diferentemente dos sensores capacitivos de polymer, os sensores de condutividade térmica oferecem medição direta da umidade absoluta, com histerese mínima e desempenho robusto em ambientes agressivos, o que os torna indispensáveis na fabricação de semiconductor, na produção farmacêutica e no controle avançado de HVAC. À medida que a digitalização e as exigências de eficiência energética se intensificam até 2035, espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta anual estável, com o índice de mercado subindo de 100 em 2025 para um patamar significativamente mais alto em 2035. Este relatório oferece uma perspectiva baseada em dados sobre tamanho de mercado, segmentação, dinâmica da cadeia de suprimentos e estratégias competitivas, ajudando fabricantes, distribuidores e investidores a navegar por um cenário em evolução. Entre os principais fatores de crescimento estão a expansão de data centers de hiperescala, que exigem controle preciso de umidade para evitar condensação e descargas eletrostáticas, a adoção de regulamentações mais rigorosas de qualidade do ar interior e a integração de sensores de umidade em sistemas de gestão predial conectados à IoT. O ambiente competitivo é moldado por fabricantes de sensores consolidados e empresas de tecnologia especializadas, com foco em miniaturização, saída digital e redução de custos para adoção em massa. O cenário-base para o mercado de sensores de umidade por condutividade térmica entre 2026 e 2035 projeta crescimento robusto, com taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de 5,8% e índice de mercado atingindo 176 em 2035 (2025 = 100). Essa perspectiva se apoia na adoção acelerada de tecnologias de edificações inteligentes, nas quais os sensores de umidade são essenciais para otimizar o consumo de energia em HVAC e manter o conforto dos ocupantes. No ambiente industrial, o avanço da Indústria 4.0 e da manutenção preditiva impulsiona a demanda por sensores confiáveis e de longa vida útil, capazes de operar em condições extremas. O setor automotivo, em especial a fabricação de veículos elétricos, desponta como aplicação de alto crescimento para sensores de umidade no gerenciamento de baterias e no controle climático da cabine. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico deve permanecer como o maior e mais dinâmico mercado, sustentada pela fabricação de eletrônicos e pelo desenvolvimento de infraestrutura na China, no Japão e na Coreia do Sul. América do Norte e Europa registrarão demanda constante de reposição e modernização de sistemas existentes, enquanto América Latina e Oriente Médio e África oferecem oportunidades incrementais em monitoramento industrial e agrícola. Restrições na cadeia de suprimentos de componentes especializados e serviços de calibração podem representar desafios temporários, mas, no geral, o mercado está preparado para uma expansão consistente até 2035. artigo.texto: Sergio Sgobbi — diretor de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais da Brasscom (Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação de Tecnologias Digitais) A aprovação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Data Centers (Redata) representa um marco histórico para a política industrial e digital brasileira. O programa cria condições para reduzir os custos de investimento em infraestrutura digital e posicionar o país de forma mais competitiva na nova economia global. No entanto, é preciso falar com franqueza técnica: o Redata, de forma isolada, não soluciona o gargalo da carga tributária sobre os equipamentos de tecnologia da informação (TI) utilizados nos data centers. Fique por dentro das notÃcias que importam para vocÃª! O programa federal suspende a incidência de PIS/Cofins (Programa de Integração Social e Contribuição para o Financiamento da Seguridade Social) e IPI (Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados) é sobre uma lista de equipamentos de tecnologia da informação (TI). Trata-se de uma medida vital em um setor altamente intensivo em capital, no qual servidores e sistemas de armazenamento representam cerca de 70% dos investimentos. Contudo, uma verdade precisa ser dita: o principal peso tributário sobre os equipamentos continua sendo o ICMS (Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços). Enquanto o debate público se concentra na desoneração federal, o ICMS responde por dois terços do total da carga tributária. Isso significa que, embora o Redata antecipe um ambiente favorável, o ganho real de competitividade será limitado caso os estados não se unam a esse esforço por meio da aprovação do convênio no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz), que permite a redução de até 90% do ICMS. A dinâmica é incontornável. Hoje, grandes operadores globais definem seus aportes comparando custos de implantação, matriz energética, segurança jurídica e incentivos tributários. Países disputam esses aportes, pois sabem que atraem inovação, geram empregos, estimulam outros setores e ampliam a capacidade digital de toda a economia. Nesse contexto, diferenças tributárias tornam-se decisivas. Quando um grupo internacional avalia instalar um data center na América Latina, o Brasil concorre com mercados que oferecem condições agressivas. Se o custo de equipamentos permanecer elevado pelo ICMS, perderemos competitividade num momento em que a demanda por infraestrutura digital cresce exponencialmente, impulsionada pela inteligência artificial e processamento em nuvem. Outro ponto que merece destaque é a inteligência estrutural do Redata. A política não se limita a benefícios tributários; ele estabelece mecanismos de habilitação para projetos de investimento e de coabilitação para empresas que fabricam ou comercializam os equipamentos. Esses instrumentos são essenciais, pois, sem eles, corre-se o risco de a desoneração não ser transferida para a economia. O objetivo do programa é assegurar que a redução tributária chegue ao investimento final e, posteriormente, ao consumidor de serviços digitais, ou seja, a verticalização dos benefícios para toda a cadeia. O sucesso do Redata não deve ser medido apenas pelos impostos reduzidos, mas pela capacidade sistêmica de diminuir o custo do processamento e armazenamento de dados. Quanto mais eficiente o processo, maior a competitividade das empresas que dependem da infraestrutura digital globalmente. Vale lembrar que o Brasil é contumaz importador de capacidade computacional, que em 2025 atingiu o deficit de US$ 7,9 bilhões. A implementação do programa precisa avançar. A regulamentação dos instrumentos de habilitação deve ocorrer com rapidez, objetividade e sem travas que desincentivem investimentos. Ao mesmo tempo, é indispensável construir uma agenda federativa com os Estados na estratégia nacional de atração de investimentos. A transformação digital tornou-se pilar do crescimento no século 21. Inteligência artificial, nuvem e economia de dados dependem de infraestrutura robusta. O Brasil possui vantagens, como matriz elétrica limpa e condição geopolítica estável. Mas essas virtudes não serão suficientes se o ambiente tributário onera os investimentos. O Redata é um passo decisivo. Contudo, seu potencial será plenamente alcançado apenas quando União e estados atuarem de forma coordenada. Sem a redução do ICMS, a política ficará incompleta. Com ela, o Brasil terá condições de se consolidar como polo global de infraestrutura, atraindo bilhões, gerando empregos e fortalecendo sua autonomia tecnológica. O desafio agora não é apenas celebrar a conquista. É garantir que ela produza todos os resultados que o país precisa para liderar a economia digital do futuro.

artigo.texto: - Gotion Power Morocco plans to begin commissioning its battery-production equipment during the week of 20 October. - The first phase of the Kenitra project represents approximately $1.3 billion in investment. - The factory will manufacture batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage, targeting African and international markets. - A separate partnership with Volkswagen’s PowerCo will produce battery materials in Morocco. Gotion Power Morocco announced on 12 October that equipment commissioning and startup would begin during the week of 20 October at its plant in Kenitra’s Atlantic Free Zone. The company says construction of the cell plant’s buildings and infrastructure is complete. The first phase is designed for 20 gigawatt-hours of annual production capacity, a planned figure rather than current output. The facility will manufacture lithium iron phosphate batteries, commonly known as LFP batteries, for customers in Morocco and elsewhere in Africa, alongside Europe, the Middle East and the United States. According to TelQuel, which reported the company’s statement issued on 12 October, commissioning will open the way to industrial cell production. Gotion Power Morocco chairman Khalid Qalam had previously indicated that sales of assembled batteries were expected before the end of the year. From investment plans to factory operations The announcement gives a more precise timetable for a project whose first production line had already been expected to start in October. Commissioning involves bringing equipment into operation and testing its performance before production can expand. It should not be confused with the factory immediately reaching its full annual capacity. Gotion’s own project information puts first-phase investment at approximately $1.3 billion and identifies a planned capacity of 20 GWh. The next commercial milestones will be consistent production, customer deliveries and the gradual increase in output. Volkswagen adds a European connection The factory’s progress comes as Gotion deepens its partnership with Volkswagen and the German carmaker’s battery subsidiary, PowerCo. On 28 September, the companies announced plans for joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco to expand production of LFP battery cells and cathode materials. The proposed Kenitra joint venture will manufacture cathode material, a key battery component. Gotion will hold 51% and PowerCo 49%, with the partners managing the venture together. That materials project is separate from the cell-production equipment scheduled for commissioning this month. Volkswagen’s announcement did not establish an October startup date for the cathode facility. Morocco is attracting investment in both finished battery cells and the materials needed to manufacture them. Why Morocco matters to the supply chain Volkswagen says its partnership with Gotion is intended to diversify supplies and strengthen Europe’s battery industry. LFP technology offers relatively competitive costs, a long service life and durability, making it attractive for more affordable electric vehicles and energy-storage systems. The companies see expanding European demand as an opportunity for their production network. For Morocco, the investment provides an opportunity to move further into battery manufacturing while serving markets beyond its borders. The project has also attracted African development financing. The African Development Bank announced approval of a loan in July to support an integrated battery-manufacturing facility in Kenitra. Its financing documents describe an initial 10 GWh project, whereas Gotion’s broader first-phase description puts capacity at 20 GWh.
