artigo.texto: Mercado global de criptografia por hardware: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Projeção do Mercado de Criptografia por Hardware até 2035: Crescimento Impulsionado pela Demanda de Data Centers e pela Conformidade Regulatória Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Criptografia por Hardware, o mercado inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de criptografia por hardware entra em uma fase de expansão sustentada, com horizonte de projeção até 2035. A criptografia por hardware, que se baseia em componentes físicos dedicados para executar funções criptográficas, oferece desempenho superior, menor latência e maior resistência à violação em comparação com alternativas baseadas em software. À medida que os volumes de dados aumentam e as ameaças cibernéticas se tornam mais sofisticadas, organizações de diversos setores priorizam uma proteção de dados robusta. Exigências regulatórias como GDPR, HIPAA e CCPA impulsionam a adoção, enquanto a proliferação da computação em nuvem e de borda cria novos vetores de demanda. O mercado abrange unidades de disco com autocrifragem, módulos de segurança de hardware, chips TPM, pen drives criptografados e outros hardwares especializados. Os principais setores de uso final incluem data centers, TI corporativa, governo, serviços financeiros e saúde. O cenário competitivo reúne fornecedores consolidados de semicondutores e armazenamento, além de empresas especializadas em segurança. Esta análise oferece uma visão orientada por dados da dinâmica de mercado, dos fatores de demanda e das considerações estratégicas para os participantes até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado de criptografia por hardware prevê crescimento constante entre 2026 e 2035, sustentado por fatores estruturais de demanda. A frequência e a gravidade crescentes das violações de dados levam as organizações a adotar a criptografia baseada em hardware como camada fundamental de segurança. Os marcos regulatórios em todo o mundo estão mais rígidos, exigindo criptografia para dados sensíveis em repouso e em trânsito, o que impulsiona diretamente a demanda por soluções de hardware em conformidade. A expansão de data centers e da infraestrutura de nuvem, impulsionada pela transformação digital e por cargas de trabalho de IA, exige criptografia de alto desempenho que somente o hardware é capaz de oferecer. No segmento corporativo, a migração para arquiteturas de confiança zero e a necessidade de proteger ambientes de trabalho remoto são catalisadores adicionais. A adoção de dispositivos de armazenamento criptografados pelos consumidores também cresce, ainda que a partir de uma base menor. Entre os entraves estão os custos iniciais elevados, a complexidade de integração e a escassez de mão de obra qualificada. No entanto, a inovação contínua, como a integração da criptografia aos processadores principais e o desenvolvimento de criptografia pós-quântica, deve atenuar esses desafios. O índice de mercado deve alcançar 185 até 2035, refletindo uma trajetória robusta de expansão. Fatores de Demanda e Restrições Principais Fatores de Demanda - Violações de dados e ameaças cibernéticas crescentes impulsionam a demanda por criptografia de hardware resistente à violação - Exigências regulatórias rigorosas (GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA) que requerem criptografia para dados sensíveis - Proliferação de data centers e infraestrutura de nuvem que exige criptografia de alto desempenho - Adoção de arquiteturas de segurança de confiança zero e tendências de trabalho remoto - Crescimento da eletrônica de consumo com recursos de criptografia integrados - Avanços em algoritmos de criptografia e integração com arquiteturas de computação emergentes Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Custos iniciais elevados e complexidade de integração de soluções de criptografia por hardware - Escassez de mão de obra qualificada para implantação e gestão - Problemas de compatibilidade com sistemas legados e ambientes de TI diversificados - Concorrência de soluções de criptografia baseadas em software em segmentos sensíveis a custos Estrutura de Demanda por Setor de Uso Final Armazenamento em Data Centers (participação estimada: 30%) Os data centers são o maior setor de uso final da criptografia por hardware, impulsionados pelo crescimento exponencial das necessidades de armazenamento de dados e pela demanda por criptografia de alto desempenho e baixa latência. À medida que provedores de serviços em nuvem e empresas ampliam sua infraestrutura de armazenamento, cresce a implantação de unidades de disco com autocrifragem (SEDs) e módulos de segurança de hardware (HSMs) para garantir a proteção dos dados sem comprometer o desempenho. A migração para interfaces NVMe e PCIe acelera ainda mais a demanda por criptografia por hardware, pois essas tecnologias exigem offload criptográfico eficiente. A conformidade regulatória, como o GDPR e exigências específicas do setor, obriga os operadores de data centers a implementar criptografia para dados em repouso. Até 2035, espera-se que a adoção de SEDs se torne padrão no armazenamento corporativo, enquanto os HSMs terão demanda crescente para gestão de chaves e aceleração criptográfica. O avanço da computação de borda e do 5G também criará novos nós distribuídos de data centers que exigirão criptografia. Entre os indicadores do lado da demanda estão a capacidade de armazenamento embarcada, os gastos com infraestrutura de nuvem e o ritmo de construção de data centers. artigo.texto: Date: 2026-10-14 04:30:17 Hong Kong, Oct 14, 2026 - (ACN Newswire) - As artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud services grow rapidly, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems are becoming increasingly important in keeping data centers running reliably. GP Energy Tech Limited (âGP Energy Techâ or theâCompanyâ), a subsidiary of Gold Peak Technology Group Limited (âGold Peakâ) (SEHK: 40), is showcasing its Nickel-Zinc (NiZn) battery system at the Hong Kong Electronics Fair (Autumn Edition), held at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Center from October 13 to 16. With Manufacturing Twins and Speed to Scale at the core of its approach, the Company is advancing the development and scalable supply of backup power solutions for AI and cloud data centers, as well as other critical infrastructure. As part of its product development efforts, the Company is embracing the promising application of NiZn batteries in UPS systems and battery backup units (BBUs) and is also exploring opportunities to provide backup power for emerging 800-volt direct current (800 VDC) architectures. Speed to Scale: accelerating commercialization through smart manufacturing Drawing on Gold Peak's more than 60 years of experience in battery design, manufacturing and sales, GP Energy Tech is leveraging the Group's expertise in electro-chemistry and high-volume Nickel-based battery manufacturing to advance its NiZn battery systems. Through smart automation and replicable production processes, the Company is accelerating the transition from technology development to commercial application. While maintaining consistent quality and reliable delivery, it flexibly expands manufacturing capacity in line with customer demand, supporting the delivery of NiZn battery solutions at scale to meet growing demand for next-generation backup power. Alan Lo, Executive Vice Chairman of GP Energy Tech said:âThe value of NiZn technology lies in its ability to meet the industry's requirements for safety, power and sustainability simultaneously. artigo.texto: Trina Storage, the energy storage division of Trinasolar, has secured a contract to supply a 50 MW/196 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) for the AEJ Nozu project in Oita Prefecture, Japan, strengthening its presence in the country’s expanding utility-scale energy storage market. The project, located in Nishihata, Nozu Town, Usuki City, was awarded under Japan’s FY2023 Long-Term Decarbonization Auction and is scheduled for completion in the third quarter of 2028. Under the agreement, Trina Storage will deploy its Elementa 2 Pro 5 MWh battery energy storage solution to support the project’s energy storage requirements. The AEJ Nozu project represents another addition to Trina Storage’s growing portfolio in Japan, where demand for grid-scale battery storage is increasing alongside renewable energy deployment. The company has been expanding its local operational capabilities to support project development, system configuration, technical consultation, delivery coordination and after-sales services. Through its Japan-based team, Trina Storage works with customers and project partners to address local technical specifications and project requirements throughout the development and operational lifecycle. These capabilities are supported by the company’s global expertise in battery cell technology, system integration and utility-scale energy storage solutions. Commenting on the development, Dr. Leo Zhao, Head of Energy Storage (APAC) at Trina Storage, said the company was pleased to contribute to Japan’s expanding renewable energy portfolio through the AEJ Nozu project. He highlighted the opportunities emerging from Japan’s evolving energy requirements and emphasized the importance of combining advanced storage technology with strong local support capabilities. In addition to the Nozu project, Trina Storage is supplying a 160 MWh utility-scale battery energy storage project in Japan’s Kyushu region, further expanding its presence in the market. The company also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with AMP-lify in September for approximately 1 GWh of grid-connected battery energy storage projects across Japan. The proposed projects will feature Trina Storage’s latest Elementa 3 series energy storage technology. These developments reflect Trina Storage’s continued expansion in Japan’s energy storage sector as the country increases investment in grid flexibility, renewable energy integration and long-duration energy storage infrastructure. With the addition of the AEJ Nozu project and its expanding pipeline of storage developments, Trina Storage is positioning itself to support Japan’s transition toward a more flexible and decarbonized electricity system. artigo.texto: The Lino Lakes City Council continues to have discussions around data centers. At the council’s most recent work session, Community Development Director Michael Grochala reviewed the city’s current land use regulations and provided an overview of data centers. “We’re hearing a lot more about them now,” Grochala said. “They’ve been around for years … but we’re seeing a lot more locally within the Twin Cities Metro Area and as a whole nationally.” What data centers do A data center is a facility that houses computer servers and related equipment used to process, store and distribute digital information. Grochala said data centers support cloud computing, artificial intelligence, data storage, online applications and other digital services. Unlike a typical office or commercial building, a data center is designed primarily to operate computer equipment. These facilities generally run continuously and require reliable electrical power, cooling systems, network connectivity and backup power, Grochala said. “The city’s zoning ordinance defines a data center as an establishment primarily involved in compiling, storing and maintaining information in digital form using a mainframe computer,” Grochala said. “The definition specifically excludes general business offices, computer-related sales establishments and business or personal service establishments.” Types and sizing considerations Data centers vary in size, ownership and function. Common types include enterprise, colocation and hyperscale facilities (see sidebar for more information). Grochala said the hyperscale data centers are driving concerns and interest. “These are much bigger facilities. These are over 200,000 square feet, some of them getting into the million-square-foot size,” he explained. “… These places are really pushing a lot of data, storing a lot of data and now computing, as AI is expanding.” Because these facilities differ in size, design and operating requirements, the appropriate location depends on the data center’s type and scale, available site infrastructure, surrounding land uses and local regulations. Potential sites may include industrial districts, technology or business parks, areas with existing or planned electrical and high-capacity fiber infrastructure, and locations with adequate water and wastewater infrastructure when water-based cooling is proposed. Under the city’s current zoning code, a data center is a permitted use in the Light Industrial (LI), General Industrial (GI) and Business Campus (BC) zoning districts. The LI district includes high-tech businesses and professional services. The GI district allows general industrial uses and services, including more intensive activities. The BC district supports employment-oriented development, including offices, services, research and development, data centers and light industrial uses. A data center proposed in one of these districts would not require rezoning, Grochala explained. However, the development would still need to comply with all applicable city building and development requirements. The city’s 2040 Comprehensive Plan provides the broader land-use framework for determining whether a proposed data center aligns with the city’s planned development pattern. Each proposal would be evaluated according to its location, design and development characteristics. Data centers may also be subject to state and regional regulations and approvals. Minnesota’s Business First Stop offers a coordinated resource for businesses and project proposers navigating state requirements. Depending on the project, those requirements may address environmental review, water appropriation and use, stormwater and wastewater, air emissions, electric generation or storage, utility interconnection, and building and plumbing standards. The city’s land use review and any applicable state or regional reviews are separate processes. A project must satisfy the requirements of each reviewing authority before the corresponding approvals or permits can be issued. Grochala said Lino Lakes’ location within the metropolitan area, access to major transportation corridors and established business campus and industrial areas may create opportunities for technology-oriented development. The city also participates in the Minnesota Technology Corridor, a regional economic development collaboration among six cities. The corridor encompasses development areas along I-35E and I-35W and identifies more than 1,500 acres of future development potential. According to the city staff report, supporting infrastructure includes proximity to I-35E, a fiber-optic backbone and two electric transmission lines. Council members share feedback, thoughts Council Member Julia Nelson clarified that no company has approached the city about building a data center. “I would be for anything that gives us the most power and control over this,” she added. Council Member Randy Rennaker, who brought this forward for discussion to the council in July, said he wants to make certain the city is protected and has the control of what type of facilities are built in the city. “I have friends and family who live in the city that can’t water their yard on a Monday or a Wednesday,” he added. “Some of these data centers are using exorbitant amounts of water. That’s just not right.” Council Member Chris Lyden asked Grochala if it would be possible to ban data centers in the specific zoning districts. Grochala said staff have not gone down the path of exploring prohibition, but the city could establish standards. There was no formal action taken by the council. It was discussion only.

artigo.texto: A joint South Korean research team has announced a finding that could accelerate the commercialization of next-generation lithium-metal batteries: a high-performance electrolyte formulation made entirely from two inexpensive, off-the-shelf solvents that battery researchers had long considered individually unsuitable — and had never thought to combine — tripling cycle life under demanding conditions compared with conventional electrolytes tested in identical circumstances. The result challenges a design principle that has dominated the field for decades. The Battery Chemistry That Could Double EV Range — and Its Long-Standing Problem Lithium-metal batteries have sat just beyond the commercial horizon for the better part of five decades. The appeal is straightforward: swap the graphite anode in today's electric vehicle batteries for lithium metal, and you can theoretically double — and in some research estimates multiply by up to ten times — the energy stored per kilogram. That translates directly into longer driving range without a heavier or larger battery pack, and into cheaper, more compact grid-scale energy storage systems. The obstacle is equally straightforward: lithium metal is exceptionally reactive. Every time a lithium-metal battery charges, the anode reacts with the surrounding liquid electrolyte. Those reactions build up a protective layer called the solid electrolyte interphase, or SEI, on the anode surface. On graphite, this layer forms once and stabilizes. On lithium metal, it cracks, regrows, and thickens with every cycle — consuming lithium and electrolyte irreversibly, promoting the growth of needle-like lithium dendrites that can short-circuit the cell, and triggering destructive side reactions at the cathode. The result is rapid capacity fade. Under the high-voltage conditions required to push maximum energy from a cell, the problem intensifies. The prevailing engineering response has been to use electrolytes that minimize the strength of the solvent's grip on lithium ions. Strongly solvating solvents — those that cluster tightly around a lithium ion in solution — raise the energy barrier for the ion to shed those solvent molecules and deposit as metal on the anode, a step called desolvation. Poor desolvation means uneven plating, which means a bad SEI, which means short cycle life. The conventional fix has been to use either expensive fluorinated solvents that bind lithium more weakly, or to dissolve lithium salts at very high concentrations to push the chemistry in a more favorable direction. Both approaches add manufacturing cost and complexity. An Unexpected Combination The team, led by Professor Song Hyun-kon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), focused instead on two commodity chemicals that the battery field had previously ruled out: ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL). Both researchers are confirmed specialists in battery electrolyte design with a track record of publication in high-impact materials science journals. Both solvents are produced industrially at large scale and are inexpensive. Both had been excluded from lithium-metal battery electrolyte design for the same fundamental reason: they bind to lithium ions too strongly. EC in particular is a workhorse of the conventional lithium-ion battery industry — it is the primary solvent in most EV battery electrolytes today — but it is well-documented as incompatible with lithium metal anodes, where its tight grip on lithium ions and its tendency to decompose continuously at the reactive lithium surface rapidly degrade the cell. Sulfolane, a polar industrial solvent with similarly high binding affinity for lithium, had been studied as a battery solvent on its own and rejected for analogous reasons. What the UNIST–KAIST team found and reported in ACS Nano on August 11, 2026, is that mixing EC and SL at a 3-to-7 weight ratio — together with a lithium salt and a small quantity of an SEI-stabilizing additive — produces an electrolyte that behaves in a way neither solvent predicts individually. What Does 'Cooperative Solvation' Actually Mean? When EC and SL molecules are present together at that ratio, strong intermolecular forces arise between them — specifically, hydrogen bonds between EC's hydrogen atoms and SL's oxygen atoms. These inter-solvent bonds pull the two molecules toward each other rather than toward the lithium ion. The result is counterintuitive: each solvent's individual binding affinity for lithium ions is weakened by the presence of the other. The team called this mechanism cooperative solvation. The mechanism works through the structure of the lithium ion's immediate environment in solution. Normally, a lithium ion in an EC-based electrolyte is surrounded by EC molecules in what is called the first solvation sheath — typically four to six molecules arranged around the ion. When EC and SL are mixed in the cooperative ratio, both solvents appear simultaneously in that first solvation sheath in a new configuration that the team verified through computational modeling. The co-localized solvents effectively share the coordination of the lithium ion, and because they are also coordinating with each other through hydrogen bonding, the total binding energy available for each solvent to hold onto the lithium is reduced. Desolvation — the step where lithium ions must shed their solvent shell before depositing on the anode — becomes easier. "Mixing two strongly binding solvents to actually weaken their interaction with lithium ions represents a new design principle that overturns conventional electrolyte design wisdom," first author Jinki Hong stated in the research announcement. artigo.texto: As the global transition toward renewable energy accelerates, the race to capture market share in storage and delivery is intensifying. Deciding between Eos Energy Enterprises (EOSE -5.16%) and Plug Power (PLUG -3.57%) is a choice between two distinct technologies. EOSE & PLUG: Performance Comparison Key Financial Metrics Eos Energy Enterprises specializes in zinc-based long-duration battery systems designed for utility and industrial applications. Plug Power focuses on building an end-to-end green hydrogen ecosystem, from fuel production to powering heavy machinery. Both companies are scaling rapidly but face different financial hurdles as they attempt to reach long-term profitability in the clean energy market. The case for Eos Energy Enterprises Eos Energy Enterprises designs zinc-based battery systems and is carving out a niche within industrial stocks. In its latest annual report, the company noted that two customers accounted for nearly 52% and 19% of revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, though it highlights the scale of its current utility-level partnerships. In FY 2025, revenue reached about $114.2 million, representing a roughly 632% increase over the previous year. The company reported a net loss of approximately $970 million for the period. This performance follows a net loss of nearly $686 million in fiscal 2024 as the company continues to invest heavily in its manufacturing capabilities. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately negative 1.0x, indicating total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets, is nearly 4.9x. Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was roughly negative $265.0 million in FY 2025. The case for Plug Power Plug Power builds an integrated green hydrogen ecosystem, deploying over 74,000 fuel cell systems globally. In its latest annual report, the company disclosed that Walmart Inc. (WMT +1.55%) was its largest customer, representing approximately a quarter of revenue. Such high customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the enterprise as it navigates the high costs of hydrogen infrastructure. In FY 2025, revenue reached about $709.9 million, which is a roughly 13% increase from the prior year. The company recorded a net loss of approximately $1.6 billion for the same period. This trend follows a net loss of roughly $2.1 billion in fiscal 2024, showing a slight narrowing of losses even as the top line remains volatile. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.0x, meaning total debt is roughly equal to shareholder equity. The current ratio is close to 2.3x. Free cash flow was approximately negative $662 million during FY 2025, reflecting the massive capital intensity required to build and operate hydrogen production facilities. Risk profile comparison Eos Energy Enterprises faces significant legal challenges from securities fraud class action lawsuits filed in 2026. These suits allege the company made misleading disclosures about its production ramp-up and quality issues at its Turtle Creek facility. The business also contends with competition from larger energy storage providers like Fluence Energy (FLNC -4.84%) and remains sensitive to changes in government subsidies. Plug Power is currently defending against multiple federal securities fraud lawsuits regarding its financial performance and Department of Energy loan status. The company suspended activities related to that loan program in November 2025, creating uncertainty about its path to low-cost capital. It also faces intense competition from established giants like GE Vernova (GEV -0.79%) while managing a complex supply chain for materials like iridium. Valuation comparison Eos Energy Enterprises is cheaper based on Forward P/E and earnings estimates, whereas Plug Power has a lower P/S ratio using sales over the past twelve months. Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers. Which stock would I buy in 2026? The current fiscal year, 2026, looks to be a major step forward for Eos Energy Enterprises. The business has already sold more products through the first half of the year than it did in all of 2025, shipping $126 million of gear to clients. The longer term should be much greater, too. Management says it has nearly $25 billion of business pipeline, meaning proposed energy storage developments Eos could bid on, and an $807 million backlog, which are firm orders for the company's products. 2026 revenue is expected to more than double. Recently, Eos scored a high-profile deal to support the PJM grid after joining with Alphabet Inc (GOOG +0.32%) and MN8 Energy on a solar energy storage project in West Virginia. Similarly, Plug Power's fuel cells run on clean-burning hydrogen, though creating hydrogen is often done in a process fueled by natural gas. Still, Plug Power sits firmly in the renewable energy niche, benefiting from many countries' moves toward green (non-fossil-fuel-derived) hydrogen. It is also benefiting from the datacenter boom and from restored tax credits that make its systems more affordable to deploy. For fiscal 2026, revenue growth is pretty good, with Wall Street analyst consensus predicting a nearly 15% increase to $812 million. The net loss is seen narrowing to about $580 million. Both businesses offer investors a way to play the rise in demand for power storage brought about by AI data center demand and the need for storage for renewable energy production. Eos, with its lower forward P/E and similar P/S ratio, seems to be the better bet for long-term investors.

artigo.texto: O Nordeste estará no centro do debate energético nacional pelos próximos 10 anos e pode atrair quase 30% dos novos investimentos em data centers de grande porte, além de ampliar a produção eólica, fotovoltaica e de gás natural. As perspectivas constam no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2036), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), sob diretrizes do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). Divulgado no último dia 8 para consulta pública, o PDE atribui a atratividade do Nordeste aos data centers à presença de pontos de chegada de cabos internacionais de fibra óptica, à elevada disponibilidade de geração renovável e ao potencial de desenvolvimento econômico regional. Apesar dessas vantagens, o subsistema Sudeste/Centro-Oeste deverá receber a maior parcela dos novos investimentos em grandes data centers, estimada em mais de 65%, enquanto o Sul ficará com os 5% restantes. >> Faça parte do canal do Movimento Econômico no WhatsApp No cenário nacional, os centros de dados ganham importância com a digitalização da economia, a expansão dos serviços de armazenamento e processamento de informações e a disseminação da inteligência artificial. O PDE projeta que o consumo de eletricidade dos data centers no Brasil alcance aproximadamente 30 terawatts-hora (TWh) em 2036. Pelo porte dos novos empreendimentos, a tendência apontada é de busca por conexão direta à rede básica de transmissão. Demanda elétrica do Nordeste cresce acima da média nacional A expansão das atividades de comércio e serviços deverá impulsionar o crescimento da carga elétrica no subsistema Nordeste. O PDE estima avanço médio de 3,7% ao ano entre 2026 e 2036, a maior taxa entre os subsistemas e superior aos 3,3% previstos para o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Segundo o relatório, a carga global nordestina deverá passar de 14.209 megawatts médios (MW médios) em 2026 para 20.462 MW médios em 2036. Esse indicador reúne o consumo final de eletricidade e as perdas verificadas entre a geração e o atendimento aos consumidores. Com isso, segundo o PDE, os data centers passam a exercer influência crescente sobre o perfil de demanda da classe comercial. Nacionalmente, a participação dessa classe no consumo de eletricidade deverá aumentar de 19% para 24% no período, enquanto a residencial recuará de 32% para 28%. Além dos centros de dados, o planejamento considera novas demandas associadas à produção de hidrogênio por eletrólise, que tendem a ocorrer apenas no segundo quinquênio, devido ao prazo mais longo de maturação dos investimentos, ainda em escala reduzida no horizonte analisado. Transmissão precisa atender novos consumidores e escoar renováveis A instalação de grandes consumidores, como data centers e plantas de hidrogênio, exigirá reforços na transmissão, segundo avaliação da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética. O PDE destaca um estudo para inserção dessas cargas no Nordeste e recomenda o Bipolo Nordeste II, que ampliará a capacidade de exportação de eletricidade da região para Sudeste e Sul. O empreendimento e as obras associadas deverão permitir a conexão de novos projetos de geração, consumo e armazenamento, além de fortalecer a estabilidade da rede e reduzir cortes de geração por restrições de confiabilidade. A redução mais ampla desses cortes, conhecidos como curtailment, também dependerá de armazenamento, resposta da demanda e maior flexibilidade das usinas. Nas simulações do plano, os cortes permanecem em patamar absoluto semelhante ao de 2026 ao longo do horizonte analisado. Trata-se de uma projeção sistêmica, sem previsão específica para regiões ou empreendimentos. Já sobre novos parques eólicos, solares e linhas de transmissão no Nordeste, o estudo indica que será necessário maior atenção aos impactos cumulativos sobre vegetação, fauna, paisagem e acesso das comunidades aos recursos naturais. O relatório também aponta riscos de conflitos pelo uso da água nas termelétricas e de pressão sobre comunidades, infraestrutura e ambientes marinhos nas atividades de petróleo e gás. Projetos de gás somam R$ 7,5 bilhões em infraestrutura As bacias de Sergipe-Alagoas, Parnaíba e Potiguar estão entre as principais contribuições à expansão da produção bruta nacional de gás natural, com uma projeção de atingir 308 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia em 2036. A produção líquida, descontados reinjeção, perdas, queimas e consumo próprio, deverá chegar a 135 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia, com destaque para o Sergipe Águas Profundas (SEAP) e os campos da Bacia do Parnaíba, no Maranhão. No Nordeste, três projetos de infraestrutura reúnem estimativas de aproximadamente R$ 7,5 bilhões. A maior parcela corresponde ao escoamento do SEAP, com R$ 6,8 bilhões, capacidade de 18 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia e operação prevista a partir de 2030. O projeto prevê processamento no ambiente marítimo e injeção direta na malha de transporte, por um gasoduto de 134 quilômetros. Na Bahia, a UPGN Miranga, da PetroReconcavo, tem investimento estimado em R$ 360 milhões e entrada prevista para 2028. A capacidade de processamento será de 950 mil metros cúbicos por dia, expansível a 1,5 milhão. Em Pernambuco, o terminal de regaseificação de GNL de Suape aparece com R$ 350 milhões, capacidade de 14 milhões de metros cúbicos por dia e operação considerada para 2027. Segundo o PDE, a ampliação da oferta de gás pode fortalecer o abastecimento industrial e a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico. Esses benefícios dependem da competitividade do combustível, da execução dos investimentos e das condições regulatórias. artigo.texto: Amwins Global Risks (AGR) is expanding its specialist commercial and industrial (C&I) insurance facility to cover battery energy storage systems (BESS) and electric vehicle charging infrastructure. The facility groups distributed assets under a single program, with deductibles scaled to individual site characteristics rather than to utility-scale norms. The structure is designed for portfolios that sit between the two ends of the existing insurance market: too small for utility-scale terms, too numerous to place site by site. Amwins has offered BESS cover through NARDAC, its specialist energy MGA, since March 2024, with capacity of up to $50 million per location backed by eight Lloyd’s syndicates. The C&I facility does not introduce new BESS cover so much as a new structure for it: a portfolio approach that groups multiple distributed sites under a single programme, with deductibles calibrated to individual asset scale rather than applied uniformly across the portfolio. The BESS insurance market has been expanding, but unevenly. A number of insurers have restricted or withdrawn capacity following battery fires in the UK and overseas, a trend documented by market participants including Allianz UK, which expanded its own BESS underwriting capability in July 2026 partly in response to gaps left by capacity withdrawals. That means brokers face a market where appetite and expertise are not evenly distributed. Allianz UK expanded its own BESS underwriting capability in July 2026, with its head of construction, engineering and energy insurance noting that early engagement with experienced underwriters is increasingly valuable given how quickly the risk landscape is developing. For C&I assets specifically, the challenge is structural as much as technical. Individual sites can be relatively small in value, but developers are assembling portfolios of dozens of them across multiple locations. Applying terms designed for a large utility-scale installation to a single C&I site can produce deductibles that are disproportionate to the asset’s value, making the insurance economically unworkable. The Amwins facility is designed to resolve that by underwriting at portfolio level while still assessing accumulated natural catastrophe exposure across individual locations. “Individual sites can be relatively small, but developers are increasingly building portfolios comprising numerous assets across multiple locations," said Tom Harries, director at Amwins Global Risks and partner at NARDAC. "Bringing those assets together allows us to underwrite them efficiently at portfolio scale, while still recognising the individual risk characteristics of each site.” The facility covers both construction and operational phases, including delay in start-up and business interruption cover. The EV charging component is primarily directed at the US market, where commercial charging infrastructure is being deployed at scale. Amwins Global Risks operates from London and places through the London market, giving US-based developers and their brokers access to London capacity for risks that the domestic US market has been slower to accommodate in structured form. Harries said the addition of BESS and EV charging reflects the increasing convergence of distributed energy technologies, and that the facility is designed to adapt as portfolios grow. “It allows us to focus on monitoring how the portfolio’s natural catastrophe exposure changes as new projects are added and gives developers the freedom to concentrate on building out their portfolios, knowing their insurance program can adapt and grow alongside them.” The C&I expansion follows AGR’s renewal and enlargement of a separate natural catastrophe facility for renewable energy projects in July 2026, which increased available capacity to $50 million per placement from $20 million and broadened cover to all major natural catastrophe perils globally. The two moves extend AGR’s distributed and renewable energy proposition across construction, operation and catastrophe layers within a matter of months.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 14 de outubro de 2026, às 12:27 Seja para as equipes criarem redes e infraestruturas corporativas no setor de varejo, saúde, serviços financeiros ou implementarem um data center de IA com velocidade e escala gigantescas, a configuração, a observabilidade e a automação dependem de um registro confiável de qual infraestrutura deve existir e como ela deve operar. Esse registro é o NetBox, disse Kris Beevers, CEO e cofundador da NetBox Labs. O NetBox é usado por empresas como Arm, CoreWeave, Kaiser Permanente e J.P. Morgan Chase para criar, operar e expandir suas redes e infraestruturas. Estamos observando um crescimento enorme, com mais de 90% das principais neonuvens usando o NetBox para projetar e escalar seus datacenters de IA, e esperamos que o NetBox alimente mais de 100 GW de capacidade de datacenters de IA até 2030. O NetBox se torna nativo do NVIDIA DSX OS A NVIDIA fez uma parceria com a NetBox Labs para tornar o NetBox uma fonte nativa de referência para o NVCM, de modo que a configuração de rede no DSX OS venha diretamente do sistema de registro que as equipes de infraestrutura de IA já usam. Isso coloca o NetBox no centro do design, do provisionamento e da operação das implementações de IA em grande escala da atualidade. O NetBox fornece os dados centrais que impulsionam a automação da configuração em todas as malhas de cluster nativas da NVIDIA. Leia mais sobre a Parceria NetBox Labs NVIDIA aqui. Contexto do NetBox em todos os dashboards da Grafana Labs A infraestrutura está produzindo cada vez mais telemetria. Mas a telemetria só mostra o que a infraestrutura está fazendo, não o que ela é: a qual dispositivo uma interface pertence, onde ela está localizada, qual função ela desempenha, quem é o proprietário dela e se ela deveria existir. Atualmente as equipes preenchem essa lacuna manualmente, com scripts ou suposições frágeis. Com a nova parceria da NetBox Labs com a Grafana Labs, o NetBox registra como a infraestrutura deve ser e a Grafana mostra o que ela está realmente fazendo. O plugin gratuito e de código aberto do NetBox, desenvolvido em colaboração com a Grafana Labs e publicado no catálogo da Grafana, transfere o contexto do NetBox em tempo real (local, função, tenant, rack, proprietário, ciclo de vida) para os dashboards e alertas da Grafana. Ele não exige alterações no pipeline, evita rótulos desatualizados e não adiciona nenhum custo de métrica. Separadamente, a plataforma Orb de código aberto da NetBox Labs agora oferece aos usuários da Grafana Cloud uma nova fonte de fluxo de rede e telemetria de pacotes. A observabilidade das redes e da infraestrutura são casos de uso populares em toda a comunidade da Grafana, e o contexto é o que separa uma parede de métricas das respostas e ações, disse Ash Mazhari, VP de Desenvolvimento Corporativo da Grafana Labs. O NetBox é o sistema de registro em que as equipes já confiam. Com a fonte de dados do NetBox em nosso catálogo e a Orb fornecendo telemetria de rede para a Grafana Cloud, nossos usuários passam a ter um entendimento mais profundo da sua infraestrutura e dos dados de rede. Leia mais sobre a Parceria entre a NetBox Labs e a Grafana Labs aqui. Novos recursos da plataforma NetBox Labs para pessoas e agentes de IA Além das parcerias, a NetBox Labs também anunciou várias novas adições à plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura da NetBox Labs. Leia mais sobre Anúncios da Plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura da NetBox Labs aqui. Somente a NetBox Labs oferece uma plataforma abrangente de inteligência de infraestrutura que aborda todas as etapas do ciclo de vida da infraestrutura, com neutralidade de fornecedores, proteções claras para agentes e a confiança dos ambientes mais exigentes do mundo, afirmou o CEO e cofundador Kris Beevers. Os anúncios de hoje sobre o produto da NetBox Labs e as parcerias com a NVIDIA e a Grafana Labs possibilitam às equipes, em qualquer estágio da sua jornada de modernização da infraestrutura, trabalhar com a confiança de quem conta com o apoio da plataforma de inteligência de infraestrutura mais potente do mundo. Estamos muito animados com o que essas parcerias e anúncios de produtos significam para nossos clientes e nossos negócios. Sobre a NetBox Labs A NetBox Labs simplifica todo o ciclo de vida da infraestrutura para os ambientes técnicos mais exigentes do mundo. Ela é a administradora comercial do NetBox, o sistema de registro de infraestrutura de código aberto no qual mais de 10 mil organizações confiam há mais de uma década. A NetBox Labs simplifica a aquisição, a modelagem, a implementação e o gerenciamento de infraestruturas tanto para pessoas quanto para agentes. Sua plataforma de inteligência de infraestrutura é a base de sistemas de missão crítica em empresas como Arm, CoreWeave, J.P. Morgan, Kaiser Permanente e Riot Games. Com sede em Nova York, a NetBox Labs é apoiada pela NGP, Notable Capital, Flybridge, IBM, Salesforce e Two Sigma. Visite https://netboxlabs.com para mais informações. artigo.texto: Ohio candidates for U.S. Senate As the country prepares to vote in this year's pivotal midterm election, the balance of power in Washington, D.C. is at stake, and once again Ohio finds itself in a decisive position. The results of our U.S. Senate race could tip the scales resulting in continuing Republican control, Democrats taking back power in Congress, or split control in the two chambers. On the table in Ohio is the remaining two years left on Vice President JD Vance's Senate term, left vacant when he became second in command following President Donald Trump winning the presidency in 2024. Governor Mike DeWine appointed then-Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted to temporarily take over that spot, and this year, Husted is running on the Republican ticket, hoping to retain the seat. On the Democratic side, Sherrod Brown is hoping to rejoin his former colleagues in the Senate, after losing his re-election bid to current Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024. Libertarian candidate Bill Redpath and Independent candidate Gregory Levy have also joined the contest. On Tuesday's edition of the "Sound of Ideas" hosted by Stephanie Haney, we'll share one-on-one pre-recorded conversations with Redpath and Levy. We previously shared Stephanie's one-on-one conversation with Brown in an episode of the "Sound of Ideas" that aired on Sept. 28. While we had an interview scheduled with Husted, his spokesperson told us he needed to reschedule due to Senate business, and never responded to our repeated requests to reschedule. The questions we've asked these candidates came from our own independent research, as well as conversations we had this summer with voters at libraries across Northeast Ohio as part of our Listen, Engage, Vote initiative. We also asked for input from our audience members on social media. Researchers are looking for ways to get people the help they need more quickly by using technology as an intervention tool, which can also be tailored to the individual. On Tuesday's episode of the "Sound of Ideas," hosted by Stephanie Haney, we share the latest edition of our "Brains on Tap" science series produced in collaboration between Ideastream and Kent State University's Brain Health Research Institute. In this installment, Ideastream's science reporter Jeff St. Clair talks with Karin Coifman about the emerging field of precision psychiatry in a public conversation recorded at Bell Tower Brewing Co. in Kent on Sept. 10. artigo.texto: BASF SE Key supplier of materials for electrode manufacturing According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Electrode Dry Coating Materials market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global market for Battery Electrode Dry Coating Materials is entering a decisive commercialization phase as cell manufacturers scale solvent-free electrode production to cut gigafactory operating costs and meet tightening VOC regulations. Dry coating eliminates solvent recovery systems, reduces energy consumption, and simplifies line footprint, but adoption is gated by a dual qualification burden: electrode performance validation and industrial-scale powder process validation. This creates first-mover advantages for integrated cell makers and specialized material formulators. The supply chain for consistent dry polymer binder powders and tailored conductive additive blends is a critical bottleneck, with scaling of formulated inputs more constrained than active material supply. Pricing power is shifting from per-kilogram material sales to solution-based models bundling formulation, process parameters, and technical support. The economic case strengthens for thick electrodes targeting high-energy-density cells and for solid-state designs where solvent incompatibility makes dry processing a technical necessity. Geographic adoption will mirror gigafactory clusters, while material supply concentrates in specialty chemical hubs, creating new trade dependencies. This report analyzes demand drivers, restraints, end-use sectors, regional dynamics, and competitive structure through 2035. The baseline scenario for the Battery Electrode Dry Coating Materials Market through 2035 assumes continued gigafactory capacity expansion, gradual dry process qualification, and regulatory pressure on solvent emissions. Under this scenario, the market grows at a 18.5% CAGR from 2025 to 2035, reaching a market index of 545 (2025=100). Growth is front-loaded in Asia-Pacific, where leading cell manufacturers are already piloting dry coating for LFP and NMC electrodes, followed by North America and Europe as local gigafactories mature. The baseline assumes no disruptive leap in alternative solvent-free technologies and that dry polymer binder powder supply expands sufficiently to avoid prolonged bottlenecks. Demand is concentrated in EV batteries, which account for the largest share, but stationary storage and solid-state batteries gain share toward 2035. Restraints include high initial capital for dry coating lines, slow qualification cycles, and limited availability of high-performance dry binders. The market remains supply-constrained for formulated dry materials until at least 2030, supporting premium pricing and strong margins for early certified suppliers. As automakers scale EV production, gigafactories face intense pressure to reduce cell costs and energy consumption. Dry coating eliminates solvent recovery systems, cutting factory OPEX and floor space, which is critical for high-volume EV battery plants. Currently, dry coating is being piloted for NMC and LFP electrodes, with early adoption by Tesla and other integrated manufacturers. Through 2035, as EV penetration rises and battery demand multiplies, dry coating adoption will accelerate, particularly for thick electrodes that boost energy density and reduce cost per kWh. Demand-side indicators include EV sales growth, battery pack price targets, and gigafactory capacity announcements. The shift to dry processing is also supported by automakers' sustainability goals, as it reduces VOC emissions and energy use. By 2035, dry coating is expected to capture a significant share of new EV battery lines, especially for premium and long-range models, while wet processes persist for lower-volume or specialty cells. These applications prioritize cost, cycle life, and safety, often using LFP chemistry, which is well-suited to dry processing. artigo.texto: The Custer County Board of Supervisors met for less than an hour on Tuesday morning inside the Custer County Courthouse. Following a public hearing late last month which saw no members of the public coming forward, the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously today to adopt the data center regulations recommended to them by the planning commission. Ahead of last week’s public hearing, Zoning Administrator Darci Tibbs explained the process that led to the regulations being drafted. “The purpose of these regulations is to not encourage or attract data centers, but to make sure that if one is proposed in Custer County, we have appropriate standards and safeguards in place to protect the health, safety, and welfare of our citizens, and to protect the ag and rural character of the county,” said Tibbs.” View the full data center regulation document here: Custer County Data Center Regulations The board also voted unanimously to put a 12 month moratorium in place regarding battery energy storage systems. This time period was stated to be so that more time could be given to researching them and to work toward regulations, much like the months long process ahead of the adoption of data center regulations. In board of equalization matters, tax corrections for the years 2023 through 2025 were made to change a stick built home to a mobile home resulting in over $2,000 back to the property owner. A motor vehicle exemption for Custer Care was also approved, at a loss to the county of $16 and change. Levy allocation requests for the upcoming fiscal year were approved unanimously for all subdivisions. View the levy allocations here: 2026-2027 Levies Custer County Sub-divisions County Assessor Elise Taylor came before the board regarding her department’s copier machine, stating that it is starting to show signs of failing. The current copier has been in use since around 2017 or 2018 and is owned, however repairs had become more frequent with parts being harder to find. Taylor said options of a $143 per month lease or purchase over $7,000 were available. Following a discussion about what budget the copier would have to come from and the fact that budgets were just passed and the copiers health was not a concern presented, discussions about its replacement fizzled out. A contract between Central Plains Valuations and the county’s assessor’s office was approved, capped at $8,000. The contract was stated to be the same as it had been since 2021. Supervisor Anne Gibbons was the lone vote of no. With no applications to cross right-of-way received, the meeting was adjourned at 9:52 AM.

artigo.texto: GLENDALE, AZ — The Phoenix area is experiencing a data center construction boom, transforming vacant lots and former farmland to meet digital demand in Arizona and beyond. Data centers keep the digital world running around the clock — streaming TV, cloud storage, banking, and artificial intelligence - but these facilities also require substantial power and water, which impact surrounding communities. DataCenterMap.com tracks locations worldwide and ranks Arizona eighth in the U.S. with 160 existing and proposed facilities statewide. Why is Arizona such a draw? "Land is inexpensive in Arizona; they require a lot of land to build," said Vijay Vittal, a professor at ASU's School of Electrical, Computer and Energy Engineering. Vittal said Arizona has also offered tax incentives and a geographic advantage "very close to the western tech markets" like California's Silicon Valley. Matt Bullock, Peoria's Mayor Pro Tem and owner of a data protection and cybersecurity company that works with data centers, echoed that assessment. "Arizona has one of the lowest seismic activity areas, unlike California or other parts of the country," Bullock said. "And because we have such wide open areas, it's very easy to get power and water infrastructure to data center locations." Data centers' demand for power and water — and the impact on nearby communities — is drawing pushback from some Arizona residents. April Butler lives near a proposed data center in Glendale called Project Eagle, also known as Project Baccara, located on Olive Avenue just east of the Loop 303. She says the project is massive. "The biggest part will be three data centers, and they're just back to back to back," Butler said. Butler and her neighbors spoke out at a Glendale City meeting in September. "I don't think we have a lot of laws in place to protect us," Butler said. "There are other states that were quicker enacting moratoriums and putting rules and guidelines in place to where it's a little bit more difficult to get those projects in." ABC15 is committed to finding the answers you need and holding those accountable. Submit your news tip to Investigators@abc15.com Peoria is also facing pushback over a large data center preparing to build there. Bullock said councilmembers are considering changes to zoning rules that would require special use permits for future data center projects or greater oversight. "To ensure they're using the reclaimed water, closed-loop [cooling systems], bring their own power, building parks and roads and things, and helping local schools," Bullock said. "That's how it should have been done all along, and now we're just catching up." As for Butler, she is standing her ground against Project Eagle. "Do you have any hope you can stop this from coming?" I asked her. "Absolutely," Butler said. A final vote on the formal land annexation and rezoning applications is expected at the Glendale City Council Meeting scheduled for October 27.

artigo.texto: Sodium-Ion Batteries and Storage Flexibility: Why Batteries are not a Bottleneck for a Fully Renewable Energy System Battery technology is frequently framed around a material bottleneck, but a recent study from LUT University researchers suggests that concern may be overstated. According to pv magazine, the analysis examines sodium-ion batteries as a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries and finds that raw material availability need not constrain the scale of storage required for a fully renewable energy system. The study notes that sodium-ion batteries rely on abundant raw materials beyond the cathode, with hard carbon replacing natural graphite in anodes and aluminum substituting for copper as the anode current collector. Previous energy system simulations pointed to stationary battery demand approaching 75 TWh of capacity by 2050, while mobile batteries were estimated to dominate at up to almost 275 TWh of capacity by mid-century. A ratio of roughly 0.8 kWh of capacity per kW of installed solar PV capacity was identified for a cost-optimized, flexible global energy system run entirely on renewable energy. Including electronics and other applications, total battery demand could exceed 350 TWh of capacity by 2050. A bottom-up assessment spanning cell-level to system-level costs found sodium-ion batteries already close to cost parity with lithium counterparts. System-level costs were estimated at about EUR120 per kWh of capacity in 2025, and applying different learning rates could bring costs down to a range of EUR28.5 to EUR51.9 per kWh of capacity by 2050. The authors conclude that batteries are ruled out as a bottleneck on both raw material and cost grounds. They also note that sodium-ion batteries can serve as a drop-in technology produced on existing lithium-ion production lines. For solar PV prosumers who both produce and consume electricity, batteries are not strictly necessary for a secure supply. A grid connection allows surplus rooftop generation to be fed into the grid and reimbursed, with electricity drawn back during periods of low or no solar yield. Rising grid electricity prices and falling battery costs may nonetheless make adding a battery economically beneficial for optimizing overall energy supply costs. An initial cost-optimization study found that PV-battery systems are widely beneficial for prosumers in terms of total energy supply cost, with electrification of heat via heating rods or heat pumps identified as key. Residential rooftop PV yields about 18% less electricity than ground-mounted systems, yet very low-cost solar PV is not a limitation. Combining with stationary battery storage enables high demand and heat cover ratios globally, and battery capacity optimization depends on whether electric vehicles are included. High benefits were found for cars capable of supplying electricity to the system through vehicle-to-home arrangements. A follow-up study examined whether seasonal hydrogen storage benefits residential PV prosumer systems. Long-term storage was found to play only a niche role for Nordic countries in an off-grid scenario, even with significant cost reduction potential. The updated optimization model showed most regions reaching grid parity by 2035, with more than half having already reached parity in 2020. Batteries were confirmed to play an important role. For on-grid cases, a maximum battery-to-PV ratio of 1.6 to 1.8 kWh of capacity per kW was found, rising to 3 to 4 kWh of capacity per kW in off-grid cases. The electric vehicle fleet is growing quickly worldwide, already accumulating battery capacity on the terawatt-hour scale and driving solar PV capacity demand. Using this capacity for power system balancing is seen as a promising solution for systems with a growing share of variable renewable generation. Smart charging alone provides flexibility by raising electricity consumption during renewable generation peaks and reducing it during deficits. Vehicle-to-grid goes further, turning electric vehicles into distributed battery storage on wheels that can supply electricity to the grid during deficit periods. A study analyzing smart charging and vehicle-to-grid confirmed substantial system benefits. These technologies allow installed utility-scale battery storage capacity to be reduced by about 50%, indirectly lowering critical material use in batteries and reducing the need for other energy storage technologies. Enabling them alone may cut total annual system costs by about 4%. Vehicle-to-grid cannot be free for the system, however. Electric vehicle owners must be incentivized to participate and compensated for battery wear. The role and impact of vehicle-to-grid will depend strongly on the cost of this service, but even at EUR50 to EUR100 per MWh it still provides system benefits. The main challenge is the public infrastructure needed for electric vehicles to charge or feed high-quality AC power into the grid whenever parked, especially during the midday PV generation peak when additional storage capacity is most valuable. Flexibility is needed to mitigate the variability of renewable energy sources arising from their weather-dependent nature. Battery energy storage systems have gained widespread attention as a potential leading technology for this role, with advantages including high energy density, rapid response, reliable power delivery, sustained discharge capability, and geographical independence. Continued reductions in battery manufacturing costs have strengthened the role of battery storage in facilitating renewable energy integration, particularly for solar PV. A comprehensive review of flexibility options across more than 1000 research articles found that compared with other storage technologies, including pumped hydro energy storage, thermal energy storage, and e-hydrogen storage, battery technologies currently offer an attractive combination of rapid response, modularity, efficiency, and technological maturity. artigo.texto: INDEPENDENCE, Mo. — KSHB 41 reporter Tod Palmer covers sports business and eastern Jackson County, including Independence. Share your story idea with Tod. — Independence approved new zoning requirements for data centers and battery energy storage systems within city limits. After several months of conversation and public hearings, the Independence City Council unanimously approved the changes Oct. 5 to its Unified Development Ordinance, or UDO, related to such projects. Independence initiated a moratorium on new data center projects, which passed in July, over the summer after Nebius broke ground in May 2026 on a hyperscale AI data factory in the Little Blue Valley and Patmos moved to build a data center farther south along Little Blue Parkway. The council approved the Nebius project in March despite strong organized opposition, which ultimately led to residents voting out several council members who supported the project. Council member Brice Stewart and Mayor Kevin King introduced a series of amendments, all of which were also adopted unanimously. One requires any new data center or BESS developments to be at least 1,000 feet from residences or other public spaces — schools, parks, recreation and playground facilities, daycares, nursing homes, hospitals or places of worship. It would allow for variances, if recommended by the city planning commission and approved by the city council. Other amendments were related to noise-impact assessments and mitigation plans, decommissioning data centers that cease operations for 12 months, and requiring generator compliance reports every six months rather than annually. The new regulations require any data center larger than 2.5 megawatts to seek a special use permit from the city. Independence, like many city and county governments, didn’t have specific zoning requirements in place for data centers and BESS projects, which “present unique land use considerations not commonly associated with traditional industrial development,” according to the Agenda Item Cover Letter. Those complicated issues include massive electrical demand, high water consumption, on-site backup power generation, consistent mechanical noise and other issues. “The City's current UDO does not contain use-specific regulations for data processing and hosting facilities,” according to the cover letter. “As interest in this development type continues to increase, staff believes additional standards are appropriate to provide clear expectations for future development while protecting surrounding properties and community resources.” —

artigo.texto: In the race for California’s 46th Congressional District, voters will choose between two candidates with differing perspectives on federal health insurance programs, data centers and more. Rep. Lou Correa, D-Santa Ana, said the rising number of uninsured Americans and the lack of affordable healthcare available to them is a result of President Donald Trump’s administration gutting the Affordable Care Act. Any structural reforms to Medicare and Medicaid can only happen once Congress reverses the cuts that were included in the Big Beautiful Bill budget package, which passed last year, said Correa, 68, who is seeking his sixth term in Congress to represent a district that covers parts of Anaheim, Fullerton and Santa Ana. “We must be more efficient in delivering healthcare services, better coordinated medical data, and more preventive care. We need to ensure that we have a cost-effective, healthy nation,” Correa said in response to a questionnaire from the Southern California New Group. His challenger is David Pan, 62, a Republican and professor of German at UC Irvine. To fix the healthcare programs, Pan said the federal government should look to privatize Medicare and Medicaid, so that private insurance companies approved by and contracted with the federal government would be the sole providers of Medicare and Medicaid benefits. But Pan’s proposal doesn’t stop there. It aligns with how he feels Congress should address rising affordability concerns: The federal government should phase out the country’s welfare and entitlement programs “and use this money to create a universal basic income of $16,000 per year for every individual 21 and older.” He called for monthly payments of $1,000 to all U.S. citizens who are at least 21 years old “and $4,000 per year could be paid into each person’s health savings account.” The savings created by privatizing Medicare and Medicaid would go toward creating this universal basic income, Pan said. “My plan would improve affordability by putting cash directly into people’s bank accounts, reduce fraud and waste in government, and still save over $1 trillion per year over the long term,” Pan said. “We would have a system that provides freedom and equal opportunity to everyone, and in which hard work leads to success.” This isn’t a new platform for Pan. He campaigned on universal basic income in his 2024 congressional bid, losing then to Correa. The two candidates for the 46th Congressional District don’t see eye-to-eye on what the top concern constituents are facing. For Correa, it’s immigration. The ramp-up of federal immigration enforcement since the beginning of 2025 has had a direct impact on the economy, especially in California, Correa said. “California today is the fourth-largest economy in the world. We lead the nation in agriculture and food production, as well as light manufacturing, biomedical, high tech, and high-tech startups, and venture capital. All these industries rely on an immigrant workforce,” Correa said. “Our economy needs immigrant workers to grow, these workers that are being deported.” As for specific policy, Correa said Congress should reform the timeline of when an immigrant can apply for a change in their legal status. Federal law allows for undocumented people to apply for a change to their citizenship if they were in the country before 1972. A bill in the House would change that date, from 1972 to seven years before that application to change citizenship is filed. (That bill, which has no Republican co-sponsors, has stalled in the House Judiciary Committee after it was introduced last year.) Correa would like to see that amendment go even further: “Let’s change the date again to 2019.” Pan, when asked what immigration policy should look like in five years, said the federal government should maintain a secure border. “In addition, we should have ways for people to immigrate legally if they go through proper procedures and are vetted,” he said. “We can establish a pathway to legal residence for law-abiding residents who contribute to our country.” Another area where Correa and Pan differ is their stance on offshore oil drilling and production in California, something the Trump administration has aggressively pushed since taking office last year. Correa, who was first elected in 2016, pointed to his record of opposing these efforts and co-sponsoring legislation to permanently ban offshore drilling off California’s coast. The West Coast Ocean Protection Act would permanently ban oil and gas exploration off the coasts of California, Oregon and Washington. The bill was introduced in April 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, where it has since stalled. While Congress needs to ensure people can afford to fill their gas tanks today, the country needs a “smart, balanced, long-term energy policy” that transitions to favor renewable energy sources, Correa said. “And we must be sure that the food we eat, including seafood, is not contaminated. Accordingly, we must protect our future food supply, and that includes our oceans,” he said. “The threat of offshore oil spills and the threat to our future food supply make offshore drilling unwise.” Conversely, Pan said he would support expanding offshore drilling here, so long as oil companies “think that it would be economically productive.” As long as oil is still comparably efficient with other energy resources, Pan said, “its production should not be suppressed.” But like Correa, Pan acknowledged that energy production must eventually transition to cleaner alternatives. “I support the expansion of all forms of energy that are economically efficient and can diversify our energy production,” he said. “Climate policy should instead focus on carbon taxes, which would generate government revenue and have a real environmental effect.” Correa has similar environmental concerns about data centers. artigo.texto: BYD Chases Global Crown Without America as Battery and Storage Bets Deepen Published on 10/12/2026 at 13:40 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD has set its sights on becoming the world's largest automaker within five years, and it intends to get there without selling a single passenger car in the United States. The Chinese group is betting on purely organic growth, steering clear of the American market for now because regulatory hurdles facing connected vehicle software of Chinese origin make entry difficult. That global ambition is only partly reflected in the share price. The stock slipped 1.9% in the latest session to EUR 8.48, extending its year-to-date decline to 21%. A day earlier, the picture had looked brighter: BYD shares closed at EUR 8.65 on Friday, up 4.2%, lifted not only by company-specific news but by a broad recovery across Chinese automakers. According to media reports, the sector's rebound was a technical countermovement after several sessions of declines, with concerns about demand in the seasonal peak quarter and trade tensions between China and the European Union already partly priced in. Closing the Gap on Toyota and Volkswagen To narrow the distance to the industry leaders, BYD is pressing ahead with production capacity outside China. Toyota sold roughly 11.32 million vehicles worldwide in full-year 2025, Volkswagen around 8.98 million, while BYD delivered about 4.60 million. In the first half of 2026, Toyota notched 5.39 million sales, against 1.81 million for BYD in the same period. Management sees local supply chains as the key to closing that gap. Beyond plants already producing in Thailand and Uzbekistan, factories in Brazil and Indonesia are under construction. In Europe, the ramp-up at the Hungarian site is imminent, with series production slated to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 once testing is complete. At the Paris Motor Show, Stella Li also held out the prospect of examining further European production locations in the medium term, with France among the candidates on the shortlist. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? Public Fleets, Trucks and a Masdar Storage Deal Alongside its consumer passenger car business, BYD is broadening its international footprint in the public sector and adjacent technology fields. Overseas sales of passenger cars and pickups climbed 67.9% to almost 790,000 units in the first half of 2026. The company now supplies police forces and government fleets in several countries, including Mexico, Pakistan, the Philippines, Austria and Hungary. The commercial vehicle segment is expanding too. At its Huai'an plant, the 150,000th commercial vehicle in company history rolled off the line on October 9 — an all-electric Q3 tractor unit, underscoring the push into heavy long-haul transport. Outside vehicle manufacturing, BYD secured a battery storage agreement for 11.275 gigawatt-hours with energy company Masdar in the United Arab Emirates during the third quarter of 2026. Blade Battery Capacity Takes Precedence Operationally, BYD reports sustained strong demand for its models equipped with fast-charging capability. To safeguard delivery capacity over the long term, the company is giving top priority to expanding production capacity for the second generation of its in-house Blade battery. At the same time, the manufacturer is widening its model range at home. Pre-orders for the second generation of the Seagull have reportedly opened, with the official market launch planned for the fourth quarter. No official pricing has been disclosed so far. Geopolitics Keep Washington Off the Map On the international stage, management is pursuing a selective expansion strategy. Executive Vice President Stella Li, cited by Reuters, described geopolitical tensions as the single biggest challenge for the company's overseas business. For that reason, BYD will not bring passenger cars to the United States for the time being. Exports to other regions remain unaffected. In September 2026, the group sold 463,561 vehicles in total, a gain of 17.0% versus the same month a year earlier. Passenger car and pickup exports accounted for 180,700 units, up 153.9% from the prior-year figure. Ad BYD Stock: New Analysis - 12 October Fresh BYD information released. artigo.texto: UND in the Conversation: Data centers make heat all year long – here’s how the ground can hold onto it until winter Moones Alamooti, Assistant Professor of Energy and Petroleum Engineering at the University of North Dakota, explains in The Conversation how data centers generate waste heat year-round, and by storing that heat underground during warmer months, communities could reuse it in winter for heating buildings, reducing energy waste and reliance on fossil fuels. Editor’s note: The following article is written by Moones Alamooti and is an excerpt of the original article published by The Conversation. You can read the full article in its original format on their website. You have probably noticed it on a hot summer day: A basement feels cool even when the air outside is baking. The ground does not heat up and cool down as fast as the air does. A few hundred feet down, it stays close to the local yearly average all year, which can be around 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 Celsius). In Verona, Wisconsin, the health software company Epic Systems has spent two decades turning that fact into infrastructure. It has drilled roughly 6,100 wells, 300 to 800 feet (90 to 240 meters) deep, that now heat and cool about 40 buildings on its own campus by using the waste heat from a 3.5-megawatt data center. What makes this setup unusual is not that Epic pulls heat out of the ground in winter – ordinary ground-source heat pumps do that in homes across the country. What’s uncommon is that Epic puts heat into the ground in summer and takes it back out months later. That matters more than it sounds because timing is what usually kills the idea of reusing a data center’s heat. Servers make heat every hour of the year. In most of the U.S., buildings need to be heated for only about four months. Piping it straight to nearby buildings works beautifully in February, but solves nothing in July. Storage is the missing piece.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich-— Greater Bay Technology has commissioned the industry's first gigawatt-hour-scale solid-state battery line. At an Oct. 13 ceremony at its Nansha headquarters, the company marked the completion of capacity upgrades for mass production. The line was retrofitted from existing capacity to produce cells classified under the national solid-state battery standard GB/T 48093.1-2026. This marks the world's first solid-state battery to roll off a mass-production line with certification from an authoritative third-party lab, according to Dong Yang, chairman of the China Automotive Power Battery Industry Innovation Alliance. Third-party tests showed the cells lost less than 0.5% of their mass after being punctured and continuously baked for six hours in a 120°C vacuum — meeting the national standard GB/T 48093.1-2026 issued in late August. That makes Greater Bay Technology the first company to clear testing under the new benchmark. The first solid-state cells roll off the line. (Image credit: Greater Bay Technology) The cells also passed every safety test under the upcoming GB 38031-2025 standard, which takes effect July 1, 2026. In a nail-penetration test, a steel needle pierced the fully charged cell without triggering a fire or explosion, and the structure remained intact. On the performance front, the batteries use a deep-eutectic-based composite solid electrolyte. Specific energy ranges from 260 to 480 Wh/kg, while cycle life matches conventional cells and supports stable fast charging. Drawing on state-backed R&D, Greater Bay Technology retrofitted and optimized portions of an existing 4 GWh liquid lithium battery line. By upgrading rather than building a heavy-asset plant from scratch, the company bridged the manufacturing gap from liquid to all-solid-state — while retaining the ability to flexibly switch between the two formats. After A-sample cells rolled off the line in April, the gigawatt-hour-scale line was upgraded and commissioned just six months later. At the ceremony, Greater Bay Technology also signed strategic pacts with the Shenzhen Vertical Take-Off and Landing Aircraft Innovation Center and Hubei Liming Lithium Industry. The deals aim to speed up the deployment of solid-state batteries across multiple applications — from electric vehicles and the low-altitude economy to embodied robots and premium energy storage.
