artigo.texto: CATL expands Seres battery capacity: what it means for Contemporary Amperex Technology stock Published on 10/13/2026 at 09:01 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Key points in brief - CATL agreed with Seres on October 11, 2026, to expand dedicated battery capacity to more than 20 GWh annually. - The October 11 agreement adds 10 to 12 GWh of annual pack capacity at Seres' Chongqing plant. - Second-quarter 2026 revenue reached CNY 147.8 billion, while net income was CNY 22.5 billion. - The Shenzhen quote was CNY 288.71 on October 13, 2026, 1.24 percent above the 52-week low. Contemporary Amperex Technology stock was quoted at CNY 288.71 on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on October 13, 2026 at 2:45 p.m. CST, as CATL expanded its battery partnership with Seres. The October 11 agreement adds 10 to 12 gigawatt-hours of annual pack capacity and takes dedicated capacity at Seres' Chongqing plant above 20 gigawatt-hours, according to East Asia Brief on October 11, 2026. What 20 GWh means for CATL The Seres project places CATL battery assembly directly inside the vehicle plant. The expansion adds 10 to 12 GWh of annual pack capacity, while the agreement gives CATL a five-year supply framework running through August 2027, East Asia Brief reported. The operating model also locks CATL into Seres' Aito vehicle range, whose cumulative deliveries equipped with CATL batteries have exceeded 1.2 million units, according to the same October 11 report. For CATL, the value is production visibility rather than a disclosed order amount because the companies did not publish construction costs or a commissioning date. Recent results show scale CATL reported CNY 147.8 billion of revenue and CNY 22.5 billion of net income for the second quarter of 2026. Revenue rose 57 percent from CNY 94.2 billion in the second quarter of 2025, while net income increased 37 percent from CNY 16.5 billion, according to Simply Wall St. The comparison also shows the pressure behind the capacity push: second-quarter profit growth trailed revenue growth by 20 percentage points. Simply Wall St reported that the second-quarter profit margin was 15 percent, down from 18 percent a year earlier, while earnings per share exceeded analyst expectations by 2.1 percent. Three dated operating milestones On July 25, 2026, CATL reported second-quarter revenue of CNY 147.8 billion and net income of CNY 22.5 billion. On September 22, 2026, its Debrecen factory began trial production after the company had produced 537,000 battery modules at the site. On October 11, 2026, the Seres agreement lifted the Chongqing plant's planned dedicated capacity above 20 GWh, with each event covered by Simply Wall St and East Asia Brief. Next results come into view CATL's board is scheduled to meet on October 20, 2026, to consider third-quarter results for the nine months ended September 30, according to Futubull. The company is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results on October 21, 2026, according to Simply Wall St. Stock stays near its yearly low The Shenzhen quote of CNY 288.71 on October 13, 2026 stood 1.24 percent above the 52-week low of CNY 285.17 and 38.33 percent below the 52-week high of CNY 468.75. CATL's market capitalization was CNY 1.3 trillion on that date, giving the Seres expansion a market setting defined by scale and a wide distance from the yearly high. The continuously updated company information is available through the Market report Shanghai Composite. artigo.texto: by Wedan Emmanuel Gnibga & Andrew A. Chien Datacenter (DC) power demand is rapidly growing to support AI workloads. With increasing pressure to reduce water consumption, DC cooling power can be up to 30% overall DC power, reducing IT power capacity. Cooling is especially power-demanding during hot periods, which often coincide with peak grid loads and insufficient renewable generation, increasing costs and carbon emissions. Exacerbating the problem is growing compute power density. Rack power densities have grown from under 20kW (2010) to more than 120kW (today), and could reach 1MW (2029). Conversely, cooling and power distribution are not scaling in density, so their space use grows in proportion. This limits DC scalability and lifetime. We explore the benefits of augmenting DC cooling with cold Underground Thermal Energy Systems (Cold UTES), a technology with no water consumption, well-suited to water-stressed regions. Cold UTES can store thermal energy in underground formations (e.g., natural reservoir or shallow rock) during off-peak times and release it to cool DCs during peak periods. Results show this can increase IT capacity by 9.8% across regions, and improve cooling power efficiency, reducing on-peak power use (e.g., 44.4% in Texas), operational carbon emissions (e.g., 10.4% in Arizona), and cooling costs (e.g., 3.4% in Arizona). Cold UTES can improve DC scalability, extending DC lifetime from one to three generations (2 to 6 years).

artigo.texto: Solidion Technology Reaffirms Commitment to Address Growing Energy Storage Needs of AI Data Centers Solidion's patented anode technology and PEAK UPS design target the space, lifespan and cost demands of AI-scale infrastructure. DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion's approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company's strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion's portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. "AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage," said Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion. "Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs." Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users. About Solidion Technology, Inc. Headquartered in Dallas, Texas with pilot production facilities in Dayton, Ohio, Solidion's (NASDAQ: STI) core business includes manufacturing of battery materials and components, as well as development and production of next-generation batteries for energy storage systems, including UPS systems serving the artificial intelligence (AI) data center market and electric vehicles for ground, aerospace, and sea transportation. Solidion holds a portfolio of over 385 patents, covering innovations such as high-capacity, silane gas free and graphene-enabled silicon anodes, biomass-based graphite, advanced lithium-sulfur and lithium-metal technologies. For more information, please visit www.solidiontech.com or contact Investor Relations. artigo.texto: How one city balances its economy and community needs on data centers Colorado Springs, Colorado wants to bring in data centers but do so in a way that’s transparent and protects quality of life. Being proactive is crucial, an economic development leader there said. In a rare move earlier this year, data center operator and developer Raeden published a website looking to dispel various concerns and “misinformation and disinformation” around a project it’s building in Colorado Springs, Colorado. Known as Project Taurus, the website promises the 50-megawatt data center on the site of a former Intel chip factory will use zero gallons of water each day for cooling, operate more quietly than the previous tenant and generate more than $3 million a year in tax revenue. The effort has not been without controversy. The Colorado Springs City Council voted last month to postpone a decision granting the project final approval until April after a contentious public hearing. But local officials said that while the approval process has been tricky, it demonstrates that Colorado Springs is trying to strike the right balance between encouraging data centers to power artificial intelligence while respecting the views of residents who may be opposed to them. Data centers are a controversial subject in communities across the country, but being transparent and getting promises from developers before they build are crucial ways to protect their constituents. “The concerns about water and power and noise are not a reason to say no; they really are conditions to say yes,” Johnna Reeder Kleymeyer, president and CEO of the Colorado Springs Chamber and Economic Development Corporation. “The way we have approached it as a community is to work to get in front of these questions.” Using former industrial sites for new data centers is a key part of Colorado Springs’ strategy, Reeder Kleymeyer said, as those sites are already zoned for industrial uses and would likely not be good candidates for anything else. The Environmental Protection Agency has already assembled information on how to reuse those brownfield sites for data centers, and it’s something Colorado Springs continues to explore. Beyond that, the city is already looking to get ahead of various concerns around power and water use. The city’s utility company, Colorado Springs Utilities, was the first in the state to put a tariff on large loads, meaning that the user pays for all the infrastructure and the power itself, without passing those costs on to residents. The House of Representatives passed a bill last month known as the Ratepayer Protection Act, designed to require states to have a strategy to have large operators pay for their own power, but it appears to be languishing in the U.S. Senate. That puts the onus on states and communities to do the work themselves, like in Colorado Springs. The city also is requiring data centers to use closed-loop water systems, meaning that water is recycled rather than putting a drain on limited water resources. Reeder Kleymeyer said it’s important for the city to be “getting in front of the issues and ensuring we are protecting the residents,” while at the same time showing it is “open for business.” Similar initiatives are set to follow in noise monitoring, which so far does not have a requirement in the city’s unified development code. Reeder Kleymeyer said Project Taurus has already agreed to monitor its noise and put up a surety bond of $1 million if they break those parameters, so they would be required to pay a penalty if they do not comply. While some data center operators have failed to be good neighbors and so stoked community anxiety, Reeder Kleymeyer said it’s incumbent on lawmakers and other senior leaders to hold their feet to the fire. And financial incentives, which have been preferred by many over the years, are not the way. “I think some data centers have earned that reason that communities are skeptical,” she said. “Not everyone has been a good player in the industry, and I think that's why it's important that people that live in the community, such as myself with an economic development organization or elected officials, we ask the questions, we get things in writing, and we make data-driven decisions, not based on emotion.” It would be “naïve” to not have data centers given the growth in AI and technology, Reeder Kleymeyer said. And it’s especially important for Colorado Springs, given its national security and military importance, to have its data housed on these shores and not elsewhere. She said that states and localities that take the time now to have forward-looking and proactive policies in place will benefit the most from data centers. “‘Never’ is not a strategy,” Reeder Kleymeyer said. “The communities that set strong terms, they're going to win for the next generation of employers. That's what we've got to be thinking about for the next 12 months to 10 years.”

artigo.texto: A Nov. 18 community forum has been set for Russell County residents who want to know more about the three or four data centers planned for the former Moss No. 3 coal mine site near Cleveland. Oasis Digital Properties, the Northern Virginia-based data center developer behind the project, will hold the forum in the conference room at the county government center at 139 Highland Drive in Lebanon, Laura Gilmer, director of the county’s industrial development authority, said in a phone interview. Ross Litkenhous, co-founder of Oasis, said the company is still working on the agenda, but the plan is to have a presentation on anything Oasis has done to date and answer questions from the community. He said he will also commit to appear before the community again before any construction begins. “We’re still very early in the process. We’re not ready to put shovels in the ground,” he said in a phone interview. “This is not a presentation where we say we’re ready to break ground tomorrow… we want to listen to them before we get to the point.” Three or four data centers could be coming to the site, a historic coal mine that was recently the site for a proposed landfill. That project was eventually rejected by county leaders, and now the data center campus is on the table as part of a deal between Oasis and the IDA. The agreement says the authority retains control of the property while Oasis takes the next steps to develop it, Litkenhous told Cardinal News. That development is contingent on finding companies to occupy the buildings. Russell County IDA members and other county officials have not answered questions about the project, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Oasis. The IDA denied a Freedom of Information Act request for documents and communications related to the project sent by Cardinal News, citing the agreement and exemptions under Virginia Code. Litkenhous said the IDA asked his team members if they would be willing to come down to share more about the project. Gilmer declined to comment further on the project but reiterated what she said at last week’s IDA meeting. “We were questioned about the details, and it really is, we can’t confirm details because they’re not there yet,” she said. “It’s not a project that’s finalized.” Litkenhous said there are no major updates on the project, and the developer is still working to match with companies that would occupy the buildings. “I hope by the time we get to the November meeting, we will have more substantive updates,” he said. “We understand this is a big deal for the community.” Since learning about the plans for the data center, some county residents have spoken out against the project. A protest is planned for Saturday, following the first held on Oct. 3. On that day, 10 people stood at the corner of Church Avenue and Main Street in Lebanon, holding signs and asking those driving by to sign a petition opposing the project. “No data centers in Russell County … NDAs do not belong in our local government. We have a right to know what’s going on at Moss 3,” Donna Ball, a resident of Cleveland, said through her megaphone. She asked questions at the last county board of supervisors meeting and did not get a response, she said. She was also part of a group of 12 who attended the IDA’s meeting last week and spoke against the project. The group cited concern over the potential impact on the Clinch River, whether there would be noise that would disturb the peace near Cleveland, the use of nondisclosure agreements and low tax rates set by the county. Russell County passed a machinery and tool tax in December 2025 at 24 cents per $100 of assessed value, an incentive to encourage development. “If you’re going to do it, do it to the best of [your] ability,” Amy Branson, a pharmacist from Castlewood, told the IDA. She encouraged its members to pursue an aggressive agreement, including a “fair tax rate,” and prepare for the power demand to ensure the cost doesn’t fall on residents. Litkenhous said Appalachian Power has untapped electricity capacity and confirmed it could provide 300 megawatts to the site. Residents brought up the bad taste they still have from past large land projects, including the failed landfill proposal and the fish farm project on the Russell-Tazewell County border that has been paused due to tariffs and gas prices. But some also noted appreciation for getting to have a back-and-forth with the IDA and said they understand the county budget is strained and solutions are needed. Still, as they heard plans for the community forum, Betsy Dickenson, a resident from Cleveland, said, “This sounds like what we went through with the trash dump.”

artigo.texto: Intelligent Flow Measurement Has Become Essential for Next-Generation Data Center Cooling As AI workloads drive higher rack densities and greater thermal demands, data center liquid cooling is becoming an increasingly important part of modern facility design. But moving from traditional air cooling to liquid-based architectures also creates a greater need to understand exactly what is happening inside critical cooling loops. This Ask the Expert explains why flow measurement for data centers is becoming essential to cooling performance, efficiency, and uptime. It explores how chilled water flow monitoring, combined with temperature and other operational data, can provide greater visibility into cooling system performance and help operators make more informed decisions about energy and water use. The discussion also examines magnetic flow meters, which are ideally suited for many liquid cooling applications and can deliver accurate measurements without introducing pressure loss. It provides insight into installation considerations, commissioning challenges, piping constraints, and the importance of measurement accuracy and repeatability as facilities scale. For teams designing, building, or operating next-generation infrastructure, understanding the role of flow measurement is becoming an important part of optimizing the cooling systems that support high-density computing. Discover how flow data can support both building management systems and data center infrastructure management (DCIM) platforms, providing greater visibility across increasingly complex AI data center cooling environments.

artigo.texto: Data centers may soon require special-use permits to build in Lawrence after a vote by the Lawrence-Douglas County Planning Commission on Sept. 21. The commission voted 6-1 to recommend that the Lawrence City Commission require that developers receive a special-use permit before building data centers in industrial zoning districts within city limits. The Lawrence City Commission voted on July 14 to pass a two-year moratorium on data center development. Drew Bealby, a city planner, told planning commissioners that, in addition to restricting data center construction, the moratorium directed planning staff to research data centers and gave them time to write policies, such as special-use permit requirements, to regulate data centers once it’s over. City commissioners will review the research before considering a ban. Previously, the development code allowed data center development without review by the planning or city commissions. For a special-use permit, projects must be presented to both commissions. The approval process allows commissioners to set approval conditions and consider potential impacts on surrounding neighborhoods. It also requires public comment. “I think we have terrifically bright people [in Lawrence], if we will just listen to you,” Commissioner Charlie Thomas said in an interview with the Kansan. “And any time we cut the people out of the process, I think we have done a disservice to any regulations that we write, so this will give people many chances to have input, and that’s what we need.” This change would require a special-use permit for data center development in Lawrence’s industrial districts, in addition to the mixed corridor and commercial center districts, which already require a special-use permit for data centers. Bealby said this change will not affect the moratorium overall. Instead, commissioners may approve a moratorium exception for data center projects approved for a special-use permit on a case-by-case basis. Data centers that are powering artificial intelligence’s growth are an issue for American communities. These issues prompted 17 members of the public to voice their concerns to the commission. Most supported a complete ban, carrying signs that said “full ban now,” “we need water” and “listen to your people.” Many told the commission that the proposed changes aren’t restrictive enough. Some described how a data center would affect local water, electricity and agriculture; others spoke about AI's growing power and its potential use in military and surveillance operations. One public commenter, Jeremy Rothe-Kushel, co-host of the podcast “The Antedote,” compared AI and data centers to nuclear weapons and nuclear weapons sites. He said U.S. adversaries may soon treat AI as a weapon and, therefore, treat data centers as military targets. “I hope we don’t go there as a world,” Rothe-Kushel said. “But we do not yet have international law, let alone treaties, like we did in terms of nuclear weapons, yet.” Rothe-Kushel said in an interview with the Kansan that data centers aren’t always bad for a community, but Lawrence needs to study how to scale and site them properly and design them with minimal ecological impacts. Dominique Sexton, member of the Coalition for Collaborative Governance, said AI will negatively impact American society and already affects children’s lives. “I mean, we don’t even understand the consequences of AI with data centers,” Sexton said in an interview with the Kansan. “We see it tied to the military-industrial complex. We see it tied to ICE in the way that it’s dehumanizing our neighbors. And these are all consequences that these young kids are growing up [with] as their normal experience. And I just worry so much about that.” Commissioner Gary Rexroad voted against the special-permit measure, arguing that the restrictions would be too broad and only large data centers should be restricted. He said he worried the measure would create an undue burden on businesses’ small data centers that handle business functions. “I really feel like this application in front of us tonight is immature,” Rexroad said. Commissioner Jane Eldredge said the measure will “provide the opportunity to learn what we need to regulate, what we don’t need to regulate.” Bealby said businesses’ small data centers used for their own operations are considered a secondary use of the property. Therefore, they will likely be exempted from the moratorium. Thomas said he knows a data center when he sees it, and waiting longer to pass restrictions is risky. “The unintended consequences of not doing this tonight, of not approving this, I think places this community more at risk,” Thomas said. This article was edited by Head News Editor Marissa Buffon. If the information in this article needs to be corrected, please contact marissa.buffon@ku.edu.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de carregadores de bateria industriais: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de carregadores de bateria industriais até 2035: implantação de BESS em escala de rede e eletrificação de veículos pesados impulsionam o crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Carregadores de Bateria Industriais, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de carregadores de bateria industriais é um habilitador essencial da transição energética, fornecendo a base de conversão de energia para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em escala de rede e para a eletrificação industrial pesada. Diferentemente dos carregadores de consumo, os carregadores industriais precisam gerenciar conversão CA/CC de alta potência, conformidade com códigos de rede e certificação de segurança, o que os torna componentes de alto valor incorporados a projetos de energia financiáveis. A demanda está se bifurcando: carregadores padronizados e otimizados em custo para BESS em contêineres, de um lado, e sistemas personalizados e ricos em recursos para suporte à rede e ambientes industriais severos, de outro. O cenário competitivo opõe gigantes diversificados da eletrônica de potência a fabricantes especializados com profunda engenharia de aplicação. As compras são dominadas por compradores sofisticados — integradores de BESS, empresas de EPC e concessionárias de energia —, que priorizam o custo total de propriedade e o serviço de longo prazo em vez do preço inicial. A resiliência da cadeia de suprimentos, especialmente para semicondutores de SiC/GaN e componentes magnéticos, continua sendo uma preocupação central. Estruturas regulatórias e códigos de rede são os principais indutores de produto, exigindo funcionalidades avançadas como suportabilidade a afundamentos de tensão e regulação de frequência. À medida que o mercado evolui até 2035, os carregadores se tornarão ativos inteligentes na borda da rede, com controles definidos por software que viabilizam a gestão ativa da rede. Este relatório oferece uma análise estruturada do tamanho de mercado, da segmentação, dos indutores de demanda, da dinâmica competitiva e das perspectivas regionais, com insights acionáveis para fabricantes, integradores, investidores e formuladores de políticas que navegam por esse cenário em rápida evolução. O cenário-base para o mercado de carregadores de bateria industriais até 2035 prevê expansão robusta, sustentada pela implantação acelerada de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em escala de rede e pela eletrificação do transporte pesado e de processos industriais. Com o avanço da participação de energias renováveis, a necessidade de infraestrutura de recarga flexível e compatível com a rede torna-se primordial, impulsionando a demanda por carregadores avançados capazes de fluxo bidirecional de energia, recursos de formação de rede e integração perfeita com sistemas de gestão de energia. Espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de 8,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 220 (2025=100). Esse crescimento não é apenas volumétrico; reflete uma mudança em direção a carregadores de maior valor, definidos por software, que atuam como ativos inteligentes na borda da rede. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico continuará sendo o maior mercado, impulsionada pelo domínio da China na fabricação e implantação de BESS, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão forte crescimento, apoiadas por incentivos de política pública e iniciativas de modernização da rede. América Latina e Oriente Médio e África surgirão como mercados de oportunidade, ainda que a partir de uma base menor. Os principais riscos incluem gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos de semicondutores especializados, atrasos regulatórios e a possibilidade de mudanças tecnológicas que perturbem as arquiteturas de produto estabelecidas. Ainda assim, a trajetória de longo prazo permanece positiva, com os carregadores sendo cada vez mais vistos como componentes estratégicos da transição energética. Indutores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Indutores de Demanda - Expansão acelerada das implantações de BESS em escala de rede para integrar energias renováveis e aumentar a estabilidade da rede. - Eletrificação de veículos pesados (ônibus, caminhões, equipamentos portuários), que exige carregadores industriais de alta potência. - Códigos de rede rigorosos que exigem funcionalidades avançadas como suportabilidade a afundamentos de tensão, regulação de frequência e capacidade de formação de rede. - Crescimento dos investimentos industriais em resiliência, com energia de reserva e microrredes, especialmente em operações remotas ou críticas. - Queda dos custos da eletrônica de potência e das baterias, melhorando a economia dos projetos de infraestrutura de recarga industrial. - Incentivos governamentais e metas de descarbonização que promovem o armazenamento de energia e a mobilidade elétrica. Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos de semicondutores especializados de alta potência (SiC/GaN) e componentes magnéticos, gerando volatilidade nos prazos de entrega. - Custos iniciais elevados e processos complexos de qualificação, sobretudo para conformidade com códigos de rede e certificação de segurança. - Falta de protocolos padronizados e de interoperabilidade entre diferentes arquiteturas de BESS e de carregadores, o que aumenta a complexidade de integração. - Escassez de mão de obra de engenharia com experti

artigo.texto: After over a year and a half since a $6 billion data center proposal arrived on Oldham County’s doorstep, the Oldham County Fiscal Court approved an ordinance establishing regulations on data centers on Oct. 6 in an 8-1 vote, Magistrate Michael Logsdon opposed. As previously reported, the regulations were made stricter in early September, effectively proposing to limit all data center developments to a maximum power capacity of 10 megawatts and capping total square footage for data center facilities to 110,000 square feet. That, alongside the previously proposed 1,000-foot setback from all residential property and 1,500 from adjoining school properties, effectively bans hyperscale data centers from the county for the time being, according to Judge Executive David Voegele. “We have designed a bill here where there is no place in this county that will fit … There is no place in this county where a data center will fit right now. It doesn’t mean that in the future it won’t fit somewhere if some other group of people sitting here decides that it’s appropriate,” Voegele said. During the public hearing for the ordinance, some residents expressed concerns regarding the language of the regulations as well as the process leading up to their approval. Sarah Little of La Grange raised concerns regarding the process of approval, specifically questioning if state law requires the regulations to be approved by the Planning and Zoning Commission again, since they were first denied by the court on Aug. 18. Kentucky Revised Statutes 100.211(3) reads: “A proposal to amend the text of any zoning regulation which must be voted upon by the legislative body or fiscal court may originate with the planning commission of the unit or with any fiscal court or legislative body which is a member of the unit. “Regardless of the origin of the proposed amendment, it shall be referred to the planning commission before adoption.” When Voegele asked County Attorney D. Berry Baxter if he would agree that the regulations “are on solid ground” to be considered, Baxter said: “We wouldn’t be here if we were not on solid ground, and that’s what our research has indicated.” Little also noted that the ordinance number — a number used to keep record of each ordinance the court passes — has changed since the Planning and Zoning Commission recommended approval in June. “I want to be wrong on this ...” Little continued. “I do want to make sure that all of those ordinance number changes are addressed so that we know what went in front of the planning commission is what you guys are considering because if it’s not, it will get overturned in court.” Amanda Dreckman of Crestwood told the court she was concerned about loopholes in the regulations, and that simply removing sections regarding “large” or “hyperscale” data centers doesn’t actually ban them. Specifically, in the definition of “medium” data centers, Dreckman pointed out that it states that only “one or more of the following criteria” must be met — e.g. either megawatt capacity or square footage — not “all” criteria, which may allow a data center development to exceed one limit if it meets another. After some discussion on possible edits, Magistrate Kevin Jeffries said that changing the ordinance too extensively could force the court to have to host another first reading, delaying the regulations’ approval further. “With this regulation going forward, whatever administration is in play or planning director is going to have to continue to monitor this,” said Planning and Development Director Ryan Fischer. “This technology is so evolving that this can’t be an ordinance that you all stick on the shelf and go, ‘good job, we have data center regulations.’ Some of the comments are correct. This is going to have to continue to be monitored as the technology changes, as the federal government continues to get involved … That’s going to be a job for all of you going forward.” Other court actions In other news, The court also conducted a second reading for a zoning change at 2616 Singleton Lane, ultimately approving Greg and Shelby Biddle’s request to change the nearly 41-acre property’s zoning form heavy industrial to agricultural. As previously reported, the Biddle’s are currently building a single-family home on the property, but want to build an accessory-dwelling unit for Greg Biddle’s father, but only one residential building is permitted per heavy industrial lot. Before final approval of the ADU, Board of Adjustments approval is required. The court also conducted a first reading on a zoning change for Sugar Babes Antiques, located at 7511 Highway 329, which is proposed to go from “C-2,” community business district, to “C-3” general business district to become the new home of woodworking company Straight Grain LLC. The second reading of the zoning change is scheduled for Oct. 20. The court also heard a presentation from Oldham County Health Department Director Matt Rhodes, which included the Board of Health’s property tax rate for this year, which is set at 2.5 cents per $100 of assessed value, which Rhodes said has stayed the same for the last decade. Rhodes said the rate expects to generate over $2.6 million in revenue. After its expenses, the health department expects to have $211,233 left over. The court also opened three bids for a pavement reconstruction project at the county recycling center. Louisville Paving’s low bid of $156,000 was chosen by unanimous vote. The court also opened bids for road salt, but only received one bidder: Morton Salt, who supplied the county’s salt last year. The bid of $110.76 per ton of salt — a roughly $13 increase from last year — was chosen by unanimous vote. The county plans to purchase 3,000 tons of road salt, which is 500 tons more than last year. artigo.texto: Por que baterias portáteis podem pegar fogo em aviões? Entenda os riscos após caso na Índia Incêndio em carregador externo levou avião da IndiGo a fazer pouso de emergência na Índia; baterias de lítio podem sofrer superaquecimento e provocar chamas intensas Por O Globo — Nova Deli Atualizado Um voo da companhia aérea indiana IndiGo precisou ser desviado para Hyderabad, na Índia, neste domingo (11), depois que uma bateria portátil pegou fogo dentro da cabine. O dispositivo estava guardado em uma bagagem no compartimento superior do avião, que seguia de Delhi para Chennai. A tripulação conseguiu controlar as chamas com extintores, e a aeronave pousou em segurança. Segundo a companhia, o voo 6E 6115 foi desviado após a detecção de fumaça proveniente do dispositivo eletrônico de um passageiro. Os passageiros desembarcaram em Hyderabad e seguiram viagem em outra aeronave. Veja o momento: O que faz uma bateria portátil pegar fogo? Os carregadores portáteis, conhecidos como power banks, utilizam baterias de íons de lítio, que armazenam grande quantidade de energia em pouco espaço. Quando danificadas, superaquecidas ou submetidas a falhas internas, essas baterias podem entrar em um processo chamado fuga térmica, no qual a temperatura aumenta rapidamente e desencadeia uma reação em cadeia. O fenômeno pode provocar chamas intensas, fumaça e liberação de gases tóxicos, dificultando o combate ao incêndio. Quais são as regras para transportar carregadores em aviões? As regras variam conforme o país e a companhia aérea. No Reino Unido, a Autoridade de Aviação Civil (CAA) estabeleceu, a partir de 27 de março de 2026, novas exigências para o transporte de baterias de lítio e carregadores portáteis. Pelas orientações do órgão, os dispositivos devem permanecer na bagagem de mão, protegidos individualmente quando não estiverem em uso. Também não devem ser recarregados a bordo nem utilizados para carregar outros aparelhos durante o voo. O limite estabelecido é de dois carregadores por passageiro. O caso na Índia ocorre após outro incidente semelhante no mês passado, quando um voo que partia da Holanda em direção ao Caribe precisou retornar após suspeita de incêndio envolvendo uma bateria portátil. Os episódios reforçam a importância de seguir as regras de segurança e verificar as restrições específicas da companhia aérea antes de embarcar.

artigo.texto: Solidion Technology Reaffirms Commitment to Address Growing Energy Storage Needs of AI Data Centers Solidion's patented anode technology and PEAK UPS design target the space, lifespan and cost demands of AI-scale infrastructure. DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (STI) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion's approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company's strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion's portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. "AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage," said Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion. "Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs." Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users. About Solidion Technology, Inc. Headquartered in Dallas, Texas with pilot production facilities in Dayton, Ohio, Solidion's (STI) core business includes manufacturing of battery materials and components, as well as development and production of next-generation batteries for energy storage systems, including UPS systems serving the artificial intelligence (AI) data center market and electric vehicles for ground, aerospace, and sea transportation. Solidion holds a portfolio of over 385 patents, covering innovations such as high-capacity, silane gas free and graphene-enabled silicon anodes, biomass-based graphite, advanced lithium-sulfur and lithium-metal technologies. For more information, please visit www.solidiontech.com or contact Investor Relations. artigo.texto: CARLOS MASTRANGELO APONTA DISPUTA POR EQUIPAMENTOS COM DATA CENTERS E ADOÇÃO DE NOVAS TECNOLOGIAS COMO DESAFIOS DO MERCADO DE FPSOs Considerado um dos pioneiros na disseminação mundial do uso de plataformas do tipo FPSO, Carlos Mastrangelo escreveu, em parceria com o também experiente executivo Jorge Mitidieri, o livro “FPSO: Legado Offshore”. A obra aborda desde as escolhas técnicas que moldaram o mercado de navios-plataformas até os atuais desafios operacionais e as tendências futuras. Em entrevista ao Petronotícias, Mastrangelo analisou os fatores que pressionam o mercado de unidades de produção offshore, como a disputa por equipamentos com setores como os de data centers e aviação, e as incertezas que afetam as decisões de investimento em projetos de petróleo e gás. O executivo também discutiu os impactos da adoção de novas tecnologias, como a inteligência artificial, e defendeu o planejamento de longo prazo e a atuação do governo para evitar sobrecargas na cadeia brasileira de fornecedores e ampliar a participação nacional nos projetos. Qual foi a proposta da obra e por que considera importante olhar para o passado ao pensar no futuro da indústria? O título FPSO: Legado Offshore pode dar a impressão de que se trata de um livro de história, voltado ao passado. No entanto, essa não é a proposta. A obra busca compreender o presente com base nos acontecimentos anteriores, de modo a projetar o futuro. A palavra “legado” está relacionada justamente ao que deixamos para as próximas gerações, oferecendo referências para que possam pensar no futuro. Para projetar o futuro, seja na vida pessoal ou nas empresas, é preciso conhecer o passado. As histórias se repetem e, infelizmente, os erros também. O livro aborda diversos aspectos dessa relação, incluindo a influência da inteligência artificial nos projetos. Por exemplo: existe um discurso politicamente alinhado de que a IA contribuirá para reduzir o número de pessoas a bordo e substituir atividades realizadas no mar. Essa redução de pessoal se concretizou em outras etapas da evolução tecnológica? No livro, fazemos um regaste histórico do que aconteceu na indústria ao longo dos anos. No início da década de 1990, surgiram as primeiras unidades com sistemas digitais no Brasil, enquanto essa transformação também começava a ocorrer em outras partes do mundo. Os computadores passaram a permitir a substituição dos sinais mecânicos de pressão por sinais elétricos, por exemplo. A expectativa inicial era simplificar os processos e aumentar a eficiência na leitura dos dados de campo. Imaginava-se que, no futuro, seria possível reduzir o número de pessoas a bordo. Ao longo do tempo, porém, embora o perfil do trabalhador embarcado tenha mudado, também houve uma tendência de aumento do efetivo a bordo, por diversos outros motivos. O livro aborda essa questão em detalhes. Inicialmente, o uso de IA pode demandar um acréscimo de demanda de atividades que hoje são executadas por pessoas que já trabalham a bordo das plataformas. Portanto, existe uma preocupação de que aconteça o mesmo que ocorreu no passado: estressar as unidades de produção por conta das novas demandas. Em síntese, a proposta da obra é relacionar o presente aos acontecimentos do passado, compreender as reações dos especialistas e abordar diferentes temas, sempre com uma perspectiva voltada também para o futuro. Falando do mercado de maneira geral, quais são hoje os principais desafios do setor que dificultam a chegada de um projeto à decisão final de investimento? A situação é desfavorável porque, de um lado, a cadeia de suprimentos enfrenta preços elevados em um mercado pressionado. Essa pressão decorre não apenas da demanda, mas também da concorrência com projetos de desenvolvimento mais simples. Um exemplo são os grandes data centers, que competem diretamente com os projetos de águas profundas. Esses empreendimentos utilizam as mesmas máquinas de geração de energia empregadas nos grandes FPSOs. Ao mesmo tempo, quem desenvolve um projeto de upstream precisa realizar estudos de viabilidade, avaliar os investimentos e estimar os prazos de retorno, considerando diferentes cenários de rentabilidade futura e a imprevisibilidade natural do negócio. Além das incertezas relacionadas ao reservatório, que são inerentes à atividade, existem as incertezas externas a ele, que também precisam ser consideradas na análise de viabilidade dos projetos. Além dos data centers, que outros setores disputam os mesmos equipamentos? A indústria da aviação também utiliza máquinas que concorrem com as demandadas pelo setor de petróleo e gás. Há ainda a disputa por chips, painéis elétricos e outros equipamentos. Trata-se de uma concorrência que envolve diversos segmentos. As grandes instalações de gás natural liquefeito (GNL), com pacotes de até US$ 20 bilhões, também fazem parte desse cenário de disputa por recursos e equipamentos. Nesse contexto, a cadeia de suprimentos precisa apresentar propostas firmes às operadoras, considerando os preços atuais e as condições de um mercado pressionado. Do outro lado, as operadoras precisam avaliar seus projetos com base nesses custos atuais, mas considerando receitas futuras cujo valor ainda é desconhecido. Falando agora sobre conteúdo local, como a cadeia brasileira de fornecedores pode ampliar sua participação e conquistar novos negócios no contexto atual? artigo.texto: NEW DELHI: India and the European Commission on Monday discussed continuing technical engagement on recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms and auditing (MRV) systems. Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal met with Gerassimos Thomas, Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union, European Commission, in New Delhi, the Power Ministry said in a release. Both sides expressed willingness to continue technical engagement on recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms; monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems; and capacity building. An MRV system is an accounting process that measures climate actions, quantifies GHG emissions, and confirms reductions. The two sides agreed to strengthen cooperation and continue dialogue on carbon markets, CBAM-related methodologies, and other areas of mutual interest. Discussions focused on India's carbon market development, the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and opportunities for enhanced technical cooperation. The secretary highlighted India's progress under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), including notifying emission intensity reduction targets for 490 industrial units and developing the domestic carbon market. He also highlighted India's progress in increasing the share of non-fossil sources in its electricity generation capacity, noting that non-fossil sources account for 308 GW of the country's total installed capacity of 558 GW. The EU side appreciated India's progress in developing its carbon market and shared updates on CBAM implementation. artigo.texto: O que a rede elétrica brasileira precisa para atender grandes data centers? Especialistas apontam como modernizar a gestão do sistema de energia para o aumento exponencial da demanda. Os grandes data centers que devem operar no Brasil, voltados ao processamento de dados de plataformas de redes sociais e inteligência artificial (IA), exigem preparação da rede elétrica. Especialistas defendem a modernização da gestão do sistema para dar conta do consumo desses empreendimentos. A demanda de eletricidade dos data centers deve crescer cerca de 12% ao ano a partir de 2027, segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Com isso, o segmento será o quinto maior consumidor de energia elétrica do País até 2030. Considerando os pedidos de ligação à rede elétrica, os projetos de data centers podem consumir até 10.721 megawatts (MW) em 2029. A demanda também deve dobrar até 2038. Veja também O QUE ESTÁ SENDO FEITO EM OUTROS PAÍSES? O desafio da conexão dos equipamentos é global. No estado de Nova York, por exemplo, o governo suspendeu a construção de novos data centers por preocupações com o impacto no consumo de energia e água. A suspensão vale até julho de 2027 para empreendimentos com potência superior a 50 megawatts. Um dos modelos adotados por empresas nos EUA é a instalação de usinas dedicadas aos data centers, isoladas da rede, explica o líder de mercado e clientes da Siemens Energy, Pedro Matos. A solução, entretanto, é transitória e pode ser menos sustentável. "Como vemos em outros países, a exemplo da Irlanda, onde o pedido de ligação à rede leva cinco anos, as empresas recorrem a uma geração temporária a gás. Quando recebem a ligação, passam a injetar energia renovável na rede", aponta. O executivo participou da Atlantic Convergence, conferência organizada pela DE-CIX que debate o futuro das infraestruturas digitais, em Lisboa. De acordo com ele, o aumento da demanda energética por data centers deve atenuar o desequilíbrio entre a geração e o consumo de energia no Brasil. "Esse equilíbrio é difícil de obter, mas, com mais potencial de consumo, com data centers e outras indústrias, será mais fácil gerir todo o sistema. Há uma oportunidade de ter um sistema ainda mais renovável", comenta. Segundo Matos, o custo da energia no País tende a cair no longo prazo, desde que o Brasil aprimore a gestão dos recursos. "No futuro, a energia será muito barata. O que pagaremos é a flexibilidade, ou seja, a capacidade de nos adaptarmos à quantidade de energia disponível naquele momento", diz. ACESSO PRIORITÁRIO À REDE ELÉTRICA NO BRASIL O acesso de data centers à rede de energia é viabilizado pela Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (PNAST). Na prática, o Ministério de Minas e Energia dará prioridade a empreendimentos considerados estratégicos. Segundo a pasta, o objetivo é fortalecer o planejamento do setor elétrico, ampliar a segurança do sistema e criar condições para que o País não perca investimentos no setor. No cálculo da capacidade disponível, o Operador Nacional do Sistema (ONS) determina o máximo valor de potência ativa que o sistema é capaz de transportar, sem apresentar violações de tensão ou fluxo de potência na região em análise, em condições normais de operação e em situações de contingência. A primeira temporada de acesso, encerrada no início de outubro, teve 367 cadastramentos de empreendimentos de geração e consumo, totalizando mais de 20 GW em solicitações. Considerando também o período transitório, o ONS analisou mais de 43 GW em pedidos de acesso à rede básica. Foram viabilizados ou habilitados 30,7 GW. INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL NA GESTÃO DE GRANDES CARGAS Ao modernizar a gestão do sistema elétrico, o ONS pode adotar ferramentas de inteligência artificial para melhorar a previsão de consumo e oferta de energia no País. "A IA ajuda a perceber quanto vai ser a demanda, a procura. Assim, começa-se a equilibrar e a entender quando é possível produzir mais para consumir mais", explica o diretor da Greenvolt, Filipe de Oliveira Lopes. Os modelos matemáticos também podem auxiliar na definição de locais para projetos de usinas renováveis e de equipamentos eletrointensivos. "Cada vez mais teremos de nos preocupar com essa questão. No Brasil, sentem-se muito as alterações climáticas. É melhor construir uma central hidrelétrica perto de zonas de cheias, é preciso entender onde vai ter o melhor impacto", comenta. EFEITO NAS COMUNIDADES Para o especialista, ao fazer a conexão de data centers, é importante que os operadores também pensem na qualidade de conexão das comunidades no entorno. Ou seja, em um ambiente adequado de instalação, as cidades próximas aos data centers não podem ter o acesso à energia prejudicado, mas sim aprimorado. "A parte social é importante. É preciso entender o data center não só em termos econômicos. Os empreendimentos podem trazer know-how para o País, gerar emprego e ajudar a gerir a energia da rede", afirma. *A colunista viajou a convite da DE-CIX para a Atlantic Convergence em Lisboa.

artigo.texto: ST. GEORGE, Utah — For decades, small data centers have quietly served as the physical backbone of the internet. But new, large-scale data centers meant to support artificial intelligence are sizing up significantly — and there’s been a corresponding increase in public scrutiny and concern about an industry long used to operating behind the scenes. WATCH | Massive Utah data centers draw scrutiny, but smaller ones have existed for years "There are quite a few already operating in Utah,” noted Shon Hiatt, a University of Southern California professor who has studied the state's data center landscape. But, he added, “the trend moving forward is bigger, larger data centers.” Utah currently has at least 48 operational data centers, according to Hiatt’s recent report for the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute. But another seven under construction will use more energy than all those that currently exist in the state combined, the report notes. Pete Ashdown, president and founder of XMission, has operated a small data center in the heart of downtown Salt Lake City for more than 25 years. He stresses that there are “two different stories” when it comes to these facilities. “It’s the traditional data centers that handles your email, handles your webpages, that have been around for decades,” Ashdown said. “And then there’s this new style of data center.” The new hyperscale data centers have sprung up largely to support the recent boom in artificial intelligence and the corresponding surge in demand for computing and processing power. “Around the time Chat GPT came out — 2022, 2023 — that was a game changer because then it started an AI race, basically,” said Bob West, the vice president of marketing for ValorC3, which operates a small data center in St. George. “And with that, it caught the data center industry kind of off guard,” he added. “There wasn't enough capacity, and people started building data centers like crazy.” That construction craze has sparked intense bipartisan blowback across the United States in recent months, with polls showing a majority of Utahns are now opposed to new data centers. Nearly 76% of respondents in a Utah State University survey released last week said they oppose or strongly oppose building new data centers in the state. And 90% said they see the amount of water a project consumes as “very important” in determining whether they would support or oppose a particular project. Hiatt said he believes the opposition also reflects broader fears about the future of artificial intelligence. "What does it mean for society? What does it mean for my job?” he said, referencing the questions many people are asking as the technology rapidly advances. “And because of that, there's this anti, negative sentiment towards AI. And now it's being shifted to the data centers.” 'A lot of misconceptions’ While the phrase “data center” raises the specter of massive, power and energy-hungry campuses with thousands of servers, those in the industry stress that these facilities are not monolithic. “I think there's just a lot of misconceptions about data centers and what we do here,” said West, with ValorC3. “Everybody thinks that, No. 1, there are these huge campuses and data centers are bad. They draw all this power; they take up all this water. And that's just not true.” ValorC3 is a colocation data center, where other businesses rent space for their own servers and hardware. Chris Damrow, the director of facilities management there, describes it as “a hotel for companies’ or individuals’ very expensive computers.” “Really what we do is provide power and cooling for other people’s computers,” he added, noting that the data center’s clients range from health care companies to financial institutions. Colocation centers are different from what have been deemed “hyperscale” data centers. Those are predominantly owned and operated by major technology companies, like Facebook or Amazon, “and they need a very, very big footprint and a lot of power,” Damrow said. WATCH | West, with ValorC3, explains the different types of data centers: ValorC3’s St. George data center has a capacity of about 4 megawatts. That’s several thousand times smaller than the Stratos data center planned for Box Elder County that has dominated headlines in recent months. In thirsty southern Utah, Damrow said ValorC3’s data center is cooled with a direct expansion system, which uses refrigerant rather than water. The trade-off of that system, though, is that it can be more energy-intensive — a resource Damrow said ValorC3 also tries to use judiciously. “If we’re not,” he noted, “we’re losing money.” About 300 miles north, XMission operates a colocation data center with an even smaller footprint than ValorC3's. The Salt Lake City facility has a capacity of just under 1 megawatt and uses a closed-loop cooling system that Ashdown compares to a car radiator. “You’re not continually putting water into your car to cool your car,” he noted. “But the air that flows through the front of your car cools off the entire system of your car. It’s just a matter of moving heat around inside the engine and out to where it can be ejected.” Asked to compare what he calls a “traditional data center” like XMission to the hyperscale ones coming online now, Ashdown argues that the latter have far more “intense” environmental impacts due to their scale. artigo.texto: Clearway Energy Group has announced the addition of 210 MW of battery energy storage capacity to its Honeycomb Energy Center portfolio in southern Utah, supported by long-term agreements with PacifiCorp. The expansion, involving an investment of approximately $400 million, aims to strengthen grid reliability, improve energy flexibility and support growing electricity demand across the region. The additional capacity will support the second phase of the Honeycomb Energy Center development, comprising three new battery energy storage facilities. With this expansion, Clearway’s energy storage portfolio in Utah will increase to seven systems, providing a combined storage capacity of 2,120 MWh. The company commissioned the first four Honeycomb energy storage facilities earlier this year. Each of the new battery storage installations will be located adjacent to an existing Clearway solar power facility operating under a power supply agreement with PacifiCorp. The integration of battery storage with solar generation is expected to improve renewable energy utilisation, support grid stability and provide greater flexibility in managing electricity supply and demand. To finance the approximately $400 million development, Clearway has secured support from a consortium of financial institutions, including KeyBank, U.S. Bank, NordLB and CoBank. Clearway Energy, Inc. has also entered into an agreement to invest in the project following the commencement of commercial operations. Valerie Wooley, Senior Vice President of Origination at Clearway, highlighted the importance of expanding energy storage infrastructure to support Utah’s growing economy. She stated that the additional facilities would contribute to grid resilience and help manage electricity costs as regional power demand continues to increase. The expansion is also expected to generate economic benefits for local communities in Beaver and Iron counties. Clearway has partnered with Rosendin for construction activities, which are expected to create at least 150 jobs. According to the company, the three new Honeycomb Energy Center projects are projected to generate approximately $37 million in additional tax revenue over their operational lifetimes. This will increase the total expected tax contributions from the Honeycomb portfolio to more than $95 million, supporting public services and infrastructure development in the surrounding communities. Clearway will also contribute an additional $60,000 annually to local schools and community organisations, bringing the total annual community contributions from the seven Honeycomb facilities to approximately $100,000. Matt Sterzer, Beaver County Economic Development Manager, acknowledged Clearway Energy’s growing contribution to the region’s energy sector, highlighting the company’s role in attracting investment, creating employment opportunities and generating additional revenue for local communities. The latest development builds on Clearway’s longstanding partnership with PacifiCorp, which has supported the development of approximately 1.4 GW of power projects since 2008. This includes more than 1 GW of capacity in Utah, representing approximately $1.5 billion in investments and establishing the state as one of Clearway’s largest operational markets. The Honeycomb Energy Center expansion reflects the increasing importance of utility-scale battery energy storage systems in supporting renewable energy integration and grid modernisation. By combining solar generation with large-scale battery storage, Clearway aims to enhance power system flexibility, improve electricity supply reliability and support Utah’s evolving energy requirements. The additional 210 MW of battery storage capacity is expected to further strengthen Clearway’s renewable energy infrastructure in the state while contributing to regional economic development and the transition towards a more resilient electricity grid. artigo.texto: Real Assets We build future energy systems and resilient infrastructure, backing emerging opportunities in technology, land and water. Foresight has today announced that Foresight Energy Infrastructure Partners II SCSp (“FEIP II”) has completed its acquisition of a 100% interest in Nivala, a battery energy storage system (“BESS”) from Fotowatio Renewable Ventures. Nivala is Finland’s largest BESS project. Nivala is a fully permitted, ready-to-build battery energy storage system project, with a 100MW/400MWh capacity located in the city of Nivala, in the North Ostrobothnia region of Finland. This investment, which is Foresight’s second in Finland, following the acquisition of Puskakorpi, an 88MW in 2021 via FEIP I, strengthens FEIP II's exposure to energy storage and grid flexibility infrastructure. With a four-hour duration, the battery is designed to participate in Finland's wholesale, intraday and ancillary services markets, a significant revenue driver for Finnish BESS, and help support the integration of renewable generation and the decarbonisation of the Finnish power system. With the acquisition, Foresight will continue to develop the project which is expected to commence commercial operations in the second half of 2028. Finland has emerged as one of the most attractive BESS markets in the Nordics, due to rapid renewable energy growth, particularly in onshore wind. Finland also carries a positive demand side story, acting as a key hub for Europe’s data centre buildout following a recent announcement from Google to invest €13bn in data centres across Finland. Together, these tailwinds increase the need for grid flexibility and BESS. Richard Thompson, Partner and Co-Manager of FEIP & FEIP II at Foresight Group, said: “The energy transition is no longer only about decarbonisation, it is increasingly about maintaining system security, reliability and resilience as electricity demand grows and economies become more electrified. As Finland sees accelerated investment in data centres and new industrial demand, we expect grid-scale battery storage to play an increasingly important role in providing flexibility, supporting grid stability and helping integrate more renewable power onto the system. Project Nivala provides immediate access to this critical infrastructure opportunity.” Javier Huergo, Chief Investment Officer of FRV, noted: “This transaction reflects FRV’s ability to create value throughout the entire development cycle of its projects and successfully execute its asset rotation strategy. The sale of Nivala allows us to crystallise the value generated during the development phases and reinvest those resources in new opportunities that will continue to drive the energy transition and strengthen our international BESS project portfolio”. artigo.texto: EnergyPathways plc (AIM: EPP), a UK-based energy transition firm, has completed a placing raising £1.75 million by issuing shares at 5.75 pence each to a sole institutional investor who requested exclusive participation. This fundraising, initially announced on 28 September 2026, will support the advancement of the company's MESH Long Duration Energy Storage project and provide additional working capital. Trading of EPP's existing ordinary shares was scheduled to resume at 7:30 a.m. on 13 October 2026 following the closure of the Capital Access Window linked to the placing. Key Points - EnergyPathways plc (AIM: EPP) focuses on the UK energy transition and the MESH Long Duration Energy Storage project - Raised £1.75 million through placing 30,434,782 new ordinary shares at 5.75p each with a single institutional subscriber - New shares expected to be admitted to AIM at 8:00 a.m. on 15 October 2026, bringing total voting rights to 282,134,998 - Investors should monitor developments on MESH asset acquisitions, institutional partnership talks, and the forthcoming Energy Independence Bill £1.75 Million Placing Finalized with Single Institutional Subscriber at 5.75p Per Share EnergyPathways confirms the successful closure of the fundraise announced on 28 September 2026, issuing 30,434,782 new ordinary shares at 5.75 pence each exclusively to one institutional investor. The new shares will rank equally with existing ordinary shares in all respects, including entitlement to dividends and distributions declared after issuance. Admission to AIM remains conditional and is anticipated at 8:00 a.m. on 15 October 2026. Post-admission, EPP’s total issued ordinary share capital will be 282,134,998 shares with no treasury shares held. Utilizing Proceeds to Acquire Assets and De-Risk MESH Project The £1.75 million raised will be allocated to accelerating the MESH project and funding working capital. EnergyPathways plans to acquire critical assets such as land, existing pipelines, and technical data to further de-risk the MESH project ahead of institutional and strategic partner investments, with active discussions ongoing. The UK Government has designated MESH as a project of "national significance," aiming to become the UK’s largest Long Duration Energy Storage project with a 300 MW, 55 GWh capacity, and storage duration exceeding 100 hours. MESH Project Aims for Hydrogen Production by 2029 and LDES Operations by 2031 The MESH initiative integrates compressed air energy storage with natural gas and hydrogen storage. Hydrogen production is targeted to commence between 2029 and 2030, with Long Duration Energy Storage operations expected from 2031 to 2032, contingent on government policy, approvals, and financing. The project could offer gas and hydrogen storage equivalent to six days of the UK’s national gas supply. Notably, wind power curtailment costs surpassed £1.5 billion last year and are projected to exceed £8 billion by 2030, underscoring the critical need for multi-day storage solutions beyond the capabilities of battery technologies. Trading Resumption and Regulatory Outlook on AIM The Capital Access Window that opened on 28 September 2026 has now closed. Trading in EnergyPathways’ existing ordinary shares was expected to recommence at 7:30 a.m. on 13 October 2026. Cairn Financial Advisers LLP serves as the company’s nominated adviser, with Fortified Securities and SP Angel Corporate Finance LLP acting as joint brokers. Investors should be aware that the MESH project timeline is subject to policy developments under the upcoming Energy Independence Bill, which represents a significant regulatory factor and project risk highlighted by the company.

Here's a map of single-copy locations. URBANA — There aren’t a lot of topics where one can expect unanimous agreement from the Champaign County Board, said board member John Farney. However, there may be at least one issue where the board’s 21 members can find consensus. “The county board is pretty unified in all things related to data centers right now — very cautious, very much in favor of having strong regulations, very much in favor of transparency,” Farney said. In that vein, two items related to this topic will be discussed at tonight’s committee-of-the-whole meeting: an ordinance prohibiting nondisclosure agreements and a resolution against property-tax incentives for hyperscale data-center developments. No final action will be taken during the meeting. “These are all commitments that we have made,” said board member Emily Rodriguez, who chairs the data-center activities task force. “We are not interested in anything that dodges taxes, for example. That’s something we all agree on on the data-center task force. We also all agree that nondisclosure agreements are bad governance and that folks should be embarrassed to sign them, and data centers should not ask that of local governments.” The proposed ordinance against NDAs states that such agreements have “become an issue with other units of government in local and national news.” If approved, the ordinance would prohibit county board members and county employees from entering into NDAs regarding county business — in any situation, not just instances where data-center developers are involved. As for the other piece of legislation, the proposed resolution would prohibit “the negotiation of tax-abatement agreements, payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements and other concessions for the development and construction of hyperscale data centers within Champaign County.” “No data-center applications have yet been submitted to the county for rural Champaign County, but rumors and public outcry have prompted the need for a formal position,” the resolution states. The two proposals come after the village of Mahomet announced on Sept. 28 that it was in talks with Clean Cloud Energy about a potential data center project in “a rural area west of Champaign” that falls within Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction. One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency. Farney, who wrote the resolution against tax incentives for hyperscale data centers, sent a draft to the board’s policy and finance committee chairs on Oct. 5. “And like a half-hour later, somebody texted me the article that says, ‘Hey, Mahomet’s saying they’re backing off,’” he said. “But I wanted to get that out there right away for the county to actually be able to do something immediately. We don’t have to go through the same processes that we do for the zoning ordinance change in order to put a policy in effect for tax breaks for developments. And so I wanted to have something on record.” When asked how payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements work, Farney said it’s his understanding that data-center developers sometimes offer to make payments to communities while also entering into agreements for long-term property-tax abatements or reductions. Farney said that such agreements end up “being a benefit to the developer and not to the taxing bodies within the area as far as collecting the full value of property taxes.” “Basically, what I’m saying is, if you want to build a data center here, then you’re going to have to do it by our ordinances, which are going to be very stringent when the data-center task force gets done with their work,” he told The News-Gazette. “You’re also going to have to play by the rules that are in place for every other taxpayer in the county, as far as the county’s portion of the tax bill goes. And so we’re not going to give any incentives for data centers. If they can make it, they’re gonna make it on their own.” It’s his hope that other governments and taxing bodies will enact similar policies and form a united front. Champaign County currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with “at least 10,000 square feet of processing area”; the ban is currently set to end in April. The county also created the data-center activities task force to draft planning and zoning regulations for such developments. A previous statement from Leslie Farmer, Clean Cloud Energy’s director of environmental and permitting, indicated that the company may still be considering the project, just not in partnership with Mahomet. “Clean Cloud Energy has decided not to seek annexation into the village of Mahomet following discussions with village leadership,” she said. “We respect Champaign County’s ongoing review of data-center regulations and will evaluate our project’s development in accordance with the framework established by the county.” Documents released by the village on Sept. 28 following a Sept. 14 Freedom of Information Act request by Mahomet resident John Bambenek show that Clean Cloud Energy began talking with Mahomet officials about the project in December. The village entered into a nondisclosure agreement with the company in early 2026 but was released from the agreement on Sept. 16. Communications between the village and Clean Cloud Energy included multiple drafts of a proposed redevelopment and annexation agreement. Both Farney and Rodriguez said that if a municipality annexes an unincorporated area, that land would no longer be subject to the county’s moratorium or zoning regulations on data centers. “I was very surprised to hear that Mahomet was in those discussions, knowing that the county was working on a data-center ordinance,” Farney said. “...
