artigo.texto: Is CATL eyeing the AI business? In the late 19th century, the founders of Standard Oil, the predecessor of ExxonMobil, began buying shares of railway companies in their personal names. Jabez Bostwick, one of the founding partners, later simply served as the president of the New York and New England Railroad Company, while another partner Camden guarded the oil-producing regions for Standard Oil and financed the Ohio River Railway at the same time. Over thirty years, these individual shareholdings quietly formed a network. In 1904, investigative journalist Ida Tarbell wrote the well-known assertion in The History of the Standard Oil Company: Standard Oil "holds shares in most of the large railway systems and has representatives on the boards of directors of almost all major railway systems". At that time, Standard Oil under the management of John D. Rockefeller was the largest crude oil extraction, gasoline and lubricant production enterprise in the United States. For Standard Oil, taking shares in railways could not only ensure that it could obtain cheap and safe oil transportation routes, but also make railway companies themselves major customers for lubricant sales. It can be said that this method guaranteed Standard Oil's position in the industry to a certain extent. The same story is still happening today. On October 6, 2026, Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that DeepSeek's new round of financing is nearing completion, with a scale ranging from 800 billion yuan to 1 trillion yuan. Tencent and CATL have once again become one of the investors with the highest capital contribution. It has been only more than four months since CATL first appeared on DeepSeek's shareholder list. As a leader in power batteries, CATL used to invest its capital in mining, materials and automobile companies: securing supply in the upstream and connecting customers in the downstream. Now, its investment tentacles are beginning to extend to large models, data centers, computing power operation, and embodied intelligence. Why does a battery manufacturer invest in AI? The story of Standard Oil provides a perspective to understand CATL. What CATL is looking for is not a new story unrelated to batteries, but the next batch of customers for batteries and electric energy, as well as new capabilities required to access these customers. In those days, oil needed to be transported by trains; today, electricity needs to be sent to data centers and supplied to robots. What CATL is trying to do is to become a shareholder at the table before the next round of demand really expands. Is the Battery Giant Chasing the AI Trend? If you make a list of CATL's investment targets in the past few years, you will find a change: in the early days, the list was densely populated with mining, materials, battery equipment and automobile companies, while now large models, data centers and robots are occupying more and more positions. This is not a sudden cross-border move. In the middle of this year, Zeng Yuqun, founder of CATL, was asked in an exclusive interview with Caijing why CATL's business boundaries are expanding wider and wider. His answer was: "All our expansions are centered on our core capabilities." One of the previous priorities was to carry out industrial layout around electric vehicles. By 2026, the CATL ecosystem has invested in more than 10 automobile enterprises in total. For example, in 2021, CATL contributed 770 million yuan to participate in the capital increase of AVATR and became its second largest shareholder. In the same year, it also participated in Zeekr's Pre-A round of financing. In addition to equity investment, CATL has also established joint battery companies with many automobile enterprises, advancing the cooperation from procurement relationships to joint R&D, production and supply. AVATR is a typical example of this strategy. In the cooperation system composed of Changan, Huawei and CATL, CATL does not just wait for new cars to be launched to receive orders, but participates in product development earlier as a shareholder and technical partner. For battery suppliers, this means the opportunity to integrate their own technologies into customers' solutions at the vehicle model planning stage. At the same time, the venture capital institutions under the CATL ecosystem, including Puquan Capital, Wending Investment, Chendao Capital and Mindong Times, have also expanded to both ends of the industrial chain: moving upstream to mining, materials and equipment to ensure supply and technical support; extending downstream to automobile enterprises, battery swapping and recycling to find markets and new business models for batteries. Direct investment and fund investment together form a network, and the role of capital has extended from obtaining returns to establishing cooperative relationships and complementing industrial capabilities. In the AI era, CATL has also begun to shift its focus. An early signal came from Qianxun Intelligence. In November 2024, Qianxun Intelligence announced the completion of the angel+ round of financing exclusively invested by Borey Capital, with an amount of tens of millions of yuan. Borey Capital is not an affiliate of CATL, but a venture capital firm established with personal capital from Li Ping, co-founder and vice chairman of CATL. On the other hand, CATL's presence can be seen in the business dealings of Qianxun Intelligence: CATL provides batteries for Qianxun's robots, and Qianxun has obtained the identity of "CATL Ecological Enterprise". Subsequently, in the field of embodied intelligence, CATL invested in Galaxea, Songyan Power, Zhongqing Robot and Weita Power. Among them, in addition to the direct investment from CATL, Puquan Capital and Chendao Capital, the industrial investment platforms under the CATL ecosystem, also participated in the investment in Galaxea and Songyan Power. artigo.texto: TOKYO - Major telecommunications provider NTT Inc. is considering building the first core data center for U.S. artificial intelligence startup Anthropic in Japan, a source familiar with the matter said Wednesday. The construction cost for the data center, to be built in a coastal area in southern Osaka Prefecture and handled by NTT Data Group Corp., is expected to total roughly 1 trillion yen ($6.3 billion), making it one of the leading projects in the country. Anthropic opened its first office in Asia in Tokyo in October last year and the launch of a data center is expected to help the company expand its business in Japan amid the AI boom. Since data centers handle confidential corporate and personal data, having domestic facilities is seen as desirable from a national security perspective and can help mitigate risks related to operations and data transfers. Japanese digital minister Toshiharu Furukawa said Tuesday the government had asked Anthropic to consider the country as a site for a data center during a meeting in Tokyo with Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, adding that the government was willing to support such a project. Anthropic is a leading developer of generative AI, and its Claude Mythos model is seen as highly capable of finding security vulnerabilities. Governments around the world have worked to strengthen ties with the startup to gain access with its technology and information.

artigo.texto: WILLIAMSBURG, Ohio — Jessica Baker sifted through an overflowing pile of political mailers she has received over the past month. Lowering costs? “That’s common sense,” she said. Reducing gas prices and utility bills? “We need that.” Party division, culture wars — it’s all there. But none of it touched the issue she wants to hear about before she votes: data centers. “My home’s under attack,” Baker, a lead organizer for the grassroots advocacy group Conserve Ohio, told MS NOW in her living room. Just a few steps away were piles of petitions and homemade maps marking where data centers are being built across Ohio. In just a few months, she said, the issue turned her from someone who was mostly apolitical into someone who ferries petitions to and from the statehouse. There isn’t a data center in her town, but there are plans to build one just a few minutes’ drive away. “Everything doesn’t stop at that property line. So, once we started realizing that they were coming everywhere, and nobody would listen, we had —” she stops herself. “There was no choice. There’s just no choice.” She pointed back at the mailers. “That’s what’s not on here: The people are not on here.” But the people will vote in November. Ohio has competitive races this year for governor, Senate and House — and Democratic wins in the congressional contests could help tip the balance of power on Capitol Hill. Ohio also has more data center-related ballot measures than anywhere else in the country: 21 of them, spread across 16 counties, mostly in areas that overwhelmingly voted Republican just two years ago. Data centers are unpopular across party lines. In a September NBC News poll, nearly half of Republican voters said they would be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building data centers in their local communities. That is making an already competitive election even less predictable, and nowhere more so than in the Senate race. Ohio has been reliably red for more than a decade. So, in theory, the race to serve the rest of Vice President JD Vance’s Senate term should be an easy win for Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to the seat in 2025. But bipartisan backlash to the state’s data center boom — and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown’s strategy of laying the blame at Husted’s feet — could return the Buckeye State to its swing-state past. More than $14 million has been spent on data center-related ads in the Husted-Brown race alone. That is six times as much as in any other Senate race in the country. Nearly all of the ads target Husted, casting him as the “face of data centers” in Ohio and attacking him for backing tax breaks for developers when he was lieutenant governor. Republicans are worried. In an August memo reported by Politico, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which works to protect and expand the GOP’s Senate majority, warned that Brown’s strategy was working and that data centers had become an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” Asked by MS NOW about that assessment, Husted sidestepped it. “People in Ohio, I can tell you, after I fought to make the data centers pay their own freight so that we could lower electricity prices, and Chuck Schumer and the Democrats blocked it — that has been an eye-opening piece of information to them,” he said. “Because they’re like, ‘What’s the truth?’ And now they know the truth that the Democrats are blocking our efforts to make data centers accountable, and that’s really been a shift here in the last week in the campaign.” Democrats did block the bill, called the Ratepayer Protection Act, before the Senate left Washington for its pre-midterm October recess. They argued it was “toothless” because it only asks companies to consider paying for the costs their data centers create, rather than requiring them to. Husted glossed over that distinction, telling MS NOW his legislation would “force data centers to pay for their own power.” Still, the fact that he spent precious time in the Senate fighting for it is a telling sign of how much the issue matters back home. It also helps explain why Brown, who is trying to win his way back to the Senate, isn’t letting up. “It really is part of the rigged system,” Brown says of data centers. “I’ve spent my career fighting against this rigged system, whether it’s Wall Street, whether it’s the oil companies, now whether it’s the tech boys. Now these data centers come in, and it shows an even more rigged system because people had no say whatsoever. Local communities had no input in what these [centers] are doing.” Baker agrees. But she doesn’t think either candidate is doing enough as both find their footing, in real time, on an issue that is rapidly reshaping politics in Ohio and beyond.

artigo.texto: Appeal for major energy storage system rejected - Published Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed. Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year. The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire. In her decision, inspector RC Kirby said such mitigation "would not be effective" in ensuring an acceptable balance between harm and benefit", stating the proposal was "not suitable for its location". A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, external. Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway. The appellant said it believed it would be about eight years before water used to fight a notional fire at the BESS would reach the drinking water source, but the inspector said there had been "insufficient evidence" to substantiate this. The appeal decision notice stated the appellant had put forward revised plans that East Devon had not had put before it. These included an increase in the size of the water tanks, relocation of some of the tanks, the separation distance between pairs of containers being 6m (20ft) apart, and other alterations. Campaigners from Devon branch of the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) and the Hawkchurch and Monkton Wyld Action Group said they were "massively relieved" plans for the site had been blocked. Devon CPRE energy spokesperson Dr Phil Bratby added: "For years, Devon CPRE has been highlighting the risks from the hazardous materials that could be released and contaminate the groundwater." Kirby said that, while the benefits of the scheme would "outweigh the moderate harm that would be caused to the Dorset National Landscape", they were "insufficient" to outweigh the "very substantial, overriding, unacceptable risks in respect of pollution of the water environment". Proponents of BESS systems highlighted their benefits in helping the nation reach net zero aspirations, notably because they could store energy. The UK government noted BESS systems used batteries, for example lithium-ion batteries, to store electricity at times when supply was higher than demand. "They can then later release electricity when it is needed. BESSs are therefore important for "the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable energy", it stated. artigo.texto: Renewable energy illustration: Chen Xia/Global Times One of the challenges emerging from India's rapid economic growth is how to meet its rising demand for electricity. The Indian Express reported that Ghanshyam Prasad, chairperson of the country's top power planner, said that India may need to add 105-150 gigawatts of coal-based power capacity by 2035, significantly more than the 97 gigawatts currently planned. The remarks come amid growing concerns over whether India's electricity supply can keep pace with rising demand. Bloomberg recently reported that smaller factories, farmers and households are facing power cuts as demand outweighs supply on the grid. Manish Dhuppad, general secretary at the Chhattisgarh Mini Steel Plant Association, was quoted as saying that small steel mills in the central state of Chhattisgarh are facing outages of 10 to 12 hours a day, forcing plants to reduce output. India's electricity challenges are complex. Yet recent signs of supply constraints suggest that ensuring a reliable power supply is becoming increasingly important as the economy expands. The focus, therefore, is shifting toward how India can expand electricity supply to meet rising demand. The paradox is that India's electricity supply challenges have emerged even as its renewable energy sector has expanded rapidly. India now ranks third globally in renewable energy installed capacity, with solar power accounting for the largest share of its renewable energy mix. As of July 31, the country's installed solar capacity had reached 164.59 gigawatts, up from just 2.8 gigawatts in 2014. The scale of this increase highlights the rapid pace of India's solar development over the past decade. The question, then, is why India's power shortages have persisted alongside rapid growth in renewable energy. One part of the answer is that some renewable electricity has not been fully utilized. Citing data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), Reuters reported that India turned away nearly 1.8 billion units of renewable electricity in July and August, even as it grappled with power shortages. CREA analysts attributed the curtailment to grid and operational constraints. In other words, India's renewable energy expansion has created a new challenge: some of the electricity generated has gone to waste because the grid has not been able to absorb it. The build-out of renewable energy has outpaced the development of transmission infrastructure. Expanding grid capacity and energy storage could offer a more effective way to address this mismatch. One area with potential is battery storage. Deploying battery storage systems could help integrate more renewable power into the grid and allow more of the electricity generated to be used. Battery storage, however, is a highly specialized industry that requires technological expertise and mature supply chains. India has invested heavily in this area and has continued to strengthen its capabilities. Yet imports and international cooperation can also offer a faster way to access advanced technologies and help address the country's immediate energy challenges. Given the scale of India's electricity needs and the importance of reliable power supply for economic development, expanding access to battery storage through trade and cooperation could be highly beneficial. China's years of experience in battery manufacturing and its extensive industrial supply chain have made it a major participant in the global energy storage sector. This creates potential areas for cooperation between China and India, which could help India expand its options as it seeks to address its energy challenges. If this potential is better realized, battery storage could become another tool for India to ease pressure on its power system and reduce the need to rely on expanding coal-fired capacity. As the global energy transition continues, whether coal can provide a long-term solution to India's growing electricity demand remains uncertain. Greater international cooperation in energy storage could help India overcome the bottlenecks holding back renewable energy and create a more balanced path for meeting future power needs. The author is a reporter with the Global Times. bizopinion@globaltimes.com.cn

artigo.texto: Israel to cap new data centers at 200 megawatts amid AI power crunch The Electricity Authority is preparing rules that would block larger facilities as developers seek grid connections totaling 27,000 megawatts, well above the country’s installed generation capacity. Data centers could account for about 20% of electricity consumption by 2030. The Electricity Authority is moving to curb the construction of large data centers by limiting the maximum capacity of any new facility to 200 megawatts, Calcalist has learned. According to sources familiar with the matter within the Electricity Authority’s plenum, a draft decision regulating data center connections to the electricity grid is expected to be released for public comment on Sunday. Meanwhile, estimates suggest that data centers could account for approximately 20% of Israel’s total electricity consumption by 2030. A data center’s power capacity determines how much computing it can support, including the training and operation of artificial intelligence models. Its electricity demand is driven by processors and the extensive cooling systems needed to keep them running. While a 200-megawatt facility would be large by Israeli standards, Noga, Israel’s independent electricity system operator, has already received connection requests for 50 facilities with higher capacities. For example, Mega DC, owned by Zahi Nahmias, is seeking to build a 1,100-megawatt facility on the site in Hadera where the Alliance tire factory operated until 2024. SDS, a company controlled by Yossi Schonfeld, has requested approval for an 875-megawatt facility in Nesher. Under the proposed rules, projects of this scale would not be eligible for approval as currently planned. According to officials familiar with the plenum’s deliberations, limiting individual facilities to 200 megawatts would allow more data centers to be built while helping protect the electricity grid. A sudden failure at a large facility could disrupt grid frequency and potentially affect the stability of the electricity supply. The global boom in demand for data centers supporting AI models has prompted Israeli entrepreneurs to race to establish facilities and submit connection requests to Noga. But the scale of the applications has raised concerns about whether the country’s electricity infrastructure can accommodate them. The total requested capacity has reached 27,000 megawatts, compared with Israel’s installed electricity generation capacity of 18,800 megawatts. Israel’s average electricity consumption is approximately 9,000 megawatts, while peak demand reached 17,300 megawatts in August 2025. The total capacity sought by data center developers therefore exceeds the country’s entire existing generation capacity, even before accounting for other electricity consumers. Data centers also pose a particular challenge because they are designed to operate continuously. Unlike many factories or other large electricity consumers, they cannot easily suspend operations without disrupting the services they provide. Their customers, including major technology companies such as Google, Microsoft and OpenAI, expect reliable, uninterrupted computing capacity. This creates a large and relatively inflexible source of electricity demand that requires long-term planning. Last June, the Electricity Authority temporarily halted the processing of new data center applications for 140 days while conducting an internal review ahead of the regulatory decision. The draft is expected to be released for public comment, followed by a three-week consultation period. The authority’s plenum will then consider objections before publishing the final framework. Notably, the draft does not appear to impose geographic restrictions on data centers. Developers could therefore apply to build facilities in areas with high existing electricity demand as well as in more remote regions. Noga is likely to find it easier to approve projects in outlying areas, where connecting a new facility may have less impact on other consumers and the existing grid. The framework is also expected to address whether data centers should be allowed to connect directly to power plants, bypassing the Israel Electric Corporation’s grid. Such an arrangement could be rejected out of concern that generation capacity intended to serve the wider public would instead be allocated to a single customer. Another issue is whether data centers could be required to disconnect from the grid at short notice. A senior executive at a data center developer said such a requirement would be a deal-breaker. The cost of installing backup generators or energy storage systems capable of supporting a 200-megawatt facility, he said, could make the project economically unviable. The executive nevertheless described the proposed 200-megawatt ceiling as reasonable. “Currently, there are no data centers of this scale in Israel, and given the electricity generation capacity, establishing massive facilities here is not feasible,” he said. “Even in the U.S., data centers are hitting a wall. Demand is enormous, but you can’t just build a 1,000-megawatt facility anywhere; there are power constraints. Furthermore, you can’t buy unlimited quantities of GPUs.” The difficulties of building data centers in the U.S. and Europe could make Israel an attractive destination for technology companies. Electricity prices in Israel are lower than in the U.S., potentially making operations more cost-effective for data center developers. The senior executive cited other advantages, including Israel’s technology sector and its experience building hardened data centers. “Israel is a technological powerhouse, a ‘Startup Nation.’ All the major players are here. Furthermore, Israel possesses expertise in constructing hardened data centers,” he said. artigo.texto: Hyundai Motor has adopted CATL’s latest thermal propagation (TP) control technology in its recently launched IONIQ V electric vehicle in China. Equipped with a Chinese-made lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, the IONIQ V is the first electric vehicle under Hyundai’s IONIQ brand priced in the 20 million won range. CATL said on Oct. 14 that the IONIQ V features its third-generation TP prevention technology, NP3.0 (No Propagation 3.0), according to battery safety materials released the previous day. This marks the first time the technology has been adopted in a Hyundai vehicle. The IONIQ V is an electric vehicle developed specifically for the Chinese market and was first unveiled at the 2026 Beijing International Auto Show in April. Launched on Sept. 29, it is produced by Beijing Hyundai, a joint venture between Hyundai Motor and Beijing Automotive Group (BAIC). Its locally discounted price ranges from 99,900 yuan to 131,900 yuan (approximately 20 million to 26 million won). Equipped with a 66.8-kilowatt-hour (kWh) LFP battery from CATL, the vehicle offers a driving range of more than 650 kilometers on a single charge under China’s Light-Duty Vehicle Test Cycle (CLTC). However, CLTC tends to produce longer range estimates than South Korea’s Ministry of Environment standard, with differences reaching as much as 200 kilometers. CATL’s NP3.0 technology is designed to help vehicles continue moving safely even after battery thermal runaway occurs. Thermal runaway is a phenomenon in which a battery’s internal temperature rises rapidly, spreading heat to neighboring cells and potentially causing fire or explosion. CATL has developed three generations of TP prevention technology since introducing NP1.0 in 2018. NP3.0 is designed to detect abnormalities within seconds of thermal runaway, warn the driver and maintain high-voltage power supply. CATL said its internal tests showed that vehicles could continue driving safely for at least five minutes after thermal runaway without losing power. The technology focuses on giving drivers enough time to move their vehicles to a safe location. Hyundai’s adoption of NP3.0 comes amid tighter battery safety regulations in China. The previous national standard, GB 38031-2020, required occupants to receive a warning at least five minutes before a fire or explosion caused by battery thermal runaway. The revised standard, GB 38031-2025, which took effect in July, strengthened requirements to prevent fires or explosions even when thermal runaway occurs. Under its “In China, For China” strategy, Hyundai has reduced costs by using locally sourced components and manufacturing facilities, enabling it to introduce a midsize electric vehicle priced in the 20 million won range. Demand for similarly affordable EVs is also growing in South Korea as Tesla rapidly expands sales with Chinese-made vehicles and Chinese automakers including BYD and Zeekr target the Korean market. Tesla sold 11,421 Model Y vehicles in South Korea in September, surpassing Hyundai’s Grandeur sedan at 8,898 units. Tesla’s Korean sales reached 89,148 vehicles in the first nine months of the year, up 104.4% from a year earlier. Hyundai’s domestic EV sales, including Genesis, totaled just 55,733 units during the same period. Hyundai has yet to decide whether to launch the IONIQ V in South Korea. Even if introduced, maintaining its Chinese-market price in the 20 million won range would be difficult. Eligibility for EV purchase subsidies is also uncertain, as the government revised its subsidy program this year to consider contributions to domestic supply chains and the use of locally sourced components. Hwang Kyung-in, head of the Strategic Industry Analysis Division at the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade (KIET), said automakers must weigh the benefits of lower costs against potential subsidy disadvantages. “Even if using Chinese batteries reduces EV production costs, companies need to assess the trade-offs if they face disadvantages in domestic subsidies,” he said. “Automakers must consider not only battery prices but also subsidies, supply chains and other factors.” Hwang added that Korean battery manufacturers also need to develop cost-competitive LFP batteries for electric vehicles, while deciding where to concentrate their limited investment resources and production capacity.

As battery technologies continue to evolve, manufacturers face growing pressure to improve energy density, extend cycle life, increase charging speed and scale production across multiple chemistries and manufacturing approaches. VOLTRICELL brings together Dow's growing portfolio of battery cell materials under a unified platform designed to support innovation across electrodes, separators, coatings and battery cell packaging applications. artigo.texto: A gigante russa de tecnologia da informação Yandex, chamada de Google da Rússia, diz que um data center da empresa nos arredores de Moscou foi atacado por um drone ucraniano. A Yandex anunciou domingo que foi danificada a infraestrutura do data center, situado na região de Vladimir, e que as suas atividades foram completamente interrompidas. O grande jornal russo Kommersant noticiou no mesmo dia que não estavam disponíveis para usuários alguns serviços da Yandex, como de solicitação de táxis e de entrega de refeições. Segundo o periódico, também ficaram parcialmente indisponíveis serviços mantidos pela Yandex no Cazaquistão e no Quirguistão — nações da Ásia Central que têm estreitos laços com a Rússia. É o terceiro ataque ucraniano a instalações pertencentes à gigante russa de tecnologia. Na quinta-feira, foi atacado um data center da Yandex em Ryazan, na região central da Rússia, e na sexta-feira, outro na região de Kaluga, vizinha a Moscou. A mídia ucraniana noticiou quinta-feira que o presidente da Ucrânia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, fez menção a um plano para revidar ataques lançados pela Rússia a data centers situados na Ucrânia.

artigo.texto: 12.10.26 – By NewsIP Bureau – New Delhi – India and the European Union discussed carbon market development, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and technical cooperation during a bilateral meeting in New Delhi on October 12, 2026. Pankaj Agarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Power, met Gerassimos Thomas, Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union at the European Commission, to exchange views on carbon pricing frameworks and implementation-related developments. The discussions covered India’s domestic carbon market initiatives, the EU’s CBAM framework and opportunities to strengthen cooperation on monitoring, reporting, verification and capacity building. Also Read: Ministry of Power clears up to 654 MW electricity export to Nepal During the meeting, Agarwal highlighted progress under India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), including the notification of emission-intensity reduction targets for 490 industrial units. The initiative forms part of the country’s efforts to develop a domestic carbon market. He also outlined the expansion of non-fossil energy capacity in India’s electricity sector. Non-fossil sources account for 308 GW of the country’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW, according to the figures presented during the meeting. These developments provided context for the exchange on carbon pricing and climate-related policy frameworks. Also Read: Power Minister Boosts Morale at NHPC’s J&K Sites The European Commission side acknowledged India’s progress in carbon market development and shared updates concerning CBAM implementation. Discussions also addressed the potential for technical engagement on the recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms and the development of monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems. Capacity building was another area identified for cooperation. These subjects are relevant to understanding how carbon pricing approaches are assessed and implemented, while the meeting provided an opportunity for both sides to exchange information on their respective policy developments. Also Read: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: Key Developments Both sides agreed to continue dialogue and strengthen cooperation on carbon markets, CBAM-related methodologies and other areas of mutual interest. The proposed continued engagement will cover technical issues, including carbon pricing mechanisms, MRV systems and capacity building. The meeting reflects an ongoing exchange between India and the European Union on carbon market policies and implementation approaches. No specific agreement on formal recognition of either side’s carbon pricing mechanism was announced in the information provided.

artigo.texto: ALPS nomeia Brian Turnbow para liderar o desenvolvimento de data centers de IA de última geração A startup italiana nomeou Turnbow para liderar sua expansão tecnológica em inteligência artificial e computação de alto desempenho, com uma abordagem de energia para computação que planeja aproveitar fontes de energia renováveis e reutilizar ativos existentes para desenvolver uma infraestrutura de computação mais sustentável. TRENTO, Itália, 15 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A ALPS anuncia a nomeação de Brian Turnbow como diretor técnico de IA. Fundada em Trentino em 2018 e com atuação em quatro continentes, a empresa aplica sua expertise em projeto, construção e operação de data centers integrados a sistemas de energia às áreas de IA e HPC. O acesso à energia é uma das principais restrições ao desenvolvimento da infraestrutura de IA. Segundo dados da Terna de 31 de agosto de 2026, as solicitações de conexão à rede elétrica de data centers na Itália totalizaram mais de 100 GW, um aumento em relação aos cerca de 30 GW no final de 2024 — um crescimento que torna a seleção do local e os prazos de conexão à rede extremamente críticos. A abordagem de conversão de energia em computação da ALPS baseia-se em uma escolha deliberada: Localizar data centers onde a energia já está disponível, inclusive fora dos principais polos, para reduzir a dependência de áreas congestionadas da rede elétrica. A empresa tem como objetivo integrar fontes de energia renováveis e revitalizar áreas industriais desativadas, reutilizando conexões de rede, edifícios e outros ativos existentes sempre que tecnicamente viável. O objetivo é desenvolver uma infraestrutura computacional mais sustentável, utilizando recursos locais e, por meio da reutilização de ativos, limitando a ocupação de terrenos e reduzindo a necessidade de novas construções. Essa expansão complementa as operações de mineração em andamento da ALPS, que continuam em linha com seu plano de negócios. Turnbow liderará a estratégia técnica de IA/HPC da ALPS, desde a avaliação de arquiteturas e locais até o engajamento com parceiros de tecnologia e industriais. A Itália será um mercado prioritário. A ALPS pretende trazer de volta à Itália sua expertise internacional e trabalhar com empresas italianas de engenharia e do setor industrial, aproveitando também sua experiência em projetos no exterior. "A Itália e a Europa possuem recursos energéticos, ativos industriais e conhecimento técnico que podemos aproveitar", afirma Francesco Buffa, CEO e cofundador da ALPS. "Por meio de nossa abordagem de conversão de energia em computação, queremos transformar o potencial energético e industrial das regiões onde atuamos em uma vantagem competitiva e ajudar a reduzir a lacuna da IA na Europa." Turnbow traz para a empresa mais de 25 anos de experiência em telecomunicações e infraestrutura digital, tendo ocupado cargos técnicos na TWT, Unidata e CDLAN. Ele é membro do conselho administrativo do ITNOG. "A infraestrutura de IA começa muito antes da implementação de GPUs", afirma Brian Turnbow. "Cada projeto deve começar com as cargas de trabalho que precisa suportar e os requisitos dos clientes, e não apenas com a energia disponível. Meu objetivo é traduzir esses requisitos em decisões de projeto coerentes, construindo capacidade computacional flexível, escalável e sustentável, ao mesmo tempo que utilizo fontes de energia renováveis e ativos existentes." Sobre a ALPS A ALPS projeta, constrói e opera data centers para aplicações de alta demanda energética e computacional, combinando conhecimento especializado em energia com engenharia e operação de data centers. Seu crescimento internacional foi apoiado pela Azimut por meio de uma transação de € 40 milhões em 2023 e um acordo de € 105 milhões em 2024. Para informações adicionais: www.alps.it FONTE ALPS

artigo.texto: Brighton singer-songwriter Bess Atwell returns to Australian stages in March 2027 with a new album due in February and a freshly released single written about her time in Quebec. Bess Atwell is heading back to Australia in March 2027, bringing songs from her forthcoming album due in February alongside the just-released single and video ‘The Act’. The Brighton-based artist last toured Australia as a headline act in 2025. That run built on the quiet momentum she has gathered since her 2021 album Already, Always and the 2024 release Light Sleeper. The new Australian dates land just after the arrival of the next full-length record, giving local audiences an early chance to hear the material live. ‘The Act’ was written about the period Bess Atwell spent living in Quebec. The track and its accompanying video are available to stream, download and watch now. It sits in the same emotionally direct lane that has defined her work: intimate storytelling delivered with melodic restraint and a clear, crystalline vocal. Bess Atwell first drew wider attention with Already, Always in 2021. The record established her as a writer capable of turning private observation into something that feels shared. Three years later Light Sleeper expanded that approach. Produced by Aaron Dessner and released through Real Kind Records (the label founded by Lucy Rose), the album added luminous textures while keeping the focus on her voice and the detail of the lyrics. Reviews noted the increased sonic range without any loss of the quiet assurance that marked the earlier work. Her path into music began with Taylor Swift songs on guitar before a Johnny Flynn concert shifted her focus toward the early 2010s London nu-folk scene. Influences such as Fleet Foxes, Bon Iver, Joni Mitchell, The National and Sharon Van Etten sit alongside later admiration for Julia Jacklin, Stella Donnelly, Phoebe Bridgers and Soccer Mommy. Those threads appear in the careful economy of her arrangements and the unflinching honesty of the words. Live, Bess Atwell has steadily moved from smaller rooms to sold-out headline shows across the UK, Europe, Canada and Australia. The songs tend to feel like confidences rather than performances: vulnerable, precise and delivered with an understated power that rewards close listening. The 2027 Australian run continues that pattern, placing her in rooms that have become familiar stops for independent artists who prioritise connection over scale. The new album remains untitled at this stage, but the February 2027 release window places it just weeks before the Australian dates. That timing suggests the tour will function as both a celebration of the new material and a continuation of the relationship Bess Atwell has been building with Australian audiences since her previous visit. Her catalogue now stretches from the 2016 debut Hold Your Mind through the 2019 EP Big Blue, Already, Always, the 2022 remix collection Already, Rearranged, Light Sleeper and the 2024 EP More Than Science. Each step has refined the same core strengths: careful melody, emotional clarity and a refusal to overstate. ‘The Act’ continues that trajectory, offering a first glimpse of the writing that will shape the next chapter. For Australian fans who caught the 2025 shows or who have followed the records from a distance, the March 2027 dates present a clear opportunity to hear the next phase of the work in rooms designed for listening. The combination of a new album, a fresh single and a return to the same cities creates a natural moment of connection between artist and audience. artigo.texto: Dow launches VOLTRICELL battery cell materials platform to advance next-generation battery innovation - VOLTRICELL materials are designed to help address performance needs in high-energy-density battery applications. - Alongside existing technologies, the introduction of VOLTRICELL means Dow can support customers across multiple stages of the battery value chain. - Dows newest battery fire protection materials DOWSIL EF-6559 and DOWSIL FC-2024 will be also on display at The Battery Show North America 2026 Dow (NYSE: DOW) announced the addition of VOLTRICELL to its existing portfolio of battery solutions at The Battery Show North America. VOLTRICELLopens in a new tab is a brand-new suite of materials designed to optimize battery manufacturing processes and improve the performance of todays battery and emerging sodium-ion, silicon-anode and solid-state battery technologies. It is Dows first material platform designed specifically for supporting optimal electrochemistry inside the cell. As battery technologies continue to evolve, manufacturers face growing pressure to improve energy density, extend cycle life, increase charging speed and scale production across multiple chemistries and manufacturing approaches. VOLTRICELL brings together Dows growing portfolio of battery cell materials under a unified platform designed to support innovation across electrodes, separators, coatings and battery cell packaging applications. The portfolio includes binders, dispersants, rheology modifiers, surfactants and specialty additives that can be selected and combined to help support performance, manufacturability and scalability. In the battery industry, there are a multitude of chemistries and cell manufacturing strategies in play today and under development for the future, said Joel McDonald, Global Technical Director for Dow MobilityScience. Battery manufacturers need materials partners that can evolve with their technology roadmaps. Through VOLTRICELL, we can help customers innovate with confidence, leveraging Dows broad toolbox to support todays cell chemistries and the next generation of energy storage. Designing Materials that Support the Whole Battery The launch of VOLTRICELL reflects Dows continued commitment to the industry and to customers across the battery value chain. By combining deep materials science expertise with application development capabilities and global technical support through its global MobilityScience Studiosopens in a new tab, Dow helps battery manufacturers accelerate innovation from cell design to system-level integration. At The Battery Show North America 2026, Dow will also showcase its latest materials to support battery fire protection including: - VORAFORCE TP1415 Polyol: a polyurethane resin system for manufacturing lightweight fiber-reinforced composites, designed to support impact resistance, corrosion resistance and flame-retardant performance in polyurethane pultrusion applications - DOWSIL EF-6559 Silicone Foam: a two-part, expanding foam for narrow, complex shapes within battery assemblies that forms a protective ceramic layer when exposed to high heat and is designed to support thermal management and electrical insulation in high-volume series production - DOWSIL FC-2024 Coating: one-part RTV coating applied to battery housings, enclosures and lids to support battery fire protection by forming a hard protective ceramic layer during a thermal event and is intended for a cylindrical, prismatic or pouch-based battery system Visitors can meet with Dow experts at Booth #3000 in Exhibit Halls A-E to explore how advanced materials are helping drive the next generation of battery innovation. For more information and to schedule a meeting with Dow at or before The Battery Show North America, visit https://www.dow.com/en-us/market/mkt-mobility/sub-mobility-electronics/app-mobility-elec-battery-systems.htmlopens in a new tab. About Dow Dow (NYSE: DOW) is one of the worlds leading materials science companies, serving customers in high-growth markets such as packaging, infrastructure, mobility and consumer applications. Our global breadth, asset integration and scale, customer-focused innovation and leading business positions enable us to achieve profitable growth and help deliver a sustainable future. We operate manufacturing sites in 29 countries and employed approximately 34,600 people as of year-end 2025. Dow delivered sales of approximately $40 billion in 2025. artigo.texto: St. Petersburg’s existing zoning rules prohibit standalone data centers, according to an Oct. 9 memo from Planning Director Derek Kilborn to Mayor Ken Welch explaining how a new Florida law relates to the city’s regulation of the facilities. The city’s land development code does not list data centers as a permitted use or special exception, and uses that are not listed are presumed prohibited unless they are similar enough to an approved use to qualify. Kilborn found no basis for treating data centers as an existing permitted use, including under the classifications for utility plants and substations. His determination follows the passage of Senate Bill 484, signed by Gov. Ron DeSantis on May 7, which preserves local governments’ authority to regulate facilities with substantial electricity and utility demands. The law also prevents large-load customers from being treated as electric substations under a state provision governing substation approvals, a distinction relevant to the city’s existing zoning classifications. To determine whether an unlisted use qualifies, St. Petersburg’s zoning code relies on the American Planning Association’s land-use classification system and the North American Industry Classification System. Kilborn wrote that neither provides a clear basis for treating data centers as similar to an existing permitted use. “For these reasons, Data Centers generally, and Large-Scale Data Centers explicitly, remain prohibited as a permitted, principal (P) or Special Exception (SE) use in the City of St. Petersburg,” Kilborn wrote. The new state law defines large-scale data centers as facilities with an anticipated monthly peak electrical load of at least 50 megawatts, calculated using the highest average load over a 15-minute interval. St. Petersburg’s determination also covers smaller standalone data centers that fall below that threshold. The restriction does not apply to data centers that serve as ancillary parts of otherwise permitted businesses, allowing supporting data infrastructure to operate alongside an approved primary use. Kilborn’s memorandum does not propose any changes to the city’s zoning code.

artigo.texto: In between jeers and boos from an audience of Elizabeth Township residents, a Bucks County-based developer laid out an initial concept for a sprawling data center campus on a 549-acre former landfill bordering the Youghigheny River on Tuesday night. Tim Hendricks, a New Hope resident, told attendees that he hopes to develop a 20-building data center campus and associated natural gas power plant at a township-organized town hall meeting. Communications between Hendricks and local officials obtained by Pittsburgh’s Public Source last week revealed several project plans presented to the township over the summer. Those plans for a 549-acre parcel on Henderson Road near the Youghiogheny River included anywhere from 11 to 28 two-story data center buildings. They were met with opposition from some residents and advocates last week, and hesitancy from the local state representative. Hendricks provided few specific details regarding the final size, scope and environmental impact of the project at the town hall, stressing that the project was still in its development phase. “A project like this obviously has an impact on the community, everybody knows that,” Hendricks said. “We don’t know anything about what’s going to get approved.” Hendricks has not formally submitted any plans to the township or applied for any permits. “Frankly, Elizabeth Township deserves better than another sales pitch about how an industrial project is going to save this community,” said Joelle Whiteman, a township resident and local organizer for the D.C.-based advocacy organization Food & Water Watch, in an interview prior to the meeting. Whiteman is also a member of Protect Elizabeth Township, an environmental advocacy organization that was originally formed to oppose a power plant previously intended for the site. Whiteman, who has been collecting signatures for a petition to stop the development, said she has signed up 350 residents. Attendees, who nearly filled most of the Elizabeth Forward Middle School auditorium, raised questions regarding the water and energy demands of the site, its proximity to houses in the area, the planned natural gas plant and noise concerns. Many in the crowd held signs and wore pins opposing the project. The crowd applauded after one resident shouted, “We don’t want this.” Hendricks said he couldn’t provide specific numbers regarding the site’s water and electricity usage, but said that there was “no way” the site would have an impact on residents’ electricity bills. He also said it would use less water than “typical factories.” The data center buildings would be 2,000 feet away from the nearest homes in the township, a community of manufactured homes called Rolling Hills Village. Noise “will not exceed anything that exists today,” Hendricks said. “Everything is designed so far back from the homes that we don’t have [noise] as an issue.” Hendricks said the data center buildings would be around 150,000 square feet each, which would total 3 million square feet, dwarfing a planned site in Springdale Borough opposed by some local residents. “We’re at step one, maybe step two. There’s probably 100 steps,” Hendricks said, adding that he hadn’t previously attended a meeting this early on in a data center process. He said he’d have to obtain permits from the township, state and potentially the Federal government. State official not convinced State Rep. Andrew Kuzma, R-Elizabeth Township, previously expressed hesitation about some aspects of the project. In an interview after the meeting, he said he is opposed to the project in its entirety. “There is no end user, there are no facts that are in writing and it’s apparent a majority of the residents are against it,” said Kuzma. At the meeting, Hendricks said he was in discussion with end users but did not identify them. Hendricks said his role in the development is to identify the property and obtain all the required permits and approvals. Another person or company would build and operate the property, he said. The proposal became public on Sept. 15, when township commission President Josh Walls announced at a commission meeting that Elizabeth had been approached about a data center project. Tuesday’s town hall was moderated by Eric Piper, a township redevelopment authority member, who asked selected questions submitted by residents. Piper said he received 330 questions from residents that he condensed into 45. Elizabeth Township by the numbers - 22.8 square miles - 12,690 population - 92% white (vs. 76% countywide) - 5.7% in poverty (vs. 11.5%) - $80,589 median household income (vs. $78,548) - $167,000 median value of owner-occupied homes (vs. $227,600) Source: U.S. Census American Community Survey data compiled by Census Reporter The site could generate $125 million in annual tax revenue for the municipality and Elizabeth Forward School District, according to Hendricks’ emails to commissioners. Hendricks reiterated the $125 million number at the town hall. The township expects to bring in around $10.6 million in revenue in 2026, according to its budget. The district brought in $52 million in revenue during the 2024-2025 school year. “Everybody wants this township to be bailed out,” Whiteman said. “Seeing a number that high, I understand why some of the elected officials are like, ‘Oh, this could really save us.’” Walls said that he could not comment on the revenue figures because they were not prepared by the township or local taxing bodies. Walls also stressed that the development is still in the discussion phase. “There’s a lot of residents with very, very serious concerns. Without adequate answers to those, I could not personally support this project moving forward,” he said. artigo.texto: With participation confirmed from 24 African countries and 45 countries globally, CMAS 2026 will bring together more than 100 speakers, over 50 investors, buyers and financiers, 20 African governments and more than 40 project developers in Kigali from 13 to 15 October. The diversity of participation reflects growing engagement with African carbon markets from governments, project developers, financiers and credit buyers. The international presence will bring African policymakers and projects into direct contact with organisations active across carbon markets globally. For Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance & Stakeholder Engagement for the Government of Nigeria, the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 represents an opportunity for continental participants to play a central role in determining how the market develops. “This gathering of the leading players in African carbon markets represents a continental ownership in driving the future of carbon markets shaped by Africans, for the benefit of Africa.” Investor and buyer participation will add an important commercial dimension to the gathering. Dedicated Investor Roundtables will provide focused opportunities for capital providers, buyers and project developers to engage directly, while meetings across the summit will allow participants to identify potential partnerships and areas for further engagement. More than 40 project developers and project representatives working across sectors including nature-based solutions, agriculture, waste, clean cooking and carbon removals will also participate, providing investors and buyers with direct exposure to projects from across the continent. For Maggie Kinyanjui, Sourcing Manager, Africa, Climate Impact Partners, greater engagement between project developers, buyers and investors is essential to building a stronger African carbon market. “Africa should not just participate in carbon markets. We should help shape them. The opportunity is to build a market that attracts capital, rewards integrity and ensures that value reaches the countries and communities delivering climate impact.” The timing also coincides with an active period for international carbon markets. These discussions will take place at a time when key international carbon market rules and mechanisms continue to evolve. The Article 6.4 Supervisory Body, which oversees the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, is holding its 23rd meeting this week in Bonn, immediately ahead of CMAS 2026. Amy Rhoades, Chief Communications & Engagement Officer, Carbon Standards, says meaningful engagement across the carbon value chain is critical to the growth of credible carbon removal solutions on the continent. “Africa isn’t waiting for global carbon markets to mature; it’s actively building them. At Carbon Markets Africa Summit, we’re not just sponsoring a conference, we’re engaging the policymakers, entrepreneurs, and buyers who are building the carbon removal ecosystem in Africa. That engagement is the future of credible CDR and that’s why Carbon Standards is in Kigali.” Against that international backdrop, discussions in Kigali will provide an opportunity for African governments and market participants to consider what developments in the global market mean in practice for the continent, while investors, buyers and project developers explore opportunities for greater cooperation. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and African Development Bank (AfDB) as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. With the summit now days away, Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director, says the breadth of participation has been particularly encouraging. “The real opportunity lies in bringing decision-makers, financiers, buyers and project developers into the same room. Those conversations can help unlock investment, strengthen project pipelines and accelerate the partnerships needed to scale African carbon markets.” The scale and diversity of participation heading to Kigali reflect a market increasingly attracting attention from governments, investors, buyers and project developers alike. As these groups come together over three days, the focus will shift from market ambition to the partnerships and transactions needed to move implementation forward. CMAS 2026 takes place from 13 to 15 October 2026 at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda.

artigo.texto: BYD has unveiled its new Atto 8 at the Paris Motor Show, a large seven-seat electric SUV capable of charging its battery from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes using the manufacturer’s latest charging technology. The Atto 8 will sit at the top of BYD’s European SUV range, above models such as the Atto 3 and Sealion 7. Measuring just over five metres long, it will compete with large electric family SUVs such as the Kia EV9, Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90. Two versions have been announced, both featuring a large 115kWh battery. The rear-wheel-drive ‘Design’ model produces 456hp and offers a claimed driving range of up to 405 miles on a single charge, while the more powerful ‘Excellence AWD’ produces 764hp and has a range of up to 374 miles. The all-wheel-drive model can accelerate from 0-62mph in 4.6 seconds, compared with eight seconds for the rear-wheel-drive version. Rapid charging The Atto 8 will be the first BYD model in Europe to use the manufacturer’s second-generation Blade Battery, introducing its new Flash Charging technology. BYD claims the battery can be charged from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or from 10% to 97% in nine minutes, when connected to a compatible charger. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, the manufacturer says a 20% to 97% charge can be completed in 12 minutes. These figures are considerably faster than the charging times currently offered by most electric SUVs, although achieving them will require access to BYD’s dedicated Flash Charging network. BYD plans to install 3,000 Flash Charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027. It has not yet confirmed how many will be located in the UK. Seven seats and plenty of equipment The Atto 8 has three rows of seats, with a 270-litre boot when all seven seats are in use. Folding the second and third rows increases luggage space to 1,960 litres, while an additional 136-litre storage compartment sits beneath the bonnet. Inside, both versions feature a 16-inch infotainment touchscreen with Google built-in, a ten-inch digital instrument display and a head-up display. Standard equipment includes leather upholstery, a panoramic glass roof and heated, ventilated and massaging seats in both the front and middle rows. Other features include three-zone climate control, wireless smartphone charging and a small refrigerated compartment that can also be used to keep food and drinks warm. The rear-wheel-drive model comes with a ten-speaker sound system, while the all-wheel-drive version gets a 21-speaker setup. When is it arriving? The BYD Atto 8 is expected to go on sale in European markets during the first three months of 2027. UK pricing, specifications and a customer delivery date have yet to be confirmed.

artigo.texto: Company Establishes Pilot Line in South Korea, Preparing 30MWh Sample Tests for North American Customers LG Energy Solution is accelerating the development of sodium-ion batteries as a potential next-generation growth driver, expanding its battery portfolio beyond conventional lithium-ion technology. The company has established a pilot production line in South Korea and is preparing to validate its technology with North American customers, positioning itself for an early entry into the emerging sodium-ion energy storage system (ESS) market. According to battery industry sources on Oct. 13, LG Energy Solution has established a sodium-ion battery pilot line at its Ochang Energy Plant in North Chungcheong Province. The company is currently conducting vehicle tests involving 12-volt and 24-volt batteries and plans to carry out sample testing for approximately 30 megawatt-hours (MWh) of sodium-ion ESS batteries with North American customers by the first half of 2027. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium instead of lithium as a key raw material, offering the potential for lower production costs and improved thermal safety. One of the technology's main advantages is the abundance and accessibility of its raw materials. Sodium is estimated to be approximately 1,200 times more abundant than lithium in the Earth's crust and can also be extracted from seawater, potentially reducing dependence on geographically concentrated supply chains. Sodium-ion technology also offers promising low-temperature performance. According to the performance figures cited in the industry, certain sodium-ion batteries can retain more than 90% of their charge capacity at temperatures as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius, although actual performance varies by cell chemistry and design. LG Energy Solution is pursuing a commercialization roadmap targeting 2027, initially focusing on automotive auxiliary batteries, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and stationary energy storage systems. The company eventually aims to expand into affordable electric vehicles as improvements in energy density make the technology suitable for a broader range of applications. It also plans to work with South Korean materials suppliers to establish a domestic sourcing network and strengthen its supply chain competitiveness. Competition is intensifying as other South Korean battery manufacturers advance their own sodium-ion development programs. Samsung SDI is developing UPS solutions for AI data centers and stationary ESS products using its proprietary technologies, with more detailed mass-production plans expected in 2027. SK On is also expanding its ESS development efforts, targeting completion of sodium-ion battery prototypes in 2027 and commercialization in 2028. Stationary energy storage is emerging as a promising initial market for sodium-ion technology because space and weight constraints are generally less demanding than those for electric vehicles. Although sodium-ion batteries typically have lower energy density than lithium-ion alternatives, their potential cost advantages and low-temperature performance could make them attractive for fixed-site applications. The South Korean government is also seeking to accelerate the commercialization of next-generation battery technologies. At a recent event, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs and the minister of climate, energy and environment pledged support for emerging technologies, including sodium-ion batteries, as part of the government's ambition to lead the next-generation battery market by 2035. Competition from Chinese manufacturers remains a major challenge. CATL, the world's leading battery manufacturer, unveiled a sodium-ion ESS product in June and announced plans for cumulative shipments of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) by the end of 2026. An LG Energy Solution representative said the company aims to establish a leading position in the emerging market by securing key technologies and supply chain capabilities at an early stage. The company's progress in customer validation, production readiness and cost competitiveness will be critical to determining how quickly sodium-ion batteries can become a commercially viable addition to its existing portfolio.

artigo.texto: China's lithium battery exports jump 36% in first three quarters; overseas plant construction and services become new competitive focus China's lithium battery exports maintained strong momentum through the first three quarters. Data released by the General Administration of Customs on October 14 showed that China's lithium battery exports grew 36.4% year-on-year in the first three quarters. More noteworthy is the structural shift: while exports to the United States declined, other markets are rapidly filling the gap, and the way Chinese battery companies participate in overseas markets is evolving from pure product supply to heavier models involving joint-venture plant construction and long-term operational services. According to customs data compiled by the Power Battery Applications Branch, lithium battery exports to the United States fell 24% in the first eight months, but exports to markets outside the U.S. grew approximately 53% on a comparable basis. This means the U.S. market shortfall has been fully offset by Europe, Asia, and other emerging markets, signaling a shift in the overseas focus of China's battery industry. Market share reshuffle: CATL gains as South Korean rivals retreat The sharp divergence in regional demand has directly redrawn the competitive landscape of the overseas power battery market. According to SNE Research, CATL's share of the non-China power battery market rose from 29% to 33.7% in the first eight months of this year, with European business maintaining growth and Asian installations increasing rapidly. In contrast, LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI—dragged down by weakening North American demand—saw their combined overseas share plunge from 37.9% to 26.8%. It should be noted that SNE Research's overseas installation figures include both batteries shipped with complete vehicles and batteries produced through overseas localization, which differs from customs export statistics. But both point to the same trend: Chinese battery companies are systematically strengthening their presence in overseas markets. BYD's domestic and overseas performance presents a stark contrast. In the first eight months, its global power battery share slipped from 17.1% to 15.1%, but its overseas share climbed from 8.2% to 11%. With domestic auto sales under pressure, vehicle operations in Europe, Asia, and South America continue to drive battery installation growth. BYD's own-brand vehicles remain the most important vehicle for expanding its overseas battery share. The second tier is catching up just as rapidly. In the first eight months, Gotion High-tech's overseas power battery share doubled to 4%, with overseas installations already surpassing Samsung SDI. EVE Energy rose from 0.9% to 2.1%, and SVOLT Energy Technology and CALB also increased their shares. Both CALB and EVE Energy entered the top ten in overseas power battery installations. Heavier cooperation models: from selling products to joint investment Independent battery makers expanding their overseas automaker client base are also being pushed to adapt to diversified technology roadmaps. Sunwoda has been supplying hybrid batteries in volume to Renault and Nissan, while CALB provides stable supply for Toyota and Mazda global models. Although the share of pure electric models in Europe is rising, conventional hybrids still account for the largest proportion, and international automakers' battery procurement is not following a single product route. The deepening of cooperation is even more pronounced. Volkswagen and Gotion High-tech have advanced to the joint-investment stage. Volkswagen wants to increase lithium iron phosphate (LFP) supply for mainstream-priced models and has pointed out that Europe lacks relevant scale production capacity. Under the announced arrangement, Gotion plans to invest approximately €1.1 billion (approximately $1.2 billion) for a 49% stake in a Spanish joint-venture plant, with the agreement still pending approval. For such partnerships, Chinese battery makers need to bring not only products and manufacturing technology, but also real capital to build local supply chains. Data released by InfoLink shows that the top five overseas energy storage cell shippers in the first half of this year were CATL, EVE Energy, BYD, Hithium, and Great Power. Hithium's strength is concentrated in large-scale storage projects, ranking second globally in utility-scale storage cell shipments. artigo.texto: Vattenfall has entered into a tolling agreement with Royal Vopak to obtain access to battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity in the Netherlands. Under the terms of the deal, Vattenfall will secure 100MW/400MW-hours (MWh) from a planned BESS near Meeden in Groningen province. The total project, developed and managed by Vopak, will have a capacity of 150MW and is expected to begin commercial operations in the second quarter of 2028. The agreement aims to support the balancing of fluctuations between electricity supply and demand as the Dutch power system incorporates increasing amounts of renewable energy. Battery storage enables the absorption of surplus electricity from renewable sources during periods of high production and can return power to the grid when demand rises or renewable output drops. According to Vattenfall, the secured BESS capacity will contribute to greater flexibility in its operations and aligns with the company’s objective to contract at least 1.5GW of BESS capacity across its core markets. Vattenfall wholesale energy head Erik Suichies said: “As the energy system becomes increasingly renewable, flexibility plays a crucial role in maintaining balance between supply and demand. Battery storage helps make better use of renewable electricity and contributes to a more reliable and efficient energy system. “We are pleased to partner with Vopak and support the development of large-scale energy storage in the Netherlands.” For Vopak, the deal represents a further step in its business expansion into electrical energy storage. Vopak battery energy storage solutions business development vice-president Jarno Veldhoven said: “With our aim to provide reliable and affordable battery systems to our customers we are excited to have Vattenfall as a long-term partner.” The partnership brings together Vattenfall and Vopak, both established players in the Dutch energy sector, and combines large-scale storage infrastructure with market expertise in flexibility optimisation. The companies aim to enhance the resilience of the Dutch electricity grid and support the integration of renewable energy sources. In July 2026, Vopak completed the acquisition of a 79% controlling interest in Green Energy Storage, a Netherlands-based developer specialising in BESS.

artigo.texto: Policy Update Anushree Khare BACKGROUND The Transformation of Industrial Carbon Pricing In the words of William D. Nordhaus: “Those who emit emissions do not have to pay to do so. Those who are affected by those emissions do not receive compensation. In short, carbon emissions represent a market failure which will require a price to be explicitly set.” During the formative years of industrial development, all forms of industry were able to treat the natural environment as their “free disposal” site for the effluents resulting from the combustion of fossil fuels. Economists recognized the discrepancy between the social cost of pollution and the private cost of pollution. They proposed remedies via tax (Pigou) or market based systems using well-defined property rights (Coase). These models provide the basis for modern-day international environmental policy. Although CO2 was historically viewed as a necessary by-product of large scale heavy industry, it is today becoming formally quantifiable and tradable on corporate balance sheets. Developing countries face two competing demands during this transition: - Expanding their primary sector to create jobs and build physical infrastructure and - Limiting emissions within an increasingly constrained global carbon budget. Market-based instruments in India initially focused on conserving energy before attempting to limit emissions directly. The Energy Conservation Act, 2001 empowered the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) to implement the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) Scheme in 2012. Under PAT, each facility would receive plant-specific energy reduction targets. Facilities achieving better than specified standards were rewarded. Energy-Saving Certificates (ESCerts) could also be traded among facilities across different industrial sectors. Although significant cumulative energy savings were realized by PAT’s application, its reliance on Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) had a fundamental flaw. It failed to ensure emissions reductions when a facility optimizes its SEC but increases its total carbon emissions due to fuel choice or expanded production such as switching to carbon-intensive captive coal or scaling clinker output. India sought to address this divergence and bring its domestic policy into alignment with its revised Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), specifically reducing the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 compared to 2005 levels. To achieve this goal, India passed the Energy Conservation Amendment Act in 2022. Subsequent to the Ministry of Power issuing notification no. F.No. 12/14/2019-EMD dated June 28, 2023, titled “Carbon Credit Trading Scheme”, India transitioned from regulating input energy efficiency denominated in Mtoe… to regulating greenhouse gas emissions intensity measured in (tCO2e) the form of Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs).With CCCs, India created a formal compliance mechanism where industrial emissions can be priced directly at the plant level. FUNCTIONING Market Design and Compliance Architecture The CCTS architecture distinguishes between two discrete but complementary markets: - a mandatory compliance market for energy-intensive sectors - a voluntary offset mechanism for non-obligated project developers Governance Nodes National Steering Committee for Indian Carbon Market (NSC-ICM): The NSC-ICM is co-chaired by the Secretary of the Ministry of Power and the Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MOEFCC). It is responsible for governing the market design as well as establishing the trajectory for the market and providing guidance with respect to the Indian Carbon Market (ICM) registry. Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE): The BEE acts as the Administrator of the market. It shall recommend sectoral trajectories; define the methodology for Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) under the Indian Carbon Market and manage the ICM registry. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC): The CERC regulates the trading of Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs) in secondary markets through the approved domestic power exchanges such as India Energy Exchange (IEX) and Power Exchange India Limited (PXIL). Accredited Carbon Verification Agencies (ACVAs): Independent third-party auditors accredited by the BEE to audit annually the amount of greenhouse gases claimed by each production unit according to ISO 14064/14065 standards. The Rate-Based Intensity Metric The CCTS is different from the EU ETS because, instead of imposing an absolute emissions limit (i.e., limiting total gross tonnage of CO₂ emitted), the CCTS applies a rate-based emissions intensity cap-and-trade system. That design represents the economic realities of emerging economies such as India: industrial capacity must expand to meet infrastructure and urbanization demands, but it must do so cleanly. The compliance metric is the Greenhouse Gas Emission Intensity (GEI), defined as follows: GEI = (Direct Scope 1 Emissions + Indirect emissions Scope 2) Gross Equivalent Production Unit - Direct emissions (Scope 1) include emissions resulting from fossil fuel combustion, calcination, catalytic reactions, and on-site chemical reductions. - Indirect emissions (Scope 2) represent electricity consumed by a facility using state- and year-specific grid emission factors provided by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). - Production units are measured per standard industry segment (for example, crude steel in metric tonnes,cement in clinker-adjusted metric tonnes; primary aluminium). PERFORMANCE The transition into CCTS is structured in multi-year compliance cycles, with the inaugural cycle covering FY 2025–26 and FY 2026–27. The scheme initially subsumes the heavy industrial sectors formerly regulated under PAT. Compliance targets are reset in triennial trajectories, requiring facilities to outpace business-as-usual technological advancements to generate surplus credits.
