artigo.texto: Planning commission weighs future of data centers in New Orleans The City Planning Commission has been tasked with recommending guidelines for data center creation in the city. Planning commission weighs future of data centers in New Orleans The City Planning Commission has been tasked with recommending guidelines for data center creation in the city. The New Orleans Planning Commission failed to approve a recommendation for data center creation guidelines Tuesday. Planning staff were tasked with creating definitions for data centers and making a recommendation for which, if any, should be allowed in New Orleans. The planning staff's recommendation was to prohibit large and hyperscale data centers, and allow small and medium data centers in certain parts of the city, with certain restrictions. According to their definitions, small data centers must be no greater than 20,000 sq. ft. and consume no more than 5 megawatts of power. Medium data centers must be no greater than 100,000 sq. ft. and consume no more than 20 megawatts of power. Large and hyperscale data centers are greater than 100,000 sq. ft. and consume greater than 20 megawatts of power. Planning commissioners decided the recommendation was not ready to go to City Council. They voted against approving the recommendation, and are now asking City Council to extend the moratorium on new data center creation. City Council approved a one-year moratorium back in January, in order to give the planning staff time to make a recommendation and come up with definitions. In the meantime, the commission is asking the planning staff to make amendments to the recommendation. They want to change the definitions for small and medium data centers. They are suggesting a small data center be reduced from 20,000 sq. ft. to 10,000 sq. ft. and the maximum usage be reduced from 5 megawatts to 3 megawatts. They also want the maximum size for a medium data center to be reduced from 100,000 sq. ft. to 50,000 sq. ft. and the maximum energy usage to be reduced from 20 megawatts to 15 megawatts. Their other suggestion is to increase the buffer between homes and data centers from 500 ft. to 1000 ft. The decision came after several people spoke against the recommendation during public comment, and a small group gathered outside City Hall ahead of the vote. The demonstration was led by members of the Party for Socialism and Liberation. They believe no type of data center should be allowed in New Orleans. They cited quality of life and environmental concerns, and said any new data center would put a strain on utilities. According to the planning staff report, it was found that many small data centers already exist in New Orleans. There are at least four operating in the downtown area. The report also says the biggest concern with new data centers is their impact on water and power usage. The item to approve a recommendation was originally on the agenda for the commission's August 25 meeting, and was deferred multiple times.

artigo.texto: Agricultural equipment has relied on diesel engines and hydraulic systems for decades, but battery-powered machinery is beginning to appear on farms across North America. This shift affects not only how equipment operates but also how farmers maintain their fleets, what skills repair technicians need, and which components fail most often. Understanding these changes helps farm operators make informed decisions about equipment purchases and maintenance planning. The Maintenance Advantage of Electric Drive Systems Electric motors contain fewer moving parts than internal combustion engines. A typical diesel tractor engine has pistons, valves, camshafts, fuel injectors, and turbochargers that require regular service intervals. Electric motors eliminate these components entirely, reducing the number of maintenance tasks. Oil changes, filter replacements, and cooling system flushes remain necessary for tractors with diesel engines, but electric alternatives require none of these services for their drive systems. This reduction in maintenance tasks does not mean electric equipment is maintenance-free. Battery packs require thermal management systems to prevent overheating, and these systems need inspection. Electrical connections must be kept clean and tight to prevent resistance that can cause heat buildup. The regenerative braking systems common in electric farm equipment need periodic checks to ensure they capture energy efficiently during deceleration. Battery Management and Replacement Costs Lithium-ion batteries degrade over time regardless of use patterns, though heavy discharge cycles accelerate this process. Most agricultural battery packs are designed to retain 70 to 80 percent of their original capacity after several thousand charge cycles. For equipment that operates daily during planting and harvest seasons, this translates to several years of service before capacity loss becomes noticeable. Replacement costs for battery packs remain the largest concern for farmers considering electric equipment. Unlike engine rebuilds, which can extend the life of diesel tractors at moderate expense, battery replacement often represents a significant portion of the equipment’s original value. Farmers must factor this eventual cost into their total ownership calculations. Some manufacturers offer battery leasing programs to spread this expense over time, though these arrangements add ongoing costs that traditional equipment does not carry. Impact on Hay and Forage Operations Hay production equipment has particularly demanding duty cycles. Balers, mowers, and rakes operate for extended periods during narrow weather windows when conditions are right for cutting and baling. Battery capacity becomes a limiting factor during these intensive work periods. A diesel-powered baler can refuel in minutes and continue working, while battery-powered alternatives require charging time that can interrupt operations during critical harvest windows. For farmers managing hay operations across Tennessee, Kentucky, and Illinois, this operational reality shapes equipment decisions. Traditional repair services remain essential for maintaining the diesel-powered fleets that most operations depend on. Facilities offering tractor repair services and agricultural equipment maintenance understand that new holland hay equipment and similar conventional machinery will continue to dominate hay production for the foreseeable future, particularly in regions where charging infrastructure is limited and work schedules are dictated by weather patterns rather than planned intervals. Training Requirements for Technicians Repair shops that have serviced diesel equipment for decades now face the need to train technicians in high-voltage electrical systems. Working on battery packs rated at 400 volts or higher requires specific safety protocols that differ fundamentally from mechanical repairs. Technicians must understand battery management systems, power electronics, and diagnostic software that reads error codes from electronic control units rather than mechanical symptoms. This training gap affects rural areas more severely than urban regions. Agricultural equipment dealers in smaller communities may struggle to justify the cost of certification programs and specialized diagnostic tools when only a handful of electric machines operate in their service area. The result is a transitional period where farmers with electric equipment may face longer wait times for repairs or need to transport machines to distant service centers with qualified technicians. Safety Considerations in Farm Equipment Electrification Electric farm equipment introduces new safety concerns alongside its operational benefits. High-voltage systems remain energized even when the equipment is turned off, creating shock hazards during maintenance or after accidents. Battery fires, though rare, burn intensely and require specialized extinguishing methods that differ from diesel fuel fires. Farmers and technicians accustomed to conventional machinery safety protocols must learn additional precautions specific to electrical systems. The silent operation of electric motors also creates situational awareness challenges. Diesel engines announce their presence with noise and exhaust, alerting nearby workers to moving equipment. Electric tractors and implements operate quietly enough that workers may not notice approaching machinery, particularly in noisy environments like grain handling facilities or livestock barns. This characteristic requires deliberate changes to farm safety practices and communication protocols among crew members. The Role of Hybrid Systems Many manufacturers are introducing hybrid equipment that combines diesel engines with electric drive systems rather than moving directly to pure battery power. artigo.texto: This transition process creates a huge demand for resources to invest in technological innovation, transform production methods, use energy efficiently, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Expanding resources for green transformation At the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance-Investment Newspaper on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh emphasized that, in addition to resources from the State budget, capital markets, and money markets, developing new market mechanisms is crucial in mobilizing resources for green transformation. According to the Deputy Governor, by establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This provides businesses with additional motivation and resources to continue investing in the transition process, instead of relying primarily on bank credit. In recent years, the banking sector has gradually improved its policy framework, promoting green credit and managing environmental and social risks in lending activities. Capital flows are directed towards areas that bring environmental benefits, especially sustainable agriculture , green energy, and projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Data from the State Bank of Vietnam shows that by the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856 trillion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. During the period 2017-2025, green credit maintained an average growth rate of over 20% per year. Outstanding loans are mainly concentrated in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; green energy accounts for nearly 28%. Notably, outstanding loans that have undergone environmental and social risk assessment reached over VND 6.2 million trillion, equivalent to more than 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy. However, according to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, the important thing for green credit is not only that the capital is disbursed to projects identified as green, but also that the results of energy saving, emission reduction, and environmental protection achieved by borrowers can be verified. From this perspective, green credit and carbon markets have a mutually supportive relationship. Credit provides resources for businesses to innovate technologically, improve energy efficiency, and thus generate emission reductions. Conversely, when carbon markets operate effectively, the recorded and commercialized emission reductions can generate additional revenue, improve cash flow, support debt repayment capacity, and enhance credit quality. Speaking at the conference, Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-in-Chief of the Finance-Investment Newspaper, argued that if the carbon exchange is the infrastructure of the market, then credit policy, the banking system, and the capital market are the driving forces for the green transition process. According to Mr. Pham Van Hoanh, a market that wants to develop sustainably needs not only an exchange, commodities, and trading regulations, but also liquidity, data, verification mechanisms, trust between buyers and sellers, and a sufficiently strong financial ecosystem. The crucial issue is how to gradually make carbon value a reliable factor in financial decisions, helping capital flow to the right, effective projects. Unblocking bottlenecks Despite the significant potential of the carbon market, translating emission reduction results into actual cash flow still faces considerable challenges. A project's ability to reduce emissions does not automatically guarantee carbon credits, buyers, or a sufficiently stable revenue stream for banks to consider granting credit. Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank, analyzed that the capital needs for emission reduction projects often arise right from the preparation and implementation phases. Meanwhile, carbon credits can only be generated after emission reduction results are measured, reported, verified, and all related procedures are completed. The time gap between investment needs and the time when carbon revenue is generated is a challenge for both businesses and credit institutions. For agriculture and forestry, the dispersed nature of production makes the cost of measuring and verifying emission reduction results relatively high. If each producer has to carry out the entire process themselves, economic efficiency is difficult to guarantee. Meanwhile, linkages through cooperatives, raw material areas, or production chains require clear data governance mechanisms and benefit sharing. Based on this practice, Agribank proposes a "two-tiered cash flow" assessment principle. In this principle, cash flow from core production and business activities remains the foundation for debt repayment; carbon revenue is only considered as a supplementary source, depending on the level of legal, technical, and commercial certainty. From an international perspective, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, noted that the carbon market provides economic incentives for emission reduction, while credit provides the capital for investments. It is estimated that Vietnam needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Of this, the capital needed for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, and for emission reduction is approximately US$114 billion. artigo.texto: South Korea is set to launch the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) next year, a platform for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits. The initiative will utilize blockchain technology to record core data, aiming to enhance the credibility of carbon credits. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il announced the finalized “Detailed Implementation Plan for the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)” after a meeting of economy-related ministers. The GVCM will facilitate the issuance and trading of carbon credits derived from international greenhouse gas reduction projects. Credits will be categorized into two types: GVCM A, usable for both regulatory compliance and voluntary environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities when host countries authorize transfers, and GVCM NA, restricted to voluntary ESG purposes. The government plans to sign letters of intent with potential participating countries at COP31 next month and is in discussions with the World Bank and Green Climate Fund to convert existing project credits. Blockchain Integration for Enhanced Credibility A key feature of the GVCM is the integration of blockchain technology for data management. Core information, including project operators, reduction volumes, unique identification numbers, and methodologies, will be recorded on the blockchain. Other data will be stored in traditional databases. This selective application of blockchain aims to balance management efficiency with data integrity and stability. Initially, credits will be issued in electronic form and traded on South Korea’s voluntary carbon market exchange. The government is considering parallel issuance in digital asset form in the future, contingent on trading volumes, the evolving digital asset legislation, and market confidence. The market’s name change from “Global Voluntary Carbon Market” to “Global Verified Carbon Market” reflects its expanded scope to include regulatory markets. Dual-Track Credit System and Governance The GVCM’s dual-track credit system differentiates based on host country authorization. GVCM A credits, with host country approval, can satisfy regulatory requirements such as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement or the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), as well as voluntary ESG activities. GVCM NA credits, lacking such authorization, are limited to voluntary corporate environmental initiatives but can be upgraded to GVCM A if corresponding adjustment approval is later granted. The government is also exploring links between the GVCM and South Korea’s domestic emissions trading scheme, provided that credibility standards, Paris Agreement Article 6 requirements, and domestic legal conditions are met. The issuing body will comprise a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is currently serving as the interim secretariat. Governance structures are designed to ensure direct participation from developing countries, allowing them to influence operational processes and gain experience in carbon market management. The project sectors will align with participating countries’ development needs and South Korea’s technological strengths, encompassing areas like mangrove restoration, agricultural waste treatment, methane capture, and energy efficiency improvements. The anticipated growth of the international carbon credit market, projected by MSCI to reach $45 billion, $250 billion by 2050, underscores the significance of standardized and credible market criteria. The GVCM aims to address current controversies surrounding credit credibility and actual reduction effectiveness by establishing clear international market criteria. The government plans to leverage networks such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) and the Asia-Pacific Carbon Market Roundtable (APCMR) to secure participating countries. Full-scale operations are expected to commence after the establishment of the issuing body next year and the specification of project structures. The GVCM initiative aligns with the broader trend of major financial institutions exploring blockchain for core operations, as detailed in reports on how major financial institutions move core operations onto blockchain networks. This move also echoes the strategic planning seen in projects like the CENTEL Blockchain Roadmap, which pairs CNT participation with network plans, as highlighted in CENTEL Blockchain Roadmap Pairs CNT Participation With Network Plans. The involvement of entities like the World Bank and Green Climate Fund in such initiatives reflects a growing institutional interest in blockchain-based solutions for global challenges, similar to how Chainlink Co-Founder presented blockchain finance at a major banking conference. Frequently asked questions - What is the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)? The GVCM is a platform South Korea will launch next year for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits, utilizing blockchain for enhanced credibility. - How will blockchain be used in the GVCM? Blockchain technology will be applied to record core data, such as project operators and reduction methodologies, to ensure the credibility and stability of carbon credits. - What are the two categories of GVCM credits? Credits are divided into GVCM A, usable for regulatory compliance and ESG activities, and GVCM NA, limited to voluntary ESG purposes, based on host country transfer authorization. - Who will be involved in the GVCM's issuing body? The issuing body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat, with plans for developing countries to participate directly. - When will the GVCM fully launch? The GVCM will fully launch starting next year, with plans to sign letters of intent at COP31 next month and establish the issuing body in the coming year.

artigo.texto: Dell shares plummeted 11% on Wednesday and dragged down other data center equipment names on mounting concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout. Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, Oracle and Super Micro all joined in the downward slide. In a report to clients on Wednesday, analysts at Barclays downgraded its rating on Dell, HPE and NetApp, "after a significant run and on enterprise AI timing." Makers of data center servers and other backend equipment have been favored on Wall Street this year on optimism that they'll be selling huge volumes of gear tied to demand for AI chips and systems for years into the future. Dell has been one of the top performers on the market, up more than 300% this year, while HPE has jumped about 160% and NetApp has doubled. However, sentiment toward the AI infrastructure space has shifted of late due in part to concerning revenue figures out of OpenAI and more broadly out of fear that rising interest rates will create a challenging environment as so much of the buildout is reliant on debt. Oracle, a heavy borrower, dropped 9% on Wednesday and is now down 33% for the year while neocloud CoreWeave plunged 15%, wiping out its gains for 2026. The Barclays analysts said they haven't seen a "meaningful AI inflection" when it comes to enterprise spending for Dell, HPE and NetApp, lowering the rating on each to the equivalent of a hold from buy. They instead attribute increased revenue to the global memory shortage and noted that infrastructure companies have passed the higher price of memory along to customers. "There is growing sentiment about enterprise AI adoption creating a hardware refresh," the Barclays analysts wrote, adding that businesses are typically allocating just 5% of their IT budgets to AI. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time." The Barclays analysts also found that only about a quarter of total enterprise AI spend is going towards hardware. They said normalizing and eventually declining memory prices could weigh on infrastructure-related revenue. Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and stocks were hit this week after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress over the weekend on a new chip structure. Micron is down 11% for the week, while South Korea's SK Hynix has tumbled 13% in U.S. trading and Western Digital has dropped more than 8%. The company also announced the successful financial close for the facility, noting that it went into commercial service on 17 September. Bocanova 2 aims to provide additional flexibility to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas electricity grid amid rising demand, particularly as data centres and other large energy consumers expand operations in the state. Located in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area, Bocanova 2 follows Bocanova 1, an earlier 150MW battery storage project at the same site. According to Nightpeak Energy, Bocanova 1 commenced commercial operation in August 2025. The combined projects form part of the company’s ongoing battery storage development in a region recognised for its fast-growing power demand. Bocanova 2 is equipped with Tesla’s Megapack 2 XL lithium-ion battery systems. It operates under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty. The financing structure included a tax equity bridge loan and a construction-to-term loan provided by MUFG Bank, while U.S. Bank supplied traditional tax equity for the project. Nightpeak Energy co-founder and CEO/chief development officer Paris Hays said: “We are seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand. “Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change. “With 300MW now operating at Bocanova, we are putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country.” Nightpeak Energy was founded in 2022. Since then, the company has developed and acquired more than 1GW of operating and de-risked capacity, including battery storage, gas-fired generation and powered land development. The company continues to develop additional flexible generation and large-load projects as part of efforts to address growing power needs in the US.

artigo.texto: Nas colinas de Águas de Santa Bárbara, um município de cerca de 7 mil habitantes no interior de São Paulo, o Patria Investimentos está testando uma nova tese climática para o seu Reforest Fund. O Patria entrou no mercado de capital natural olhando para uma das apostas mais recorrentes da transição climática: o carbono. Acabou encontrando uma oportunidade menos óbvia – e bem mais saborosa: o avocado. É na região centro-oeste do estado de São Paulo que a gestora está investindo cerca de R$ 100 milhões para produzir a fruta, ainda pouco conhecida dos brasileiros. O projeto combina produção agrícola, restauração ambiental e geração de créditos de carbono. O Patria comprou duas fazendas que juntas somam mil hectares, e fechou uma parceria com a Jaguacy, que é um dos maiores produtores e exportadores brasileiros da fruta e vai tocar a operação. Hoje o Brasil produz pouco mais de 60 mil toneladas do abacate Hass, uma variedade criada na Califórnia há um século e que reina no avocado toast e nas saladas dos americanos. Boa parte da produção nacional é voltada para a exportação. O Reforest Fund foi desenhado para combinar diferentes fontes de capital – e diferentes interesses. De um lado estão investidores que olham para a agenda de restauração, biodiversidade e descarbonização. De outro, o capital mais tradicional, que precisa enxergar retorno, risco e previsibilidade de receita. “Ao longo do desenho do fundo, a pergunta era quanto da exposição ao mercado de carbono queríamos ter. É uma solução relevante, porque muitos dos esforços de descarbonização passam pelo mecanismo de offset. Mas o mercado tem se desenvolvido de uma forma que exige soluções mais customizadas. A gente sabia que o avocado preenchia essa lacuna,” disse Pedro Faria, sócio do Pátria e co-CEO da vertical de high growth. O fundo nasceu com a meta de mobilizar R$ 2 bilhões — e já chegou perto disso. Na primeira rodada, anunciada pelo Patria em 2025, foram captados R$ 100 milhões com a Desenvolve SP, a agência de fomento do Governo de São Paulo; David Vélez, o fundador do Nubank; Teresa e Candido Bracher, reconhecidos ambientalistas; e o Enseada, o family office dos Larragoiti. Mais recentemente, o fundo atraiu novos investidores – entre eles a Vale – e chegou a R$ 160 milhões. No momento, o Patria está em negociações com investidores institucionais internacionais. Outra frente de captação vem de instrumentos de capital catalítico – que aceitam maior risco, menor retorno ou prazos mais longos . No início do ano, o fundo foi um dos sete selecionados na chamada pública de mitigação climática que vai destinar R$ 4,3 bilhões em aportes do BNDESPar. Nessa frente, o veículo pode receber até R$ 500 milhões. Além disso, o Patria também vai acessar recursos do Fundo Clima e do terceiro leilão do Eco Invest. Os recursos do capital catalítico funcionam como uma espécie de colchão para atrair investidores. “O capital catalítico passa a ser uma camada de proteção. Nesse modelo, o dinheiro que pode ser ‘perdido’ é utilizado antes dos recursos do investidor tradicional,” disse Faria. A lógica adotada é que cada investidor também possa enxergar uma porta de entrada diferente para o mesmo ativo. Para uma empresa com metas de descarbonização e restauração, o projeto entrega atributos ambientais. É o caso da Vale, que entrou no fundo para acessar os créditos gerados pelo sequestro de carbono. Já para um investidor financeiro, a produção agrícola e a receita associada aos créditos ajudam a compor a equação de risco e retorno. “No nível da operação é um arranjo agroflorestal, no nível do fundo é um arranjo multifacetado de investidores entrando em cotas,” disse o executivo. Foi nesse desenho que o avocado ganhou espaço. Estima-se que o mercado global da fruta movimente cerca de US$ 20 bilhões por ano. O Brasil ocupa hoje a sétima posição entre os produtores, mas, na visão de Faria, tem condições para avançar bastante. “Quando você olha a questão de custo, competitividade e acesso a dinheiro, não há nenhuma razão para que o Brasil não esteja entre os três maiores produtores mundiais de avocado.” Para o Patria, os mercados europeu e asiático são o foco para a exportação. Em 2025, Japão e Chile passaram a importar a fruta do Brasil. A parceria com a Jaguacy, que cultiva 1200 hectares de avocado e atende clientes como Carrefour e Pão de Açúcar, garante não só a operação das fazendas como também o acesso à infraestrutura de processamento e aos canais de distribuição. A região de Águas de Santa Bárbara escolhida não foi por acaso. As propriedades estão em uma área de solo fértil, altitude adequada e disponibilidade de água, mas que também passou por ciclos de agricultura, pecuária e monoculturas que degradaram parte do território. O cultivo será feito em sistema agroflorestal, combinando as fileiras de avocado com espécies nativas, que protegem as árvores frutíferas contra potenciais danos causados pelo vento. Dos quase 1 mil hectares, a previsão é plantar cerca de 100 hectares neste semestre. A primeira colheita virá em quatro anos. O projeto também servirá como laboratório para o que pode vir depois. O Patria já identificou café e cacau como próximas culturas a serem desenvolvidas e vê espaço para levar o modelo a outros biomas. Para Faria, as mudanças climáticas estão tornando a produção de alimentos uma questão cada vez mais estratégica para o capital. A demanda global cresce, enquanto eventos climáticos mais frequentes aumentam o risco de choques de oferta. É essa combinação que transforma a agricultura resiliente em uma tese de investimento: produzir mais, restaurar áreas degradadas e, ao mesmo tempo, construir cadeias de alimentos menos vulneráveis às mudanças do clima. O avocado do Patria deverá ganhar mesas mundo afora. O carbono, por sua vez, fica como crédito para o planeta.

artigo.texto: With participation confirmed from 24 African countries and 45 countries globally, CMAS 2026 will bring together more than 100 speakers, over 50 investors, buyers and financiers, 20 African governments and more than 40 project developers in Kigali from 13 to 15 October. The diversity of participation reflects growing engagement with African carbon markets from governments, project developers, financiers and credit buyers. The international presence will bring African policymakers and projects into direct contact with organisations active across carbon markets globally. For Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance & Stakeholder Engagement for the Government of Nigeria, the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 represents an opportunity for continental participants to play a central role in determining how the market develops. “This gathering of the leading players in African carbon markets represents a continental ownership in driving the future of carbon markets shaped by Africans, for the benefit of Africa.” Investor and buyer participation will add an important commercial dimension to the gathering. Dedicated Investor Roundtables will provide focused opportunities for capital providers, buyers and project developers to engage directly, while meetings across the summit will allow participants to identify potential partnerships and areas for further engagement. More than 40 project developers and project representatives working across sectors including nature-based solutions, agriculture, waste, clean cooking and carbon removals will also participate, providing investors and buyers with direct exposure to projects from across the continent. For Maggie Kinyanjui, Sourcing Manager, Africa, Climate Impact Partners, greater engagement between project developers, buyers and investors is essential to building a stronger African carbon market. “Africa should not just participate in carbon markets. We should help shape them. The opportunity is to build a market that attracts capital, rewards integrity and ensures that value reaches the countries and communities delivering climate impact.” The timing also coincides with an active period for international carbon markets. These discussions will take place at a time when key international carbon market rules and mechanisms continue to evolve. The Article 6.4 Supervisory Body, which oversees the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, is holding its 23rd meeting this week in Bonn, immediately ahead of CMAS 2026. Amy Rhoades, Chief Communications & Engagement Officer, Carbon Standards, says meaningful engagement across the carbon value chain is critical to the growth of credible carbon removal solutions on the continent. “Africa isn’t waiting for global carbon markets to mature; it’s actively building them. At Carbon Markets Africa Summit, we’re not just sponsoring a conference, we’re engaging the policymakers, entrepreneurs, and buyers who are building the carbon removal ecosystem in Africa. That engagement is the future of credible CDR and that’s why Carbon Standards is in Kigali.” Against that international backdrop, discussions in Kigali will provide an opportunity for African governments and market participants to consider what developments in the global market mean in practice for the continent, while investors, buyers and project developers explore opportunities for greater cooperation. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and African Development Bank (AfDB) as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. With the summit now days away, Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director, says the breadth of participation has been particularly encouraging. “The real opportunity lies in bringing decision-makers, financiers, buyers and project developers into the same room. Those conversations can help unlock investment, strengthen project pipelines and accelerate the partnerships needed to scale African carbon markets.” The scale and diversity of participation heading to Kigali reflect a market increasingly attracting attention from governments, investors, buyers and project developers alike. As these groups come together over three days, the focus will shift from market ambition to the partnerships and transactions needed to move implementation forward. CMAS 2026 takes place from 13 to 15 October 2026 at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda.

artigo.texto: Julio Friedman, chief scientist at Carbon Direct, warned a captive audience to “proceed with caution” regarding space-based data centers (SBDCs) during a talk at the Press Building on Monday. The event, hosted by the Precourt Institute of Energy, summarized an upcoming report about the dangers of space-based data centers. Friedman spoke alongside David Sandalow, inaugural fellow at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, and Roger Aines, the former energy program chief scientist at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The trio, along with a few other scientists, has spent the last few months researching the scientific and social implications of sending data centers into space. Sending data centers into space doesn’t actually mean sending a large megaton computer into orbit. According to Sandalow, a single SBDC will consist of “approximately 10,000 satellites, orbiting in a constellation.” These satellites would all communicate with each other to avoid collisions and operate as a singular, large data center. They would orbit along the terminator — the line that separates dusk and dawn — and “as a result, have access to 24/7 solar power,” as Sandalow explained. The swarms of satellites would have to be in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) to stay close enough to devices on Earth and avoid lag. Scientists are developing SBDCs to address the rising need for compute, the processing power required to run large AI models. By 2030, “700 large launches a year are going to be required to put roughly 10% of projected global AI compute in space,” Sandalow said. This year, SpaceX has launched under 120 rockets. All three presenters warned that innovation and development without extensive testing would lead to several problems. “The American Astronomical Society says that with the larger climate of these constellations, you will see more satellites than stars in a nice sky, particularly [at] dawn and dusk,” Sandalow said. “There is a very significant risk of cascading collisions [that] might render portion[s] of the lower orbit unusable for communication satellites or other types of uses in use.” Sandalow also warned that a sudden increase in rocket launches and landings could re-threaten the ozone layer, which has recovered tremendously under the Montreal Protocol, an international treaty that phased out ozone-depleting substances like chlorofluorocarbons. “Aluminum oxides and the soot are particularly bad because those create surfaces for the surface chemistry that destroys the ozone,” Friedman said, detailing the effects of two emittants released by rocket launches. Sandalow also emphasized the importance of energy, as it’s “at the core of so many aspects of human life,” he said in an interview with The Daily. “[I’ve] seen students paying very close attention to global warming threats, because I think that’s going to make a huge difference in our ability to solve this problem.” Arpita Kalra, director of marketing and engagement at the Precourt Institute of Energy, said the institute hosts these events to expose students to diverse perspectives. “We organize a lot of these seminars, and most of our seminars are open to the public,” Kalra said. The Precourt Institute of Energy organizes roughly 200 events a year, according to Kalra. Cheng Ma, a visiting political science and anthropology researcher from Berlin, said he found the event “quite interesting.” He attended the talk to stay informed on conversations concerning data center development. “We still talk about different [geopolitical] boundaries[except] now it’s space,” he said, describing space as a new frontier in international development. Sandalow emphasized the importance of staying informed, especially for students. “[Energy] is a multigenerational problem. So we need the younger generation really focused on this issue,” he said.

artigo.texto: Johannes Linder, Director, System Design & Innovation at BELECTRIC, a member of the Elevion Group, shared ideas on optimizing system designs for PV-plus-storage hybrid power plants, particularly in Germany, at the TaiyangNews Solar Power Plants & Storage Conference 2026. His presentation focused on hybrid system design optimization for engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) firms and investors. Linder shared a German co-located PV + battery energy storage system (BESS) system design case study with a 1:1 PV + BESS AC-coupled configuration as a reference project. In 2024, BELECTRIC simulated the project and found that a 58 MW BESS size corresponds to the project's highest Net Present Value (NPV). NPV, which indicates how much value a project is expected to add to a business in current monetary terms, is considered a key performance indicator (KPI) for optimization. Back then, the company could adjust BESS and PV size by optimizing the ratio of fixed-tilt and tracker-based systems within a given land area to get maximum BESS revenues. Linder argued that although these optimization types still apply to grey BESS, which charges itself from either PV or the grid, Germany has changed a few frameworks. These include regulations backed by grid oversizing, such as flexible grid connection agreements (FCAs), grid connection restrictions for grey BESSs, right balancing between the grid operator's acceptance and project profitability, and a focus on green BESS. Green BESS allows only renewable energy to charge it. From an investor's perspective, the company follows optimized system design in three stages: 1) Set the project frameworks; 2) Define technology and design parameters; and 3) Check sensitivities/critical assumptions. However, Linder noted that these procedures make hourly battery simulation challenging, with many possibilities and scenarios. The company has adopted a ‘practical’ four-step approach to address challenges. They are: pre-selection of PV system designs, BESS optimization for pre-selected designs, PV + BESS market value analysis and clustering, and simulation of all relevant scenarios. In a nutshell, this clustering of market value analysis reduces the need to handle too many simulations. Linder shared a case study for a PV + green BESS hybrid plant system design with an AC-coupled system architecture, no grid restrictions, and within 33 ha of land in Central Germany, following these steps. The simulation results showed that the optimized BESS size is 40% of PV MWp with a corresponding backup duration of 4 hours. For PV + BESS optimization, a 45 MWp PV array mounted on a fixed mounting structure with a 3P module mounting architecture at a 10° inclination angle showed the highest NPV and ranked first. In comparison, modules mounted on trackers, those installed along the east-west (E-W) direction, and those mounted vertically relative to flat land ranked at 178, 782, and 3,005, respectively.

artigo.texto: Na manhã de 14 de outubro de 2026, o jornal Finanças e Investimentos, em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã, organizou o seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde" em Hanói . Em seu discurso de abertura no workshop, o Sr. Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-Chefe do Jornal de Finanças e Investimentos, afirmou que, na busca pelo objetivo de crescimento verde e pelo compromisso com emissões líquidas zero até 2050, o Vietnã está gradualmente aprimorando instrumentos políticos e mecanismos de mercado para mobilizar recursos para o processo de transição verde. O lançamento do mercado doméstico de carbono em 29 de junho de 2026 não apenas marca a formação de um novo mercado, mas também exige a consolidação de um ecossistema financeiro para garantir seu desenvolvimento eficiente e sustentável. Se as bolsas de carbono são a infraestrutura do mercado, então a política de crédito, o sistema bancário e o mercado de capitais são as forças motrizes por trás da transição verde. Dentro desse ecossistema, a política de crédito desempenha um papel fundamental na canalização de recursos financeiros, apoiando empresas e indivíduos a investirem em atividades de redução de emissões e conectando os objetivos de desenvolvimento sustentável aos fluxos de capital da economia . Em outras palavras, a transformação verde deve, em última análise, se traduzir em investimentos concretos: investimentos em tecnologias mais limpas, uso mais eficiente de energia, mudanças nos processos de produção, desenvolvimento da agricultura de baixa emissão, proteção e desenvolvimento florestal, tratamento de resíduos, desenvolvimento de energias renováveis e construção de cadeias de suprimentos mais sustentáveis… E para que esses projetos sejam implementados na prática, é necessário um sistema financeiro capaz de identificar, valorizar, alocar e gerenciar fluxos de capital verde. O arcabouço legal para o mercado de carbono do Vietnã foi estabelecido pela Lei de Proteção Ambiental de 2020 e detalhado por meio de diversos documentos. Mais recentemente, incluem-se o Decreto 29/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta o mercado interno de carbono, e o Decreto 112/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta o mercado internacional de resultados de redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. Ao mesmo tempo, o Vietnã também adquiriu experiência na comercialização dos resultados da redução de emissões no mercado internacional. Em março de 2024, o Vietnã recebeu, pela primeira vez, US$ 51,5 milhões do Banco Mundial, referentes a 10,3 milhões de toneladas de resultados comprovados de redução de emissões no âmbito do Programa de Redução de Emissões da Região Centro-Norte. Segundo o editor-chefe do jornal Finanças e Investimentos, a negociação de cotas de emissão no sistema de negociação, que será implementada a partir de 29 de junho de 2026, não se trata apenas da formação de um novo mercado. Mais importante ainda, ela cria uma nova abordagem para a avaliação econômica das atividades de redução de emissões. No entanto, também precisamos reconhecer, de forma realista, que a formação de um novo mercado de carbono é apenas o começo. Um mercado sustentável precisa de mais do que apenas uma bolsa de valores, commodities e regulamentações comerciais. Ele também requer liquidez, dados, mecanismos de verificação, confiança entre compradores e vendedores e um ecossistema financeiro robusto para dar suporte aos participantes do mercado. Ao mesmo tempo, essa jornada rumo à sustentabilidade ainda levanta muitas questões que precisam de respostas de todas as partes. Quais gargalos precisam ser abordados no arcabouço legal do mercado de carbono e nos mecanismos financeiros desse mercado? Como o capital verde pode fluir para os projetos certos? Como os bancos podem avaliar as oportunidades e os riscos de um projeto verde? Como as empresas podem demonstrar a eficácia de sua transformação e atrair capital não apenas de bancos, mas também se conectar mais estreitamente com fontes de capital de médio e longo prazo do mercado de capitais? E como o valor do carbono pode se tornar gradualmente um fator confiável nas decisões financeiras das partes interessadas relevantes? O editor-chefe do jornal Finanças e Investimentos enfatizou que, para responder a essas perguntas, o jornal está organizando o seminário de hoje com o tema "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando os Fluxos de Capital Verde". Quando as empresas percebem os benefícios econômicos da redução das emissões, os bancos e as instituições do mercado de capitais conseguem gerir os fluxos de capital de forma eficaz, os investidores percebem o valor e os produtores beneficiam proporcionalmente, então o mercado de carbono cria verdadeiramente um novo impulso para a economia. Com esse espírito em mente, o jornal Finance and Investment espera que a conferência se torne um fórum substancial para que agências reguladoras, bancos, empresas, especialistas e organizações troquem ideias, forneçam feedback e busquem soluções viáveis.

artigo.texto: Planning for development is notoriously local in Pennsylvania, but one of the largest and most contentious building proposals in the region is now heading into a county-run public input process. Springdale Borough is one of around two dozen municipalities in Allegheny County that do not have ordinances establishing their jurisdiction over subdivision and land use decisions. Instead, the county carries out the process. Over the next two weeks, Allegheny County Economic Development’s (ACED) Planning Division will hold public meetings as part of this process for the proposed development of a data center campus, which has drawn opposition from residents of the borough and the surrounding community due to concerns over noise, air pollution and transparency from the developer Allegheny DC Propco LLC. The first meeting, which will be held virtually tonight, has even drawn a watch party organized by Save Allegheny Valley Environment (SAVE). SAVE Treasurer Marty Garrigan said that group has been educating residents on the process dictated by the county’s SALDO, or Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance. For Garrigan, the preferred outcome would be a denial. “We’re hopeful. In the worst case scenario, they would approve this with conditions. But that’s a scary thought, too,” he said. Anna Jewart, who serves as land use counsel for Allegheny DC Propco LLC, which recently rebranded as Dynamo DC, said that the SALDO process for major developments can be broken down into three steps: zoning approval at the local level, approval of the preliminary land development plan and final approval of the plan. The developer is on the second step. The ACED Planning Division has 90 days from its Oct. 28 meeting at Springdale Borough Municipal Building to issue its decision, she said. The county will accept written comments through Nov. 30. A preliminary approval would not allow Allegheny DC Propco to start building any structures or complete any grading work, she said. But because the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development Standards now require local approvals to be complete before data center developers apply for Department of Environmental Protection permits, Jewart said an approved preliminary plan would allow Allegheny DC Propco to apply for those. “This is a big hurdle. And it takes a lot of work, a lot of engineering. But there is much more that has to be done still,” she said. One application, dozens of issues Last December, Allegheny DC Propco received approval from Springdale Borough Council to build the data center complex as a conditional use. The borough also granted the developer six variances. Lessons of Springdale: Towns must prepare if they want any say over data centers At the municipal level, the preliminary plan submitted as part of the SALDO process typically provides a broad overview of what’s being proposed, said Brigitte Meyer, a staff attorney for the environmental advocacy organization PennFuture. But that also depends on the town’s zoning ordinance and the level of detail it requires. The county’s SALDO requires preliminary applications to include a range of documents, including a description of the project and its purpose and maps of the development’s proposed location and surrounding developments. Depending on a site’s conditions, a developer might also have to submit reports that assess soil contamination, landslide proneness and subsidence risk. Allegheny DC Propco’s preliminary plan proposes transforming 47 acres of the former Cheswick Generating Station site into a data center campus that would include power generators, utility yards and stormwater facilities to support its operations. In response to the 182-page application, ACED’s Planning Division asked for correction of several inconsistencies. Some of those issues include: - Certification from the Allegheny County Health Department that it was notified about the proposal, as required, wasn’t included in the application. Notification to the Health Department would also trigger air pollution requirements for the facility, according to the county’s review. - Several concerns surrounding the application’s treatment of the St. Mark’s Lutheran Church cemetery, which sits to the west of the proposed data center campus. The review notes that there’s a call to move earth in proximity to existing headstones there, and a proposal to relocate access to the cemetery would require building a bridge. - Despite the plan showing that parts of the site are contaminated with methylnaphthalene and arsenic, the application did not signal that any remediation had been done. Two consultants — Mackin Engineers and Consultants and GFT Infrastructure, Inc. — also conducted reviews of the plan on behalf of the county and borough. Similar to the county’s internal review, the third parties took issue with missing or incomplete information throughout the plan. Jewart, counsel for the developer, said that the length of the county’s review was not surprising for a plan of this size. She also said that it’s standard for these reviews to include several reminders to obtain certain permits, some of which she said the developer cannot apply for at this time due to the state’s GRID Standards. Allegheny DC Propco has submitted a letter in response to the county’s review, she said, and plans to submit an updated plan ahead of the Oct. 28 meeting. In June, county Sustainability Director Brittany Prischak said the county is working on a model data center development ordinance that municipalities can adopt, but that the county was still figuring out its role in the evolving space. Harrisburg also has a role. According to the state’s data center permit tracker, the developer already has state water obstruction and encroachment permits, but still has to submit permit applications related to erosion control and brownfield cleanups. Mia Hollie is the economic development and housing reporter for Pittsburgh’s Public Source. She can be reached at mia@publicsou

artigo.texto: New BYD Act 8: everything we know The new 7-seater electric SUV, which made its debut at the Paris Motor Show, sits at the top of the brand’s European range. It is set to arrive on European markets in 2027 Key points BYD unveiled the new Atto 8 – a seven-seater electric SUV that will sit at the top of the Chinese brand’s range – in a world premiere at the Paris Motor Show. Measuring 5.04 metres in length, 1.99 metres in width and 1.76 metres in height, the new Atto 8 features a three-row seating layout, complemented by a 270-litre boot capacity that expands to 1,960 litres when the second and third rows are folded down. The exterior design stands out for its Matrix LED headlights, slim daytime running lights and all-new light clusters, whilst the spoiler and aerodynamic features improve the car’s aerodynamic efficiency. There are two versions of the new SUV, both powered by the same second-generation 115 kWh Blade Battery. BYD Act 8: high-tech interiors Inside, the 2.39 m² panoramic roof, the 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster, the 26-inch head-up display and the 15.6-inch central touchscreen with Google Built-in immediately catch the eye. The seats in the first two rows are heated, ventilated and feature a massage function, whilst those in the third row have adjustable headrests. Three-zone climate control and leather upholstery come as standard. The standard equipment is rounded off by a 50 W on-board wireless charging pad and several USB Type-C ports. BYD Act 8: available engines The entry-level version of the BYD Atto 8 is the rear-wheel-drive Design model, which features a single 340 kW electric motor – equivalent to 462 cv – with a maximum torque of 365 Nm. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in 8 seconds. The 115 kWh battery delivers a range of 653 km, the highest in the range. At the top of the range is the Excellence AWD. A second motor on the front axle is added to the rear motor to provide all-wheel drive. Power rises to 570 kW, equivalent to 775 cv, whilst torque reaches 775 Nm and acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h takes 4.6 seconds. The battery capacity remains unchanged at 115 kWh, but the combined range stands at 602 km – a result attributable to the presence of the second motor and the all-wheel drive system. BYD Atto 8: battery and charging Both versions feature the second-generation 115 kWh Blade Battery. This is the same technology that the Chinese brand uses in its flagship models, characterised by a high level of safety and remarkable energy density. New to the European market is the introduction of Flash Charging technology: for the first time on a BYD car sold in Europe, the battery can go from 10 per cent to 97 per cent in just 9 minutes. This places the new Atto 8 amongst the models with the fastest charging times in its segment. The combination of such a generous battery, two clearly differentiated power levels and ultra-fast charging makes the Atto 8 one of the most technically innovative new models amongst the seven-seater electric SUVs currently on the market.

artigo.texto: Professor da Universidade Estadual da Califórnia em Fullerton compara a expansão digital à infraestrutura de óleo e gás. Quando um data center chega a uma cidade, a promessa costuma aparecer na forma de arrecadação, aluguel de terrenos e obras de infraestrutura. O impacto mais persistente, porém, pode ficar longe dos usuários que utilizam serviços de nuvem, videoconferências e plataformas digitais. Uma pesquisa conduzida por David Adams, professor associado de Administração Pública da California State University, Fullerton, nos Estados Unidos, aponta que a expansão desses complexos segue uma lógica semelhante à do setor de petróleo e gás: o benefício se espalha, enquanto parte importante do custo permanece no território onde a instalação funciona. A análise foi apresentada em entrevista publicada em 12 de outubro de 2026 e reúne estudos do professor sobre energia, água, infraestrutura e atuação do poder público. Segundo a California State University, Fullerton, havia cerca de 7.000 edifícios de data centers em operação, propostos ou em construção nos Estados Unidos em 1º de setembro de 2026, com aproximadamente 2.100 unidades operando em cerca de 1.400 locais. O lugar escolhido depende de cabos e eletricidade Os data centers são estruturas que concentram servidores responsáveis por armazenar, processar e distribuir dados. Para funcionar, precisam de conexão rápida com redes de fibra óptica e fornecimento contínuo de energia. Por isso, o levantamento de Adams identificou uma tendência de localização próxima às rotas de cabos já existentes e às áreas com oferta energética considerada mais conveniente. Essa escolha produz efeitos diferentes dos gerados por uma fábrica tradicional. O empreendimento pode recolher impostos sem necessariamente criar uma grande demanda por moradias, escolas, transporte coletivo ou contratação permanente de trabalhadores. Para municípios e condados, a combinação parece vantajosa: entra uma nova fonte de receita, mas a população não cresce na mesma proporção. O problema aparece quando a análise considera o ciclo completo da instalação. Um campus de grande porte pode consumir eletricidade equivalente à de uma cidade pequena. Além disso, muitos equipamentos precisam ser resfriados continuamente, o que pode ampliar a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos, especialmente em regiões sujeitas a secas. A água economizada pode reaparecer na usina O sistema de resfriamento cria uma escolha difícil. Quando o operador utiliza ar para reduzir o consumo direto de água, a instalação tende a demandar mais eletricidade. Se essa energia for produzida em uma usina que também utiliza água, parte do consumo apenas muda de lugar dentro da cadeia de fornecimento. Esse deslocamento torna o impacto menos visível para a comunidade. A água pode não ser retirada diretamente pelo data center, mas ainda ser necessária na produção da energia que mantém os servidores ligados. A consequência é uma disputa por recursos que envolve empresas, concessionárias, governos locais, órgãos reguladores e moradores. A comparação com o petróleo e gás se estende ao risco de abandono. Adams avalia que a evolução tecnológica pode tornar determinados complexos pouco úteis ou economicamente inviáveis, deixando uma infraestrutura de grande porte sem função. O paralelo é feito com poços abandonados e órfãos, cuja manutenção e recuperação podem acabar recaindo sobre o poder público. O caso do Arizona expõe a divisão de responsabilidades Um episódio em Tucson, no Arizona, mostra como a aprovação pode atravessar várias instituições. Um empreendimento associado à Amazon Web Services adquiriu terras no condado, mas encontrou resistência da cidade para obter acesso à água. O projeto foi redesenhado para utilizar resfriamento a ar e, depois, buscou autorização para a conexão elétrica junto à Arizona Corporation Commission, reguladora estadual do setor de energia. Enquanto moradores participaram de manifestações e o conselho municipal rejeitou o projeto, a comissão estadual aprovou o acordo de fornecimento de energia. Como o condado já havia negociado o terreno, as decisões tomadas por diferentes órgãos produziram um resultado que contrariava a posição expressa no município. A situação, segundo Adams, deixa o público diante de uma dúvida prática: qual governo tem, de fato, poder para interromper ou alterar a instalação? O pesquisador afirma que um único empreendimento pode envolver até 15 governos, com participação de estados, municípios, condados, distritos especiais e comissões reguladoras. A fragmentação dificulta a fiscalização e pode fazer com que moradores procurem a instituição errada para apresentar reclamações sobre água, energia, zoneamento ou impactos ambientais. O que a experiência pode ensinar à Amazônia O debate também interessa aos estados amazônicos, onde a expansão da infraestrutura digital convive com rios estratégicos, sistemas elétricos ainda desiguais e municípios com capacidade administrativa variada. Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Pará, Rondônia, Roraima e Tocantins podem enfrentar discussões semelhantes caso novos complexos de processamento de dados sejam planejados na região. A principal lição é que a autorização não deveria considerar apenas a área ocupada ou a arrecadação esperada. artigo.texto: UK bespoke raw materials company Avocet Materials Group is developing specialist lithium-ion battery components in Cheshire for high-performance applications including Formula One (F1), aerospace, defence, electric vehicles and energy storage, as it expands its advanced manufacturing and research capabilities. The family-owned business has established a 29-strong manufacturing and R&D operation in Holmes Chapel, producing components it says were previously manufactured only in Asia. It exports 99% of its battery products to international markets including China, Japan and the US. At the heart of its technology portfolio are lead tabs, small but critical metal components that connect a lithium-ion battery cell to an external circuit. Their properties can affect battery weight, conductivity and reliability, making precision manufacturing essential for demanding applications. One of Avocet’s innovations is Flyweight, a bimetallic lead tab designed for pouch cells and used in F1 battery applications to reduce battery system weight. The company is also developing DryTab, a next-generation surface technology that has secured government backing through the DRIVE35 programme. Avocet moved from specialist metals distribution into manufacturing during the Covid-19 pandemic. Supported by a £1.4m Innovate UK grant through the Advanced Propulsion Centre and further investment, it now operates through three businesses: Avocet Precision Metals, Avocet Battery Materials and Avocet Research Centre. Kieren Hall, CEO, said: “When you think that five years ago we didn’t manufacture anything, what we’ve achieved is pretty remarkable. We’ve built a manufacturing operation from scratch, developed our own technology and we’re now making specialist components for lithium-ion batteries in Cheshire for some of the most demanding applications in the world. “We’re exporting 99% of our battery products and selling into countries with some of the biggest battery industries in the world, including China and Japan. For a business of our size to be competing internationally at that level is something we’re incredibly proud of.” Turnover has grown from £1.5m to £3.5m, with sales increasing by around 25% this year. To support further expansion, Avocet is working with Made Smarter North West on manufacturing systems and digital infrastructure. The company has secured a £13,000 grant towards a £75,000 enterprise resource planning system, scheduled to go live in January 2027. The system will integrate operations across the business and support productivity and capacity growth. Avocet is also exploring automated inspection technology and artificial intelligence to improve manufacturing efficiency and decision-making as it develops its battery technology portfolio. artigo.texto: Los Angeles plans floating solar and iron-flow battery system on Encino Reservoir to generate and store electricity Los Angeles is pushing its green shift forward by deploying floating solar on a reservoir. The United States is actively pursuing its national climate goals to meet rising energy demands more sustainably. However, urban regions with the highest consumption and emissions struggle to raise renewable capacity. Ultimately, unused municipal reservoirs and floating photovoltaics can unlock local energy resilience, meeting rising demands more sustainably. Spatial limitations are a major bottleneck, which is why developers are turning to floatovoltaics. Will Los Angeles’ latest approved project serve as a vital blueprint for other cities? How U.S. cities struggle to progress in the clean transition The United States currently ranks 19th in the global renewable energy transition. Domestically, clean power generation accounts for 30% of total electricity supply. Despite this, the nation is still far from reaching its national climate mandates. This is because urban centers have concentrated, dense populations, industrial hubs, commercial infrastructure, and heavy transit networks. Cities’ extreme density accounts for more than 70 percent of global energy-related carbon emissions. In the U.S., electricity consumption and building operations drive roughly 40 percent of national greenhouse gas output. As industrial and transport electrification and AI data center infrastructure expand, power consumption will continue to surge. Consequently, energy demand is rising much faster than new power generation capacity can be added. This leads to a growing supply gap, threatening the stability of regional grids. To bridge this gap, rapid deployment of utility-scale renewable energy sources is key. Unfortunately, urban planners face significant spatial and economic hurdles. Structural obstacles faced in cities trying to go green Solar power has become a core pillar in America’s renewable energy shift, with capacity reaching major milestones in recent years. Currently, the nation’s total operational solar capacity is 299.4 gigawatts. However, this generation is highly concentrated in specific regions, and cities still face challenges raising solar production. Traditional utility-scale photovoltaic facilities require vast open land, roughly 5 to 10 acres per megawatt. Densely built urban regions cannot provide this footprint. Furthermore, U.S. permitting bottlenecks slow solar growth. This is because developments must navigate overcrowded grid distribution, complex zoning laws, and historic preservation rules. Additionally, limited undeveloped real estate in cities commands a premium market price. These high land acquisition costs make urban ground-mounted photovoltaic projects uneconomical. As a result, urban planners are forced to turn to dual-use infrastructure like floatovoltaics to generate localized clean power. In Los Angeles, a floating solar pilot project has been approved after the LADWP filed a formal Notice of Determination. The floatovoltaics project on the Encino Reservoir California’s solar-and-storage portfolio is set to increase, with the San Fernando Valley region of Los Angeles leading in innovation. A new floating solar project will be constructed directly on the Encino Reservoir. LADWP owns and manages the 960-acre site, which means private land acquisition was completely bypassed. The project will comprise a 5-megawatt floatovoltaic array covering 10 acres of the reservoir surface. There will also be a 30-kilowatt mounted solar system spanning 4,000 square feet on adjacent land. A 5-megawatt iron-flow battery system will ensure long-duration energy storage. Meanwhile, on-site transformers, inverters, and switchgear will be connected directly to an existing distribution line. The project achieved fast-tracked approval Regulatory review was quickly completed by filing a Mitigated Negative Declaration under CEQA. This bypassed a lengthy Environmental Impact Report. Environmental evaluations confirmed no significant ecological impact. By bypassing standard zoning delays, construction can proceed rapidly. With the environmental clearance completed, LADWP can proceed to procurement and development. The goal is to operationalize this project as a core clean energy pilot. The combined deployment of floating solar and local battery storage creates a vital blueprint for other urban regions nationwide. Ultimately, unused municipal reservoirs and floating photovoltaics can unlock local energy resilience, meeting rising demands more sustainably. Anke Maree is a writer with a clear and engaging editorial style. Her work focuses on making complex topics accessible, informative, and relevant for readers across different areas of interest.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Daily presents a selection of the latest developments from China's automotive industry. Here are the key stories in this edition. CATL, SERES Deepen Strategic Partnership On October 10, 2026, CATL and SERES Group signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement in Chongqing. All AITO-branded vehicles have been equipped with CATL batteries since the brand's launch, with cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million vehicles. The two companies will continue their full-range battery partnership and deepen cooperation in three areas: Production capacity: Accelerate Phase II construction of the battery plant within SERES' super factory, with planned annual capacity of 10–12 GWh. Combined annual capacity for Phases I and II will exceed 20 GWh once completed. Charging services: Cooperate on fast-charging networks and battery services to build a full-lifecycle service system. Global expansion: Jointly explore overseas markets in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia. Geely Galaxy ZJ700 Hits Market On October 10, 2026, Geely officially launched the Galaxy ZJ700, its first AI-powered all-terrain SUV, offering six variants. Built on Geely's GTA new-energy off-road architecture, the SUV combines advanced driver assistance, off-road capability and premium comfort. Its Qiankun H7 driver-assistance system uses a Thor-U chip delivering 700 TOPS of computing power. The sensor suite includes a 192-line LiDAR, three millimeter-wave radars, 11 high-definition cameras, 12 ultrasonic radars and two wading radars. The vehicle supports highway and urban Navigation on Autopilot (NOA), point-to-point parking navigation and multi-scenario automated parking assistance. Power comes from Geely's Leishen EM-T off-road hybrid system, combining a 2.0TD off-road hybrid engine with electric motors. Key performance figures include: Combined power: 830 kW Battery capacity: 47.14 kWh Pure electric range: 305 km Combined range: 1,770 km Fast charging: 10% to 80% in 10 minutes, with 6C charging support Wading depth: 800 mm Additional off-road features include mechanical differential locks and dual-chamber closed air suspension with CCD continuously variable damping. The SUV also supports a minimum turning radius of 3.36 meters and a "Waltz Turn" maneuver. GEENER, Wolfspeed Ink Deal Wolfspeed and GEENER recently signed a memorandum of understanding in Hangzhou to cooperate on silicon carbide (SiC) power modules. GEENER will prioritize Wolfspeed's SiC bare dies for integration into its next-generation power module platform, initially targeting applications such as main inverters for new-energy vehicles. Wolfspeed will leverage its established 200 mm SiC production lines to develop bare dies that meet or exceed GEENER's performance requirements, while providing stable supply and commercial support. The two companies will jointly engage with leading Chinese automakers on high-voltage electric vehicle platforms, aiming to secure vehicle design wins. The partnership combines Wolfspeed's SiC chip technology and manufacturing capacity with GEENER's expertise in module design, packaging and reliability validation. Beyond electric vehicles, the companies also see potential applications in AI data centers, where reliable power modules and stable supply are increasingly important.

artigo.texto: A infraestrutura de nuvem da Yandex, uma das maiores empresas de tecnologia da Rússia, enfrenta uma grave crise após ataques com drones danificarem três de seus data centers. Os incidentes, registrados em outubro de 2026, provocaram interrupções operacionais e instabilidade em serviços de armazenamento, computação e inteligência artificial, levantando preocupações sobre a capacidade da empresa de manter suas operações durante emergências físicas. As instalações atingidas ficam em Sasovo, Kaluga e Vladimir. Entre os serviços afetados estão componentes do Yandex Cloud, o armazenamento compatível com S3, o Kubernetes e o Yandex Disk. Clientes também relataram falhas em requisições, dificuldades para baixar arquivos e respostas HTTP de erro. Diante do cenário, a empresa recomendou que os clientes recorressem a seus planos de recuperação de desastres enquanto a infraestrutura permanecesse instável. O episódio expõe uma fragilidade importante da computação em nuvem: embora os serviços pareçam funcionar de maneira virtual e distribuída, eles dependem de instalações físicas que podem ser danificadas. Para empresas que hospedam aplicações críticas, a crise reforça a necessidade de manter backups independentes, redundância geográfica e planos de continuidade operacional. Ataques com drones interrompem operações em três data centers da Yandex A sequência de ataques atingiu três instalações importantes da Yandex em poucos dias, reduzindo a capacidade disponível para executar aplicações e atender às solicitações dos clientes. A empresa, frequentemente comparada ao Google pelo conjunto de serviços digitais que oferece na Rússia, opera plataformas de busca, armazenamento, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. A interrupção simultânea de diferentes instalações representa um desafio maior do que a falha isolada de um servidor. Quando um data center inteiro deixa de operar, milhares de componentes podem ficar indisponíveis, incluindo servidores, sistemas de armazenamento e equipamentos de rede. A recuperação também depende das condições físicas do local e da possibilidade de transferir as cargas de trabalho para outras instalações. Sasovo, Kaluga e Vladimir foram atingidas em sequência Os incidentes foram registrados em três localidades russas durante outubro de 2026. Em Sasovo, na região de Riazan, um ataque ocorrido na noite de 7 para 8 de outubro provocou danos graves e levou ao desligamento da instalação. O local abriga parte da infraestrutura de computação utilizada pela Yandex, inclusive em atividades relacionadas à inteligência artificial. Em Kaluga, outro ataque, registrado em 9 de outubro, danificou módulos do data center e comprometeu parte de sua capacidade operacional. Embora a interrupção tenha sido parcial, a perda de recursos contribuiu para aumentar a pressão sobre a infraestrutura restante. Já em Vladimir, um ataque em 11 de outubro levou à suspensão das operações da instalação. A sequência dos incidentes reduziu a margem disponível para redistribuir serviços e manter a capacidade habitual da plataforma. Os episódios também levantaram preocupações sobre a concentração de recursos computacionais em instalações sujeitas a riscos físicos. Mesmo quando uma empresa mantém vários data centers, a redundância pode ser insuficiente se os locais compartilharem dependências ou se a capacidade remanescente não suportar a demanda. Yandex Cloud entra em modo de operação de emergência Durante a crise, a Yandex reconheceu dificuldades operacionais e orientou clientes a utilizar seus planos alternativos de recuperação de desastres, conhecidos pela sigla DR, de Disaster Recovery. Esse tipo de recomendação indica que a recuperação pode exigir mais do que uma manutenção convencional. A perda de instalações inteiras demanda avaliar equipamentos, reconstruir capacidade computacional, verificar a integridade dos dados e restabelecer as dependências necessárias para os serviços voltarem a funcionar. A ausência de uma previsão definitiva para a recuperação integral também dificulta o planejamento das empresas afetadas. Sem uma estimativa confiável, administradores precisam decidir se aguardam a normalização, transferem aplicações ou ativam ambientes alternativos. O cenário demonstra por que planos de contingência devem prever interrupções prolongadas, em vez de considerar apenas falhas temporárias de rede ou indisponibilidade de componentes individuais. Kubernetes, S3 e APIs enfrentam instabilidade A crise atingiu diferentes componentes do Yandex Cloud, plataforma utilizada para hospedar aplicações, armazenar dados e executar cargas de trabalho empresariais. Entre os serviços citados nos relatos sobre a interrupção estão Kubernetes, Object Storage compatível com S3, Container Registry, Console, APIs, IAM e serviços de bancos de dados. Também foram relatados problemas em componentes relacionados à inteligência artificial, incluindo o AI Studio. Os efeitos variam conforme o serviço e suas dependências. O Kubernetes, por exemplo, pode reiniciar contêineres e redistribuir aplicações entre nós disponíveis, mas não consegue compensar automaticamente a perda de toda uma instalação quando faltam capacidade computacional, armazenamento ou componentes essenciais do plano de controle. O armazenamento compatível com S3 também merece atenção. Muitas aplicações utilizam esse tipo de serviço para guardar documentos, arquivos de usuários, registros e cópias de segurança. Se as operações de leitura e gravação falham, o problema pode se propagar para sistemas que dependem desses dados. Da mesma forma, a instabilidade nas APIs e no IAM pode prejudicar a autenticação, o gerenciamento de recursos e a execução de operações automatizadas. Assim, uma interrupção física pode afetar tanto os usuários finais quanto as equipes responsáveis pela administração da infraestrutura.
