artigo.texto: I am writing today to address an integral piece of our local and national discourse: the debate over data centers. I am writing to challenge a recent letter I read in the local newspaper: “Nobody wants a data center in their backyard” (Sept. 8, Morgan Hill Times and Gilroy Dispatch). I respect the author’s perspective; many residents do not want data centers in their community, as there are negative externalities associated, such as water and power usage and the unsightliness of the power facilities associated with it. However, I believe that when it comes to such a contentious issue, we must tread carefully and treat the subject with the nuance it deserves. This article quickly served to attack the character of those in favor of data centers saying “the people who want the data centers are the same ones who never want them in their own neighborhood.” I, for one, can unequivocally refute this—I would love for more data centers to be built in San Martin, where I live, and Gilroy, where I was born and went to elementary school. Data centers are an opportunity to employ both blue collar and white collar workers—something that Gilroy would gladly take more of. Counties which host data centers experience a rise in local employment, total wages, median household income, business growth, construction revenue and tax revenue. I would love this for the South Valley, where I grew up, and in which not a single family member of mine worked, because of the lower wages compared to the rest of the Bay Area. The article continues to poke at Gilroy Mayor Greg Bozzo, and in reference to why he was allowing the data centers to be built, said he was “looking forward to an early and comfortable retirement.” The insinuation that Bozzo is looking out for his personal interest is a blatant attack on his character. As for how this got passed through without input from other stakeholders, the approved facility is more than a half mile away from the nearest residential area. The data center is being built in an area inhabited by the 145 Gilroy Outlets and other big box retailers and businesses. While I agree community input should be vital in a project like this, it is understandable that the Gilroy City Council would approve a project like this in an area which has hundreds of neighboring businesses, and no housing in close proximity. There are 107 data centers currently operating in Santa Clara County, and I contend this is a great thing. Data centers store data such as personal photos and database information for businesses. They stream media, like movies and TV shows into our homes. They help with cybersecurity, which protects local and corporate businesses from data breaches. They power online services, such as social media, online banking and the online print of the Morgan Hill Times, Gilroy Dispatch and Hollister Free Lance. They make our modern lives possible. When it comes to data centers, there are many issues that will arise. Seeing them in the community we live in and love can be difficult. It can seem that big tech companies and powers outside our control are dictating how our communities change. I am writing to say that these are entirely valid criticisms, but there are positive changes that come along with their construction, and they can serve to better our lives and the generations in the South Valley after us. Ellis Richardson San Martin

artigo.texto: Know Data centers prohibited under St. Pete’s city code According to Planning Director Derek Kilborn, data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. Standalone data centers, including large-scale facilities used to power artificial intelligence, are prohibited under St. Petersburg’s existing zoning regulations, according to a new memorandum from the city’s planning director. In an Oct. 9 memo to Mayor Ken Welch, Planning Director Derek Kilborn clarified how the facilities are classified under the city’s land development code. He concluded that data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. The determination comes as local governments across Pinellas County consider how to regulate the rapidly expanding industry amid concerns about electricity consumption, water resources and land availability. St. Petersburg’s zoning code contains a matrix identifying permitted land uses. Data centers are not included, and city regulations presume that uses not specifically listed are prohibited. Kilborn also examined whether data centers could qualify as similar to other permitted uses, including utility infrastructure, but found no sufficient justification. “For these reasons, Data Centers generally, and Large-Scale Data Centers explicitly, remain prohibited as a permitted, principal (P) or Special Exception (SE) use in the City of St. Petersburg,” Kilborn wrote. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Senate Bill 484, which recognizes the infrastructure and environmental challenges of large utility users, like data centers, last May. However, DeSantis preserved local authority over land use regulation in the same bill, which took effect July 1. Under the new law, a large-scale data center is defined as a facility with an anticipated monthly peak electrical demand of at least 50 megawatts at a single location. St. Petersburg’s determination applies to standalone data centers regardless of whether they meet that threshold. The memo follows similar actions elsewhere in Pinellas County. Pinellas Park approved a one-year moratorium on data center development in August. Additionally, in September, county commissioners adopted a resolution restricting large standalone facilities in unincorporated areas. Unlike those actions, St. Petersburg’s memorandum simply clarifies that standalone data centers are already prohibited under existing regulations, and presumably no further action is needed to overhaul the law. It was not indicated whether the city has received any recent data center development proposals, or whether officials are considering changes to the zoning code.

artigo.texto: Pennsylvania launches interactive data center permit tracker amid environmental concerns PENNSYLVANIA (WHP) — Pennsylvania has launched a public map that will allow the public to track proposed data centers that are seeking environmental permits. The data center tracker is operated by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). The interactive map shows the locations of proposed data center projects in the Commonwealth and includes a list of environmental permits for each project and their status. Data centers have continued to be a point of contention in Pennsylvania, including as a talking point in the debate between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Shapiro started off the debate saying he's been listening to concerns of the people, and after doing so, drafted the "strictest guardrail in the nation" for data centers. He said it is important to protect air and water and that it must include local benefits. Meanwhile, Garrity discussed individual cases where people are fighting against data centers in their own backyard. Over the weekend, the Swatara Township Board of Commissioners approved community benefits agreements for a pair of proposed data centers. RELATED | Swatara Township approves community benefits plan for data center projects The types of permits and/or authorizations often associated with large-scale data centers include: - Earth disturbance and stormwater management - Wetland and waterway encroachment - Storage tanks - Air quality - Sewage facilities planning - Clean water To track the status of a permit authorization, use the DEP's permit tracker.

The battery supports a driving range of over 1,500 km on a single charge, with almost no performance degradation after more than 600,000 km of driving, and has a lifespan exceeding 5,000 cycles. Furthermore, it features 6C fast-charging technology that can charge the battery from 30% to 80% remaining capacity in just 9 minutes. Changan Automobile will begin full-scale commercial production of the Golden Bell all-solid-state battery in 2027, following vehicle road tests in 2026. This joint battery production and all-solid-state battery development is a strategic move for Changan Automobile, which faces profit pressure per vehicle, to reduce costs for core components such as batteries and secure cost competitiveness. artigo.texto: NDSU forum tackles data centers, AI FARGO, N.D. (Valley News Live) - Dozens of people attended a forum at NDSU’s Memorial Union Wednesday night looking for answers about artificial intelligence and data centers. Applied Digital is building a data center in Harwood, with another proposed in Harmony Township by Geronimo Power. Students weigh in on AI’s role Michael Nelson, a student at NDSU, said he has been interested in data center infrastructure for the last couple of years. “I’ve been interested in data center kind of infrastructure the last couple of years. North Dakota is a big component to that. I just think it’s beneficial for everybody to kind of learn a little bit more. Whatever side you’re on of it, I think learning about the issue is highly valuable,” Nelson said. Will electric bills go up? Experts say there is not a one-size-fits-all answer to whether the data centers will lead to higher electric bills. Officials at Cass County Electric Cooperative said they don’t want to interrupt service because of data centers. Paul Matthys, President and CEO of Cass County Electric Cooperative, said the cooperative has large investments to make in generation for its members. “If we can take some of the revenue from those large data loads and help pay for some of the costs that we will have to incur, to build new power generation for our legacy load, that will help drive down pressure on rates,” Matthys said. AI’s growing presence While discussion around data centers continues, AI continues to become more popular. Robert Mayo, a Research Specialist at the Challey Institute for Global Innovation and Growth, said AI systems can function as tutors. “Those systems can function as very effective user-friendly tutors. It’s also been bad because it allows students to basically plagiarize sometimes in a way they shouldn’t,” Mayo said. AI is impacting NDSU students’ everyday lives. “It’s kind of a double-edged sword. You can become dependent on it obviously to some degree, just like I think everybody does. But if you use it the right way, you can create study sets for yourself,” Nelson said. Cooperative says it must adapt quickly As data centers multiply, Cass County Electric Cooperative says it has to adapt just as fast. “We have to evaluate, make decisions and ensure that we’re not taking any unnecessary risks for the cooperative or our members,” Matthys said. artigo.texto: A re-engineered lead-acid battery system aimed at helping businesses cut power bills is now operating in Geelong, with its developer seeking to make energy storage cheaper and easier to install. New Zealand energy storage company ArcActive has switched on the pilot at Deakin’s new Renewable Grid-Connected Battery Testing Facility at its Waurn Ponds campus, with support from Origin Energy. Related article: Partnership to accelerate Allegro Energy’s flow battery tech ArcActive aims to make battery storage cheaper and easier to install, allowing more businesses to store solar electricity for later use and buy less power when prices are high. Its system builds on lead-acid technology already used to support critical infrastructure, including telecommunications, hospitals, and data centres. ArcActive has redesigned the batteries’ internal structure, using a fabric framework to support the material that stores and releases energy. The design aims to extend cycling life while preserving low cost, making lead-acid more attractive for everyday energy storage. The pilot operates within Deakin’s renewable energy microgrid, which provides electricity generation and storage for operational use. ArcActive CEO Stuart McKenzie said the pilot was a step forward in making battery storage accessible to more businesses. “The cost of installing a battery goes beyond the battery itself. Businesses also need to account for engineering work, approvals, insurance and safety measures. If they don’t know what their site will need or how much it will cost, they can be reluctant to invest.” McKenzie said using lead-acid technology offered a familiar starting point. “It is a technology that engineers, approval authorities and insurers already know. There are established pathways for approving and insuring these installations, which is an important starting point when you want to put batteries alongside businesses and occupied buildings.” ArcActive is targeting commercial and industrial businesses that could benefit from storage but face costs and complexity that can prevent projects from proceeding. Related article: Sicona acquires US firm and New Orleans battery facility “We want businesses to be able to deploy storage through a more standardised, repeatable process, with greater confidence about the cost, the approval requirements and the financial return,” McKenzie said.

artigo.texto: Russia's President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting with members of the government via videoconference in Moscow on June 23, 2026. | Gavriil Grigorov/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Ukraine’s strikes on data centers inside Russia aimed to disrupt military planning and communication services. There were also reports of another kind of disruption: to customers waiting for their dinner from food-delivery apps. Kyiv’s drone strikes on three Yandex data centers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir saw delays and interruptions for thousands of businesses and households that rely on Yandex's cloud infrastructure, including e-commerce, digital payment platforms and apps of food delivery and car services. Ukrainian drones on Wednesday targeted a major Sberbank data center in Russia’s Saratov region, though a senior company executive said it hadn’t affected operations. After the strikes on Russian data centers, Kyiv noted that Moscow has already repeatedly targeted its digital infrastructure. “Ukrainians wanted to show Russians that two can play this game,” a senior official familiar with the operation told POLITICO, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. Advertisement The attacks and counter-attacks point to a new frontline in war: the infrastructure powering the digital economy. The attacks on the buildings that supply compute power are akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that both militaries and civilians depend on. It may weaken an enemy's war effort but can also bring everyday life to a standstill. Experts say the cost of rebuilding in Russia will be particularly high as the centers require scarce materials that must be imported. “Obtaining a large amount of equipment to replace what was destroyed is not going to be easy,” said Oleg Shakirov, a cyber policy and international security researcher, noting that most hardware needs to be imported and that is complicated by high global demand and sanctions on Russia. “To be honest, no one really knows what’s the actual damage. Since two data centers are still offline, we can assume that it’s significant,” said Shakirov. Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that normalizing strikes to data centers could have a new set of dangerous consequences. “These strikes likely breach International Humanitarian Law and it’s a big risk when global populations increasingly rely on digital services,” he told POLITICO. Advertisement When servers become targets Data centers have entered the crosshairs of other recent armed conflicts. During the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran earlier this year, drone strikes hit three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. Since data centers can serve civilian and military purposes simultaneously, the legal status of targeting them is far from straightforward. Kubo Mačák, an expert on international humanitarian law, said a data center must meet two conditions to qualify as a military objective under the Geneva Conventions: it must make an effective contribution to military operations and destroying it must offer a “definite military advantage.” A delivery robot from Russian tech giant Yandex moves through Moscow. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images “If you know that they are storing military intelligence or that they're using the data center to power military artificial intelligence tools,” Mačák said, there could be grounds to consider it a military objective. Following the most recent strikes of the Yandex data centers, users on social media platform X reported a sudden drop in automated bot activity, including from accounts associated with pro-Russian, pro-Trump and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narratives. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seized on the reports to boast that the strikes had made social media less toxic, even as independent researchers and national research institutes found no evidence they specifically disrupted any Russian disinformation campaigns. Advertisement Mačák said that even if a data center is being used to “let's say, run some trolls or these bot farms to interfere with elections abroad … that would not be sufficient.” In other words, hosting propaganda bots does not, by itself, make a data center a lawful military target. The dual-use quandary has often focused on the targeting of energy infrastructure, which has been frequent in the Russia-Ukraine war. On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for rising fuel prices. He has since called for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, although the existence of any ceasefire agreement remains disputed. As data centers become increasingly central to national economies, they will become more consequential targets. A senior NATO official granted anonymity to discuss the matter told POLITICO that data centers are already considered potential targets and that the alliance is factoring their vulnerability into its planning. NATO allies recognize that their data centers could come under attack in a conflict, the official said: “We would get it in a fight.” Veronika Melkozerova in Kyiv contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: BYD Energy Storage showcased its MC-Cube-XT and BYD Haohan BESS at Solar & Storage Live UK 2026 The former product features 12 cube-type cabinets in a 7,550 × 2,438 × 2,896 mm container frame, while the latter combines 4 cubes on a common base frame The company also displayed its Battery-Box HVB/HVE/HVM+ storage, and Power-Box residential hybrid inverters BYD Energy Storage, the energy storage arm of well-known Chinese car maker BYD, showcased its latest product lineup at Solar & Storage Live UK 2026 for utility and residential customers. The company displayed its MC-Cube-XT and BYD Haohan utility battery energy storage systems (BESS), both built around long, thin, and blade-shaped battery packs. Traditional BESS accommodates multiple battery stacks within a 20- or 40-ft container. Instead, the displayed products combine multiple cabinet-based storage sections within a container frame. MC-Cube-XT consists of 12 cube-type cabinets and features 1,980 Ah blade-type batteries, for a total storage capacity of 6,437 kWh. It measures 7,550 × 2,438 × 2,896 mm (W × D × H). In comparison, BYD Haohan uses 4 cubes with a higher battery capacity (2,710 Ah) for a total storage capacity of 14,568 kWh. The company says its size is comparable to a standard 20 ft container. The two BESS systems have a rated full-load DC power output of 1,608 kW and 1,820 kW, respectively. BYD also showcased its GC Flux series bidirectional power conversion system (PCS) station at its booth. The above products can be charged or discharged from or to the grid via this PCS, offering a maximum rated capacity of 7,000 kW. The company specifies a maximum conversion efficiency of 99% and an overload capacity of up to 300% for 10 seconds. For residential applications, the company introduced its Battery-Box HVB/HVE/HVM+ storage and Power-Box hybrid inverters (3-phase) at the show.

artigo.texto: Publicado em 14 de outubro de 2026 A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) participou da primeira edição do Data Center World Brasil, realizada entre 6 e 8 de outubro em São Paulo. O evento reuniu líderes dos setores de data centers, infraestrutura digital, cloud computing e inteligência artificial para debater os principais desafios e oportunidades da transformação digital. A EPE foi representada pelo Consultor Técnico Daniel José Tavares de Souza no painel “Expansão na Era da IA: Decisões que Definem Bilhões em Investimentos”. Entre os principais debates esteve o papel estratégico da energia para a expansão da infraestrutura digital. Em sua participação, Daniel destacou que conectividade, profissionais qualificados e investimentos financeiros não são suficientes para viabilizar um projeto de Data Center sem a disponibilidade de energia e de margem de conexão. A transmissão e a geração de energia aparecem como pontos fundamentais para acompanhar o crescimento acelerado do setor. O principal desafio apresentado pela EPE está na diferença entre os cronogramas de implantação. Um grande data center pode começar a operar em dois ou três anos. Já uma obra de transmissão exige pelo menos cinco anos de execução, considerando a complexidade de construção de linhas de transmissão e subestações, além dos processos de licenciamento ambiental. Quando são incluídos os estudos e o planejamento, o intervalo entre a decisão de expansão e a entrada em operação da infraestrutura pode alcançar sete anos. “Enquanto isso, os data centers estão entrando”, observou Daniel. Apenas para o estado de São Paulo, já foram recomendados mais de R$ 7 bilhões de investimentos em obras de transmissão para viabilizar margem de conexão para cerca de 7 GW no total. Além de São Paulo, também foi recomendado pela EPE um montante de R$ 5,7 bilhões em obras de transmissão na região Nordeste, com o intuito de viabilizar margem de conexão de 4 GW para grandes cargas. Por fim, foi reforçada a mensagem de que a EPE mantém a interlocução com grandes players de data centers e segue acompanhando os processos de acesso, como a PNAST, para identificar os locais de maior procura e avaliar a probabilidade de concretização dos empreendimentos, que são importantes insumos para os estudos realizados pela EPE. 14/10/2026 - A EPE publica o Roadmap para Fortalecimento da Resiliência do Setor Elétrico Brasileiro em Resposta às Mudanças Climáticas, estudo que consolida uma avaliação sistêmica dos potenciais impactos das mudanças do clima sobre o sistema elétrico brasileiro e propõe estratégias e medidas para ampliar sua capacidade de adaptação. 14/10/2026 - A EPE, o ONS e a CCEE realizarão online, no dia 21 de outubro, das 9h às 12h30, o Workshop sobre os Processos de Previsão de Carga, voltado aos representantes dos agentes do setor elétrico. O evento será transmitido pela plataforma Webex. 13/10/2026 - A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) publica o Informe Técnico “Iluminação Pública como Vetor de Transformação Digital e Eficiência Energética nas Cidades”, que apresenta um panorama do setor no Brasil e propõe caminhos para ampliar a eficiência, a qualidade dos serviços e a integração da iluminação pública ao planejamento urbano e energético. 13/10/2026 - Pela primeira vez, a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) disponibiliza em inglês o Informe de Monitoramento sobre a Política de Exploração e Produção (E&P) de Petróleo e Gás, edição de 2026, e seu respectivo Fact Sheet. 09/10/2026 - Estudo sobre fungibilidade e precificação de certificados de descarbonização, selecionado entre os três melhores trabalhos da ROG.e na categoria Diversificação Energética e Soluções de Baixo Carbono, ajuda a entender o que o mercado de biometano pode aprender com a experiência do CBIO

artigo.texto: Andhra Pradesh has issued a tender for 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh of standalone BESS with four-hour storage duration Winning bidders will sign 12-year BESPAs with state discoms Projects need to be set up across three locations under a build-own-operate model Andhra Pradesh has launched a call for the deployment of 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh of standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity at selected project locations across the state. As the bid coordinator, the Andhra Pradesh Power Coordination Committee (APPCC) may procure up to 25% additional BESS capacity for each project under a green shoe option, amounting to 125 MW/500 MWh each for Projects 1 and 3, and 50 MW/200 MWh for Project 2. The tender documents state that the additional capacity will be included in the contracted capacity if allocated. To be set up under a build-own-operate (BOO) model, the capacity will be established at three locations. Of the total, 500 MW/2,000 MWh will be located at Dr. M.V. Ramana Reddy Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant (RTPP). Another 250 MW/1,000 MWh will come up at the Talaricheruvu RE Project, and 500 MW/2,000 MWh at the NP Kunta RE Project. The entire 1,250 MW translates into 4-hour storage capacity. Bidders are required to design the BESS under Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreements (BESPAs), ensuring the system can charge and discharge at a C-rate of 0.25. It must also be capable of being charged and discharged in blocks of either 50 MW/200 MWh or 100 MW/400 MWh, alone or in combination up to the total rate capacity specified for each location. Interested BESS developers are invited to submit bids for the grid-connected projects, each of which will be tendered, evaluated, and awarded separately, with tariffs determined independently. No viability gap funding (VGF) is available for these projects. APPCC has launched the call on behalf of AP discoms, namely Andhra Pradesh Central Power Distribution Corporation Limited (APCPDCL), Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APEPDCL), and Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APSPDCL). State discoms will enter into a 12-year BESPA with the winning bidders to secure energy storage facilities on an on-demand basis. APPCC issued the tender on October 7, 2026. It will accept bids till November 23, 2026. Details of the tender are available on the APEPDCL website. Under its Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, Andhra Pradesh targets 25 GWh of BESS and 22 GW of pumped storage hydropower capacity by 2029 to accommodate growing renewable energy capacity. It also aims to add 78.5 GW of solar and 35 GW of wind capacity between 2024 and 2029.

artigo.texto: NYK-Led Consortium Develops Floating Data Center Concept for Ports A Japanese consortium led by shipping giant NYK Line has developed a new port-based floating data center concept designed to accelerate the commercialization of offshore data centers while addressing growing constraints on land availability, electrical power and construction timelines. The consortium, comprising Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK), NTT FACILITIES, Eurus Energy Holdings and MUFG Bank, envisions floating data centers moored alongside existing port quays, leveraging established shoreside infrastructure and local energy resources. Unlike floating data centers positioned farther offshore, which could directly utilize large-scale renewable energy sources such as offshore wind, the port-based model offers easier access, established telecommunications connectivity and more conventional power supply arrangements. The approach could enable deployment in locations ranging from major metropolitan ports to smaller regional harbors, potentially opening new opportunities for port authorities seeking to diversify waterfront infrastructure and services. The consortium sees the port-based concept as an intermediate step toward more ambitious offshore installations, where accessibility, telecommunications connectivity and independent power supply systems remain significant technical challenges. Under the initiative, NYK will oversee project development and business strategy. NTT FACILITIES will handle technical verification of data center design, construction and operations, while Eurus Energy will explore renewable power integration, particularly offshore wind. MUFG Bank will evaluate financing opportunities and potential business partnerships. The companies believe floating data centers could provide an alternative to conventional land-based facilities as global demand for digital infrastructure continues to expand. No construction timetable, project location, investment value or computing capacity was disclosed.

artigo.texto: Before it was fully contained, the Hawk Fire that started in August in Reno, Nevada, burned 15,085 acres, destroyed 48 homes and other structures, claimed the life of one person, and forced the evacuation of 42,000 residents. The cause of the wildfire remains under investigation. The Hawk Fire is one of thousands of wildfires that have burned across the United States this year, but a photo of that particular fire caught my attention for one reason. There's no vegetation. It is not burning in forest land but is burning in a desert environment with little fuel on the ground. Granted, Reno sits in an arid, dry region and wildfires are not uncommon. Wildfires are burning with a greater intensity than ever before and are much more difficult to control because the effects of climate change greatly exacerbate these already existing dry conditions. Wildfire seasons are much longer and not just contained to the western part of the country. Extreme weather events are occurring daily throughout the world. Just look at the record flooding that has hammered many parts of West Virginia in recent years. Severe weather events dominate our daily news cycle. The problem is here now We can no longer speak of climate change as a phenomena that will impact our lives in the future. We are in a climate crisis now and it is clearly the number one environmental issue facing mankind today. Water temperatures in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean, where El Niño is measured, have been at record levels for more than three months straight. El Niño’s effects are already evident worldwide. The pattern has contributed to more frequent heat domes, persistent temperature records in Peru, deadly storms in Chile, destructive hurricanes in Hawaii, floods across the United States and the Atlantic hurricane season’s record calm so far. Ocean temperatures in the central Pacific are on a record trajectory. They’re projected to reach an average peak of around 4.1 degrees Celsius above average in December — about a degree higher than a record-breaking El Niño in 2015 — leading to catastrophic weather events this fall and winter. A new UN Environment Programme report released in early September warns that global warming is likely to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold within the next few years. Even if governments fulfill their current pledges, temperatures will peak at 1.8 degrees Celsius, with some models indicating a rise above 2degrees. Every fraction of a degree above 1.5 degrees Celsius heightens the risks of extreme weather, heat waves, floods, and dangerous climate tipping points. The current crisis can be compared to leaning back in a chair: for a while, nothing happens, but eventually the chair tips over. Our climate is now at that tipping point. Action is needed There is only one way out of this crisis: end fossil fuel use as quickly as possible so global temperatures can decline. There is no alternative. It is frustrating to watch West Virginia’s political leaders fall short of the skills and vision needed to lead the state in the 21st century. Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s commitment to attracting data centers to the state is predicated on the false premise that it will benefit the state economically by increasing coal and natural gas production. Even the most backward countries across the globe are moving away from that insane idea. On Sept. 14, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the repeal of most of the Biden administration's greenhouse gas requirements for U.S. power plants and West Virginia’s politicians responded like lemmings. Attorney General J.B. McCuskey praised the move in a news release. Gov. Morrisey said, “Today marks an important victory for reliable, affordable American energy after years of fighting federal efforts to shut down West Virginia’s coal and natural gas industries.” The state’s entire congressional delegation fully supported the move as well. West Virginia suffers Is there no hope for West Virginia? The state’s current political leadership lacks the skills required to hold office. Their backward views on climate change are deeply reactionary, willfully ignorant, and betray a profound lack of understanding of the issue.” Unfortunately, I believe their views also accurately reflect those of the majority of the citizens of the State. We must phase out coal and natural gas from our energy portfolio now! I fear West Virginia’s political system is incapable of producing leaders intelligent enough to guide the state in the direction it must go.

artigo.texto: DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion's approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company's strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion's portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. "AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage," said Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion. "Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs." Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users. About Solidion Technology, Inc. Headquartered in Dallas, Texas with pilot production facilities in Dayton, Ohio, Solidion's (NASDAQ: STI) core business includes manufacturing of battery materials and components, as well as development and production of next-generation batteries for energy storage systems, including UPS systems serving the artificial intelligence (AI) data center market and electric vehicles for ground, aerospace, and sea transportation. Solidion holds a portfolio of over 385 patents, covering innovations such as high-capacity, silane gas free and graphene-enabled silicon anodes, biomass-based graphite, advanced lithium-sulfur and lithium-metal technologies. artigo.texto: In Bessemer, Alabama, a secrecy pact with the developer of a proposed $14.5 billion data center didn’t just keep city officials quiet. It required them to destroy records. In Salem, Oregon, a city council member learned of her city’s nondisclosure agreement only when the public did. In Pine Island, Minnesota, officials knew about a project for two years before residents heard a word. One resident told lawmakers the democratic process there had been “hijacked by big tech.” These aren’t isolated lapses. That’s how the artificial intelligence boom is being built: deals negotiated behind closed doors, with elected officials contractually barred from telling constituents what enterprise is coming, how much electricity and water the facility will consume, and what tax breaks it will get. The AI train has left the station. Secrecy is a choice, and it’s the wrong one. When University of Mary Washington sociologist Eric Bonds filed public records requests across Virginia, the nation’s data center capital, he found nondisclosure agreements in 25 of 31 localities. Why would any official sign away the public’s right to know? Towns and states are competing for these investments, and a developer that doesn’t get its secrecy can take its billions elsewhere. Red and blue states alike have signed. And the pushback is just as bipartisan: Republicans and Democrats in Congress have joined forces on a bill to ban the agreements. What do these contracts hide? Sometimes just the business’s name. In Spotsylvania County, Virginia, an agreement with Amazon kept the company’s water use confidential. Residents drink from that same public system, yet they couldn’t find out how much Amazon would draw from it. The industry’s argument isn’t frivolous. Once landowners learn a data center is the buyer, prices soar, Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition told Spotlight PA. Fair enough, for a land deal. That doesn’t require hiding a facility’s water and power use from the people who will live beside it. Microsoft said in March that it would end its nondisclosure agreements with local governments. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman has since written that the company “ no longer use(s) nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies” it works with. Distrust breeds backlash: Garman counts more than 100 data center moratoriums under consideration nationwide. In Monterey Park, outside Los Angeles, 88% of voters banned data centers outright. Ending nondisclosure agreements only lets us see the bill. It doesn’t decide who pays it. That’s settled piecemeal, by utility commissions, county boards and water agencies, each with its own rules. Government often approves a data center with the same scrutiny as a shopping mall, by zoning boards never designed to handle infrastructure of national consequence. We’ve done this before. America didn’t build the interstate highway system by letting every county haggle over asphalt. It set national standards and built one network. The AI build-out deserves the same. Ohio offers a start. When data center demand outran central Ohio’s grid, regulators required large new facilities to pay for at least 85% of their expected power, for up to 12 years, whether they use it or not. The rules weeded out speculative projects, let new hookups resume, and aim to keep households from paying for power some server farm has reserved. Manufacturers have challenged it in court. However, it answers the question nondisclosure agreements never do: Who pays? California has gone further. Laws by San Diego state Sen. Steve Padilla and others order regulators to set separate electricity rates so data centers, not households, cover their grid upgrades, and require developers to report projected power demand when seeking local permits. Pima County, Arizona, went after the secrecy itself, capping nondisclosure agreements at two years and requiring disclosure at least 90 days before any county vote. Now, take these models national. Permit server farms like power plants. Before any council or county board approves a land sale, rezoning or tax break, require developers to disclose power, water and incentives. And make data centers pay. The servers are coming either way. What’s still up for a vote is whether Americans get to see the deal, and whether they’re the ones stuck paying for it.

artigo.texto: Ucranianos usaram drones para atingir três dos maiores data centers da Yandex, provocando quedas de serviço que revelam fragilidades na estratégia digital russa. Como começou a campanha de drones russos contra a Ucrânia? Em setembro passado, a Rússia iniciou uma série de ataques aéreos contra infraestruturas críticas ucranianas, incluindo centros de dados e redes de telefonia móvel. O objetivo declarado era interromper comunicações e limitar o acesso à internet em Kiev, afetando cerca de cem mil residências. Esses ataques faziam parte de um plano maior que também visava a rede elétrica, ferrovias e até blocos residenciais. Qual foi a reação da Ucrânia aos ataques russos? Como resposta direta, a Ucrânia passou a mirar instalações russas que sustentam serviços digitais essenciais. Em outubro, drones ucranianos atingiram um data center da Yandex na região de Sasovo, ao sudeste de Moscou, danificando equipamentos que hospedam dois dos três supercomputadores usados para treinar o modelo de IA YandexGPT. Que importância têm os supercomputadores da Yandex? Os dois sistemas afetados – batizados de Chervonenkis e Lyapunov – são baseados em gpus nvidia a100, reconhecidas pela alta performance em tarefas de aprendizado de máquina. O Chervonenkis registra cerca de 29,4 petaflops, ocupando a posição 101 no ranking Top500 de supercomputadores, enquanto o Lyapunov oferece 20,0 petaflops, posicionando‑se em 161. Essa capacidade permite à Yandex desenvolver modelos de linguagem avançados, aproximando‑se do que empresas como Google e Microsoft oferecem. Por que a infraestrutura russa parece vulnerável? Especialistas ligados ao círculo pró‑Kremlin, citados por pesquisadores independentes como ChrisO_wiki, alertam que a economia digital da Rússia está excessivamente centralizada. A maioria dos serviços de nuvem, busca e IA está concentrada em poucos data centers controlados por gigantes como a Yandex. Quando esses pontos críticos são atingidos, o efeito dominó pode comprometer desde serviços de streaming até plataformas de pagamento. O que o modelo descentralizado da Ucrânia oferece? A Ucrânia tem investido em soluções distribuídas, com provedores menores e redes peer‑to‑peer que dificultam a interrupção total. Essa arquitetura resiliente pode se tornar um exemplo para outros países que buscam reduzir a dependência de grandes provedores e melhorar a segurança nacional. Quais são as possíveis consequências para os usuários russos? - Interrupções temporárias em serviços de busca, mapas e assistentes virtuais da Yandex. - Impacto nas plataformas de e‑commerce que dependem da infraestrutura de nuvem da empresa. - Risco de atrasos nas atualizações de modelos de IA, prejudicando a competitividade da Rússia no mercado global. - Pressão para que o governo russo invista em redundância e diversificação de provedores. Como a comunidade tech brasileira deve interpretar esse conflito? Para os profissionais e entusiastas de tecnologia no Brasil, o episódio serve como alerta sobre a importância da arquitetura distribuída. Empresas que ainda dependem de um único provedor de nuvem podem considerar estratégias de multi‑cloud ou edge computing para mitigar riscos semelhantes. Além disso, o caso evidencia que a guerra digital pode ser tão decisiva quanto os combates tradicionais, influenciando políticas de segurança cibernética em todo o mundo. O que ainda não está claro sobre os danos aos supercomputadores? Até o momento, não há informações oficiais sobre o grau de comprometimento dos chips Nvidia A100 dentro dos sistemas Chervonenkis e Lyapunov. A complexidade de reparar ou substituir esses componentes pode levar semanas, e a Yandex ainda não divulgou um plano de recuperação detalhado. Para ficar no radar Os próximos dias serão críticos para observar como a Rússia reagirá a esses ataques. Se a estratégia de retaliação incluir novas ofensivas cibernéticas ou reforço de defesas físicas, o cenário digital da região pode mudar rapidamente. Enquanto isso, profissionais de TI no Brasil podem usar o caso como estudo de caso para reforçar a importância de arquiteturas resilientes e de um planejamento de continuidade de negócios robusto.

artigo.texto: LOWELL — The Lowell residents who attended the city’s second meeting on data centers were virtually unanimous in their feedback to restrict future growth of the facilities in every district in the city. “The only way to protect our community from the environmental impacts that we know are caused by these data centers, particularly when these data centers are put in environmental justice neighborhoods, is to prohibit them … ,” the participants at Table No. 4 said during their presentation. The community engagement event was hosted on Oct. 7, by the Department of Planning and Development at the Senior Center on Broadway Street in the Acre neighborhood. Residents give city planners feedback More than 50 participants broke into a dozen small groups to discuss DPD’s two zoning options for consideration by the City Council for regulating data centers in the city, part of an overhaul of Lowell’s outdated zoning code. Option 1 is restricting future data center growth to 15 megawatts with climate-friendly infrastructure. Option 2 is that data centers are prohibited in every district. Lowell is currently home to a 352,000-square-foot data center in the city’s Sacred Heart neighborhood. Markley Lowell LLC operates the state-of-the-art data-storage and cloud-computing colocation data center that rents secure space to more than 500 clients to run their own technology. Its systems power and provide routing to a wide variety of private companies, state and local governments, internet companies and universities, including UMass Lowell. The privately owned company has faced some local headwinds, driven in part by consistent neighborhood opposition, as well as a national angst over the unchecked growth of hyperscale projects that are the backbone of the artificial intelligence revolution. Residents in the economic justice neighborhood have consistently testified to noise and air quality concerns, ongoing and disruptive construction projects and violations of approved permitting. “We say these are the rules in place, you can build your data center,” the moderator for Table No. 1 said. “Who’s going to enforce those rules? What are we going to do to make sure that they’re following them? And if they’re not, what is going to happen? Because we’ve seen it in other places where they come in, they say, ‘This is what we’re going to do,’ and then they far exceed that and it harms the community and the damage has already been done.” Markley Lowell only data center operating in Lowell Markley Lowell was not on DPD’s data center zoning agenda, but its shadow loomed over the residents’ workshopped conversations. When the Markley Group purchased the derelict and long-vacant former Prince Pasta plant in Lowell for $4 million in 2015, Lowell welcomed the high-tech center with a $77 million tax break. Over the past 10 years, the company embarked on a dramatic renovation and expansion, with founder and CEO Jeff Markley claiming to have invested at least $650 million in the site and related developments to date. The company’s power profile has expanded from seven to 23 diesel-powered backup generators, 16 chillers and two water towers to secure its growing energy needs. And despite significant pushback from both residents and the City Council, the company has continued to expand its footprint in Lowell. Both Markley Lowell and Jeff Markley have purchased multiple properties in and around its existing facility at 1 Markley Way. City lacks zoning on data centers The City Council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium March 10 to allow the city to develop zoning around data centers in Lowell. Under the city’s existing zoning, the data center company is not required to divulge its long-term development plans for any of its new sites. But the parcels either contain or are colocated to generators of the scale needed to power data centers, perhaps even artificial intelligence. The company’s website recently added “Now available for your generative AI workloads.” DPD Deputy Director Camilo Espitia reminded participants that Markley’s current projects are “locked in.” “Whichever option we go with today is irrelevant to where Markley stands today,” he said. “They are grandfathered in and that business will keep operating. This is intended for any other land that has not been touched by data centers or that hasn’t been subdivided in the future for any other type of developer including Markley themselves.” At the end of the almost two-hour session, Assistant City Manager and DPD Director Yovani Baez-Rose thanked the community for their feedback. “We appreciate the fact that you’re taking time out of your personal lives to sort of help us frame what our community is going to look like moving forward,” she said. In late October to early November, DPD will present the data center ordinance to the City Council Zoning Subcommittee, followed by a final draft of the zoning ordinance to the council in early to mid-December. A Planning Board public hearing will be held in January, and the council will hold a public hearing and hold a vote later that month.

artigo.texto: Data center development divides candidates and communities Pennsylvania governor and representative races are both taking strong stances Data center development divides candidates and communities Pennsylvania governor and representative races are both taking strong stances Data center development has become a major topic in western Pennsylvania this fall, with residents and officials debating regulations and community concerns as elections approach. Kristin Kanthak, an associate professor of political science at the University of Pittsburgh, said, "One of the big issues of this election, it seems, is artificial intelligence. For example, we've seen the governor candidates come down on different sides of that issue, and parties are really trying to figure out where they sit on that." More than a dozen data center sites have been proposed or explored in western Pennsylvania, and the state is aware of at least 100 proposals across Pennsylvania, most of which are still in the early stages. Shapiro, Garrity Stances Gov. Josh Shapiro has issued an executive order requiring developers to meet stricter commitments before the state reviews their permit applications. "You've got to generate your own power, and the developers and the tech companies have to pay for it. You've got to protect our air and water, and most importantly, you have to earn the support of the local community first," Shapiro said. State Treasurer Stacy Garrity, Shapiro’s challenger, has called for a temporary pause on data center development to allow municipalities time to update their zoning regulations. "I heard the same thing. They're not against data centers, but they want time to get their zoning updated," Garrity said. What Local Officials are Saying Local officials, who make zoning decisions, are staying in office as regular elections for Pennsylvania’s local offices are held in odd-numbered years. Some state representative and congressional races also feature candidates representing municipalities involved in data center development. In Elizabeth Township, where a data center has been proposed, Republican State Rep. Andrew Kuzma is running against Democrat Dylan Altemara. Kuzma addressed the issue at a recent town hall, saying, "I am a state representative, meaning that I represent the people that live here. And if 95% of them are taking a position, I am 100% with them because that is my job as a state representative." Altemara shared a statement at the town hall calling for more transparency in development plans from the township. With just weeks left before the election, many residents are still deciding which candidates will best address their concerns about data center development. Some are advocating for stricter regulations, while others are calling for a complete halt to the projects.

artigo.texto: On October 14 in Hanoi, VIR held a seminar on credit policy and the carbon market, where experts focused on discussing the links between credit policy, the carbon market, and the capital market, with a view to identifying solutions to mobilise financial resources for the green transition. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV), said the Party, state, and government had introduced key policies and guidelines in recent years to promote green growth, energy transition, and a low-carbon economy, supporting Vietnam’s commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. “This transition requires substantial investment in technological innovation, changes to production methods, greater energy efficiency, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction,” Canh said. “Alongside funding from the state budget and capital and money markets, market-based mechanisms, including the carbon market, are needed to mobilise additional resources and create economic incentives for businesses to proactively reduce emissions.” “By establishing emission allowances, measuring emissions reduction results, and determining transaction prices for emission allowances and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism for converting emissions reduction results into economic value. This gives businesses additional incentives and resources to continue investing in the green transition, rather than relying primarily on bank credit,” he said. The government issued Decree No.29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange in January, establishing the legal framework for the organisation and operation of the market and the trading of GHG emission allowances and carbon credits. The initial pilot market has been established with a scale of more than 511 million tonnes of CO2, equivalent to the emission allowances allocated to facilities in three major emitting industries, including thermal power, iron and steel, and cement for the 2025-2026 period. The pilot phase will run until the end of 2028, before the market transitions to full mandatory operation from 2029. Commercial banks will participate in the market as settlement banks, with BIDV serving as the sole settlement bank during the pilot phase. From the banking sector’s perspective, Canh said it was important to clearly recognise the respective roles of green credit and the carbon market in the green transition. “First, green credit provides capital for investment and technological innovation, creating resources for the development of green industries and sectors and thereby generating emissions reduction results. The emissions reductions achieved by projects financed with bank capital, in turn, provide the foundation and commodities for the development of the carbon market,” Canh stated. “Conversely, an effectively functioning carbon market will enable businesses to generate revenue and maintain stable cash flows from emissions reduction results to support their production and business activities, while improving their credit quality. Businesses will also be better positioned to purchase carbon credits to meet the stringent standards applicable to imports and exports,” he added. Regarding green credit, Canh explained that the key consideration was not merely whether funds had been disbursed to a project classified as green, but also whether the borrowing customer had demonstrated measurable results in energy savings, emissions reduction, and environmental protection. “Measurement, reporting, and verification of emissions reduction results, together with the trading of emission allowances and carbon credits on the carbon market, can provide additional information for monitoring the environmental performance of projects. This, in turn, can help credit institutions assess the effectiveness of capital utilisation and strengthen the management and supervision of green capital flows,” he said. In practice, the banking sector has proactively implemented various measures in recent years to promote green credit and direct capital towards industries and sectors that deliver environmental benefits and reduce GHG emissions. The SBV has gradually refined the policy framework and issued orientations and guidelines on green credit and environmental and social risk management. It has also encouraged credit institutions to develop strategies and internal processes, as well as introduce credit products aligned with green growth objectives. This is particularly important in the context of developing green and low-carbon financing channels. Speaking at the event, Canh said that since green credit was first introduced in 2017, the sector had expanded in both credit scale and the participation of credit institutions. As of the end of June this year, outstanding green credit had exceeded VND 856 trillion, up 9.87 per cent from the end of 2025. Average annual growth exceeded 20 per cent over the 2017-2025 period, with lending concentrated primarily in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, which accounted for more than 31 per cent, and green energy, which accounted for nearly 28 per cent. Outstanding loans that had undergone environmental and social risk assessments exceeded $240 billion, representing more than 31.33 per cent of total outstanding credit across the economy. “This result reflects the banking system’s commitment and efforts to support the green transition of businesses and the economy. When the carbon market operates effectively, emissions reduction results can be converted into financial resources for the businesses themselves. Accordingly, the development of the carbon market can help ease pressure on green credit resources,” said Canh. “Rather than relying predominantly on their own capital, the state budget, or bank credit to finance their transition needs, businesses will have additional opportunities to generate resources from their own emissions reduction results. In the long term, this will help diversify financing sour

artigo.texto: Did Ukraine’s strikes on data centers really silence Russian bots? Russia's army of bots is apparently offline. At least, that's according to chatter on social media and even Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Over the past week, Ukrainian drones struck three data centers belonging to Yandex, the tech giant often called "Russia’s Google." The first strike happened on Oct. 8, followed by a second attack on Oct. 9. On Sunday, Oct. 11, a third strike damaged a Yandex data center in the Vladimir region, east of Moscow. The company said operations at that facility were completely suspended and some of its services were unavailable, according to the BBC. The attacks disrupted Yandex services, from its AI chatbot to its smart home devices. Per the BBC, the military strikes were meant to target "places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine." You May Also Like Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelenskyy said "everyone noticed" a drop in Russian bot activity on social media after the strikes. On X, Reddit, and elsewhere, users in several Western countries reported seeing less right-wing activity in their feeds, from pro-GOP accounts in the U.S. to supporters of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Czech member of the European Parliament Tomáš Zdechovský also pointed to claims that online support for the AfD had dropped after the strikes. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. The prediction market Polymarket’s X account was among those amplifying the claim. Take that with a grain of salt, though, as the account has a tendency for posting breaking-news-style claims without sources or verification. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. Much of the buzz traces back to a report from U24 Media, the media arm of United24, a platform run by the Ukrainian government. To its credit, U24’s own report is careful about what the numbers can and can’t prove. It cites an Oct. 12 analysis by The Deep Dive of data from Cloudflare Radar, which monitors internet traffic. According to that analysis, automated web traffic from Yandex’s network fell sharply after Oct. 8 and nearly disappeared by Oct. 11. At one point, it measured just 0.3 percent of the chart’s peak, compared with 88.2 percent at the same hour a week earlier. U24 also cites German tech publication t3n's report of a similar plunge — with bot traffic dropping to about 0.4 percent of the previous week’s level before bouncing back to around 20 percent later in the day on Oct. 11. The catch is that "automated traffic" and "Russian propaganda bots" aren’t the same thing. Automated traffic is any request sent to a website by software rather than a person. Most of it is mundane, e.g., search engine crawlers indexing pages or monitoring tools checking whether sites are up. Because Yandex runs Russia’s biggest search engine, its network constantly sends out crawlers to index the web. Knocking its data centers offline would bring traffic to a halt regardless of whether a single troll account went quiet. As U24 itself notes, the measurements show a sharp drop in automated network activity, but they can’t tell us whether propaganda bots disappeared or whether damaged infrastructure simply stopped producing ordinary automated traffic. The numbers also track how much traffic Yandex’s network sent relative to its peak, not how many social media accounts were active. Mashable has yet to see published evidence tying Russian influence operations on X or Reddit to Yandex’s servers specifically. Many of the claims to that effect are sourced from the same Cloudflare Radar and Deep Dive data reports that we cited here. Influence campaigns can run on infrastructure anywhere, and the accounts posting the content don’t have to live on Yandex’s network at all. It's easy to see why the claim has caught on, as social media platforms are rife with hyper-polarization fueled by ragebait political engagement. However, not all political content online comes from Russian bots. As The Atlantic's Ali Breland writes, operatives based in Eastern European countries like Latvia are paying people to post pro-GOP talking points — $3 for every 1,000 views. That also doesn’t mean the strikes had no effect online. Per U24, the bombings have found a way to rattle Russia’s internet, including widespread outages. Whether it also silenced Russia’s online propaganda machine is a much bigger claim. He has a Master's in Journalism from the University of North Texas and is a proud orange cat father. His writing has also appeared in PC Mag and Mother Jones. In his free time, he cooks, loves to sleep, and greatly enjoys Detroit sports. artigo.texto: By Charlotte Underwood JACKSBORO, TN (WLAF)- County commissioners briefly discussed data centers at Monday’s county commission workshop, saying that the county needed to pursue education regarding data centers. TOP PHOTO: Left to right- Lonnie Weldon, Ralph Davis, Chris Stanley, Suzette Davenport, Johnny Bruce and Beverly Hall. Commissioner Lonnie Weldon brought the topic up at the close of Monday’s workshop, saying he had attended the Tennessee Governor’s Economic Development Conference in Chattanooga. He and several other commissioners attended that conference. “We sat in on one of the meetings on data centers, I don’t know what the commission thinks of data centers or what they know about data centers, but there are multiple kinds of data centers. I think they would be willing to come and speak to the commission about data centers, whether it’s a good thing or a bad thing,” Weldon said, adding that he thought the citizens had a “misconception about data centers” because of all the “bots that have been on the internet, telling how bad they are.” “Not all data centers are bad, they are profitable for the county, but if the commission likes, we could probably get in touch with them and have them come talk to the commission about data centers … there’s a good side, they can also talk to you about what we might want to do to keep data centers from coming here, but its up to the commission if they want to pursue that info,” Weldon said. Commissioner David Greene spoke briefly on the topic as well, saying he felt more education was needed on data centers. “I kind of agree with you on that, there’s good and there’s bad and I was all bad until I went and listened to them talk about that. I just think it’s an opportunity we keep an open mind to. I am not saying we do them or don’t do them, but I think we need to educate ourselves about them, because the one that I was in, they have some that are self-contained units, you fill the water one time basically and it does for several months as they recirculate it – they generate their own power. Good or bad, I don’t know, but the one that I sat in on that talked about it, they said that 75% of the negativity on social media on them was done by bots and those bots are owned by Chinese companies, they are trying to create the negativity about it because they want China to be the leading developer of AI,” Greene said. Weldon said that there were data centers that the county needed to “guard from” since Campbell County “does not have zoning.” “The ones that you hear the most negativity about is the hyper skill data centers that use all the water, and all has the loud noises, that is probably the one that the county needs to guard from, where you hear all the social media about the noise that you hear from it, or all the water that they use or power that they use and take away. The way I take it, this latter one is something the county needs to guard against because we don’t have zoning, that is something that we probably need to look at, but most of these others are self-contained and they are money makers,” Weldon said. Commissioner Chris Stanley, who also attended the conference in Chattanooga said there “were several counties there who were talking about how they were making money off of it, of course, I went into the meeting kind of like David, I thought they were all bad, but it did look like there are several different kinds, I think it would be good to hear both sides, and educate ourselves on it and the biggest thing right now is, and I know zoning is a bad word in the county and we are not trying to say zone your property, and I am not on the planning commission, but they probably need to talk about zoning for data centers and the only places that they can go, because I think right now, there is no zoning, no law against them moving in next door,” Stanley said. artigo.texto: Brightray Science Inc, a majority-owned subsidiary of BUUU Group Limited, has announced that its wholly owned subsidiary Brightray Veridian Pte. Ltd. has signed a letter of intent (LOI) with an unnamed US-based mission-critical infrastructure partner for a planned 10 MW AI data center project in Indiana, United States. This is, according to a press release, Brightray’s first project LOI signed in the US and an important step toward expanding into the world’s largest data center market. Under the LOI, Brightray will deploy a prefabricated data center solution. The implementation is subject to final agreement on technical specifications, commercial terms, the project schedule, and definitive contract documentation. “Entering the US market is an important step in Brightray’s international development. The US has enormous data center demand, and customers face real pressure to turn their AI investments into usable computing power as quickly as possible. Our entry point is delivery: with Brightray prefabricated data center solution, we move more of the work into the factory and run manufacturing in parallel with on-site works, with the aim of shortening the delivery period for this project to within one year,” said Bin Wang, Brightray founder. By taking this approach, Brightray says it can deliver the 10 MW AI data center within a year. That timeline covers the entire schedule, including design finalization, permitting, international shipping, on-site foundation and ancillary works, installation, and commissioning. “We look forward to working further with our partner on the technical solution and implementation arrangements and to building delivery experience in the US market through this 10MW project. Addressing the power, cooling and space requirements of next-generation AI equipment, we aim to bring the efficiency advantages of our prefabricated data center solution to the project and lay the foundation for the further expansion of our US business,” said Wang. If this agreement is finalized and the project delivered, it could serve as a blueprint for Brightray’s expansion into the US market. Grid capacity constraints, community opposition, and infrastructure bottlenecks can significantly delay data center buildouts in the US market, a problem Brightray looks to want to solve. Despite the constraints, US data center investments have nearly doubled since 2024, according to Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, and demand for AI will only push that growth higher with the US data center market expected to be worth US$ 494.49 billion by 2031.

artigo.texto: ND counties talk about how to handle data centers BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - The North Dakota Association of Counties said that data center construction should be considered on a county-by-county basis. The Association held its annual meeting this week in Bismarck. The group said questions about the size of data centers, proximity to urban and rural areas and potential tax benefits differ between counties. These differences are why it’s necessary for counties to have individualized zoning and planning rules. “There’s obviously people that are highly opposed, but we’re still gathering facts, getting the right information out there,” said Association President Nick Moser. “That’s one great thing about this event, is getting that information and getting the proper information to people is huge.” In Moser’s own county, Cavalier, data centers are not allowed within one mile of town. The noise from data centers only reaches 50 decibels at this distance, according to research. Moser encourages public hearings to ensure the correct information is being given to people. The new edition is based on the premium trim and is limited to 150 units. BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition The ultra-limited Festive Edition (150 units) was specifically introduced to capitalise on the Indian festive shopping season. It offers high-end buyers exclusivity through a unique Tan and Black interior treatment, maintaining momentum for a model that has quickly become one of BYD India's top sellers. Interior and Exterior Features The Sealion 7 festive edition features an 82.56 kWh Blade Battery and a rear-mounted electric motor that delivers 230 kW (308 hp) and 380 Nm of torque. The electric SUV can accelerate from 0 to 100 kmph in 6.7 seconds and has a claimed driving range of 567 km under the NEDC testing cycle. The Electric SUV is equipped with BYD's Cell-to-Body (CTB) technology, which integrates the battery pack into the vehicle's structural architecture. The festive edition also features torque adaptation control, which manages torque delivery based on traction conditions. These features were already seen in the premium model. The car comes with a 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen infotainment system, quilted Nappa leather seats, and a panoramic glass roof with an electric sunshade. It also comes with a dual-tone cabin treatment. It has 11 airbags and a five-star Euro NCAP rating. Other attributes include a DYNAUDIO system, ventilated front seats, driver's memory seats, a 360 camera, an ADAS suite, a panoramic glass roof, a powered tailgate, double-glazed glass, and a 12-speaker system. The Sealion 7 measures 4,830 mm in length, 1,925 mm in width, and 1,620 mm in height, with a 2,930 mm wheelbase. The cargo capacity is 500 litres at the back, expandable to 1,789 litres, and the frunk holds 58 litres. The Sealion 7 Festive Edition extends that approach, bringing a distinctive Tan & Black interior to the premium variant in a limited run for the festive season. At its core, it retains the technology, safety and performance that define the Sealion 7, while offering customers a differentiated expression of the model. Its biggest strengths are the Blade Battery, premium interior, 308 bhp performance and extensive equipment. The main point to remember is that this special edition is essentially the existing Premium variant with a different cabin colour scheme.

artigo.texto: Data center boom puts Republicans in a bind before midterm elections A year ago, there weren't many voters talking about data centers. Now, the massive facilities being built to satisfy the enormous computing needs of the AI boom have become one of the most explosive issues of the 2026 midterms, and their construction is opening a divide between the Trump administration and Republicans running in state and federal races this fall. When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, most data centers were being built in blue states. But by 2025, 68% of data centers online were in red states. Now, 75% of data centers under construction and 80% of data centers in the planning stage are in predominantly Republican states, according to new data from Cleanview Research, an independent energy market intelligence company tracking data center development. "Red states have more of a history of accepting large, energy intensive, infrastructure projects — even those that might have detrimental effects on communities," said Chris Millay, a data center analyst at the macroeconomic consultancy Greenmantle. He also points to the relative lack of environmental regulation and the availability of open land as reasons rural states are receiving more investment. President Trump sees the AI race as critical to the economy and national security, and he's one of data centers' biggest boosters. At a recent Ohio rally, he said of data centers, "We want them … look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio — you can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." He has repeatedly dismissed public opposition to data centers, posting on Truth Social that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." Mr. Trump has also resisted regulation, though he has called on developers to give back to local communities through education, lower taxes, job creation and energy cost protections. Red states may be hosting most of the boom, and increasingly, communities living next to data centers are pushing back. People who live near data centers have reported concerns about their property values, noise, higher energy bills and resource depletion. Meanwhile, calls for moratoriums are spreading through communities across the country. Overall, opposition to data centers outweighs support by 30 points, with polls showing the majority of Republicans oppose the construction of data centers near them. "It's such a consensus issue it's really impossible to take the other side," said Millay. "When voters see a politician who supports data centers, they think, 'Well, how am I going to trust him with my job?'" Some of the president's closest allies have begun to break with him on the issue. In Texas, which has the most data centers under construction, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott has paused environmental permits and grid connections for new data centers. Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is in a surprisingly close race against Democrat Gina Hinojosa. In Texas' tight Senate race, the Republican nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, wants to end Texas' sales tax break for data centers. He has also said they should be held criminally liable if they power AI chatbots that endanger children. Data centers seem to be the single issue where Democratic and Republican candidates sound nearly identical. In Ohio, Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, said in a press release, "I am calling on our Statehouse to pass a conditional moratorium on data centers." Her GOP opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, has gone further. He vowed to "issue an executive order on my first day in office to immediately halt the approval of any new data center project announcements in Ohio," and to keep that pause in place until lawmakers pass his "Ohioans-First" law, which would require data centers to provide free electricity to surrounding residents. A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that data centers are a weak point for Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, with voters favoring his opponent by an 11-point margin on the issue. Campaigns have spent $45 million this year on ads that mention data centers — most of them in opposition — according to AdImpact. In Georgia, where candidates have spent nearly $13 million on ads mentioning data centers — more than any other state — the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Rick Jackson, is sticking with Mr. Trump. While the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, is calling for a temporary moratorium on construction, Jackson says the decision should be left up to local officials. Jackson made the case for data centers at a recent press conference, saying he wanted "to educate people on the benefit if they want [a data center]." Some counties, he said, expect they "will have zero property taxes after the data center goes in." Effingham County, where OpenAI plans a $20 billion data center, has pledged to use some of that revenue to cut homeowners' property taxes. Because most of the next wave of data centers is largely planned in states Mr. Trump won in 2024, the choices Republican candidates make, siding with voters or with the president, could decide whether those projects are paused, made more expensive or even canceled.
