artigo.texto: Marblehead could move to ban data centers under a new zoning bylaw, following a discussion at the Planning Board’s Oct. 13 meeting. Planning Board Chair Marc Liebman raised the possibility of prohibiting data centers in town, citing concerns about their impact on communities and pointing to similar efforts underway in Salem. “There’s all kinds of reasons why data centers create a strain on the communities they’re in,” Liebman said. Data centers are facilities that house computer servers and other equipment used to store, process and distribute digital information. Large facilities, including those supporting artificial intelligence, can consume substantial amounts of electricity and water and require extensive infrastructure. Liebman said several town officials have expressed interest in exploring a prohibition and wanted to gauge the Planning Board’s willingness to pursue one. “There are many people in various parts of town government who wanted to test our appetite for defining data centers and coming up with a bylaw to prevent data centers from existing in Marblehead,” he said. “I fully support that.” The Salem City Council approved a data center ban earlier this month. Liebman said one of the biggest challenges is developing a legal definition of a data center. He proposed working with Select Board members, Planning and Community Development Director Brendan Callahan and town staff to develop draft language for the Planning Board to review at its November meeting. The proposal could then be brought before Town Meeting for consideration. No formal vote was taken, and no specific restrictions or exemptions were proposed. The discussion was preliminary, with the board agreeing to explore the idea further. ADU approvals highlight multigenerational housing needs Earlier in the meeting, the board considered three accessory dwelling unit applications, approving two and continuing a third amid concerns about whether the proposed designs complied with the town’s 900-square-foot limit.

artigo.texto: Data center developer offers residents of Kansas town $1,000 each for 10 years Amid a pronounced public backlash against data center construction in the U.S., one real estate developer is making an offer it hopes will win over one Kansas community: money. Digital Realty is offering every household in De Soto, Kansas, where it plans to build a data center, $1,000 in utility and property tax credits for 10 years. "Digital Realty builds critical infrastructure that enables the modern economy, and we believe we also have a responsibility to help strengthen the communities that make this growth possible," Andy Power, the developer's president and CEO, said in a statement on Wednesday. The offer is part of a $20 million community investment Digital Realty is pledging in De Soto as the company paves the way for a 280-acre data center site. The company said the project, which will eventually cover 1,400 acres, will provide recurring tax revenue, create jobs and deliver other economic benefits to local residents. Digital Realty, a publicly traded company based in Austin, Texas, with a market worth of more than $67 billion, said in a news release that it is working with De Soto to finalize distribution of the $1,000 credits to households. The company, whose clients include Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Nvidia, expects to create 250 permanent jobs for local suppliers and contractors once the site is complete. The initial phase of development will also support "thousands of construction jobs over time," Digital Realty said in its news release. A recent CBS News poll found that more Americans oppose than favor building a new data center in their area, citing concerns that the facilities harm the environment, drain local resources and raise utility costs.

A ofensiva registrada no domingo (11) forçou a paralisação completa das operações na unidade afetada, resultando no bloqueio instantâneo e na indisponibilidade de serviços populares da plataforma, como aplicativos de transporte por aplicativo e entregas de refeições. Os impactos do ataque transpassaram as fronteiras nacionais e atingiram nações vizinhas da Ásia Central, como o Cazaquistão e o Quirguistão, onde usuários relataram instabilidade e interrupção parcial no funcionamento de diversos ecossistemas digitais da empresa. O bombardeio representa o terceiro ataque coordenado contra instalações estratégicas da empresa tecnológica em poucos dias, após unidades no centro da região de Ryazan terem sido atingidas na quinta-feira (8) e outra instalação na região de Kaluga ter sido alvo na sexta-feira (9). As incursões táticas ucranianas integram uma estratégia deliberada de retaliação contra a infraestrutura de dados russa em resposta aos contínuos bombardeios efetuados contra centros de tecnologia e processamento de informações na Ucrânia. artigo.texto: South Korea plans to launch the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) in 2027 to facilitate trading in carbon credits generated by overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects. The system will classify credits according to host-country approval, use blockchain to record key project information and rely on the Korea Exchange (KRX) for trading. The government is also considering digital-asset-based credit issuance and links with its domestic emissions trading scheme. Key Overview - Launch target: 2027. - Market: Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM). - Trading platform: Korea Exchange (KRX). - Credit categories: GVCM A and GVCM NA. - Technology: Blockchain-based records of key project and emissions-reduction information. - Future options: Digital-asset issuance and possible links with South Korea’s domestic emissions trading scheme. - International cooperation: Participation by other countries and potential conversion of selected World Bank and Green Climate Fund project outcomes into GVCM credits. South Korea Prepares to Launch an International Carbon Market South Korea is preparing to establish an international marketplace for carbon credits generated through overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects, with full operations targeted for 2027. The initiative, called the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM), is designed to support the issuance and trading of credits while addressing concerns about the credibility and consistency of carbon markets. The government discussed the detailed implementation plan at a ministerial meeting on international economic affairs on 12 October 2026, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il. Under the proposed system, verified emissions-reduction outcomes from overseas projects will be converted into carbon credits that can be traded through the Korea Exchange. Depending on the relevant approvals, the credits could support corporate environmental activities and certain regulatory obligations, including national climate targets. The initiative represents a move beyond a market limited to voluntary corporate offsetting. The government has replaced the earlier name, Global Voluntary Carbon Market, with Global Verified Carbon Market to reflect the broader intended uses of eligible credits. Two Credit Categories Will Determine How Credits Can Be Used A central feature of the framework is the distinction between credits approved for international transfer by the host country and those without that approval. Credits classified as GVCM A will be eligible for specified compliance uses, including contributions towards the investing country’s nationally determined contribution (NDC) and compliance with international aviation requirements under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). They may also support corporate environmental, social and governance activities. Credits classified as GVCM NA will initially be restricted to voluntary corporate environmental activities. Their permitted uses could expand if the host country subsequently grants the required transfer approval. This distinction matters because approval by the country hosting a carbon-reduction project affects whether the resulting credits can be used towards international climate commitments. It also provides a basis for separating credits intended for voluntary claims from those eligible for specified compliance purposes. The two categories of carbon credits are therefore central to the proposed market’s structure and the conditions under which buyers can use the credits they acquire. Blockchain Records to Support Credit Credibility South Korea plans to use blockchain technology to strengthen the traceability of carbon credits. Key information, including project operators and emissions-reduction volumes, will be recorded on the blockchain to help establish a more transparent record of the credits issued. The system is intended to improve confidence in transactions in a market where the credibility of claimed emissions reductions has been a longstanding concern. Better access to project information can help participants track the origins and reported outcomes of credits. The government also plans to use the Korea Exchange as the trading platform. The approach combines blockchain-based information management with an established exchange infrastructure for trading the credits. However, blockchain records alone cannot guarantee that a project has delivered the emissions reductions it claims. The effectiveness of the framework will also depend on project assessment, reliable measurement and verification, and compliance with the applicable approval requirements. Context is everything. This remains under review rather than a confirmed feature of the initial launch. The government will need to consider the relevant legal framework, market conditions and the reliability of the proposed infrastructure before deciding how digital-asset issuance might operate. It is also examining whether GVCM credits could be linked to the domestic emissions trading scheme and greenhouse gas target management system, subject to the necessary conditions. Such a link could create additional uses for eligible credits, although the proposal has not yet been confirmed as an operational arrangement. artigo.texto: Project doubles capacity of Bocanova site in one of the country's fastest-growing electricity load centers HOUSTON and OAKLAND, Calif., Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nightpeak Energy announced today the successful financial close and commercial operation of its 150 MW, two-hour duration Bocanova 2 battery storage project in Southeast Texas. The project reached commercial operation on September 17, doubling the Bocanova site's capacity to 300 MW and adding significant flexibility to the ERCOT grid as data centers and other large loads drive rapid growth in electricity demand. Bocanova 2 is the second phase of Nightpeak's battery storage development in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area. The first 150 MW phase, Bocanova 1, began commercial operation in August 2025. Bocanova 2 uses Tesla's Megapack 2 XL battery storage systems. Operating under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty, the project was financed through a tax equity bridge loan and construction-to-term loan with MUFG Bank. U.S. Bank provided traditional tax equity. Paris Hays, Co-founder and CEO/CDO, Nightpeak Energy, said, "We're seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand. Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change. With 300 MW now operating at Bocanova, we're putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country. We're grateful to the City of Alvin, Brazoria County, and the local community for their support in bringing Bocanova to life." Since its founding in 2022, Nightpeak has developed and acquired a portfolio of over 1 GW of operating and de-risked capacity spanning gas-fired generation, battery storage and powered land development, and continues to advance an additional pipeline of flexible generation and large-load projects to meet growing demand in the U.S. About Nightpeak Energy Nightpeak Energy develops, owns and operates flexible power generation and large-load enablement assets that help meet growing electricity and AI demand while supporting a reliable, lower-carbon electric grid. Applying a technology-agnostic approach across gas-fired generation, energy storage, renewables, and large-load project types, the company combines generation and load into integrated solutions for its customers. Nightpeak is a portfolio investment of Energy Spectrum Partners VIII, LP, which is an infrastructure-focused private equity fund based in Dallas, Texas. artigo.texto: Para analisar a relação entre crédito verde e o mercado de carbono sob a perspectiva de um banco comercial, a Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank , fez uma apresentação no seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", organizado pelo jornal Finanças e Investimentos em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã, em 14 de outubro. O mercado de carbono abre novas oportunidades para créditos verdes. No contexto internacional, a precificação do carbono tornou-se uma ferramenta econômica cada vez mais importante. O relatório do Banco Mundial "Estado e Tendências da Precificação do Carbono 2026" identifica 87 políticas de precificação direta do carbono em todo o mundo, abrangendo mais de 29% das emissões globais de gases de efeito estufa; essas ferramentas geram mais de US$ 107 bilhões em receita orçamentária em 2025 e o preço médio direto do carbono é de quase US$ 21/tCO₂e. Esses números não implicam um preço único para todos os créditos, mas demonstram que os custos das emissões estão sendo cada vez mais incorporados às decisões de investimento e negócios. A Sra. Ha afirmou que, para o Agribank, essa questão está diretamente ligada aos seus clientes e áreas de atuação. A agricultura , os agricultores e as áreas rurais são significativamente impactados pelas mudanças climáticas e têm espaço para redução de emissões na produção de arroz, pecuária, silvicultura, energia de biomassa, tratamento de resíduos e economia circular. Portanto, a questão central não é "se o banco comprará e venderá créditos", mas sim "como o banco pode financiar o processo de geração de resultados de redução de emissões e quando o valor do carbono é suficientemente certo para influenciar as decisões de crédito?". O arcabouço legal para o mercado de carbono do Vietnã foi estabelecido pela Lei de Proteção Ambiental de 2020 e detalhado por meio de diversos documentos. De 2022 até o presente, a lista de empresas obrigadas a realizar inventários de gases de efeito estufa aumentou de 1.912 para 2.441, um aumento de quase 28%. Em 2022, a Decisão 01/2022/QD-TTg listou 1.912 estabelecimentos; em 2024, a Decisão 13/2024/QD-TTg listou 2.166 estabelecimentos, um aumento de 254 estabelecimentos, representando aproximadamente 30% do total das emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa; e em 2026, a Decisão 42/2026/QD-TTg listou 2.441 estabelecimentos, um aumento de 275 estabelecimentos. Em relação aos créditos verdes, a Decisão 21/2025/QD-TTg sobre critérios ambientais e a Lista de Classificação Verde fornece uma base para a identificação de projetos verdes, e a Decisão 46/2026/QD-TTg sobre orientações para a determinação de projetos verdes e projetos que atendem aos critérios da economia circular contribui para a criação de novos projetos verdes, desbloqueando capital, expandindo os padrões para a economia circular e os critérios ESG. No entanto, é importante ressaltar que a inclusão de um projeto na lista de classificação verde não significa automaticamente que ele possua créditos de carbono e, inversamente, um projeto com créditos não atende automaticamente às condições para a concessão de créditos. A Decisão 42/2026/QD-TTg, em vigor a partir de 25 de setembro de 2026, atualiza a lista de setores e instalações que devem realizar inventários de gases de efeito estufa, ampliando ainda mais a base de dados para a gestão de emissões. De acordo com dados da HNX, o código de cota VN2025 para o período de conformidade de 2025-2026 possui um volume total de 511.473.846 tCO₂e, alocado a 110 instituições; o primeiro dia de negociação é 29 de junho de 2026 e o último dia de negociação é 24 de dezembro de 2027. Esta é uma transição significativa da estrutura política para a infraestrutura de negociação propriamente dita. No entanto, os dados publicamente disponíveis na HNX mostram que, durante esses dias de negociação, tanto o volume quanto o valor negociado foram zero. Isso não significa que o mercado não tenha potencial, mas sugere que os bancos não devem presumir que já exista um preço de referência estável ou liquidez abundante para usar diretamente na avaliação de pedidos de empréstimo. O Vietnã também possui experiência na comercialização de resultados de redução de emissões no mercado internacional. Em março de 2024, o Vietnã recebeu US$ 51,5 milhões do Banco Mundial por 10,3 milhões de toneladas de resultados comprovados de redução de emissões no âmbito do Programa de Redução de Emissões da Região Centro-Norte. A lição importante não está em dividir US$ 51,5 milhões por 10,3 milhões de toneladas para formar um "preço de referência", mas sim em que os resultados ambientais só se tornam fluxo de caixa quando há uma metodologia clara, dados, verificação, contrato e mecanismo de compartilhamento de benefícios. Proposta para facilitar o fluxo de capital verde vinculado ao mercado de carbono. Segundo representantes do Agribank, em meados de 2026, o total de ativos do Agribank ultrapassará 2,7 trilhões de VND, o capital mobilizado ultrapassará 2,5 trilhões de VND e a carteira de empréstimos para a economia ultrapassará 2 trilhões de VND. Em agosto de 2026, a carteira de empréstimos para agricultura, agricultores e áreas rurais atingirá mais de 1,34 trilhão de VND, representando 64,7% do total de empréstimos. Em 31 de julho de 2026, todo o sistema contará com mais de 58.000 grupos de empréstimo, com mais de 910.000 membros e um total de empréstimos pendentes superior a 216 trilhões de VND. Essa é uma vantagem única para a coleta de dados, a organização do financiamento ao longo da cadeia de valor e a implementação de modelos de redução de emissões em áreas de produção dispersas. Em relação ao crédito verde, até o final de março de 2026, o saldo total de crédito verde do Agribank atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND. Em 2026, o Agribank continuará a implementar um programa de crédito verde de 3 trilhões de VND para client

artigo.texto: The global energy storage market is moving fast. Battery costs have fallen sharply, installations are accelerating, and projects are being built in markets where governments have yet to set a 2030 storage target. So, if the market is already delivering, why do governments still need targets? Because deployment alone does not guarantee that storage will be built at the scale, in the places or on the timelines needed to support the energy transition. Global energy storage additions reached a record 118 GW in 2025, including 108 GW of batteries. Battery additions have increased seventeenfold in five years, and deployment is already outpacing current national targets. Yet, Ember’s latest analysis finds that national 2030 storage targets total just 822 GW across 99 countries and the EU. That is nearly three times the ambition assessed at COP29, but still 45% below the global pledge to reach 1,500 GW by 2030 (see Global Storage Targets Reach 822 GW, 45% Below COP29 Goal). The apparent contradiction is important. The market is moving, but government planning has not caught up. The case for storage is increasingly clear in solar markets. Solar generates most of its electricity during daylight hours, while demand continues into the evening and night. Batteries can store surplus daytime generation and release it when needed, helping reduce curtailment, ease pressure on grids, and make better use of renewable capacity. That is why countries with ambitious solar targets often have ambitious storage targets too. But the relationship is far from universal. Of the world's 20 largest solar markets by installed capacity in 2025, eight still have no storage target for 2030. The lack of a target has not stopped deployment everywhere. The US has installed roughly 52 GW of utility-scale batteries, Germany has around 30 GWh of battery storage installed, and Saudi Arabia has connected a 7.8 GWh project, the world's largest single battery project. These examples show that market forces and grid needs can drive investment without an explicit national target. But they do not mean targets are unnecessary. They show that deployment can move ahead while government planning lags behind. Other markets have made less progress on both targets and installations. Without a clear signal of future ambition, investors may have less certainty about the scale and timing of demand. Where storage development remains limited, the absence of a target can mean a missed opportunity to unlock investment and make better use of existing and planned solar capacity. A national target is not a substitute for a functioning market. Nor does announcing a number guarantee that projects will be built. Targets need to be supported by effective policies, investment frameworks and grid planning. But they can help align these elements. A credible target gives investors a clearer indication of the scale of future deployment governments expect. It can help guide decisions on procurement, grid development, and the coordination of storage with new renewable generation. It can also draw attention to gaps between planned renewable capacity and the flexibility needed to integrate it. The distinction matters because storage is not just about adding up gigawatts. It is about ensuring that the right amount and type of storage is available where and when the power system needs it. A national target should therefore be connected to the country's broader energy plans, including its renewable capacity ambitions and grid requirements. The global picture also shows how concentrated the recent increase in ambition has been. China raised its 2030 storage target to 460 GW in its 15th Five-Year Plan, while the EU set its first bloc-wide target at 200 GW in June 2026. Together, they account for more than 80% of national storage targets worldwide. This is significant progress, but it is not evidence of a broad-based shift in government planning. Most other major solar markets have not substantially increased their storage ambition since COP29. The stakes will rise as electrification expands. More electricity use across transport, buildings and industry can reduce dependence on fossil fuels, but only if power systems can supply that electricity reliably and increasingly from clean sources. The Global Electrification Pledge being advanced ahead of COP31 aims to raise electricity's share of final energy demand from around 20% to 35% by 2035. Delivering on that ambition will require more than electrifying end uses. It will also require sufficient renewable generation, grid infrastructure and storage to meet demand when it occurs. The storage market has already demonstrated that it can scale rapidly. Ember's analysis suggests that even if annual battery additions grow much more slowly than they have since 2020, the world could still reach the 1,500 GW pledge by 2030. Falling battery costs are helping make that possible. The challenge now is to translate this momentum into reliable power systems. Governments do not need to dictate every investment decision or set targets just to have them. They do need credible plans that give markets direction and ensure deployment meets system needs. Storage is booming, which is reason enough to raise ambition, not abandon it. This matters even more as the world enters the Age of Power, with electricity taking on a growing role across all sectors. Targets can help turn a fast-growing market into a more coordinated build-out of the flexibility needed for a renewables-powered, increasingly electrified world.

artigo.texto: Desbloquear fluxos de capital verde através dos mercados de crédito e de carbono. Juntamente com a expansão do crédito verde, espera-se que o mercado de carbono crie recursos financeiros adicionais, reduzindo a pressão de capital sobre as empresas em processo de transformação verde. O saldo devedor em crédito verde ultrapassou 856 trilhões de VND. O crédito verde está em expansão, contribuindo para o fluxo de capital para setores que apoiam a transformação verde. No entanto, a necessidade de investimentos de grande porte e longo prazo exige o desenvolvimento de canais adicionais de mobilização de capital, incluindo o mercado de carbono. Em seu discurso no seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", organizado pelo jornal Finanças e Investimentos em 14 de outubro, o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã, Nguyen Ngoc Canh, afirmou que, no processo de alcançar a meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050, a demanda por capital para inovação tecnológica, transformação dos métodos de produção, uso eficiente de energia e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa está aumentando. Embora outros canais de mobilização de capital verde estejam se desenvolvendo, o crédito verde continua a desempenhar um papel crucial na transição para um modelo de crescimento de baixo carbono. Segundo o vice-governador, o setor bancário tem implementado proativamente diversas soluções para promover o crédito verde, direcionando fluxos de capital para indústrias e setores que trazem benefícios ambientais e reduzem as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Paralelamente, o Banco Central do Vietnã está aprimorando gradualmente o arcabouço político, emitindo diretrizes e instruções sobre crédito verde e gestão de riscos ambientais e sociais, e incentivando as instituições de crédito a desenvolverem estratégias, processos internos e produtos de crédito alinhados às metas de crescimento verde. Os resultados da implementação mostram que a escala do crédito verde se expandiu. No final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde atingiu mais de 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025. Durante o período de 2017 a 2025, a taxa média de crescimento foi superior a 20% ao ano. Os empréstimos em aberto concentram-se principalmente nos setores de agricultura , silvicultura, pesca e conservação da biodiversidade, representando mais de 31%; o setor de energia verde representa quase 28%. Além disso, os empréstimos avaliados quanto aos riscos ambientais e sociais ultrapassaram 6,2 milhões de VND, representando mais de 31,33% do total de empréstimos em aberto em toda a economia . De acordo com o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, esses resultados demonstram o compromisso do sistema bancário em apoiar a transformação verde dos negócios e da economia. De fato, no Banco de Desenvolvimento Agrícola e Rural ( Agribank ), o crédito verde está sendo implementado em conjunto com os setores de produção e grupos de clientes que necessitam de transformação. Até o final de março de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde do banco atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND. Em 2026, o Agribank continuará a implementar um programa de crédito verde de 3 trilhões de VND para clientes individuais e um programa de 50 trilhões de VND para financiar a agricultura limpa e de alta tecnologia. Você também pode gostar Um programa notável é o programa de empréstimos que vincula produção, processamento e consumo no âmbito do Projeto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável para 1 milhão de hectares de arroz de alta qualidade e baixa emissão no Delta do Mekong, com um valor mínimo de 30 trilhões de VND. A Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank, acredita que a agricultura, os agricultores e as áreas rurais são significativamente impactados pelas mudanças climáticas e que há espaço para redução de emissões em setores como o cultivo de arroz, a pecuária, a silvicultura, a energia de biomassa e o tratamento de resíduos. Portanto, a questão não se resume apenas a fornecer capital para atividades produtivas, mas também a financiar o processo de criação de resultados mensuráveis e verificáveis de redução de emissões. O crédito é um canal crucial para o fluxo de capital; no entanto, o Sr. Bui Minh Giap, economista-chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, acredita que o crédito bancário por si só não consegue suprir todas as necessidades de capital para a transformação verde. Estima-se que o Vietnã necessite de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Desse total, a necessidade de adaptação e aumento da resiliência é de aproximadamente US$ 254 bilhões, enquanto a redução de emissões requer cerca de US$ 114 bilhões. Somente o setor elétrico necessita de aproximadamente US$ 136 bilhões em investimentos para o desenvolvimento da geração e transmissão de energia entre 2026 e 2030. O Sr. Bui Minh Giap afirmou: "Os bancos são um canal importante para o fluxo de capital, mas não podem, sozinhos, atender às necessidades de capital de longo prazo para financiamento verde e financiamento de conversão." Portanto, é necessário combinar crédito com títulos verdes, títulos de conversão, capital próprio, financiamento misto, garantias e mecanismos de compartilhamento de risco. Cada tipo de risco precisa ser alocado a partes com capacidade de gestão adequada. O mercado de carbono precisa gerar valor econômico real. Juntamente com os créditos verdes, espera-se que o mercado de carbono desbloqueie mais recursos para as empresas, convertendo os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico. artigo.texto: Unlocking green capital flows through credit and carbon markets. Along with the expansion of green credit, the carbon market is expected to create additional financial resources, reducing the capital pressure on businesses undergoing green transformation. Outstanding green credit reached over 856,000 billion VND. Green credit is expanding, contributing to the flow of capital into sectors supporting green transformation. However, the need for large and long-term investments necessitates the development of additional capital mobilization channels, including the carbon market. Speaking at the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that, in the process of achieving the goal of net zero emissions by 2050, the demand for capital for technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is increasing. While other green capital mobilization channels are developing, green credit continues to play a crucial role in the transition to a low-carbon growth model. According to the Deputy Governor, the banking sector has proactively implemented many solutions to promote green credit, directing capital flows into industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Along with this, the State Bank of Vietnam is gradually perfecting the policy framework, issuing guidelines and instructions on green credit and environmental and social risk management; and encouraging credit institutions to develop strategies, internal processes, and credit products that align with green growth goals. The implementation results show that the scale of green credit has expanded. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856,000 billion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. During the period 2017-2025, the average growth rate was over 20% per year. Outstanding loans are mainly concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; the green energy sector accounts for nearly 28%. In addition, loans assessed for environmental and social risks reached over 6.2 million billion VND, accounting for more than 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy . According to Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, these results demonstrate the banking system's commitment to supporting the green transformation of businesses and the economy. In fact, at the Agricultural and Rural Development Bank ( Agribank ), green credit is being implemented in conjunction with production sectors and customer groups with a need for transformation. By the end of March 2026, the bank's outstanding green credit balance reached nearly VND 30,000 billion. In 2026, Agribank will continue to implement a VND 3,000 billion green credit program for individual customers and a VND 50,000 billion program to finance clean, high-tech agriculture. You may also like One notable program is the lending program linking production, processing, and consumption under the Sustainable Development Project for 1 million hectares of high-quality, low-emission rice in the Mekong Delta, with a minimum scale of 30,000 billion VND. Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank, believes that agriculture, farmers, and rural areas are both significantly impacted by climate change and have room for emission reduction in sectors such as rice cultivation, livestock farming, forestry, biomass energy, and waste treatment. Therefore, the issue is not only about providing capital for production activities, but also about financing the process of creating measurable and verifiable emission reduction results. Credit is a crucial channel for capital flow; however, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, believes that bank credit alone cannot meet the entire capital needs for green transformation. It is estimated that Vietnam needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Of this, the need for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, while emission reduction requires about US$114 billion. The electricity sector alone needs approximately US$136 billion in investment for power generation and transmission development between 2026 and 2030. Mr. Bui Minh Giap affirmed: "Banks are an important channel for capital flow, but they cannot alone meet the long-term capital needs for green financing and conversion financing." Therefore, it is necessary to combine credit with green bonds, conversion bonds, equity capital, mixed financing, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms. Each type of risk needs to be allocated to parties with appropriate management capabilities. The carbon market needs to create real economic value. Along with green credit, the carbon market is expected to unlock more resources for businesses by converting emission reduction results into economic value. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, by establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the market creates incentives for businesses to proactively invest in green transformation. The Deputy Governor argued that when the carbon market operates effectively, the results of emission reductions can become a source of financing for businesses themselves. This would give businesses the ability to generate additional resources from their emission reductions, helping to reduce pressure on equity capital, the budget, and bank credit. artigo.texto: To analyze the relationship between green credit and the carbon market from a commercial bank's perspective, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank , delivered a presentation at the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam on October 14th. The carbon market opens up new opportunities for green credit. In the international context, carbon pricing has become an increasingly important economic tool. The World Bank's State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026 report identifies 87 direct carbon pricing policies worldwide, covering more than 29% of global greenhouse gas emissions; these tools generate over $107 billion in budget revenue in 2025 and the average direct carbon price is nearly $21/tCO₂e. These figures do not imply a single price for all credits, but they demonstrate that emission costs are increasingly being internalized into investment and business decisions. Ms. Ha stated that, for Agribank, this issue is directly linked to its customers and operating areas. Agriculture , farmers, and rural areas are both significantly impacted by climate change and have room for emission reduction in rice production, livestock farming, forestry, biomass energy, waste treatment, and the circular economy. Therefore, the central question is not "whether the bank will buy and sell credits," but rather "how can the bank finance the process of generating emission reduction results, and when is the carbon value sufficiently certain to influence credit decisions?" The legal framework for Vietnam's carbon market is established by the 2020 Environmental Protection Law and further elaborated through various documents. From 2022 to the present, the list of businesses required to conduct greenhouse gas inventories has increased from 1,912 to 2,441, a nearly 28% increase. In 2022, Decision 01/2022/QD-TTg listed 1,912 establishments; in 2024, Decision 13/2024/QD-TTg listed 2,166 establishments, an increase of 254 establishments, accounting for approximately 30% of the total national greenhouse gas emissions; and in 2026, Decision 42/2026/QD-TTg listed 2,441 establishments, an increase of 275 establishments. Regarding green credit, Decision 21/2025/QD-TTg on environmental criteria and the Green Classification List provides a basis for identifying green projects, and Decision 46/2026/QD-TTg on guidance for determining green projects and projects meeting circular criteria contributes to creating new green projects, unlocking capital, expanding standards for the circular economy and ESG criteria. However, it is important to emphasize that a project on the green classification list does not automatically mean it has carbon credits, and conversely, a project with credits does not automatically meet the conditions for granting credit. Decision 42/2026/QD-TTg, effective from September 25, 2026, updates the list of sectors and facilities that must conduct greenhouse gas inventories, further expanding the data base for emission management. According to HNX data, the VN2025 quota code for the 2025-2026 compliance period has a total volume of 511,473,846 tCO₂e, allocated to 110 institutions; the first trading day is June 29, 2026, and the last trading day is December 24, 2027. This is a significant transition from the policy framework to the actual trading infrastructure. However, publicly available data at HNX shows that during these trading days, both trading volume and value were zero. This doesn't mean the market lacks potential, but it suggests that banks shouldn't assume a stable reference price or deep liquidity already exists to use directly in loan application assessments. Vietnam also has experience commercializing emission reduction results on the international market. In March 2024, Vietnam received US$51.5 million from the World Bank for 10.3 million tons of verified emission reduction results in the North Central Region Emission Reduction Program. The important lesson is not in dividing US$51.5 million by 10.3 million tons to form a "benchmark price," but in that environmental results only become a cash flow when there is a clear methodology, data, verification, contract, and benefit-sharing mechanism. Proposal to facilitate the flow of green capital linked to the carbon market. According to Agribank representatives, by mid-2026, Agribank's total assets will exceed VND 2.7 trillion, mobilized capital will exceed VND 2.5 trillion, and outstanding loans to the economy will surpass VND 2 trillion. By August 2026, outstanding loans for agriculture, farmers, and rural areas will reach over VND 1.34 trillion, accounting for 64.7% of total outstanding loans. By July 31, 2026, the entire system will have over 58,000 loan groups with more than 910,000 members and total outstanding loans exceeding VND 216,000 billion. This is a unique advantage for gathering data, organizing financing along the value chain, and bringing emission reduction models to dispersed production areas. Regarding green credit, by the end of March 2026, Agribank's total outstanding green credit reached nearly 30,000 billion VND. In 2026, Agribank will continue to implement a 3,000 billion VND green credit program for individual customers and a 50,000 billion VND program to finance clean, high-tech agriculture. Within the Sustainable Development Project for 1 million hectares of high-quality, low-emission rice in the Mekong Delta, Agribank is implementing a loan program linking production, processing, and consumption with a minimum scale of 30,000 billion VND. This platform is particularly suitable for testing how to manage data, cash flow, and carbon benefits in an organized production chain. artigo.texto: EnergyPathways plc (LSE:EPP) has raised £1.75 million through a share placing with a single institutional investor to support the development of its MESH long-duration energy storage project and provide additional working capital. The UK energy transition company issued the new shares at 5.75 pence each, with the proceeds intended to fund further project development activities, including the potential acquisition of land, pipelines and technical data associated with MESH. The placing involves the issue of 30,434,782 new ordinary shares, which are expected to be admitted to trading on AIM on 15 October 2026. Following admission, EnergyPathways will have 282,134,998 ordinary shares in issue, with the newly issued shares representing approximately 10.8% of the enlarged share capital. The company also confirmed the closure of its Capital Access Window following completion of the fundraising process. Trading in its existing ordinary shares is scheduled to resume on 13 October 2026. EnergyPathways said the additional funding will allow it to progress work on MESH, a proposed integrated energy storage development designed to combine compressed air, natural gas and hydrogen storage infrastructure. The company intends to use part of the proceeds to acquire assets and technical information considered necessary for advancing the project through its development stages. These acquisitions are intended to reduce project development risks and support future discussions with institutional investors and strategic partners regarding potential financing arrangements. MESH has been designated as a project of national significance by the UK Government, according to the company. The proposed development is designed to store surplus electricity generated by wind farms and make energy available when required, using a combination of long-duration storage technologies and associated gas infrastructure. EnergyPathways is targeting a power capacity of approximately 300 megawatts and an energy storage capacity of 55 gigawatt-hours, with the proposed system designed to provide more than 100 hours of storage. The company believes the project could contribute to reducing the amount of wind-generated electricity that is curtailed when supply exceeds demand or transmission capacity. Management also expects the proposed infrastructure to provide additional flexibility to the UK electricity system by enabling stored energy to be dispatched during periods of lower renewable generation. The project includes plans for natural gas and hydrogen storage facilities, alongside infrastructure intended to support future hydrogen production and energy supply.

artigo.texto: Northfield council moves away from data center ban, toward tiered regulation After more than two hours of public comment and council discussion, the Northfield City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday night to reduce the required setback between data-processing facilities and parks or trails from roughly three-quarters of a mile to 200 feet. But the setback change was only part of the story. In a separate motion, the council also directed staff to explore a tiered regulatory framework for data-processing facilities as part of the upcoming Land Development Code update, looking beyond just power consumption to include water use and other emerging concerns. The change to the setback had been in the works since 2024, when the city passed an ordinance regulating data-processing facilities. That ordinance required a 3,950-foot setback from any existing or planned park, trail, or recreational feature. It also required a 200-foot setback from residential structures. Community Development Director Scott Wopata acknowledged the moment was about more than one number. “This one’s going to be hard,” he said. “In any example I look at around Minnesota or the Midwest or nationally, there aren’t a lot of examples where communities have figured out a way to have this conversation and learn from each other and to empathetically see things from different perspectives. There’s a lot of negative examples of how elected officials and staff members in different cities have signed NDAs, dismissed the public, not listened to public concerns.” Wopata framed the night as an effort to rebuild public trust after a year of conversations that started long before any application existed. “In 2024, we put a moratorium on all data-center development so that we could develop policies before we had a project application,” Wopata said. “That is what we did. We have been following those best practices.” The city’s regulations include 17 performance standards covering noise, water use, glare, vibrations and more. They also require a conditional use permit triggered by any water use. “If we read anywhere anything about data centers, [there] is a very well documented track of negative externalities,” Wopata said. “There are water quality issues. There’s water quantity issues. There are stories of communities losing water pressure. There’s stories of communities where residents have seen significant spikes in their utility bills because the data centers moved in and this corporate development has happened.” But he also drew a distinction between prohibition and regulation. “Regulating is often a more strategic and sophisticated and just successful approach than prohibition,” Wopata said, listing alcohol and cannabis prohibition as negative examples from history. “Bringing something into the light and regulating it can often help ameliorate some of the biggest harmful negative externalities.” City Planner Mathias Hughey explained the rationale for the change. The 3,950-foot setback made every industrial parcel in the city undevelopable, and it was originally drafted without a clear rationale. “This is still much more restrictive than other industrial uses,” Hughey said. Hughey said the planning commission had separately recommended that data-processing facilities be prohibited outright and that staff research a tiered regulatory framework. Because that recommendation was not part of the published public hearing notice, the council had to proceed with the setback item as written. Competing priorities More than a dozen residents spoke during public comment, most urging the council to keep the moratorium or reject the setback change. One Northfielder, Trisha Brunk, even led the room through a song. Councilor Kathleen Holmes acknowledged the volume of opposition in the room but said the council has to weigh competing priorities. “While there is a high number of people who have spoken out against data centers, we, those of us decision makers, policymakers up here, have to hold many priorities,” she said. “And while we have heard the thoughts, the feedback, the opinions on data centers, I would say probably all of us here more often and more frequently hear ‘Lower our taxes.’ … I take this as the belief that the path forward is through regulation and not prohibition.” Councilor Jessica Peterson White said she saw parallels to hog feedlot debates from the early 2000s. “But when we were talking about hog feedlots, the scale was a really important part of the conversation,” she said. “I don’t have a clear sense myself of what scale of data center or other types of development is where we should set a regulation, but I believe that the regulations that we have make it vanishingly unlikely that we will get a hyperscale data center, and that seems good.” She also addressed the equity dimension. “There is a history in this country of affluent white communities sort of offshoring their industrial needs to communities that don’t have the same resources, don’t have the same organizing power, and those industrial uses are then underregulated and create issues for poorer and less white communities,” she said. “And I hope we don’t play a role in that.” No one is saying ‘Let’s build a huge data center’ Councilor Davin Sokup said he was voting yes despite his own uncertainty. “But I just really want to highlight that what we’re considering here tonight, I think, in my opinion, does show an openness to having a data center in Northfield,” he said. “I’m not willing to say that it couldn’t possibly be that in the future.” Councilor Chad Beumer said he understood the distrust but believed the city’s regulations were already strong. “I don’t think there’s a single person sitting up here that is saying, ‘Let’s build a huge data center out there that’s going to burn up all kinds of energy and waste a whole bunch of water,’” he said. “I think our ordinance 1098 clearly artigo.texto: Vattenfall has awarded Fluence Energy a contract to supply and support a large-scale battery energy storage facility at the Brunsbüttel site, currently the location of a decommissioned nuclear power plant in Germany. The agreement includes both the delivery of the storage system and long-term service for the facility, which will have a capacity exceeding 1GW-hour (GWh) and an output of 254MW. The project is expected to become operational by the end of 2028. Once completed, the Brunsbüttel project will be among the largest battery energy storage system (BESS) installations in Germany and represents Vattenfall's most substantial battery commitment so far. The facility will be built using Fluence's Gridstack Pro 5000 platform, which incorporates battery systems and associated power conversion equipment. It also includes an energy management system designed to enhance grid resilience and support renewable energy integration. Fluence is responsible for providing a turnkey solution covering engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning, along with ongoing long-term service to help maintain performance over the facility's lifespan. The four-hour BESS is designed to respond to fluctuations in electricity supply and demand as Germany experiences increasing amounts of wind and solar generation and growing price volatility. Vattenfall solar and batteries head Claus Wattendrup said: "Projects like this battery storage facility play an important role in strengthening the resilience of the energy system and enabling the continued integration of renewable power generation. "Together with Fluence as our long-term partner, we are creating a flexible asset that can respond to changing electricity market needs for many years to come. "The project will further strengthen our portfolio of flexibility solutions and support the transition away from fossil fuels." The company reached a final investment decision last month to build the Brunsbüttel BESS facility. Construction is set to begin in 2027, with grid connection planned to the 50Hz, 380kV transmission network by late 2028. The new installation will nearly double Vattenfall's existing battery storage portfolio. "Vattenfall selects Fluence for 1GWh Brunsbüttel battery storage project" was originally created and published by Power Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: Lexington extended its temporary ban on data center construction. Mercer County rejected regulations that would allow hyperscale data centers. And a Carroll County ethics board is looking into dealings surrounding a proposed hyperscale data center. As local governments in Kentucky are weighing and making decisions on potential hyperscale data centers, some Kentuckians came to Frankfort to tell state lawmakers that they need to do more to regulate large data centers — not put that burden on local governments. Just a few months away from when state lawmakers meet again in Frankfort, catch up on the latest data center news in this round-up as reported by the Lantern and other news outlets from around Kentucky. Kentuckians tell state lawmakers to act More than 60 people from across the state, ranging from Pike County to Daviess County, came to a committee room earlier this month to lay out a number of concerns they have about hyperscale data center proposals and their potential impacts on electricity ratepayers, rural land and the state’s natural resources. The gathering was for a “listening session” on data centers organized by Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, who is preparing legislation on data center regulations for when the GOP-controlled state legislature meets again next year. Rep. Josh Bray, R-Mount Vernon, the vice-chair of the Kentucky House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, is also preparing legislation on data centers. A few of those speakers told the state lawmakers at the meeting that local governments shouldn’t be expected to regulate data centers on their own. “Finally, stop expecting local officials without specialized technical, legal, environmental, or utility expertise to negotiate billion-dollar industrial development deals on equal footing with the wealthiest companies on Earth,” said Diane Floyd of Mercer County. Local government decisions Meanwhile, local governments including Mercer County have been hearing public commentary and taking votes on whether to regulate hyperscale data centers or allow them at all. The Mercer County Fiscal Court through a unanimous voice vote in late September rejected proposed regulations that would have allowed the placement of hyperscale data centers next to a coal-fired power plant. Opponents of the regulations argued the land near the power plant was also relatively close to Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill, a historic site preserving structures of the Kentucky Shakers religious community. In Kentucky’s second-largest city of Lexington, the city council voted to move forward with potential data center regulations and also a temporary ban, or moratorium, on data center construction in the city through October 2027, according to public radio station WEKU. In Carroll County, Kentucky Public Radio reported in late September that frustrated community members have filed local ethics complaints arguing that several city council members for the Carroll County seat of Carrollton should have abstained from votes to sign land deals with a prospective hyperscale data center because of conflicts of interest. Carroll County is home to two proposed large data centers, one of them by Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, which is also building a hyperscale data center in West Louisville. Other communities, including the Christian County seat of Hopkinsville, are moving forward with proposed data center regulations, or, in the case of the Scott County seat of Georgetown, looking at an outright ban on hyperscale data centers.

artigo.texto: A migração da inteligência artificial corporativa para sistemas agênticos está mudando a proporção entre componentes nos data centers. Na avaliação da AMD, a arquitetura tradicional, que costumava operar com um processador central para cada quatro ou oito GPUs dedicadas à inferência, caminha para uma razão próxima de 1:1 — e, em cenários de alta concorrência, a demanda por CPU pode superar a das GPUs. O motivo, conforme a empresa, é que a IA agêntica não depende apenas do modelo de linguagem rodando no acelerador. Segurança, middleware, repositórios vetoriais, orquestração, APIs e gestão de memória exigem uma camada robusta de processamento central. Quando a CPU é subdimensionada, as GPUs ficam ociosas à espera de dados, o que amplia a latência e encarece a operação. A AMD defende que a métrica de avaliação passe a ser a capacidade de vazão por rack considerando limites energéticos, de espaço e de refrigeração, e não o desempenho de componentes isolados. Para a fabricante, o avanço dos projetos-piloto para a produção em larga escala depende de um ecossistema equilibrado de CPUs e aceleradores, com conectividade de baixa latência, para sustentar o retorno sobre o investimento. Você pode acompanhar as análises, lançamentos e principais novidades sobre tecnologia em tempo real aqui na SpaceMoney.

artigo.texto: The US is set to have access to about 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium over the next decade following a new agreement to produce the critical mineral using advanced lithium extraction technology. The GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) and refining technology was developed by Energy Exploration Technologies (EnergyX). The Texas-based firm specializes in lithium extraction and critical mineral production. On Monday, October 12, EnergyX announced that it signed a binding, 10-year, take-or-pay agreement with Singaporean global commodity trader Trafigura to supply lithium from two major projects in Texas and Chile. The supply will support electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and other industries that depend on battery materials. The company said commercial production is scheduled to start in 2028. “Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” Teague Egan, EnergyX founder and CEO, disclosed. A new extraction method The US produces about 6,600 US tons (6,000 metric tons) of lithium annually. This accounts for less than one percent of the global production. Moreover, it relies on net imports for more than 50 percent of the lithium it consumes. To address this, EnergyX came up with the GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology. More from Energy See All Backed by more than 150 patents, the approach extracts lithium from mineral-rich brines and refines it into materials suitable for batteries. The novel process works by separating lithium directly from liquid brines. EnergyX has already tested the method in labs, pilot facilities, and demonstration plants in the US and Chile. In April 2026, it commissioned its Project Lonestar lithium production plant in Texas, which is the largest DLE lithium production plant in the country. At the same time, the company is also working on another major lithium project in Chile called Black Giant. It has a planned annual production capacity of around 57,871 US tons (52,500 metric tons). The two projects will produce different lithium products. Black Giant will supply lithium carbonate, while Project Lonestar will produce lithium hydroxide. Both materials are essential for rechargeable batteries used in EVs and energy storage systems. Commercial operations Under the agreement, Trafigura will buy 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium products over the next decade. The deal covers 66 percent of the planned first-phase output from Project Black Giant, as well as 30 percent from Project Lonestar. Meanwhile, EnergyX is also talking to other potential buyers to secure customers for 80 percent of its planned production. At current lithium prices of about USD 18,100 per US ton (roughly USD 20,000 per metric ton), the deal could generate over USD 2 billion in revenue over its lifetime. “A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product,” Egan stressed in a press release. “It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.” EnergyX has also secured financial support for its expansion plans. This includes a USD 225 million investment from energy company Eni for Project Black Giant and a USD 690 million letter of intent from the US Export-Import Bank for potential debt financing. “We are pleased to support EnergyX as it develops its lithium projects in Chile and the US,” Daniel von Arx, Trafigura’s head of battery metals, stated. He added that long-term deals are important for starting production and securing reliable supplies of critical minerals.

artigo.texto: Under the draft regulations, facilities drawing 20 megawatts or more would be barred from using drinking water in open cooling systems, required to run on 100% clean power, and limited to 25 hours a year for backup generator testing. The proposed policies follow weeks of community outreach in which city residents expressed many of the same anxieties over data centers that have been growing nationwide. While the projects promise millions of dollars in revenue for cities that welcome them, they also bring massive energy and water demands alongside quality-of-life concerns like noise pollution. The new draft regulations target large data centers and other tech facilities drawing massive amounts of electricity and water. To cut down on environmental harm, facilities would be banned from using drinking water in open cooling systems, which continuously lose water rather than recirculating it. Sites would also need built-in sound barriers, shielded lights that point downward to prevent neighborhood glare, and mandatory annual city checkups on their power, water, and sewer usage to ensure they stay within legal limits. The proposals also set new expectations for developers and neighbors. Companies would be required to comply with state "prevailing wage and skilled and trained workforce requirements" and notify residents within a 1,500-foot radius of a proposed site. The city is also weighing new developer fees to fund local affordable housing and strengthen the power grid, while ensuring tax dollars from equipment sales remain in San Jose. "The standards are intended to mitigate potential impacts related to energy consumption and sourcing, water use, air quality, backup power generators, and other environmental factors, and to outline a clear and consistent process for community notification and engagement," the city said in a statement. City officials emphasize that the proposals are only a first draft and that residents can still help shape them during a special community forum next Thursday, Oct. 15, from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at San Jose City Hall Council Chambers and online via Zoom. Following Thursday's meeting, staff will present the final draft standards and accompanying ordinances to the Planning Commission on Nov. 18. The proposals are expected to reach the City Council on Dec. 8, with a second and final vote set for Dec. 15. San Jose's push for local oversight echoes a statewide effort to rein in data centers driven by the artificial intelligence boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven bills aimed at protecting electric customers from paying for grid upgrades needed for data centers, forcing transparency on water usage, and curbing environmental exemptions for these facilities. While other Bay Area cities have enacted temporary bans on data centers — prompted by pushback from communities concerned about environmental, health, and quality-of-life impacts — San Jose has taken a different route. Mayor Matt Mahan said the city is opting for a more tailored approach that addresses community concerns item by item through specific regulations. "We have found a middle path. We have not defaulted to unfettered capitalism, nor have we put our head in the sand and tried to ban change," Mahan said. "And I believe we have an opportunity and a responsibility to regulate technological change to make it work for people." The city projects multimillion-dollar deficits over the next two years — though smaller than the $50 million shortfall it grappled with this year due to stagnant revenues and rising costs. With each data center projected to generate between $3 million and $7 million annually, the city is relying on these developments to help secure its financial future. City officials said public feedback gathered across multiple outreach events directly shaped the proposed rules, pointing to generator limits and environmental monitoring as community-driven additions. "There were a lot of concerns that we heard that we weren't aware of," said Deputy City Manager Manuel Pineda, highlighting public input on noise and sewer impacts. "We're setting up some pretty robust programs to monitor those... and address any issues that come up through our process." Mahan emphasized the process is not finished and encouraged the community to continue weighing in. "We have two months and at least three large public meetings to go," Mahan said. "This is very much an iterative process with the community. So we're continuing to listen. I hope that community members will take time to review the standards and let us know what isn't clear or seems lacking so that we can continue to improve." ©2026 Silicon Valley, Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

artigo.texto: Microsoft is planning to build fewer data centers at its sprawling complex in Mount Pleasant. In January, the Mount Pleasant Village Board approved the site plan for the company to build nine data centers as part of an expansion of its plans in the village. The company is now amending that down to seven data center buildings. “We continue to refine the design and layout of our expansion parcels in the Village of Mount Pleasant,” a Microsoft spokesperson wrote in a statement. “The changes in no way reflect a reduction in our ambition, they have been made to ensure faster development, allowing us to access this increased capacity quicker. We will continue to evolve our design and keep the community updated prior to beginning any vertical construction.” Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. While there are fewer buildings in the updated plan, the total square footage of building space is greater. The updated plan has over 5.8 million-square-feet of building space, up from the just over 5.2-million-square feet in the plan approved by village officials earlier this year. “There’s two fewer buildings than the last site plan you saw, but they are actually slightly larger in square footage,” said Samuel Schultz, the community development director for the village. On Wednesday, the Mount Pleasant Plan Commission unanimously approved the amended site plan. The village board is expected to vote on it later this month. As part of the updated plan, Microsoft plans to build an office and storage building, a guardhouse and two substations at the site. Sean Ryan, a spokesperson for the village, said the 5.8 million-square-feet figure includes the data center buildings, as well as the offices and guard houses. It does not include the two utility substations, he said. Schultz said Microsoft’s plans could continue to change. He said the square footage for the site, “will likely fluctuate, maybe up, maybe down, over time.” The estimated taxable value per acre is also decreasing under the updated plan, down from around $10 million in the original plan, to around $7.7 million in the amended plan. Ryan said compared to earlier this year, “planners are using a more conservative estimate now for what the possible future value of the buildings would be.” “And this is just a more careful way to approach this exercise and know that in the end, if these buildings are built, it would result in a net positive in terms of the financials for the community,” Ryan said. “It would show that even under these more careful conservative predictions of the future taxes that these buildings would generate, the potential property tax revenue still far exceeds the cost of service,” he added. The plan commission approved the updated site plan with more than a dozen conditions Wednesday. Village Trustee Nancy Washburn, a member of the plan commission, made a motion to add a condition for Microsoft to look to add “noise protection” to a portion of the site. In June, Microsoft announced its first data center facility in Mount Pleasant, known as “Fairwater,” was operational. Construction on Microsoft’s second data center in the village is expected to be completed in 2028. Microsoft was sued in July due to noise complaints from residents who live nearby. Some people who live near the development have also complained about construction noise and dust, light pollution, traffic and a changing rural landscape. The company also plans to build a data center project on around 240 acres in Kenosha about 8 miles away from the tech giant’s campus in Racine County. artigo.texto: Nobody wants a data center in their backyard. So a developer from Natick came up with a novel idea: Sink a data center under the ocean off Downeast Maine, and harness the motion of the extraordinarily strong tides there to power it. He says it’s a solution that could neutralize some of the main objections to data centers — they use up too much fresh water and energy, and they release too much heat. “Tidal currents are free, continuous, and completely predictable, unlike wind or solar,” said developer Louis Wolfson. “And the ocean naturally cools things without touching a single drop of drinking water.” But it turns out people don’t like underwater data centers either. Though the idea at this point is little more than “an idea on a bar napkin,” as the Eastport city manager put it, opposition is building fast. In August, the City Council announced a 180-day moratorium on data center development. The council and the local port authority are opposing the project. And a group of residents has organized — Eastport Residents for Healthy Oceans — in part around their concern that if the developer gets an initial permit for a study, it could be harder to stop the project. They and others say the bay just feels too precious and fragile to risk. Already, thanks to the rapidly warming waters of the Gulf of Maine, species are being stressed and pushed north to cooler water. Some species — like one commonly called the flat periwinkle — are already gone. Others — like green crabs — were brought here in larger numbers by warming waters. “I don’t think anybody’s for it,” said Jared Hagan, a co-owner of Picnic, a coffee shop in Eastport. The concept first surfaced in February, when Wolfson, a Needham real estate developer and lifelong Cape Cod surf-caster, put forward a proposal with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for a preliminary permit to construct a 15-megawatt underwater data center powered by the tides. The tides off Eastport are some of the strongest in the continental United States, often gaining some 20 feet between high and low tide. The preliminary vision includes a roughly 80-foot-wide, 11-foot-tall frame made of marine-grade reinforced concrete that would be sunk to the seafloor. Inside would be 40-foot long cylinders with steel-pressured hulls. The project would be powered by up to 50 turbines for generating tidal energy and connected to land by 1.5-mile subsea cable to a facility on Kendall Head. Data centers on land have become the rare point of agreement in the United States — residents in red and blue states alike oppose them, and dozens of projects have been delayed or canceled as a result. High on the list of concerns are energy usage, high water demands, and heat. Recent research led by a team at the University of Cambridge found that AI data centers on land can increase the nearby land surface temperature — between 2.7 and 4.3 degrees Fahrenheit, on average. In theory, that’s why moving a data center off the land, and into the water, could help. Much of the energy used for data centers comes from the need to constantly cool the servers by circulating fresh, cool water around the structure. Placing a data center underwater — particularly in a place with constant, massive tides, Wolfson says — could solve that problem. And the concept isn’t just theoretical. In 2015, Microsoft sank a small prototype of an underwater data center off the coast of California, running it for three months before hauling it out for assessment. Three years later, it launched the real thing off the coast of Orkney, an archipelago off mainland Scotland. “It was a totally new concept,” said Jason Schofield, managing director of Green Marine, an Orkney-based marine services company that was contracted to install the data center and remove it at the project’s completion. He said the project was a huge success. Installation was fast and easy. The data center had one-eighth the failure rate of a comparable land-based one. When Schofield went to remove the data center, he said crabs and other marine life were present on the ocean floor; photos of the shipping-container sized structure were covered in algae, barnacles, and sea anemones. But Microsoft’s track record with Project Natick doesn’t seem to mean much in Eastport. Like many locals, Elijah Brice, a 24-year-old lobsterman, worries about how a sunken data center could affect marine life in Passamaquoddy Bay, where he tends some 800 lobster traps. The tides there are “just such a crazy physical force,” Brice said recently, taking a quick break from the boat house he’s building. When he heads into the waters off Kendall Head, he said he brings heavy gear, including a 100-pound anchor, but still, it’s hard to keep it from moving. “You could probably put a 100-ton excavator or some, like, massive machine on the bottom, and the tide would roll that around until it’s crushed like a little Tonka truck.” He worries that force that strong could damage the data center and pollute the waters. Even without that, he wonders what any generated heat would do to lobster and other species in the area. Wolfson, the project’s developer, said he respects these kinds of concerns, but it’s still early in the process. What he’s looking for at this point is a permit that would allow him to spend two years figuring out if a plan is even feasible by conducting baseline environmental studies and silt-scour engineering, which would let him know how the tides affect the silt-beds and the seafloor. “We should have done a better job early on making it clear that this is a quiet, early study, not construction,” he said. “The concerns about fishing, sound, and the harsh water are all fair points, and they’re what the multiyear study is meant to figure out.” He’s excited enough about the possibilities of tide-powered data centers that he has also proposed an underwater AI data center in Upper Cook Inlet, Alaska, the stretch of water just below Anchorage that boasts among the greatest t
