artigo.texto: N.A.N. Silox GreenMet Pvt. Ltd., the joint venture between N.A.N. GreenMet and Belgium’s Silox Group, has appointed Vijay Pasupathy as Chief Executive Officer as the company receives Consent to Establish (CTE) and moves forward with groundbreaking for its ₹1,400 crore lithium-ion battery recycling and critical metals facility at Naidupeta, Andhra Pradesh. The company has also earmarked additional investment beyond the initial ₹1,400 crore outlay to accelerate its downstream expansion into precursor cathode active material (pCAM) and cathode active material (CAM) manufacturing, actively pursuing global technology partnerships. Vijay brings over two decades of industrial leadership across strategy and operations, having previously served as Executive Vice President at Epsilon Advanced Materials, alongside senior roles at Orbia and EY. He will lead N.A.N. Silox GreenMet through plant execution at Naidupeta and drove the company’s expansion into engineered cathode materials. To execute the industrial buildout, N.A.N. Silox GreenMet has assembled a high-caliber leadership team, appointing Rakesh Patel as Chief Operating Officer, Harish Aich as Chief Technology Officer, M. Sri Rama Krishna Murthy as Deputy CFO, Partha Reddy as Chief Supply Chain Officer, and Alisha Abbas as Head of HR. The team brings deep domain expertise across metallurgy, mineral processing, and large-scale plant execution from Hindalco, Shell, ExxonMobil, Adani’s Kutch Copper, and Hyundai. Bridging the Midstream Battery Gap in India The Naidupeta facility will feature an ultimate capacity of 40,000 tonnes per annum (TPA) of shredding and 20,000 TPA of hydrometallurgical processing, deployed in phases. The plant’s hydrometallurgical technology will produce high-purity, battery-grade salts designed directly as feedstock for downstream pCAM and CAM synthesis. By linking battery recycling directly with cathode material manufacturing, the company aims to establish domestic capabilities to process recovered critical metals into cell-ready materials, reducing India’s reliance on imported East Asian cathode supplies. India’s battery ecosystem is scaling rapidly at the cell manufacturing level, but the country remains heavily dependent on overseas supply chains for processed cathode materials. With Consent to Establish secured and groundbreaking underway at Naidupeta, N.A.N. Silox GreenMet is focused on executing its lithium-ion battery recycling and hydrometallurgical facility while pursuing global technology partnerships to expand into domestic pCAM and CAM manufacturing. This expansion aims to strengthen India’s battery manufacturing value chain by enabling recovered critical metals to be processed into high-value battery materials within the country. Naivedya Agarwal, Director and Co-founder, N.A.N. GreenMet, said: “We are delighted to welcome Vijay as CEO alongside a heavily experienced operational leadership team at this pivotal stage. With groundbreaking underway at Naidupeta, our downstream pCAM and CAM expansion will ensure that critical minerals recovered in India are processed further and reused to build new batteries domestically.” Jean-Christophe Bogaert, Chairman, Silox Group, said: “With Vijay and the new leadership team on board, Silox’s advanced hydrometallurgical technology transitions into large-scale industrial execution in India. Our expertise in high-purity metal extraction will be central as we build out the Naidupeta facility and advance discussions on pCAM and CAM technology partnerships.”

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – What was meant to be a stop on the campaign tour for Arizona’s attorney general deep in the heart of Mesa became a one-topic free-for-all instead on Wednesday night. The city of about 500,000 people, near Phoenix, is where Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes came to lay out her vision for data center development. But most of the town hall at the Eagle Community Center was spent talking about a particular 38-acre tract of land in the southern fringes of the Phoenix city limits. As The Center Square covered on Wednesday morning, Mayes’ calls for a data center moratorium have been met by raised eyebrows and criticism from business officials, including executives from the state and Phoenix area chambers of commerce. One such criticism has come from the campaign of Mayes' opponent in the Nov. 3 general election, Republican State Senate President Warren Petersen of Gilbert. His campaign manager, Chad LeBeau, said there's a lack of consistency regarding data center development in Arizona. “Kris Mayes has spent years trying to get data centers to come to Arizona," LeBeau said in an email to The Center Square. "Now that she's on the ballot, she wants a total halt, a position even Governor [Katie] Hobbs rejects. Mayes doesn't have a policy; she has a poll. When the winds shift, she flips.” Regardless, that opposition couldn’t beat back the mood in the East Valley on Wednesday night, with dozens of attendees taking to the microphone to discuss the hot-button subject, forcing Mayes’ staff to cut the meeting at 7 p.m., two hours after it began. The 150 or so attendees in the 180-seat gym at the Eagle Community Center were red-hot and bothered by the Menlo Digital data center development in Ahwatukee, a bedroom community that’s technically part of Phoenix, albeit on the southern side of South Mountain. As the crowd settled in for the two-hour town hall, with attendees passing time by knitting or scrolling their phones between questions, Mayes admitted what Phoenix Chamber CEO Danny Seiden and others said — that she has no legal authority to issue a data center moratorium on her own. Instead, the former member of the Arizona Corporation Commission called on that body, as well as the Arizona Legislature and fellow Democrat, Hobbs, to do the work needed to “press time out” on the industry. “I am limited to the tools that I have as your attorney general, which is the bully pulpit and nuisance law,” Hobbs told the crowd Wednesday. More than half of the people in attendance raised their hands when Mayes asked if they came to discuss the Menlo development. One such attendee was Tina Charon, who has lived in Phoenix for more than 30 years, spending her career as a project manager for a semiconductor manufacturing firm. Charon told The Center Square that the development in her backyard has disturbed her quality of life, spurring her to join a neighborhood activism group called the Ahwatukee Community Alliance. Charon said she hoped her state's attorney general would fight the very industry that Charon worked for, helping her sleep better at night. "We're all hoping that she can intervene and do anything to help reduce the nuisance in our lives," Charon told The Center Square. "This is going to impact thousands of homes of people who were there well before that data center was even a dream. So I'm hoping she'll help in some way." Mayes cited her past work on the ACC as a reason why she will seek to use the state’s nuisance law. That law applies to everything from being “injurious to, indecent, offensive to the senses” to selling, offering to sell, transferring or disseminating items deemed to be offensive within 2,000 feet of any public or private school, public park or residential neighborhood. “One of the things that has alarmed me the most, which is that it seems very obvious to me, and this is one of the reasons that we formally intervened in opposition to the Arizona Public Service and Tucson Electric Power rate increases," Mayes said at the town hall. “We were in opposition to those proposed rate increases in front of the Arizona Corporation Commission, because we are opposing a 14% APS rate increase and a 13% TEP rate increase because I believe it's unnecessary, unjust, and is being fueled by data centers, at least in part.” In her post-town hall press scrum, Mayes addressed what she’d like to see from the data center and AI industries at large, to satisfy her concerns. Chief among them is having residents have more of a say in where and when such facilities are built, with Mayes pitching the idea of having a neighborhood, town or entire city voting on data center development before they can break ground on them. “You have to ask yourself, 'Why would you drop an industrial-scale, hyper-scaled AI data center in the middle of Ahwatukee?' ” Mayes told reporters. “And so, number one, pick the right place. I'm not flatly against data centers. Maybe there is a place in the middle of almost nowhere Arizona where these things would be appropriate, where maybe a community would want one. “But it is very obvious that they are choosing locations that were designed for a lower scale, lower level commercial operation, and then they are somehow flipping that into this gigantic industrial facility that can give off constant noise and pollution and possibly even constant air pollution if they're using diesel generators to power them at any time, and so there's a lot to be investigated here," she said.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Virtual event Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline By Canary Media Lithium-ion batteries could do so much for AI data centers and the power grid. They’re cheaper than the fossil-gas turbines that tech giants are building at gigawatt scale for their “AI factories.” They can cushion the cost of building out grid infrastructure and power plants just to serve data centers’ peak energy demands. And they’re much cleaner than the diesel backup generators almost all data centers rely on. So why haven’t on-site batteries taken off yet with the computing crowd? It comes down to costs and benefits. Data center developers and operators often see fossil fuels as more reliable for 24/7 power. And industry watchers say the companies are leery of adding batteries unless they see a clear payback — or if they simply can’t do without them. Data centers have in fact relied for decades on a type of battery known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. It’s essentially a bank of batteries — most of them old-fashioned lead-acid chemistries — that connects to servers and other computing gear to keep them running smoothly in case utility power flickers or fails. Much like backup generators, they don’t do anything useful except during emergencies. With the right technological fixes, however, lithium-ion batteries that sit between the grid and the data center complex could perform this task, and solve a host of other problems. Specifically, they could serve as shock absorbers to prevent the kind of power disruptions, caused by data centers dropping off the grid unexpectedly, that are emerging as a major threat to grid stability. That’s the idea behind startup ON.Energy’s new AI UPS. According to CEO and cofounder Alan Cooper, it’s the result of roughly a half-decade of technology development, aimed at delivering what he described as “the new standard for connecting the data center to the grid.” The trick has been to prove that these centralized systems are capable of performing the critical tasks they need to. Earlier this year, ON.Energy concluded trials at the nation’s premiere grid testing facility showing that its technology works. Now, with a 5-gigawatt order from major AI data center developer Crusoe, ON.Energy is preparing to put this centralized UPS system to the test at commercial scale. “The grid sees a battery that’s always charging, and the load sees a battery that’s always outputting perfect quality power,” Cooper said. “In an oversimplified way, it smashes together BESS” — the industry term of art for grid-scale battery energy storage systems — “and UPS into a single asset.” ON.Energy isn’t the only company building batteries for this purpose, said Shahil Shah, chief engineer at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, formerly known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Shah is in charge of the grid simulator lab that tested the AI UPS system at multi-megawatt configurations. He’s also overseeing tests of a similar battery system from Prevalon Energy, and some others he said he can’t name yet. Besides providing UPS services, these technologies aim to solve a growing problem created by the rapid buildout of data centers, Shah said. “Many power system operators are coming up with requirements to make sure that the data center loads — the large loads — don’t negatively impact the reliability of the grid.” Data centers are uniquely challenging for utilities and grid operators to manage for a couple of reasons. First, their appetite for power can rise and fall dramatically, depending on how much computing they’re doing at any moment. And those changes can happen really fast, Shah said — “say, from 5% to 100% in a few milliseconds. You’re hammering the grid if you do that.” Second, data centers’ sensitivity to fluctuations in grid power quality can trigger them to disconnect from the grid and switch to UPS and backup generators at a moment’s notice, leading to massive unexpected drops in power demand that threaten to throw grid balances out of whack. Grid operator PJM Interconnection has recorded a handful of such multi-gigawatt drop-offs in recent years, including one in July where nearly 4 gigawatts of data center load in Virginia disconnected. Utilities and grid operators like PJM need to carefully balance supply and demand to avoid voltage and frequency fluctuations that can, in the worst case, lead to region-wide grid collapses. Many grid operators require big solar and wind farms to configure their systems to avoid tripping offline in response to grid voltage disturbances. Now data centers have become large enough to represent similar trip-off risks. The North American Electric Reliability Corp., which oversees the U.S. and Canadian electric systems, has targeted large “computational loads” for new requirements on this front, and Texas utility regulators instituted similar requirements this year. ON.Energy’s AI UPS is designed to handle those kinds of power isolation services, Cooper said. “Our double-conversion technology, which we’ve patented, is basically the process of fully electrically decoupling the load from the power generation source,” he said. “We’re using the fastest-response, best-in-class inverters in the market.” That technological sophistication adds up to a relatively simple solution for the utilities and grid operators, he said. “We’re basically a really predictable utility-scale battery that just sits and takes power from the grid.” To be clear, data centers need to be designed ahead of time to use ON.Energy’s AI UPS system, Cooper said. To illustrate the point, he showed me aerial photos of a Crusoe data center campus under construction. The parts of the campus built first include a central building that will house traditional UPS systems, he said. artigo.texto: Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal held a bilateral meeting with European Commission Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union Gerassimos Thomas in New Delhi to discuss India’s carbon market development, the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and technical cooperation. Discussions covered carbon pricing, emissions monitoring, reporting and verification systems, and capacity building. Key Highlights - Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal met EU Director-General Gerassimos Thomas in New Delhi to discuss carbon markets and CBAM. - India highlighted emission intensity reduction targets notified for 490 industrial units under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. - Non-fossil energy sources account for 308 GW of India’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW, according to the Ministry of Power. - India and the EU agreed to continue technical dialogue on carbon pricing, emissions monitoring and verification, and capacity building. New Delhi, Oct 14: Secretary, Ministry of Power, Pankaj Agarwal held a bilateral meeting with Gerassimos Thomas, Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union at the European Commission, in New Delhi to discuss India’s carbon market development, the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and opportunities for enhanced technical cooperation. The meeting focused on strengthening engagement between India and the EU on carbon pricing frameworks, emissions accounting and approaches to managing the climate-related aspects of international trade. During the meeting, Agarwal highlighted India’s progress under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), including the notification of emission intensity reduction targets for 490 industrial units and the development of a domestic carbon market. The scheme is part of India’s efforts to establish a framework for carbon credit trading and encourage industries to reduce the emissions intensity of their operations. The discussions also covered India’s progress in expanding non-fossil energy capacity as part of its broader energy transition. Agarwal noted that non-fossil sources accounted for 308 GW of India’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW. The expansion of non-fossil capacity is an important element of India’s strategy to diversify its energy mix and advance its climate and sustainability objectives. The meeting provided an opportunity to discuss the relationship between domestic carbon market mechanisms, industrial decarbonisation and international approaches to carbon-related trade measures. The European Commission delegation appreciated India’s progress in developing its carbon market and shared updates on the implementation of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Both sides expressed willingness to continue technical engagement on the recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms, monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, and capacity building. They agreed to strengthen cooperation and maintain dialogue on carbon markets, CBAM-related methodologies and other areas of mutual interest. The India–EU meeting highlights the growing importance of technical cooperation on carbon pricing, industrial emissions and climate-related trade measures. Continued dialogue on the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme and CBAM methodologies could help both sides improve mutual understanding of their respective frameworks and identify areas for further cooperation.

artigo.texto: BYD's Atto 8 Charges In Less Time Than You'll Spend Scrolling Netflix Tonight BYD’s Flash charging tech can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. - BYD's electric Atto SUV charges faster than any rival – with the right charger. - The 115-kWh Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. - Most potent version makes 764 hp and gives a 374-mile WLTP electric range. Fast electric SUVs are nothing new. But BYD's new Atto 8 is fast in a straight line and at the charging station. You might even spend less time topping up the battery than you would pumping gas into a combustion SUV and paying for it. The Atto 8 made its European debut at this week's Paris Motor Show, and on the stand, it doesn't look particularly groundbreaking. Sure, it's BYD's first three-row vehicle for Europe, where it will take on the new Skodq Peaq. But the design, a predictable mashup of existing BYD styling cues, is entirely forgettable. Review: The BYD Seal 6 Is A Perfectly Adequate EV Sedan, But That's About It It's a different story under the skin. The Atto 8 is powered by BYD's second generation Blade battery, and the generous 115 kWh capacity is actually the least interesting thing about it. Because the real story is the Atto 8's ability to charge that huge battery from 10-97 percent full in only nine minutes. And you can cut that almost in half by settling on a 10% to 70% fill, pulling the plug before the charge rate slows for the final push. Even in chilly (-30 C) weather, a 20-97 percent charge is done in 12 minutes. That compares with a 10% to 80% fill time of 28 minutes for the new Skoda Peaq. BYD's Flash Charging technology makes those feats possible, but only if you can find a Flash charger. The automaker is still building the infrastructure, so they're few and far between right now, although BYD says 3,000 Flash stations will be live across Europe by the end of 2027. Choose 456 HP Or 764 HP Both versions of the 198-inch (5 m) SUV get the same battery and charging capabilities, but not the same powertrain. The entry level Design comes with a 456 hp (462 PS / 340 kW) electric motor and rear-wheel drive. That might sound like a solid number of horses, but the weight of the huge battery means zero to 62 mph takes a leisurely 8 seconds. Atto 8 Excellence adds a second motor, boosting overall output to 764 hp (775 PS / 570 kW), and chopping the sprint time to 4.6 seconds. But it also chops the available range. The RWD 8 can over a respectable 405 miles (652 km) on a fill, and the dual-motor SUV, a less impressive 374 miles (602 km). 26-Inch Head-Up Display The Atto 8's flagship status in BYD's lineup means it comes loaded with standard equipment, including a panoramic glass roof, a 26-inch head-up display, and heating, ventilation and massage functions for both the front seats, and the outer pair in the middle row. Both models get dual 50W smartphone chargers, and Excellence models attempt to justify their name with a refrigerator. Will it also be excellent value? We'll find out later this year, closer to the spring 2027 on-sale date, by which time BYD might have plumbed in a few more Flash chargers.

artigo.texto: - Council seeks community input on data centers. Members of the Sioux Falls City Council's Regulatory Oversight Committee are meeting several times over the next couple months to put together regulations and ordinances related to data centers. And they want to hear from community members along the way. - Meetings will be held at 6 p.m. on Nov. 9, Nov. 30 and Jan. 4, with the goal to present final recommendations to the full council on Jan. 12. - "We’re trying to make sure that people can understand where we came from and what exactly the guardrails are that we’re putting in place," Councilor James Oppenheimer said. "So this is really an exercise in transparent governance." - There's also an opportunity to share feedback online on the city's website. - It's also unclear if any of these new ordinances or changes would impact the proposed Gemini data center in northeast Sioux Falls. Merkouris said the council has asked the city for a legal opinion on that. - Smithfield, take two. After having its initial conditional use permit overturned in court, Smithfield is going to re-apply, a Smithfield executive told The Dakota Scout this week. Find the full story here. - Erickson names next parks director. Mayor Christine Erickson on Tuesday announced the appointment of Brett Kollars as the city's next parks director. Kollars currently serves as the assistant director for the parks and recreation department, and has been interim director since Don Kearney retired this spring. His appointment now goes before the City Council for final approval. - Remembering Katherine Frank. Minnehaha County Sheriff's Deputy Katherine Frank, 26, died Monday after being shot in the line of duty on Friday night. The Sheriff's Office has established a memorial in her honor at the Law Enforcement Center on 4th and Minnesota, for those who wish to pay their respects. There's also a GoFundMe from the Minnehaha County Deputies Association that's raised more than $73,000 as of Tuesday night. - Frank's friends and colleagues shared memories of her life with Sioux Falls Live and Dakota News Now, and The Dakota Scout provided some important context on just how rare these types of incidences are in our community. artigo.texto: As ações da Enerflex Ltd. (NYSE:EFXT) sobem 5% nas negociações pré-mercado de terça-feira, após a empresa anunciar um contrato para fornecer mais de um gigawatt (GW) de equipamentos de geração de energia a gás natural com baixas emissões para um empreendimento de data center na América do Norte. O contrato amplia a presença da Enerflex no mercado de infraestrutura de energia dedicada para suporte a instalações de inteligência artificial e computação digital. Em conjunto com os projetos anunciados anteriormente, incluindo aproximadamente 450 megawatts (MW) divulgados em 1 de outubro de 2026, o novo acordo aumenta a carteira de projetos de geração de energia a gás natural da empresa para mais de 1,75 GW. As entregas referentes ao atraso estão programadas para se estender até 2028. Enerflex garante importante contrato de geração de energia para data centers O contrato recém-adjudicado está inserido na área de Sistemas de Engenharia da Enerflex e abrange o projeto, a engenharia, a fabricação e a montagem de unidades de geração de energia a gás natural. O equipamento será implantado em um centro de dados em desenvolvimento na América do Norte, fornecendo capacidade dedicada de geração de eletricidade. O projeto utilizará uma configuração “atrás do medidor”, permitindo que a energia seja fornecida diretamente à instalação sem a necessidade de conexão à rede elétrica convencional para o sistema de geração. Esses arranjos podem suportar grandes instalações industriais e de computação que exigem fontes de alimentação de energia substanciais e confiáveis. A Enerflex descreveu o equipamento como uma tecnologia de geração a gás natural com baixas emissões, embora o anúncio não tenha especificado dados de desempenho de emissões nem comparações com sistemas de geração alternativos. A empresa também não divulgou o valor financeiro do contrato, a identidade do cliente ou a localização exata do centro de dados. A carteira de pedidos de geração de energia ultrapassa 1,75 GW A Enerflex afirmou que sua carteira de projetos de geração de energia a gás natural para consumidores finais agora ultrapassa 1,75 GW. O total inclui o contrato mais recente para mais de 1 GW de capacidade e contratos previamente anunciados, incluindo aproximadamente 450 MW divulgados no início de outubro. A carteira de pedidos representa o trabalho contratado que a empresa espera executar nos próximos anos. A previsão é de que as entregas continuem até 2028, fornecendo um cronograma das atividades futuras de fabricação e execução de projetos. O aumento reflete a crescente demanda por infraestrutura dedicada à geração de eletricidade, à medida que os desenvolvedores expandem a capacidade dos data centers. No entanto, a empresa não forneceu uma discriminação detalhada do valor financeiro da carteira de pedidos nem do reconhecimento de receita esperado por ano. O cronograma e a rentabilidade de cada projeto dependerão dos prazos de fabricação, dos custos de execução e dos termos contratuais. A Enerflex planeja investir US$ 100 milhões em sua unidade fabril Para dar suporte à sua crescente carteira de projetos, a Enerflex autorizou um investimento de aproximadamente US$ 100 milhões em suas instalações e capacidades de Sistemas de Engenharia. Desse montante, US$ 15 milhões estão incluídos na previsão de despesas de capital da empresa para 2026. O programa de investimento tem como objetivo fortalecer os recursos de fabricação e operacionais necessários para executar contratos de geração de energia em larga escala. A Enerflex afirmou que os projetos serão entregues por meio de suas operações de fabricação na América do Norte. O investimento planejado surge em um momento em que a empresa expande seu papel no fornecimento de infraestrutura de energia modular para instalações com alto consumo energético. O anúncio não forneceu uma alocação detalhada do investimento restante nem especificou o cronograma para todas as despesas planejadas. A infraestrutura de IA impulsiona a demanda por energia dedicada A Enerflex atribuiu o crescimento de sua carteira de pedidos de geração de energia à demanda decorrente do desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital. Os grandes centros de dados exigem um fornecimento substancial de eletricidade para operar equipamentos de computação, sistemas de rede e infraestrutura de refrigeração. A geração de energia instalada no próprio local de consumo pode fornecer uma fonte alternativa de energia para instalações que buscam capacidade dedicada sem depender de uma conexão convencional à rede elétrica para essa geração. Paul Mahoney, presidente e diretor executivo da Enerflex, destacou a demanda por esses sistemas. “A demanda por energia confiável e de primeira qualidade que não exija conexão à rede elétrica, e que dê suporte ao desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital, continua a crescer”, disse Mahoney. “O nosso sucesso em garantir mais de 1,75 gigawatts em carteira de pedidos destaca as capacidades únicas da Enerflex em fornecer soluções integradas de design, engenharia, fabricação em grande escala e execução de projetos para geração de energia atrás do medidor.” Os comentários destacam o foco da administração no fornecimento de sistemas integrados de geração de energia para grandes projetos de infraestrutura. Os contratos podem gerar receita adicional com serviços A Enerflex afirmou que sua crescente carteira de pedidos de geração de energia pode criar oportunidades que vão além da entrega inicial dos equipamentos. Isso inclui o comissionamento, a instalação e os serviços pós-venda associados às unidades geradoras. A empresa também identificou uma demanda potencial por suporte digital por meio de seu ecossistema de Gestão de Desempenho de Ativos ReliaCore. Os sistemas de gestão de desempenho de ativos podem ajudar os operadores a monitorar equipamentos, avaliar as condições de operação e gerenciar as necessidades de manutenção. artigo.texto: The zoning amendment, filed by Mayor Dominick Pangallo in July, defines data centers within the city’s zoning ordinance, as a “facility, or portion thereof, primarily designed or used to house computer servers and related information technology infrastructure for the storage, processing, management, or transmission of electronic data.” City staff and legal counsel determined that data centers were already not an allowed use under the current zoning, but there was no language until now to explicitly define a data centers and prohibit its construction in the city. All councilors favored moving some version of the zoning amendment forward. Most of the discussion Thursday night centered around what version of the amendment would prevent potential loopholes for developers to exploit without inadvertently banning routine data processing uses for businesses such as hospitals and telecommunications. During a committee meeting Sept. 30, Councilor at-Large Ty Hapworth made a revision to specify that “a data center shall not include such computer servers and related information technology infrastructure that is accessory, incidental, and subordinate to a lawful principal use at the same facility or a portion thereof, however stored. This exception does not cover a separate business providing data storage, server hosting, distributing processing, or similar technology to third parties.” Several councilors agreed they need to revisit the new zoning change in the coming months, saying that what the mayor initially filed left them with little flexibility to more carefully define data centers without banning routine data processing. Legally, the council is unable to substantially change the language beyond the “four corners” of what was originally proposed in July. Since the council plans to revisit the matter soon, councilors Lydia King and Jason Sydoriak said it would be best to exclude Hapworth’s amendment in order to prevent potential loopholes. “We can all agree that nothing we can pass tonight is a comprehensive data center ordinance,” King said. “There is a lot of nuance that would go into (that), so anything we do tonight is effectively temporary... (But) by further clarifying accessory uses, we may have inadvertently introduced additional loopholes that would make this harder to hold up against in court if someone wanted to come and say they didn’t like a ruling they got from the city.” Other councilors disagreed. “I think this language is valuable to keep in here,” said Ward 6 Councilor Katelyn Holappa. “If this use is ‘accessory, incidental, and subordinate to a lawful principal use’ — all of those three things together, such as a hospital having a server room, we’re not making that impossible. That could cause problems for businesses that we’re not intending to put in here.” The vote to include Hapworth’s proposed language passed, with just King and Sydoriak in opposition. The committee had also approved a motion to strike language previously recommended by the Planning Board adding the language “and has an aggregate power demand of 2 Megawatts or higher” to the end of the definition of data centers. Councilors shared concerns that a use of up to 1.9 megawatts could still result in harmful impacts associated with data centers such as heat and noise. Ultimately, the council unanimously approved the zoning change to ban data centers, with plans to revisit the issue in the coming months to draft language that would give a more comprehensive definition of data centers. © 2026 The Salem News (Beverly, Mass.). artigo.texto: Energia DHL amplia rede global de logística especializada em baterias Companhia reúne mais de 20 instalações e prepara novos centros na Europa para atender aos setores automotivo, industrial e de armazenamento de energia A DHL está ampliando sua rede internacional de logística especializada em baterias, formada atualmente por mais de 20 instalações. A estrutura atende fabricantes de veículos elétricos, empresas industriais e projetos de energia, oferecendo serviços que vão do transporte de componentes e apoio à produção ao armazenamento, reparo e encaminhamento de baterias para reciclagem. A companhia prevê novas unidades na Europa até 2027. A rede reúne operações de três divisões do grupo — DHL Supply Chain, DHL Global Forwarding e DHL Express — para integrar transporte, armazenagem, procedimentos aduaneiros e serviços pós-venda. Segundo a empresa, os centros especializados também realizam diagnóstico, testes, carregamento, condicionamento e recebimento de equipamentos devolvidos pelos clientes. A expansão acompanha o aumento da utilização de baterias em diferentes atividades. Além dos automóveis elétricos, os equipamentos são empregados em máquinas industriais, operações de mineração e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Alguns conjuntos pesam mais de 50 toneladas, o que exige veículos apropriados, equipamentos para movimentação de cargas pesadas e planejamento específico das entregas. O transporte desses produtos também está sujeito a requisitos de segurança. De acordo com a DHL, a classificação de baterias como mercadorias perigosas e as diferenças entre as regras aplicáveis ao transporte marítimo, aéreo e terrestre impõem cuidados com acondicionamento, documentação e fiscalização aduaneira. “A logística de baterias é fundamentalmente diferente das cadeias de abastecimento tradicionais”, afirmou Francisco Milián, responsável pela área de logística de entrada para a produção da DHL Supply Chain na Europa, Oriente Médio e África. Segundo ele, os clientes demandam serviços em todas as etapas, desde o fornecimento às fábricas até o recondicionamento, as devoluções e a reciclagem. Novas instalações Na Alemanha, a DHL disponibilizou recentemente 13 mil metros quadrados de armazenagem adaptada a baterias na cidade de Halle. Outra instalação está sendo preparada na Hungria, com início das atividades previsto para 2027. Nos Países Baixos, o grupo está construindo um centro em Holtum, com 17 mil metros quadrados para armazenagem e serviços especializados em baterias de alta tensão. A previsão é de que a operação comece no início de 2027. O empreendimento ficará próximo de instalações já utilizadas para atendimento à indústria automotiva, formando um complexo voltado também a sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Segundo a empresa, a concentração de atividades em centros especializados permitirá reunir operações de transporte internacional, liberação aduaneira, distribuição e atendimento após a venda. O serviço é destinado tanto à indústria automotiva quanto a fabricantes de equipamentos, empresas de energia e projetos relacionados a minerais críticos. Transporte de energia A DHL também atua na movimentação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, do inglês Battery Energy Storage Systems. Esses conjuntos armazenam eletricidade para utilização posterior e podem ser empregados em projetos de energia renovável e infraestrutura das redes elétricas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a companhia transportou mais de 1.100 unidades BESS para diferentes mercados. Segundo o grupo, as entregas podem exigir transporte multimodal, içamento de cargas de grande porte e deslocamentos até áreas remotas, além do cumprimento das normas aplicáveis ao manuseio de mercadorias perigosas. O crescimento dessa atividade ocorre paralelamente à instalação de fábricas de baterias em diferentes regiões. A DHL aponta que a concentração de parte da produção na Ásia e a demanda em mercados como o europeu movimentam matérias-primas, produtos químicos, componentes, equipamentos industriais e baterias prontas entre continentes. “A transição energética está criando corredores comerciais e padrões de cadeias de abastecimento inteiramente novos”, afirmou Hendrik Venter, CEO global da DHL Supply Chain. De acordo com o executivo, fabricantes e operadores estão reorganizando suas redes para atender à produção de veículos elétricos, ao armazenamento de energia e aos empreendimentos de fontes renováveis. A logística para o setor de novas energias integra a Strategy 2030, plano de negócios do DHL Group. A área contempla oito segmentos: energia eólica, solar, veículos elétricos e baterias, armazenamento de energia em baterias, carregamento de veículos elétricos, infraestrutura de redes, hidrogênio e combustíveis alternativos.

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Advancing American Freedom Foundation wants Congress to see how much electricity data centers use. It also wants states to reveal how much their data center tax breaks cost. The conservative group made those recommendations in a paper by Kevin Dayaratna. He’s the president of AAFF’s Institute for Statistical Policy Analysis. The paper argues that lawmakers and utilities need better information before deciding data center policy. He said these policies impact state budgets and utility costs. “There is no precise aggregate measure of how much electricity data centers consume,” Dayaratna wrote. He used Ohio as an example of where this would’ve helped. The state projected that its data center sales tax exemption would cost about $136 million in 2025. Its tax department later told reporters it would cost $1.569 billion, according to published reports. That’s more than 11 times the first estimate, the paper says. The department also shared those figures with a news outlet instead of posting them on a state website. Texas had something similar happen. In February 2023, the state projected that its data center exemption would cost $130 million in fiscal year 2025. By January 2025, that estimate ballooned to $1.016 billion. “States should publish these figures and review these exemptions on a fixed schedule,” Dayaratna wrote. The paper also looks at power forecasts changing. In 2022, Georgia Power expected demand to grow by less than 400 megawatts by 2031. A year later, it raised that estimate to 6,600 megawatts. Dayaratna thinks both low and high forecasts hurt customers. Too little power can cause shortages, too much can raise electric bills, he noted. The paper cites projections saying data centers may use 9% to 17% of American electricity by 2030. AAFF wants Congress to make the Energy Information Administration require regular data collection of this information. EIA announced voluntary pilot studies in March. That pilot program covers just 196 companies. “Congress should make this collection broader and more permanent,” Dayaratna wrote. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 includes a reporting requirement. Senators introduced it last month. Section 2114 would make power companies report how much electricity data centers use. Data centers wouldn’t have to file any new reports. AAFF also wants states to let private utilities use separate power grids to serve data centers. The power company and its customers would negotiate prices and finance their own systems. They would still have to follow environmental, siting and safety laws. Dayaratna says this would protect other utility customers from paying for infrastructure upgrades to benefit data centers. The paper says charging data centers higher electric rates could help, but they would still use the same power grid as everyone else. AAFF also wants to make it easier and faster to build power plants and connect them to the grid. It supports using different energy sources without any emissions rules. The group doesn’t want to ban new data center construction, it says. It wants states to fix power supply shortages and make adding more electricity to the grid easier.

artigo.texto: The Chinese battery manufacturer leads with 26,574 patent families, supported by substantial research investment and rapid advances in power and solid-state battery technologies. China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) has surpassed South Korea’s LG Energy Solution to become the world’s leading company in battery patent holdings, highlighting China’s growing influence in the global battery technology sector. According to data released on October 6 by intellectual property consulting firm PatSnap, CATL recorded 26,574 simple patent families between October 2016 and September 2026. This places it ahead of LG Energy Solution, which holds 22,597 patent families, creating a gap of nearly 4,000. Simple patent families group patent applications covering the same core invention across different countries or regions. This method provides a clearer comparison of companies’ technological contributions while avoiding duplicate counting of identical inventions. CATL Strengthens Its Position in Battery Innovation The latest rankings reflect a significant shift in the battery industry, where Japanese and South Korean manufacturers historically held leading positions in research and development. LG Energy Solution now ranks second, while Panasonic has dropped out of the top ten with 4,994 patents. Toyota remains the only Japanese company among the leading ten. CATL’s growing patent portfolio is backed by substantial research spending. The company has invested more than 100 billion yuan, equivalent to approximately $14.9 billion, in cumulative research and development. PatSnap data further indicates that CATL holds 27,402 battery patents overall, including 16,722 filed during the past three years. These recent filings account for 61% of its total portfolio, demonstrating the pace of its technological expansion. Power Battery Patents Lead the Industry CATL has established a particularly strong position in power battery technology, holding 19,539 patents. Its portfolio is approximately 2.2 times larger than that of the second-ranked domestic competitor. During the past three years, CATL filed 12,084 power battery patents, significantly exceeding the 4,384 recorded by its closest domestic rival. Its recent filings also approach the combined 14,500 patents held by companies ranked second through fifth. Solid-State Battery Research Gains Momentum CATL is also expanding its presence in solid-state battery development, a technology widely viewed as important for the next generation of energy storage. The company holds 3,538 patents in this field, more than twice the total of its second-ranked domestic competitor. Of these, 2,763 were filed during the last three years, nearly matching the combined 2,891 patents recorded by domestic companies ranked second through tenth. The figures underline CATL’s growing technological lead and the increasingly prominent role of Chinese manufacturers in shaping the future of battery innovation.

artigo.texto: Data Centers and Public Health The rapid growth of AI and other digital services like search engines and cloud storage and computing is driving a major expansion of data center construction across the United States. As rapid expansion continues, it is necessary to account for related health impacts. Data centers can affect communities and their health in a variety of ways, including air pollution from the burning of fossil fuels, water use and pollution, excessive noise and light pollution, and land use and development. New facilities that are powered by fossil fuels can add to existing pollution and health burdens in communities already facing environmental injustices. Data centers are often placed and operated in the same communities already disproportionately impacted by environmental injustices: low-income, rural, immigrant/refugee, Indigenous communities and other communities of color, and other marginalized populations. It’s important to understand how data centers can affect health and the role public health professionals can play to advocate for transparent decisionmaking and protective policies. Latest Updates - Data Centers and Health: Understanding the Impacts and Taking Action AI data centers are expanding rapidly across the U.S., with growing implications for air and water quality, noise, energy costs and public health. This four-part webinar series equips health professionals and advocates with the evidence, messaging and actionable strategies needed to respond. Watch the recordings. - Q&A with NAACP: Addressing the growing environmental harms of AI data centers | Public Health Newswire From rising emissions to local air, water and noise pollution, AI data centers pose growing concerns about environmental justice and health equity. The NAACP has long been on the front lines of environmental justice and is addressing new threats as they arise. This March 2026 Q&A from Public Health Newswire talks with the NAACP to learn how communities and health professionals can respond. Read the article. How a Data Center Can Affect Health Energy, Air Pollution and Climate Health The energy demand created by data centers can drive grid expansion and fossil fuel energy generation, which can worsen air pollution, amplify the effects of climate change and create affordability concerns for households. Impact on Energy Grid In some areas, utility companies may need to expand or upgrade the power grid to meet data centers’ energy demand. Depending on how these upgrades are funded, this can increase energy costs for surrounding communities, contributing to financial stress and mental health impacts. Inadequate energy access can increase the risk of heat- and cold-related illnesses, such as heat stroke and inadequate blood circulation. Long-term socioeconomic implications of financial hardship can include food insecurity, increasing health disparities and chronic stress. Air Quality Data centers that rely on fossil fuels can increase air pollution, contributing to respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, neurological disorders and reduced fertility. One high-growth model suggests that data centers may contribute to approximately 600,000 asthma cases in 2028, with an estimated public health cost over $20 billion. Climate Change Added CO₂ from data center operations accelerates climate change, contributing to more severe heat waves, storms and floods, which are all events that endanger both data centers and nearby communities and compound health risks ranging from heat stroke and respiratory illness to trauma and mental health impacts. The water consumption by data centers may exacerbate growing water scarcity caused by climate change and drought. Data centers can release excess heat that may raise temperatures in nearby neighborhoods. Some researchers have documented increased air temperatures up to 4°F, and this heat impact spanned approximately a third of a mile from the data center. Added heat may increase cooling needs and compound heat-health risks for people who are most vulnerable or unable to afford air conditioning. Water Use, Quality and Scarcity Cooling systems can strain local water supplies and raise concerns about water quality, drought and equitable access. The cooling systems used in data centers can strain local water resources and negatively impact water quality. There are also some concerns around incorporation of chemicals like PFAS in the cooling systems. These forever chemicals are long-lasting in the environment and high levels are linked with some cancers. The changes to water supply and quality may increase the risk of waterborne diseases, water scarcity, pollution ingestion and poor maternal outcomes. Noise, Light and Sleep Health Around-the-clock cooling equipment, fans, generators and construction can create disruptive noise, while nighttime lighting can interfere with sleep and daily rhythms. Noise Pollution Cooling systems, back-up diesel generators, fans and other machinery contribute to constant noise production, which can cause chronic sleep disturbance and stress, with the possibility of long-term conditions such as cardiovascular impacts. Noise pollution is of particular concern for children as it can impact cognition and may have lifelong health impacts. Light Pollution Data centers require lighting throughout the night which can disrupt the circadian rhythm of individuals exposed, impacting melatonin production, sleep cycles, mental health, cardiovascular health and overall quality of life. Beyond the Facility: Supply Chains and E-Waste Construction, mineral extraction and electronic waste create health and environmental impacts beyond the data center site. Beyond the direct health impacts of data centers, the processes required to build and maintain the facilities, such as mining rare-earth metals and concrete production, also impact health outcomes. artigo.texto: Ask most people what BYD does and they will say electric cars. That is true, and it undersells the company by a wide margin. BYD is a Chinese multinational manufacturing conglomerate that builds rechargeable batteries, stationary energy storage, solar panels, semiconductors, forklifts, and entire monorail systems. The car business is the loudest part. It is not the whole company, and it was not even the first. BYD Company Ltd. operates across electronics, autos, renewable energy, and rail transit. That spread is not an accident of acquisition. It is the result of a battery maker deciding, over three decades, that it could build the things its batteries power, then the things that move those things, then the infrastructure they run on. To understand BYD you have to start before the cars existed. Wang Chuanfu founded BYD to make rechargeable batteries in February 1995, formally registered as Shenzhen BYD Battery Company Ltd. Before that he worked as a vice supervisor at Beijing's Nonferrous Research Institute. He saw an opening as Japanese companies shifted from NiCd toward higher-value nickel-metal hydride and lithium-ion chemistries, and he went after the segment they were leaving behind. The early strategy was labor, not automation. BYD built its business on manual labor rather than the capital-intensive, highly automated processes Japanese rivals used, and that approach, combined with in-house production of key machinery, cut its unit costs to roughly five or six times lower than Japanese competitors. It worked. BYD won an order from Sanyo in 1996 that marked its arrival in the global supply chain, and by July 2002 it had surpassed Sanyo to become the world's leading NiCd battery maker, accounting for 65% of global production. The car business came later. BYD Auto was established in 2003. For a battery company that had just won the NiCd crown, building cars was the logical place to put all those cells. BYD is well known for its Blade Battery, and one sits in every BYD EV. The headline feature is safety: it has passed the nail penetration test, and its compressive strength reaches 445 kN, the equivalent of a 45-ton truck. The warranty runs eight years or longer, covering 310,685 miles and in some cases up to 621,371 miles. BYD does not keep the batteries to itself. It functions as an OEM battery supplier, and FinDreams Battery, its subsidiary, ranked as the world's number-two EV battery producer in 2024, holding 17% of the EV battery market behind CATL. Its customers include rivals. The Toyota bZ3, a China-only sedan co-developed with BYD, runs a BYD Blade Battery underneath, and regulatory filings show Tesla has fitted BYD cells in the Model Y. BYD Energy Storage was founded in 2008 and specializes in energy storage solutions. According to its website, it has rolled out industrial and residential projects in 110 countries. The scale here is genuinely large and often overlooked in all the EV coverage. In 2025, BYD topped global Battery Energy Storage System shipments at more than 60 GWh, displacing Tesla - the first year it held the number one BESS position worldwide. That gave BYD a 13 percent global BESS market share, against Tesla's 10 percent, per Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Tesla shipped 46.7 GWh of storage that year. The grid-scale battery business, in other words, is now another market where BYD leads and Tesla follows. The most surprising corner of BYD is the one where it stopped being a parts supplier and became a civil engineering firm. SkyRail is an advanced monorail; its carriages ride on an elevated single beam that supports and guides them, and BYD built the entire system - vehicles, tracks, stations, and communication systems. The R&D project ran five years, mobilized more than 1,000 engineers, and cost over 600 million euro, with total SkyRail investment exceeding $1 billion. The pitch is cost. SkyRail runs about a fifth of what a subway costs to build, with construction taking as little as two years - one third the time a subway takes, helped by prefabricated track beams. It can move 10,000 to 30,000 passengers per hour in one direction. BYD positions it for cities worried about the financial burden of a subway. It has launched lines in Shenzhen and Sao Paulo, Brazil. The grand plan was bigger: an initial rollout across more than 200 Chinese cities was cut back sharply once Beijing moved to curb local government debt. The vertical integration shows up in the financials. BYD's net profit in 2025 was CNY 32.62 billion, roughly $4.72 billion, and it earned 1.25 times more net profit than Tesla while pulling in 1.23 times the revenue. It sold 2.81 times as many vehicles. That volume comes at a lower price per car - a domestic average selling price around CNY 141,000, about $20,400 - but the batteries, electronics, and storage businesses give BYD revenue streams Tesla does not have. It is not all up and to the right. BYD's 2025 revenue grew only 3.46%, its slowest in six years, net profit fell 18.97% - its first yearly profit drop in four years - blamed on a fierce domestic price war that squeezed margins. Overseas is now the profitability lever: exports passed the 1 million mark for the first time, hitting 1.05 million, a 145% jump, and overseas operations rose to 38.65% of revenue. If you want to track BYD as the conglomerate it actually is, read past the vehicle delivery numbers. Its 2025 annual report is filed on the Shenzhen exchange under 002594.SZ and on HKEX under 01211.HK, where the segment breakdowns show handset revenue and the rest. Watch the energy storage shipments, since that is where BYD just overtook Tesla. And keep an eye on U.S. legislation banning Chinese vehicle software from 2027 and Chinese hardware from 2030, on top of existing 100 percent tariffs on Chinese EVs - the regulatory wall that will decide how much of this empire ever reaches American roads. artigo.texto: Morocco prepares to launch Africa’s first battery gigafactory Gotion Power Morocco plans to begin equipment commissioning in Kenitra, advancing major investment in battery manufacturing KENITRA, Morocco (MNTV) — Morocco is preparing to advance its electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry as Gotion Power Morocco plans to begin commissioning production equipment at its Kenitra gigafactory during the week of October 20. Moroccan subsidiary of China’s Gotion High-Tech announced the timetable for starting up equipment at the industrial facility, which is intended to produce lithium iron phosphate battery cells. The project’s first phase represents an investment of approximately 13 billion Moroccan dirhams, equivalent to about $1.3 billion, and targets an initial annual capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours. Located in Kenitra’s Atlantic Free Zone, the facility is designed to serve the automotive and energy storage industries. Its potential markets include Morocco, other African countries, Europe, the Middle East and the United States. Construction began in September 2025, with the company’s buildings and infrastructure completed over approximately 13 months. The project required large-scale shipments of production equipment from China, supported by Moroccan port and customs authorities. Gotion Power Morocco president Khalid Qalam described the equipment startup as an initial step toward developing a wider battery manufacturing ecosystem in the country. The company has recruited more than 400 Moroccan employees, including engineers, technicians and production workers. Many received training at Gotion facilities in China before joining the Kenitra project. The company expects the gigafactory to create more than 2,300 direct jobs when fully developed. Its longer-term plans include expanding production capacity and manufacturing battery materials for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. The project also forms part of a broader partnership involving Gotion and Volkswagen’s battery subsidiary, PowerCo. The companies announced a separate Moroccan joint venture in September to produce lithium iron phosphate cathode materials. That venture is expected to involve an investment of approximately €480 million, or about $547 million, with planned annual production capacity of 100,000 metric tons. The developments strengthen Morocco’s ambitions to attract advanced manufacturing investment and establish a larger role in international electric vehicle supply chains.

O lançamento reúne os principais sistemas necessários à operação de uma infraestrutura de tecnologia da informação (TI), incluindo energia, climatização, monitoramento e segurança. artigo.texto: Netbox Labs Faz Parceria com a NVIDIA e a Grafana Labs e Anuncia Novas Adições à Plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura NetBox para Agregar a Camada de Inteligência para Data Centers de IA e Criação de Infraestrutura Corporativa AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 14 de outubro de 2026 CABO CANAVERAL, Flórida, Oct. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Centro Espacial Kennedy — A NetBox Labs, empresa criadora do NetBox, o sistema de registro para redes e datacenters, anunciou hoje parcerias com a NVIDIA e a Grafana Labs, além de uma série de novos recursos da plataforma, na primeira conferência NetBox Evolve. Juntos, esses anúncios ampliam a posição do NetBox como a camada de inteligência central para a infraestrutura tecnológica mundial. - A NVIDIA agora está integrada ao NetBox como uma fonte de verdade nativa do NVIDIA Configuration Manager (NVCM), o componente de orquestração de rede do NVIDIA DSX OS. Com a aceleração da implementação da infraestrutura de IA, essa parceria coloca o NetBox no centro de como a infraestrutura de IA é projetada, provisionada e operada. - A Grafana Labs e a NetBox Labs lançaram um plugin oficial do NetBox no catálogo da Grafana. Ele leva o contexto da infraestrutura em tempo real para os dashboards e alertas da Grafana, viabilizando que as equipes de rede e de data centers atribuam significado aos seus dados. - A Plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura da NetBox Labs foi ampliada com novos produtos e recursos. O NetBox Designs se junta ao NetBox Visual Explorer e ao NetBox Asset Lifecycle para acelerar o design e o planejamento, a aquisição e o gerenciamento de implementações de data centers e redes. Além disso, novos agentes e recursos de operações de IA ajudam todas as equipes a automatizar sua infraestrutura com base no contexto independente de fornecedores do NetBox. Por fim, uma grande variedade de novas integrações e novos dashboards para o NetBox Analytics ajudam as equipes a inserir mais dados no NetBox e a entender rapidamente sua infraestrutura. Seja para as equipes criarem redes e infraestruturas corporativas no setor de varejo, saúde, serviços financeiros ou implementarem um data center de IA com velocidade e escala gigantescas, a configuração, a observabilidade e a automação dependem de um registro confiável de qual infraestrutura deve existir e como ela deve operar. Esse registro é o NetBox, disse Kris Beevers, CEO e cofundador da NetBox Labs. O NetBox é usado por empresas como Arm, CoreWeave, Kaiser Permanente e J.P. Morgan Chase para criar, operar e expandir suas redes e infraestruturas. Estamos observando um crescimento enorme, com mais de 90% das principais neonuvens usando o NetBox para projetar e escalar seus datacenters de IA, e esperamos que o NetBox alimente mais de 100 GW de capacidade de datacenters de IA até 2030. O NetBox se torna nativo do NVIDIA DSX OS A NVIDIA fez uma parceria com a NetBox Labs para tornar o NetBox uma fonte nativa de referência para o NVCM, de modo que a configuração de rede no DSX OS venha diretamente do sistema de registro que as equipes de infraestrutura de IA já usam. Isso coloca o NetBox no centro do design, do provisionamento e da operação das implementações de IA em grande escala da atualidade. O NetBox fornece os dados centrais que impulsionam a automação da configuração em todas as malhas de cluster nativas da NVIDIA. Leia mais sobre a Parceria NetBox Labs NVIDIA aqui. Contexto do NetBox em todos os dashboards da Grafana Labs A infraestrutura está produzindo cada vez mais telemetria. Mas a telemetria só mostra o que a infraestrutura está fazendo, não o que ela é: a qual dispositivo uma interface pertence, onde ela está localizada, qual função ela desempenha, quem é o proprietário dela e se ela deveria existir. Atualmente as equipes preenchem essa lacuna manualmente, com scripts ou suposições frágeis. Com a nova parceria da NetBox Labs com a Grafana Labs, o NetBox registra como a infraestrutura deve ser e a Grafana mostra o que ela está realmente fazendo. O plugin gratuito e de código aberto do NetBox, desenvolvido em colaboração com a Grafana Labs e publicado no catálogo da Grafana, transfere o contexto do NetBox em tempo real (local, função, tenant, rack, proprietário, ciclo de vida) para os dashboards e alertas da Grafana. Ele não exige alterações no pipeline, evita rótulos desatualizados e não adiciona nenhum custo de métrica. Separadamente, a plataforma Orb de código aberto da NetBox Labs agora oferece aos usuários da Grafana Cloud uma nova fonte de fluxo de rede e telemetria de pacotes. A observabilidade das redes e da infraestrutura são casos de uso populares em toda a comunidade da Grafana, e o contexto é o que separa uma parede de métricas das respostas e ações, disse Ash Mazhari, VP de Desenvolvimento Corporativo da Grafana Labs. O NetBox é o sistema de registro em que as equipes já confiam. Com a fonte de dados do NetBox em nosso catálogo e a Orb fornecendo telemetria de rede para a Grafana Cloud, nossos usuários passam a ter um entendimento mais profundo da sua infraestrutura e dos dados de rede. Leia mais sobre a Parceria entre a NetBox Labs e a Grafana Labs aqui. Novos recursos da plataforma NetBox Labs para pessoas e agentes de IA Além das parcerias, a NetBox Labs também anunciou várias novas adições à plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura da NetBox Labs. - Agora em versão de pré-visualização pública, o NetBox Designs oferece modelos reutilizáveis para um projeto de infraestrutura rápido. As equipes definem um local, um rack ou um plano de IP uma vez e, em seguida, podem repetir o processo para implantações em grande escala. O NetBox Asset Lifecycle então acompanha os objetos planejados ao longo da lista de materiais, do pedido de compra, do envio e da instalação. - O NetBox Analytics ganhou vários dashboards prontos para uso esta semana para ajudar as equipes a entender seus complexos ambientes de infraestrutura. artigo.texto: In recent weeks, Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton have adopted increasingly tough rhetoric against data centers, promising to crack down on hundreds of facilities that failed to disclose required information about their water use over the past five years. But the law that Texas political leaders are invoking carries a maximum fine of just $500 — a potentially negligible penalty that’s just a blip for large companies. Data centers use millions of gallons of water a year to run their facilities and cool their servers. Under state law, facilities that fail to complete required water-use surveys can be charged with a Class C misdemeanor, punishable by up to a $500 fine, and barred from certain state funding and environmental permits. But some experts say those consequences have significant limitations, raising questions about whether the state has the tools to force compliance from an industry expanding rapidly across Texas. State officials don’t know whether misdemeanor penalties have been issued against data centers, and the facilities aren’t eligible for state funding. Increasing fines for Class C misdemeanors in the Water Code would require state legislation. Lawmakers do not convene in Austin for the 2027 legislative session until January. “The governor is like, ‘Let’s enforce the laws on the books that weren’t being enforced.’ That’s not much in the way of incentive,” said Kathryn Guerra, who leads a watchdog campaign at the environmental nonprofit Public Citizen. “If those are the laws that we already have and nobody’s enforcing them, the data centers know.” Abbott’s office defended its enforcement crackdown by saying that the water board, along with other agencies including the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and the Public Utility Commission of Texas, will work together. “No other state agency will approve data centers until the Public Utility Commission, ERCOT, and the Water Development Board have the information they need to make informed decisions,” said Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary. Mahaleris added that the governor has recommended that data centers pay for their own electric infrastructure, use less water-intensive cooling technologies and add power generation to the state’s power grid. Cameron Poursoltan, the director of energy policy at Texas for the Data Center Coalition, said the organization, which represents many data center operators, supports annual water reporting because state and regional planners need accurate data to build a water plan that meets the needs of all Texans. The state already requires large water users, including data centers, to complete annual water use surveys. The Texas Water Development Board, the state agency tasked with overseeing the state’s water planning process and financing water projects, uses responses to assess the current demand and to plan for water needs 50 years into the future. But data centers have largely ignored the surveys. Or some argue they haven’t received them. Last year, 329 data centers were surveyed. Only about 30% responded. One lawmaker described the response rate as “pretty pathetic” at a legislative hearing this summer, despite the requirement being written into state law. Some data center operators have defended the low response rate, saying they have not received a survey. “Data centers take water stewardship extremely seriously,” Poursoltan said. He added that the organization has worked with TWDB to resolve “significant contact information and data discrepancies that contributed to the TWDB Water Use Survey’s initial lower response rate.” Tracking data centers in Texas The survey has long been the state’s only way to track how much water the rapidly expanding data center industry uses. Another effort to collect the information by the PUC this year has been voluntary and also had a low response rate. Now, amid growing scrutiny of data centers and their demands on Texas’ dwindling water supply, Abbott and Paxton are asking state agencies to enforce the existing law. The enforcement push comes as both Republicans face competitive elections and opposition to data center development grows. A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released in August found that 57% of Texas voters opposed building a data center in their community. Republicans remained closely divided, with 45% supporting while 43% opposed local data center construction. Meanwhile, 75% of registered Texas Democrats oppose data centers. The water board, which collects the surveys to help plan the state’s water needs, has historically had little ability to enforce the requirement. Abbott has directed the agency to notify local prosecutors about noncompliant facilities, while Paxton has launched an investigation. But the board says it has no authority to prosecute violations itself, and state officials don’t know if fines have been issued against data centers. The state’s next steps could reveal how much leverage officials actually have. artigo.texto: Bulgaria’s net electricity exports surged by 62% in annual terms from the beginning of the year to early October. They reached 3.5 TWh, compared to 2.16 TWh in the same period last year, driven primarily by increased generation from renewable energy sources, supported by energy storage systems. Data from Bulgaria’s transmission system operator (TSO) Electricity System Operator (ESO) show that the country produced 12.24% more electricity year-on-year, while domestic consumption grew by 8.45%, according to the Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity (APSTE). Power generation from renewable energy sources reached 11.5 TWh, up by nearly 34% from the previous year. Renewables have accounted for nearly 80% of the country’s total power generation growth. The expansion of energy storage systems has been particularly remarkable The expansion of energy storage systems has been particularly remarkable. From the start of the year until October 4, grid-scale batteries delivered 1,720 GWh of electricity to the power system. It is a more than ninefold increase from just 190 GWh that was recorded a year earlier. This enabled cheap electricity generated during the day to be stored and used during hours of higher demand and higher prices, APSTE pointed out. Of note, Bulgaria’s BESS capacity is approaching 6 GW / 17 GWh. Eurelectric earlier said that 5.4 GW of BESS capacity accounts for 22.8% of total generation capacity in the country, making it one of the global leaders. Bulgaria remained a net exporter during the challenging summer in the region APSTE stressed that the benefits of the new energy mix became particularly clear during the summer. Despite prolonged heatwaves and low water levels on the Danube river that constrained nuclear and hydro power generation across the region, Bulgaria remained a net exporter and maintained prices lower than neighboring markets during key periods. This success was driven by a combination of solar power plants, battery storage, and the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant (NPP). Gazdov: While neighboring markets suffer from high prices and power shortages, Bulgaria generates and stores more and more of its own electricity “While neighboring markets suffer from high prices and power shortages, due to constraints on their nuclear plants and high natural gas prices, Bulgaria generates and stores more and more of its own electricity. This translates into more competitive prices for households and businesses, greater energy security, and a stronger position on the regional energy market,” APSTE chairman Nikola Gazdov explained. A striking example occurred on October 8, when Unit 6 of the Kozloduy NPP underwent planned maintenance and Unit 5 operated at reduced capacity due to low water levels on the Danube. Despite these constraints, in the early afternoon photovoltaic systems were producing nearly 4,300 MW, exceeding total national demand of 4,100 MW, while batteries were charging at over 4,000 MW, storing cheap electricity for peak evening demand, the update reads. Wind is the solution for cheaper electricity in the winter However, APSTE warned that the successful expansion of solar energy and batteries is not enough. In the winter, solar generation decreases while demand rises. To secure more of cheap domestic power during the colder months, Bulgaria must accelerate wind energy deployment. Since 2020, PV capacity in the country has grown by about 600% to nearly 7 GW, while BESS capacity is close to 6 GW / 17 GWh. APSTE estimates that total investments in photovoltaics, batteries, and related infrastructure since 2020 have reached approximately EUR 7 billion. However, Bulgaria has only 716 MW of installed wind capacity, with no major new wind farm built since 2013. Wind power complements solar with a different daily and seasonal generation profile, capable of providing substantial power output during winter, APSTE added. Gazdov: Sun and batteries have significantly enhanced Bulgaria’s energy security “Sun and batteries have significantly enhanced Bulgaria’s energy security amid one of the most severe energy crises. This is very important, but it is not enough. We must build on this success by attracting investment into wind power as well,” he said. This road will secure cheaper local electricity not only in the summer, but also in the winter, Gazdov added. Achieving this does not require new subsidies, but clear rules and a genuine easing of construction procedures for new capacity, in his view. According to APSTE, Bulgaria could attract over EUR 4 billion in additional private investment in wind farms and energy storage systems by 2030, provided institutions ensure predictable regulations and remove unnecessary administrative constraints, including for projects located outside renewable energy acceleration areas.
