artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Why AI Data Center Cooling Needs to Get Smarter AI is pushing data center cooling to its limits, so the real advantage comes from integrating smart sensing, motor control, and power management into a single responsive, failure-anticipating system. The job of a data center cooling system is simple in concept: absorb heat where it isn’t wanted and move it where it can be released safely. AI is making that job much harder, pushing rack power past 100 kW, with some AI clusters expected to exceed 1 megawatt within the next few years. Operators racing to add AI capacity must deploy quickly while protecting uptime, managing energy use, and safeguarding valuable hardware. There is no single way to cool an AI data center. The right architecture depends on rack power, workloads, and facility requirements. Engineers typically reserve the most advanced liquid cooling for AI racks, while other approaches serve standard workloads and facilities without existing water infrastructure. Liquid cooling is becoming increasingly important, but this mix of approaches adds complexity: mitigating leak risk, supporting multiple architectures at once, and ensuring that cooling responds precisely as thermal demands change. Moving heat more efficiently is no longer enough. The next step is to make cooling systems more intelligent through real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management. Together, these technologies can make cooling more responsive, reduce energy consumption, and maximize uptime while laying the foundation for AI-enabled predictive maintenance. Why Smarter Control Matters Consider what happens when a liquid-cooled rack develops a leak. Many of today’s rack installations use on-off valves that stop the coolant when a sensor detects a leak, shutting down the entire rack until technicians can locate and fix the leak source. With a whole rack at stake, detection must be reliable. Yet the most common leak sensors, moisture-sensitive resistive ropes, can be limited in both accuracy and response time. A more intelligent approach could detect leaks faster and control coolant flow at the server-tray level, helping keep unaffected parts of the rack running. That points to three capabilities working together: real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management. Real-Time Motor Control Keeps Coolant Moving Inside the coolant distribution unit (CDU), pumps and fans form the mechanical heart of the cooling loop. Reliability is the top priority. Depending on the CDU placement, a single pump failure can take an entire rack – or worse, an entire row – of AI computing equipment offline. Real-time motor control helps keep that system stable. Microcontrollers process sensor data and adjust performance accordingly, while motor drivers run pumps and fans efficiently. Motor control also extends to the server tray. Valves at the CDU typically open or close, but linear valves at the tray level can regulate coolant flow much more precisely. As power density inside the tray continues to rise, that level of precision becomes more important. Precision Flow Sensing Tracks Coolant at the Tray Precise flow control requires precise flow measurement, so linear valves at the tray work alongside accurate flow sensors. Together, they enable more granular control of GPU and CPU die temperatures. How the sensor is installed matters, too. Conventional flow sensors are inserted into the coolant line, creating an additional potential leak point. Non-invasive ultrasonic sensing can avoid that risk while also making installation easier and faster. Moisture-sensitive resistive ropes are still commonly used for leak detection. Still, concerns about accuracy and response time are pushing engineers to evaluate alternatives such as humidity sensors, capacitive sensors, and negative-pressure CDU designs. Flow readings also contribute to a broader operating picture. Combined with temperature, humidity, and pressure sensors, they can help detect changes that any single sensor might miss. High-Efficiency Power Management Keeps Cooling Lean The pumps and fans cooling AI racks consume power themselves, so their efficiency matters. Power management and motor control meet in the pump drive, where gallium nitride (GaN) power devices can improve overall pump-system efficiency by up to 2% compared with traditional silicon while enabling a smaller form factor. In server trays that still combine air and liquid cooling, fans remain critical, and many are shifting from 12 V to 48 V to reduce power consumption and improve efficiency. Power delivery is evolving as well. CDU pumps already operate on input voltages ranging from 48 V DC to 380 V AC. As 800 V high-voltage DC (HVDC) distribution gains traction in parts of the industry, operators will need pumps designed to support it. Edge AI Lays the Groundwork for Predictive Maintenance Sensing can also become predictive. Edge AI can process data from a cooling system’s full sensor array, an approach known as “sensor fusion,” enabling faster response times and lower latency. That matters for leak detection, which remains a bottleneck for reliable liquid cooling. Sensor fusion can improve detection speed and accuracy. It also opens the door to predictive maintenance for pumps and other critical mechanical components. Combined with tray-level flow control, edge AI and sensor fusion point toward cooling systems that sense changing conditions, anticipate problems, and adjust automatically. Building Intelligence into Every Architecture No single cooling design fits every AI data center, and mixed architectures are likely to serve the industry for years. But every architecture, from rear-door heat exchangers to immersion tanks, shares many of the same building blocks: sensors to measure conditions; motor control to drive pumps, fans, and valves; power management to supply them

artigo.texto: Rapid City surveyed citizens in a town hall to get to the bottom of the ongoing data center debate. The results were clear – most believe data centers are at best necessary evils, at worst drains on natural resources which should be banned from city limits. Though no public comment session was held at Wednesday’s event, over 220 residents had their anonymous surveys shared over the course of the night. The answer was overwhelming, though not universal, in opposition to data centers. The results of this survey, which will be published online to take for the coming weeks, will be used to inform policy on the allowances for data centers in the states second largest city. Jeff Shelton is a Democrat running for the District 32 Senate seat. Though not the crux of his campaign, he wants strict controls on data center development in the state. He said this isn’t surprising. “I think that we got some very clear responses that what we don’t want is any large-scale data centers," Shelton said. "Even on the smaller side on things that aren’t covered by (SB)135, I saw some strong opposition there.” Shelton refers to Senate Bill 135, otherwise known as the data center bill of rights, which passed last session. Data center opposition is bipartisan in nature, and Shelton said the bill needs more fine tuning. “A mistake that was made with Senate Bill 135 that I hope to address if I’m elected in the Senate, is to have more comprehensive definitions to make sure that when we say ‘data center,’ we mean a drain on our resources and something meaningfully harmful to our communities," Shelton said. "I think if we’re not careful we really run the risk of missing the mark.” That is what Rapid City is hoping to hash out specifically with municipal policy. This builds off the platform of SB135, hoping to fill in the gaps Shelton refers to with specifics relating to size and resource consumption of the data center. Jessica Olson is the city planning manager. “They also gave the city the ability to limit, prohibit, or other ways regulate data centers," Olson said. "That is what’s we’re talking about doing today, for ten megawatts or greater.” Below is the handout given to survey takers with details on scope and size of data centers in question and their status under currently drafted policy.

artigo.texto: Residents weigh in on year-long data center pause CHARLOTTE, N.C. – Dozens of people sounding off about whether Charlotte should move forward with data centers in the city. City council hosted a public hearing to extend the data center moratorium. Across the country, conversations about data centers have been getting heated but the discussion at the government center Monday night was subdued. More than 30 residents on both sides of the argument signed up to speak at the hearing. Back in June, the council voted in favor of a data center moratorium that runs out in November. The moratorium temporarily paused any new data center applications or development. This did not stop projects that are already under construction like the large scale data center under construction in University City. The moratorium was supposed to give staff time to research potential ways to regulate data centers and address environmental concerns. The city started a task force and hosted forums for residents to weigh in while working on regulations. More than 100 days later the work isn’t done. “Staff need additional expertise and capacity to develop the tools needed to ensure responsible data center development,” Heather Bolick, Chief Sustainability & Resiliency Officer for City of Charlotte said. “An extension of the moratorium would allow us to develop needed tools.” Some residents encouraged the city to speed up the process of writing regulations for data centers. “We believe that this moratorium is an impractical tool that risks sending the wrong signal about our region’s economic readiness,” Rob Nanfelt, Executive Director of Real Estate and Building Industry Coalition said. “However, since city staff and council require more time to study infrastructure impacts, we firmly believe the path forward lies in collaboration, not exclusion.” Other residents say the city cannot afford to rush the process to regulate data centers. “The purpose of a moratorium is not to stop progress; is to create the space for informed progress,” Rev Dr Janet Garner Mullins, Charlotte resident said. “Tonight is not about whether data centers belong in Charlotte. It’s about whether or not Charlotte has done enough homework before writing rules that would shape our future.” Some councilmembers suggested city staff research what other cities are doing to regulate data centers. Council will vote on whether to extend the moratorium at the October 22nd meeting. If passed the action would extend the moratorium until October of 2027.

artigo.texto: The flagship seven-seater is BYD’s first vehicle in Europe to feature its second-generation batteries and Flash Charging tech, delivering over 400 miles of range. BYD launches new flagship Atto 8 in Europe “BYD is all about turning intelligence into reality,” Stella Li, the company’s executive vice president, said on Monday. The Atto 8 is the “perfect example,” Li added, featuring its latest breakthrough tech, including its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging system. Introduced at the Paris Auto Show, the flagship SUV is the first BYD vehicle to feature its Flash Charging system, enabling it to recharge just as fast as filling up at the gas station. It takes just five minutes to charge from 10% to 80%. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. According to BYD, that’s about a third of the time rival SUVs take to go from 10% to 80%. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it requires only 12 minutes for the vehicle’s battery to recharge from 20% to 97%. Measuring 5,040 mm long, 1,996 mm wide, and 1,760 mm tall, the Atto 8 is about the size of other full-size electric SUVs, such as the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. BYD’s flagship SUV comes in two all-electric variants with the choice of rear- and all-wheel-drive powertrains. The Design RWD model has a single rear motor producing 456 hp (340 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD said delivers a 0 to 62 mph time of eight seconds. Powered by a 115 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, the Atto 8 offers an impressive WLTP range of up to 405 miles (600+ km). For example, BYD said the flagship SUV offers enough electric range to drive from London to Edinburgh. The Atto 8 Excellence AWD, on the other hand, adds a front electric motor for a combined output of 764 hp (570 kW) and 572 lb-ft (775 Nm) of torque. The added power delivers a sports-car-rivaling 0- 62 mph acceleration time of 4.6 seconds and a WLTP range of 374 miles. Inside, natural light fills the spacious cabin thanks to a 2.39m2 panoramic glass roof. Both Atto 8 variants have a 10.25″ digital instrument cluster, a 26″ head-up display, and a 15.6″ central infotainment touchscreen with Google Built-in. BYD said the Atto 8 is specifically tailored for those looking for a “zero compromise” seven-seat SUV. The front seats and outer seats of the middle row feature heating, ventilation, and massage functions. Rear passengers get their own air-conditioning control panel. All seats are upholstered in genuine leather. The Design RWD model features a 10-speaker sound system, while the Excellence AWD gains a 21-speaker DiSound audio system, plus an added front refrigerator. With the second and third rows folded, the Atto 8 offers up to 1,960L capacity. Even with all three rows up, the full-size SUV offers 270L of luggage space. Plus, there’s a 136L frunk (front trunk). BYD said dealers in Europe will begin selling the Atto 8 in the first quarter of 2027. Prices have yet to be announced, but given it will be positioned above the Ti 7, a plug-in hybrid seven-seat SUV, it will likely start at slightly over £47,995 ($65,000) on the road in the UK. In Europe, BYD currently sells the Tang, an electric seven-seat SUV. In Germany, the BYD Tang typically starts at €75,000 ($84,000), but it’s currently on sale for €47,990 ($54,000).

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center 14 de outubro de 2026, às 03:42 SAN JOSE, Califórnia, 14 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), anunciou hoje um portfólio expandido de sistemas, racks e trocadores de calor de porta traseira (RDHx) certificados como Open Compute Project Accepted(TM). Com o suporte do DCBBS, o portfólio de soluções pode ser incorporado em implantações completas de ponta a ponta, em escala de rack e cluster. “O boom da IA redefine a forma como os data centers são projetados, construídos e implementados, e a Supermicro lidera essa transformação com o DCBBS”, disse Charles Liang, presidente e CEO da Supermicro. “Ao integrar computação, redes, energia, refrigeração avançada, software e serviços em soluções validadas em escala de rack, ajudamos os clientes a simplificar a complexidade e acelerar o caminho da inovação até a produção. O DCBBS possibilita que os clientes reduzam o TTM e o TTO ao oferecer infraestrutura essencial de IA de forma mais rápida e eficiente.” As soluções OCP da Supermicro já estão disponíveis; clique aqui para saber mais. Ao aproveitar as melhores práticas da comunidade OCP e o design e serviços do DCBBS, os operadores de data centers podem aumentar a densidade de computação e a eficiência energética para cargas de trabalho de IA e HPC com base em uma infraestrutura aberta e validada em escala de rack — desde sistemas e barras de distribuição até o resfriamento em nível de rack e de data centers — para implementar soluções de alta densidade de forma mais eficiente e acelerar o tempo de lançamento no mercado (TTM) e o tempo de operação (TTO). “Os clientes precisam de uma infraestrutura aberta e flexível que possa ser dimensionada de acordo com as demandas em rápida evolução da IA, ao mesmo tempo que se adapte à realidade de seus data centers”, disse Dirk Van Slyke, vice-presidente de Marketing da OCP. “Ao reunir sistemas, racks, energia e refrigeração aceitos pelo OCP em soluções validadas em escala de rack, a Supermicro ajuda os clientes a simplificar a integração, maximizar a capacidade e a eficiência das instalações e acelerar a implantação da infraestrutura de IA de produção.” Os racks ORv3 e ORW substituem as fontes de alimentação e os cabos individuais por servidor por uma barra de distribuição CC centralizada de 48 V, permitindo que os clientes otimizem seus sistemas de CPU e GPU para racks de computação de maior densidade. Essa densidade é ainda mais reforçada pelo sistema de resfriamento líquido DLC-2 Direct-to-Chip da Supermicro, que remove o calor de forma mais eficiente de CPUs, GPUs e outros componentes críticos, enquanto o calor residual pode ser removido do rack por meio de unidades de resfriamento ORv3 RDHx especialmente desenvolvidas, sem a necessidade de adaptações adicionais nos sistemas de ar-condicionado do data center. As unidades RDHx da Supermicro podem ser montadas na parte traseira de racks ORv3 e ORW, removendo o calor residual do ar de exaustão dos servidores antes que ele entre na sala do data center. O portfólio abrange capacidades de refrigeração de 10 kW a 120 kW, oferecendo aos operadores uma maneira prática de aumentar a densidade de racks tanto em novas instalações de IA quanto em data centers existentes. Os modelos alimentados por corrente contínua conectam-se à barra de distribuição do rack para reduzir a quantidade de cabos, enquanto os designs incluem ventiladores redundantes N+1 para garantir o tempo de atividade e um sistema anticondensação inteligente para evitar danos causados pela umidade a outros componentes dentro do rack. Os operadores podem monitorar e gerenciar todo o portfólio de componentes DCBBS, por meio do SuperCloud Composer®, utilizando protocolos padrão do setor. Além disso, os softwares da Supermicro, como o SuperCloud Director, o SuperCloud Automation Assistant e o SuperCloud Developer Console, possibilitam que as empresas gerenciem e operacionalizem todos os aspectos das modernas fábricas de IA, centros de dados corporativos e infraestrutura NeoCloud, por meio de uma solução unificada de controle de software. Como parte do portfólio do DCBBS, a Supermicro também oferece um portfólio abrangente de soluções de rede para IA, que variam de switches Ethernet 800G e 1.6T com refrigeração a ar ou líquida, incluindo plataformas Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) de última geração baseadas no silício de comutação Broadcom Tomahawk 6, otimizadas para racks EIA ou ORv3. O sistema operacional de rede SONiC Advanced da Supermicro Enterprise oferece aos clientes a flexibilidade de selecionar a arquitetura de rede que melhor atenda às suas necessidades de desempenho, energia, escalabilidade e implantação, à medida que a IA e os ambientes de data center de grande escala continuam a evoluir. A linha Supermicro DCBBS também incluirá sistemas de switches NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics, os primeiros switches Ethernet coembalados com SerDes de 200 Gb/s. Baseada no ASIC Ethernet NVIDIA Spectrum-6 de 102,4 Tb/s, a tecnologia Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics oferece eficiência energética 5 vezes superior, MTBI 10 vezes maior, tempo de atividade 5 vezes mais longo para aplicações de IA e tempo de implementação 1,3 vezes mais rápido, em comparação com redes baseadas em transceptores plugáveis. A tecnologia Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics já está em produção. Visão geral do portfólio: o amplo portfólio de soluções da Supermicro incorpora muitos padrões baseados na comunidade, o que permite que data centers mais rápidos e otimizados sejam colocados em operação mais rapidamente. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Flex adiciona módulos de IA fabricados em fábrica ao portfólio de data centers modulares Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Em 12 de outubro de 2026, a Flex anunciou um portfólio ampliado de soluções modulares pré-fabricadas para data centers, projetadas para acelerar a implantação de fábricas de IA de próxima geração. O portfólio inclui os novos Axiom AI Modules, que integram energia, computação de alta densidade e resfriamento líquido avançado em sistemas fabricados em fábrica, que, segundo a Flex, podem reduzir os prazos de implantação em até 50% em comparação com a construção tradicional. O portfólio ampliado faz parte do segmento de Infraestrutura de Nuvem e Energia da Flex, que a empresa planeja separar e transformar na Axiom Solutions International, Inc., uma empresa independente de capital aberto, no primeiro trimestre do ano-calendário de 2027. A Flex afirmou que, à medida que a infraestrutura de IA cresce em escala e densidade de potência, os operadores de data centers enfrentam complexidade cada vez maior na distribuição de energia, no resfriamento, na integração da computação e na implantação. Chris Butler, que deverá ocupar o cargo de diretor de tecnologia e estratégia da Axiom, afirmou que atender a essa demanda em escala exige mais do que melhorias incrementais. Em vez disso, descreveu uma abordagem em nível de sistema que combina tecnologias de energia, computação e resfriamento com manufatura avançada para simplificar a integração, acelerar a implantação e fornecer fábricas de IA em escala. Por dentro dos Axiom AI Modules Segundo o comunicado, os módulos integram componentes essenciais da infraestrutura de IA em três categorias. Um rack de energia de 800 VDC oferece conversão e distribuição de energia de alta eficiência para a infraestrutura de IA de 800 VDC de próxima geração e a computação de alta densidade. Unidades avançadas de distribuição de resfriamento fornecem resfriamento líquido para controlar o calor gerado por cargas de trabalho de IA que consomem muita energia, enquanto racks de TI de alta densidade integram servidores de IA, redes e interconexões de alta velocidade para dar suporte à computação de IA de próxima geração em escala. A Flex afirmou que transferir a integração de infraestruturas complexas do local do data center para um ambiente de fábrica controlado permite montar, integrar e testar os módulos em paralelo ao desenvolvimento do local, reduzindo a complexidade no local e ajudando os clientes a disponibilizar capacidade de IA mais rapidamente. Uma página de recursos da Flex publicada em 12 de outubro de 2026 informa que os módulos são pré-fabricados e comissionados em um ambiente de fábrica controlado, com racks de TI e a infraestrutura de suporte essencial integrados em um único sistema antes do envio. Os módulos incluem estruturas de corredores, unidades de distribuição de líquido refrigerante, redes secundárias de fluidos, painéis de energia remotos, controles, sistemas de distribuição elétrica, sistemas de gerenciamento da qualidade da água e componentes de segurança e detecção de vazamentos. Prazos de implantação estimados A página de recursos apresenta uma comparação estimada entre a implantação modular pré-fabricada e a construção tradicional com estrutura montada no local para um projeto de fábrica de IA, tomando como referência os 18 meses, ou 78 semanas, da construção tradicional. Nesse modelo, afirmou a Flex, os Axiom AI Modules podem reduzir os prazos de implantação em até 50%, de 78 semanas para apenas 39 semanas. A Flex atribuiu a aceleração a cinco fatores: padronização do projeto e integração em fábrica; fabricação em fábrica e construção no local em paralelo; redução da instalação, dos testes e do comissionamento no local; controles integrados e testes no nível dos racks; e menos alterações em etapas avançadas, retrabalho e falhas de instalação em campo. A empresa declarou que os prazos e as economias reais de implantação variam conforme o escopo do projeto, as condições do local, os requisitos de projeto e outros fatores. Presença industrial e separação da Axiom A Flex afirmou que está desenvolvendo ativamente soluções modulares pré-fabricadas para hiperescaladores em suas unidades em todo o mundo, com o apoio de mais de três milhões de pés quadrados de capacidade dedicada à fabricação de infraestrutura de data centers nos Estados Unidos. Em conexão com a separação proposta, Flex apresentou à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC), em 5 de outubro de 2026, uma declaração de procuração no formulário Schedule 14A. A declaração de procuração foi enviada ou divulgada por outros meios aos acionistas para solicitar sua aprovação das propostas relacionadas à cisão. A declaração de registro da Axiom no formulário Form 10, referente às suas ações ordinárias, foi apresentada à SEC em 15 de setembro de 2026. Em um comunicado separado, de 5 de outubro de 2026, a Flex informou que havia firmado um acordo para vender US$ 2,0 bilhões em ações preferenciais conversíveis Série A da Axiom a fundos afiliados à General Catalyst e à Koch Equity Development, além de coinvestidores, com um valor empresarial inicial de US$ 37,5 bilhões para a Axiom. Revathi Advaithi, CEO da Flex e futura CEO da Axiom, afirmou que o investimento “fornece financiamento por meio de capital próprio para nossa aquisição da EPC Power, anunciada recentemente, e permitirá que a Axiom tenha um balanço sólido enquanto nos preparamos para nos estabelecer como uma empresa independente de capital aberto”. As ações preferenciais conversíveis pagam dividendos em dinheiro de 10,0% ao ano antes da separação. Depois dela, a taxa cai para 6,0% ao ano se pagos em dinheiro ou 7,0% ao ano se pagos na forma de dividendos não pecuniários, sujeita a aumentos após o quinto aniversário da separação e a certos outros ajustes. A General Catalyst terá o direito de indicar um diretor para o conselho da Axiom após a conclusão da separaç

artigo.texto: No último mês, em conversa com o líder de uma indústria intensiva em energia, ele se mostrou surpreso porque vinha conversando com outros líderes de setores relevantes da economia real e encontrava, na maioria deles, pouco conhecimento e nenhuma ação sobre a precificação de carbono em andamento no Brasil. O assunto já tem lei, tem cronograma e terá consequência direta no caixa de quem estiver no rol de regulados. Mesmo assim, ainda está longe da pauta de nossas lideranças. Pouco depois, a cena foi diferente, mas dizia o mesmo. Em uma conversa sobre carbono e questões de competitividade, uma liderança de inovação de um grupo multinacional pontuou: “o Brasil tem que fazer isso direito”, ao que eu respondi: “Quem é o Brasil?” Pergunto a você que lê esta coluna e atua em um setor da economia real: quem é o Brasil que deve agir proativamente para que nosso framework regulatório de precificação de carbono seja redigido com adequação técnica, visão prática para assegurar que seja exequível, cronograma compatível e incentivos econômico-financeiros apropriados? Quem é o Brasil que deve agir proativamente para materializar nossa vantagem comparativa (em termos de disponibilidade de capital natural e de matriz elétrica) em competitiva para prosperarmos econômica e socialmente neste novo cenário de mundo em 2026? Na minha opinião, o “Brasil” somos nós, a economia real que emprega, emite gases de efeito estufa, depende de água, de solo, de clima estável, gera PIB. Nossos reguladores escrevem as normas, mas a eficácia delas será diretamente proporcional a quanto a economia real conseguirá (ou quererá) colocar em prática. Conteúdo técnico, ritmo, viabilidade prática e incentivos devem ser resultado de trabalho colaborativo de alta qualidade entre reguladores e regulados. Evolução reativa: a falta do foresight estratégico Amy Webb, futurista e CEO do Future Today Strategy Group, publicou uma reflexão que descreve com precisão o que vejo na agenda da liderança brasileira quando os temas são clima e natureza. Os CEOs descrevem a própria empresa como “adaptativa”, evoluindo de forma reativa: a empresa só muda depois que a pressão chega e a seleção natural faz o resto. Não há foresight estratégico. O argumento central dela me interessa por uma razão prática. Quem enxerga uma restrição se formando cedo, nos sinais fracos, nos rascunhos regulatórios, nos movimentos de concorrentes e de financiadores, ganha algo raro: a possibilidade de contribuir para essa inovação e de escolher entre várias saídas. Quem espera a pressão chegar, no caso, a regulamentação de carbono ser publicada, tem que cumprir (ou se aventurar no judiciário brasileiro). Interessante também é a lista de desculpas que ela ouve, como “esperar para ver qual padrão vence, achar que o conselho jamais aprovaria, ter prontidão para implementar ou ter feito um piloto”. Quando o tema é clima e natureza, com frequência ouço variações dessas frases em conversas com lideranças. Sinais evidentes A precificação de carbono está quase passando do ponto de precisar de foresight estratégico para se materializar como pressão instalada. O mundo já precificou ou está precificando carbono. Mecanismo de ajuste de carbono na fronteira da União Europeia, o CBAM, começou a produzir plenos efeitos desde janeiro deste ano. Já a lei antidesmatamento está prevista para entrar em vigor a partir de 1º de janeiro de 2027. Fundos de pensão, a exemplo do NBIM e do Nest, demandam a incorporação da avaliação de riscos e oportunidades de clima e natureza nas decisões de alocação de capital. No Brasil, nossos bancos estão sujeitos a regulação de clima e natureza desde 2021, com implementação gradual e atualizações, não apenas para refinar dados e quantificá-los, mas também para incorporar diretrizes de reporte financeiro de sustentabilidade e clima padronizadas globalmente. As seguradoras estão no mesmo caminho, com regulação para gerenciamento de riscos e oportunidades de clima e natureza desde 2022 e recente consulta para atualização visando harmonização do disclosure com referidos padrões globais. Especificamente para a regulamentação do mercado de carbono aplicável às indústrias, temos cronograma previsto em lei, que demanda conclusão em dezembro de 2026, e cronograma do Executivo que vem sendo cumprido. Por que sair da evolução reativa Na lógica da Amy Webb, a empresa que se diz adaptativa tem uma única tentativa diante do ambiente e o ambiente decide o resultado. O foresight estratégico permite rodar essa extinção como simulação, antes de vivê-la no resultado da companhia. Para a economia real brasileira, a janela dessa simulação é agora, porque as regras de precificação de carbono ainda estão sendo escritas. Na minha perspectiva, a precificação de carbono altera a estrutura de custos, o acesso a capital, a relação com a cadeia de valor (clientes e fornecedores) e a competitividade na exportação. Quem avalia antecipadamente esses efeitos decide estratégia, investimento, contrato e portfólio com várias opções à mesa. Quem cruza os braços e aguarda a regulamentação, escolhe entre compliance ou litígio. O ciclo de investimento (capex) de uma indústria intensiva em energia é longo, uma decisão de investimento tomada hoje carrega o custo de carbono de décadas. Isso importa a dois públicos: a economia real que compõe o setor regulado e todos aqueles que compõem a cadeia de valor dos regulados. O custo do carbono, uma vez precificado no regulado, impactará a cadeia nos contratos, preços e critérios de compra e venda. A mesma lógica vale para a natureza: a lei antidesmatamento da Europa, citada acima, tende a chegar à cadeia dos exportadores brasileiros. Sair da inércia exige líderes capazes de enxergar o valor do foresight como ferramenta de gestão, com rotina, métrica e responsabilidade. Aplicando essa realidade para nossa regulamentação de carbono em andamento, isso significa entender: inventário de emissões, intensidade por produto e qualidade do dado; cenários de preço, aborda

artigo.texto: - The BRICS Business Council has proposed a voluntary carbon market framework for agriculture and nature-based solutions, with farmers positioned to receive most credit-sale proceeds. - The plan calls for shared carbon accounting standards, digital monitoring and links to existing international carbon registries. - Projects in India involving rice cultivation and soil carbon illustrate how carbon-credit revenue could support more sustainable farming practices. Intergovernmental organization BRICS, bringing together eleven major emerging markets and developing countries of the world, has proposed a framework for agricultural carbon credits intended to channel climate finance directly to farmers while expanding the supply of nature-based credits available to corporate buyers. The proposal was presented by the bloc’s Agribusiness Working Group at the BRICS Business Council’s annual meeting in New Delhi, as reported by India’s The Economic Times. The council included the recommendations in its annual report, which was submitted to BRICS leaders at the closing ceremony of the group’s 18th summit. In addition to the five original member states, namely Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, six new members have joined in recent years: Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The proposed BRICS voluntary carbon market would cover agriculture and nature-based solutions. It would remain open to domestic and international buyers and connect with established voluntary carbon registries, rather than operate as a separate system. The framework also calls for a common carbon classification system across member countries, allowing carbon sequestered through farming practices to be measured and credited on comparable terms. A shared digital platform for monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) would aim to reduce the costs that have made carbon markets difficult for smallholder farmers to access. Indian Projects Offer A Potential Model Under the proposal, farmers, farmer organizations and Indigenous communities would be the primary beneficiaries, receiving most proceeds from credit sales. Companies seeking to address emissions and financial institutions developing green portfolios would provide buyer demand, while governments could use the system to support national climate commitments and attract green finance. Existing projects in India offer examples of how the approach could work. Google has agreed to buy 1 million credits over four years from Bengaluru-based Mitti Labs, supporting changes in irrigation practices among more than 70,000 smallholder rice farmers across three states. The project aims to cut methane emissions by about half and water use by nearly 40%. Relevant: Google To Buy 1M Rice Methane Carbon Credits From India’s Mitti Labs The proposal’s wider ambitions face a practical challenge: making carbon measurement and verification affordable across fragmented agricultural landholdings. Pilot projects between BRICS members are intended to test compatibility between systems before broader implementation. The framework’s success will depend on whether credit revenue reaches farmers promptly while maintaining credible verification and affordable participation. artigo.texto: Chinese battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Company Limited (CATL) announced that it has signed a new long-term strategic cooperation agreement with local automaker Seres Group, strengthening their existing long-term partnership. CATL confirmed that since Seres launched the Aito brand, all Aito models have been equipped with CATL batteries, with cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million units to date. The two companies have now agreed to deepen strategic collaboration across three key areas: Production Capacity Expansion: the two companies plan to accelerate the implementation of Phase 2 of the 'Plant in Plant' project at Seres' manufacturing hub in Chongqing, which involves adding 10–12 GWh of annual battery production capacity, bringing total battery production capacity to over 20 GWh. Supercharging and Energy Replenishment Ecosystem: CATL and Seres will focus on expanding supercharging networks and battery services, creating a full-lifecycle service system to further enhance the user experience. Global Market Development: the two companies also plan to work together to explore overseas markets, including in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, bringing "high-quality products and services" to more global customers and supporting the transition to intelligent electric mobility in key markets. "CATL, Seres strengthen their long-term battery partnership" was originally created and published by Just Auto, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: The California Energy Commission will revise and recirculate its environmental review of a proposed 300-megawatt battery energy storage project near Vacaville after determining that significant new information requires another round of public review. The announcement is a development in the state’s review of the proposed Corby Battery Energy Storage System, which drew more than five hours of public comment at a Sept. 1 hearing in Vacaville. Local officials and residents urged the commission to reject the project, citing concerns about fire safety, groundwater contamination, agricultural land and the facility’s proximity to future development. In an Oct. 7 update to the Solano County Board of Supervisors, Deputy County Counsel Holly E. Tokar said the commission determined that the project’s Staff Assessment/Draft Environmental Impact Report requires “significant new information” and will be recirculated at a future date for another 60-day public comment period. Tokar said the county’s comments may have contributed to the commission’s determination and told the Board the continued review is good news. “In my view, this is the best-case scenario at this stage in the process,” she wrote. “We will now wait to see what changes the CEC makes to its DEIR, recommendation, and proposed conditions of approval, and plan to submit another set of comments once the next iteration of the Draft EIR is released.” Officials will also monitor proposed regulatory changes to the state’s permitting process for energy storage projects, Tokar said. The commission has scheduled a remote workshop for Nov. 2 to discuss proposed changes to the process established under Assembly Bill 205. Written comments on the proposed regulatory changes are due Nov. 10. The next version of the Corby project’s environmental review, along with any revised recommendations and proposed approval conditions, will help determine how the state proceeds with the application. The commission has not announced a new timeline for its decision on the project. The proposed project would occupy approximately 40 acres of unincorporated land near Kilkenny and Byrnes roads, about 250 feet southeast of Vacaville’s jurisdictional boundary and roughly five miles northeast of downtown. The facility would be capable of storing up to 1,200 megawatt-hours of electricity. Plans include battery units, a project substation, inverters, fencing, a sound barrier, roads, drainage facilities, and other infrastructure. At the Sept. 1 hearing, Vacaville Mayor John Carli and other local officials urged the commission to reject the project at the proposed location, citing agricultural land preservation and the city’s plans for future residential and commercial growth. Local officials emphasized that they support battery energy storage as a technology but oppose placing a large-scale facility on the Corby site. Solano County Supervisor Mitch Mashburn pointed to the county’s battery energy storage ordinance and Measure T, the voter-approved orderly growth regulation, arguing that state permitting authority does not erase the importance of local land-use policies. Residents also raised concerns about lithium-ion battery fires, potential groundwater contamination, noise, risks to nearby homes and the facility’s proximity to future development. Some questioned the environmental report’s analysis of potential impacts on groundwater resources used by nearby communities and agricultural operations.

artigo.texto: To keep up with artificial intelligence, Illinois needs batteries big enough to keep its air conditioners running on hot summer nights and to replenish its electrical grid during winter storms lasting for days. The state took a step in this direction Monday when Richardson Electronics said it would expand production of commercial-scale storage batteries at its factory in La Fox, a suburb west of Chicago. Richardson, a diversified manufacturer of power products, expects to sell batteries worldwide. But company officials say they’ll deploy many of their batteries in Illinois because of the state’s hefty tax incentives for renewable power and for batteries that make solar and wind less intermittent. When layered on top of each other, Illinois and federal tax incentives add up to almost the entire cost of one of Richardson’s storage batteries, said Scott DuBois, director of the company’s storage operations. The battery, which the company plans to build at its La Fox site next summer, would be able to store 5 megawatts of power and will cost about $3 million. It will be the largest battery ever connected to the grid by an Illinois company, Richardson officials said. Without more batteries, Illinois will be even more reliant on dirty, expensive electricity imports from other states and more likely to delay the natural gas power plant closures it’s planned for years to clean the air. “We are depending on out-of-state resources to essentially keep the lights on,” said Matthew Tomc, vice president of regulatory policy and energy supply for Ameren, which serves customers in downstate Illinois. “There are many states building new generation, but it’s not built yet. So there are reliability issues first and foremost,” Tomc said. “And it raises the risk that you have price spikes seasonally, namely in the summer, right when you’re trying to meet those capacity requirements.” Tomc’s not alone in sounding the alarm. PJM Interconnection, the regional grid that includes northern Illinois, 12 other states and the District of Columbia, could face 13 days of service interruptions a year by 2030 in a worst-case scenario, Pennsylvania regulators said last month. PJM’s longstanding goal has been to have just one day of service interruptions every 10 years. Prices already are climbing. Commonwealth Edison customers in northern Illinois pay an average residential bill of $141 per month, according to Heatmap News and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. That’s up just 4% since 2021, partly because PJM imposed price caps last year. Ameren customers downstate pay an average of $224, up 51% in five years. The downstate area is part of the Midwest Independent System Operator grid or MISO, which also serves 14 other states from Mississippi to North Dakota as well as Manitoba. To blunt further increases, Richardson and its supplier Gotion, a Chinese-owned company with a $2 billion factory in Manteno, Illinois, start with 4,500 battery cells, each about the size of a college textbook. For their biggest batteries, they will then stack, weld and seal the battery cells, cooling equipment and electronic controls inside a metal box resembling a 20-foot shipping container. DuBois wouldn’t give a precise estimate for how big Richardson’s battery business will get. But he said he expects exponential growth. Gil Quinones, ComEd’s chief executive, is thinking big, too. “If the majority of our residential, commercial and industrial customers put in batteries, that’s going to be a big win for the state,” Quinones said. “It could increase the capacity utilization for the grid we’ve already paid for, and have a chance to really put downward pressure on prices for everybody,” Quinones said. Because Richardson sees itself as an engineering specialist rather than a high-volume manufacturer, it will focus on customized storage systems for so-called microgrids. These are clusters of solar and wind operators that can either supply electricity directly to nearby users or buy and sell power as a group into the regional grid. One of the company’s first orders, for example, came from a microgrid serving seven remote communities in Alaska. Illinois needs more batteries to unlock the full potential of its growing wind and solar capabilities, according to consultants to the Illinois Power Agency and other state regulators in a report last month. Illinois will need 50 gigawatts of installed solar and wind capacity by 2050 to get close to its goal of using only non-carbon sources to generate electricity by then, the agencies said. But regional grid operators still regard wind and solar as too intermittent. As a result, the state will be able to count only about 6 gigawatts of its renewable output as the baseload power electricity grids need to operate around the clock. With additional batteries, Illinois could make its solar panels more productive and reliable by, for example, storing the power they generate during the day and then pumping it into the grid or nearby homes and businesses after the sun goes down. In addition to more batteries, the Ameren service area downstate will need 9 gigawatts of out-of-state imports by 2045, according to the Sept. 24 consultant report to the IPA. That’s more than half the Ameren area’s total requirement of 16 gigawatts of round-the-clock power in 2045. The ComEd service area will need 4 gigawatts of out-of-state imports, or about 13% of its baseload requirement. The imports will include power produced by new natural gas plants that Illinois ratepayers will help build in other states. Illinois can’t build these plants because of the state’s clean air rules. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it has amended the At-the-Market ("ATM") Issuance Sales Agreement (the "Agreement"), dated June 18, 2026, by and between the Company and Spartan Capital Securities, LLC, as sales agent (the "Agent"), reducing the aggregate amount that may be sold pursuant to the Agreement from Three Hundred Million Dollars ($300,000,000) in shares of the Company's Class A common stock, par value $0.001 per share (the "Common Stock") to One Hundred Million Dollars ($100,000,000), including the shares of Common Stock that have been sold pursuant to the Agreement through an amendment to the Agreement (the "Amendment"). The Company has sold 121,827,841 shares of Common Stock and raised approximately $49.8 million in gross proceeds, or approximately $0.41 per share, pursuant to the ATM. "Based on our current capital plans, we do not believe the additional $200 million of ATM capacity is currently necessary," said Will Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data. "Reducing the size of the ATM reflects our commitment to disciplined capital management while preserving financial flexibility to support our AI data center strategy. We believe that our equity is significantly undervalued and this $200 million reduction will limit the dilution to our equity and is in the best interests of our stockholders. Our focus remains on deploying capital prudently and building long-term value through the buildout of our Michigan AI data center (the "Facility") to initially support the 20 megawatts of critical compute capacity of our neocloud customer. It is our intention to augment the Facility buildout costs with debt financing and preliminary estimates on the existing buildout indicate that the Facility will support project debt financing between $100 million to $150 million." The Company may evaluate capital markets options in the future as appropriate and in the best interests of the Company and its stockholders. This press release shall not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy, nor shall there be any sale of shares of the Common Stock in any state or other jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or other jurisdiction. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. artigo.texto: From pressures facing Iowa farmers to the costs of major industrial projects, Iowa’s U.S. Senate candidates outlined their priorities and challenged each other’s records in their second and last debate Tuesday night. Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, D-Council Bluffs, and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, faced off in their second debate for U.S. Senate hosted by WHO-13 in Des Moines. The candidates continued to highlight hot button issues, discussing the importance of agriculture and economic developments throughout the state. The debate also covered immigration enforcement, rural healthcare, and Social Security with the candidates offering differing approaches to border security, access to care, and retirement benefits. Questions about transgender athletes in women’s sports and congressional stock ownership prompted further exchanges, alongside criticism of each other’s voting records and personal finances. On agriculture and economic development, the candidates debated how to expand markets for Iowa farmers and attract investment while protecting taxpayers from the costs and risks of major projects. Agriculture continues to be a top priority The candidates offered differing views on tariffs and farmland ownership, with both emphasizing the need to support Iowa farmers. Turek criticized the administration’s tariffs and said they have hurt farmers by limiting markets and increasing costs. He supports targeted tariffs to protect American manufacturing but opposed those he said burden agriculture and small businesses. “Our farmers rely on open markets and free trade more than any other group,” he said. He also called for year-round E-15 sales, mandatory out-of-origin labeling, and a federal right-to-repair law allowing farmers to repair their equipment. He urged Congress to pass a farm bill before adjourning. Hinson defended tariffs as a tool to counter unfair trade practices while acknowledging farmers’ uncertainty. She said she has raised their concerns directly with President Donald Trump and pointed to agricultural exports and trade negotiations as signs of progress. “Nobody loves tariffs, but what I like even less is an unlevel playing field for Americans and for our farmers,” she said. Hinson emphasized preventing foreign adversaries from purchasing agricultural land, particularly near sensitive military sites. Turek agreed restrictions on foreign ownership were important but said large corporations posed the greater concern, pointing to pressures facing small family farms. Data centers, industrial projects raise economic questions Both candidates opposed a federal moratorium on new data centers but differed on how to oversee the projects and who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support them. Turek demanded no further tax breaks for multinational tech firms and suggested requiring closed-loop water circuits that reuse water to reduce data centers’ consumption of local water supplies. “We should be doing what we can to protect Iowa and to protect the tax rates here,” he said. He opposed using taxpayer funds for the reopening of the Duane Arnold nuclear plant — a facility near Palo, northwest of Cedar Rapids, that shut down in 2020 — if most energy is diverted to Google. Hinson, on the other hand, maintained that data center regulation should occur at the local level rather than through a federal moratorium and supports reopening Duane Arnold to help meet rising electricity demand. “It is really critical that we have enough energy production in this country to handle the necessary needs of whether it’s a data center or another big energy consumer,” she said. “We want to reinvigorate American manufacturing in this country.” Questions about taxpayer protections extended to the proposed steel plant in southeast Iowa, with both candidates saying Iowans should not bear infrastructure costs if the project falls through. Turek said he supported the $15 billion Masabi Metallics steel plant’s job potential but questions the risks associated with a $770 million federal loan given the company’s history of bankruptcy. He argued companies should cover their own infrastructure. “There’s no upfront state money,” he said. “The incentives are only there if they provide the actual jobs and metrics achieved.” Hinson said she views the plant as critical for national security and the domestic steel supply chain, though she agrees taxpayers should not be held liable if the project fails or is scaled back. “We need definite accountability measures built in,” Hinson said. “And I think what’s important about the policies we’ve put into place is that they are going to supercharge potential future investments just like this one.”

artigo.texto: LOGAN, Utah — Before a crowd here at Utah State University on Tuesday night, Republican Congressman Blake Moore and Democratic challenger Peter Crosby debated a number of big issues facing the newly-formed Second Congressional District. It was a collegial, policy-focused debate where they presented their views for northern Utah. Both were quizzed on data centers, a particularly hot topic in the district, where celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary's plans for a massive data center have sparked significant public protest. Both candidates agreed local control is best. "Data centers are a part of our immediate future, right? There's no question. We're all using cellphones. We're all, you know, doing some type of AI utilization and whatnot, but the issue is, we cannot have this kind of situation take over the way that it did and that people have to be brought along," Moore said, pointing to what was being done on a congressional level. "There's good, strong legislation that should have passed in the Senate, but it didn't, to make sure electricity costs don't go up for residents and the Department of Defense is doing a unique thing where they're going to start to use more of their resources and their land in a more productive way, which is a good change that's happening." Crosby said he had been involved in some of the pushback on data centers. "I think as we talk about the future of data centers in Utah specifically, we have to acknowledge that local control is oftentimes being ignored because external pressure coming from the top down is forcing a decision against the will of local residents," he said. "That's inappropriate. I am all for a future where local communities decide whether or not that kind of infrastructure is appropriate for them, and what we have seen in Box Elder is a direct counter to that reality." The two expressed a desire to save the Great Salt Lake, but offered differing viewpoints on water policy. "I don't want the federal government making water policy for the state of Utah," declared Crosby. "I think that's a bad road to head down. The state of Utah has to decide: Are we a state that grows to 10 million people? Are we a state that decides to fully invest in Silicon Slopes? Are we a state that decides to maintain local resiliency in agriculture? We can't have all three." But Moore said he has already been passing legislation to help the lake, though he acknowledged President Trump's pledge of a billion dollars for the lake is unlikely to get through Congress. "We were able to do bite-size projects to help funding the support from different elements of the of the lake that the state is actually leading a lot of the effort and then of course you're seeing the White House now get involved, so it's nice to be able to see a throughput," he said. Crosby was critical of Moore's votes on President Trump's Big, Beautiful Bill. Moore defended his work to mitigate tariffs, even noting that he had removed some of the harsher impacts on a major northern Utah employer. "There is a lot of pain with this and every time that Procter and Gamble has reached out to our office, we've gone and actually successfully been able to mitigate their issues," Moore said. "If I may say, Procter and Gamble, that's great, but none of the small business owners seem to receive the same attention," Crosby countered in a rebuttal. But the candidates both pledged ongoing support for Hill Air Force Base and bolstering northern Utah's aerospace industry. They also supported agriculture, a major industry in the area. The poll commissioned by the Utah Debate Commission that put the two men on stage on Tuesday night shows a closer race than some might like. Voters surveyed had Moore in the lead at 39%, with Crosby close behind at 34%. Nearly 11% of voters remained undecided and third-party candidates took the rest. Speaking to FOX 13 News after the debate, Moore believed voters would stick with him. "We’re confident where we are, we’re going to continue to drive the message home and I look forward to the opportunity to continue on the things I've been working on," he said. Crosby told FOX 13 News after the debate he and volunteers for his campaign would be out engaging voters. artigo.texto: O Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã promove a transformação verde e a redução das emissões. Aumentar a conscientização sobre a redução de emissões, promover práticas ecológicas e o uso eficiente de recursos são tarefas essenciais realizadas pelo Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã para contribuir com o alcance dos objetivos de desenvolvimento sustentável. Integrar a transformação verde nas atividades sindicais. O Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã (VCPTU) desenvolveu recentemente um plano para organizar campanhas de conscientização, treinamentos e workshops com o objetivo de aprimorar o entendimento de dirigentes, membros e trabalhadores do sindicato em relação à redução de emissões, à transição verde e ao desenvolvimento econômico de baixo carbono. O plano visa fortalecer o papel dos sindicatos na promoção de práticas sustentáveis, utilização eficiente de recursos e proteção ambiental, garantindo, ao mesmo tempo, os direitos e interesses dos trabalhadores durante o período de transição. De acordo com as diretrizes do Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã, os sindicatos filiados integrarão a disseminação de informações sobre créditos de carbono, práticas de economia de energia, uso eficiente de recursos e redução de emissões em suas atividades sindicais, adequadas às suas condições específicas. Além disso, promoverão a reutilização, a reciclagem e a redução de resíduos, e incentivarão a aplicação de soluções sustentáveis e ecologicamente corretas para a produção, os negócios e o consumo. Por meio dessas atividades, o Sindicato contribui para a formação de um estilo de vida sustentável, promovendo a produção verde e o consumo de baixo carbono, protegendo o meio ambiente e adaptando-se às mudanças climáticas. A Confederação Vietnamita de Sindicatos (CĐXDVN) também orienta todos os níveis de sindicatos a participarem proativamente, contribuindo com ideias para a construção e o aprimoramento de mecanismos, políticas, leis , programas e projetos relacionados à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, inventários de gases de efeito estufa, desenvolvimento de mercados de carbono, gestão de créditos de carbono, transição verde e proteção da camada de ozônio. Dá-se ênfase ao conteúdo diretamente relacionado aos trabalhadores, contribuindo assim para o aumento da competitividade nacional, a integração proativa na comunidade internacional e a conquista dos objetivos de desenvolvimento verde e sustentável. Você também pode gostar Além disso, o incentivo à participação de entidades econômicas, empresas e trabalhadores na criação, negociação e utilização de créditos de carbono baseia-se em princípios de mercado, transparência, concorrência leal e eficiência. Os créditos de carbono são reconhecidos como uma força motriz para a inovação tecnológica, a melhoria da eficiência energética e de recursos e a promoção do desenvolvimento sustentável. Na promoção da transição verde e da redução das emissões, o Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã enfatiza o papel do sindicato no monitoramento da implementação das diretrizes do Partido, das políticas e leis estatais nessas áreas, bem como no desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono e na garantia da transparência em sua implementação. O monitoramento também se concentra na implementação de políticas e programas que apoiam a transformação tecnológica, a economia de energia, a produção mais limpa e políticas relacionadas. Por meio disso, os sindicatos em todos os níveis compilam e relatam prontamente as questões emergentes, especialmente o impacto da transição verde e da redução de emissões no emprego, na renda, nas condições de trabalho, na segurança e saúde ocupacional e nos direitos e interesses dos trabalhadores. É dada especial atenção aos grupos de trabalhadores que correm o risco de serem afetados pela transição, a fim de abordar prontamente as questões relacionadas aos direitos dos trabalhadores e às condições de trabalho. Paralelamente às suas atividades de monitoramento, o Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã visa integrar a redução de emissões, a utilização eficiente de recursos, a conservação de energia, a economia circular e a adaptação às mudanças climáticas ao movimento "Verde - Limpo - Bonito, Garantindo a Segurança e Saúde Ocupacional" e a outros movimentos de emulação relevantes. Com base nas condições reais, os sindicatos em todos os níveis, unidades e empresas incentivam seus membros e trabalhadores a propor e implementar iniciativas e modelos para economia de energia, uso eficiente de recursos, redução de emissões e proteção ambiental. Essas iniciativas devem estar vinculadas ao objetivo de melhorar as condições de trabalho, prevenir acidentes e riscos e construir uma cultura de segurança no local de trabalho. Identificar, elogiar e replicar iniciativas e modelos práticos e eficazes que sejam adequados às condições de produção e negócios das empresas e às atividades sindicais também recebe atenção, a fim de incentivar soluções com aplicação prática. Além de promover e incentivar práticas sustentáveis, o Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã concentra-se em aprimorar as habilidades de seus dirigentes em diálogo e negociação coletiva. O sindicato também incentiva a inclusão de critérios para a construção de uma cultura de segurança no trabalho na avaliação da qualidade dos acordos coletivos de trabalho, utilizando-os como base para revisar e premiar órgãos, unidades e empresas com bom desempenho em segurança e higiene no trabalho. Outra tarefa é promover a aplicação da tecnologia da informação e da transformação digital na disseminação, gestão, monitoramento e avaliação da segurança e saúde ocupacional. O Sindicato dos Trabalhadores da Construção Civil do Vietnã visa construir gradualmente um banco de dados para orientar e gerir o trabalho, melhorando assim a eficácia da implementação de ativida

artigo.texto: Flex Expands Prefabricated Modular Data Center Portfolio to Accelerate AI Factory Deployment Integrated solutions combine power, compute and cooling to speed deployment by up to 50% News summary - Introduces AI Modules that integrate power, compute and cooling in prefabricated modular solutions to accelerate AI factory deployment by up to 50% - Enables faster deployment of next-generation AI infrastructure through factory-built, integrated systems - Strengthens Flex's Cloud and Power Infrastructure portfolio, which Flex plans to separate into Axiom Solutions International, Inc. (Axiom), in the first quarter of calendar 2027 SAN JOSE, Calif. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Flex (NASDAQ: FLEX) today announced an expanded portfolio of prefabricated modular data center solutions designed to accelerate deployment of next-generation AI factories. The portfolio includes new AI Modules that integrate power, high-density compute and advanced liquid cooling into pre-engineered, factory-built systems, enabling customers to reduce deployment timelines by up to 50% compared with traditional construction approaches. The expanded portfolio is part of Flex's Cloud and Power Infrastructure (CPI) segment, which Flex plans to separate into Axiom, an independent publicly traded company, in the first quarter of calendar 2027. "Meeting the demands of AI infrastructure at scale requires more than incremental improvements. It requires rethinking how power, compute and cooling work together as a system," said Chris Butler, expected Chief Technology and Strategy Officer at Axiom. "Our system-level approach brings these critical technologies together with advanced manufacturing to simplify integration, accelerate deployment and deliver AI factories at scale." As AI infrastructure grows in scale and power density, data center operators face increasing complexity across power delivery, cooling, compute integration and deployment. Addressing these challenges requires a more integrated approach to designing and deploying the critical infrastructure that supports next-generation AI factories. The Axiom AI Modules integrate critical AI infrastructure into pre-engineered, factory-built systems, including: - 800 VDC Power Rack: Delivers high-efficiency power conversion and distribution for next-generation 800 VDC AI infrastructure and high-density compute. - Advanced cooling distribution units (CDUs): Provide liquid cooling to efficiently manage the increasing heat generated by power-intensive AI workloads. - High-density IT racks: Integrate AI servers, networking and high-speed interconnects to support next-generation AI compute at scale. By shifting complex infrastructure integration from the data center site to a controlled factory environment, the Axiom AI Modules are assembled, integrated and tested in parallel with site development. This approach reduces on-site complexity and helps customers bring AI capacity online faster. Flex is actively building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers across its global footprint, including more than three million square feet of dedicated data center infrastructure manufacturing capacity in the U.S. With deep expertise across power, compute, cooling and systems integration, Flex has the scale and capabilities to support rapid AI infrastructure deployment across regions. artigo.texto: SINEXCEL Completes PCS Shipment for 100MW/400MWh Energy Storage Project in Chile VALLENAR , Chile , Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SINEXCEL (300693.SZ) has shipped all StellaON 1250K power conversion systems for RelyEZ Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd.'s 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage project in Chile. The four-hour system in Atacama will charge during lower-demand periods and discharge at peak times, supporting grid flexibility and project returns. On-Schedule Delivery Supports Project Execution Large-scale overseas projects require production, inspection, and shipment schedules to remain closely aligned with on-site construction. SINEXCEL completed the full PCS order on schedule, helping RelyEZ Energy protect the timetable for transport, installation, commissioning, and grid connection. For a project of this scale, delays in a single batch can narrow the construction window. Coordinated delivery reduces uncertainty and helps local teams plan the next stages. StellaON 1250K PCS Built for Atacama's Demanding Conditions Energy equipment in Atacama must operate in an environment that can include high temperatures, dust, and sand. The StellaON 1250K PCS has a maximum efficiency of 99% and a rated-power efficiency of 98.5%. It supports operation from -40°C to 60°C, maintains full power output at 55°C, and has an IP65 protection rating. Maintaining rated output in high temperatures can reduce power derating and the need for additional capacity. Higher conversion efficiency also limits energy losses across repeated charge-discharge cycles, supporting stable operation and long-term returns. Strengthening Local Service Capabilities Across the Americas Following shipment, the project will move into on-site installation and commissioning. SINEXCEL has a dedicated after-sales team in Latin America and seven service centres across the Americas. Technical requests can receive a response within 30 minutes, backed by round-the-clock support and a seven-day spare-parts guarantee. SINEXCEL has deployed more than 17GW of energy storage capacity across over 5,000 projects and works with more than 600 partners in 60+ countries and regions. Following shipment, the Chilean project moves into its on-site delivery phase. SINEXCEL will continue to expand its local operations across Latin America, providing customers with support throughout the project lifecycle. About SINEXCEL Founded in 2007, SINEXCEL is a pioneer in energy storage, EV charging, and power quality solutions. With 17 GW of installed storage, 200,000 EV DC chargers, and nearly 20 million amperes of Active Harmonic Filters deployed, SINEXCEL partners with industry leaders to empower energy freedom. artigo.texto: A aceleração da transformação digital e a demanda por inteligência artificial convertem a infraestrutura de dados em um ativo estratégico. Por Misto Brasil – DF O Brasil consolida sua posição como o principal polo de infraestrutura digital da América Latina, concentrando 71% da capacidade de data centers em construção na região. Segundo dados do relatório Latin America Data Center Report, elaborado pela JLL, o país responde também por 48% da capacidade instalada em operação na América Latina, impulsionado pelo avanço da nuvem e da inteligência artificial. Leia – Senado aprova incentivo a instalação de data centers Leia: o que são data centers? Muita energia e informação A matriz elétrica baseada em fontes renováveis (hidrelétrica, eólica e solar) representa um diferencial competitivo para atração de investimentos globais. No entanto, o funcionamento de estruturas de missão crítica exige sistemas elétricos, climatização e automação integrados para evitar interrupções operacionais. “Um data center precisa ser concebido como um ecossistema integrado. Sistemas elétricos, climatização, automação, conectividade, segurança e prevenção de incêndios devem funcionar de maneira coordenada”, analisa Marco Alberto Silva, CEO do Grupo Engemon. O executivo acrescenta que a sinergia entre engenharia e tecnologia otimiza prazos e custos: “A integração entre engenharia, construção, tecnologia, operação e manutenção permite antecipar interferências, acelerar a implantação e entregar uma infraestrutura mais segura”. - Liderança regional: Concentração de quase metade das operações latino-americanas e expansão de 20% no inventário de colocation. - Vantagem energética: Matriz limpa e adoção de certificações como LEED e ISO atraem projetos focados em metas de descarbonização. - Gargalos estruturais: Desafios de conectividade, formação técnica e segurança regulatória ainda distanciam o país dos polos mundiais. A evolução do setor dependerá da capacidade do mercado em converter abundância energética em capacidade computacional efetiva frente à concorrência internacional.
