artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Announces Plans for up to $33.5 Million in Tokenized Series D Preferred Stock Offering Following 52 consecutive monthly Series D dividend payments, the Company plans to expand access to eligible investors through blockchain-based RWA platforms LAS VEGAS , Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced plans to tokenize up to 1,340,947 shares of its 13.00% Series D Cumulative Redeemable Perpetual Preferred Stock (the "Series D Preferred Stock"), representing approximately $33.5 million in potential gross proceeds at an assumed offering price of $25.00 per share. The Company intends to use the net proceeds primarily to finance the continued development, construction and expansion of its Michigan AI data center campus, including power distribution, cooling systems, utility improvements and customer deployment infrastructure and potentially for working capital purposes. The proposed initiative would be expected to create an additional financing channel for the Company by bringing an established, publicly traded preferred security to eligible investors through digital securities platforms in the United States and international markets. An Established Preferred Security The Series D Preferred Stock trades on the NYSE American under the symbol GPUS PD and carries a 13.00% annual cumulative dividend based on its $25.00 per-share liquidation preference, equivalent to $3.25 annually or approximately $0.2708333 monthly per share. The Company has reported 52 timely consecutive monthly dividend payments since the security was first issued in June 2022. Dividends are payable when declared by the Board of Directors, and historical payments do not guarantee future dividends. The security is perpetual and has no stated maturity. The Company expects the tokens to represent interests in the underlying Series D Preferred Stock, with its economic and legal rights preserved under the final structure. Implementation would be pursued through appropriate securities-market participants, technology providers, custody arrangements and transfer infrastructure, subject to applicable securities laws and jurisdictional restrictions. No specific exchange, trading venue or international listing arrangement has been finalized. Financing Structure and Common Share Considerations The contemplated offering would issue Series D Preferred Stock rather than Class A common stock. Because the Series D Preferred Stock is not convertible into Class A common stock except in extremely limited and exceptional circumstances, the Company does not expect this financing to result in additional Class A common shares at issuance or through ordinary conversion thereafter. This statement relates solely to the contemplated offering and does not preclude future issuances of Class A common stock in other financings or transactions. Additional preferred stock would increase the Company's preferred dividend obligations and liquidation preferences and could reduce cash flow available to the Company and its common stockholders. Management intends to evaluate those obligations against anticipated operating cash flow, existing commitments and capital expenditure requirements. William B. Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data, stated, "Our priority is to secure capital that advances the Michigan campus and supports its long-term development. Tokenization could broaden the investor audience for our established preferred security and add a financing channel as we build our AI infrastructure business. We intend to evaluate this approach with careful attention to its cost, our liquidity needs and the interests of our stockholders." Financial Outlook Supports Evaluation of Series D Financing Hyperscale Data previously announced consolidated financial guidance for the year ending December 31, 2027, projecting revenue of approximately $300 million to $350 million and Adjusted EBITDA of approximately $60 million to $80 million. Management believes its Adjusted EBITDA outlook supports evaluating additional Series D Preferred Stock financing, as anticipated growth in operating profitability could help sustain the associated preferred dividend obligations while funding long-term infrastructure investment. In assessing the amount and timing of any financing, the Company intends to consider expected cash generation, existing obligations, liquidity needs and capital expenditure requirements. The guidance is preliminary and reflects management's expectations regarding future business performance. Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP measure and does not represent cash flow available for preferred dividend payments or assure the Company's ability to pay those dividends. The Company cannot provide a quantitative reconciliation of its projected Adjusted EBITDA to the most directly comparable measure calculated under GAAP, which in this case would be net income or loss, because certain components required to calculate net income or loss cannot presently be reasonably estimated without unreasonable effort. These components include future interest expense, income taxes, depreciation and amortization, stock-based compensation, impairment charges, acquisition-related expenses and changes in the fair value of financial instruments. These items are likely to be material to the Company's future GAAP results. The Company intends to provide further updates on the timing, structure, implementation and distribution arrangements for the proposed offering. There can be no assurance that the offering will be completed, that the full contemplated amount will be raised or that a secondary trading market for the tokenized securities will develop. artigo.texto: Supermicro Expands Integrated Open Compute Project Portfolio to Accelerate Rack-Scale AI Data Center Deployments - Integrated Open Compute Project (OCP) based portfolio spans rack-scale AI/HPC systems, ORv3 and ORW racks, 48V DC power, networking, and liquid cooling solutions to enable higher-density compute in existing and new data centers - Portfolio extends from infrastructure to intelligent operations with DCBBS Coolants, in-rack CDUs, switches, and Supermicro System Management Software Suite for infrastructure management - Supermicro DCBBS brings these OCP-based technologies together into integrated rack-scale solutions, simplifying and speeding deployment across compute, power, networking, and cooling for a faster Time-to-Online (TTO) SAN JOSE, Calif. , Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), an AI, Enterprise, Storage, and 5G/Edge Total IT Solution Provider featuring Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), today announced an expanded portfolio of Open Compute Project Accepted™ systems, racks, and rear door heat exchangers (RDHx). Supported by DCBBS, the solutions portfolio can be incorporated into complete end-to-end rack- and cluster-scale deployments. "The AI boom is redefining how data centers are designed, built, and deployed, and Supermicro is leading this transformation with DCBBS," said Charles Liang, president and CEO of Supermicro. "By integrating compute, networking, power, advanced cooling, software, and services into validated rack-scale solutions, we help customers simplify complexity and accelerate the path from innovation to production. DCBBS enables customers to reduce TTM and TTO by delivering essential AI infrastructure faster and more efficiently." Supermicro's OCP solutions are now available, click here to learn more. By leveraging OCP community best practices and DCBBS design and services, data center operators can increase compute density and energy efficiency for AI and HPC workloads based on an open and validated rack-scale foundation—from systems and busbar to rack-level and data center cooling—to bring high density solutions online more efficiently to accelerate Time-to-Market (TTM) and TTO. "Customers need open, flexible infrastructure that can scale with the rapidly evolving demands of AI while fitting the realities of their data centers," said Dirk Van Slyke, vice president of Marketing, OCP. "By bringing OCP-accepted systems, racks, power and cooling together in validated rack-scale solutions, Supermicro is helping customers simplify integration, maximize facility capacity and efficiency, and accelerate the deployment of production AI infrastructure." The ORv3 and ORW racks replace per-server power supplies and cables with a centralized 48V DC busbar, allowing customers to optimize their CPU and GPU systems for higher density compute racks. This density is further supported by Supermicro's DLC-2 Direct-to-Chip liquid cooling, which removes heat more efficiently from CPUs, GPUs, and other critical components, while residual heat can be removed from the rack by purpose-built ORv3 RDHx's without requiring additional retrofit of data hall air conditioning systems. Supermicro RDHx units can be mounted to the rear of ORv3 and ORW racks and remove residual heat from server exhaust before it enters the data hall. The portfolio spans 10 kW to 120 kW of cooling capacity, giving operators a practical way to increase rack density in both new AI facilities and existing data centers. DC-powered models connect to the rack's busbar to reduce cabling, while designs include N+1 redundant fans to ensure uptime and a smart anti-condensation system to prevent moisture damage to other components inside the rack. Operators can monitor and manage the entire portfolio of DCBBS components, through SuperCloud Composer® using industry-standard protocols. Further, Supermicro's software, such as SuperCloud Director, SuperCloud Automation Assistant, and SuperCloud Developer Console, enables organizations to manage and operationalize all aspects of modern AI factories, enterprise data centers, and NeoCloud infrastructure, through a unified software control solution. As part of DCBBS portfolio, Supermicro also delivers a comprehensive portfolio of AI networking solutions, ranging from air and liquid-cooled 800G and 1.6T Ethernet switches including next-generation Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) platforms built on Broadcom Tomahawk 6 switching silicon, optimized for EIA or ORv3 racks. The Supermicro Enterprise Advanced SONiC Networking Operating System gives customers the flexibility to select the networking architecture that best meets their performance, power, scalability, and deployment requirements as AI and large-scale data center environments continue to evolve. Supermicro DCBBS will also include NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics switch systems, the first co-packaged Ethernet switches with 200Gb/s SerDes. Built on the 102.4 Tb/s NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Ethernet ASIC, Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics delivers 5x better power efficiency, 10x greater MTBI, 5x longer uptime for AI applications and 1.3x faster time to deployment, compared to pluggable transceiver-based networks. Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics is in production now. Data centers have become a central issue in Oklahoma’s midterm elections, with gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei (R) saying he supports them with guardrails, and Democratic nominee Cyndi Munson promising a day-one moratorium. Related Story: Mike Mazzei and Cyndi Munson share their stances on Oklahoma data center development Driven by affordable land, access to power, and growing demand for cloud and AI services, companies ranging from global tech giants to regional providers are expanding their presence in Oklahoma. According to the US Data Center Map, data as of Oct 2026. https://dcmap.us, Oklahoma has: - 64 data center projects overall - 34 operational data centers - 6 data centers under construction - 20 data centers planned - 2 paused data center projects - 2 inactive data centers Below is a running list of data center projects across the state. This article will be updated as new facilities are announced, approved, or completed. Claremore Project Mustang (Approved) Project Mustang is an approved data center development at the Claremore Industrial Park by Beale Infrastructure. Plans call for multiple data center buildings and office space, with power supplied by Grand River Dam Authority and water and wastewater services provided by the City of Claremore. City leaders say the property is already zoned for industrial use and that the developer would pay for required infrastructure upgrades. The Claremore City Council approved plans Monday, May 18, for “Project Mustang.” Claremore City Hall reached standing-room capacity during the meeting, with dozens of people waiting outside and rotating in to comply with fire code limits. Public comment lasted nearly two hours before the council voted on the proposal. Related Story: Claremore approves Project Mustang data center plan The agreement allows Beale Infrastructure to seek a 25-year ad valorem tax exemption for each phase of the project. Company representatives said the development would still contribute more than $250 million toward Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programs over time. Some residents have raised concerns about water usage, environmental impacts and transparency. City officials and the developer say the project would not raise taxes or utility rates and could bring long-term investment and jobs. Muskogee County Google Data Centers (Summit and Council Hill) (Early Development) Google plans to build two new data center campuses near Summit and Council Hill as part of a $9 billion investment in Oklahoma. The facilities are expected to support Google’s cloud and AI services, including Search, Maps and Google Cloud. The company says the projects will be paired with clean energy agreements expected to add hundreds of megawatts of renewable power to Oklahoma’s grid. Construction timelines have not been released. Related Story: Google to build two data centers in Muskogee County as part of $9B Oklahoma investment In April, OG&E announced that it will power the Muskogee data centers as well as a data center coming to Stillwater (see below) “OG&E is pleased to support Google and together advance growth in our home state, ensuring our current customers benefit from data center expansion that meets the technology needs of the 21st century economy at some of the lowest rates in the country,” said Sean Trauschke, Chairman, President and CEO of OGE Energy Corp. “This unique agreement is a model for future data center partnerships and forms the basis for a new large-load tariff that OG&E will submit in the coming weeks that protects our current customers from bearing the costs of this growing demand and Oklahoma’s goals for economic growth.” Core Scientific (Under Construction) Core Scientific has partnered with Port Muskogee to develop a 100 MW high-performance computing (HPC) data center in Muskogee at 1525 W 43rd St S . Scheduled to become operational in 2026. A second Core Scientific data center is planned for Muskogee at 4800 S 24th St W. Oklahoma City American Tower EDC Oklahoma (Planned) American Tower EDC Oklahoma is a construction-ready edge data center* development located at 1309 Northeast 122nd Street in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. According to American Tower, the facility would be on 83.5 acres and provide 4MW of capacity. The American Tower EDC Oklahoma company says that zoning has been approved and that the facility can be ready in 18 months once a customer signs an anchor lease. *An edge data center is a smaller, decentralized facility positioned near the source of data generation. Cerebras Systems operates a 10-megawatt data center in Oklahoma City in partnership with Scale Datacenters. The facility supports large-scale AI computing and uses a closed-loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling system. CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus - 3 Data Centers (Under Construction) The CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus is planned to be an expansive location with a total capacity of 200MW covering at least three data centers. The project was set to break ground at the end of 2025; however, its construction appears to have been impacted by OKC’s data center moratorium. It is planned for the area near 2000 S Council Rd. Cogent Data Center (Operational) The Cogent Data Center in Oklahoma City is 5,294 square feet of colocation space designed for 42U cabinets. The Cogent data center is what’s known as a “carrier hotel,” meaning that it has equipment, space, and/or bandwidth available for rental to retail customers. artigo.texto: It doesn't seem that long ago when the idea of a data center meant a few shrugged shoulders, a couple of confused looks and at best a few questions along the line of: "What is a data center?" It turns out what we call data centers aren't new. They were originally called Electric Numerical Integrator and Computers. In 1945, they weighed 27 tons, occupied 300 square feet of space and used punch cards for data storage. Then, throughout the 1960s, these behemoths became more efficient, took up less room and started storing information in memory, and IT was developed to run various systems. From the 1980s through the '90s, computers became smaller and faster, personal computers entered homes, and during the "dot com boom," the first data centers emerged, housing hundreds and then thousands of servers. Jumping forward to 2012, 38% of organizations were using cloud services. Cloud service providers needed data centers, and since then, more and more of those digital warehouses have been built. Alas, a computer engineer will probably disagree with my terminology, but I think of data centers as where my 6,500 iPhone photos, my 342 audiobooks, my Amazon movies and my emails are "warehoused." Then, in mid-2024, a disdain for data centers became the one thing that could bring rural, suburban and urban dwellers together. The one thing that Democrats and Republicans, folks who love the president and folks who love AOC, and just about all of our races can agree on is that we all seem to hate data centers. And we all share our disdain, fears and loathing for these large ugly facilities on social media, which utilize data centers. Data centers use a lot of electricity, are terribly ugly, and depending on where they are built, use a great deal of water. The largest data centers can use up to 450,000 gallons a day. Neighbors complain of incessant noise, vibrations and the noxious fumes produced by massive diesel generators used for backup power. They are like oil refineries: We all know they must exist, but perhaps just out of our field of view. There are 7.2 million of these structures worldwide, and they act as the backbone of the world economy. You cannot watch an episode of "Slow Horses" or "Downton Abbey" on Apple TV without a data center. You cannot order anything from Amazon without these big ugly boxes. The largest centers use the same amount of water that 450 homes use daily for sprinkler systems. A typical 18-hole golf course uses roughly 312,000 gallons per day. Mowing your lawn for an hour produces smog-forming emissions equivalent to driving a car from 45 to 100 miles. Lawn fertilizers contribute to 56% of the total nitrogen and phosphorus found in our local streams. Do you know what else uses tens of billions of kilowatt-hours of electricity along with millions of gallons of water a day? They are loud, obnoxious to live near and create billions of gallons of runoff during every rain? Amusement parks. The point? Yes, we need greater regulatory management of data centers at the federal and state levels. They need to be built in a manner and location where the amount of water and energy utilized can be lowered to more manageable levels. But are you willing to put down your phone? Are you willing to go back to DVDs? Willing to rush to Walgreens to print off every picture on your iPhone? Are you willing to send a letter via the U.S. Postal Service? Maybe pay your bills with a check, instead of online? Or, utilize an old fashioned paper catalog from L.L. Bean for your next purchase? The point is, that, no, we won't do any of those things, because most of us like the ease and speed these data centers bring to our everyday lives. We need our collective digital addictions. Thus, we need data centers. We need to use common sense when it comes to data centers: Take a method and try it, if it doesn't give the public the desired outcome, admit it, and try something else. But above all, try something. ______ David Barto is a Hamilton County native, director of a nonprofit, gardener and amateur historian. Reach him at David Barto@Collegedale.Foundation.

artigo.texto: TI unveils new ADC to enable nanosecond-level telemetry and minimize downtime in AI data centers As AI workloads increase in volume and complexity, Texas Instruments is delivering the essential solutions needed to power, monitor and optimize AI data centers News highlights: - TI's ADC34DSO75 is the industry's highest performance 3 gigasamples per second ADC, enabling 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution – thousands of times faster than what current solutions offer. - The LMI800PS is the industry's first 800V isolated hot-swap controller, replacing a complex discrete solution requiring five integrated circuits with a single high-density package that delivers in-rush current and power path protection. - The LMK6B is a bulk acoustic wave-based oscillator that delivers best-in-class jitter performance and power-supply rejection ratio. SAN JOSE, Calif. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Texas Instruments (TI) (Nasdaq: TXN) debuted the first analog-to-digital converter (ADC) to enable 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution. As AI workloads rapidly increase, data center operators face significant challenges around power instability, inadequate real-time monitoring and signal degradation, all of which can lead to costly downtime. TI is addressing these challenges through its new ADC device and other analog solutions designed to tackle the challenges of scaling artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructures. Demonstrations on display in TI's booth, No. E45, at OCP include: - Real-time nanosecond-level telemetry: TI's ADC34DSO75 is the industry's highest performance 3 gigasamples per second (GSPS) ADC, enabling 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution – thousands of times faster than what current solutions offer. Existing monitoring solutions often fail to detect the nanosecond-level power-rail glitches that cause costly, unplanned downtime in data centers. By combining ultra-high-speed sampling with advanced on-chip digital signal processing in a small form factor, the ADC34DSO75 detects and captures transient fault events in real time. As the industry's first solution to offer fully remote, event-based telemetry, the device eliminates the need for on-site debugging and oscilloscopes. By providing continuous, high-resolution monitoring of low-voltage, high-current power rails, the ADC34DSO75 helps data centers minimize downtime – which can cost operators hundreds of thousands of dollars an hour – while optimizing grid power efficiency. This compact, efficient solution offers hyperscalers unmatched remote diagnostic capabilities at a fraction of the size and cost of conventional monitoring methods. - Reliable high-voltage power delivery: The LMI800PS is the industry's first 800V isolated hot-swap controller, replacing a complex discrete solution requiring five integrated circuits with a single high-density package that delivers in-rush current and power path protection. The integration of an isolated bias supply and PMBus telemetry reduces board area by more than 60% and simplifies high-voltage designs. The LMI800PS enables safe power insertion and fast fault isolation, meeting safety standards with 5kVrms reinforced isolation and more than 8mm creepage. This prevents a single load failure from disrupting the shared power bus and maximizes data center stability. Supporting both ±400V and 800V distributions, the device provides a scalable solution for diverse rack architectures, accelerating the deployment of high-efficiency power systems required for next-generation AI infrastructures. - Ultra-low jitter signal integrity: The LMK6B is a bulk acoustic wave (BAW)-based oscillator that delivers best-in-class jitter performance and power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR). As data center transmission rates approach 3.2Tbps, the margin for timing error shrinks significantly, and even minute jitter can increase bit error rates and cause system instability. The LMK6B provides industry-leading jitter performance of 9.6fs at 625MHz, ensuring reliable performance and preserving signal integrity for next-generation, AI-driven networking infrastructures. "As AI workloads drive massive scale, the need for real-time visibility and architectural stability has never been greater," said Karthik Vasanth, vice president and general manager for TI's Data, Converters and Clocks business unit. "By delivering industry-leading solutions for high-speed telemetry, advanced power protection and precision timing, TI is enabling hyperscalers and operators to design the next generation of AI data centers with optimized performance and minimal downtime." More details Also at OCP, TI Power Electronics Engineer David Reusch will present "800V Data Center DC/DC Design Considerations, Topology Comparisons and Trade-Offs," on Oct. 15 at 2:45 p.m. in room 230A. See ti.com/ocp for more information. For more information on the ADC34DSO75, read the technical article "The power glitches AI data centers can't see." About Texas Instruments Texas Instruments Incorporated (Nasdaq: TXN) is a global semiconductor company that designs, manufactures and sells analog and embedded processing chips for markets such as industrial, automotive, data center, personal electronics and communications equipment. At our core, we have a passion to create a better world by making electronics more affordable through semiconductors. This passion is alive today as each generation of innovation builds upon the last to make our technology more reliable, more affordable and lower power, making it possible for semiconductors to go into electronics everywhere. Learn more at TI.com. artigo.texto: Trending PANAMA -- Conversations surrounding Battery Energy Storage Systems have been held in the recent past in the village of Panama, and during their most recent meeting the village board dove more into the research behind the hazards associated with the systems. Originally, the village was meant to have someone who has done research on BESS as they appear around the county come to talk, but as that person could not make it, the village board looked at the research that was sent along to them at their October meeting. Mayor William Schneider said BESS are being seen more in the northern parts of the county, but it is anticipated that they will start to drift towards the areas around the village soon, so the village is looking to be prepared, especially with the increase in usage of solar farms. The man who sent the research to the village is a scientist and aerological engineer, who has worked with the town of Ripley on this subject as well, outlining some potential hazards with BESS. "One of the things that can create an issue is if they start a reaction and overload and start a fire," Schneider said. "These particular lithium ion thermal batteries, they call them runaway events, and what happens is they cannot be put out with water or foam and it basically has to burn until the modules in the container are consumed." The additional problem with that, Schneider said, is that there are several containers or modules that sit close by each other, so if one was to catch on fire the process could cause issues with the one sitting next to it and cause that one to catch on fire as well. Emergency responders then have to cool the existing ones that are not on fire until the first one burns out, and there is no time frame on how long that could take, needing to be done continuously and for many hours. "The problem is if the cooling issue were to stop somehow or be prolonged, the other units could start a chain reaction," Schneider said. Other potential issues about BESS that connect to the fire issue that were outlined for the village include the possibility of toxic runoff that could get into the groundwater and surrounding water ways, along with toxic gases that can come off as containers fail, meaning responders need full respiratory protection and that, Schneider said, would most likely mean the hazmat team would have to come in as well, and residents would likely have to be evacuated. Schneider also addressed liability concerns with the companies that come in and build the systems, with the liability then falling back on the municipalities and residents. "So this is something we're going to need to take a look at," Schneider said. "I've reached out to the town because I want to know what their language is on these systems, and then I'm also going to reach out to the lawyer to find out if the town has a particular law regarding these, do we have to reinvent it for the village or does that also cover us as we are inside the town itself. I know that can be a sticky point in certain circumstances, so I want to make sure we have all of our t's crossed and i's dotted." While nobody has asked about putting these systems in the village, Schneider said it is something the village needs to prepare for as they are not sure what will happen once nearby proposed solar farms are put in and functioning. It was noted that the village does not have to put in BESS, and the thought would be that the village would not due to the dangers. "Especially in a village that is one square mile and 450 residents and we have major waterways and most everybody's got groundwater, we don't have a public water system, these are all very high concerns," Schneider said. "I'm also very concerned as a retired emergency services and hazmat responder. It's dangerous for everybody all the way around." Schneider added that emergency services are not prepared for something like these systems either, citing similar potential dangers that come with fires in electric vehicles, though those are on a smaller scale. After talking with the town and lawyers, Schneider said the village could come back with a resolution against allowing BESS in the village, if that is the way everyone decides that they want to go. Conditional use permits or variances were also discussed, as technology has the ability to change years into the future. Having to deal with electric buses as the state continues to push for them was also brought up and noted that the village will have to deal with that at some point as well. "There's all of these little intricate things that we don't know enough about right now," Schneider said. "We need to see how some of this plays out. So, the safe thing would be to do this, cover the bases, and then as technology increases, gets better, safer, then the village can relook at the issue again." The village also briefly discussed upcoming fall related items, including Trick-or-Treat hours being from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. on Halloween, and village leaf pickup being scheduled for November 4, with a rain date of November 5. Residents are also asked to bring their leaves out to the curbside for leaf pickup.

Set us as preferred California has always hidden the true price of progress somewhere beyond the horizon. The water arrives from a distant river. The electricity crosses a mountain range. By the time the benefits reach us, the damage has been assigned elsewhere. Now the future is arriving in windowless buildings. Data centers are rising from industrial corridors and farmland with the appetite of cities. They pull electricity by the hundreds of megawatts. Inside, servers build fortunes. Outside, residents open their utility bills and wonder what will remain. Before California approves another facility, every host community deserves an answer: What will this project make better here? Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven laws that begin to make the hidden costs visible. Until those are in effect, a company could arrive with the appetite of a city and quietly leave its bill for wires and water with people who never asked for it. Now utility regulators must reckon with what it takes to serve that appetite. The rates and connection terms are meant to make new users shoulder their share of the grid and the electricity it must supply, instead of loading those costs onto a family studying its bill. Regulators must now make that promise real. The water, too, must come into the open. Data centers are water guzzlers, using huge volumes for cooling. Before construction, a developer must show where that water will come from, how the facility will fare in drought and who will pay for the new pipes. After the servers begin to hum, estimates must give way to actual water use. State planners will gain an account of energy consumption and efficiency. A town needs numbers it can see. And the project can no longer pass under a blanket environmental exemption. A quicker path through court is reserved for facilities that meet demanding conditions on clean power, water and protection of ratepayers. In California, speed must be earned. These laws draw a floor beneath the bargain. They do not guarantee that a neighborhood gains something lasting from the land, power and water it commits. California should establish a “community benefit standard” for every new data center and major expansion. Protect the resources of the place. Pay every cost the project creates. Then deliver a public benefit that residents can see, measure and enforce. The first requirements are obligations, not generosity. Developers must disclose projected electricity demand, water consumption, emissions, noise and infrastructure needs. That includes drought, extreme heat and nearby projects. Households cannot pay for capacity reserved by a corporation that may never use it. No company should receive applause for obeying environmental law. Efficient cooling is not a community gift when the machinery is necessary to run the servers. A research grant cannot excuse an unacceptable water plan. Public benefits cannot purchase permission to pollute a neighborhood or drain an aquifer. Only after those tests are met does the additional bargain begin. Each major project should fund at least one substantial technology program tied to an identified public need. Residents and public agencies would help choose the priority. California should measure what changes, not what gets announced. One developer might finance advanced water reuse with a local district beyond what is required to address its own demand. The compact would state how much freshwater demand must be eliminated, how savings will be verified and who will operate the system. Buying equipment would not count. Producing verified water savings would. Another facility might guarantee computing capacity to California hospitals and universities studying rare diseases, cancer or wildfire behavior. The agreement would specify secure access, support and computing hours, and bind the tenant. Researchers would receive usable capacity, not whatever remains after commercial customers finish. A third project could finance batteries and controls that keep a clinic, cooling center or water system operating during an outage. The equipment must serve the public in an emergency. Backup power reserved for company servers would not qualify. Every project must still provide a direct local benefit. A statewide research program may supplement that commitment, but it cannot replace it. The compact would name beneficiaries, funding, responsible parties, milestones and penalties for failure. Its duties would survive a sale or tenant change. Independent verification would report delivery, not spending. If one method underperforms, the agreements between data centers and communities should permit another. The obligation itself remains. Contribution levels should reflect project size. Small facilities could pool resources. Large campuses could not divide themselves into smaller applications to escape responsibility. Broader innovation contributions should be legally sound and separate from required mitigation. Projects with unacceptable impacts should be rejected or relocated. Those meeting environmental standards and securing credible, enforceable benefits deserve coordinated reviews and clear timelines. The Legislature has drawn the line against making families pay for the servers that power someone else’s fortune. The industry can meet that line by showing, in public and before construction, how it will protect the grid and water system. Then it can show what it will build for the people living outside its walls. For too long, California has sent the rewards of progress in one direction and the damage in another. If our communities are asked to power the future, that future must also power them. Dean Florez is a former California Senate majority leader, representing portions of the Central Valley. artigo.texto: Chuyển đổi số từ dữ liệu: [Bài 4] Xây nền tảng số cho thị trường carbon Dữ liệu hạn ngạch phát thải khí nhà kính, tín chỉ carbon, các tổ chức tham gia thị trường carbon tại Việt Nam được quản lý tập trung, thống nhất trên một nền tảng số. O setor de agricultura e meio ambiente está focado na padronização, interconexão e exploração de bancos de dados, na inovação de métodos de gestão e no atendimento às pessoas e empresas. Em resposta ao Dia Nacional da Transformação Digital, em 10 de outubro de 2026, com o tema "Da arquitetura, plataforma e dados a resultados tangíveis", o jornal Agricultura e Meio Ambiente publica uma reportagem especial intitulada "Transformação Digital a partir de Dados", esclarecendo o papel dos dados na inovação de métodos de gestão, na melhoria da eficiência operacional, na otimização do uso de recursos e no atendimento às pessoas e empresas. A transição para uma governança orientada por dados. O Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas (Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente) desenvolveu e implementou o Sistema Nacional de Registro de Cotas de Emissão de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono. Em junho de 2026, o sistema começará a operar em paralelo com a bolsa de carbono nacional. Isso pode ser considerado um passo significativo na transformação digital do setor agrícola e ambiental, contribuindo para a modernização da gestão estatal em resposta às mudanças climáticas e para o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono no Vietnã. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, Vice-Chefe do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono (Agência de Mudanças Climáticas), o sistema ajuda a transformar os métodos de gestão, passando de processos administrativos tradicionais para um ambiente digital. Através do sistema, os dados sobre quotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa, créditos de carbono e participantes do mercado são gerenciados de forma centralizada e uniforme em uma plataforma digital. Os dados garantem precisão, transparência, rastreabilidade e controle sobre as flutuações históricas. Em particular, o Sistema Nacional de Registro é um componente crucial da infraestrutura digital que serve à operação do mercado de carbono do Vietnã, desempenhando um papel de ligação entre a gestão estatal e as atividades relacionadas à custódia, negociação e pagamento de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. “A construção deste sistema não só atende aos requisitos operacionais do mercado de carbono doméstico, como também cria uma base para a conexão e troca gradual de dados com os mecanismos de cooperação internacional sobre carbono, conforme o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris. Isso apoiará o alcance das metas de redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, a transição verde e o compromisso do Vietnã de atingir emissões líquidas zero até 2050”, afirmou o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong. As principais funções do sistema O sistema nacional de registro serve para gerenciar de forma centralizada e uniforme as operações relacionadas ao registro, emissão de códigos, rastreamento de propriedade, transferência e uso de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono, em conformidade com a lei . Você também pode gostar O Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas está oferecendo treinamento para organizações e empresas sobre como participar do mercado de carbono. Foto: Trung Nguyen. Em primeiro lugar, o sistema facilita o cadastro, a configuração e a gestão de contas eletrônicas para agências e organizações participantes do mercado de carbono. Isso inclui o gerenciamento de informações dos titulares das contas, o controle de transações e o monitoramento do saldo de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono para cada conta. Essas atividades são realizadas eletronicamente, simplificando o processo de cadastro, aprimorando as capacidades de controle e aumentando a eficiência do processamento de transações. Para quotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono, o sistema registra e armazena informações sobre as quotas alocadas e os créditos de carbono elegíveis; atribui códigos, gerencia a quantidade, o status e o histórico de alterações de cada unidade de carbono. Por meio de uma gestão centralizada e unificada, o sistema permite o rastreamento das quotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e dos créditos de carbono ao longo de sua existência e utilização. Isso garante transparência, rastreabilidade e reduz o risco de dupla contabilização e reutilização de uma mesma unidade de carbono. A imagem ilustra o número de série da quota de emissão de uma organização/empresa. Foto: VNEEC . Além disso, o sistema suporta operações relacionadas a depósitos, saques, transferência de titularidade fora da bolsa, uso de créditos de carbono para compensar emissões, pagamento, transferência e empréstimo de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa, conforme regulamentado. O sistema está conectado e troca dados com sistemas de custódia, negociação e pagamento para garantir a sincronização entre as informações de registro e as atividades de negociação no mercado nacional de carbono. Além das funções já mencionadas, o sistema também permite pesquisar, agregar, analisar estatisticamente e gerar relatórios com dados sobre o registro e o uso de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. Essas funções auxiliam os órgãos de gestão estatal no monitoramento das operações de mercado, na verificação e cruzamento de informações e na supervisão do cumprimento das normas pelas instalações emissoras. Os dados também contribuem para o planejamento e a implementação de políticas de redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa e desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono no Vietnã. Preparativos passo a passo para o lançamento oficial do mercado de carbono. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, no próximo período, o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente continuará a concentrar-se no aperfeiçoamento, aprimoramento e expansão das funções do Sistema Nacional

artigo.texto: O mercado de carbono abre fontes adicionais de capital para empresas em transição para energias sustentáveis. O mercado de carbono pode gerar receita a partir da redução de emissões, ajudando as empresas a diversificar seus recursos de investimento e a reduzir a dependência de crédito bancário. No entanto, para que a valoração do carbono influencie as decisões de empréstimo, é necessário superar os obstáculos legais, de dados e de fluxo de caixa. No seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", realizado em 14 de outubro, o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, Vice-Governador do Banco Central do Vietnã (SBV), afirmou que um mercado de carbono que funcione de forma eficiente ajudará a transformar os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico , criará recursos adicionais para as empresas e contribuirá para reduzir a pressão sobre o crédito bancário. Para cumprir seu compromisso de emissões líquidas zero até 2050, o Vietnã está acelerando o crescimento verde, a transição energética e a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Esse processo exige investimentos significativos em inovação tecnológica, ajustes nos métodos de produção e melhoria da eficiência energética. Além do orçamento estatal, dos mercados de capitais e do crédito bancário, o mercado de carbono pode se tornar um canal para complementar esses recursos. Em 29 de janeiro de 2026, o Governo emitiu o Decreto nº 29/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta o mercado interno de carbono. De acordo com as informações apresentadas na oficina, o mercado encontra-se atualmente em fase piloto, com mais de 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente em quotas de emissão alocadas a instalações dos três setores: energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento, durante o período de 2025-2026. A fase piloto se estenderá até o final de 2028, antes da transição para a operação obrigatória plena a partir de 2029. Segundo o vice-governador do Banco Estatal do Vietnã , Nguyen Ngoc Canh, o crédito verde e o mercado de carbono têm uma relação complementar. O crédito verde fornece capital para que as empresas invistam em tecnologia, desenvolvam produção verde e reduzam as emissões; o mercado de carbono cria um mecanismo para que esses resultados se tornem bens negociáveis. A receita proveniente do comércio de carbono, se estabelecida de forma consistente, pode sustentar o fluxo de caixa e melhorar a capacidade de pagamento de dívidas de uma empresa. A mensuração, o relato e a avaliação dos resultados da redução de emissões também fornecem informações adicionais para que as instituições de crédito avaliem a eficácia da utilização do capital e gerenciem os riscos dos empréstimos verdes. No final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde atingiu mais de 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025. Durante o período de 2017 a 2025, a taxa média de crescimento foi superior a 20% ao ano. Os empréstimos pendentes concentram-se principalmente nos setores de agricultura , silvicultura, pesca e conservação da biodiversidade, representando mais de 31%; a energia verde representa quase 28%. Você também pode gostar Dadas as significativas necessidades de capital para a transformação verde, o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono contribuirá para a diversificação das fontes de financiamento, criando incentivos adicionais para que as empresas invistam em tecnologias limpas e reduzindo a dependência de empréstimos bancários. Na perspectiva dos bancos comerciais, a Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank , acredita que incorporar o valor do carbono nas decisões de crédito exige determinar a confiabilidade dos resultados da redução de emissões e a capacidade de converter esse valor em fluxo de caixa real. A agricultura, a silvicultura e a economia circular têm um potencial significativo para reduzir as emissões, desde a produção de arroz e a pecuária até o tratamento de resíduos. Essas são também áreas em que o financiamento bancário pode ser vinculado a modelos de produção sustentáveis. No entanto, um projeto que atenda a critérios ambientais não gera automaticamente créditos de carbono; da mesma forma, possuir créditos de carbono não garante automaticamente a elegibilidade para empréstimos. Os bancos ainda precisam avaliar a viabilidade do plano de negócios e a capacidade de pagamento do projeto. Segundo a Sra. Ha, para que a valoração do carbono apoie as atividades de concessão de créditos, é necessário esclarecer a propriedade, os direitos de alienação e os benefícios decorrentes dos resultados da redução de emissões; e melhorar a qualidade do sistema de medição, reporte e avaliação. Quando os dados não são suficientemente confiáveis, os benefícios não são claros ou o mercado carece de um preço de referência estável, os bancos têm dificuldade em considerar a receita de carbono como uma fonte confiável de pagamento de dívidas. Os custos de levantamento, elaboração de relatórios e avaliações também podem se tornar uma barreira para cooperativas, pequenas empresas e áreas de produção dispersas. A padronização de dados, a redução dos custos de avaliação e a produção organizada ao longo da cadeia de valor ajudarão muitos projetos a acessar capital verde. Você também pode gostar Até o final de março de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde do Agribank atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND. O banco está implementando programas de empréstimo para apoiar a agricultura limpa e de alta tecnologia, bem como a integração entre produção, processamento e consumo de arroz de alta qualidade e baixa emissão no Delta do Mekong. A Sra. Ha argumentou que é necessário aprimorar ainda mais o arcabouço legal relativo aos direitos aos créditos de carbono, desenvolver a infraestrutura de dados, reduzir os custos de avaliação e construir um mecanismo de compartilhamento de riscos para projetos em seus estágios iniciais. artigo.texto: A Finnish battery startup facing sustained accusations from industry rivals that its technology is overstated or outright fraudulent has released new independent test data showing its solid-state cells deliver more than their rated capacity at temperatures that would degrade or destroy a conventional lithium-ion battery. Donut Lab, which has previously claimed its cells can charge in minutes and offer high energy density, commissioned a second evaluation by VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, the country’s state-run research institute. The results, published by Donut Lab this week, focus specifically on thermal performance, examining how the battery behaves at 80°C and 100°C, temperatures at which standard lithium-ion cells begin to suffer serious performance loss and pose safety risks. Standard lithium-ion batteries are very sensitive to heat, with an upper operating temperature limit of typically around 60 to 70 degrees Celsius. High temperatures increase the risk of damage to battery cells and shorten their service life. High temperatures can also cause accelerated reactions inside the cell, and in the worst case, the risk of thermal runaway increases significantly. The Donut Battery does not use flammable liquid electrolytes, the component most responsible for thermal runaway in conventional cells. That difference in architecture is what VTT’s tests were designed to quantify under real thermal stress. The methodology was straightforward. Engineers placed the cell on an aluminium profile, secured a steel plate on top to apply light pressure and reduce hot spots, then measured capacity in stages at each temperature. At 176°F, the battery delivered about 110% of its rated capacity, showed better efficiency than at room temperature, and the cell showed no visible changes after the test. At 212°F, the battery used roughly 107% of its capacity and recharged back to 4.15 volts with the same capacity as at room temperature. Although the pouch lost vacuum at that temperature, the active materials remained fully functional. The efficiency gain at elevated temperatures is explained by basic electrochemistry. Heat reduces the internal resistance of a cell, which in turn reduces the voltage drop during discharge, allowing more of the stored energy to be extracted as usable output. In a liquid-electrolyte battery, that benefit is overwhelmed by accelerating degradation chemistry. In Donut Lab’s solid-state design, the degradation mechanism is largely absent, allowing the efficiency benefit to dominate instead. “The battery’s full capacity was utilised with excellent results at both 80 and 100 degrees Celsius, and it was possible to discharge it at a 1C discharge rate at 80 degrees and a 0.5C discharge rate at 100 degrees without any increase in temperature. The battery’s properties did not change even at 100 degrees, and it functioned normally when recharged, which demonstrates the convincing performance of the Donut Battery even in extremely hot conditions. This confirms that the battery is exceptional not only in terms of performance but also in terms of safety,” said Ville Piippo, CTO at Donut Lab. The results carry practical implications beyond the laboratory. Batteries that tolerate extreme heat without cooling system support could reduce the weight, complexity, and cost of thermal management in electric vehicles, particularly relevant for markets in desert climates where ambient temperatures routinely exceed the operating ceiling of conventional packs. Industrial applications including grid storage, aerospace, and military systems have similarly been constrained by the thermal sensitivity of existing battery chemistry. The tests also represent a deliberate shift in how Donut Lab is managing its public credibility. After bold claims generated skepticism rather than investment interest, the company is now building its case incrementally through third-party data published openly, letting the numbers do the work that press releases could not. For automakers in the US and companies focused on energy storage, having batteries that can handle extreme heat is absolutely essential. Batteries that can endure high temperatures not only lessen the strain on cooling systems but also enhance safety in sweltering regions like Arizona, Texas, and Nevada. Whether the technology proves durable at manufacturing scale remains the central unanswered question, but on the narrow question of what the cells do under extreme heat, the independent record now says they perform better than anything currently in mass production.

artigo.texto: SC Senate candidates clash over data center expansion in debate COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS) - During Sunday’s debate in South Carolina’s heated U.S. Senate race, data centers became a big point of contention for all three candidates. Republican Sen. Darline Graham, along with challengers Dr. Annie Andrews and Kasie Whitener, were asked Sunday if they supported data center moratoriums and if they’d support federal regulations. Andrews, the Democratic challenger, pushed Graham on her stance on data centers. “She [Graham] thinks we need to all get with the program and build data centers faster and faster,” said Andrews. “So why does ‘Data Center Darline’ think we need to do that? Because data center companies and AI companies have spent millions to prop up her campaign.” Graham fired back. “Since we’re name-calling here. obviously, you don’t know my stance on data centers. I’m concerned about data centers too, but let me be clear here: I think there needs to be community involvement when it comes to data centers,” the senator responded. Whitener, running as a Libertarian, said she feels local communities need to have a voice when it comes to building new data centers in their area. “It is a local issue,” Whitener said. At least six Midlands communities have voted to temporarily pause data center development, with others also doing so across the state. More South Carolinians are raising concerns about possible impacts of those data centers, including water consumption and higher energy bills. “These data centers are being built in communities’ backyards without any community input,” said Andrews. Andrews said her data center plan includes a two-year moratorium. Graham criticized the proposal, citing national security concerns and what she argued is a growing threat from China. “Under her Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country because in two years, China is going to be so far ahead, we’re going to be in so much trouble,” said Graham. Whitener doubled down on her stance. “Your community should be talking to one another and figuring out what’s best for you, and again you don’t need the government’s permission to do that,” Whitener said. Meanwhile, South Carolina state lawmakers are set to reassess statewide regulations on data centers when they return for the next legislative session in 2027. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – As San Antonio prepares to add more guardrails for where data centers can go in the Alamo City, the question now is how exactly the regulations will work. At a Wednesday council meeting, staff briefed council members on two options, which boiled down to having a defined set of restrictions or making each data center project get council approval on a case-by-case basis. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones also tossed in a third option of her own that would also require council approval for new data centers, as well as requirements like replacing double the greenspace eliminated during construction. Data centers have become a hot button topic in Texas politics, raising concerns about issues from their power and water use to noise or air quality concerns. Councilman Ric Galvan (D6) says his Northwest Side district has the majority of the city’s data centers and has been the one leading the charge for data center regulation. For him, requiring council approval over each project is necessary. “I do not believe it is enough for residents just to know about the project. It is important for their public officials to also make clear where they stand on the project and to move it forward or not, depending on what the conversations look like,” he said. Development Services Director Amin Tohmaz says data centers are currently allowed in most areas of the city, except residential ones. The two options staff presented, though, would restrict them to areas zoned for industrial and heavy commercial uses, like warehouses or regional shopping centers. The first option with more baked-in regulation came mainly out of stakeholder discussions, staff said. It would require data centers to be 500 feet from areas like schools or housing, have certain landscaping, be set back 50 feet from the property line, and not be over the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone. The other option, which was largely born out of a previous council discussion, wouldn’t have those same restrictions, but council would be able to institute similar ones on a case-by-case basis and would have the ultimate say over whether to allow a project. Jones suggested a hybrid model with mandatory council approval and several other requirements, including a 45-day pre-filing notice and enclosing backup generators as much as possible. It was unclear, however, if the “1,000-foot setback from the perimeter” she called for appeared to be meant as an extension of the proposed 500-foot buffer between data centers and certain other sites, instead of the “setback” distance from a data center to its own property line. When reached for clarification Wednesday, the mayor’s chief of staff offered an interview on Thursday but did not provide an explanation. City staff have said that while individual council consideration for a project would provide more flexibility, it would also mean less predictability and certainty, which is what they say are what developers are looking for. Councilwoman Misty Spears (D9) said she didn’t like any of the options and worried about losing out on data center projects. “If we put too many restrictions here, they’re not even going to look at us,” she said. “They’re going to go, ‘Nah, I’ll just go to Medina County, and then I’ll put what I want there,’ and then it still affects your air quality. And it still affects — or presumably affects your air quality.” The zoning commission is expected to discuss options next week, and the council will actually vote on Oct. 29. Read also:

artigo.texto: Carbon price signals must be strong enough to guide investment flows. At the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam on October 14th, Mr. Dang Tai An Trang, Deputy General Director of the Vietnam Stock Exchange (VNX), stated that the development of the carbon market needs to be considered in relation to the goals of emission reduction, economic efficiency, and the ability to mobilize resources for green transition. According to Mr. Trang, the green transition has become a clear trend worldwide , creating new demands on production and business activities. For example, the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is setting emission requirements for certain groups of imported goods, including iron and steel. For Vietnamese export businesses, proactively investing in domestic emission reduction technologies not only helps meet international standards but also limits carbon costs incurred when exporting goods to markets with strict regulations. This allows businesses to retain financial resources for reinvestment, instead of having to pay additional emission-related expenses. However, the Deputy General Director of VNX also noted that the green transformation process needs a roadmap that is appropriate to the actual conditions of the economy. In the context of Vietnam's high growth target, the transformation of technology, energy, and production methods requires very large capital investments. If the transformation pressure occurs too quickly, exceeding the adaptability of businesses, compliance costs could affect business efficiency and overall growth. Notably, according to Mr. Trang, the driving force behind businesses' green transformation stems from both legal requirements and market pressures. Besides international commitments, the demands of consumers, trade partners, and investors are increasingly becoming factors driving businesses to improve environmental standards. In this context, the carbon market is expected to become an important economic tool, helping businesses quantify emission costs and incorporate environmental factors into investment decisions. Regarding the Vietnamese carbon market, Mr. Trang argued that one should not only look at the volume or value of transactions in the initial phase to assess operational efficiency. More importantly, the market must gradually develop price signals, thereby helping businesses calculate the costs and benefits of emission reduction activities. From a financial perspective, Mr. Trang compared the carbon market to the bond market. Just as the bond market requires a long-term yield curve as a basis for pricing and investment decision-making, the carbon market also needs a sufficiently clear price signal so that participants can predict and calculate economic efficiency. Having a carbon price reference point makes it easier for businesses to quantify emission costs, assess compliance risks, and determine the benefits of investing in green technologies. This is especially important for large-scale projects with long investment and payback periods. However, to generate reliable price signals, the market must have goods that meet standards, a transparent information system, and an effective monitoring mechanism. According to the Deputy General Director of VNX, a crucial requirement is to build a measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) system to ensure the quality of emission quotas and carbon credits traded. Simultaneously, it is necessary to improve information disclosure standards and strengthen supervision to prevent market manipulation and the risk of "greenwashing." Regarding VNX, Mr. Trang stated that technical infrastructure and technology are not major obstacles thanks to existing experience in operating the stock market. The more important issue lies in building a transparent operating mechanism, ensuring the quality of securities, and strengthening the confidence of participating entities. Beyond just the carbon market, VNX representatives also mentioned the possibility of developing financial instruments to support green transition in the stock market. According to Mr. Trang, in the initial stages, developing green bonds may be easier than establishing criteria for identifying green stocks. This is because green bonds are linked to the use of capital for projects that meet environmental standards, while determining whether a business truly meets green standards requires a comprehensive assessment of its production and business operations. Based on the ESG index that has been in operation since 2017, Mr. Trang believes that it is necessary to continue improving the in-depth green indexes, providing investment funds and investors with more tools to identify businesses, thereby supporting capital allocation. Furthermore, standardizing environmental data and establishing mechanisms for information sharing between banks, regulatory agencies, and investors are also crucial. This will help businesses reduce information provision costs while supporting financial institutions in improving the efficiency of project appraisal and selection. The carbon market needs more goods and participants. Adding to the perspective on the progress of building and operating the domestic carbon market, Mr. Do Thanh Lam, Specialist in the Legal Department, Ministry of Finance, said that Vietnam has made significant progress in institutional and transaction infrastructure, but the development of the market still faces limitations in terms of goods and the number of participating entities. According to Mr. Lam, developing the carbon market is an interdisciplinary task requiring coordination among many regulatory agencies. artigo.texto: Os sinais relativos ao preço do carbono devem ser suficientemente fortes para orientar os fluxos de investimento. No seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", organizado pelo jornal Finanças e Investimentos em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã em 14 de outubro, o Sr. Dang Tai An Trang, Vice-Diretor Geral da Bolsa de Valores do Vietnã (VNX), afirmou que o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono precisa ser considerado em relação às metas de redução de emissões, eficiência econômica e capacidade de mobilizar recursos para a transição verde. Segundo o Sr. Trang, a transição verde tornou-se uma tendência clara em todo o mundo , criando novas exigências para as atividades de produção e negócios. Por exemplo, o Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) da União Europeia está estabelecendo requisitos de emissão para certos grupos de mercadorias importadas, incluindo ferro e aço. Para as empresas exportadoras vietnamitas, investir proativamente em tecnologias nacionais de redução de emissões não só ajuda a cumprir as normas internacionais, como também limita os custos de carbono incorridos na exportação de mercadorias para mercados com regulamentações rigorosas. Isso permite que as empresas preservem os recursos financeiros para reinvestimento, em vez de terem que arcar com despesas adicionais relacionadas às emissões. Contudo, o Vice-Diretor Geral da VNX também observou que o processo de transformação verde precisa de um roteiro adequado às condições reais da economia. No contexto da meta de alto crescimento do Vietnã, a transformação da tecnologia, energia e métodos de produção exige investimentos de capital muito elevados. Se a pressão da transformação ocorrer muito rapidamente, ultrapassando a capacidade de adaptação das empresas, os custos de conformidade podem afetar a eficiência dos negócios e o crescimento geral. Notavelmente, de acordo com o Sr. Trang, a força motriz por trás da transformação verde das empresas decorre tanto de exigências legais quanto de pressões de mercado. Além dos compromissos internacionais, as demandas de consumidores, parceiros comerciais e investidores estão se tornando fatores cada vez mais importantes que impulsionam as empresas a aprimorarem seus padrões ambientais. Nesse contexto, espera-se que o mercado de carbono se torne uma importante ferramenta econômica, ajudando as empresas a quantificar os custos de emissão e a incorporar fatores ambientais em suas decisões de investimento. Em relação ao mercado de carbono vietnamita, o Sr. Trang argumentou que não se deve analisar apenas o volume ou o valor das transações na fase inicial para avaliar a eficiência operacional. Mais importante ainda, o mercado deve desenvolver gradualmente sinais de preço, ajudando assim as empresas a calcular os custos e benefícios das atividades de redução de emissões. Do ponto de vista financeiro, o Sr. Trang comparou o mercado de carbono ao mercado de títulos. Assim como o mercado de títulos exige uma curva de rendimento de longo prazo como base para a precificação e a tomada de decisões de investimento, o mercado de carbono também precisa de um sinal de preço suficientemente claro para que os participantes possam prever e calcular a eficiência econômica. Ter um ponto de referência para o preço do carbono facilita para as empresas a quantificação dos custos de emissão, a avaliação dos riscos de conformidade e a determinação dos benefícios do investimento em tecnologias verdes. Isso é especialmente importante para projetos de grande escala com longos períodos de investimento e retorno do investimento. No entanto, para gerar sinais de preços confiáveis, o mercado precisa de produtos que atendam aos padrões, um sistema de informações transparente e um mecanismo de monitoramento eficaz. Segundo o Diretor-Geral Adjunto da VNX, um requisito crucial é a construção de um sistema de medição, reporte e verificação (MRV) para garantir a qualidade das quotas de emissão e dos créditos de carbono negociados. Simultaneamente, é necessário aprimorar os padrões de divulgação de informações e fortalecer a supervisão para prevenir a manipulação do mercado e o risco de "greenwashing". Em relação à VNX, o Sr. Trang afirmou que a infraestrutura técnica e a tecnologia não representam grandes obstáculos, graças à experiência já existente na operação do mercado de ações. A questão mais importante reside na construção de um mecanismo operacional transparente, na garantia da qualidade dos títulos e no fortalecimento da confiança das entidades participantes. Além do mercado de carbono, os representantes da VNX também mencionaram a possibilidade de desenvolver instrumentos financeiros para apoiar a transição verde no mercado de ações. Segundo o Sr. Trang, nos estágios iniciais, desenvolver títulos verdes pode ser mais fácil do que estabelecer critérios para identificar ações verdes. Isso porque os títulos verdes estão vinculados ao uso de capital em projetos que atendem a padrões ambientais, enquanto determinar se uma empresa realmente atende a esses padrões exige uma avaliação abrangente de sua produção e operações comerciais. Com base no índice ESG em operação desde 2017, o Sr. Trang acredita que é necessário continuar aprimorando os índices verdes mais detalhados, fornecendo aos fundos de investimento e investidores mais ferramentas para identificar empresas e, assim, apoiar a alocação de capital. Além disso, a padronização de dados ambientais e o estabelecimento de mecanismos para o compartilhamento de informações entre bancos, agências reguladoras e investidores também são cruciais. Isso ajudará as empresas a reduzir os custos de fornecimento de informações, ao mesmo tempo que apoiará as instituições financeiras na melhoria da eficiência da avaliação e seleção de projetos. artigo.texto: Sign up for The Brief, The Texas Tribune’s daily newsletter that keeps readers up to speed on the most essential Texas news. This article is co-published with El Paso Matters and ProPublica as part of an initiative to report on local control of government. Sign up to receive ProPublica’s biggest stories as soon as they’re published. Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition. Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places. Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms. A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso. The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters. The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months, as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune. But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than two million cars in a year. They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University of California, Riverside. “The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said. Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately. “We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.” The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them. Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not. New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away. Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said. “This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?” Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region. State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break, which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune. New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030. The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time.
