artigo.texto: The European Union Emissions Trading System: What Can We Learn from the Proposed Changes to One of the World’s Longest-Running Carbon Pricing Policies? This issue brief dives into key proposed changes to the European Union Emissions Trading System and their implications for several industrial products. Introduction On July 17, 2026, the European Commission published a proposal to revise the EU emissions trading system (ETS). ETS revisions tend to happen roughly every five years to account for changes in the European Union’s overall climate policy and the global economy. Earlier this year, the European Union confirmed its climate target for 2040 of reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 90 percent relative to 1990. In this issue brief, we review some of the key proposed changes to the ETS design, especially as related to allowance allocation and other design elements that are relevant to industrial product regulation. 1. Allowance Supply: More Supply and a More Flexible Supply As a cap-and-trade system, the EU ETS shrinks the allowance supply each year by a fixed amount—the linear reduction factor. Under the current trajectory, no new allowances would be issued after 2039. Under the proposed new trajectory, the cap is lowered more gradually, especially after 2036, so that it will not reach zero until 2048. For reference, in 2025, total ETS emissions were 1,009 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, a 51.8 percent reduction compared to 2005 (the ETS launch year). Figure 1 shows the development of the ETS allowance supply and emissions covered by the system since 2013. Figure 1. EU Emissions Trading System Allowance Supply and Emissions by Sector, 2013–2025 The European Union proposes to create room for additional ETS supply through the purchase of 260 million international carbon credits (funded by selling ETS allowances). This would increase domestic emissions in exchange for more international reductions, but only if the credits can be procured in the desired quantity and quality. If not, the ETS cap will still be reduced commensurately. Another source of additional supply is permanent carbon removals. The European Union proposes that companies under the ETS can also buy units certified under its carbon removal certification mechanism and use these for compliance. Because permanent carbon removal is costly, likely exceeding the ETS allowance price, it is unclear if the volumes of removals will be significant. 2. Allowances Allocated for Free: More Conditionality, More Benchmarks? Free allocation in energy-intensive industries in the EU ETS has been justified as a compensation mechanism against the risk of carbon leakage risk. With protecting industrial competitiveness as a goal, making free allocation conditional (e.g., on low-carbon investment) has been resisted. This may be changing, as the commission suggests making it conditional on companies submitting transition plans for their facilities that align with the European Union’s climate neutrality goals. Twenty percent of free allowances may face even stricter rules, as operators will need to prove that they invested the value in actual decarbonization of their facilities. Unlike with the other allowances, this 20 percent would not be allocated ex ante but several years later, after verification of the investments. Although conditionalities like this may be heavily contested during the upcoming legislative process, the proposal reflects a core challenge in free-allocation design. It carries a high opportunity cost in foregone auction revenue that could be used to finance green industrial policy. Shifting free allocation from a compensatory logic to directly supporting low-carbon investments can be a way to bridge a period when allocation mostly benefits conventional, higher-emitting producers to one where it benefits lower-carbon producers as a decarbonization coinvestment mechanism. Figure 2. Free Allocation and Verified Emissions in the EU Emissions Trading System The European Union’s carbon border adjustment mechanism also fits here, as it will gradually replace free allowances. However, the proposal suggests a more gradual phaseout of free allowances to sectors included in the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), so the effective price for CBAM certificates will not reflect the full ETS price for a few years longer (until 2038), as the price is adjusted for the share of free allocation (see Figure 3). The full CBAM payment obligation depends on not just this CBAM factor but the emissions embedded in imported goods. If actual emissions data cannot be verified, default values apply as a fallback approach, which act as an intensity benchmark. Figure 3. Current and Proposed Phase-In of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism 3. Benchmarks: Technical Allocation Rules Can Affect Decarbonization Incentives A more technical change to free allocation concerns benchmarks. These are set at the product level and should ensure that free allocation volumes are “benchmarked” to the 10 percent most efficient EU installations for a given product. However, some industrial facilities yield many different products (e.g., refineries or the chemicals industry). In these cases, input-based fallback benchmarks are used that relate more to generic industrial processes (heat and fuel consumption, expressed as GHG emissions per terajoule of input) than to products (expressed in output terms as tons of GHG per ton of product). Examining the evolution of ETS benchmarks can provide insight into policy design choices that also are relevant when considering product carbon intensity standards—a topic that Resources for the Future will work on over the coming year. artigo.texto: Ampotech and Buskowitz Energy Collaborate to Deliver Integrated Energy Solutions Combining Energy Efficiency, Solar and Battery Storage SINGAPORE, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ampotech and Buskowitz Energy are collaborating to help commercial and industrial customers in the Philippines unlock greater energy savings and sustainability through an integrated approach combining energy efficiency, rooftop solar, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and AI-powered energy management. The collaboration combines Buskowitz Energy's solar development, engineering, EPC, PPA and battery storage capabilities while Ampotech provides energy efficiency solutions and its AmpoCloud AI-powered energy management platform, enabling customers to integrate and manage multiple energy assets through a unified platform. Combining renewable generation with energy efficiency Under the collaboration, Ampotech identifies commercial and industrial projects where customers can benefit from a combination of energy efficiency measures, rooftop solar PV and/or BESS. Buskowitz provides the renewable energy and energy storage infrastructure, while Ampotech supports the efficiency side and provides the digital intelligence layer through AmpoCloud. This integrated approach is designed to help customers move beyond generating renewable energy alone by also improving how energy is measured, managed and optimized across their facilities. Buskowitz Energy has extensive experience in commercial and industrial solar deployment in the Philippines, with capabilities spanning project development, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC), power purchase agreements (PPAs), and operations and maintenance (O&M). Over 3 MWp of projects currently in development Ampotech and Buskowitz are currently working together on 3.3 MWp of solar projects as part of Ampotech's engagement with PEZA locator companies in the Philippines. The collaboration is intended to support businesses operating within economic zones as they look for practical ways to manage rising energy costs, increase renewable energy adoption and improve operational efficiency. Ampotech has been actively working with PEZA and its locator companies to demonstrate how digital energy solutions can support energy efficiency, ESG data management and the integration of distributed energy resources such as solar PV and BESS. Exploring AI-powered management of existing solar assets Beyond new projects, Ampotech and Buskowitz are also discussing a separate Proof of Concept (POC) to deploy Ampotech's distributed energy resource management application across Buskowitz's existing solar portfolio. "Solar is an important part of the energy transition, but maximizing the value of a facility's energy system requires visibility and optimization across on-site generation, storage, and demand," - William Temple, CEO and Co-Founder of Ampotech. "Our collaboration with Buskowitz allows us to combine renewable energy deployment with energy efficiency and AI-driven energy management, helping businesses take a more integrated approach to reducing energy costs and improving sustainability." The proposed POC would explore how centralized digital monitoring and AI-driven analytics can provide greater visibility across distributed solar assets and support more efficient asset management. This initiative builds on Buskowitz's established commercial and industrial solar portfolio and its experience in asset monitoring, performance reporting, technical support, and ongoing operations and maintenance. "As our solar portfolio continues to grow, we see opportunities to leverage technology and data to improve how we monitor and manage our assets. Through this collaboration, we look forward to exploring how AI-powered analytics can complement our existing capabilities and support more efficient operations as we continue delivering reliable renewable energy solutions to our customers" — James Buskowitz, CEO, Buskowitz Energy Toward smarter, integrated energy systems The collaboration reflects a broader shift in how commercial and industrial facilities approach energy management. Rather than treating solar generation, battery storage and energy efficiency as separate initiatives, Ampotech and Buskowitz are exploring an integrated model in which these assets can work together as part of a smarter energy system. Through the collaboration, the companies will continue to identify suitable projects, develop integrated energy solutions and explore opportunities to apply digital intelligence across existing and new renewable energy assets. About Ampotech Ampotech provides intelligence driven energy solutions for commercial and industrial clients in Asia Pacific. With over 10 years of experience developing, deploying, and maintaining AI-enabled internet of things and energy asset solutions in the real estate and renewable energy sector, Ampotech is at the forefront of the transition to an AI-native energy sector. For more information visit our website. About Buskowitz Energy Buskowitz Energy is an energy infrastructure company with deep solar expertise. It develops, finances, builds, operates and supplies energy for Philippine businesses under contracts of 20 to 25 years. Founded in 2016, it has delivered more than 300 installations and is financed by international lenders and by institutional infrastructure investors. Website: www.ampotech.com SOURCE Ampotech

artigo.texto: Charlotte residents urge city to extend data center construction pause ‘I hope the council would do the right thing and go at least another year’ CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV) - As Charlotte leaders consider whether to extend a pause on new data centers, a group of residents in east Charlotte are urging the city to keep the freeze in place for another year. Cristopher Scalise, co-founder of STOP East Charlotte Data Center, lives about a mile from the site of a proposed 40,000-square-foot data center on Hood Road. “I wasn’t shocked to hear they wanted to put something up here, but I’m surprised at the scope of it and the size of it, right smack in the middle of a sea of residential properties,” Scalise said. The 150-day moratorium, which halts new data center development, expires Nov. 5. Scalise served on a city task force that studied data centers and potential concerns, including noise and water and energy use. He is now urging the city to extend the moratorium until it can develop policies to address possible harms. “I hope the council would do the right thing and go at least another year because, as we found on the task force, there is an enormous, enormous amount of work that still needs to be done,” Scalise said. “We’re not ready to move forward as a city on this issue.” This week, Scalise launched a webpage where residents can review timelines, key points and other research related to the first 75 day “learning period” during the moratorium. It can be accessed by clicking here. Though he is no longer on the task force, Scalise encouraged neighbors to stay involved and keep pressing elected officials for answers. “It needs to be consistent and loud,” he said. “And there needs to be this continual growth of a resistance movement that is putting constant pressure on elected officials to do the right thing for the right reason.” The City Council is expected to hold its final public hearing on a possible moratorium extension Monday night. A vote is anticipated in two weeks. Copyright 2026 WBTV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: BYD Atto 3 Gets New Atlantis Gray Colour Option in India BYD has replaced Surf Blue with Atlantis Gray on the Atto 3, which continues to offer two battery options, up to 521km of claimed range, and the same equipment list. BYD has introduced a new colour option for the Atto 3 electric SUV in India, with Atlantis Gray replacing the previously available Surf Blue. The change is limited to the exterior colour palette, with no reported updates to the SUV's features, battery packs, or performance. The Atto 3 continues to be offered in multiple variants. Also Read: BYD Denza India Entry Confirmed; Here's What to Expect BYD Atto 3: What's Changed? With Surf Blue discontinued, the BYD Atto 3 is now available in four colours: Atlantis Gray, Cosmos Black, Ski White and Harbour Grey. The SUV retains its existing design, including full-LED lighting, chrome and black exterior elements, a panoramic sunroof and either 17-inch or 18-inch wheels, depending on the variant. BYD Atto 3: Battery The electric SUV is available with 49.92kWh and 60.48kWh battery packs. Both use an electric motor that develops 201bhp and 300Nm of torque. The smaller battery offers an ARAI-certified range of 468km, while the larger unit has a claimed range of 521km. BYD claims a 0-100km/h acceleration time of 7.3 seconds. For charging, the smaller battery supports DC fast charging at up to 70kW, while the larger pack supports up to 80kW. The cabin features a 12.8-inch rotating touchscreen, wireless smartphone connectivity, wireless charging and a six-speaker audio system. Other equipment includes a powered tailgate, a 360-degree camera, an NFC key card, tyre pressure monitoring and auto-hold. The front seats are electrically adjustable, with six-way adjustment for the driver and four-way adjustment for the front passenger. Safety equipment comprises seven airbags, Level 2 advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and disc brakes on all four wheels, with ventilated discs at the front. The BYD Atto 3 is priced from Rs 24.99 lakh to Rs 34.49 lakh (ex-showroom), depending on the variant. The new colour has not brought a price increase, and the SUV's existing specifications remain unchanged.

artigo.texto: Local Georgia Democrats presented a united front against data center development Monday morning when State Sen. Harold Jones issued statements in alongside other local Democratic Party representatives in a press event at a storefront campaign hub downtown. Jones emphasized a contrast between the positions of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms and her Republican opponent Rick Jackson regarding data centers projects popping up throughout the state. “The key is we do not want data centers for small communities. We do not want our electric bills to go up. We do not want Rick Jackson to profit from data centers as he has in healthcare,” said Jones, alluding to Jackson having declined going up against Bottoms in the Atlanta Press Club election debate also scheduled for Monday night. Speaking alongside Jones were Parin Amin, chair of the Columbia County committee of the Georgia Democratic Party, and Cathi Frederiksen, chair of the Georgia Democrats’ 12th Congressional District committee. All three speakers underscored Jackson’s investment in a data center development project in Texas. “Just listen to what the Texas residents say. It’s the same thing as people in Appling and Harlem. They said it’s sold out, that the community was not involved, the [nondisclosure agreements] kept it all quiet, and they forced it down at the very last minute,” said Amin, referencing the data center developments—two out of three that have thus far been approved by the Columbia County Board of Commissioners—that have sparked controversy for most of this year. “The first time most of us heard about it was at a planning and zoning meeting, and they came, they packed the house, but they didn’t listen to us. We can do much better than the self-enriching governor for Georgia.” Frederiksen, who also chairs the Georgia Democratic Rural Council, likewise referred to a $20 billion project by artificial intelligence company OpenAI to build a data center in Effingham County, Ga., signed off by that county’s development authority last year amid claims by county leaders that it could lead to eliminating the county’s property tax. “[Rick Jackson] needs to divest today. Not after the election, but today,” said Frederiksen. “Georgia is a hotbed for data center growth. Our next governor will make decisions about land, water, power bills, and who gets a seat at the table, those decisions will shape the state for generations. We cannot afford to have someone with millions invested in data centers making these calls.” Jones outlined candidate Bottoms’ plan for data center development in Georgia: to impose a statewide moratorium to make way, he says, for a thorough investigation into their potential ramifications, to eventually discern the best course of action to regulate data centers. “I think that’s the key, because when we talk about going back in January and all of a sudden now we’re just going to try to create these ordinances, we’re going to try to create these guardrails,” he said. “What we really need to do is study the issue a little bit more, and I think that’s what she is talking about for us to make an informed decision about what we should do from a state perspective, so I think her plan is a good common sense plan about how we ought to go about doing things.” The media conference comes amid Jackson’s scheduled appearance with Governor Brian Kemp Monday evening in a Republican rally at the Columbia County Exhibition Center in Grovetown, a stop along Jackson’s campaign tour. Skyler Andrews is a reporter covering general reporting with The Augusta Press. Reach him at skyler@theaugustapress.com.

artigo.texto: - Supermicro expands its Open Compute Project portfolio with integrated AI racks, networking, power and cooling - Standardized 21-inch rack designs aim to simplify deployment of increasingly power-hungry AI systems - The move reflects growing demand for preintegrated infrastructure as server manufacturers compete to deliver complete AI clusters Supermicro is expanding its portfolio of open-standard AI infrastructure, betting that preintegrated racks, cooling systems and networking will help data center operators bring increasingly complex AI installations online faster. The company announced the expansion at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose this week, adding OCP-accepted systems, racks and rear-door heat exchangers to its Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) portfolio. The objective is to deliver more of the infrastructure required for AI computing as a validated system, rather than leaving customers to integrate servers, networking, power distribution and cooling separately. That’s an increasingly important proposition as AI infrastructure moves beyond individual servers toward entire racks and clusters, with growing demands on power delivery and heat removal. Supermicro’s expanded portfolio includes OCP Open Rack version 3 (ORv3) and Open Rack Wide (ORW) designs, centralized 48-volt DC power distribution, direct-to-chip liquid cooling, rear-door heat exchangers and management software. The ORv3 architecture uses wider, 21-inch equipment bays rather than the conventional 19-inch mounting format common in enterprise data centers. It also replaces individual server power supplies and associated cabling with centralized rack-level power distribution. Supermicro is supporting both open-rack and conventional EIA rack designs, allowing customers to select architectures appropriate to their existing facilities. Cooling becomes part of the system Power and cooling are central to the announcement. As GPUs and CPUs become more powerful, the amount of heat generated by densely packed computing equipment is becoming a major constraint on AI data center design. Supermicro’s expanded portfolio includes direct-to-chip liquid cooling and rear-door heat exchangers designed to remove residual heat from server exhaust before it enters the data hall. The company said its rear-door heat exchangers provide cooling capacities ranging from 10 kW to 120 kW, while a separate in-rack coolant distribution unit supports up to 250 kW of cooling capacity. The approach could help operators increase rack density without relying entirely on conventional room-level air conditioning, although actual performance will depend on the configuration and the facility’s cooling infrastructure. Emilio Guerrero, a Supermicro product manager speaking at the OCP event, described the shift toward more efficient power delivery and cooling. “It is a new way to deliver power more efficiently to the servers,” Guerrero said, adding that the design could support 97% heat capture. From server supplier to infrastructure integrator The announcement also reflects a broader change in the competitive position of server manufacturers. Increasingly, customers are buying complete, prevalidated computing environments rather than assembling individual components themselves. ABI Research identified this shift in its assessment of leading AI server suppliers, naming Supermicro, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Cisco as its five highest-ranked vendors. The research firm highlighted the growing importance of modularity, integrated cooling and deployment services alongside conventional server performance. It also identified openness as an increasingly important consideration, with organizations such as OCP helping establish hardware standards that can simplify upgrades and reduce dependence on proprietary designs. For Supermicro, supporting OCP specifications offers a way to combine hardware from multiple semiconductor suppliers within standardized rack-scale architectures. The company’s portfolio includes systems built around processors and accelerators from Nvidia, AMD and Intel, alongside high-performance Ethernet networking and liquid-cooling infrastructure. But open hardware standards do not necessarily eliminate vendor dependency. Operators must still consider compatibility across management software, networking, accelerators and cooling systems when selecting integrated platforms. Supermicro is also expanding its management software portfolio, including tools for monitoring and automating infrastructure across AI factories, enterprise data centers and cloud environments. That creates an interesting competitive tension: customers want the flexibility associated with open standards, while suppliers increasingly differentiate themselves through their ability to integrate and manage the complete infrastructure stack. For data center operators, the attraction is straightforward. The faster a validated AI cluster can be installed, powered, cooled and connected, the sooner it can begin delivering computing capacity. Whether standardized rack-scale infrastructure can materially reduce deployment times and costs across different facilities remains an important question. Supermicro has outlined the engineering approach but has not provided comparative deployment data in its announcement. For an industry pouring enormous amounts of capital into AI computing, that distinction is worth watching. artigo.texto: - AI workloads are pushing data centers beyond siloed management of facilities and IT resources - Operators increasingly need orchestration layers that can coordinate infrastructure in real time, not just monitor it - The payoff could be better capacity utilization, fewer performance bottlenecks and tighter control over cost and reliability Data centers have historically operated as a collection of little kingdoms, with facilities teams managing power and cooling while IT teams wrangled servers and networks. But the rise of AI and high-performance computing is making this model harder to sustain. Rather than optimizing for their own distinct metrics, data center systems increasingly need to be orchestrated together. What we’re talking about here isn’t too different from the idea of co-design between hardware and software that you might be familiar with. As GPU clusters push rack densities higher and workloads fluctuate faster, factors like compute placement, power availability, cooling capacity and even network behavior have become critical to squeezing the most out of constrained compute and power resources. That shift is creating demand for a new kind of control layer, PADO AI, Hammerhead AI and Texas Instruments told Fierce. The risk if data center operators can’t rise to the task? “Performance breaks first, followed by cost control,” PADO AI’s CEO Wannie Park said. “Poor coordination rarely causes immediate catastrophic physical failure. Instead, it triggers a domino effect across the stack,” with cascading effects hitting performance, cost controls, reliability, cooling efficiency and then network capacity, he said. “We are moving rapidly toward a software-defined control plane where compute, networking, power and cooling operate as a single, holistic optimization domain.” What does a data center orchestration layer look like? At its core, orchestration means moving beyond visibility into active coordination. Data center operators already have plenty of telemetry coming from servers, GPUs, switches, power systems and cooling equipment. The harder problem is turning those siloed feeds into a control layer that can decide, in real time, how to place workloads, adjust cooling, avoid simultaneous power peaks and make fuller use of the capacity already inside the facility. As Hammerhead AI CEO Rahul Kar explained, the goal is not simply to optimize cooling, compute or power independently, but to co-optimize them. Today, there isn’t “one large system or large system of systems that is trying to bring everything together for a common outcome,” Kar said. “If you can coordinate, orchestrate across all these different silos and bring data and controls together, you can squeeze out not only more power, but also more compute from both newer infrastructure as well as the existing infrastructure.” For instance, he added, you could use machine learning and AI to forecast when peak power utilization might happen within a data center and then use an orchestration system to control cooling, compute and anything else behind the meter as a means of managing through that peak. But coordination depends on physical infrastructure that can measure and control what is happening inside the facility. Karthik Vasanth, VP and GM for Texas Instruments’ Data Converter Business Unit, said the company is looking at data center power and cooling “in a holistic manner,” from power efficiency and telemetry to temperature sensors, leak detection and pump controls. "It has to be coordinated, because it is now a complete system solution," he said. "You cannot just say, 'I have the power, but…I don't know how to do the cooling or monitor the cooling.'" To make a coordinated system work, Park said time-synchronized telemetry is needed across four key layers of data center infrastructure: compute (servers and chips), connectivity (switches and network), thermal management (cooling systems) and electrical (power distribution systems). What roles do humans and AI have in data center orchestration? Of course, all of this data would be too much for a human to sift through and react to in real-time. So, AI and automation have a role to play here. “Automation and AI should act as the high-speed nervous system of modern data centers—handling sub-second telemetry, predictive adjustments, and real-time co-optimization across compute, power and cooling,” Park said. But that doesn’t mean humans disappear from the loop. Park said people still play a crucial role in setting strategy, governing risk, establishing policies across different infrastructure domains and stepping in when unusual failure scenarios arise. Humans are also needed to define the guardrails and weigh trade-offs that AI systems may not be able to fully measure or resolve on their own.

artigo.texto: The Poway City Council unanimously approved to ban large, third-party data centers used for artificial intelligence applications throughout the city. The ordinance approved by council members on a second reading Oct. 6 amends the Poway Municipal Code and the South Poway Specific Plan to prohibit data centers in all zones of the city. The ordinance states the city of Poway wishes to protect and preserve the public safety, health, welfare, resources and quality of development throughout the city through effective land use and planning. Mayor Steve Vaus said large-scale data centers “have very real impacts” when the item was introduced for a first reading on Sept. 15. “We are the first in the county to say no to AI data centers and I expect we will not be the last,” Vaus said during the Oct. 6 second reading of the item on the consent calendar. A staff report stated there is increasing evidence that these types of data centers use significant water and electricity and result in a strain on water and electricity infrastructure, and have an adverse impact on utility rates. Additionally, concerns include potential negative impacts on air quality, noise and increased fire risks. Vaus said banning AI data centers is a land use issue rather than a technology issue. There is a finite amount of land in the South Poway Business Park, he said. “Once that is consumed, we don’t get it back,” Vaus said. “AI data centers are simply not the highest and best use (of the land). “Local control means making these decisions before someone else makes them for us,” he added. Councilmember Anita Edmondson, who proposed the ban with Vaus, said the ban is not about entering philosophical debates over the merits of AI. Instead, her concern is with providing jobs, she said. “AI data centers are largely automated,” according to the staff report. “While they may result in temporary construction jobs, there is a lack of local, long-term jobs and economic growth provided when compared to traditional industrial, manufacturing and office uses that would otherwise be permitted in the city’s commercial areas, specifically including (the business park).” The data centers were identified in the staff report as computer servers that use high-density clusters of specialized accelerators such as graphics processing units and tensor processing units, and any associated data storage systems, for third-party entities that store, process, train or support AI applications. Speaker John Szlyk said data centers have high energy needs, the equipment needs to be cooled with large volumes of water, and they produce a constant humming noise. They also limit job growth because most of the jobs of these types of data centers are associated with maintenance of the facility, he said. Szlyk thanked the council for acting expeditiously to ban the AI data centers and requested that similar action be taken to lay down rules for pickleball courts in residential neighborhoods. Councilmember Christopher Pikus said banning AI data centers is about making the best use of limited land. Instead of an automated data center, the city could have businesses that hire people who live and shop in the community and contribute to its success, he said. “I want the business park to be a business park for everyone, not just a mausoleum for data storage,” Pikus said. “Ultimately, some proposal will come along. We have to get a regulation in place before someone drops a permit application on our desk.” Although Councilmember Jenny Maeda proposed placing a five-year moratorium on the development of AI data centers instead of a complete ban, the suggestion was not supported by the other council members.

artigo.texto: Standalone data centers, including large-scale facilities used to power artificial intelligence, are prohibited under St. Petersburg’s existing zoning regulations, according to a new memorandum from the city’s planning director. In an Oct. 9 memo to Mayor Ken Welch, Planning Director Derek Kilborn clarified how the facilities are classified under the city’s land development code. He concluded that data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. The determination comes as local governments across Pinellas County consider how to regulate the rapidly expanding industry amid concerns about electricity consumption, water resources and land availability. St. Petersburg’s zoning code contains a matrix identifying permitted land uses. Data centers are not included, and city regulations presume that uses not specifically listed are prohibited. Kilborn also examined whether data centers could qualify as similar to other permitted uses, including utility infrastructure, but found no sufficient justification. “For these reasons, Data Centers generally, and Large-Scale Data Centers explicitly, remain prohibited as a permitted, principal (P) or Special Exception (SE) use in the City of St. Petersburg,” Kilborn wrote. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Senate Bill 484, which recognizes the infrastructure and environmental challenges of large utility users, like data centers, last May. However, DeSantis preserved local authority over land use regulation in the same bill, which took effect July 1. Under the new law, a large-scale data center is defined as a facility with an anticipated monthly peak electrical demand of at least 50 megawatts at a single location. St. Petersburg’s determination applies to standalone data centers regardless of whether they meet that threshold. The memo follows similar actions elsewhere in Pinellas County. Pinellas Park approved a one-year moratorium on data center development in August. Additionally, in September, county commissioners adopted a resolution restricting large standalone facilities in unincorporated areas. Unlike those actions, St. Petersburg’s memorandum simply clarifies that standalone data centers are already prohibited under existing regulations, and presumably no further action is needed to overhaul the law. It was not indicated whether the city has received any recent data center development proposals, or whether officials are considering changes to the zoning code.

artigo.texto: Impact Carbon Appoints Christopher Morgan Zink CEO to Drive Carbon Market Growth - Leadership Transition: Christopher Morgan Zink takes over as CEO, bringing nearly two decades of experience in international carbon finance and compliance markets. - Climate and Development Impact: Impact Carbon’s programmes reach more than 1.2 million households with efficient cooking solutions and 24 million students with safe drinking water. - Carbon Market Expansion: The company is positioning for growth as demand shifts towards high-integrity carbon credits, Article 6 mechanisms and compliance markets. Impact Carbon has appointed Christopher Morgan Zink as Chief Executive Officer, effective September 30, strengthening its leadership as international carbon markets move towards stricter integrity standards and expanding compliance demand. Zink joins from Conservation International, where he served as Vice President and led the organisation’s global carbon finance activities. His appointment comes as governments and corporate buyers increasingly seek verified emissions reductions with measurable development benefits. The leadership transition places an experienced carbon finance executive at the helm of a company operating across Uganda, Nigeria and Kenya. Leadership Change Positions Impact Carbon for Expansion Zink brings nearly two decades of experience spanning conservation finance, government policy and commercial carbon markets. Before joining Conservation International, he spent 15 years working in climate and carbon finance with the Swedish government and Dutch energy trading company Eneco. His experience covers both public and private carbon financing mechanisms, providing expertise as international markets adapt to new regulatory frameworks. Impact Carbon’s founders, Evan Haigler and Tim Neville, will remain closely involved in the business. Zink will assume responsibility for day-to-day operations and strategic execution. Announcing his appointment, Zink said: “I just started as CEO of Impact Carbon. Impact Carbon is one of the longest-running carbon project developers in the market. Nearly twenty years of taking energy-efficient cooking and safe drinking water to scale, now across Uganda, Nigeria and Kenya, through every phase of the carbon market. The scale is real: well over a million households cooking on efficient stoves, and 24 million students with safe water at school. I’m still wrapping my head around these numbers.” Carbon Finance Supports Millions Across Africa Impact Carbon has spent nearly two decades developing carbon programmes that combine emissions reductions with measurable social benefits. Its energy-efficient cooking initiatives have reached more than 1.2 million households, primarily in Uganda and Nigeria. These programmes use carbon finance to support access to improved cooking technologies, potentially reducing fuel consumption and associated emissions. The company also develops and manages carbon programmes supporting Impact Water, a major provider of school-based safe drinking water. Impact Water currently serves more than 24 million students across 60,000 schools in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda. By supporting safe drinking water access, these programmes can reduce reliance on boiling water, which often requires biomass fuels. The approach connects carbon finance with broader development priorities, including public health, education and access to cleaner energy. Article 6 and Compliance Markets Shape Growth Strategy Impact Carbon has historically structured its projects with compliance markets in mind, using voluntary carbon markets to support programme development. Its experience spans the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), South Korea’s Emissions Trading System (ETS), and emerging opportunities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The company is also targeting demand associated with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). RELATED ARTICLE: Climate Impact Partners Certifies Lob’s Carbon Neutral Offering Article 6 enables international cooperation on emissions reductions, including transfers of mitigation outcomes between countries under agreed accounting requirements. For project developers, these mechanisms create potential access to new buyers while increasing expectations around verification, authorisation and environmental integrity. Zink described the company’s growth ambitions: “The company is in a growth phase, and the market is moving in the direction I have long believed it should: towards higher-quality units, Article 6 and compliance demand. I believe in the long-term fundamentals of carbon finance as a way to pay for things that work for climate and people, in the places that need them most. That is what Impact Carbon does.” African Carbon Markets Enter a New Phase Zink’s initial engagements include visits to Impact Carbon’s operations and partners in Kenya and Uganda. He is also scheduled to speak at the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali before travelling to Nigeria. His appointment comes amid growing scrutiny of carbon credit quality, particularly around additionality, emissions accounting and the durability of project benefits. For investors and corporate buyers, Impact Carbon’s strategy reflects the increasing importance of connecting verified climate outcomes with established delivery systems. Its expansion will depend on maintaining programme integrity while navigating evolving compliance requirements and buyer expectations. Across Africa, the broader challenge remains translating carbon market demand into reliable financing for climate and development projects. Impact Carbon’s leadership transition places that challenge at the centre of its next phase of growth. artigo.texto: BISMARCK, N.D. (PSC) – The North Dakota Public Service Commission (PSC) will hold a public hearing on Friday, October 23, regarding a proposal to construct a battery energy storage system in Cass County, North Dakota. Harmony Storage, LLC (a subsidiary of Geronimo Power, LLC) is requesting a siting permit for a 200-megawatt battery energy storage system with a four-hour duration to store excess power. The project also includes associated inverters, transformers, underground cables and other ancillary facilities such as fencing, roads, storm water facilities and a Battery Management System. The project will connect to the Harmony Solar collector substation via underground collection lines. The estimated cost of the project is $249 million. The Project will be capable of storing surplus power from the Harmony Solar collector substation and the existing electric grid when production exceeds system demand (oversupply). If the grid has excess energy (e.g., during periods of low demand), this energy will be routed and stored by the project for later release. Developers say the project will enhance reliability and will be able to deliver surplus energy to the grid by storing low-cost, excess generation from the Harmony Solar Project and surplus power from the grid. The Project will then be able to discharge the stored energy into the grid at times of increased demand. The project would be located on approximately 9.73 acres within the 74-acre project area in Harmony Township and would be adjacent to the planned Harmony Solar Project, which has already been permitted by the Commission. The location is approximately 4.2 miles north of Mapleton, 7.4 miles northeast of Casselton and 10.3 miles northwest of Fargo. Details for the public hearing are as follows: Friday, October 23, 2026 at 10 a.m. Central Time in the Days Inn Hotel & Governorâs Waterpark, RV Park & Fitness Center 2050 Governorâs Drive Casselton, ND 58012 The hearing provides an opportunity for members of the public to contribute to the PSCâs official record. Any comments from members of the public must be received at a hearing to be part of the record. People with concerns or support/opposition for the project are encouraged to attend the hearing and present their information. Information received after the hearing will not be part of the official record and cannot be used as a basis for the Commissionâs decision unless certain additional procedures are followed.

artigo.texto: India's Battery Storage Capacity Projected to Climb Sharply Through 2032 India's annual battery storage installations are expected to roughly double each year through the 2032 fiscal year, according to a report by Nuvama cited by Indian media, as the renewable energy buildout pulls in more investment for battery energy storage systems. The Nuvama analysis places total BESS capacity in India at 302 gigawatt-hours by 2032, compared with 6.3 GWh at present, a trajectory the analysts describe as a compound annual growth rate of 91% over the period. The Central Electricity Authority offers a more conservative view, estimating BESS installations of 236 GWh by FY32 and 1,840 GWh by 2047. The India Energy Storage Alliance said last month that rising renewable capacity will require more battery storage to support growth and give the grid greater flexibility. Discussions at the IESA Chennai Connect 2026 indicated that India would need about 888 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2035-36 to serve growing electricity demand and to integrate renewable power reliably. Ashok Jhunjhunwala, an Institute Professor at IIT Madras, described energy storage as one of the defining technologies of India's energy transition, adding that renewable energy must remain central while being backed by storage to create a stronger, more reliable and increasingly affordable power system. India has recognized the need to scale up battery storage installations substantially to keep pace with rapid renewable energy growth. Authorities plan to introduce a regulation from July 1, 2027 that would require developers of solar and wind projects to install battery storage at project sites, a step aimed at better managing renewable output and reducing curtailments. Even with a major solar and wind installation boom in recent years, India has struggled to fully use those capacities because output has often been curtailed when battery storage is unavailable. - 1. artigo.texto: The Sioux County Board of Supervisors advanced proposed data center regulations on another 4–1 vote Tuesday, October 13, following public questions about enforcement, electricity costs, agricultural impacts, and protections for neighboring properties. Supervisor Dan Altena again cast the lone opposing vote, matching the board’s September 29 decision. The amendment to County Ordinance No. 1, the county’s zoning ordinance, now moves to a third and final reading October 27 at 9 a.m. County Zoning Director Shane Walter said the proposed language had not changed between the first and second readings. He explained that the county already has a conditional-use process for industrial projects but developed additional requirements to address the particular demands of data centers. Oversight, Utilities, and Neighbor Protections Questions during Tuesday’s hearing included who would verify compliance and whether penalties would be substantial enough to discourage violations. Walter said independent studies would be required before a facility could open, with periodic reviews afterward. The county zoning director would ultimately be responsible for ensuring that oversight occurs. He said a separate fine schedule would be established, although the amounts had not yet been determined. The discussion also addressed the potential to shut down an operation that failed to comply with required agreements. On electricity, Walter pointed to the proposed 25-megawatt limit and argued that using existing, underutilized infrastructure at the former Bison project site near Hull could help spread costs among more users. He also said applicants would be responsible for necessary infrastructure improvements. “So they have to enter an agreement with the provider to do that, so that that cost is borne entirely by the applicant and not consumers,” Walter said. Other protections discussed included closed-loop cooling, setbacks, and noise limits measured at neighboring homes rather than at the data center itself. Walter said technology improvements could reduce resource demands over time. The proposal also includes a community betterment fund. Walter said the initial contribution amount and the structure of subsequent payments would be determined later. Altena Cites Residents’ Reservations Altena acknowledged the work that had gone into the proposed rules and Path One’s efforts to explain its plans through public meetings. However, he said residents who had contacted him remained uneasy about bringing a data center to the county. “I think people are still scared and worried and would like to take some time and let somebody else try it first before we do is what I’m hearing,” Altena said. He later emphasized that he recognizes the value of technology in agriculture and law enforcement. His concern, he said, was residents’ reluctance to be among the first nearby communities to host such a facility—not opposition to using data. Altena also pushed back on any suggestion that Sioux County would lose access to data services without a local center. Agriculture and the Facility’s Lifespan Students from MOC-Floyd Valley’s FFA attended as part of their preparation for an agricultural issues contest. Their questions prompted discussion about how data processing relates to farming and how the proposed rules would protect agricultural resources. Supervisor Craig Hoftyzer said he was speaking about data centers generally, rather than the specific local proposal. He pointed to precision spraying technology that identifies individual weeds instead of treating an entire field. “So instead of broadcasting chemicals over an entire field, you’re using probably seventy to eighty percent less chemicals,” Hoftyzer said. He also described combine technology that uses cameras and satellite imagery to anticipate changing crop conditions. “And the combine is automatically adjusting settings, RPMs, and ground speed to be most efficient. And the operator is not even doing that,” Hoftyzer said. Walter said the county’s approach seeks to balance agricultural preservation with industries that support the local economy. Questions about decommissioning also led to a discussion of how long a data center could operate. After Walter offered a tentative estimate of 10 to 20 years, Path One representative Gyles Uhlenhopp said the building itself could have a significantly longer life than the equipment inside it. “There’ll be a process where we have to upgrade on the inside for a variety of reasons, but that doesn’t mean that we’ll tear down the facility. That means you make an upgrade and you move from there,” Uhlenhopp said. Uhlenhopp also said smaller data centers have existed throughout the internet’s history, distinguishing them from the much larger facilities receiving national attention. Final Reading Scheduled October 27 Walter said changes could still be made before final approval, but revised language would need to return to the Planning and Zoning Commission for review and a recommendation to supervisors. Tuesday’s vote advanced the zoning amendment; it did not approve a specific data center application. Walter said Path One is interested in submitting an application if the ordinance is approved. The third and final reading is scheduled for October 27 at 9 a.m. If approved at that reading, the amendment would take effect upon publication. The proposed ordinance is available for the public to review at siouxcounty.org. Sioux County’s data center moratorium for its unincorporated parts remains in effect.

artigo.texto: City of Taylor moves forward with data center despite pushback from community TAYLOR, Texas - The city of Taylor is one step closer to getting another massive data center and power plant despite strong pushback from the community. City leaders say the deal gives them regulatory control and millions in potential revenue, but residents remain firm that they don't want these in their backyards. Data center coming to Taylor The backstory: The city of Taylor approved a development agreement for the "Taylor Technology Campus," formerly known as Project Mustang. The decision paves the way for big watt digital and powerhouse data centers to annex and develop a 664-acre campus at 3301 FM 112, east of city limits. The project is a 500-megawatt data center and a 750-megawatt natural gas-fired power generation facility. What they're saying: "Without an agreement, the land would remain in Williamson County, which has no zoning authority or ability to regulate noise, setbacks, water use or light pollution," said Daniel Seguin with the city of Taylor. Developers initially withdrew their zoning application last month. The city says it worked with the developers to make sure they’d meet regulatory standards. With the agreement, the land will be annexed into the city. "The agreement requires a 300-foot setback from the north, east and west property lines and a 700-foot setback from the south line to protect nearby homes. It limits noise to approximately 65 decibels, requires the site to meet dark site lighting standards and requires the two backup generators be tested," said Seguin. Some Taylor residents oppose the massive development The other side: While the city highlights the $28-million-dollar investment, residents made it clear they are against it. "It is very clear what we want. It's very clear that we don’t want this project, that we don’t want the gas plants, that we don’t want the data centers, that we don’t want all of this large revenue that's pouring in because we want our community, we want multifamily housing, we want intermediate housing we want small businesses," said resident Carrie D’Anna. "This isn't going to benefit anyone in Taylor. They say you can get the money, money sounds good, but we need to care about human lives, they should be more about human lives," said another resident. This isn't the first time residents have clashed over proposed data centers in Taylor. Last year, the city approved a separate 135,000 square foot data center on Carlos Parker Boulevard amid similar concerns regarding noise, light, water and air pollution. The Source: Information from the City of Taylor, Taylor residents, previous coverage and reporting by FOX 7 Austin's Jenna King

artigo.texto: - Michigan’s data center boom has brought with it some exaggerated claims from supporters and critics - Bridge spoke with experts to get their take on everything from economic benefits to local control - Among the takeaways, data centers indeed pose environmental concerns, but they aren’t raising electricity rates — at least not yet Few issues are as controversial today as data centers, which polls show are overwhelmingly opposed by Michigan residents. Amid the debates, there are plenty of exaggerated claims from both opponents and supporters. Bridge spoke with some of the leading experts in the field to separate fact from fiction. Despite assurances from state leaders that Michigan is a fitting destination to build warehouse-scale server farms across hundreds of acres, projects have been met with considerable pushback from a public worried about everything from their potential environmental impact to the unpredictable nature of artificial intelligence itself. Claim: Data centers are a new thing for Michigan What the experts say: No, but their scale is much, much bigger. “A data center is the most fantastic economic development opportunity in the last 150 years,” said business leader and former US ambassador John Rakolta Jr. before the Detroit Policy Conference this year. His company, Walbridge, is leading construction of one of the state’s largest projects: Oracle’s 1.4-gigawatt data center complex in the farmlands of Saline Township. It’s also a partner in the proposed 282-acre Google data center in Van Buren Township. Data centers have been in Michigan for decades — tucked inside office parks, university buildings and industrial parks. They’ve generally gone unnoticed as they’ve powered our email, streaming services and websites. By some estimates, there are upward of 70 commercial data centers operating in Michigan powering our digital information ecosystem. Rakolta was referring to a new class of “hyperscale” data centers that are far bigger, more powerful and more expensive. Tech companies like Meta and Amazon plan to spend trillions of dollars on AI infrastructure through 2030 with thousands of projects underway, saying the technology will usher in a new era of cost savings, increased productivity and domestic industrial development. A new generation While a standard data center facility used for cloud computing may draw around 50 megawatts of energy, the increasingly sophisticated AI systems powering large language models and neural networks require magnitudes more power. Related: - Where Michigan governor candidates stand on data centers, the environment - Survey: Michigan local leaders sour on data centers, want more regulations - Ypsilanti Township eyes moratorium on power transmission to slow U-M data center “The technology is turning data centers into a new class of industrial infrastructure,” said Hengguang Li, director of the Institute for AI and Data Science at Wayne State University. “It’s nothing like the data centers we built 30 years ago.” Near Grand Rapids, Switch, a Las Vegas company, operates what is likely Michigan’s biggest functioning data center. Appearing as a modern pyramid jutting up from the freeway, the sprawling data center in Gaines Township has expanded for AI in recent years, with a planned electrical capacity of 237 megawatts. With the growth of AI, the US and Michigan are promoting data center development to buoy the economy. In 2024, the Michigan Legislature exempted qualifying data centers from Michigan’s 6% sales and use tax. Several proposals for what the state views as “enterprise” data centers have since materialized, while communities are debating the tax breaks. Claim: Data centers move in with little regard to nearby communities What the experts say: Developers have overridden local decisions in the past, but communities can be proactive about regulation. Companies wanting to build data centers are looking for large parcels of land and access to electricity, fiber connectivity and water, said Jean Hardy, an MSU associate professor who researches digital development in rural communities. Often, that means farmland. Communities are pushing back. No fewer than 30 have enacted moratoriums on data center development. Critics say their communities are being singled out because they’re perceived as less regulated, Hardy said. Some worry that massive tech companies are able to steamroll rural locales as they scramble to effectively control data center development. Many communities in the state had not given industrial development “any serious consideration” in a long time, according to Sarah Mills, director of the Center for EmPowering Communities at the University of Michigan’s Graham Sustainability Institute. “I don’t suggest to communities that they make a data center ordinance. I think instead they should update what they expect out of industrial development,” Mills told Bridge. In Saline Township, some residents felt data center developers were able to “bully their way in.” After the township officials denied zoning for the project, developers sued, and the board settled citing expensive legal fees in fighting the lawsuit. Attorney General Dana Nessel and several environmentalists are challenging the Michigan Public Service Commission and DTE over its decisions to permit the project, saying the process was “fast-tracked” despite apparent “red flags.” Claim: Data centers are raising electricity rates What the experts say: Not true, at least for now. In promoting a responsible growth pledge for data centers, Whitmer said families “have been protected from any rate increases due to data center development.” Michigan’s residential electric rates are higher than the US average and lead the midwest. But that trend is “not related to data centers,” according to Erik Nordman, director of the Institute of Public Utilities at Michigan State University. artigo.texto: 09/10/2026 O desembargador Rafael Paulo, do Tribunal Regional Federal da 1ª Região, determinou que a ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) conclua em 48 horas a análise de pedidos de medida cautelar relacionados ao acesso ao sistema elétrico de três data centers da Pahlavan. A empresa saiu vencedora da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026, finalizada nesta semana, mas tenta desde já ter a garantia do aumento do montante de energia a ser usado da rede em 2029. A decisão, expedida na segunda-feira (6), ainda assegura que, até a deliberação da reguladora, não sejam adjudicadas propostas vencedoras na 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026 para conexão à rede na Subestação Replan, em São Paulo. Conforme a liminar, eventual capacidade remanescente do barramento na proporção dos montantes de uso de energia solicitados pela Pahlavan não poderá ser comprometida até a decisão da ANEEL. Segundo o desembargador, o restante do procedimento competitivo “prosseguirá regularmente quanto a todas as demais margens” e a determinação em questão não se trata de “reconhecimento de prioridade, reserva de capacidade ou autorização para contratação, energização ou incremento de carga”. Assim, os efeitos da liminar encerrarão após com deliberação da ANEEL, independentemente do resultado. A Pahlavan já tinha entrado com um primeiro pedido de cautelar na agência para ter a garantia do aumento do MUST (Montante de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão), que foi negado. Um recurso foi interposto na ANEEL em setembro, com novo pedido de cautelar, mas ainda não foi analisado pela reguladora. A empresa alega que seus três projetos de data centers são de grande porte, situados em Paulínia (SP), e que foram estruturados sob o regime anterior de acesso à transmissão, antes da Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão). No entanto, após o novo modelo, o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) apontou a inviabilidade dos incrementos de acesso pretendidos pela empresa. Os projetos entrariam em operação de forma escalonada, com uso da energia do sistema indo de 71 MW (megawatts) para 157 MW por unidade em 2029. Os empreendimentos já tinham portaria do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), atos autorizativos da ANEEL e pareceres de acesso e CUSTs (Contrato de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão) assinados. artigo.texto: A battery storage facility proposed for South Orange County won’t get built after residents spent years protesting the project, claiming it would be too close to homes and arguing it would pose too great of a wildfire risk. The company proposing the project officially withdrew their application last month after pressing pause on the facility as they looked for different site options. Compass Energy Storage, the company behind the proposal, withdrew their application to the California Energy Commission on Sept. 1. Their notice said the company wasn’t able to find a suitable location for the battery storage facility within their budget. “This notice is based on the inability to locate an alternative suitable site in proximity to the point of interconnect and due to changed economic conditions associated with the Project,” reads the notice, signed by Ricky Davis, vice president of Compass Energy. The project would have created a facility on 13 acres of land on the northern edge of San Juan Capistrano with lithium-iron-phosphate batteries connected to the energy grid to store excess power and release it back into the grid when necessary. These facilities — known as Battery Energy Storage Systems — are generally viewed by supporters as a positive step toward clean energy solutions since the batteries can help store and provide surplus energy, helping reduce the need for additional fossil fuel generation at high-need times. But similar facilities have also turned into fire hazards elsewhere within the state. A battery storage facility known as Moss Landing in California’s Monterey County ignited in January 2025, causing the evacuation of about 1,500 residents and complaints of health concerns like headaches, coughing and sore throats. There have also been multiple fires at battery energy storage facilities in San Diego County over the past few years, including at the Terra-Gen facility in Valley Center, the Gateway Energy facility in Otay Mesa and at the SDG&E facility in Escondido. Those facilities utilized an older battery technology, known as nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries, whereas the proposed Compass project would have used lithium iron phosphate batteries. A resident group known as BLESSIN — Ban Lithium Energy Storage Systems in Neighborhoods — spent years railing against the project proposed in OC, arguing the proposal would create a severe wildfire risk near schools and homes. During the Laguna Niguel City Council meeting on Oct. 6, Mayor Gene Johns commended several of the group’s leaders for successfully killing the project. “That was a 13-acre facility they were going to build — 1,500 feet away from homes here in Laguna Niguel,” Johns told members of the resident group during the meeting. “Because of your efforts, you put together a great group of people with great knowledge, and you fought a $80 billion worldwide company and showed them it was unsafe and it didn’t belong here.” Assemblymember Laurie Davies also attended the meeting to commend the community for their efforts. “These are community superheroes,” Davies said. “You came together and we were able to get the California Energy Commission to actually come here,” she said. “When they left, they said this was the most respectful community.” Tim Lineberger — spokesperson representing Engie North America, the parent company of Compass Energy — thanked the California Energy Commission and the community’s engagement in a Saturday email to Voice of OC. “While this specific project has been suspended, ENGIE remains committed to working with Orange County, local jurisdictions across California, and the CEC to advance clean, reliable, affordable, and safe electricity solutions for Californians,” Lineberger wrote. The San Juan Capistrano City Council voted multiple times to prohibit the construction of new commercial energy storage systems after the applicant previously submitted requests at the city level. After the city rejected the project, the applicant turned to the state instead, filing an application through the California Energy Commission, which had the power to bypass the city’s previous rulings and approve the project. A host of elected officials also spoke out against the project, including Supervisor Katrina Foley, Rep. Mike Levin, Assemblymember Diane Dixon and San Juan Capistrano city leaders. Cathleen Pryor, BLESSIN president, said the group supports clean energy but only when community members are engaged within the planning process to ensure safety for families and homes. “We support responsible clean energy development,” Pryor said. “At the same time, clean energy infrastructure must be carefully evaluated and appropriately located.” “Residents should never be excluded from decisions affecting the safety of their homes, animals, families, evacuation routes, open spaces and quality of life.” Angelina Hicks is the Voice of OC Collegiate News Service Editor. Contact her at ahicks@voiceofoc.org or on Twitter @angelinahicks13.

artigo.texto: Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas on Cost Globally, Says Report Wood Mackenzie finds four-hour battery storage cheaper than gas peaking across 43 markets worldwide. October 13, 2026. By EI News Network Four-hour battery energy storage systems (BESS) are now cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines (OCGTs) across all 43 markets where both technologies were modelled, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) report. The report attributes the shift to gas turbine shortages and fuel price volatility, which are raising gas peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing is driving storage costs down. In the Middle East and Africa, four-hour battery storage costs are estimated at USD 120/MWh in 2026 and are projected to decline by 33 percent to USD 80/MWh by 2035. The report said that storage is becoming more cost-competitive than gas peaking across every gas market in the region. Utility-scale solar remains the lowest-cost power generation technology in the Middle East and Africa, with single-axis tracker solar averaging USD 37/MWh in 2026. Its levelized cost is forecast to fall to USD 24/MWh by 2035. Solar costs in Saudi Arabia and the UAE are expected to drop below USD 20/MWh by 2033. China continues to set the global benchmark for grid-scale battery storage costs, with its levelized cost of storage more than 55 percent below the Asia Pacific regional average of USD 134/MWh. Manufacturing scale and integrated domestic supply chains are driving the cost advantage. Wood Mackenzie expects the Asia Pacific average to decline to USD 92/MWh by 2036 as competitively priced Chinese equipment influences regional markets. The report also found that single-axis tracker solar is the lowest-cost new-build generation technology in 43 of the 48 markets modelled, while onshore wind leads in the remaining five. Across Latin America, solar PV with single-axis tracking remains the cheapest generation option in 2026. Solar costs are projected to decline by 38 percent by 2060, while average onshore wind LCOE is expected to fall from USD 73/MWh to USD 58/MWh by 2030. In Europe, solar PV remains the most cost-competitive generation technology. However, battery storage turnkey capital expenditure increased by about 2 percent in 2026, marking its first annual rise in three years, as battery cell prices rebounded by around 10 percent from their 2025 lows. In North America, tariffs, trade restrictions and supply-chain constraints are putting pressure on solar costs. Meanwhile, growing electricity demand from data centres and constraints on gas-generation equipment supply are keeping thermal power investment costs elevated. Wood Mackenzie said that falling storage costs and competitive renewable energy resources are increasingly challenging the economic case for new gas peaking capacity. The report identifies battery storage as an increasingly important technology for integrating solar and wind generation and supporting power system planning. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Driven largely by the increased computing needs of artificial intelligence (AI), data centers are running out of power to grow. In the U.S., data centers are on track to consume as much as 12 percent of total U.S. electricity by 2028. Thirty percent of a data center’s total power draw comes from cooling the infrastructure. A new study looks at a way to ease that strain: pairing data center cooling systems with an emerging geothermal technology called Cold Underground Thermal Energy Storage (Cold UTES). Cold UTES stores cold water underground during off peak hours and draws it back up to meet cooling demand when it’s needed most. Unlike a conventional battery, it can hold that stored cooling capacity for weeks or even an entire season. To test the idea, Andrew Chien, the William Eckhardt Distinguished Service Professor of Computer Science at the University of Chicago, and his University of Chicago co-author Wedan Emmanuel Gnigba modeled Cold UTES equipped data centers in three major U.S. markets: Virginia, Arizona, and Texas—regions chosen for their differing climates and grid conditions. Across the three sites, Cold UTES increased available IT power capacity by 9.8 percent. The biggest gains were seen in Arizona’s hot, dry climate, where capacity rose by 11 percent. “The key benefit of Cold UTES is that is enables data centers to make better use of their grid interconnection capacity, reducing pressure on the grid for power, and enabling AI companies to run more GPUs,” says Chien of the broader research effort behind the technology. “Given the more than $10 billion price tags on AI data centers, the 11 percent increase we have demonstrated could mean savings of billions of dollars. Cold UTES ability to create flexible cooling is a powerful new way to make and operate data centers.” The technology also improved cooling efficiency and eased pressure on space constrained equipment like rooftop dry coolers, the study finds, extending how long a facility can keep scaling before it outgrows its physical footprint. The research is part of a broader Cold UTES collaboration funded by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Geothermal Technologies Office, which also includes the National Laboratory of the Rockies, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and Princeton University. “With data center operators and grid planners racing to keep pace with AI-driven power demand, the findings point to underground cold storage as one option to accelerate AI capacity at lower cost and reducing the need to build new data centers and new power plants,” Chien says.

artigo.texto: Dar es Salaam – State Minister in the Vice President’s Office for Union and Environment Hamad Masauni has rejected an allegation that the government has handed forests to Saudi or Omani companies for carbon-credit trading, calling it false and pledging to leave public office if it is proved. Masauni was responding on October 11 to a claim attributed to CHADEMA Deputy Chairperson John Heche that forests had been given to the two Gulf states, which were collecting the proceeds. Speaking during a visit to inspect environmental conditions in Dar es Salaam, Masauni said: “If he can substantiate what he said, I will quit being a minister, quit Parliament and leave Chama Cha Mapinduzi.” The minister said carbon trading was not confined to forests or the transfer of title to land. He cited opportunities in clean energy, waste, agriculture, mining and forestry, and said the government had created an institution to regulate the sector. A carbon credit is a tradable unit representing a verified reduction, avoidance or removal of one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. In practice, a project developer may sell credits to companies seeking to compensate for emissions they have not yet eliminated, while the underlying land remains subject to Tanzania’s land and environmental laws. The 2022 Carbon Trading Regulations and national guidelines established the basic framework for project registration, approval, monitoring and benefit sharing. In 2025, Parliament gave the National Carbon Monitoring Centre a statutory mandate to register projects, verify and certify credits, manage transactions and promote international cooperation. The market extends beyond forests. The guidelines cover clean energy, waste, agriculture, industrial processes, forests and blue-carbon ecosystems such as mangroves, while requiring non-community projects to explain how local communities will participate and benefit. NCMC requires developers to establish land rights or community agreements, register their project, select a standard and complete baseline, monitoring and verification processes before selling credits. Masauni said in August that 117 projects had been registered by July, and announced four approved projects led by Burn Manufacturing, AP Energy Group with Sayari SA, Water Mission International Tanzania and Bridge Carbon Tanzania. The centre currently lists nine ongoing projects and 1.117 million credits issued, suggesting that the larger government figure includes projects at different registration or assessment stages. READ MORE: Carbon Credits Trading: A New Form of Africa’s Colonialism? Carbon Tanzania, a nature-based credit developer, and the Tanzania National Parks Authority are among the better-known players through a six-national-park project announced in 2023. Internationally, Tanzania also signed a June 2026 memorandum with Singapore on possible Article 6 cooperation under the Paris Agreement. The Chanzo could not identify a Saudi or Omani project that owns Tanzanian forests or receives national carbon revenues. The more direct Gulf connection, however, is a preliminary 2023 agreement with UAE-based Blue Carbon, reported as covering about eight million hectares of forest reserves. Saudi Arabia is also a significant regional buyer and marketplace builder. Its sovereign wealth fund and Saudi Tadawul formed the Regional Voluntary Carbon Market Company, which auctioned more than 2.2 million credits in Nairobi in 2023, most originating in the Middle East and Africa. The sector’s rapid growth has also prompted scrutiny. Then-Vice President Philip Mpango said in 2025 that limited public understanding and the dominance of a small number of brokers were barriers. At the same time, Maasai representatives and advocacy groups have raised concerns about consent, benefit sharing and grazing restrictions in proposed northern soil-carbon projects.
