artigo.texto: First the city, now the county debates a data center temporary moratorium A narrow vote with four commissioners abstaining moves a proposed pause on data centers in unincorporated Shelby County to a second reading. MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Shelby County commissioners narrowly advanced a proposed temporary moratorium on data centers in unincorporated areas outside city limits Monday, despite questions about whether a pause is necessary when no projects are currently identified in those areas. The measure passed its first reading in a 5-4 vote, with four commissioners abstaining. It must clear another vote and a third reading before the commission can make a final decision. Supporters argue the county should establish regulations before a data center developer proposes a project, while opponents have raised concerns about the county’s legal authority and whether a moratorium is the right approach. Commissioner Erika Sugarmon, who represents District 12 and introduced the ordinance alongside Commissioner Henri. E. Brooks, said the proposal is intended to give the county time to establish rules before data center development becomes a possibility in unincorporated areas. “The problem is if we don’t have anything in place and the data centers decide to move in... then there’s no such thing as ex post facto laws,” Sugarmon said. “That’s illegal. So if they move in, they come in without regulations.” Dr. Sugarmon emphasized that the goal is not to prevent data centers from coming to the county permanently, but to ensure rules are established before development begins. Other commissioners, like Commissioner Amber Huett-Garcia, who represents District 13, raised concerns about the county’s legal authority and the language of the proposed ordinance. Huett-Garcia is proposing an alternative focused on establishing regulatory guardrails rather than imposing a temporary moratorium. “I think we have citations incorrect about what our powers really are,” Huett-Garcia said. “And the attributed powers of city council are different from those of county government. So, I want us to clean this up at a minimum.” Huett-Garcia also pointed to infrastructure considerations, including the fact that unincorporated Shelby County does not have independent power and water infrastructure. Her proposal would focus on clarifying the county’s authority and determining what regulations it can establish for potential data center development. Some young residents who have followed the debate said they feel regulatory protections alone may not go far enough. Jasmine Bernard, a 17-year-old Shelby County resident, argued that the county should consider a moratorium and regulatory guardrails together rather than as competing options. “But if these guardrails and these extra ordinances mean that we will not be passing the moratorium, then we’re not actually solving the full issue, and we’re not getting to the root cause of what’s harming our communities,” Bernard said. “So we need guardrails and a moratorium. You can’t pick one or the other.” Hayden Wakefield encouraged residents to make their voices heard by contacting commissioners and representing their districts in the discussion. “I feel like if all of us spoke out and all of us represented each district, then they would listen to us more, and more things would be passed exactly like this,” Wakefield said. The proposed moratorium now moves to a second reading, where commissioners will have another opportunity to debate and vote on the measure before a final decision. The discussion comes as Memphis City Council considers its own temporary moratorium on data centers. Dr. Sugarmon said coordination between the county and city will be important because regulations adopted within Memphis could affect surrounding unincorporated communities. For now, commissioners must decide whether to pursue a temporary pause on data center development, establish regulatory guardrails or consider a combination of both approaches. The commission’s next vote will determine whether the proposed moratorium advances toward final approval. The Memphis City Council will vote on the municipal data center moratorium October 20. artigo.texto: Protesters call for oversight of data centers, Flock cameras at Michigan Capitol LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - Dorr Township resident Rachel McGrady-Hawley joined protesters on the Capitol steps Wednesday calling for more oversight before data center projects move forward. McGrady-Hawley said her life turned upside down after learning about a data center development proposed across the street from her home. “And my focus went from guiding my child through her senior year, from trying to stop this data center campus from going in across the street from my home. And that’s what my life has been like since,” McGrady-Hawley said. Residents oppose neighborhood data centers “We just don’t feel like it’s a good fit for our community, we don’t believe that data centers belong in neighborhoods,” McGrady-Hawley said. Marjorie Steele with the Economic Development Responsibility Alliance of Michigan said the issue has united people from all walks of life. “Michiganders as a whole across the political aisles are tired of being ignored. They are tired of having projects that they don’t want forced on them, and they are tired of their politicians telling them that there’s nothing they can do,” Steele said. Supporters of data center developments claim they create local jobs and boost the local economy and tax revenue. Surveillance concerns raised Attendees also spoke out against the use of Flock cameras and other automated surveillance methods. “I haven’t met a single Michigander who is in favor of this kind of AI-automated surveillance,” Steele said. Law enforcement officials have said the cameras make a difference in solving serious crimes. Attendees said regardless of who represents them at the Capitol, communities will continue to speak up at the local level. “These issues that we’re all battling, they’re non-partisan, they’re about all of us. And it turns out we Michiganders have a lot more in common, you know, than we have different,” Steele said. Candidates weigh in The protest was hosted by Libertarian candidate for Michigan’s governor, Anthony Hudson. Hudson said he invited the other candidates, Jocelyn Benson and John James, to participate, but they did not attend. Both Benson and James shared their stances on data centers in a recent debate, in which they called for guardrails and protections for local communities. artigo.texto: Green credit partners with the carbon market, unlocking capital flows for businesses. (Chinhphu.vn) - Green credit provides capital for businesses to transform their technology, while the carbon market opens up opportunities to generate revenue from emission reductions. According to Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh, these two tools can complement each other, enhancing the efficiency of mobilizing and utilizing green capital. The carbon market opens up additional resources for green transition. Speaking at the workshop "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) Nguyen Ngoc Canh emphasized that fulfilling the COP26 commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 requires significant resources for technological innovation, energy transition, and greenhouse gas emission reduction. Besides the state budget, capital and monetary markets, the carbon market plays a crucial role in mobilizing resources, transforming emission reduction results into economic value, and encouraging businesses to proactively transition to green. Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange, along with the pilot phase in 2025-2026, with a scale of over 511 million tons of CO₂ equivalent across three sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement, creates the legal basis for the development of the carbon market. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, green credit and the carbon market have a complementary relationship. Green credit provides capital for businesses to invest in clean technologies, save energy, and reduce emissions. Conversely, an efficiently functioning carbon market can help businesses generate revenue from emission reductions, improve cash flow, and enhance debt repayment capacity, thereby contributing to improving the quality of bank credit. For green capital to be effective, the issue is not just about funding projects identified as green, but also about measuring and verifying the results of energy savings, emission reduction, and environmental protection. Measuring, reporting, and evaluating emission reduction results, as well as trading in carbon quotas and credits, will provide additional data for credit institutions to assess capital efficiency, monitor projects, and manage risks. Connecting green credit with the carbon market will help unlock resources for businesses to transform their technology, reduce emissions, and move towards sustainable growth. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, since the start of green credit implementation in 2017, this activity has expanded both in terms of credit scale and the level of participation of credit institutions. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit is expected to reach over VND 856,000 billion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. In the context of growing capital demand for green transformation, the carbon market is expected to open up additional financial resources, reducing pressure on bank credit. According to the Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, during the period 2017-2025, green credit is expected to grow by an average of over 20% per year, with expansion in both scale and the number of participating credit institutions. Capital flows are primarily concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; green energy accounts for nearly 28%. Notably, outstanding loans assessed for environmental and social risks reached over 6.2 trillion VND, accounting for over 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy. However, the capital needs for green transition remain enormous. According to Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, Vietnam estimates it needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Specifically for the electricity sector, the estimated investment needed for developing power sources and grids during the 2026-2030 period, according to the revised Power Development Plan VIII, is approximately 136 billion USD. According to Mr. Giap, the carbon market creates economic incentives for emission reduction, while credit provides capital for businesses to invest. Both tools are only effective when the project has a viable cash flow, the ability to repay debt, and verifiable emission reduction results. Revenue from carbon credits can come from selling credits, energy savings, or reduced quota purchase costs. However, banks need to assess the likelihood of credit approval, output, selling price, verification costs, and timing of collection before including this revenue source in their debt repayment plan. At the workshop, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank , stated that Agribank's green credit outstanding reached nearly 30,000 billion VND by the end of March 2026. Developing a measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) system, standardizing data, and reducing verification costs for small businesses and cooperatives are also crucial conditions for expanding their market access. Furthermore, it is necessary to develop the demand for carbon credits, ensure transparency in payment standards and conditions; and utilize guarantees, preferential capital, and technical support to address specific project risks. artigo.texto: A Green Credit estabelece parcerias com o mercado de carbono, desbloqueando fluxos de capital para empresas. (Chinhphu.vn) - O crédito verde fornece capital para que as empresas transformem sua tecnologia, enquanto o mercado de carbono abre oportunidades para gerar receita com a redução de emissões. De acordo com o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã, Nguyen Ngoc Canh, essas duas ferramentas podem se complementar, aumentando a eficiência na mobilização e utilização do capital verde. O mercado de carbono abre recursos adicionais para a transição verde. Em seu discurso no workshop "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", realizado em 14 de outubro, o vice-governador do Banco Estatal do Vietnã (SBV), Nguyen Ngoc Canh, enfatizou que o cumprimento do compromisso da COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050 exige recursos significativos para inovação tecnológica, transição energética e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Além do orçamento estatal, dos mercados de capitais e monetários, o mercado de carbono desempenha um papel crucial na mobilização de recursos, na transformação dos resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico e no incentivo às empresas para uma transição proativa para energias verdes. O Decreto nº 29/2026/ND-CP sobre a troca de carbono no mercado interno, juntamente com a fase piloto em 2025-2026, com uma escala superior a 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente em três setores: energia térmica, ferro e aço e cimento, cria a base legal para o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono. Segundo o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh, o crédito verde e o mercado de carbono têm uma relação complementar. O crédito verde fornece capital para que as empresas invistam em tecnologias limpas, economizem energia e reduzam as emissões. Por outro lado, um mercado de carbono eficiente pode ajudar as empresas a gerar receita com a redução de emissões, melhorar o fluxo de caixa e aumentar a capacidade de pagamento de dívidas, contribuindo assim para a melhoria da qualidade do crédito bancário. Para que o capital verde seja eficaz, a questão não se resume apenas a financiar projetos identificados como verdes, mas também a medir e verificar os resultados em termos de economia de energia, redução de emissões e proteção ambiental. A mensuração, o relato e a avaliação dos resultados da redução de emissões, bem como a negociação de cotas e créditos de carbono, fornecerão dados adicionais para que as instituições de crédito avaliem a eficiência do capital, monitorem projetos e gerenciem riscos. Conectar o crédito verde ao mercado de carbono ajudará a desbloquear recursos para que as empresas transformem sua tecnologia, reduzam as emissões e avancem rumo ao crescimento sustentável. Você também pode gostar O crédito verde ultrapassou 856 trilhões de VND. Segundo o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh, desde o início da implementação do crédito verde em 2017, essa atividade se expandiu tanto em termos de escala de crédito quanto no nível de participação das instituições de crédito. Até o final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde deverá ultrapassar 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025. No contexto da crescente demanda de capital para a transformação verde, espera-se que o mercado de carbono disponibilize recursos financeiros adicionais, reduzindo a pressão sobre o crédito bancário. Segundo o vice-governador do Banco Estatal do Vietnã, durante o período de 2017 a 2025, o crédito verde deverá crescer em média mais de 20% ao ano, com expansão tanto em escala quanto no número de instituições de crédito participantes. Os fluxos de capital concentram-se principalmente na agricultura , silvicultura, pesca e conservação da biodiversidade, representando mais de 31%; a energia verde representa quase 28%. Notavelmente, os empréstimos pendentes avaliados quanto aos riscos ambientais e sociais atingiram mais de 6,2 trilhões de VND, representando mais de 31,33% do total de empréstimos pendentes em toda a economia. No entanto, as necessidades de capital para a transição verde continuam enormes. De acordo com Bui Minh Giap, economista-chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, o país estima que precisa de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Especificamente para o setor elétrico, o investimento estimado necessário para o desenvolvimento de fontes de energia e redes durante o período de 2026 a 2030, de acordo com o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisado, é de aproximadamente 136 bilhões de dólares. Segundo o Sr. Giap, o mercado de carbono cria incentivos econômicos para a redução de emissões, enquanto o crédito fornece capital para que as empresas invistam. Ambas as ferramentas só são eficazes quando o projeto apresenta fluxo de caixa viável, capacidade de pagamento da dívida e resultados verificáveis de redução de emissões. A receita proveniente de créditos de carbono pode advir da venda de créditos, da economia de energia ou da redução dos custos de aquisição de cotas. No entanto, os bancos precisam avaliar a probabilidade de aprovação do crédito, a produção, o preço de venda, os custos de verificação e o cronograma de recebimento antes de incluir essa fonte de receita em seu plano de pagamento de dívidas. No workshop, a Dra. artigo.texto: Washington County, VA approves zoning ordinance for battery storage facilities Washington County, Virginia, is clamping down on where large-scale battery storage facilities can be built. On Tuesday night, the Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a new zoning ordinance that takes effect immediately. The law restricts utility-scale battery facilities—the kind often used by data centers—strictly to manufacturing zones. Officials say the rule ensures these facilities stay close to existing power lines and substations to keep taxpayer costs down. It also guarantees that no project can start without explicit local approval. Moving forward, any developer looking to build a battery storage site in Washington County must first secure a special exception vote from the board.

artigo.texto: Schrödinger Research Published in Nature Reveals New Insights into Lithium-Ion Battery Chemistry New study uncovers multi-lithium ion clustering in common battery electrolytes, paving the way for improved battery performance and design NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 14, 2026-- Schrödinger, Inc. (Nasdaq: SDGR) today announced the publication of new research in Nature that reveals critical insights into the atomic-scale structure of lithium-ion battery (LIB) electrolytes. In a joint study with researchers from Columbia University and the New York Structural Biology Center, the team discovered new insights that challenge long-held assumptions of the fundamental chemistry of lithium-ion batteries, including multi-lithium ion complexes that may play an important role in electrolyte behavior and battery function. These new mechanistic insights into electrolyte behavior have the potential to transform battery development from empirical trial-and-error toward predictive design to high-throughput, rational, computationally-driven design for higher-capacity, faster-charging, and longer-lasting batteries. The research, which leveraged Schrödinger’s physics-powered computational platform, addresses a long-standing bottleneck in energy storage design. LIB electrolytes are crucial for battery performance, influencing properties such as conductivity, viscosity, salt dissociation, and electrochemical stability. LIB electrolytes also drive the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase, which is the critical protective film on the battery anode that dictates battery lifespan and safety. However, a detailed atomic-level understanding of how electrolyte structure impacts these properties had remained limited. Utilizing Schrödinger’s advanced machine learning force field technology, the team simulated LIB electrolytes at unprecedented accuracy and scale. These simulations showed that lithium ions frequently form clusters coordinated by ethylene carbonate solvent molecules without the presence of anions, a fundamental structural phenomenon previously unrecognized. “Simulating complex battery systems has historically forced scientists to choose between quantum precision and large-scale simulation. Our machine learning force field technology eliminates that trade-off,” stated Mat Halls, senior vice president, materials science, of Schrödinger. “Predicting these multi-lithium complexes and validating them experimentally demonstrates that our platform can detect previously inaccessible chemical phenomena to accelerate materials discovery.” “Using Schrödinger’s proprietary, advanced machine learning force fields, we discovered lithium ions in batteries actually group together into clusters in the absence of anions, and that these clusters are what drive the creation of the protective film on the battery's surface,” stated Richard Friesner, co-founder and member of the Board of Directors at Schrödinger, and William P. Schweitzer Professor of Chemistry at Columbia University. “Predicting this unexpected chemistry computationally and confirming it experimentally demonstrates that Schrödinger’s physics-powered platform can accurately model the hidden atomic details of batteries. Furthermore, these results suggest that many, if not most, complex chemical systems are now amenable to predictive physics-based simulation using machine learning force fields to atomic resolution.” Key Findings: - Multi-Lithium Ion Clustering: In standard battery electrolytes, up to 40% of lithium ions group together into multi-ion clusters, with clustering becoming even more prevalent at higher salt concentrations. This finding upends the long-held assumption that lithium ions remain predominantly isolated in solution. - Accurate Experimental Validation: The machine learning force field simulations demonstrate strong agreement with a wide range of condensed-phase experimental data, including NMR spectra, electrolyte density, viscosity, ionic conductivity, and diffusion coefficients, confirming the physical reality of the predicted multi-lithium clusters. - Electrochemical Implications: Quantum chemical calculations indicate that these multi-lithium clusters have uniquely facile reduction potentials, suggesting they are key intermediates in the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase, which is critical for battery longevity and safety. - Foundation for Rational Electrolyte Design : The insights gained provide a fundamental understanding that can guide the rational design of next-generation electrolytes with enhanced performance, stability, and charge rates. This research is ongoing and is supported by funding from Gates Ventures. About Schrödinger Schrödinger is transforming molecular discovery with its computational platform, which enables the discovery of novel, highly optimized molecules for drug development and materials design. Schrödinger’s software platform is built on more than 30 years of R&D investment and is licensed by biotechnology, pharmaceutical and industrial companies, and academic institutions around the world. Schrödinger also leverages the platform to advance a portfolio of collaborative and proprietary programs. To learn more, visit www.schrodinger.com, follow us on LinkedIn. artigo.texto: Power Integrations and Ideal Power Collaborate on Efficient, Always-On Solid State Circuit Breakers for 800 VDC AI Data Centers Collaboration addresses protection, control, and power conversion challenges in emerging 800 VDC AI Infrastructure SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 12, 2026-- Power Integrations (NASDAQ: POWI), the leader in high-voltage integrated circuits for energy-efficient power conversion, and Ideal Power Inc. (NASDAQ: IPWR), developer and provider of its innovative and widely patented B-TRAN® bidirectional semiconductor power switch, today announced a collaboration to deliver a solid-state circuit breaker (SSCB) solution providing fast, efficient, always-on protection that scales with the 800 VDC transition in AI data centers. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261012559063/en/ The companies will collaborate on a new architecture combining Power Integrations’ 1700 V InnoMux-2 power conversion ICs with Ideal Power’s B-TRAN® switches to deliver a self-powered, intelligent, ultra-fast SSCB. They have also demonstrated a working prototype and are working on a reference design. Rising voltages and rack power levels in AI data centers create a need for innovative approaches to circuit protection. Mechanical circuit breakers are too slow to protect sensitive rack equipment, while existing electronic breakers introduce losses, reducing system efficiency. Further, electronic breakers must be powered from the 800 V bus. In the next generation intelligent SSCB architecture, the InnoMux-2 IC converts 800 V into isolated power for gate-drive, control electronics, sensing, and auxiliary circuitry. Ideal Power’s B-TRAN® switch uses that intelligence to protect the 800 V power path to the AI computing load. The InnoMux-2 IC features 1700 V PowiGaN technology, which can operate from an 800 VDC bus with significant margin. The IC provides multiple independently regulated outputs instead of a conventional architecture with one isolated PSU followed by multiple DC-DC converters. The result is a highly efficient, self-powered protection solution that eliminates the need for an external auxiliary supply while enabling ultra-fast fault isolation. “As AI data centers move toward 800 VDC power architectures, the industry must address new challenges in power conversion, control, and protection at the system level,” said Chris Jacobs, senior vice president of marketing and product strategy at Power Integrations. “By combining Power Integrations' 1700 V InnoMux-2 IC with Ideal Power's innovative bidirectional solid-state circuit protection, we are helping enable intelligent 800 VDC power architectures that improve efficiency, resiliency, and scalability in next-generation AI data centers.” “High efficiency, ultra-fast fault interruption is essential for enabling the migration to 800 VDC AI data centers and energy infrastructure. Traditional protection methods are proving to be inadequate. Mechanical breakers are too slow, while previous semiconductor-based breakers have historically been disqualified by high power loss,” said David Somo, CEO of Ideal Power. “Power Integrations offers a unique combination of 1700 V GaN capability, multiple independently regulated outputs, high integration, and a compact solution footprint that is well suited to our 800 VDC solid-state circuit breaker architecture, which must meet demanding power efficiency requirements and strict mechanical constraints.” Resources For further information on Power Integrations, please visit the resource page on the web site. About Power Integrations Power Integrations, Inc. is a leading innovator in semiconductor technologies for high-voltage power conversion. The company’s products are key building blocks in the clean-power ecosystem, enabling the generation of renewable energy as well as the efficient transmission, conversion and consumption of power in applications ranging from milliwatts to megawatts in applications such as AI data centers, EVs and high-voltage direct current infrastructure. For more information, please visit www.power.com. About Ideal Power Inc. Ideal Power (Nasdaq: IPWR) is the developer and provider of its innovative and widely patented B-TRAN® bidirectional semiconductor power switch. B-TRAN® offers compelling advantages over conventional technologies and addresses the demanding standards of today’s solid-state circuit protection and intelligent power delivery systems. It features very low conduction losses that deliver improved power efficiency, thereby reducing energy consumption and providing cost savings. The unique bidirectional capability of B-TRAN® simplifies the design, control, and diagnostics of solid-state power solutions while enabling smaller, lower cost systems. B-TRAN® delivers compelling advantages for a broad spectrum of applications including solid-state circuit breakers, static transfer switches, battery disconnect units, and EV contactors that are widely used in data centers, industrial power systems, energy grid and storage systems, and electric vehicles and charging infrastructure. For more information, visit the Company’s website at www.IdealPower.com, on LinkedIn, on Twitter, and on Facebook. artigo.texto: Rivian and Redwood Materials Expand Partnership to Span the Lifecycle of the Battery Redwood will now recycle Rivian’s battery scrap and end-of-life packs as well as provide energy storage for its manufacturing plant IRVINE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 14, 2026-- American automaker Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) and energy technology company Redwood Materials today announced a major expansion of their partnership, establishing Redwood as one of Rivian's key partners to enabling end-to-end energy solutions—recycling Rivian’s production scrap and end-of-life EV batteries, as well as providing stationary battery storage at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. Through the partnership, Redwood collects Rivian EV battery packs through Rivian’s nationwide network of service centers when they are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. Redwood then evaluates each battery pack to determine whether to repurpose it for energy storage—deployed directly at Rivian's manufacturing facilities or at other locations—or to recycle it. Redwood will now also recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian's manufacturing operations. This new scope of the partnership builds on the existing work, announced in April 2026, that is deploying 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage from repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker's manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. “Giving Rivian battery packs a second life in stationary storage is a massive unlock for the energy transition," said RJ Scaringe, Rivian Founder and CEO. "By partnering with JB and the Redwood team, we're turning retired EV batteries into a powerful tool to make the grid more reliable and lower energy costs for everyone.” "Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials," said JB Straubel, Redwood Materials Founder and CEO. "Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.” When EV batteries reach the end of their useful lives in vehicles, they often still have substantial useful energy capacity for second-life applications, such as stationary storage. Energy storage applications with repurposed batteries can ease stress on the grid during periods of high electricity demand, improving grid reliability while reducing energy costs for the user, as well as the grid at large. During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, these packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. When paired with Rivian—and other—EV battery packs, Redwood's proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving. Once batteries are no longer useful in energy storage applications, or where scrap is generated during manufacturing, they can be recycled. Redwood's advanced process is capable of recycling and recovering critical minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper at rates exceeding 95 percent, encouraging the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the United States. This expanded partnership reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. As grid connections take years to secure and conventional infrastructure remains supply-constrained, companies increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem—recovering materials, managing recycling, and deploying storage as a single system rather than separate vendors. Rivian’s work with Redwood is a model for that approach: one partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery, built to move faster than the grid alone can. About Rivian Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) is an American automotive technology company that develops and manufactures category-defining electric vehicles as well as vertically integrated technologies and services. Through innovation across its electrical architecture, end-to-end software, autonomous driving platform, artificial intelligence and propulsion, the company creates vehicles that excel at work and play while accelerating the global transition to zero-emission transportation and energy. Rivian vehicles are manufactured in the United States and are sold directly to consumer and commercial customers. Whether taking families on new adventures or electrifying fleets at scale, Rivian vehicles all share a common goal—preserving the natural world for generations to come. Learn more about the company, products, and careers at www.rivian.com. About Redwood Materials Redwood Materials is building the U.S. stockpile of critical materials and deploying large-scale energy storage. Founded by JB Straubel, the company produces lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper, and cathode active material at scale in the U.S., manufactures key components for advanced batteries, and deploys energy storage systems that power data centers and the nation’s grid. Redwood is expanding domestic capacity for next-generation energy storage and strengthening U.S. energy dominance. Learn more at www.redwoodmaterials.com. artigo.texto: Em outubro de 2026, drones ucranianos atingiram um centro de dados de inteligência artificial da Yandex, empresa russa frequentemente chamada de “o Google russo”, e tiraram a estrutura de operação, segundo a Ars Technica. A publicação Ars Technica não divulgou a data exata nem a localização da instalação atingida. Também não foram informados números sobre prejuízos financeiros ou quantidade de servidores danificados. A Yandex domina serviços de busca, mapas e plataformas digitais na Rússia, e expandiu sua infraestrutura para processamento de inteligência artificial. A empresa não se pronunciou publicamente sobre o incidente, segundo a Ars Technica. O ataque ao centro de dados de IA demonstra que a guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia passou a mirar a infraestrutura computacional que sustenta tanto a economia de guerra quanto sistemas de vigilância. A computação de alto desempenho se tornou um ativo estratégico. Diferentemente de alvos tradicionais, a neutralização de um data center de IA compromete a capacidade de processamento massivo de dados, essencial para logística, inteligência e monitoramento em tempo real. A Ars Technica destacou que o ataque representa um precedente em conflitos armados, ampliando o escopo de alvos para infraestrutura digital crítica. Segundo a Ars Technica, a paralisação do centro de dados interrompeu serviços associados à Yandex, mas a extensão do impacto sobre usuários e clientes corporativos não foi detalhada. O episódio consolida a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial como frente de batalha na guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia, de acordo com a Ars Technica.

artigo.texto: Federal regulators on Friday rejected PJM’s plan for curtailing large loads that failed to procure their own capacity, finding it would intrude into state authority and unfairly single out new large loads. Regulators did approve PJM’s proposed large load registry, a centralized database to be managed by the grid operator which will track all current and prospective loads of 50 megawatts or more. PJM’s proposed “Interim Resource Adequacy Service,” part of its broader framework for shielding consumers from the cost of serving data centers, would have curtailed data centers and other large loads that don’t bring their own new capacity, and assigned the responsibility for curtailing them to states. Notably, it would have curtailed those loads at the earliest stages of emergency grid conditions, before customers enrolled in voluntary demand response. For the tech companies and aggregators already signing a flurry of these so-called bring-your-own-capacity deals in the region, the rejection is certainly a setback, said Mary Yang, former regulatory counsel for PJM and chief operating officer at 804 Advisory. But it’s not necessarily a dealbreaker for BYOC, she added. Many of those deals were already in limbo, she added, ready and waiting to close, but not yet signed because companies were waiting for more clarity on how exactly BYOC rules would work. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s ruling, though not unexpected, gives them no relief. Now, Yang added, the uncertainty “is going to keep dragging,” in part because PJM is juggling a number of competing priorities, and re-writing IRAS rules isn’t likely to be the top one. “It does slow down the development of these more innovative bilateral mechanisms to solve some of these problems,” Yang added. “There’s a point at which it becomes challenging to wait longer. We are seeing anecdotally a lot of people saying ‘Okay, PJM needs to sort itself out, let’s go to a different region that’s got more certainty.” But aggregators — including those like Voltus who are pushing distributed energy resources for BYOC deals — aren’t particularly worried about the ruling, in large part because most stakeholders expect states to implement IRAS regimes of their own. The real regulatory momentum in PJM is in the hands of states, Yang added. And now, with the approval of PJM’s large load registry, states will have the data they need to shape their own standards. An expected setback Last week’s ruling was largely anticipated, particularly because FERC had already instructed PJM to rework its plan for securing new supply to meet load growth, including via a centralized, one-time auction. For distributed resource aggregators looking to sign bring-your-own-distributed-capacity deals with hyperscalers, the delay in the backstop auction was generally seen as positive, because it provides more time for inking those agreements. But the rejection of IRAS is more complicated, and more consequential for other parts of the country, where grid operators are watching closely to see how PJM’s attempt at curtailment plays out. In another potential setback for aggregators, FERC also rejected the grid operator’s proposed rules for BYOC deals, which would have allowed large loads to avoid IRAS curtailment. FERC highlighted as problematic several elements that aggregators had applauded as expanding potential participation. For example, PJM proposed locking in resource capacity accreditation values for 10 years, which FERC said would give those resources preferential treatment — and in the long run, would risk counting capacity they can’t actually provide, and shifting costs onto existing ratepayers. PJM’s plan would also have allowed distributed capacity to be delivered anywhere in the market, rather than within the specific, constrained zone where a large load is located. That approach, FERC said, doesn’t take into account transmission constraints between the data center and the distributed resources, and could “exacerbate the resource adequacy shortfall.” That said, it isn’t clear from FERC’s ruling whether the commission is rejecting those features outright, or seeking stronger justification for them, Yang explained. A future design for IRAS could still preserve similar benefits in a different form. For generators, the ruling’s impact will largely depend on the details of a specific deal, Yang said. In some cases, signing a bilateral deal as soon as possible may become more attractive given the ongoing uncertainty over the central procurement auction. But other generators considering bilateral agreements might see the delays as useful wiggle room to see whether it will make sense for them to instead get in on the central auction. Looking ahead IRAS drew pushback from stakeholders including merchant generators, state utility regulators, and the AI companies themselves. Supporters of the plan, including Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, argued that targeting non-capacity-backed large loads for curtailment would prevent the financial and operational strain of interconnecting data centers from being shifted onto everyday consumers. For data centers, their biggest problem with PJM’s approach had to do with curtailment authority, Yang said. In its plan, PJM assigned the responsibility of enforcement to states and utilities, meaning those entities and not the grid operator would ultimately decide which large loads get curtailed when, and by how much. The concern among data centers was that even if they do bring new capacity, they could still be asked to curtail. FERC, in its ruling, said PJM is welcome to refile an alternative proposal for IRAS, but laid out strict guidelines for what would have to be overhauled. artigo.texto: - Meta built a massive AI data center cluster in Ohio - And it innovated several new infrastructure techniques for that data center - Now, the company is building the world's biggest data center in Louisiana OCP GLOBAL SUMMIT, SAN JOSE, CALIFORNIA — The Open Compute Project (OCP) conference has been around for about 15 years, but 2026 is definitely its biggest year, so far. About 15,000 people are attending the sold-out conference to get together and talk about compute hardware. And more specifically, to talk about compute hardware and infrastructure for AI. A speaker from Meta Platforms kicked off the conference this afternoon with his presentation about Meta’s AI data centers. And he kind of blew everyones’ minds. Santosh Janardhan, head of Global Infrastructure with Meta, first talked about solving multiple problems for the company’s huge data center complex in New Albany, Ohio, which is named Prometheus. And then he gave a preview of Meta’s new, gargantuan data center in Richland Parish, Louisiana. Prometheus includes over 30 structures, millions of miles of fiber-optic cables and tens of thousands of GPUs. “Constructing it ended up being quite an epic journey,” said Janardhan. One of the first problems Meta had to solve was the networking between all the different structures. Historically, data centers have been built as a single building, under one roof. But in the case of Prometheus with its multiple structures, the distances between the buildings would have caused unacceptable time delays for connectivity. “When you do AI training, it moves forward at the speed of the slowest conversation that you can have between two GPUs,” said Janardhan. “The physics is simple. You essentially want to create a lossless network.” To do this, Meta created what Janardhan called an “Ethernet super spine.” He said, “You take the spines of all the buildings in the region, string them together and aggregate them locally.” The advantage is that there are no stops, so no single points of failure. “And the other thing to understand here is that this thing is fast — tens of petabits a second,” he said. “You can transmit the whole Library of Congress in less than 30 seconds.” (For a deeper technical dive into Meta’s data center inter-building networking, check out this blog.) He also noted the massive amounts of fiber optic cable needed for Prometheus, showing the below photo of some of the cables. “Each one of those pipes that you see are serving actually thousands of strands of fiber,” he said. “In fact, if you aggregate all the network fiber we have in Prometheus, it's about three to four million kilometers of fiber. You can go to the moon and back, four times. The physical manifestations of AI training truly boggles your mind.” Another problem that Meta solved was speeding up the construction of buildings. Historically, data centers have been built with steel and concrete. But Meta re-thought that because it wanted to build its data centers faster. So, it decided to build tents, instead. “Each one of our tents is the length of minimum two football fields, he said. These are humongous. And this takes months to build, not years. Because time-to-market matters.” But he said the tents are “fairly robust” — rated for a category 1 hurricane — “because you’re putting in billions of dollars’ worth of equipment in it.” While it was reimagining everything about data centers, Meta figured — why not also reformulate concrete? Janardhan said, “I don't think people understand how much concrete is used in the world. And it’s not great for the environment. It takes a lot of energy and water to create concrete. And when cities are paved with too much concrete, it creates an unpleasant heat-island effect, which contributes to more global warming. "So what we did is we fundamentally went after the composition of concrete,” said Janardhan. “We built an AI tool to rethink how concrete works, and the new concrete that we ended up getting uses 19% less carbon, cures 43% faster, and is completely cost-neutral.” Meta is open sourcing its AI tool for the concrete formulation. “All of you can go and use it,” he said. “Use it in your data center. Use it in your backyard.” Hyperion will be even bigger Now, Meta is taking the lessons it’s learned from Prometheus and applying them to its next AI data center cluster — Hyperion, in Louisiana. “That’s going to be absolutely mammoth,” said Janardhan. It's a five-gigawatt cluster at a single location. To the best of my knowledge, it’s the biggest data center on the planet. It covers about 4,000 acres.” At this point in his speech, the audience was in awe with the magnitude of Meta’s innovation and the sheer scale of its projects. But then, Janardhan said, “What matters is what runs on this, right? At the end of the day, every call, every message, every interaction, every post you do on one of the properties, that has real meaning to someone, right?” And then the audience realized that this was all for properties such as Facebook and Instagram, and that blew the wind out of the sails for many of us. artigo.texto: Lexington extended its temporary ban on data center construction. Mercer County rejected regulations that would allow hyperscale data centers. And a Carroll County ethics board is looking into dealings surrounding a proposed hyperscale data center. As local governments in Kentucky are weighing and making decisions on potential hyperscale data centers, some Kentuckians came to Frankfort to tell state lawmakers that they need to do more to regulate large data centers — not put that burden on local governments. Just a few months away from when state lawmakers meet again in Frankfort, catch up on the latest data center news in this round-up as reported by the Lantern and other news outlets from around Kentucky. Kentuckians tell state lawmakers to act More than 60 people from across the state, ranging from Pike County to Daviess County, came to a committee room earlier this month to lay out a number of concerns they have about hyperscale data center proposals and their potential impacts on electricity ratepayers, rural land and the state’s natural resources. The gathering was for a “listening session” on data centers organized by Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, who is preparing legislation on data center regulations for when the GOP-controlled state legislature meets again next year. Rep. Josh Bray, R-Mount Vernon, the vice-chair of the Kentucky House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, is also preparing legislation on data centers. A few of those speakers told the state lawmakers at the meeting that local governments shouldn’t be expected to regulate data centers on their own. “Finally, stop expecting local officials without specialized technical, legal, environmental, or utility expertise to negotiate billion-dollar industrial development deals on equal footing with the wealthiest companies on Earth,” said Diane Floyd of Mercer County. Local government decisions Meanwhile, local governments including Mercer County have been hearing public commentary and taking votes on whether to regulate hyperscale data centers or allow them at all. The Mercer County Fiscal Court through a unanimous voice vote in late September rejected proposed regulations that would have allowed the placement of hyperscale data centers next to a coal-fired power plant. Opponents of the regulations argued the land near the power plant was also relatively close to Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill, a historic site preserving structures of the Kentucky Shakers religious community. In Kentucky’s second-largest city of Lexington, the city council voted to move forward with potential data center regulations and also a temporary ban, or moratorium, on data center construction in the city through October 2027, according to public radio station WEKU. In Carroll County, Kentucky Public Radio reported in late September that frustrated community members have filed local ethics complaints arguing that several city council members for the Carroll County seat of Carrollton should have abstained from votes to sign land deals with a prospective hyperscale data center because of conflicts of interest. Carroll County is home to two proposed large data centers, one of them by Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, which is also building a hyperscale data center in West Louisville. Other communities, including the Christian County seat of Hopkinsville, are moving forward with proposed data center regulations, or, in the case of the Scott County seat of Georgetown, looking at an outright ban on hyperscale data centers.

artigo.texto: Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle Establish OCP Working Group to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security - New Open Compute Project (OCP) working group: Companies form a new working group to standardize on a silicon-based and attested secure integrated hardware security module (HSM) solution for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure. - Strengthening cloud security: Secure key caching and attestation cryptographic key lifecycle management at the server level will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads. - Open technical specification: Initial draft of technical specification to be released at OCP Global Summit in October 2026 , paving the way for broad industry adoption of in-server security for data centers. SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 13, 2026-- Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), Microsoft Corporation and Oracle today announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure. To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads. Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party. “An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security,” said Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell. “By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry.” “As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important,” said Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure. “Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security.” “An open specification for integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM) capabilities is an important step toward enabling cryptographic operations where data is processed, protecting keys within a hardware security boundary and supporting cryptographic verification of workload integrity,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure at Oracle. “This effort aims to establish a common foundation for adoption across the industry.” About OCP and the New Security Working Group The Open Compute Project (OCP) is a collaborative community focused on redesigning hardware technology to efficiently support the growing demands of compute infrastructure. As founding members of the new OCP working group, Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle will collaborate with the broader OCP community to publish a joint technical specification, with an initial draft targeted for release around the 2026 OCP Global Summit and version 1.0 to follow. The companies plan to demonstrate the new technology in their exhibit booths and during Security Track presentations at the OCP Global Summit (October 12-15) at the San Jose Convention Center in San Jose, California. Organizations interested in participating in the security working group are encouraged to join through the Open Compute Project. Trusted by the world’s leading technology companies for over 30 years, we move, store, process and secure the world’s data with semiconductor solutions designed for our customers’ current needs and future ambitions. Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we’re ultimately changing the way tomorrow’s enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better. artigo.texto: Credo Launches Short-Reach Micro-Emitter Optics (SRMO) Standardization for AI Data Center Scale-Up and Scale-Out Applications Joined by Initial Participants Including Leading Hyperscaler and Optical Technology Solution Providers AFL, ams OSRAM, BizLink, Foxlink, Heraeus Covantics, SENKO, and YOFC Under the OCP Networking Project SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 12, 2026-- Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd (Credo) (NASDAQ: CRDO), an innovator in providing connectivity at scale through fast, reliable, and energy-efficient system solutions, alongside prominent optical technology providers, today announced the launch of the Short-Reach Micro-Emitter Optics (SRMO) Workstream dedicated to developing a specification within the Open Compute Project (OCP) Community that will define a new class of high-speed data center interconnects. Among the first to join with Credo include a leading hyperscaler as well as AFL, ams OSRAM, BizLink, Foxlink, Heraeus Covantics,SENKO, and YOFC, bringing together expertise spanning the full optical connectivity stack to advance the development of the wide, parallel optical connectivity ecosystem. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261012753816/en/ Credo, alongside prominent optical technology providers, has announced the launch of the Short-Reach Micro-Emitter Optics (SRMO) Workstream dedicated to developing a specification within the Open Compute Project (OCP) Community that will define a new class of high-speed data center interconnects. The SRMO Workstream was initiated to address the need for interoperable interconnects as wide, parallel micro-emitter technology drives new form factors across rapidly evolving scale-up and scale-out fabrics in AI data centers. Micro-emitter technology brings new ways of moving volumes of data, while dramatically improving reliability, power efficiency, and bandwidth density. Arrays of micron-scale light sources make up the transmit side of an optical link. Rather than pushing a few optical channels to extreme data rates, many micro-emitters operate in parallel at optimal individual speeds, enabling layer zero redundancy to improve reliability. The SRMO Workstream was initiated to address the need for interoperable interconnects as wide, parallel micro-emitter technology drives new form factors across rapidly evolving scale-up and scale-out fabrics in AI data centers. The specification, targeted for OCP approval in 2027, will address requirements for link power, efficiency, signaling, parallelism, physical form factors – including module and connector footprint, link budget, and compliance. By defining specifications, the SRMO Workstream aims to give data center operators, hyperscalers, and system designers access to a broad ecosystem of interoperable components with supply chain resiliency, accelerating time to deployment and fostering continued innovation in optical connectivity. “As AI workloads scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accelerators, the industry needs a standardized approach to wide, parallel optical connectivity — not a patchwork of components that do not fit together or interoperate,” said L.K. Bhupathi, Associate Vice President of Product at Credo. “Launching the SRMO Workstream reflects Credo’s commitment to solving the interconnect challenges facing AI infrastructure collaboratively, alongside those who will build, deploy, and depend on this ecosystem. We believe that defining specifications, developed through industry collaboration, is the fastest path to bringing wide, parallel optics to scale.” “We continue to advance our micro-emitter, micro-receiver and 3D packaging technologies enabling next-generation wide and parallel AI optical interconnects that support very high bandwidth density,” said Ashkan Seyedi, Vice President and General Manager of Digital Photonics Interconnect at ams OSRAM. “Joining the SRMO Workstream is an important part of our strategy to bring the benefits of reliability, efficiency, and simplicity to connectivity in the AI data center.” “Realizing the power and density benefits of a micro-emitter approach depends on getting the physical connector interface exactly right, especially as channel counts scale into the thousands,” said Obie Roy, Vice President of Strategic Commercial Development at SENKO Advanced Components, Inc. “The SRMO Workstream represents an important industry effort to establish a common connector interface that can bring a new level of density and reliability in next-generation data center architectures.” More information about the SRMO Workstream can be found here. artigo.texto: Credo Unveils 1.6T ZeroFlap Active Light Cable, Industry's First Row-Scale, Wide-Parallel Optical Interconnect for AI Data Centers Micro-Emitter-Based, Pluggable Solution Targets Scale-Out and Front-End Connectivity Up to 50m with Copper-Class Reliability at Lower Power and Reduced Cable Bulk SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 12, 2026-- Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd (Credo) (NASDAQ: CRDO), an innovator in providing connectivity at scale through fast, reliable, and energy-efficient system solutions, today shared details of its 1.6T ZeroFlap active light cable (ALC), the industry’s first row-scale, wide-parallel optical interconnect solution built for AI scale-out and front-end networks. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261012663213/en/ Credo's ZeroFlap Active Light Cable (ALC) is based on a dense array of micro-emitters and photodetectors coupled with flexible, lightweight fiber bundles, designed to draw 12W per cable-end in a pluggable form factor. With targeted reach up to 50m alongside 100 million hours mean time between failures (MTBF), Credo’s ZeroFlap ALC is designed to deliver the reliability, power efficiency, and reach required for next-generation AI infrastructure. The ZeroFlap ALC is based on a dense array of micro-emitters and photodetectors coupled with flexible, lightweight fiber bundles, designed to draw 12W per cable-end in a pluggable form factor. With targeted reach up to 50m alongside 100 million hours mean time between failures (MTBF), Credo’s ZeroFlap ALC is designed to deliver the reliability, power efficiency, and reach required for next-generation AI infrastructure. The 1.6T ALC architecture will be featured in Credo’s booth at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit this week in San Jose. News Highlights - Credo's ZeroFlap ALC will bring wide-parallel, micro-emitter optics to row-scale reach, closing the mid-reach gap between copper's distance limits and the power and cost overhead of traditional pluggable optics. - The cable splits 200G lanes into many low-rate optical channels using simple NRZ modulation, avoiding the power and latency costs of complex DSP-based signal processing. - Built-in channel redundancy and ZeroFlap link monitoring enable hitless failover, with target reliability of 100 million hours MTBF and bit error rates better than traditional optics. - The ZeroFlap ALC is designed to draw 12W per cable-end, roughly 30% less than comparable active electrical cables (AECs), is 10x lighter than AECs and extends the reach to 50m enabling row-scale connectivity. As AI clusters expand across data center rows, operators need connectivity that combines greater reach with reliable, energy-efficient operation. Credo’s 1.6T ZeroFlap ALC will extend the reliability principles behind its field-proven AEC solutions to a new optical architecture. Micro-emitter technology harnesses optical arrays that make up the transmit side of a link. Rather than pushing a few optical channels to extreme data rates, many micro-emitters operate in parallel at optimal individual speeds. This shift from “fast-and-narrow” to “slow-and-wide” enables lower power per bit along with optical links protected with redundancy. “For decades, optical transceivers have prioritized data rate per fiber. Our 1.6T ZeroFlap ALCs are engineered with reliability as the first-order concern,” said L.K. Bhupathi, Associate Vice President of Product at Credo. “The scale-up and scale-out links that form the densest connections in AI data centers demand higher reliability than traditional optics were designed to provide. Credo’s ALCs bring copper-class reliability to these links, enabling larger GPU clusters and higher-throughput connectivity for massive-scale AI deployments.” “As the speeds and distances required for AI exceed the capabilities of copper, there is a gap opening between copper cables and more expensive, power-hungry traditional pluggable optics," said Scott Wilkinson, Lead Analyst, Optical Components at Cignal AI. "Credo’s ZeroFlap ALC addresses this gap with a unique approach that provides row-scale reach while maintaining the reliability and low-cost benefits of AECs.” Credo’s 1.6T ZeroFlap active light cable (ALC) solution will be shipping in 2027. Today, at the OCP Global Summit, Credo President and CEO Bill Brennan will present “Wider. Slower. Better: Optics That Can Beat Copper” at 3:20 p.m. in room LL21DE of the San Jose Convention Center. Credo’s micro-emitter technology and its latest portfolio of copper and optical interconnect solutions will be demonstrated at the OCP Global Summit Expo Hall in Credo Booth B2, October 13-15, 2026. artigo.texto: Keysight Expands Active and Passive 1.6T Copper Interconnect Validation for Scale-Out Data Centers Validating digital-layer error performance is the next step for high-speed interconnects after completing optical and electrical layer compliance testing SANTA ROSA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 14, 2026-- Keysight Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: KEYS) today announced the Functional Interconnect Test Solutions (FITS)-16CH digital-layer error performance validation system, expanding Keysight’s FITS portfolio for optical, active copper, and passive copper interconnects. With 16 transmit and 16 receive channels, FITS-16CH has twice the channel density of FITS-8CH, and is designed to validate complete interconnect assemblies across research and development, product design, manufacturing, and pre- and post-production AI and network infrastructure deployments. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261014439659/en/ With 16 transmit and 16 receive channels, Keysight’s FITS-16CH enables digital-layer error performance validation of 1.6T optical and copper interconnects. As interconnect speeds increase, testing only the physical-layer does not provide a complete view of system-level error performance. FITS-16CH combines bit error ratio (BER) and forward error correction (FEC) measurements at the digital layer to evaluate how complete interconnect assemblies perform under real-world conditions. The platform enables 106G and 212G lane-rate validation for today’s 800G interconnects and emerging 1.6T technologies. FITS-16CH supports validation across a broad range of optical and electrical interconnects. These include full-retimed optics (FRO), active optical cables (AOCs), linear-retimed optics (LRO), linear pluggable optics (LPO), active copper cables (ACCs), active electrical cables (AECs), passive direct attach cables (DACs), and high-speed copper flyover cables used in networking and high-performance computing equipment. The platform also supports development and manufacturing workflows for silicon chips, networking equipment, and interconnect products, as well as performance benchmarking for data center operators. Key capabilities include: - Higher channel density for complete-assembly validation: With 16 transmit and 16 receive channels, FITS-16CH is designed to test fully assembled interconnects using two Module Compliance Boards (MCBs) with independent channel groups and MCB controls, enabling teams to validate interconnect performance on more lanes simultaneously, ensuring a high degree of system-level qualification. - Broad interconnect support and insertion-loss capability: A large insertion-loss budget supports signals across lossy channels and customer fixtures, enabling validation of a broad range of optical and copper interconnects, including active copper and high-speed copper flyover cables. - Automated lane tuning: The FITS Windows 11 graphical user interface integrates FITS-16CH with the Keysight DCA-X to automatically calculate optimal transmit finite impulse response (FIR) tap settings and open the electrical eye. The automated process can reduce tuning time to a few minutes compared with manual tuning that can take hours, days, or even weeks. - Flexible integration and automation: FITS-16CH can integrate as a transmitter or receiver with Keysight data communications analyzers (DCAs), high-performance bit error ratio testers (BERTs), and UXR real-time oscilloscopes. The platform supports automated validation workflows with Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (SCPI) API support, automatic real-time charts and data tables, pass/fail flagging, and PDF and .csv report generation. The solution reduces validation complexity by using the common FITS software framework, providing a familiar environment across the FITS portfolio. Ameet Suri, Vice President of Product, Credo Technologies, said: “The tighter margins at 1.6T make it essential to evaluate active electrical cable performance at the system level, not in isolation for each link. Keysight's solutions give Credo a practical way to test our AEC cables during development and qualification, so issues surface sooner and designs reach production with greater assurance.” Ram Periakaruppan, Vice President and General Manager, Network Test & Security Solutions, Keysight, said: "As interconnect speeds increase, manufacturers need to validate more lanes simultaneously on many types of interconnects without adding unnecessary complexity to their labs. FITS-16CH expands our functional interconnect validation portfolio with the capacity, flexibility, and automation needed to help engineers move from product development and qualification to mass production with greater confidence." Resources About Keysight Technologies Keysight (NYSE: KEYS) serves technology innovators as a mission-critical design enablement partner for the world’s most complex engineering challenges. By connecting market-leading design, emulation, and test solutions across the full life cycle, Keysight helps engineering teams accelerate innovation, reduce risk, and bring new technologies to market faster. Customers across AI infrastructure, communications, industrial automation, aerospace and defense, automotive, semiconductor, and general electronics rely on Keysight to bridge virtual design and physical reality, enabling confident decisions earlier. Learn more at www.keysight.com. artigo.texto: Adani Enterprises, Jabil Sign MoU for 50:50 Data Center Hardware Joint Venture - The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) sets out a proposed joint venture (JV) between Jabil and Adani for building a multi-gigawatt AI infrastructure platform in India — spanning AI racks, servers, networking, power and cooling systems. - The proposed JV aims to serve India’s accelerating data center demand, with industry forecasts projecting capacity of 5–8 GW by 2030 and more than $50 billion in planned hyperscaler spending across data center, cloud and AI ecosystems. - The companies estimate the global market opportunity at more than $3 trillion over the next seven years, as investment in AI compute infrastructure continues to surge. - Once established, the JV would serve the world’s leading AI ecosystem players — from hyperscalers and neoclouds to data center operators and enterprises — with infrastructure Made-in-India forIndia and for the world. NEW DELHI, India & ST. PETERSBURG, Fla.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 13, 2026-- Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), the flagship company of the Adani Group, and Jabil Inc. (NYSE: JBL), a global engineering, supply chain and manufacturing company, have signed a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) setting out the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble artificial intelligence (AI) and data center equipment in India. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261013719250/en/ Mr. Gautam Adani, Chairman, Adani Group (left), and Mr. Mike Dastoor, CEO, Jabil (right). The companies have signed a non-binding MoU setting out the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble artificial intelligence and data center equipment in India. The proposed joint venture remains subject to execution of definitive agreements and satisfaction of applicable approvals and customary conditions. The MoU follows the June 2026 announcement of Adani Group and Jabil’s intent to establish a strategic alliance to develop an AI and data center infrastructure manufacturing ecosystem in India. Mr. Gautam Adani, Chairman, Adani Group, said: “The AI revolution will demand far more than just breakthroughs in algorithms. It will require an entire new industrial architecture where energy, hyperscale infrastructure, advanced computing and precision manufacturing converge to power the intelligence economy.” “At Adani, our vision is to expand up the AI value chain evolving from powering and hosting AI infrastructure to engineering and manufacturing the critical systems that will define the next generation of computing.” “Our proposed joint venture with Jabil marks a strategic step towards this future, combining Jabil’s world-class engineering and manufacturing capabilities with Adani’s integrated strengths in energy, infrastructure and data centers to help build the physical backbone of the global AI economy.” Mr. Mike Dastoor, Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Jabil Inc., said: “The signing of this MoU is the next step forward in our shared efforts to establish a scaled AI infrastructure manufacturing platform in India, a market we believe will become increasingly important for both domestic and global AI infrastructure demand. Integrating Jabil’s 60 years of engineering and manufacturing expertise with Adani’s significant infrastructure and energy capabilities, we can bring our rack-level data center solutions to more hyperscalers in India and around the world. We look forward to building on the work we started together in June.” Manufacturing AI Hardware in India The joint venture would manufacture and assemble AI racks, servers, storage and networking equipment used in data centers. The racks would house high-performance computing systems for AI applications and other digital services. The portfolio would also include equipment required to power and cool these systems, including power distribution units, liquid-cooling systems and transformers. The venture is expected to have multi-gigawatt AI rack manufacturing capacity, supporting computing systems with a combined power capacity of several gigawatts. It would also provide installation and commissioning services. India’s Data Center Opportunity India’s data center capacity is projected to reach 5–8 gigawatts (GW) by 2030, driven by AI adoption, cloud expansion and data localization. The venture would provide a manufacturing base in India to serve domestic demand and support exports. The companies estimate the global market opportunity at more than $3 trillion over the next seven years, driven by investment in AI computing. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, provides a framework for personal data protection. This legal safeguard, complemented by the Union Budget 2026 tax holiday for data centers until 2047, is expected to support investment in domestic data infrastructure. The venture is aligned with Adani Group’s $100 billion commitment to develop 5 GW of green-energy-powered, hyperscale AI-ready data centers by 2035. The proposed venture would add hardware manufacturing to the Group’s presence across infrastructure, energy, logistics and data centers. For Jabil, which reported $36 billion in revenue in fiscal year 2026, the venture would expand its engineering and manufacturing footprint in India’s data center market. The company has also expanded its data center capabilities through the acquisition of Hanley Energy Group, which provides critical power and energy management solutions, and Mikros Technologies, which specializes in liquid-cooling solutions for high-performance computing systems.
