artigo.texto: EdgeConneX Enters Australia in Partnership with Stockland, with Hyperscale Data Center Campuses Planned in Sydney and Melbourne Chris Maher appointed Managing Director for Australia to lead EdgeConneX’s growth and market development strategy SYDNEY--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 14, 2026-- EdgeConneX®, a pioneer in global Build-to-Suit and Build-to-Density digital infrastructure solutions, today announced its entry into the Australian market through a 50-50 joint venture partnership with Stockland (ASX: SGP). The companies plan to develop, own, and operate a portfolio of hyperscale data center campuses across Australia, starting with Sydney and Melbourne. The EdgeConneX Stockland Data Center partnership combines Stockland's land, development, and project management expertise with EdgeConneX global experience delivering data center solutions for large content, cloud, and AI providers. Following the establishment of the JV partnership, EdgeConneX and Stockland are advancing an initial portfolio of hyperscale data center campuses in Sydney and Melbourne, with 450MW of power secured, and progressing additional power applications and planning. “Our partnership with EdgeConneX brings together Stockland’s local development capabilities and EdgeConneX’s international hyperscale and AI Factory experience. Together, we are creating a strong platform to support the responsible growth of Australia’s digital economy,” said Justin Louis, Chief Investment Officer, Stockland. To lead its Australian business and market development strategy, EdgeConneX has appointed Chris Maher as Managing Director for Australia. EdgeConneX has also joined Data Centres Australia (DCA), the nation's leading industry body for data centers and AI infrastructure, as a principal member, working alongside DCA's growing base of 100+ diverse members to advance the digital infrastructure opportunity in Australia. Maher brings more than 20 years of experience across digital infrastructure, asset management, and finance in Asia Pacific and the United States. Over the past two decades, he has played a leading role in establishing and growing major digital infrastructure businesses, with extensive experience in data center development and operations, and large-scale infrastructure investment. With deep sector experience, a strong understanding of the Australian market, and a track record of leading complex infrastructure businesses, Maher is well positioned to lead EdgeConneX’s Australian business and support the company's continued growth in the region. “Australia has a significant opportunity to become a leading market for digital infrastructure and AI,” said Chris Maher, Managing Director, Australia, EdgeConneX. “Digital infrastructure and the technology it enables are transforming the way we live and work, from healthcare to agriculture and mining. I'm excited to join EdgeConneX at such a pivotal moment and to build, with our partners and customers, the sustainable digital foundations Australia needs.” Belinda Dennett, Chief Executive Officer, Data Centres Australia: "We are delighted to welcome EdgeConneX as a member and contributor to the growing Australian market for hyperscale data centers. Australia has a significant opportunity to lead the region in sustainable data center development, capturing economic and strategic advantage through the current wave of global AI infrastructure investment. I would like to congratulate Chris Maher on his appointment and look forward to working with EdgeConneX and Stockland as they establish their presence." The appointment comes amid strong momentum in the Australian market. According to DCA's latest Economic Impact report, with its abundant renewable energy, Australia is uniquely positioned to power the region's AI demand sustainably, turning clean energy into a digital export. The report estimates that capturing the AI export market could add up to $4.1 billion in additional annual economic activity by 2030 and support up to 17,120 more jobs, a net addition on top of the projected economic activity and job creation from meeting domestic demand. “Australia is one of the fastest-growing infrastructure hubs in the region,” said Kelvin Fong, Managing Director, Asia Pacific, EdgeConneX. “It offers strong fundamentals such as renewable energy for long-term sustainable infrastructure investment, and with Chris leading our local team, we look forward to supporting our customers as they grow in this market.” EdgeConneX is a leader in sustainable data center development and operations. For three consecutive years, the company has been recognized as an industry leader in Structure Research's annual State of the Environmental report for its strong balance of transparent ESG reporting, innovative use of closed-loop water-free cooling systems, energy efficiency, and renewable energy adoption. About EdgeConneX Backed by EQT Infrastructure, part of the global investment organization EQT, EdgeConneX provides a full range of sustainable infrastructure solutions worldwide. We work closely with our customers to offer choices in location, scale, and type of facility, from Build-to-Suit to Build-to-Density. EdgeConneX is a global leader in anytime, anywhere, and any scale data center services for a diverse portfolio of industries, including Cloud, AI, Content, Networks, and more. With a mission dedicated to taking care of our customers, our people, and our planet, EdgeConneX strives to Empower Your Edge. artigo.texto: Residents in an Indonesian data-center hub ran out of patience, and water, before officials did. On October 5, about 300 people in Batam blocked the road into Nongsa Digital Park, demanding the taps that had gone dry for months get turned back on. Protesters from the Sambau neighborhood, armed with empty jerry cans and plastic bottles, swarmed the compound's access road and refused to move. According to the Jakarta Post and the Star, residents said their piped water supply had been cut off, in some cases for three to six months, while the data centers next door kept running. One protester, Andi Lalang, put it plainly to reporters: since construction of the data center began, the neighborhood's water has been severely affected, and the supply has simply stopped. The anger wasn't sudden. This was the latest in a string of protests that had built over the previous two months, including a late-September demonstration at the Nongsa Special Economic Zone management office. Residents watched reservoir levels fall even as new server halls kept rising around them. A BP Batam official defused the immediate standoff. BP Batam is the state agency that runs the free-trade zone where Nongsa Digital Park sits, and the official promised piped water would be restored within two days, with six tanker trucks dispatched to deliver emergency supply. By Wednesday, water was back for roughly 53% of the affected households. For the other half, nothing had changed, and residents told local outlets they're ready to block the road again if the taps run dry a second time. BP Batam disputes the obvious reading. Denny Tondano, BP Batam's deputy for commercial affairs, denied that the data centers caused the shortage at all, pointing instead to a prolonged dry season driven by El Niño. That explanation runs into a problem of its own making. Local reports have described the data centers in Nongsa Digital Park as being served through a dedicated BP Batam pipeline connected to the Duriangkang Reservoir. The surrounding residential neighborhoods depend on the smaller Nongsa Reservoir instead - the one that's been running low. Two systems, two outcomes, same drought. The numbers ahead are the real warning. Nine data centers are planned or under construction in Nongsa Digital Park. Once they're all running, the complex will need roughly 285 megawatts of power and about 29 million liters of water a day, according to reporting compiled by Katadata and Earth Journalism Network. Combined with at least one additional large facility nearby, that adds up to something like 8.4% of Batam's entire water supply. All of it consumed by server cooling systems, in a city that can't yet guarantee piped water to the neighborhood next door. A single large AI data center can use up to 5 million gallons of water daily. That's roughly what a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people needs - which gives some sense of scale for what nine of them, fully built, would actually draw. Firmus has delayed its expected ASX IPO timetable after The Australian reported a major Nvidia partnership tied to a 360 megawatt AI factory in Batam, Indonesia. The deal could cover up to 170,000 Nvidia accelerators and support $US25 billion to $US30 billion in first-six-year revenue from committed offtake contracts. - Nvidia AI factory capacity building - ASX listing delayed for data center Batam has spent the last two years marketing itself as Southeast Asia's answer to Singapore's land-constrained data center market: close enough to Singapore for low-latency links, cheap enough on land and power to undercut it. Global Voices reported in April that the island's AI-ready data center boom has moved fast on approvals and slower on the utility planning that's supposed to back it up. The Jakarta Post has been tracking the strain since at least August. That's when it first reported that data center expansion in Batam was threatening both water and electricity supplies for ordinary residents - months before anyone blocked a road over it. None of this is abstract for the people who live there. Frankly, a resident who hasn't had running water in half a year doesn't much care whether El Niño or a new server farm caused it. They care that the facility across the street never seems to run dry. That's the actual story inside the AI infrastructure boom that doesn't show up in a chip shortage headline or a power purchase agreement: the water gets allocated first to the machines, and the humans wait for a tanker truck. Six trucks bought BP Batam two days of calm. The reservoir math behind nine data centers didn't go anywhere. artigo.texto: Rapidly rising computing density is pushing traditional systems to the limit. In particular, the demands for AI data center cooling are reshaping operating strategies. Rather than transitioning to liquid cooling data centers, operators are increasingly adopting hybrid cooling architectures that use liquid for the highest-density equipment while retaining efficient airflow to manage equipment cooling throughout facilities. Operators are looking to better understand data center fan efficiency. They are learning that advanced fans and rear-door heat exchangers combined with intelligent controls, monitoring, and adaptive operation can improve cooling performance while reducing energy consumption and freeing limited power resources for actual computing. Reliability is equally critical as cooling equipment must operate continuously under demanding conditions. Digital twins predictive maintenance can contribute to improved efficiency and increased uptime by better targeting maintenance and allowing operators to evaluate higher rack densities, cooling upgrades, and operating strategies before making capital investments. Finally, operators concerned about supply-chain risks are looking toward local-for-local manufacturing. Producing critical cooling equipment closer to customers can shorten lead times, reduce transportation and tariff risks, and provide regional manufacturing redundancy. artigo.texto: Tower Semiconductor and Semtech Expand SiGe Partnership to Scale Power-Efficient Analog Connectivity for Data Centers Multi-year agreement expands dedicated capacity across Tower's global fab network to support the companies’ growth in optical and copper interconnects for next-generation AI infrastructure MIGDAL HAEMEK, Israel & CAMARILLO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 13, 2026-- Tower Semiconductor (Nasdaq/TASE: TSEM), the leading foundry for high-value analog semiconductor solutions, and Semtech Corporation (Nasdaq: SMTC), a leading provider of high-performance semiconductors powering AI data center networking and intelligent, connected Internet of Things ("IoT") devices worldwide, today announced an expanded multi-year agreement that builds on the companies’ 20-year partnership. Under the agreement, Semtech will invest in securing dedicated silicon germanium (SiGe) capacity at Tower in support of its strong design wins and demand for AI Data Center optical interconnect components. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261012105819/en/ AI’s next constraint is power, and a growing share of that power is spent moving data rather than computing it. As AI clusters scale across racks, rows and campuses, the energy cost of moving each bit is becoming central to how much useful work each accelerator can deliver. Each step in the speed roadmap, from 800G to 1.6T and on to 3.2T, raises the requirements for bandwidth, reach and power per bit, and increases the importance of the high-speed analog front end that drives and receives the signal. Semtech’s signal integrity portfolio, including transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs), modulator and laser drivers and linear equalizers, is built on Tower’s SiGe process technology and serves fully retimed optics (FRO), linear pluggable optics (LPO), linear receive optics (LRO), near-packaged optics (NPO), eXtra-dense pluggable optics (XPO), linear equalizers on PCB and active copper cables (ACC). Semtech believes that, together, these products position it to address copper links within the rack and optical links across the data center as the industry moves to its next generation of architectures. A testament to the results of the partnership is Semtech’s recent Optical Component Innovation (Chip/Wafer) award at the European Conference on Optical Communication (ECOC) 2026. The award recognizes Semtech’s 224 Gbps per Lane TIA Family for Linear Pluggable Optics built on Tower’s leading-edge SiGe technology. Tower and Semtech continue to work closely not only on capacity but also on joint technology roadmap designed to secure product leadership in multi-generational AI data center interconnects. The secured capacity spans Tower’s fabs in the United States, Israel and Japan, adding supply resilience and geographic diversification to Semtech’s manufacturing strategy. Building on current production, the agreement gives Semtech additional supply assurance as demand for its SiGe-based products is expected to grow across a broadening base of customer programs and end markets. “Connectivity is now a primary factor in how far AI systems can scale,” said Hong Hou, Semtech President and Chief Executive Officer. “Our customers are scaling interconnect bandwidth quickly and at massive scale. Meeting that demand requires long-term capacity planning and commitment with our manufacturing partners. Tower has been a trusted partner to Semtech for 20 years, and we are very pleased with our partnership agreement that secures dedicated SiGe capacity across three regions to grow across copper and optical interconnects, from 800G and 1.6T today through 3.2T and beyond.” “It is a source of profound satisfaction that our partnership with Semtech has grown so strong,” said Russell Ellwanger, Chief Executive Officer, Tower Semiconductor. “Together, we are driving truly accretive, platform-level solutions that help advance their designs delivering best-in-class figures of merit across present-generation, next-generation and N+2 technologies. By qualifying these solutions well ahead of market need, we both stand fully prepared for immediate implementation as the market moves into these generations. In doing so, we are the key drivers of the technologies carrying the market forward, ensuring a continual expansion of our already leading market share in optical transceiver connectivity within this high-growth market." For additional information about Tower’s SiGe and SiPho technology platforms, visit here. About Tower Semiconductor Tower Semiconductor Ltd. (NASDAQ/TASE: TSEM), the leading foundry of high-value analog semiconductor solutions, provides technology, development, and process platforms for its customers in growing markets such as consumer, industrial, automotive, mobile, infrastructure, medical and aerospace and defense. Tower Semiconductor focuses on creating a positive and sustainable impact on the world through long-term partnerships and its advanced and innovative analog technology offering, comprised of a broad range of customizable process platforms such as SiPho, SiGe, BiCMOS, mixed-signal/CMOS, RF CMOS, CMOS image sensor, non-imaging sensors, displays, and integrated power management (BCD and 700V). Tower Semiconductor also provides world-class design enablement for a quick and accurate design cycle as well as process transfer services including development, transfer, and optimization, to IDMs and fabless companies. To provide multi-fab sourcing and extended capacity for its customers, Tower Semiconductor currently owns one operating facility in Israel (200mm), two in the U.S. (200mm), and two in Japan (200mm and 300mm) which it owns through its 51% holdings in TPSCo and shares a 300mm facility in Agrate, Italy with STMicroelectronics. artigo.texto: China is accelerating construction of massive data centers as competition with the United States over artificial intelligence continues to grow. A CNN report published October 13 highlights developments in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, where nearly 90 data center projects are planned. The area offers affordable land, access to renewable energy, and a climate that helps reduce cooling costs. The expansion is part of China’s broader effort to strengthen its AI infrastructure. Beijing has announced a $560 billion initiative covering computing and information systems over five years. China’s construction efforts also benefit from government coordination and fewer local development obstacles than some projects face in the United States. However, building more facilities does not automatically translate into greater computing capabilities. US export restrictions continue to limit Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI processors, while American technology firms maintain significant advantages in computing resources and investment. The growing demand for electricity also makes renewable energy an important consideration for both countries. China’s expansion illustrates how infrastructure, energy availability, and access to advanced technology have become central factors in the global AI competition.

(NASDAQ: RELL) today joined state and industry leaders to announce Richardson Electronics’ expanded manufacturing of locally produced battery energy storage systems and plans to install its first onsite battery energy storage system demonstration project. This initiative is a critical step toward scaling locally made battery energy storage solutions that strengthen grid reliability, support renewable energy integration, and store energy for use during periods of high demand while helping ease supply-related energy costs. “For generations, manufacturing has been part of northern Illinois’ identity, and Richardson’s announcement demonstrates how that sector continues to shape our region’s economic future,” said ComEd President and CEO Gil Quiniones.“ComEd is committed to supporting business growth by making the grid investments needed to deliver industry-leading reliability at rates that are well below the average commercial and industrial rates for the top 20 largest metropolitan areas.” Richardson, a legacy manufacturer based in La Fox, is currently building the largest commercial battery storage system in Illinois. Its planned operational expansion will help scale the development and distribution of these products. By storing electricity for use during periods of peak demand, battery storage can support a more resilient grid, integrate additional clean energy resources, and help ensure Illinois has the energy capacity needed to power future economic growth. “Safe, reliable and affordable energy is critical to the success of Illinois’ manufacturing sector and will require new generation, transmission investment and new technologies such as battery storage,” said Mark Denzler, President & CEO of the Illinois Manufacturers’ Association. “Richardson Electronics and ComEd’s announcement of a next-generation 5 MWh commercial battery storage system is a great example of manufacturing innovation and ingenuity that will help drive growth and economic development in Illinois.” Battery energy storage systems can charge when electricity is available and discharge when it is needed, helping customers manage energy use and support a more flexible electric system. artigo.texto: Qnity Extends Thermal Management Solutions for Advanced Memory Cooling for AI Data Centers New Laird™ Graphite-over-Foam and Thermal Interface Material solutions expand Qnity's thermal portfolio, helping engineers cool high-density memory modules in AI data centers WILMINGTON, Del.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 13, 2026-- Qnity Electronics, Inc. (“Qnity”) (NYSE: Q), a premier technology solutions leader across the semiconductor value chain, today introducedtwo new advanced memory cooling solutions leveraging Laird™ Graphite-over-Foam (GOF) and Laird™ Thermal Interface Material (TIM) technologies. Both advanced solutions help data center designers keep high-density memory systems, including Double Data Rate 5 Dual In-line Memory Module (DDR5 DIMM) modules cool, reliable, and serviceable as AI pushes memory density and power to new levels. "As AI workloads place greater demands on memory bandwidth, capacity and speed, keeping memory modules cool is critical to sustaining performance and reliability," said Chuck Xu, President, Interconnect Solutions, Qnity. "We're working side by side with customers to extend the Laird thermal expertise they already rely on to advanced memory cooling, so they can improve reliability, simplify assembly, and scale AI infrastructure faster." Leveraging its established Laird™ thermal interface and gap-filling technologies, Qnity's latest Laird™ GOF and Laird™ TIM solutions were designed with DDR5 DIMM architectures used in AI servers and high-performance computing in mind. As memory capacities and power consumption continue to increase, modern server platforms can deploy up to 48 DDR5 memory modules in densely packed DIMM rows, creating significant thermal management challenges. The latest Laird™ GOF and TIM solutions enable system designers to optimize thermal performance while addressing critical mechanical considerations including dimensional tolerances, assembly requirements, serviceability, and long-term reliability. By powering efficient heat transfer while accommodating manufacturing and assembly variations, these advanced materials help improve system reliability, streamline assembly processes, and support the growing performance demands of next-generation AI data centers. Learn more about how Qnity is powering the next leap in electronics at www.qnityelectronics.com. About Qnity Qnity is a premier technology solutions provider across the semiconductor value chain, empowering AI, high-performance computing, and advanced connectivity. From groundbreaking solutions for semiconductor chip manufacturing, to enabling high-speed transmission within complex electronic systems, our high-performance materials and integration expertise make tomorrow’s technologies possible. More information about the company, its businesses and solutions can be found at www.qnityelectronics.com. artigo.texto: Jakarta (ANTARA) - The government is determined to ensure that carbon trading generates significant economic benefits for local communities, especially those actively involved in environmental restoration efforts, Indonesian Environment Minister Jumhur Hidayat said. He underscored the importance of enabling grassroots communities, indigenous peoples, and local residents to reap economic gains from carbon trading during a technical guidance session on carbon economic value and climate-resilient low-carbon development for regional leaders in Jakarta on Tuesday. Hidayat stressed that the government is working to ensure that carbon trading creates opportunities not only for major investors but also for residents directly connected to natural ecosystems that require restoration and conservation. The minister noted that the extent of benefits received by communities could serve as a measure of the integrity of carbon trading activities in Indonesia. He further emphasized that the equitable distribution of economic benefits is one of the key indicators of a high-integrity carbon market. For example, he pointed to the economic potential of mangrove restoration, which can absorb around 3,000 tons of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare annually. Assuming each carbon credit is valued at between US$50 and US$60, he added, a hectare of mangroves could generate an estimated value of around US$150,000. He went on to say that a mangrove restoration project could also help strengthen community empowerment efforts, as it would typically require workers over a period of three to four years. Hidayat described the carbon economy as a more responsible development approach, stressing the need to move away from conventional models that often drive economic growth at the expense of environmental sustainability and social equity. The government, he added, views the new approach as a way to position carbon trading as a scheme that supports environmental restoration while generating tangible economic benefits for local communities. artigo.texto: Weighing the options: Council discusses data center regulation SAN ANTONIO - The nationwide issue of data centers has landed at the feet of San Antonio city leaders. City Council discussed preparations ahead of time in its Wednesday meeting. There hasn't been confirmed plans for a new data center in San Antonio, Wednesday's conversation outlined the council's options if that day ever comes. "The existing code does not regulate data centers and we need to come up with some requirements," said one city staff member. City council members discussed changes to its Unified Development Code (UDC), which outlines rules for land development and construction in the city. The council discussed options to help regulate any potential data centers. District six councilman Ric Galvan has spearheaded community outreach on the issue. "This is our opportunity for the city of San Antonio to have a say in any new data center developments here in our city," the councilman said. On Tuesday, the councilman hosted a townhall meeting getting community input on the possibility of new data center projects. "I do not believe it is enough for residents just to know about the project," Galvan said. "It is important for their public officials to also make clear where they stand on the project and to move it forward or not, depending on what the conversations look like." City staff presented the council with two options: The first restricts data centers to industrial or commercial areas. They'd have to be at least 500 ft. from housing, buildings, and landscaping — and out of the Edwards Research Recharge Zone. Any center falling outside of those guidelines would need to come to the council for special authorization. Option two keeps all of those requirements; it also requires any data center plans to go before council first. "I maybe see this completely differently for many in the room because I see this as the new frontier for our country," District 9 Councilwoman Misty Spears said. Councilmembers Spears and district 10 Marc Whyte opted to give the centers a chance while also protecting San Antonio's own. "Look, we're in financially difficult times now," Whyte said. "If all of a sudden they're not coming here and we're not getting that additional revenue.. I mean that is not going to be good for the city." Wednesday's meeting was just a briefing. The council will meet on the issue again on Oct. 29. We'll keep you updated as we continue following this process.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Regulação de data centers avança nos Estados, e 8 dos 16 projetos de 2026 criam restrições ou ônus Publicado 13/10/2026 • 11:10 | Atualizado há 2 dias OpenAI é processada em oito estados nos EUA devido a preocupações com a segurança do ChatGPT Bank of America contratou 1.000 terceirizados para corrigir falhas de software expostas pelo Mythos da Anthropic Trump vai recorrer da decisão que impede a Casa Branca de banir a MS NOW, a CNN e a Politico Netflix demite mais de 1.000 funcionários, cerca de 6% de seu quadro, em meio à desaceleração do crescimento ASML divulga resultados acima da expectativa do mercado, carteira de pedidos até 2030 e ações puxam índices europeus KEY POINTS Os Estados brasileiros passaram a discutir a regulação de data centers, e metade dos 16 projetos apresentados nas assembleias legislativas em 2026 cria restrições ou ônus aos empreendimentos. O levantamento mapeou 20 projetos de lei e de lei complementar sobre o tema em 11 assembleias, entre 2025 e outubro de 2026. Em todo o ano de 2025 foram quatro iniciativas, e o número saltou para 16 no acumulado deste ano. Os dados constam em estudo da Innova Assuntos Públicos obtido pelo Valor. Dos 20 textos, nove são restritivos, sete favoráveis, dois combinam incentivos e exigências e dois são neutros. No ano passado, as propostas favoráveis eram maioria. O estudo associa a reação ao aumento da insatisfação popular com a expansão dos data centers nos Estados Unidos e à mobilização de movimentos sociais locais. O avanço de investimentos e de anúncios nos Estados, possivelmente aliado a estratégias de comunicação consideradas insuficientes com a população local, também ajuda a explicar o crescimento das propostas. Para a Innova, a onda regulatória mostra que o debate ganhou força. Por outro lado, os projetos favoráveis estão mais avançados, pois são os únicos que já viraram lei. “O levantamento mostra que a regulação dos data centers está chegando aos Estados e em ritmo acelerado. Isso não significa que essas propostas vão ser aprovadas amanhã, mas mostra que a sociedade e os parlamentares estaduais estão olhando para esses empreendimentos com muito mais atenção do que há um ano”, diz Fernanda Arbex, autora do estudo e sócia da Innova. Segundo ela, chama a atenção a velocidade com que o debate se espalha. Textos apresentados em um Estado reaparecem quase iguais em outro, e parte das regras está sendo decidida fora das assembleias, em conselhos ambientais. Fernanda alerta ainda que as empresas que entraram cedo nesses debates, com dados e diálogo com as comunidades locais, terão mais chances de contribuir para regras previsíveis, em vez de apenas reagir a elas depois. Os nove projetos restritivos ainda estão em comissões, mas são mais incisivos, com vedações, multas, tetos de potência e plebiscitos. Já os favoráveis costumam ser autorizativos ou estabelecer diretrizes gerais, com incentivos tributários e simplificações. Os textos restritivos aparecem no Ceará, em Minas Gerais, no Pará, no Rio de Janeiro, no Rio Grande do Sul e em São Paulo. A energia surge de forma indireta, sobretudo como condição para a concessão de incentivos. O uso de água é a frente em que o movimento aparece de forma mais disseminada. Os cinco projetos sobre o tema impõem alguma restrição, com diferentes graus de exigência. Em São Paulo, duas propostas determinam o uso exclusivo de água de reúso, inclusive por data centers em operação, e preveem multa mensal de R$ 50 mil e paralisação em caso de reincidência. As exigências também alcançam a transparência. No Pará, um projeto prevê um painel público com indicadores de desempenho hídrico e energético dos data centers. No Ceará, outra proposta estabelece diretrizes de transparência e de inclusão das comunidades nos benefícios dos empreendimentos. “São exigências de menor custo, que tendem a se espalhar”, avalia a consultoria. Na energia, os Estados atuam por condições indiretas. No Rio de Janeiro, uma proposta condiciona incentivos ao uso de energia limpa com geração própria, exigência que pode conflitar com contratos de energia renovável no mercado livre. No Ceará, um projeto trata da sustentabilidade energética nas Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (ZPEs). Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC No licenciamento, o caso mais restritivo identificado pelo estudo está no Rio Grande do Sul. Uma proposta exige estudo prévio de impacto ambiental para cargas acima de 2 megawatts (MW) e limita a soma dos grandes consumidores a 50% da potência média do Estado. O texto também prevê plebiscito para empreendimentos a partir de 20% dessa potência, gatilho estimado em cerca de 700 MW. Em Minas Gerais, outra proposta busca restringir os procedimentos simplificados de licenciamento e prevê consulta prévia a comunidades tradicionais. Além dos projetos de lei, o levantamento identificou dois atos de conselhos ambientais e 22 requerimentos e indicações apresentados em assembleias estaduais, 17 deles em 2026. Os requerimentos não criam obrigações para os empreendimentos, mas incluem pedidos de informações, questionamentos e propostas dirigidas ao poder público. Minas concentra 14 desses instrumentos, 13 apresentados em bloco em 2026. A maioria trata de um único empreendimento em Uberlândia e cobre rede elétrica, segurança hídrica, competência do município para licenciar e participação da população. Um deles pede que data centers de inteligência artificial entrem na lista de atividades licenciáveis por norma do órgão ambiental, sem passar pela Assembleia. Ceará e Goiás já aprovaram normas voltadas à atração dos empreendimentos. No Ceará, a lei de julho de 2026 criou licenciamento escalonado por porte e potencial poluidor, além de prever cessão de áreas públicas e desoneração de ICMS. Como o ICMS será extinto em 2033, as concessões nesse sentido são temporárias. Em Goiás, a legislação combina incentivos, zonas

artigo.texto: FAIRFIELD – Residents who live near a Northeast Fairfield development project that is under consideration for a 150 MW data center are urging Fairfield City Council members to impose a citywide moratorium that will halt the project’s advancement. About 30 residents gathered at a community meeting on Oct. 7 and made plans to contact Fairfield City Council members to request that they discuss imposing a moratorium on data centers at the Oct. 20 council meeting. On Monday, Fairfield Vice Mayor Pam Bertani announced on social media that she will make a motion for a moratorium on data centers at the Oct. 20 council meeting. Bertani, who is also a mayoral candidate, had previously stated in her campaign materials that she would call for a moratorium as mayor. San Francisco and Oakland approved temporary moratoriums on data centers earlier this month and the city of Dixon approved a similar moratorium on Sep 30. At the Oct. 7 community meeting, one of the central concerns voiced by community members was the possibility that the project could be developed “by right,” meaning it could go forward based solely on whether it meets pre-established zoning and planning requirements. Community member Alicia Minyen, who lives in the Foxboro Knolls area of Vacaville about a half-mile from the project site, spoke at the meeting and presented a series of documents released in a public records request. Minyen said that the documents indicate that the city staff has already greenlit the data center project and that she had emailed the Fairfield City Council to express her concern. In her letter, Minyen cited a City of Fairfield email from Director of Community Development David Zellers to a representative of the project developer, North Point Development. Zellers wrote, “As this relates to a data center use in Planning Area 6, that use has been identified as ‘by right’ and therefore it would not fall under the purview of the review by staff or another body.” “Planning Area 6” refers to a Master Planned Unit Development Permit for a 289-acre industrial park with 4.6 million square feet of industrial buildings located near the intersection of Canon Road and North Gate Road in the northeast corner of Fairfield bordering Vacaville. The permit was approved by the planning commission on August 23, 2023. It covers broad conditions of development related to utilities, traffic patterns and architectural requirements but further permitting is still required to develop a project in that area. Fairfield Planning Commission Chair and mayoral candidate George Kennedy, who was among the six members of the Planning Commission who voted to approve the permit in 2023, said during last week’s meeting that at the time, no one had heard of data centers so the possibility that one could be built at the site was not contemplated. He said that the developers had envisioned an Amazon warehouse and that the commission had rejected an amendment that would have allowed truck loading bay doors to face the street. Kennedy said that when he recently learned that the developer of the industrial park was considering a data center, he realized that the city needed to set guidelines for data center projects. “We need a policy on data centers to control where they go in this city and how they go in,” Kennedy said. “Because we don't know about the electricity. We don't know about the water. We don't know about the noise. We don't know about the environmental [impacts] because it's changing rapidly.” Kennedy proposed a policy that would require noise analysis and testing, disclosure of water and power use as well as prioritization of efficient methods and technology. Kennedy posted a petition for the proposal that has gathered 98 signatures. According to Kennedy, any policy or moratorium would not function retroactively, so if the developer were to submit their project application before the policy is approved, then it would not apply to the project. Fairfield city spokesperson Bill Way said that the developer has not submitted a formal application for a project. Documents released in a public records request made by community member Joseph Joyce, who runs the Facebook page “I’m From Fairfield Too”, indicate that the city of Fairfield Community Development Department has been working with developers on the data center project for over a year and a half. Part of that work has involved producing a draft addendum to the existing environmental impact report to accommodate “a new PG&E-owned substation, interconnection, and related appurtenances to support the development of energy-intensive industrial uses, such as data centers or advanced manufacturing uses that may locate within Planning Area 6.” Gayle Mahoney, who has lived in Fairfield since 1980 and now lives about a mile and a half away from the project site, said that her main concern is the project’s water usage and how the community will be affected in drought years. She added that she is also concerned about electricity use and that the city may be selling residents short. “We give away too much, bringing new businesses in,” she said. “They get all these property tax credits. I don’t want the project at all but it should at least have to be all solar. Don't give them anything. These are billionaires, right?” Jason Smith, who lives at the One Lake subdivision which is about three-quarters of a mile from the project site, said that many of his neighbors already purchased at the top of the market, so any lost property value due to a data center is a big concern. “We were sold a vision here, and that vision was community and peaceful surroundings," Smith said. “This overshadows that vision that we bought into. If you are going to do this in our backyard you need to come to us first.” Minyen and Kennedy suggested that meeting attendees send emails to city officials and council members expressing their concerns about the project and to show up at the Fairfield City Council Meeting on Oct. 20 to ad

artigo.texto: Segundo o Conselho de Administração das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação e Parques Industriais da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh (HEPZA), o projeto AI Factory Data Center no Parque Industrial Tan Phu Trung, comuna de Cu Chi, recebeu um Certificado de Registro de Investimento em julho de 2026, com um capital registrado total de US$ 2,1 bilhões. O projeto de centro de dados de US$ 2,1 bilhões na cidade de Ho Chi Minh enfrenta dificuldades devido a divergências sobre os preços da eletricidade. A incerteza em relação à aplicação de tarifas de eletricidade industriais ou comerciais ao centro de dados da AI Factory no Parque Industrial de Tan Phu Trung está impactando o planejamento financeiro e o andamento da implementação do projeto de US$ 2,1 bilhões. No entanto, a falta de consenso sobre a precificação da eletricidade para data centers está dificultando o processo de implementação. Se forem aplicadas tarifas comerciais em vez de tarifas industriais, os custos operacionais do projeto aumentarão significativamente, impactando o planejamento financeiro, a capacidade de obter financiamento e o cronograma de início das obras. Na conferência socioeconômica sobre os primeiros nove meses do ano, com foco na implementação de projetos de investimento e medidas de estímulo na cidade de Ho Chi Minh, realizada em 15 de outubro, a HEPZA propôs que o Comitê Popular da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh designasse o Departamento de Indústria e Comércio para liderar e coordenar com a Companhia de Eletricidade da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh a revisão e orientação da aplicação de preços de eletricidade adequados. Caso a questão ultrapasse a competência da cidade, esta deverá buscar orientação do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio e do Grupo de Eletricidade do Vietnã (EVN). O projeto SGI-HCM Campus foi concebido para se tornar um complexo de data center e inteligência artificial de grande escala, abrangendo mais de 12 hectares, com capacidade de TI de 200 MW e capacidade para operar 100.000 GPUs. O projeto, uma colaboração entre a Kinh Bac Urban Development Corporation, a Accelerated Infrastructure Capital e o VietinBank , tem previsão de início para o quarto trimestre de 2026. Anteriormente, o início do projeto estava previsto para 29 de agosto, mas foi adiado. Além de resolver as questões relacionadas aos preços da eletricidade, a HEPZA recomenda que a cidade acelere o investimento em projetos de infraestrutura de grande escala, incluindo o Complexo Portuário de Cai Mep Ha (a jusante), o Centro Logístico e a Zona Funcional Industrial, Urbana e de Serviços, com um investimento total proposto de 204.658 bilhões de VND. A unidade também solicitou que a cidade delegue prontamente a autoridade de gestão estatal sobre a Zona Franca de Ho Chi Minh associada ao porto de Cai Mep Ha e coordene com os departamentos e agências relevantes para resolver definitivamente as questões pendentes relativas aos preços dos terrenos e às taxas de arrendamento de terrenos em zonas industriais nos meses restantes do ano. A Zona Franca de Ho Chi Minh, conectada ao porto de Cai Mep Ha, foi estabelecida em 23 de julho de 2026, abrangendo uma área de mais de 4.174 hectares nos bairros de Tan Phuoc e Tan Hai. Esta zona está planejada em três áreas funcionais, compreendendo oito subzonas adjacentes. O plano de desenvolvimento prevê foco em investimentos em infraestrutura e atração de investimentos durante o período de 2026 a 2030; operação plena durante o período de 2031 a 2035; e, após 2035, desenvolvimento acelerado da economia marítima. Segundo o Sr. Le Van Thang, Diretor do Departamento de Ciência e Tecnologia da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh, desde o início de 2026, a cidade tem atraído muitos projetos de centros de dados de inteligência artificial com investimento estrangeiro, incluindo projetos de grande escala. Atualmente, a cidade de Ho Chi Minh possui 20 centros de dados operacionais e 9 projetos de centros de dados propostos. Alguns projetos notáveis estão concentrados no Parque Industrial Tan Phu Trung, projetos do Grupo G42 e na área do Parque de Alta Tecnologia. Devido à crescente demanda por eletricidade, o Comitê Popular da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh solicitou aos departamentos e agências competentes que elaborem planos para garantir o fornecimento de energia elétrica aos centros de dados da cidade. Assim sendo, o Departamento de Ciência e Tecnologia foi incumbido de liderar e coordenar com o Departamento de Indústria e Comércio, a HEPZA (Autoridade de Zonas de Processamento de Energia Elétrica), o Conselho de Administração do Parque de Alta Tecnologia e os investidores em infraestrutura, a fim de trabalhar diretamente com os investidores para atualizar a localização, a escala, a capacidade de projeto, a demanda de eletricidade para cada fase, a capacidade de pico, o tempo de operação previsto e o plano de expansão do projeto. A cidade também solicitou uma lista completa de centros de dados operacionais, em funcionamento e com investimentos insuficientes, como base para o desenvolvimento de um plano de fornecimento de energia. Para centros de dados com alta demanda de energia, o plano de fornecimento de energia deve ser calculado em conjunto com a capacidade de fornecimento dos sistemas de energia regionais e municipais, garantindo que as necessidades sejam atendidas em cada fase do investimento. Instalações de projeto com localização, capacidade, cronograma e compromissos específicos dos investidores claramente definidos terão prioridade.

artigo.texto: Enlight and ENERTRAG Start Construction of 840 MWh Battery Storage at Bertikow Enlight Renewable Energy and partner ENERTRAG have marked the start of work on Bertikow, an 840 MWh battery storage project in Brandenburg, several parameters of which remain to be disclosed. Enlight Renewable Energy and its partner ENERTRAG have officially started construction of Bertikow, an 840 MWh battery energy storage project located in Brandenburg, Germany. Enlight announced the event following a ceremony marking the start of works. The project joins other storage construction efforts under way internationally, such as that of Leader Energy, which broke ground on a 100 MW battery energy storage project in Malaysia. An 840 MWh project in Brandenburg According to Enlight, Bertikow represents another step in expanding its presence in the European energy storage market. The company says large-scale storage is becoming more important to the flexibility and reliability of electricity grids as renewable energy expands across Europe. At the ceremony, Marko Liposcak, General Manager of Enlight Europe, addressed attendees on behalf of Enlight. artigo.texto: URBANA — After hearing public outcry over environmental impacts, noise concerns, and other uncertainties about data centers, the Champaign County board unanimously approved a resolution on Oct. 13, prohibiting tax abatements for hyperscale data center construction. The resolution states that “The policy of Champaign County, Illinois shall be to not negotiate any property tax abatement agreement, any payment in lieu of taxes agreement, or any other concession to facilitate the development and construction of any hyperscale data center within Champaign County, Illinois.” This means that if a data center company wants to build in Champaign County, they will still have to pay their fair share in taxes. District 3 Republican John Farney said during the meeting that he hopes local governments will pass a resolution similar to the county. He’s been spreading the word to leaders he knows at the local level in hopes of forming a cohesive county-wide plan on dealing with data centers. Farney said municipalities can even take the language of the resolution, as long as it means getting the word out that the government shouldn’t be helping data center companies. “Municipalities, townships, if there’s some unit of government that you represent, get this language to them. Tell them to steal it,” Farney said. “We just need to say, if your idea is so great, you don’t need to have us help you finance it.” District 8 Democrat Stephanie Fortado praised the move by the board and echoed Farney’s hope that other governments follow in the footsteps of the County Board. “This is seeing a problem that’s out there, and then thinking about how we could put policy in place to address that issue, and then giving a blueprint to other agencies,” Fortado explained. “This is absolutely what we as elected officials should be doing.” According to the resolution, no companies have reached out to the Champaign County Board about the construction of a hyperscale data center in Champaign County, but limiting the tax breaks they can receive may dissuade corporations from trying to move in. At this time, local governments can still negotiate tax abatements or other forms of payment, if they choose to allow data center construction. It just won’t apply to the county tax bill. Public concern continues to grow over the long term effects of data centers on the environment, and the Champaign County Data Center Task Force is working to develop a data center ordinance to ensure any future data centers follow strict environmental and operational standards. The county’s one-year moratorium on large scale data center construction expires in April 2027.

artigo.texto: (WEG/Divulgação) Repórter Publicado em 15 de outubro de 2026 às 06h00. A Ucrânia atingiu nesta quarta-feira, 14, o maior data center da Rússia, em Balakovo, em novo ataque contra a infraestrutura digital do país, segundo a Reuters. A ofensiva afetou serviços usados por milhões de pessoas e destruiu supercomputadores ligados ao desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial. A Ucrânia atingiu na quarta-feira, 14, o maior data center da Rússia, em um novo ataque deste tipo na guerra entre os países, que caminha para cinco anos de duração. A ofensiva aconteceu em Balakovo, na região sul do país. O local é de propriedade do Sberbank, um dos maiores bancos e empresas de tecnologia do país, que pertence ao grupo Yandex, conhecido como o Google russo. As informações são da agência de notícias Reuters. Fundado em 1997 como um mecanismo de busca, o Yandex se transformou em uma das principais infraestruturas digitais do país, reunindo serviços que vão de transporte e comércio eletrônico a pagamentos e inteligência artificial. Por causa da ação ucraniana, serviços usados diariamente por milhões de pessoas foram interrompidos, como e-mails, aplicativos de táxi e sistemas eletrônicos de acesso a condomínios em Moscou. A Rússia tem leis rígidas que exigem que dados de consumidores sejam armazenados dentro do próprio território russo, o que expõe data centers a riscos em um cenário de guerra com a Ucrânia. O ataque a mais um data center se soma a uma sequência registrada na semana passada, quando três locais parecidos foram atingidos, todos de propriedade da Yandex. A tendência reflete uma nova preocupação do conflito entre Rússia e Ucrânia, mas também uma nova estratégia de guerra. Mas qual a tática por trás da destruição de data centers em um conflito como esse? Os data centers atingidos são da Yandex, empresa que abriga supercomputadores, agora destruídos, responsáveis pelo processamento e desenvolvimento da Inteligência Artificial, no país. Danos a essas máquinas podem provocar atrasos no avanço dessa tecnologia, que se torna cada vez mais importante no campo de batalha. Segundo Rodrigo Gava, CTO da Vultus Cibersecurity, a IA facilita a descoberta e a exploração de vulnerabilidades, inclusive em infraestrutura crítica. "Usar IA na defesa e corrigir falhas mais rapidamente será cada vez mais decisivo para o ritmo do conflito", afirma ele. John Park, especialista em Inteligência Artificial e engenheiro de software da AGI Inc, diz que muitos dos supercomputadores destruídos nos ataques utilizam chips avançados, caros e difíceis de obter. "No caso da Rússia, as sanções internacionais tornam a compra e a substituição desses equipamentos ainda mais complicadas. Mesmo chips de gerações anteriores podem ser difíceis de encontrar", diz Park à EXAME. Park também afirma que "alguns drones já conseguem reconhecer imagens, acompanhar objetos e navegar com menos intervenção humana". Ao mesmo tempo, ao atacar alvos dentro do território russo, como os data centers, a Ucrânia repete a estratégia de levar a guerra cada vez mais ao cotidiano do cidadão russo, como já fez em outras ofensivas, que também provocaram interrupções em serviços do cotidiano da população. A Ucrânia atingiu o maior data center da Rússia, localizado em Balakovo, no sul do país, segundo a Reuters. A matéria afirma que o local pertence ao Sberbank, um dos maiores bancos e empresas de tecnologia da Rússia. O ataque interrompeu e-mails, aplicativos de táxi e sistemas eletrônicos de acesso a condomínios em Moscou. Esses serviços são usados diariamente por milhões de pessoas. Os ataques podem prejudicar a infraestrutura digital russa e atrasar o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial, tecnologia cada vez mais importante no campo de batalha. Na semana anterior, outros três data centers de propriedade da Yandex também foram atingidos. Os supercomputadores atingidos processavam e desenvolviam sistemas de inteligência artificial na Rússia. Segundo John Park, engenheiro de software da AGI Inc, muitas dessas máquinas usam chips avançados, caros e difíceis de substituir devido às sanções internacionais contra o país. A inteligência artificial ajuda a identificar e explorar vulnerabilidades em infraestruturas críticas, segundo Rodrigo Gava, CTO da Vultus Cibersecurity. John Park também afirma que alguns drones usam IA para reconhecer imagens, acompanhar objetos e navegar com menos intervenção humana. Os ataques dentro do território russo provocam interrupções em serviços usados pela população, como aplicativos de transporte e sistemas de acesso a condomínios. A estratégia repete outras ofensivas da Ucrânia que afetaram atividades cotidianas dos cidadãos russos.

artigo.texto: ZTE's David An Shares TCO-Optimized AI Factory Vision ZTE Expert David AN Shares TCO-Optimized AI Factory Vision at Data Centre World Singapore 2026 October 12, 2026 Sponsored by ZTE SINGAPORE, September 30, 2026, at Data Centre World (DCW) Singapore 2026, David AN, Director of ZTE CTO Group, delivered a keynote titled "From Data Center to AI Factory, TCO-Optimized AIDC" in the DCW Keynote Theatre. The presentation outlined how the explosive growth of AI is transforming data centers from traditional facilities into integrated AI factories, and why the industry must optimize the entire AI factory lifecycle - not individual components—to achieve sustainable total cost of ownership (TCO). AN opened by highlighting the rapid acceleration of global computing demand. Inference now drives 70% of intelligent computing growth, while global daily token usage has increased by 1,000 times in just two years. By 2032, global data center scale is projected to reach 246 GW, with AI data centers (AIDC) accounting for 52% of that capacity. This surge is placing unprecedented pressure on power, cooling, architecture, and deployment. "AI is pushing traditional data center architecture to its limits," said David AN. "The industry must restructure power systems to dynamically match load demand, reduce transmission loss, and rethink how compute, power, and cooling work together. " The presentation identified three industry trends: 1. Power Becomes the New Bottleneck. Data center power is evolving from a single grid input to multi-energy synergy and generation-storage-distribution-consumption linkage. The system must match power with computing load in real time across day/hour, hour, minute, second, and millisecond levels. Technologies such as 800V HVDC, solid-state transformers (SST), and multi-level energy storage are essential. 2. Cooling Must Follow Compute Density. Low-density data halls (≤40 kW) can rely on air cooling with PUE ≤1.25. High-density halls (60–240 kW) require air-liquid hybrid cooling with PUE ≤1.15. Ultra-high-density AI halls (≥600 kW) demand full liquid cooling with PUE ≤1.09. Cooling must evolve alongside chip and rack trends to support the next generation of AI workloads. 3. AI Infrastructure Must Evolve at GPU Speed. Traditional site-assembled construction is too slow. The industry is moving toward modularity and prefabrication, full-unit transport, on-site assembly, and joint commissioning. With 90% MEP modularization, delivery periods can be reduced by 50%. This approach also enables phased investment, synchronized power and cooling matching, and sustained technology roadmap evolution. ZTE's vision is to optimize the AI factory as one system that integrates the co-design and coordination of computing, power, and cooling. This system is characterized by synergy management, energy saving, flexible adaptability, and rapid delivery. ZTE's end-to-end AI infrastructure capabilities span power, cooling, and prefabricated data centers. Key solutions include 800V HVDC power modules, safe lithium batteries, intelligent busbars, cold-plate and immersion liquid cooling, fan walls, and fully prefabricated data centers. With more than 20 countries, 500+ cases, 400,000 cabinets, more than 3,200MW, and 3.5 million square meters of delivered projects, ZTE has established itself as a leading end-to-end data center solution provider. Since entering the modular data center field in 2009, the company has continuously advanced prefabricated and green data center technologies, solidifying its competitive position in the global data center market. About the Author: David AN, ZTE Expert

artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council unanimously passed a new regulation on data centers Monday night, changing the city’s zoning code to ban them in mixed-use zones. The zoning code change will no longer allow data centers as a permitted use in the mixed-use office institutional zone district. Recommended Stories There are no other mixed-use zones in the city that allow data centers. Data centers are still allowed by right in four other zone districts, including airport district, accident potential zone, business/tech and medium industrial. They are conditionally allowed in mixed-use regional activity center and mixed-use airport districts. Areas zoned mixed-use office institutional can be used for office space, multifamily housing, schools, and “related low-impact” use near residential areas, according to city code. During the public hearing for the zoning change, eight people spoke in support. All of them said the city needs to do more to regulate or ban data centers. One speaker told the council to add a moratorium on data centers anywhere in Aurora, and then outright ban them. “All this change would do is add an extra hoop for these companies to jump through. Zoning changes will not address the real problems of these data centers,” he said. “A ban is the only solution to this problem.” Dozens of other people spoke during public comment Monday night in opposition to data centers, notably the Trident Data Center that is proposed to go near Green Valley Ranch if approved. Plans for the new data center, which is proposed to sit at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue, have already been through two formal city reviews and a third is underway, an Aurora spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. The land where Trident is proposed to go is zoned industrial, which is a permitted-use zone for data centers, meaning they do not have to go to a public hearing. Residents in surrounding neighborhoods have spoken out against Trident, saying they worry about noise, health impacts, and strain on utilities like water and energy. Mark Freeman, a spokesperson for the project’s company, Vantage Data Centers, said the company is committed to working with city leaders, residents and other stakeholders to address their concerns. The company plans to hold a neighborhood meeting later in October to hear from residents, Vantage spokesperson Misty Allen said. A date and location for the meeting have not yet been set, but Allen said Vantage will be in touch with neighborhood and homeowner groups. “Vantage respects the mayor’s position yet believes it is important that the project be evaluated based on verified facts,” Freeman said in an email to The Denver Gazette on Friday. “Our goal is to develop infrastructure that supports economic growth while being a responsible neighbor and steward of local resources.”

artigo.texto: Marisa Wanzeller, Geraldo Campos Jr. e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou na terça-feira (13) o requerimento de urgência para votação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), que altera a forma de custeio da contratação de baterias. A votação foi simbólica, com votos contrários registrados pela oposição e pelo partido Novo. Dessa forma, a proposta não passará pelas comissões temáticas e irá direto para o plenário. Pela legislação atual, os custos de contratação de baterias serão arcados exclusivamente pelos geradores. O projeto retira essa obrigação dada pela Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (15.269/2025). Assim, as baterias seriam pagas pelos usuários finais do sistema, tanto geradores quanto consumidores. Interlocutores relatam que o tema atualmente divide o governo, que teme o impacto nas tarifas. O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) teria feito oposição a acelerar a tramitação da matéria na Câmara e já indicou ser favorável à regra atual de que o custeio deve ser feito por quem “deu causa” à contratação das baterias. Segundo uma fonte do setor, o governo sinalizou que “ainda não há posicionamento favorável ao projeto”. Para os agentes, a falta de apoio do governo coloca em risco a própria viabilidade do leilão, que está agendado para dezembro deste ano. Por ora, a votação do mérito da matéria deve ficar apenas para depois do segundo turno das eleições, segundo informou o autor do projeto, deputado Arnaldo Jardim, e o líder do PT na Câmara, deputado Pedro Uczai (PT-SC). O tema foi debatido durante a reunião de líderes partidários na tarde de terça. Ainda não há definição sobre quem será o relator do mérito do projeto de lei. O deputado Arnaldo Jardim disse que irá se encontrar com o presidente da Casa, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), nesta semana para discutir as opções. Leilão em dezembro A forma de custeio da contratação de baterias é um dos maiores empecilhos para a realização do leilão de armazenamento, previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro, avaliam interlocutores do setor. Isso porque a definição sobre quem paga acaba afetando os lances, que precisam precificar os riscos de inadimplência. A expectativa é que o PL seja apreciado antes do certame. Agentes de diferentes segmentos de geração e armazenamento divulgaram um manifesto conjunto em defesa do projeto na última sexta-feira (9). No documento, afirmam que o PL “é urgente para retomar a neutralidade tecnológica, coerência e segurança jurídica no setor elétrico”. Na avaliação das entidades, o desenho de remuneração pelos geradores produz um “desalinhamento entre a natureza sistêmica do serviço, a distribuição de seus benefícios e a incidência legal de seus custos”. Assinam a carta a Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), a Abiape (Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia), a ABIHV (Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde), a Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), a Absolar (Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica) e a Apine (Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica). ANEEL Com o texto da Lei 15.269/2025 em vigor, a ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) iniciou o processo de regulamentação do modelo de custeio. A proposta está em consulta pública até 9 de novembro e prevê que os geradores paguem o encargo de acordo com a sua flexibilidade. Se aprovada, as usinas intermitentes, que não geram de forma firme, devem pagar 100% do encargo. Já os geradores que são mais flexíveis devem pagar menos, entre 75% e 25% do encargo. Assim, usinas eólicas, solares e nucleares pagariam mais, as térmicas um pouco menos, e as hidrelétricas o menor patamar. A MMGD (Micro e Minigeração Distribuída), a princípio, não entraria no rateio.

artigo.texto: Em sua apresentação no seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", organizado pelo jornal Finance and Investment em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã em 14 de outubro, o Sr. Bui Minh Giap, economista- chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, compartilhou suas ideias sobre as necessidades de capital associadas à redução de emissões e como atender a essas necessidades por meio de crédito e mercados de carbono. Não existe um modelo único que sirva para todos os países. Antes de discutir a mobilização de capital, o Sr. Giap sugeriu analisar as necessidades de capital. Estima-se que o Vietnã precise de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB por ano. Desse total, US$ 254 bilhões são necessários para adaptação às mudanças climáticas e aumento da resiliência, e aproximadamente US$ 114 bilhões para redução de emissões. Especificamente para o setor elétrico, o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisado estima uma necessidade de US$ 136 bilhões em investimentos para o desenvolvimento da geração e transmissão de energia entre 2026 e 2030. A estratégia nacional de combate às mudanças climáticas visa atingir o pico das emissões até, no máximo, 2035, seguido por uma rápida redução para emissões líquidas zero até 2050. Inicialmente, são necessários investimentos em energia limpa, na rede elétrica e em eficiência energética; posteriormente, o foco será direcionado para a produção industrial, o transporte, a agricultura e o tratamento de resíduos. Os requisitos de capital são substanciais, mas o financiamento só será liberado quando os projetos forem considerados eficazes, viáveis financeiramente e quando os índices de redução de emissões forem verificáveis. O mercado de carbono oferece incentivos econômicos para a redução de emissões, enquanto o crédito fornece o capital para que as empresas façam os investimentos necessários. Essas duas ferramentas só se complementam de forma eficaz quando as instituições de crédito têm capacidade para avaliar o desempenho ambiental, a transição do cliente, o fluxo de caixa dos créditos de carbono e a capacidade de pagamento de cada projeto. Um projeto de redução de emissões pode economizar energia, reduzir os custos de compra de cotas ou gerar receita com créditos de carbono. Para projetos que visam a venda de créditos de carbono, a instituição emissora precisa considerar a probabilidade de aprovação dos créditos, a produção real, os compradores, o preço de venda, os custos de verificação e o cronograma de pagamento. Contratos de compra de longo prazo podem reduzir o risco de produção, mas não garantem que a empresa irá gerar e entregar créditos suficientes. Dependendo do projeto específico, as instituições de crédito oferecem pacotes de financiamento adequados; estes podem incluir apoio na preparação da documentação, avaliação técnica e obtenção de fundos, condições e taxas de juro adequadas. Portanto, a carteira de financiamento deve incluir ambos os grupos: Atividades Verdes, que englobam atividades que já cumprem os critérios ambientais; e Atividades de Transição, que são atividades que atualmente não cumprem os critérios verdes, mas que possuem planos viáveis de redução de emissões, metas e prazos claros e resultados verificáveis. O economista-chefe do ADB também afirmou que a experiência internacional demonstra que não existe um modelo único que se adapte a todos os países. Alguns bancos centrais fornecem apoio financeiro direto; outros concentram-se na monitorização de riscos, na manutenção de sistemas de dados e no reforço da capacidade das instituições de crédito. A China combina ambas as abordagens com seu instrumento de financiamento para redução de emissões, implementado durante o período de 2021 a 2027. Para empréstimos elegíveis relacionados a energia limpa, eficiência energética e tecnologias de redução de emissões, o Banco Popular da China oferece financiamento com juros baixos equivalente a 60% do valor do empréstimo. A instituição financeira seleciona o tomador, realiza a devida diligência e é responsável pela decisão de concessão do empréstimo. O Japão aplica um mecanismo de financiamento para instituições de crédito com base no tamanho dos empréstimos e em projetos que atendam aos critérios de resposta às mudanças climáticas. Singapura e o Banco Central Europeu (BCE) concentram-se na gestão de riscos. Singapura apoia as instituições de crédito no estabelecimento de sistemas de governança, na avaliação de riscos ambientais e no desenvolvimento de planos de financiamento para a transição. O BCE incorpora o risco climático na supervisão bancária, na análise de cenários e na análise de impacto de riscos. A partir de 2026, o BCE também considerará a vulnerabilidade a choques climáticos ao avaliar determinados títulos corporativos utilizados como garantia em financiamento verde e financiamento para a transição. Portanto, a lição para o Vietnã é a necessidade de combinar o apoio ao investimento com a gestão de riscos, observou o Sr. Giap. Primeiro, é necessário fortalecer os critérios, os dados e a capacidade de avaliação; em seguida, um programa piloto para apoiar o financiamento de empréstimos elegíveis pode ser implementado. Independentemente das ferramentas utilizadas, as instituições de crédito ainda devem realizar suas próprias avaliações e ser responsáveis pela qualidade dos empréstimos. “Quero enfatizar que os bancos são um canal importante para o fluxo de capital, mas não podem, por si só, atender às necessidades de capital de longo prazo para financiamento verde e financiamento de conversão. artigo.texto: METLEN and Karatzis Group of Companies have inaugurated Greece’s largest standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) in Larissa, Thessaly. With a power capacity of 330 MW and an energy storage capacity of 790 MWh, it is also one of the largest facilities of its kind in Europe. The project was delivered through the strategic partnership between METLEN and Karatzis Group of Companies, via a joint investment vehicle in which they hold stakes of 49% and 51%, respectively. The inauguration was attended by Prime Minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Minister of Environment and Energy, Stavros Papastavrou, and representatives of the Greek Parliament and regulatory and productive bodies, as well as of local authorities. The new BESS facility is an energy infrastructure project of strategic importance, as storage, grid works, and interconnections are essential preconditions to attract investment and strengthen the production base of both Greece and Europe. The Thessaly storage facility also illustrates the importance of mature projects, modern infrastructure and companies with the scale and expertise to turn investment plans into operational assets. It is a flagship project for the new energy era and an important step towards building the productive capacity that will underpin the next chapter of Greece’s economic growth. METLEN undertook the construction, operation and maintenance of the facility, drawing on its international experience in complex energy storage projects. Mitsotakis referred to the new facility as an important step towards building the Greece of the future. He highlighted the contribution of the investment to the energy security and competitiveness of the country, congratulating METLEN and Karatzis Group for the completion of the project. Evangelos Mytilineos, Executive Chairman of METLEN, said: “I am particularly proud that today, here in Thessaly, we are inaugurating Greece’s largest standalone energy storage facility in Eastern Europe and one of the largest across the EU. This project reflects the new reality of the energy system, as storage, alongside grids and interconnections, is essential if we are to use the clean energy we generate with efficiency and provide businesses and consumers with a more reliable and predictable energy supply. I would like to thank our partners at Karatzis Group, Antonis Karatzis personally, and everyone at METLEN who contributed to the delivery of this landmark project.” Antonis Karatzis, Chairman and CEO of Karatzis Group of Companies, added: “Today marks an important milestone for Karatzis Group and for the country’s energy future. Our participation in a storage project of this scale reflects our strategic choice to invest in infrastructure with a long-term horizon and a meaningful value for the Greek economy. Together with METLEN, we are showing how two leading Greek companies can combine strengths, expertise and willingness to invest, delivering projects to international standards, increase the use of renewable energy, strengthen grid stability and enhance Greece’s energy security. For us, this project marks the beginning of a new era in which we intend to play an active and meaningful role.” The investment is implemented with loan support from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility – NextGenerationEU. artigo.texto: South Korea plans to launch its Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) in 2027, establishing a framework for issuing and trading carbon credits generated by overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects. The initiative will allow eligible credits to be traded on the Korea Exchange and potentially used for corporate environmental, social and governance (ESG) activities and national emissions reduction commitments. Deputy Prime Minister and Economy and Finance Minister Lee Hyung-il chaired a meeting of economic ministers in Seoul on October 12, where the government finalized the detailed implementation plan. The framework builds on a roadmap announced in December 2025 and outlines the market’s operating structure, credit verification requirements and governance arrangements. A central feature of the GVCM will be the selective use of blockchain technology to record critical carbon credit information, including project operators, emissions reduction volumes, unique identification numbers and approved methodologies. Other information will remain in conventional databases, creating a dual-track system intended to balance data integrity, operational efficiency and system stability. Carbon Credits to Trade Through Korea Exchange Initially, the government will issue credits in standard electronic form for trading through South Korea’s voluntary carbon market exchange. Authorities will consider introducing digital asset-based issuance alongside conventional credits as market activity develops, taking into account trading volumes, regulatory developments and investor confidence. The government has also renamed the initiative from the Global Voluntary Carbon Market to the Global Verified Carbon Market. The revised designation reflects its intention to accommodate credits that qualify for use in both voluntary corporate initiatives and regulated emissions reduction programs. The framework establishes two credit categories based on whether the country hosting an emissions reduction project authorizes the international transfer of the resulting credits. GVCM A credits will receive host-country authorization and may qualify for regulatory purposes, including national climate commitments under the Paris Agreement and the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). They may also support corporate ESG initiatives. GVCM NA credits, which lack the required authorization, will initially be restricted to voluntary corporate environmental activities. These credits could subsequently be upgraded to GVCM A status if the host country grants the necessary approval and corresponding adjustments. South Korea is also evaluating whether GVCM credits could eventually be integrated into its domestic emissions trading system or greenhouse gas target management framework. Any such integration would depend on verification standards, compliance with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and applicable domestic legal requirements. Governance Framework to Include Developing Countries The proposed issuing organization will comprise a board of directors, a technical oversight committee and a secretariat. The board, representing participating countries, will establish policy direction and supervise technical governance. The technical committee will oversee matters such as credit issuance, while the secretariat will manage issuance procedures, credit records and registry operations. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is serving as the interim secretariat. A dedicated secretariat is expected to be established when the market officially launches. The governance structure is designed to give developing countries a greater role in decision-making while respecting their sovereignty over emissions baselines, operating rules and sustainable development priorities. Eligible project categories will reflect participating countries’ development needs and South Korea’s technological capabilities. Potential initiatives include mangrove restoration, agricultural waste management, methane capture and energy efficiency improvements. The government is also discussing cooperation with international institutions, including the World Bank and the Green Climate Fund, to convert emissions reductions from existing projects into GVCM credits. International Carbon Market Growth Drives Strategy International carbon trading is attracting greater attention as countries seek additional ways to meet their Paris Agreement commitments. Many governments face difficulties achieving their 2030 nationally determined contributions through domestic emissions reductions alone. However, inconsistent standards and concerns about the environmental effectiveness of some credits have raised questions about the credibility of international carbon markets. South Korea sees an opportunity to address these concerns through a standardized system combining verification, traceability, and clear rules governing credit eligibility. Projections from MSCI cited in the government’s assessment indicate that the carbon credit market could reach $7 billion to $35 billion by 2030 and $45 billion to $250 billion by 2050. To attract participants, South Korea plans to work with GGGI through international networks, including the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework and the Asia-Pacific Carbon Market Roundtable. At the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, scheduled for November 2026, the government intends to pursue letters of intent with interested countries. A climate investment forum planned for December will further promote the initiative. The government aims to identify priority project sectors during 2026, establish the issuing body in 2027, and finalize project structures before beginning full-scale operations. The GVCM is intended to strengthen confidence in cross-border carbon credits while creating a framework through which verified emissions reductions can support corporate climate initiatives and eligible national targets.
