artigo.texto: Colorado can help lead data center construction — in space | PODIUM Across Colorado, proposals for new data centers are running into fierce opposition. Residents are worried about noise, water use, health risks and high electricity costs. Six municipalities, including Denver, have imposed bans, caps or moratoriums while they figure out how these massive facilities could affect their communities. Local officials cannot ignore voters’ concerns. But the response to new data centers can’t simply be “no” because there’s too much at stake. Abundant computing power is critical to U.S. medical and scientific progress, military and intelligence capabilities and economic growth. Recommended Stories So it’s exciting Colorado may soon have an opportunity to play a key role in developing another option: moving some of that computing infrastructure off the ground and into space. In June, Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper joined Texas U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz in introducing the NEW HORIZON Act, which would direct the Department of Defense to establish a pilot program to test orbital data centers and space-based cloud computing. Currently in early-stage development by well-known companies like Google, SpaceX and Amazon — as well as new entrants like Starcloud and Sophia Space — orbital data centers would put computing, storage and networking equipment aboard state-of-the-art platforms in low-Earth orbit. Then, instead of sending data collected by satellites back to Earth, the orbital facilities would process and store much of that data in space. Sen. Hickenlooper’s proposed program would start small, testing whether orbital computing can quickly, safely and reliably process satellite imagery, national-security information, weather observations and other data already being generated in space, while also assessing key cybersecurity and compatibility issues. But there’s much bigger potential here. If powerful computing systems work reliably in space, we may be able to move into orbit some of the intensive computing now performed in massive ground-based data centers. That would allow us to expand America’s computing capacity without putting so much pressure on local power grids, water supplies and communities. Colorado is an obvious place to start making this happen. Aerospace is one of our defining industries, and we’re also home to important military installations, research universities, federal laboratories and innovative startups. As Sen. Hickenlooper put it, “Space innovation and military preparedness are Colorado’s bread and butter.” It won’t be easy. Launching equipment into space is expensive — and incredibly complex. Computers in orbit have to withstand intense radiation, and keeping powerful processors cool is a serious engineering challenge. Space-based data facilities would also mean more orbital congestion, debris and collision risks. And when something breaks, sending someone up to fix it is a lot harder than calling a technician to a building in Denver or Colorado Springs. But those aren’t reasons to walk away. Rather, as many tech-industry leaders have argued, they’re reasons to start innovating and experimenting with new technologies, including the power systems, cybersecurity, heat management and radiation-resistant hardware that could make commercial orbital data centers possible. Colorado can demonstrate leadership quickly. State agencies, universities, aerospace employers, federal installations and startups can pursue research funding, host demonstrations, train workers and ensure Colorado companies are competing to participate in NEW HORIZON pilot programs. Orbital data certainly won’t arrive soon enough to resolve today’s thorny local disputes. But decisions we make today could determine where the new orbital computing industry takes root in the years to come. Colorado can get there early — creating jobs, developing new national security technology and giving future policymakers another way to meet America’s growing demand for computing power. The fights over data centers happening across Colorado highlight why this idea is worth pursuing. Communities shouldn’t have to choose between protecting their residents and resources and building the infrastructure America needs to power the next generation of innovation. Colorado has the scientific talent, national-security expertise and industrial capabilities to help find another way: up. Kyle Shannon of Denver is chief executive of Storyvine and founder of AI Salon. Dave Cavossa of Washington, DC., is president of the Commercial Space Federation.

artigo.texto: Vikram Solar Subsidiary Plans 7.5 GWh BESS Assembly Plant in Tamil Nadu VSL PowerHive plans to expand from battery storage system assembly into cell manufacturing, building towards an integrated domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem. October 13, 2026. By News Bureau VSL PowerHive, a wholly owned subsidiary of Vikram Solar, has announced plans to establish a 7.5 GWh per annum Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly plant at Oragadam, near Chennai, Tamil Nadu. The facility is designed to scale up to 15 GWh in later phases and will anchor PowerHive's broader roadmap to build 30 GWh of total battery manufacturing capacity by 2030. Spread across approximately 1.65 lakh sq. ft., the facility is slated for inauguration in January 2027, with commercial operations expected to begin in April 2027. The development comes at a time when energy storage has moved to the centre of India's clean energy agenda. As solar and wind capacity grows, storage has become critical to keeping the grid stable, shifting renewable power to evening peaks and enabling round-the-clock clean energy. The Central Electricity Authority projects that India will need about 47 GW /236 GWh of energy storage by 2031-32. Meeting this need at scale will require a strong domestic manufacturing base and reduced reliance on imported systems. Complementing that, PowerHive's ambitions extend well beyond assembly. The company will move into cell manufacturing with a 7.5 GWh programme from 2028, a key step towards building a fully integrated battery manufacturing ecosystem in India, from cell to system. Backing this roadmap, PowerHive is developing indigenous battery technologies and has already initiated multiple patent filings to strengthen its technology ownership and reduce reliance on imported know-how. Once operational, the plant will assemble Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP)-based energy storage systems for utility-scale and Commercial and Industrial (C&I) applications. The portfolio will include 5.016 MWh and 6.25 MWh liquid-cooled BESS containers, PowerHive's P261 battery cabinets, utility-scale energy storage systems and renewable energy-integrated storage solutions, all to be manufactured in India under the Make in India initiative. Gyanesh Chaudhary, Chairman and Managing Director, Vikram Solar, said, "Storage is the bridge between India's renewable ambition and round-the-clock clean power. As the country scales up solar and wind, the ability to store that energy reliably will define the next phase of the transition and that capability must be built in India. The new plant is a decisive step in that direction and extends Vikram Solar's role in the clean energy value chain from generating power to storing it." Arun Mittal, CEO, VSL PowerHive, said, "Energy storage is what makes renewable power dependable, and demand for it in India is rising faster than ever. With this development, we are setting out to build world-class battery manufacturing capability in the country, starting with 7.5 GWh of assembly and progressing to cells and an integrated ecosystem. Our aim is to give utilities, developers and industries a future-ready, domestically built storage partner for the decades ahead." Through the upcoming facility, PowerHive plans to create skilled jobs, develop local talent in advanced storage solutions and strengthen the local industrial ecosystem, supporting Tamil Nadu in building a thriving clean-tech industry. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: The ongoing festive season has brought a curated update to BYD’s electric SUV portfolio in India. The premium Sealion 7 is now available in an exclusive Festive Edition; however, this package does not introduce extra mechanical power or a new battery layout. Instead, BYD has focused its attention on elevating the cabin experience, offering this special edition in a strictly limited run of 150 units nationwide. The BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition enters the market priced at Rs 50.60 lakh (ex-showroom). It is based directly on the high-spec Premium trim, which carries a sticker price of Rs 49.90 lakh, positioning this limited-run model at a premium of Rs 70,000 over the standard variant. What is new on the Sealion 7? The primary differentiator for the Festive Edition is found entirely within the interior. It introduces a sophisticated Tan and Black dual-tone theme that seamlessly accents the leather-appointed seats, layered dashboard, door cards, and the floating center console. The rest of the extensive equipment list is carried over directly from the high-end Premium trim. Core feature highlights include: - 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen - 10.25-inch driver display - Head-up display - Panoramic glass roof with electric sunshade - Ventilated front seats - Driver seat with memory function - Powered tailgate - 19-inch alloy wheels - 360-degree camera - 11 airbags - Level 2 ADAS - 12-speaker Dynaudio sound system - Dual-zone climate control - Double-glazed glass - All-LED lighting The SUV also gets leather upholstery, ambient lighting and auto-tilting ORVMs with memory function. On the exterior, the Festive Edition retains the identical styling cues, aerodynamic character lines, and 19-inch alloy wheels of the regular Premium variant, keeping changes strictly interior-focused. Battery and performance Under the skin, the Festive Edition uses the same 82.56kWh battery pack as the standard Premium model. This battery powers a rear-mounted permanent-magnet synchronous electric motor that puts out a healthy 308bhp and 380Nm of peak torque. BYD claims a 0-100km/h time of 6.7 seconds. The claimed range stands at 567km on the NEDC test cycle. The battery uses BYD’s Blade Battery technology and Cell-to-Body construction. The Sealion 7 also gets Intelligent Torque Adaptation Control, or iTAC, as part of its electric powertrain setup. The Festive Edition is offered only with the Premium specification. BYD has limited production to 150 units across India, making it a fairly small run. BYD Sealion 7 price in India What else from the brand? Beyond the core BYD lineup, the manufacturer is actively preparing to venture deeper into the ultra-luxury EV segment by introducing its premium sub-brand, Denza. Having officially teased its Indian entry, the luxury marque is widely expected to debut with two flagship models: the Z9 GT and the D9. The Denza Z9 GT is a high-performance electric shooting brake driven by a massive 122.5kWh battery pack and a triple-motor layout, generating a staggering 1,156hp and achieving a 0-100km/h sprint in just 2.7 seconds. Concurrently, the Denza D9 will cater to the executive segment as a large, ultra-luxurious electric MPV featuring a plush three-row, 2+2+3 seating configuration with individual rear captain’s chairs.

artigo.texto: Back in my corporate days, I started every new project with one rule: you can't control what you don't measure. Twenty years in energy added a second half to it. You can't sell what you can't prove. In the power business, nobody ever asked me to take my own word for anything. The meter did the talking instead. It sat at a defined point, recorded continuously, and both sides of every contract trusted it. Today I develop AI data centers and keep running into the opposite problem. Operators measure everything, from GPU utilization and node uptime to power draw and temperature at the rack, yet almost none of it counts outside their own control room. It's their own data, collected their own way and shown when they choose to show it, so enterprise customers and capacity buyers end up taking the operator's word for what a facility actually delivered. Hyperscalers get past that on brand and scale. Mid-market operators cannot, and as I see it, that's one of the biggest commercial handicaps they carry. It has nothing to do with how well they run their sites. The market has noticed. Buyers now use independent assessments of AI cloud operators to decide where their workloads go. The money side has noticed too. CoreWeave's $8.5 billion facility, secured against its infrastructure and a contract with a strong customer, has a fixed-rate tranche priced at around 5.9%, while its own unsecured five-year bonds sit close to 10%. Part of that gap is the hardware pledged behind the deal, but the rest, as I read it, is a contract that gave lenders something to rely on beyond the company's own word. Lenders will finance what they can check. With no record of your own, you borrow against someone else's name or pay a few hundred basis points more, and deals take longer either way. The dashboard was never built to answer this Here's a distinction I keep coming back to. A dashboard answers the operator's question: "How is my facility performing?" The person across the table is asking something else: "Can I rely on this when I sign a contract?" Running the first instrument harder won't answer the second. In my experience, three things separate a record somebody else can rely on from good monitoring. The readings need to be collected in a way the other side recognizes, at a defined point and interval, just like the meter. The record needs to be continuous, bad quarters included, because a history with the worst months taken out isn't really a history. And it has to stay blind to what customers are actually computing, the way a meter sees kilowatt-hours but not what you use them for. What I'd start writing down today You don't need new instrumentation for any of this, just a decision about what to keep and the discipline to keep it. Building uptime isn't the best place to start, because a building can be up while half the chips inside it are failing. I'd track how many contracted GPU hours actually turned into usable work after failures, restarts, and degraded links. The industry calls this goodput, and it's what a customer is really paying for. I'd keep the incident history beside it: what failed, how often, and how fast it was replaced. How an incident was resolved is something an outsider can check. Then there's how a site behaves when power gets tight, and that's the one I'd pay most attention to, because the grid side has made up its mind. This May, after incidents in which a gigawatt or more of computing load dropped off the grid unexpectedly, NERC, North America's grid reliability body, issued a rare top-level alert. It told grid operators to tighten how large computing loads are studied, tested, and connected. Load behavior now has to be measured to a standard, rather than described by the operator. Finally, I'd write the methodology down: what's measured, where, how often, who may check it, how long it's kept. That costs almost nothing and gets skipped most. A two-year record can't be built backwards, which is why I'd start now. A power plant with a certified generation and dispatch history talks to the market very differently from one showing its own charts, because a stranger can act on it without knowing or liking the operator. The meter is coming Every mature infrastructure industry eventually got its meter. Electricity has certified metering, and telecom carriers that compete every day still settle with each other against a shared record. AI infrastructure is young and still runs mostly on trust and brand, and I don't think that phase lasts. When a neutral way to record what a facility delivered arrives, I expect it to favor the operators who kept honest, continuous records all along, and that's where a mid-market operator can actually win against a hyperscaler. You don't win in infrastructure by promising the most. The winner is the one who can prove what they've already delivered. artigo.texto: Egypt to Host Rosatom-Teletech Energy Storage Assembly Facility of 500 MWh per Year Rosatom and Egypt's Teletech sign an agreement to set up local assembly capacity for lithium-ion storage systems, with staff training and a gradual ramp-up of production. The Energy Storage Business Unit of Rosatom's Fuel Division and Egyptian technology company Telecom and Technology Co. (Teletech) have signed an agreement to establish local assembly facilities in Egypt. The agreement also provides for personnel training and a gradual expansion of production capacity. According to the two partners, the planned facilities would have a potential production capacity of 500 MWh per year. Battery storage is the subject of other recent announcements, such as Turbo Energy bringing 62.5 MWh of energy storage online across three Spanish industrial sites, or Nala Renewables starting construction of a 125 MW/250 MWh project in Finland. An agreement concluded on the sidelines of Egypt Energy 2026 The agreement was concluded in connection with the Egypt Energy 2026 Exhibition and Conference. Rosatom and Teletech took part in a session there titled "Powering Resilience: The Future of Energy Storage Systems." The session addressed the growing role of energy storage technologies. Discussions on localized production and the product portfolio continued on the sidelines of the conference. A signing ceremony followed the session. Murad Aslanov, Director of Rosatom's Country Office in Egypt, represented the Energy Storage Business Unit. Teletech's Chief Technology Officer represented the Egyptian company. Lithium-ion solutions across the full technological cycle During the session, Rosatom presented its capabilities in lithium-ion energy storage systems. The company says it develops solutions across the full technological cycle, from the development and production of electrodes, cells, battery management systems (BMS) and modules to finished traction batteries and stationary energy storage systems. The applications cited include integrating storage with renewable energy sources, improving the reliability of electricity supply, compensating for fluctuating loads and deploying lithium-ion systems in autonomous power systems. The cooperation is expected to serve as a platform for deployment in the electric power industry, telecommunications, data centers, oil and gas, and other industrial applications. Localization and import-reduction objectives According to Murad Aslanov, building local capacity for energy storage systems can support grid stability as renewable energy expands, reduce dependence on imported technologies and external supply chains, and develop domestic technical expertise. He says the collaboration supports Egypt's 2030 vision. Teletech's Chief Technology Officer states that the partnership combines lithium-ion storage technology with local implementation capabilities and will help strengthen supply chain flexibility. Both parties link the assembly facility to Egypt's Sustainable Clean Energy Plan 2030, which prioritizes diversification of the national energy mix, greater integration of renewable energy sources and the localization of advanced energy technologies. Under the agreement, local assembly of battery energy storage systems (BESS) is expected to help reduce dependence on imported technologies. It is also expected to support grid stability and strengthen domestic technical capabilities. Rosatom adds that the local presence will expand its ability to bring Russian technological solutions to international markets, while adapting its portfolio to the requirements of local energy infrastructure. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: Na manhã de 14 de outubro de 2026, o jornal Finanças e Investimentos, em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã, organizou o seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", com foco na discussão das relações entre a política de crédito, o mercado de carbono e o mercado de capitais, buscando, assim, soluções para desbloquear recursos financeiros para o processo de transição verde. Em seu discurso de abertura no workshop, o Vice-Governador do Banco Estatal do Vietnã, Nguyen Ngoc Canh, elogiou a iniciativa do jornal Finanças e Investimentos de organizar o workshop "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono : Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde". Este é um fórum prático para que agências de gestão, instituições de crédito, empresas e especialistas participem e troquem ideias sobre um tema cada vez mais importante para a transformação verde da economia : a mobilização e a utilização eficaz de capital para esse processo. Em cumprimento ao compromisso assumido pelo Vietnã na COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050, o Partido, o Estado e o Governo emitiram diversas políticas e diretrizes importantes para promover o crescimento verde, a transição energética e o desenvolvimento de uma economia de baixo carbono . Essa transição exige recursos significativos para investimentos em inovação tecnológica, transformação dos métodos de produção, uso eficiente de energia e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Nesse contexto, além dos recursos do orçamento estatal e da mobilização dos mercados de capitais e monetários, é necessário desenvolver simultaneamente outros mecanismos de mercado para mobilizar mais recursos e criar incentivos econômicos para que as empresas reduzam proativamente as emissões, incluindo o mercado de carbono . Por meio do estabelecimento de cotas, da mensuração dos resultados da redução de emissões e da formação de preços de transação para cotas e créditos de carbono , o mercado de carbono cria um mecanismo para converter os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico. Isso proporciona às empresas motivação e recursos adicionais para continuarem investindo no processo de transição verde, em vez de dependerem principalmente do crédito bancário. Em 29 de janeiro de 2026, o Governo emitiu o Decreto nº 29/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta a bolsa de carbono nacional, criando um arcabouço legal para a organização e operação do mercado e da negociação de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono . O mercado piloto está sendo inicialmente estabelecido com uma escala superior a 511 milhões de toneladas de CO2, equivalente às quotas de emissão atribuídas às instalações nos três principais setores emissores: energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento, durante o período de 2025-2026. A fase piloto terá duração até o final de 2028, antes de entrar na fase de operação obrigatória completa a partir de 2029. Neste mercado, os bancos comerciais participam como bancos liquidadores; durante a fase piloto, o BIDV é o único banco liquidador do mercado. O vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh afirmou que, da perspectiva do setor bancário, é necessário reconhecer claramente o papel do crédito verde e do mercado de carbono no processo de transição verde. Em primeiro lugar, o crédito verde fornece capital para investimento e inovação tecnológica, criando recursos para o desenvolvimento de indústrias/setores verdes, resultando, assim, na redução das emissões. As reduções de emissões provenientes de projetos financiados por bancos criarão a base e as commodities para o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono . Por outro lado, um mercado de carbono que funcione de forma eficiente apoiará as empresas, fornecendo-lhes receitas estáveis e fluxo de caixa provenientes da redução de emissões, o que sustentará suas atividades de produção e negócios, melhorará a qualidade de seu crédito bancário e lhes permitirá comprar créditos de carbono para atender aos rigorosos padrões das atividades de importação e exportação. Para atividades de crédito verde, é importante não apenas que os fundos desembolsados para um projeto sejam identificados como verdes, mas também que os resultados de economia de energia, redução de emissões e proteção ambiental alcançados pelo tomador do empréstimo sejam verificados. A mensuração, o relato e a avaliação dos resultados de redução de emissões, bem como a negociação de cotas e créditos no mercado de carbono , podem fornecer informações adicionais para monitorar os resultados ambientais de um projeto. Isso ajuda as instituições de crédito a avaliar a eficácia da utilização do capital e aprimorar a gestão e a supervisão dos fluxos de capital verde. Segundo o Vice-Governador, na realidade, ao longo dos últimos anos, o setor bancário tem implementado proativamente diversas soluções para promover o crédito verde, direcionando fluxos de capital para indústrias e setores que trazem benefícios ambientais e reduzem as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. O Banco Central do Vietnã aperfeiçoou gradualmente o arcabouço político, emitiu orientações e diretrizes sobre crédito verde, gestão de riscos ambientais e sociais, e incentivou as instituições de crédito a desenvolverem estratégias, processos internos e produtos de crédito adequados às metas de crescimento verde. Embora outros canais de mobilização de capital verde estejam se desenvolvendo, o crédito verde continua a desempenhar um papel crucial como um importante recurso para o desenvolvimento de indústrias/setores verdes e para apoiar a transição do modelo de crescimento para uma economia de baixo carbono . Desde os primeiros anos de implementação do crédito verde (2017) até o presente, as atividades de crédito verde expandiram-se tanto em termos de escala de crédito quanto no nível de participação das instituições de crédito. No final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde atingiu mais de 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025

artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência de PL sobre divisão de custos de baterias Votação do mérito deve ficar para depois das eleições; projeto impacta leilões de dezembro A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou o regime de urgência do projeto de lei 3.716 de 2026, que altera a divisão dos custos de contratação de baterias no setor elétrico. A proposta enfrenta divergências entre agentes do setor, e ainda não há prazo para a votação no Legislativo. A aprovação do texto pode afetar os primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia em larga escala no Brasil, marcados para dezembro. Com a aprovação da urgência, o projeto passa a tramitar de forma acelerada e pode ser votado diretamente no plenário da Câmara, sem precisar passar pelas comissões temáticas. O texto ainda precisa ser analisado pelos deputados e, se aprovado, seguirá para o Senado. A expectativa do setor é que a votação do mérito do projeto só aconteça depois das eleições. Os leilões estão marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, com contratos de 15 anos e início do fornecimento previsto para agosto de 2028. Em setembro, o diretor da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Gentil Nogueira, afirmou que uma alteração na legislação às vésperas dos leilões poderia levar ao adiamento das disputas por até 30 dias, para permitir a adaptação das regras. De autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), o PL 3.716 de 2026 propõe revogar um dispositivo da lei 15.269 de 2025 que determina que os custos da contratação de reserva de capacidade por baterias sejam pagos exclusivamente pelas empresas geradoras de energia. Com a mudança, as despesas passariam a seguir a regra geral da reserva de capacidade e seriam divididas entre os usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo consumidores e autoprodutores. A proposta é apoiada por associações ligadas à geração de energia solar e eólica, além de produtores independentes e empresas de armazenamento. As entidades argumentam que as baterias beneficiam todo o sistema elétrico ao armazenar eletricidade para utilização nos horários de maior demanda. Por isso, defendem que o custo seja distribuído de maneira proporcional entre os beneficiários. Manutenção da regra atual Do outro lado, as distribuidoras defendem a manutenção da regra atual. A Abradee (Associação Brasileira de Distribuidores de Energia Elétrica) argumenta que a expansão das fontes renováveis, especialmente solar e eólica, contribuiu para a necessidade de contratar baterias. Na avaliação da entidade, os geradores devem arcar com os custos, uma vez que os consumidores já financiam a expansão dessas fontes por meio de subsídios incluídos nas tarifas de energia. Em nota, a Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) classificou a aprovação da urgência como um “avanço” para ampliar a segurança jurídica dos leilões. A entidade defende a mudança na divisão dos custos, mas afirma que a discussão no Congresso não deve comprometer o calendário dos leilões. Eis a íntegra (PDF – 166 kB). A associação alerta que um eventual adiamento pode comprometer a entrada dos sistemas de armazenamento em operação em 2028 e aumentar o risco de deficit de potência e de apagões em períodos críticos de atendimento. Durante uma audiência pública que inaugurou as contribuições dos agentes do setor para o edital do leilão, o adiamento foi discutido. Beneficiados pelo PL em discussão no Congresso temem que o certame seja realizado antes da eventual aprovação da lei. A Aneel, até o momento, tem assegurado que manterá o cronograma, salvo se a lei for alterada durante os 30 dias que antecedem o leilão. Nesse caso, poderá adiar em até 30 dias a realização do certame para que empresas possam adaptar suas propostas.

artigo.texto: Eskom has launched a process to select a strategic partner to help deliver the 1.5GW Tubatse pumped-storage scheme, a landmark project in Limpopo set to become South Africa’s largest energy-storage programme. As a flagship development in Eskom Green, an unbundled renewable energy subsidiary of the state power utility, the project will provide the long-duration energy storage needed to integrate increasing volumes of renewable energy into the national grid, strengthen energy security and support South Africa’s transition to a more resilient, low-carbon electricity system. “As South Africa advances its energy transition, long-duration storage will be essential to maintaining a reliable and resilient power system. Tubatse will provide the flexibility needed to integrate increasing volumes of renewable energy while strengthening grid stability and security of supply,” Eskom group CEO Dan Marokane said in a statement on Tuesday. Last week, electricity & energy minister Kgosientsho Ramokgopa said the government would prioritise the procurement of 4,600MW of battery energy storage systems and 5,000MW of gas-to-power under its integrated resource plan unveiled last year. The combined allocation of 9,600MW responds to the electricity system’s immediate requirements for storage, flexibility and dispatchable supply amid increasing curtailment, which occurs when available generation cannot be accommodated due to network constraints or operating conditions, including periods when supply exceeds demand. South Africa plans to build 14,000km of new high-voltage transmission lines over the next decade, at an estimated cost of R440bn, to connect new wind, solar, battery storage and gas generation projects to the national grid while strengthening the network to support changing electricity flows. The just-launched request-for-qualification process for Tubatse is the first stage of a competitive exercise to identify a partner with the financial strength, technical expertise, development experience and long-term commitment required to advance the scheme, Eskom said on Tuesday. The proposed facility will provide about 21 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage through four reversible pump-turbine units. A gigawatt-hour is a unit of total energy equal to 1-billion watt-hours (Wh) delivered or consumed over an hour. Able to generate at full output for up to 14 hours, the scheme will help balance the power system, support greater renewable energy integration and enhance grid reliability. Eskom Green is targeting up to 6GW by 2030, with plans to expand its clean energy portfolio to 21GW by 2035 and up to 32GW by 2040, including 5GW of hydro and pumped storage. “Tubatse is … a cornerstone of Eskom Green’s ambition to develop the infrastructure required for a modern, low-carbon electricity system. By combining Eskom’s development experience with private-sector expertise and investment, we aim to unlock the full potential of this project while supporting economic growth, localisation and skills development,” Eskom group executive for renewables Rivoningo Mnisi said. Tubatse will store surplus electricity when demand is low and release it during peak demand, when wind and solar output drops, or when the grid is under strain. This will help reduce wasted renewable energy, make better use of existing generation and strengthen security of supply. The project has been classified as one of the top 12 national priority projects by Infrastructure South Africa and forms part of the country’s just transition programme towards cleaner renewable energies. Tubatse builds on more than two decades of Eskom’s experience in operating and maintaining pumped storage schemes and conventional hydropower plants, including the delivery of the 1,332MW Ingula pumped storage scheme commissioned in 2017. The power utility currently operates 2,732MW of pumped storage capacity across Drakensberg, Palmiet and Ingula, as well as 661MW of conventional hydroelectric capacity, primarily at Gariep and Vanderkloof. The required land has been secured, environmental authorisation has been granted for the scheme, and key technical studies and access-road designs have reached an advanced stage, Eskom said. Grid connection studies have also advanced, and the department of water & sanitation has confirmed water availability from De Hoop Dam. “Together, these milestones distinguish Tubatse from an early-stage concept and provide prospective partners with the opportunity to invest in an advanced development platform where critical enabling work is either complete or well progressed,” the utility said. artigo.texto: Madison County planning commission votes against battery energy storage facility Madison County’s Planning Commission has given a unanimous unfavorable recommendation for zoning changes to allow a proposed battery energy storage facility. IPR’s Thomas Ouellette reports. Audio Transcript Developers with Jupiter Power want to build two battery energy storage system facilities in the county. Battery storage facilities hold surplus energy from a local power grid in large lithium batteries until it’s needed in times of peak power use. These kinds of facilities do not generate any power on their own. As part of hours of deliberation, Nat Drucker with Jupiter Power addressed several concerns from residents – like capping the number of total batteries, draining water to an independent system, and taking precautions against fire. “We hope that all of this shows and demonstrates that we are absolutely willing to work with people.” Drucker said. “And we’re working to do this better, and to provide this very important piece of infrastructure that is going to help keep this county, and this part of Indiana, moving forward.” The rezoning was proposed last month with the planning commission, but Jupiter Power developers at that meeting requested a continuance to better respond to concerns and questions. Despite that new information, members of the public remained firmly against the battery storage facility. Former Madison County Council member Ben Gale was among them. “So the numbers we’re seeing up here, I don’t buy them,” he said. “I’ve been through the process before, I see how it works, and the promises made up front are never what ends up working.” Officials with Jupiter Power say neither project involves a large building. The sites instead feature “container-based” energy storage. After the unfavorable recommendation, the project will now move to the county commissioners to consider and vote on the rezoning request. If it were to be approved in Madison County, Jupiter Power says the first site, Liberty 1, would start construction in 2027 and be operational in 2028. Indiana Michigan Power has an agreement with Jupiter Power to purchase the battery storage facility upon its completion. The second site, Liberty 2, is significantly bigger, and has a longer development time. No long-term ownership of the site has been determined yet. Thomas Ouellette is our reporter and producer. Contact him at thomas.ouellette@bsu.edu.

artigo.texto: On the morning of October 14, 2026, the Finance and Investment Newspaper, in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam, organized the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows," focusing on discussing the linkages between credit policy, the carbon market, and the capital market, thereby seeking solutions to unlock financial resources for the green transition process. In his keynote address at the workshop, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh highly appreciated the initiative of the Finance and Investment Newspaper in organizing the workshop "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" today. This is a practical forum for management agencies, credit institutions, businesses, and experts to participate and exchange ideas on an issue that is becoming increasingly important for the green transformation of the economy : mobilizing and effectively utilizing capital for this process. In fulfillment of Vietnam's commitment at COP26 to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the Party, State, and Government have issued many important policies and guidelines to promote green growth, energy transition, and the development of a low -carbon economy. This transition requires significant resources for investment in technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. In this context, in addition to resources from the state budget and mobilization from the capital and money markets, it is necessary to simultaneously develop other market mechanisms to mobilize more resources and create economic incentives for businesses to proactively reduce emissions, including the carbon market. Through the establishment of quotas, measurement of emission reduction results, and the formation of transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This provides businesses with additional motivation and resources to continue investing in the green transition process, instead of relying primarily on bank credit. On January 29, 2026, the Government issued Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP regulating the domestic carbon exchange, creating a legal framework for organizing and operating the market and trading of greenhouse gas emission quotas and carbon credits. The pilot market is initially being established with a scale of over 511 million tons of CO2, equivalent to the emission quotas allocated to facilities in the three major emitting sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement, during the 2025-2026 period. The pilot phase will last until the end of 2028, before entering the full mandatory operation phase from 2029. In this market, commercial banks participate as settlement banks; during the pilot phase, BIDV is the sole settlement bank in the market. Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that, from the perspective of the banking sector, it is necessary to clearly recognize the role of green credit and the carbon market in the green transition process. First, green credit provides capital for investment and technological innovation, creating resources for the development of green industries/sectors, thereby resulting in reduced emissions. The emission reductions from projects funded by banks will create the basis and commodities for the development of the carbon market. Conversely, an efficiently functioning carbon market will support businesses by providing them with stable revenue and cash flow from emission reductions, which will support their production and business activities, improve their bank credit quality, and enable them to purchase carbon credits to meet the stringent standards of import and export activities. For green credit activities, it is important not only that the disbursed funds for a project are identified as green, but also that the results of energy savings, emission reduction, and environmental protection achieved by the borrower are verified. Measuring, reporting, and evaluating emission reduction results, as well as trading quotas and credits in the carbon market, can provide additional information to monitor the environmental outcomes of a project. This helps credit institutions assess the effectiveness of capital utilization and enhance the management and supervision of green capital flows. According to the Deputy Governor, in reality, over the past years, the banking sector has proactively implemented many solutions to promote green credit, directing capital flows into industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The State Bank of Vietnam has gradually perfected the policy framework, issued orientations and guidelines on green credit, environmental and social risk management; and encouraged credit institutions to build strategies, internal processes, and develop credit products suitable for green growth goals. While other green capital mobilization channels are developing, green credit continues to play a crucial role as an important resource for developing green industries/sectors and supporting the transition of the growth model to a low -carbon economy. From the early years of green credit implementation (2017) to the present, green credit activities have expanded both in terms of credit scale and the level of participation of credit institutions. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856 trillion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025, with an average growth rate of over 20% per year during the 2017-2025 period, mainly concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries and biodiversity conservation (accounting for over 31%), and green energy (accounting for nearly 28%). artigo.texto: Veja o resumo da notícia - O mercado de carbono no agronegócio brasileiro é visto como promissor, mas pode ser uma ilusão para a realidade econômica do setor. - A aventura do mercado de carbono revela-se pouco rentável para o produtor rural, devido aos altos custos de mensuração e taxas de intermediários. - A regra de adicionalidade impede que produtores pioneiros monetizem o estoque de carbono preservado, premiando apenas os retardatários. - Esquemas voluntários e fragmentados, com altos custos de transação, carecem de eficácia e falham em gerar valor real, segundo economistas. - O caminho viável para o campo envolve a valorização do carbono na cadeia de suprimentos, acesso a crédito verde e ganhos de produtividade. Para muitos o mercado de carbono representa a próxima grande safra do agronegócio brasileiro mas quando confrontada com a realidade econômica do setor pode ser uma grande ilusão. Para o produtor rural, essa aventura revela-se muitas vezes pouco rentável. Nos solos tropicais, onde o carbono possui dinâmica complexa e instável, a comprovação do sequestro exige amostragens físicas caras e auditorias rigorosas. Como o sequestro líquido anual no plantio direto costuma ser inferior a uma tonelada por hectare, os altos custos de mensuração e as taxas cobradas por intermediários devoram a margem financeira, deixando para a fazenda um retorno meramente residual. Soma-se a isso a perversidade da regra de adicionalidade, que exige que a prática mitigadora seja nova, impedindo que o produtor pioneiro monetize o estoque que preserva há décadas e premiando apenas o retardatário. Essa dispersão contratual ilustra os alertas de economistas como William Nordhaus (premio Novel de 2018) e Robert Stavins: esquemas voluntários, fragmentados e repletos de custos de transação carecem de eficácia e falham em gerar valor real. O caminho viável para o campo não passa pela especulação de papéis, mas sim pela valorização do carbono dentro da própria cadeia de suprimentos, pelo acesso a crédito verde e pelos ganhos diretos de produtividade e resiliência que um solo vivo naturalmente proporciona e mecanismos como RenovaBio.

artigo.texto: The Kremlin in Moscow is investigating how much financial loss Yandex -- which supports AI and search in Russia -- has incurred after last week's drone attack on three of its data centers. One of the data centers is used to train its AI models. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was too early to assess whether users had suffered financial losses from outages, Reuters reported. Asked by Reuters whether the government was considering a mechanism to compensate users, he said Yandex was "currently facing difficulties," adding that "the matter is being discussed by the government, but the company is taking urgent steps to address the consequences of the attack." Media reports in Russia are calling Yandex,Russia’s largest technology company." Last week it announced that two of its data centers were struck by drones. “Serious" damage was reported at all three locations. advertisement advertisement In a statement posted on Friday, Yandex said operations at its Sasovo facility were “completely halted,” while part of the infrastructure in Kaluga was “disabled.” The Vladimir facility was taken completely offline on Sunday, according to the company. "Data centers are the 'iron heart' of Yandex," according to a post on the company’s website translated into English from Russian. “Their operability is critical for services that have become part of people's everyday lives. Millions of users check traffic and build routes, listen to music, watch movies, order groceries, and get answers to questions. Our technologies help hundreds of thousands of companies run their businesses: taking orders, serving customers, and interacting with partners.” Following the attacks on the Sasovo and Kaluga facilities, a third Ukrainian drone strike hit Yandex's Vladimir data center on Sunday, Oct. 11, forcing a complete shutdown of operations at that site. The Sasovo data center is noted for housing two of Yandex's top supercomputers equipped with Nvidia A100 chips used to train its YandexGPT AI models. Chinese conglomerates represent one of the largest foreign ad segments on Yandex today that leverages search, video, and geotargeted navigation ads across Yandex Maps and Navigator, according to Google Gemini. These recent targeted drone strikes hit a company still trying to recover from a recent restructuring following a corporate split in 2024. Yandex is based in Russia. It has retained the brand’s name and continues to operate as Russia's leading search engine and AI lead. Its Dutch parent company rebranded as Nebius Group. Yandex still dominates domestic search with the most market share in the region, but it is currently battling infrastructure challenges after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted several of its data centers and supercomputers. In 2024, Yandex NV, the parent company of the Russian search engine at the time, agreed to sell its assets in Russia to a group of local investors for $5.2 billion in one of the largest corporate exits from Russia since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. Nebius Group, which now focuses on AI, found that its shares fell 2% on Tuesday -- opening at $200.50 versus a prior close of $210.06, while trading volume reached nearly 6.94 million shares, according to MarketBeat. The company does not sell advertising space or operate an advertising network. Unlike its predecessor Yandex, focused on digital advertising, Nebius has completely exited the consumer-facing ad-tech industry.

artigo.texto: Eskom lança rodada de qualificação para programa de 6 GW de renováveis e armazenamento A Eskom, estatal de energia elétrica da África do Sul, iniciou uma etapa de solicitação de qualificação (RFQ) para selecionar desenvolvedores de energia renovável para a fase inicial de uma iniciativa destinada a implantar até 6 GW de capacidade de geração renovável e armazenamento em escala de utilidade. Segundo comunicado da empresa, essa primeira fase representa um conjunto inicial de projetos que chega a até 6 GW, abrangendo energia solar fotovoltaica (PV), sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), energia eólica e tecnologias renováveis adicionais.A própria Eskom fornecerá projetos que incluem não menos de 2 GW de solar fotovoltaica, além de 1 GW / 4 GWh de BESS, que os parceiros estratégicos selecionados poderão complementar com projetos próprios ou originados por eles. Esses parceiros formarão uma lista de colaboradores pré-qualificados para codesenvolvimento e coinvestimento, cuidando do desenvolvimento, do financiamento e da implementação ao longo de um prazo de cinco anos. Os desenvolvedores que se qualificarem serão convidados a participar de rodadas competitivas de contratação posteriores, por meio de uma ou mais solicitações de propostas (RFPs). O portfólio pretendido inclui projetos originados pela Eskom em terrenos de propriedade da estatal e em locais de geração atuais, além de projetos de propriedade de parceiros estratégicos ou originados por eles, que poderão ser desenvolvidos, adquiridos ou executados em conjunto com a Eskom ou sua divisão Eskom Green. Espera-se que cada projeto seja organizado por meio de uma sociedade de propósito específico (SPV) dedicada e com patrimônio segregado, com financiamento estruturado principalmente em uma estrutura de project finance com recurso limitado ou sem recurso. Em julho, a Eskom apresentou a Eskom Green como parte de uma abordagem de reestruturação mais ampla que abrange o esforço de desmembramento iniciado em 2023. Pressão financeira e reformulação do mercado Mesmo com esses passos, a Eskom continua a enfrentar pressão financeira. A estatal ainda depende de geração a carvão e de usinas de pico movidas a diesel. Os gastos com diesel permanecem na casa das centenas de milhões de randes sul-africanos, embora tenham caído consideravelmente em comparação com o ano anterior. Ao mesmo tempo, a África do Sul avança com reformas no mercado de eletricidade, entre elas propostas para criar um mercado atacadista de eletricidade que pode alterar a posição da Eskom no setor elétrico. Analistas alertaram que medidas regulatórias que favoreçam os ativos a carvão da Eskom poderiam desestimular o investimento privado e corroer ganhos de eficiência, possivelmente elevando os custos de eletricidade de longo prazo para os consumidores. A capacidade solar instalada total da África do Sul agora ultrapassou 10 GW, após 1,6 GW ter sido adicionado em 2025. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado de células solares e diodos emissores de luz na África do Sul, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. Cobertura do Produto Abrange diodos emissores de luz (LEDs) semicondutores e dispositivos semicondutores fotossensíveis, incluindo células solares, fotodiodos e fototransistores, conforme as definições do Prodcom 26112220 e do Prodcom 26112240. A base de medição da produção é expressa em unidades. Incluídos - Diodos emissores de luz (LEDs) semicondutores - Células solares fotovoltaicas de silício cristalino - Células solares de filmes finos - Fotodiodos - Fototransistores - Outros dispositivos semicondutores fotossensíveis Excluídos - artigo.texto: Media gets first look at Project Jupiter AI data center in Santa Teresa Oracle and Stack Infrastructure offered a first glimpse of Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, highlighting its progress, technology, and workforce impact. Media gets first look at Project Jupiter AI data center in Santa Teresa Oracle and Stack Infrastructure offered a first glimpse of Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, highlighting its progress, technology, and workforce impact. Media crews were invited for the first time to tour Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, which began building within the past year. The tour showcased several aspects of the roughly 1,400-acre campus, including energy solutions, construction progress, and workforce details. Oracle highlighted Bloom Energy's fuel cell technology, which uses natural gas to generate electricity without burning it. The company explained that this system will reduce air pollution and water usage. Visitors were also shown Building A, one of four planned data center buildings, and its cooling system. "It's a closed-loop cooling system, and so what that means is the project is not continuously consuming water for data center operations," Josh Timberlake, SVP of site strategy at Stack Infrastructure said. The equipment staging area was another stop on the tour, where materials and equipment are managed. Stack Infrastructure, the company developing and building the campus, shared workforce details, saying, "We have just about 4,400 construction workers working here full time. 1,200 of those are New Mexicans. Over 600 of those are from Doña Ana County." The tour concluded inside one of the data halls, where rows of server racks will eventually fill the space. Over the past year, Project Jupiter has faced community concerns regarding water use, air quality, and transparency. During a Q&A session, Oracle executives addressed these concerns, saying, "We're committed to New Mexico at this point. So we're making sure we do everything right. We're taking the feedback we need to adjust something. We keep adjusting till we get to making sure we come through on our New Mexico economic benefit." Oracle noted that this was the first time media had been allowed inside the construction site but assured it would not be the last. The company emphasized its commitment to keeping the community informed as construction progresses. Stack Infrastructure stated that the number of construction workers on-site is expected to grow to nearly 7,000, and hiring for permanent data center operations jobs has already begun.

artigo.texto: It’s a common myth that ostriches bury their heads in the sand when frightened or agitated. Ostriches actually don’t do that. But apparently, some local politicians do. Officials in the Columbia County city of Hudson last week proposed a six-month moratorium on battery energy storage systems — designed to store energy generated from solar arrays and wind turbines — after being approached by a couple of companies about the city’s codes. It turns out the city didn’t have an answer for the companies because it has nothing in its codes about the facilities. That leads to an obvious question: How does any community in New York — a state that seven years ago passed a major long-term initiative to battle climate change — go this long without taking some local initiative to regulate these systems? State law doesn’t require local governments to develop their own municipal regulations for the systems, but it should. These facilities can have major local impacts that might not be prioritized in state-level regulations, including the impact on local property values, rural character and quality of life. Local government officials can play a significant role in where such facilities are located and the conditions for approval. They should not only not be hiding from local regulations, they should be aggressively pursuing them. In fact, in an editorial on Wednesday, we supported the town of Duanesburg’s effort to assume authority from the state to manage large-scale energy projects — citing the town’s years of adapting its comprehensive plan, local zoning codes and local laws to address these projects. Hudson is in the opposite situation. The good news for Hudson and other communities that have similarly avoided addressing this growing issue is that the state has plenty of information and advice available for them. Hudson officials can start by checking out the website of the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) website. Among a significant amount of information, the website features a 46-page “Battery Energy Storage System Guidebook for Local Governments.” The guidebook includes a model law to help local government officials adopt legislation and regulations and a model permit to help local officials establish requirements for electrical and structural plan review necessary for permitting. In addition, NYSERDA offers free technical assistance for planning and zoning board members, code officials, first responders and others. Sticking one’s head in the sand doesn’t make a problem go away. It just makes it more difficult to deal with. Fortunately, Hudson officials have time and access to state resources to help them. They should use the time afforded by the moratorium to get caught up.

artigo.texto: St. Joseph City Council postponed vote on data center study contracts ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (KQTV) -- The St. Joseph City Council postponed two ordinances related to zoning and development guidelines for potential data center projects on Monday evening. The council postponed the ordinance after questions arose about whether the proposed consultants do business with data centers. One company recommended for a contract denied having business ties to data center development. "Any affiliation with data centers or data center developments was asked. I want to drill down on that with one company in particular that was mentioned," City Manager, Mike Schumacher said. During the meeting, several residents urged council members to consider how data center development could affect the community, with some also raising concerns about the proposed contract with GBA Inc. GBA Inc. provides turnkey data center services for handling the entire planning, designing, construction and maintenance process. The council is considering a contract with GBA Inc. for up to $42,440 to study data center development and recommend zoning changes and development guidelines. The review would address electric and water infrastructure, land use, environmental impacts, public services, costs and community concerns. "You're not gonna get accurate, fair information from somebody that makes their living building data centers," St. Joseph resident, Debra Miller said. "I opposed spending over $42,000 for a company that you can't trust is going to give you the best results that take in the consideration of the residents of St. Joe." The council is also considering a contract with Renew Missouri Advocates for up to $10,750 for community outreach and legal services related to data center development. The firm would also recommend zoning updates and potential changes to the city’s code of ordinances. One resident also urged the city to revise the ordinance language. "Please amend these bills and work toward that goal, and then I will say thank you for pursuing zoning restrictions, and regulations that protects the health, and well being of the citizens of St. Joseph," St. Joseph resident, Deb Ballin said. The council plans to review the language of both proposed ordinances before bringing them back for a vote at its next meeting. The council voted on a development plan for Bryan St. Joseph Apartments. The complex would be at 5408 N. Pointe Drive, behind the YMCA. The ordinance will allow the city to issue up to $40 million in bonds to help Bryan St. Joseph Apartments LLC build a 180-unit market-rate apartment complex. The project will receive property tax abatements on the improvements and a sales tax exemption on construction materials. The council voted to withdraw the request to add 55 parking spaces along Southwest Parkway between Fleeman Street and Mason Road. The school district requested the ordinance be withdrawn because they want to continue to evaluate the parking needs at Benton High School. The next city council meeting will take place on Monday, Oct. 26th, in the Council Chambers at City Hall.

artigo.texto: BYD reveals Atto 8 in new fully-electric iteration; previously PHEV only BYD has revealed the all-electric Atto 8 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The flagship electric SUV has up to 653km of claimed range and a new Flash Charging technology that can charge the battery from 10 to 97 percent in just nine minutes. New Delhi: BYD has expanded its flagship Atto 8 SUV lineup by introducing a fully electric version at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Joining the existing plug-in hybrid (PHEV) model, the new Atto 8 EV offers strong performance, a large battery pack, and the Chinese manufacturer’s latest charging technology. The biggest highlight is BYD’s new Flash Charging system, which makes its debut on the Atto 8 EV. The technology promises exceptionally short charging times, allowing the battery to gain a substantial amount of charge in just a few minutes. The electric SUV will be available in rear-wheel-drive (RWD) and all-wheel-drive (AWD) configurations, with the latter producing a combined 775hp. In terms of design, the electric version remains largely identical to its plug-in hybrid counterpart, apart from a few EV-specific changes. BYD Atto 8 EV: Battery, range and performance The BYD Atto 8 EV uses a 115kWh battery pack across both powertrain configurations. Buyers can choose between a single-motor rear-wheel-drive setup and a more powerful dual-motor all-wheel-drive version. The RWD variant produces 462hp and 365Nm of torque. BYD claims it can accelerate from 0 to 100 kph in eight seconds, while delivering a WLTP-certified driving range of up to 653km. The AWD model uses two electric motors to generate a combined output of 775hp and 775Nm. With the additional power and traction, the SUV can complete the 0-100 kph sprint in a claimed 4.6 seconds. However, its WLTP range is slightly lower at 602km. One of the most significant developments introduced with the Atto 8 EV is BYD’s Flash Charging technology. The system is designed to drastically reduce charging times, making longer journeys more convenient. As per BYD, the technology can replenish the battery from 10 to 97 per cent in just nine minutes. The manufacturer also claims that charging from 0 to 70 per cent takes only five minutes. BYD says the system can maintain impressive charging performance even in extremely cold conditions. At temperatures as low as -30 degrees Celsius, the battery can reportedly be charged from 20 to 97 per cent in approximately 12 minutes. These figures show the maker’s claimed charging capabilities. It is with actual charging times depend on factors such as charger compatibility, battery temperature and charging conditions. BYD Atto 8 EV: Exterior design The Atto 8 EV carries over most of its styling from the PHEV version. The most noticeable differences are the redesigned aerodynamic alloy wheels and the absence of an exhaust outlet. At the front, the electric SUV features a closed-off grille, matrix LED headlights and a curved LED daytime running light strip. The lower bumper incorporates black trim and functional air intakes intended to help cool the vehicle’s components. A LiDAR sensor is placed on the roof, indicating the presence of advanced driver-assistance hardware. The side profile of the Atto 8 EV features black alloy wheels with aerodynamic inserts, prominent wheel arches and slim roof rails. A chrome accent runs from the front fender towards the front doors, while black cladding covers the lower portion of the doors. At the back, the SUV gets distinctive infinity-knot-inspired LED tail lamps, connected by a design element incorporating an illuminated BYD badge. A roof-mounted spoiler completes the exterior styling. BYD Atto 8 EV: Interior and features On the inside, the Atto 8 EV shares its dashboard design and overall layout with the plug-in hybrid version. The cabin has a 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster and a large 15.6-inch touchscreen infotainment system. A three-spoke steering wheel houses physical buttons and scroll controls, while the dashboard incorporates slim air-conditioning vents and extensive soft-touch leather surfaces. The SUV offers a seven-seat configuration arranged in a 2+2+3 layout, with individual seats in the second row. Boot space sits at 270 litres, identical to the PHEV model. However, the fully electric Atto 8 benefits from an additional 136-litre front storage compartment, or frunk, made possible by the absence of a combustion engine. Comfort features include heating, ventilation and massage functions for both the first- and second-row seats. Other equipment highlights include a panoramic glass roof, three-zone automatic climate control and a 21-speaker DiSound audio system. The SUV also comes with two 50W wireless smartphone chargers and a front-mounted refrigerator capable of cooling its contents to -6 degrees Celsius or heating them to 50 degrees Celsius. In international markets, the BYD Atto 8 EV will compete with other large electric SUVs, including the Kia EV9, Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Skoda Peaq. Click for more latest Auto news. artigo.texto: If Amendment 3 passes in November, it will not only annually take nearly $12 billion away from public safety, roads, parks and other government services, but it will also create a system where the majority of homeowners become a financial drag on the very local governments from which they expect and demand services. If government is supposed to “run like a business,” as we’ve heard so many times before, then the most logical business response would be to deprioritize any future expansion of a sector that creates costs with no financial recuperation while fast tracking sectors that can fill the financial holes for existing residents. Local governments are limited in the revenue they can raise to provide the services people expect. Property taxes are a big chunk of that revenue, which local governments also leverage as a required match to secure federal and state dollars for major projects like stormwater management, flood control, beach renourishment and even affordable housing projects. Often, every dollar cut from property taxes is really a double or even triple loss for major infrastructure projects. To complete these projects to create livable cities, local governments will have no choice but to try and replace most of the lost funds due to Amendment 3. Thus, Amendment 3 could easily usher in an era of mega data centers and other industrial projects that promise the property taxes needed to fill the hole left by homesteaded properties often contributing zero dollars to local services. Indeed, Florida TaxWatch is already pitching local governments and citizens to drop opposition to data centers on the grounds they could generate $1 billion in property tax revenue. Right now, with data center projects in heavy demand, there’s no doubt these could be some of the biggest projects available to fill that sudden property tax hole. As Amendment 3 forces a major shift of tax collections to non-homestead properties, local governments are also likely to raise the millage (“taxes per $1,000 of value”) to fill the $12 billion hole. This will increase taxes on local businesses and multi-family housing like apartments — and, of course, increase the rent for those living there. It will also increase taxes for those newer homeowners with higher assessed values. To keep current funding levels, Orange County millage would need to increase by 20% for property owners still paying taxes, while fire and police millage would need to increase by more than 23%. Bedroom communities like Belle Isle, Oakland, Ocoee and Winter Garden would need more than 40% increases. On the flip side, Amendment 3 will take nearly 50% of existing homeowners off the non-school tax rolls. Since homeowners have also been protected with a 3% annual cap via Save Our Homes, the current assessed value of many homes is below $250,000, even if the market value of that home has substantially increased well beyond that in the last decade. And once taxable value becomes $0, it doesn’t matter how much millage is increased because anything multiplied by $0 is still $0. As a result, Amendment 3 will make new single-family homes (or even owner-occupied condos) much, much less attractive for local government to zone or move along in the permitting process. And it’s inevitable that projects with higher value homes will get more attention. Projects proposing more affordable housing with smaller houses and smaller lots will be de-prioritized. Indeed, for population growth, the best avenue for local governments will be multi-family apartments that are not owner-occupied and will continue to pay the higher property tax rates. All of this is not to say that Florida doesn’t have property tax issues. We continue to punish new entrants into the market by resetting assessed values when the home changes hands, which results in newer homeowners paying vastly higher amounts than their neighbors simply because they bought their first home a few years later. If property taxes are supposed to reflect services, Florida needs to reform property taxes to bring about fairness among all similar homeowners. But wiping half of homeowners off the rolls — most of whom will be longtime homeowners — while leaving most newer homeowners holding the bag along with renters and businesses, is not the ticket to prosperity that some organizations seem to think it is. So unless someone wants to vastly increase the likelihood of a mega data center in their community while also reducing the chances their kids have of moving into a home they can afford, we should say no to Amendment 3 and demand a better ballot proposition built on fairness for all taxpayers and residents. Scott Randolph is Orange County’s Tax Collector.

artigo.texto: Containerized Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Technology Innovation Key Trends, Growth Drivers and Opportunities Introduction to containerized BESS technology Containerized Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) technology is transforming the way utilities, independent power producers, and commercial enterprises store, manage, and dispatch electricity. Powered by lithium-ion and emerging sodium-ion chemistries, advanced battery management systems (BMS), power conversion systems (PCS), thermal management, and cloud-based energy management software, modern containerized BESS units deliver real-time control and grid-scale flexibility. From utility-scale renewable integration and peak shaving to commercial microgrids, EV charging hubs, and remote industrial sites, the technology is becoming an integral part of the global energy transition and the decarbonization of power networks. History of containerized BESS technology The containerized BESS industry has evolved from small stationary battery banks and UPS installations into modular, factory-assembled, plug-and-play energy storage ecosystems. Advances in lithium-ion cell density, power electronics, liquid cooling, fire suppression, and digital monitoring have enabled containerized systems to support renewable firming, frequency regulation, demand response, and resilience for critical infrastructure. Standardized 20-foot and 40-foot containers now allow rapid deployment, scalable capacity expansion, and lower installation costs compared with traditional brick-and-mortar storage plants. Benefits of containerized BESS technology Containerized BESS technology offers numerous advantages across utility, commercial, industrial, and residential environments: - Rapid deployment through factory-built, pre-tested modular containers. - Scalable capacity that can be expanded block by block as demand grows. - Enhanced grid stability, frequency regulation, and renewable energy firming. - Lower installation, civil work, and land acquisition costs. - Seamless integration with solar, wind, EV charging, and microgrid ecosystems. Current market size and growth trends of containerized BESS industry The containerized BESS market is experiencing robust growth as renewable penetration, grid modernization, and energy security become mainstream priorities. According to MarketsandMarkets, the global containerized BESS market size was valued at USD 13.87 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 35.82 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 20.9% from 2025 to 2030. Rising adoption of utility-scale storage, commercial microgrids, and AI-driven energy management continues to accelerate market expansion across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. Key drivers and factors influencing the future of containerized BESS technology AI, IoT, 5G, cloud analytics, and edge intelligence are enabling more capable containerized storage systems across industries. - artigo.texto: Data Centers Voters in Six States Will Decide Future of Data Center Construction September 24, 2026 | Kim Miller October 13, 2026 | Billy Culleton Key Takeaways: The sheer power demand from data centers has recently pushed state lawmakers to consider new policies that allow large energy users to access dedicated power sources without everyday ratepayers shouldering the cost. These arrangements, called "behind-the-meter" or "bring-your-own-power," share the same goal: addressing public concern over rising electricity costs while giving data center developers alternatives to lengthy utility interconnection queues. While utilities and large-load users have long negotiated power purchase agreements for generation, state policymakers are seeking to make behind-the-meter arrangements more common and easier to establish. This type of legislation saw more activity in 2025 than in 2026 but is likely to remain of interest to state lawmakers as more data centers connect to the grid. Last year, seven states enacted legislation allowing data centers to source their own energy. In May 2025, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt (R) signed SB 480, which exempts large users from being defined as public utilities if they provide their own electricity. The bill also allows data centers to contract with regulated and non-regulated utilities to house onsite generation. Ohio lawmakers followed suit by enacting a sweeping energy bill (HB 15) that removes barriers for large energy users to self-generate power, either directly or through a third party. In addition, the bill removed previous rules requiring self-generation sources to be located on a customer's premises. In Utah, lawmakers created a pathway for behind-the-meter generation by allowing large-load users to enter the competitive market if an agreement is not reached with the utility within 90 days. SB 132 allows data centers to source energy from the grid through a third-party supplier or from a source entirely separate from the grid. Texas, a state known for its energy production, also enacted a major bill in 2025 that addressed behind-the-meter options for data centers. SB 6, which broadly sets standards for how data centers can interconnect with the grid, allows large-load users to connect directly to an existing stand-alone generation source. The bill also requires utility regulators to direct data centers to source energy from backup generators during emergency power situations. Finally, New Hampshire lawmakers allowed off-grid power generation for large users, with the main caveat being that they have to be completely independent of the grid (HB 672). Bills that create this type of arrangement, called "consumer-regulated electricity" (or CRE) were also considered in Maryland (HB 1219 & SB 947), Illinois (HB 4163), New Jersey (A 5431), and New York (S 8037). However, none of these bills advanced out of their committee of origin. Behind-the-Meter Behind-the-meter refers to energy generation or storage systems that are located on the customer's side of the utility meter, allowing large users like data centers to generate or source their own electricity independently from the main utility grid. These arrangements can reduce reliance on the grid and help avoid passing costs onto other ratepayers. Consumer-Regulated Electricity (CRE) Consumer-regulated electricity (CRE) is a system where large energy users, such as data centers, operate their own private electricity networks or source power independently, rather than relying solely on traditional public utilities. This model allows for greater flexibility and can help large users avoid regulatory and cost structures imposed on standard utility customers. Some behind-the-meter bills explicitly make it possible for multiple large users to source off-grid power through microgrids. As part of their efforts to attract more data center development, West Virginia lawmakers created a microgrid program (HB 2014) that allows data centers to operate in certified microgrid districts. The law gives the state authority over local governments in regulating microgrids as part of its effort to attract data center users to West Virginia. In New Mexico, lawmakers enacted microgrid legislation that is more regulatory in nature. HB 93 allows customers to enter agreements with investor-owned utilities in the state for microgrid operation, including generation and distribution for onsite use. By the time legislative sessions kicked off in January 2026, data centers had become one of the most contentious issues facing lawmakers, especially at the local level, where moratoriums were being enacted. Because of this, the politics of enacting laws that speed up the process for data centers to connect to the grid became more challenging. New Jersey lawmakers enacted a pro-clean-energy measure (A 796) that directs the state's Board of Public Utilities to create energy rates that encourage large loads to bring their own generation and storage, as long as it comes from non-carbon-emitting sources. Additionally, lawmakers in Arizona (HB 4097) and Virginia (SB 751 & HB 1087) considered bills that provide pathways for large users to source behind-the-meter power. In Louisiana, a failed attempt (SB 490) to create a pathway for behind-the-meter power sourcing encouraged the Louisiana Public Service Commission (LPSC) to open its rulemaking docket on private-use electrical networks. Meanwhile, proposals in Connecticut and Maryland made behind-the-meter generation a requirement to enter the market rather than an option that data centers could exercise. Maryland's SB 596 and HB 940 banned large-load customers from connecting to the grid unless 25% of their capacity is met by either backup storage or a demand-response program. Connecticut's HB 5469 requires load customers of 50 MW and above to receive 100% of their electricity from a colocated source or off-grid supplier.
