artigo.texto: Last year, the Springdale Borough council gave the green light for a new massive data center to be built in the small town outside of Pittsburgh. But it's actually Allegheny County that will give the project final approval — and organizers say there's still an opportunity for the public to weigh in. The Springdale data center could draw as much power at one time as nearly 200,000 homes. It has gotten pushback from locals worried about noise, pollution, property values, and rising utility bills. Marty Garrigan has been organizing against the center with the group Save Allegheny Valley Environment (SAVE). He said it’s not too late to push back on the computing warehouse “Many people thought that this whole thing was a done deal when the borough voted in favor of it,” Garrigan said. “But the county has the final say here.” Springdale Borough Council voted to grant the project a conditional use permit in December. Several members of council said during the vote that they did not want the data center in the borough, but felt they had to approve the application to avoid a costly lawsuit. Allegheny County must approve the center’s land development plan before the project can move forward. The plan lays out the details of how the facility would be built, connected to utilities, and landscaped. County staff made 97 comments on the data center’s preliminary application, noting errors and unanswered questions. For example, the comments note that “no evidence has been provided” that conditions related to noise mitigation will be met. A virtual hearing is set for Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 6 p.m. An in-person hearing is scheduled for Oct. 28 at 6 p.m. at the Springdale borough building. Written comments will be accepted until Nov. 30. “This is an opportunity for us to increase public awareness and relay the dangers that this behemoth poses,” Garrigan said. Garrigan’s group plans to drive a billboard truck around the area for the next two weeks, to remind people that the center is “not a done deal.” SAVE is hosting an in-person gathering for the county’s virtual hearing at the Pittsburgh Shrine Center at 1877 Shriners Way in Harmar Township. Garrigan said volunteers can help people register to speak during the hearing. The group has also launched a fundraiser for possible legal and expert fees if the data center does get county approval and the fight moves to the courts. “We've had an estimate from an attorney who's fought these kinds of things before that would be $20,000 to continue on with the fight for an appeal to the county,” Garrigan said. “And that's just the first level of courts.” The data center, which has been dubbed “Springdale Dynamo” in a nod to the area’s industrial history, is financially backed by the New York-based hedge fund Davidson Kempner. A website for the project shows it could draw up to 240 megawatts of power, up from the company’s original proposal of 180 mw. Recent increases in electricity prices have been attributed to the projected growth of data centers and other heavy power users.

artigo.texto: Franklin County residents, groups sue to stop data center rezoning and projects FRANKLIN COUNTY, Mo. (First Alert 4) - Two organizations and neighboring landowners have filed separate but similar lawsuits challenging Franklin County’s data center regulations and the rezoning for data center projects approved on September 15. Pacific ROOT Coalition and Franklin County Rural Coalition, along with their attorneys, formally announced the lawsuits Wednesday. On September 15, the Franklin County Commission unanimously approved the rezoning for a data center project near Villa Ridge by Shaw Nature Reserve. The commission approved rezoning for a second project south of Pacific off Highway O in a 2-1 decision. Bill and Janet Hubbard live on a five-generation farm south of Pacific. Their front porch view looks onto the land where a data center is planned. “From where those power lines are, that’s where the buildings will start. There’s going to be 16 of them. The height of them, that entire hilltop will be leveled, and they will put buildings on them,” Bill Hubbard said. “For me, it’s preserving this country’s farmland. People nowadays want to know where their food is coming from. They don’t want it imported from anywhere else. So the best farmers in the world, and that produce the best products, reside here in America. And we can’t afford to keep losing those,” Julie Carr said. The Hubbards and their daughter, Julie Carr, are not named plaintiffs in the lawsuit filed against the project near their farm, but they said they welcome it. “It gives us hope that perhaps we will get this put on the back burner or put someplace else,” Bill Hubbard said. “Or stop it completely. One of the big issues for me in particular, as a retired educator, are our schools and our students. My grandson attends a local school, and it will be a mile from Crooked Creek,” Janet Hubbard said. “That there is hope that we’re not going to be devastated, that our entire community won’t be sacrificed for, for lack of a better word, carpetbaggers coming in from out of state, taking over the community, and potentially upping our electrical bills, lowering the water table so that our wells, definitely our springs, we were already told that the springs would be drying up if they do drill wells,” Bill Hubbard said. The Hubbards expressed multiple environmental and health concerns, along with what it could mean to residents and kids. “Right now we’re hearing the little hum of a fan for a blow-up Halloween decoration. If it’s a diesel generator, it’s going to be a whole different story. If it’s just the 16 buildings, it’s going to be louder than a vacuum cleaner. That’s what they say. It’s like, ‘oh, the decibel level compares to a vacuum cleaner.’ Okay, 16 vacuum cleaners running 24-7, seven days a week for the rest of your life,” Janet Hubbard said. “It’s on multiple levels where it can hit us in a way that’s not in our best interest or anyone else’s,” Bill Hubbard said. Zach McMichael, an attorney at Capes Sokol representing Pacific ROOT Coalition, said the lawsuit has been filed and a Franklin County judge issued a writ of certiorari. “We’re looking to get the zoning overturned. We’re also trying to make it so the county commission has to do this again the right way and give the residents of Franklin County a fair opportunity to be heard on their concerns and to actually weigh those concerns when they make a future decision,” McMichael said. Both lawsuits make similar arguments: that no studies were conducted to determine environmental and utility impacts, that the rezoning constitutes illegal spot zoning by changing the classification of the properties to differ from surrounding land, and that the approval process was flawed. “Our claims are both to the substance and the procedure. So, the substance, we believe this is illegal spot zoning. So, what the county commission has done is they’ve taken one single parcel to benefit one particular property owner and given them an A zoning and a C of W zoning. So, it’s spot zoning that doesn’t comport with the master plan. And it isn’t for the public welfare,” McMichael said. “We also think procedurally, they didn’t follow the steps that Missouri law requires. We think they put unreasonable restrictions on the residents and the citizens of Franklin County at these public hearings. And they didn’t give proper notice,” McMichael said. The attorneys on Wednesday said filing the lawsuits isn’t saying that the county acted illegally; that is for the court to decide, and this goes beyond the issue of data centers to making sure the correct process is followed. “Beltline picked up their party toys and they went to the county and they sold them a bill of goods. You will make millions of dollars in tax revenue. And I think that’s when the commissioners at the county level stopped listening. So it’s very, very troubling that our county commissioners, who should be representing us, seem to be working for the carpetbaggers,” Janet Hubbard said. McMichael said the case will likely be decided based on details specific to the proposed site. “This case in Franklin County and these zoning cases normally are very site-specific. And so it’s going to be really based on what is this project and what is it going to do in Franklin County, just south of the Pacific,” McMichael said. Franklin County, its commissioners and the developers named in the lawsuit did not respond to requests for comment. Georgia-based Beltline Energy, the developer for the project near the Hubbards’ property, has said when promoting similar projects: “The responsible development of data centers is both a local opportunity and a national priority. artigo.texto: Vantage Data Centers has agreed to look at alternative sites for a data center proposed next to Green Valley Ranch, a member of the Aurora City Council said Wednesday night. Councilmember Rob Andrews met with representatives from Vantage Wednesday night and has it “on good authority” that the company is looking for new locations in Aurora for the Trident Data Center, he said. Recommended Stories Vantage did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation from The Denver Gazette. The information was disclosed by Andrews around 11 p.m. Wednesday. “Economic development should not come at the expense of our existing neighborhoods,” Andrews said in a video about the meeting posted to his social media channels. Andrews called on other councilmembers and the mayor to help him identify alternative locations away from residential areas for the data center, he said. Trident is the latest project by Vantage Data Centers, which has 30 data centers in 12 countries. The company submitted the application for Trident to the city on Aug. 25, 2025. As currently proposed, the data center would be two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. The current proposal puts the data center at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue. Those plans have already been through two formal city reviews and a third is underway, a city spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. In recent weeks, members of surrounding Green Valley Ranch communities, including The Reserve, a 55+ community, have raised their voices in opposition to the data center, saying they worry about negative health impacts, declining home values, and tapped utilities. Vantage representatives have countered that they take measures to mitigate impacts to surrounding communities, saying their goal is to be a “responsible neighbor and steward of local resources.” This story is developing and will be updated.

artigo.texto: NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Before Nashville's next large data center can power up, it will have to clear a new set of rules aimed at limiting the impact these facilities can have on surrounding communities. Metro Council approved new zoning regulations for data centers in July, creating five classifications based on factors including size and electrical load. The regulations prohibit the largest category, campus data centers, countywide. Councilmember Rollin Horton, a sponsor of the legislation, described Nashville's approach this way during an interview with NewsChannel 5: "Nashville has passed some of the strictest rules and regulations protecting all of Davidson County from the dangers of data centers." The regulations followed significant public debate over data center development in Nashville, particularly after plans emerged for a DC BLOX facility next to the Nashville Zoo. In July, more than 100 people spoke in opposition to data center development during Metro Council public hearings. Under Nashville's new framework, allowable data centers face different requirements depending on their size. Small data centers have a 100-foot separation requirement from specified sensitive uses, while medium facilities generally face a 500-foot requirement. Large facilities face a 2,640-foot, or half-mile, separation requirement. Sensitive uses identified by the framework include residences, schools, daycares, religious institutions, parks and zoos. A new Metro Data Center Impact Assessment & Policy Recommendations compared Nashville's regulations with policies being adopted or considered in other communities. It found Nashville's requirements for small and medium facilities generally align with other jurisdictions, but said the half-mile buffer for large facilities makes Nashville"somewhat of an outlier." "We set very strict distance requirements, especially compared to other cities," said Horton. "And so I think it's important not just that we look at how we can continue to improve our regulations, but make sure that there's no effort to water down or weaken them." The regulations include more than where facilities can be built. They require closed-loop cooling systems, establish daytime and nighttime noise limits, require 24-hour noise monitoring and require utilities to confirm they have capacity to serve a proposed project. New data centers must also provide renewable energy systems accounting for at least 15% of annual power use. Despite concluding that the city's framework provides a strong foundation for addressing many known risks, Metro's report identifies several issues officials say warrant further evaluation. Among them are vibration, increases in background noise and potential contaminants in wastewater discharged from cooling systems. Nashville currently limits data center noise at the property line to 65 decibels during the day and 55 decibels at night. But the report says the city could consider another safeguard limiting how much a facility can increase the existing background noise around it, even if it remains below those absolute limits. Vibration is another area Metro says needs further research. The new regulations do not establish a separate vibration limit or require a vibration impact assessment comparable to the required noise assessment. Metro also wants to further study wastewater from closed-loop cooling systems. The report says that discharge can potentially contain substances including heavy metals and PFAS and recommends determining whether existing contaminant standards adequately capture potential data center process-water impacts. The report does not say Nashville's water has been contaminated by data centers. "I think we have the strictest and most comprehensive rules in the entire country. That said, this is a very fast-evolving industry. So I think it's important that we continue to monitor how the industry develops and make sure that our rules and regulations stay one step ahead of the industry," said Horton. Perhaps one of the biggest questions is what happens when Nashville's framework encounters a new proposal. Metro's report says the city has yet to apply the new regulatory framework to a new data center proposal, meaning some challenges remain relatively unknown. The report recommends several changes to how Metro implements the rules, including required pre-application coordination, completeness reviews and phased approvals tied to utility milestones. It also recommends forming a working group involving Metro, Nashville Electric Service and the Tennessee Valley Authority to develop compliance procedures, coordinate enforcement and determine whether additional resources will be needed as applications, inspections and monitoring begin. A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou, nesta terça-feira (13/10), o requerimento de urgência para o projeto de lei 3716/2026, que altera o rateio dos custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento (BESS). O PL, de autoria de Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), altera a Lei nº 15.269/2025, que estabelece que o custo do armazenamento é arcado pelas geradoras de energia. A nova proposta estabelece a divisão dos valores com os consumidores. O pedido de urgência foi apresentado à Mesa, nesta terça, pelos deputados Danilo Forte (PP/CE), Evair Vieira de Melo (Republicanos/ES), Vitor Lippi (PSD/SP) e Isnaldo Bulhões Jr. (MDB/AL). Agora, o texto segue direto para plenário. O PL ainda não tinha sido distribuído para nenhuma comissão. A matéria é apoiada por diversas organizações do setor que esperam a mudança na divisão do rateio antes dos leilões de baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) defende que o avanço da proposta é importante para ampliar a segurança jurídica para os certames e que a legislação estabelece um tratamento desigual para o armazenamento. “A aprovação da urgência representa um avanço para que o Congresso discuta o tema com a celeridade necessária. Em paralelo precisamos olhar para o prazo dos leilões: o sistema elétrico necessita de potência adicional em 2028, e é plenamente possível corrigir a isonomia no rateio enquanto prossegue o cronograma”, disse o diretor-executivo da Absae, Fabio Lima, em nota. Já a Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine) considera que a aprovação sinaliza uma sensibilidade do Congresso Nacional em relação à necessidade de debater o tema. “A tramitação célere é fundamental para o setor, tendo em vista que a matéria ainda será submetida à análise do Senado Federal”, afirmou a associação, em nota. O tema integra as prioridades da Agenda Legislativa de 2026 da Apine, que busca por soluções estruturais para os cortes de geração de energia (curtailment) .

Quick Read Big tech’s giant data center proposals have touched raw nerves in several Minnesota towns, sparking firestorms of criticism aimed at local government leaders, some of whom signed non-disclosure agreements to keep project details secret until after elected officials approved the plans. Seeing how data centers have churned up local politics and spurred newcomers to run for office, some city administrators came together to seek help. The end result is a new toolkit developed by researchers at the University of Minnesota to help local government officials better understand and weigh the pros and cons of having Google, Meta or some other big tech company build a massive data center in their community. "The way we've been framing it is how do you proactively address a data center?” said Elise Harrington, a University of Minnesota public affairs professor who is the tool kit project lead. “How do you think about it before you have one?" It’s the culmination of a year of research by the University of Minnesota and the Freshwater Society, a water conservation nonprofit. It was developed to help city leaders separate facts from fiction and to guide what city codes they can enact to mitigate environmental impacts if big tech pitches in their city next. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Arming local leaders with facts Harrington and her group of researchers released the tool kit last Friday afternoon in Rochester, where dozens of city planners, administrators and elected officials from cities and towns across southeast Minnesota gathered for a workshop to learn about the tool kit and try it out. Al Roder, city administrator for the nearby town of Byron, is part of the reason this tool kit exists in the first place. He and some of his peers in other southeast Minnesota cities had been talking a couple of years ago about how they could prepare for the seemingly inevitable arrival of data center proposals. “We just started having a conversation about data centers and how do we answer all these questions with facts instead of emotions?” Roder said. “Because so much of what I hear is emotional arguments for or against. Where are the facts?” He had observed how these emotions had created deep rifts in cities like Pine Island, about 20 minutes away, after Google proposed its Project Skyway data center there, dividing residents into heated factions of those who support the data center and those who vehemently oppose it. Roder and his counterparts in nearby Stewartville and Lewiston wanted to get ahead of such controversies. If Google or some other big tech company came to Byron, Roder wanted to be armed with facts and have city rules preemptively laid out for prospective data centers. “These are rules that we decided before we were in the heat of battle,” Roder told MPR News. “These are the conditions that we would find acceptable for our community. It's easier to do that before somebody's knocking on the door.” So they reached out to the community development folks at the University of Minnesota Extension for help gathering facts they could use to guide these discussions. What does the tool kit include? The guide, which will be made available to the public Wednesday, includes sections on how data centers can impact energy and water usage, and how these impacts can be regulated at the local level to manage environmental impacts. It also includes guiding questions for city leaders to ask if they get an inquiry from big tech about a data center proposal as well as examples of how to address data centers in local code. That’s why Greg Krushke attended the workshop. He's the community development manager for the city of Owatonna, and he’s in the midst of modernizing the city’s zoning and subdivision code that was developed back in the 1980s. He hopes the tool kit will help inform how they write the code and what is included in it. He said it’s especially helpful to come together with peers at a workshop like this one to talk with one another and share experiences. "What are they learning from others, and how can we be able to apply some of this and be able to use it to help ourselves and our neighbors?" Krushke said. A regional approach Andi Sutton, executive director of the Southeast Regional Sustainable Development Partnership with University of Minnesota Extension, said she was thrilled that so many local government decision makers showed up for Friday’s workshop in Rochester. Local data center decisions are not made in a vacuum, and she hopes the workshop, which has convened leaders from across the region, will spark these conversations early since the environmental impacts of data centers don’t stop at city borders. That’s especially true in southeast Minnesota, which has a unique geologic landscape. It’s made of karst, a type of rock that’s very porous. “It means that the way that water moves through our region is different from other parts of Minnesota,” Sutton explained. “We have sensitive aquifers. We have water that’s in use for agricultural purposes, for ecosystem purposes. So what one community does with the water that they have will very quickly and inevitably have an effect on another community.” Sutton hopes this workshop jump starts these conversations and leads local planners to ask their neighbors questions as they weigh the pros and cons of data center proposals; questions like, “Who is my neighbor in terms of energy, water, infrastructure or roads?” “All of these questions get pushed to their limits by data centers as a development opportunity,” Sutton said. “We're so grateful that we're able to h

artigo.texto: Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) systems are renowned for low electricity generation costs, but their intermittent and non-dispatchable generation poses significant challenges to grid stability and curtailment. Concentrated solar power (CSP), equipped with thermal energy storage (TES), can provide firm, dispatchable power, but its wide deployment is constrained by high capital and operating costs. To address limitations of PV and CSP systems, this study proposes an operation strategy for hybrid PV-CSP plants to utilize the thermal storage capacity of CSP systems. The proposed strategy utilizes stable power supply and grid capacity constraints to guide TES systems operation, providing a methodology for determining supply target power, followed by system simulation, techno-economic evaluation and capacity parameter optimization. Over an annual simulation, the hybrid plant achieved an average monthly target-fulfillment rate of 93.5 %, indicating robust operational performance. The effects of various capacity parameters on system operation are evaluated, with capacity allocation optimized based on metrics of levelized cost of energy (LCOE) and channel utilization rate (CUR). Analysis of capacity parameters demonstrates that the rated output power of CSP systems exerts the most substantial impact on hybrid system operations. Optimization results demonstrate that configuration combining large-scale PV with thermal energy storage-dominated CSP systems (Mode I) could achieve 40–50 % CUR at 0.06–0.07 $/kWh LCOE, while the hybrid system pairing small-scale PV with large-capacity CSP plants (Mode II) attains 70–80 % CUR with 0.08–0.086 $/kWh LCOE. PV-CSP hybrid power systems effectively address operational challenges inherent in sole PV and CSP systems. Bo Wang, Tao Ma, Yanjun Dai, Wentao Xie, Peng Xue, Simulation and techno-economic optimization of a PV-CSP hybrid system with thermal energy storage under stability-oriented operation strategy, Journal of Energy Storage, Volume 150, 2026,120371, ISSN 2352-152X, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.est.2026.120371

artigo.texto: O Valor Econômico informa que a expansão dos investimentos em data centers no Brasil começa a provocar uma reação regulatória nos Estados, com propostas que vão da concessão de incentivos locais a novas exigências sobre uso de água, licenciamento ambiental e transparência. Dos 16 projetos apresentados nas assembleias estaduais em 2026, oito criam restrições ou ônus aos empreendimentos. As propostas favoráveis eram maioria no ano passado, segundo levantamento da Innova Assuntos Públicos obtido com exclusividade pelo Valor. O estudo mapeou 20 projetos de lei e de lei complementar sobre data centers em 11 assembleias legislativas entre 2025 e outubro de 2026. Em todo o ano de 2025 foram registradas quatro iniciativas, valor que saltou para 16 no acumulado deste ano até outubro. Dos 20 projetos, nove são restritivos, sete favoráveis, dois misturam incentivos e exigências e dois são considerados neutros. Itaipu emite alerta de cheia no rio Paraná A Comissão Especial de Cheias da Itaipu Binacional divulgou, no domingo (11), um boletim hidrológico indicando perspectiva de elevação rápida do nível do Rio Paraná nos próximos dias, com risco de impactos em estruturas e residências do lado brasileiro do rio. No domingo, por volta de 10h, a cota registrada do rio era de 110,4 metros na Ponte de Amizade, em Foz do Iguaçu (PR). A projeção é de que o nível poderá subir até 115,10 metros na segunda-feira (12) e até 115,14 metros na terça (13), segundo o boletim. Paulo. Crucial no desenvolvimento de São Paulo, o complexo foi fundado pela Light em 10 de outubro de 1926 e está hoje sob gestão da Emae (Empresa Metropolitana de Águas e Energia), cujo controle a Sabesp assumiu em fevereiro deste ano. A usina fica em Cubatão (SP) e continua em plena atividade. Ainda mantém parte de suas características originais, mas já não opera da mesma forma como fazia no passado. Desde 2012, afinal, a Henry Borden trabalha sob o regime de disponibilidade. Funciona assim: em vez de vender energia ao mercado, ela recebe para garantir que sua produção esteja sempre à disposição do ONS, o operador nacional do sistema elétrico, que pede eletricidade sob demanda — que costuma ser solicitada quase todos os dias. As empresas miram o leilão de gás da União, marcado pela Pré-Sal Petróleo S.A. (PPSA) para 22 de outubro. O edital do certame, publicado na semana passada, admite a habilitação de indústrias que ainda estão no mercado cativo. Quem entra assim fica obrigado a comprar por meio de comercializadora. O prazo da primeira etapa de habilitação terminou ontem (12/10). Na habilitação, a empresa deve enviar o protocolo de pedido de migração e indicar o estado onde está localizada a unidade industrial que vai receber o gás. O estado pode ser trocado depois, mas só com o aval da PPSA. De acordo com a reportagem, a expectativa é que a fila de migrações no Rio enfim destrave, após o acordo assinado entre o governo do Rio, a Agenersa e a Naturgy, para encerrar a disputa judicial sobre a abertura do mercado no estado. artigo.texto: However, there may be at least one issue where the board's 21 members can find consensus. "The county board is pretty unified in all things related to data centers right now — very cautious, very much in favor of having strong regulations, very much in favor of transparency," Farney said. In that vein, two items related to this topic will be discussed at tonight's committee-of-the-whole meeting: an ordinance prohibiting nondisclosure agreements and a resolution against property-tax incentives for hyperscale data-center developments. No final action will be taken during the meeting. "These are all commitments that we have made," said board member Emily Rodriguez, who chairs the data-center activities task force. "We are not interested in anything that dodges taxes, for example. That's something we all agree on on the data-center task force. We also all agree that nondisclosure agreements are bad governance and that folks should be embarrassed to sign them, and data centers should not ask that of local governments." The proposed ordinance against NDAs states that such agreements have "become an issue with other units of government in local and national news." If approved, the ordinance would prohibit county board members and county employees from entering into NDAs regarding county business — in any situation, not just instances where data-center developers are involved. As for the other piece of legislation, the proposed resolution would prohibit "the negotiation of tax-abatement agreements, payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements and other concessions for the development and construction of hyperscale data centers within Champaign County." "No data-center applications have yet been submitted to the county for rural Champaign County, but rumors and public outcry have prompted the need for a formal position," the resolution states. The two proposals come after the village of Mahomet announced on Sept. 28 that it was in talks with Clean Cloud Energy about a potential data center project in "a rural area west of Champaign" that falls within Mahomet's extraterritorial jurisdiction. One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency. Farney, who wrote the resolution against tax incentives for hyperscale data centers, sent a draft to the board's policy and finance committee chairs on Oct. 5. "And like a half-hour later, somebody texted me the article that says, 'Hey, Mahomet's saying they're backing off,'" he said. "But I wanted to get that out there right away for the county to actually be able to do something immediately. We don't have to go through the same processes that we do for the zoning ordinance change in order to put a policy in effect for tax breaks for developments. And so I wanted to have something on record." When asked how payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements work, Farney said it's his understanding that data-center developers sometimes offer to make payments to communities while also entering into agreements for long-term property-tax abatements or reductions. Farney said that such agreements end up "being a benefit to the developer and not to the taxing bodies within the area as far as collecting the full value of property taxes." "Basically, what I'm saying is, if you want to build a data center here, then you're going to have to do it by our ordinances, which are going to be very stringent when the data-center task force gets done with their work," he told The News-Gazette. "You're also going to have to play by the rules that are in place for every other taxpayer in the county, as far as the county's portion of the tax bill goes. And so we're not going to give any incentives for data centers. If they can make it, they're gonna make it on their own." It's his hope that other governments and taxing bodies will enact similar policies and form a united front. Champaign County currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with "at least 10,000 square feet of processing area"; the ban is currently set to end in April. The county also created the data-center activities task force to draft planning and zoning regulations for such developments. A previous statement from Leslie Farmer, Clean Cloud Energy's director of environmental and permitting, indicated that the company may still be considering the project, just not in partnership with Mahomet. "Clean Cloud Energy has decided not to seek annexation into the village of Mahomet following discussions with village leadership," she said. "We respect Champaign County's ongoing review of data-center regulations and will evaluate our project's development in accordance with the framework established by the county." Documents released by the village on Sept. 28 following a Sept. 14 Freedom of Information Act request by Mahomet resident John Bambenek show that Clean Cloud Energy began talking with Mahomet officials about the project in December. The village entered into a nondisclosure agreement with the company in early 2026 but was released from the agreement on Sept. 16. Communications between the village and Clean Cloud Energy included multiple drafts of a proposed redevelopment and annexation agreement. Both Farney and Rodriguez said that if a municipality annexes an unincorporated area, that land would no longer be subject to the county's moratorium or zoning regulations on data centers. "I was very surprised to hear that Mahomet was in those discussions, knowing that the county was working on a data-center ordinance," Farney said. "... I knew immediately, 'OK, this is how the data-center developers are trying to do an end-around around the county and any other entities that are trying to regulate this.'" Rodriguez said that the situation in Mahomet resulted in "broken trust," making it important for the county to "codify" its position. artigo.texto: Salix council clarifies no data center moratorium in place, approves MOU with Google SALIX, Iowa (KTIV) - Conversations continue in Salix, Iowa, over 900 acres of annexed land and plans for a data center project. Wednesday night, the Salix City Council agenda included three items involving data centers. One stemmed from the council’s September meeting, when the council discussed a “Memorandum of Understanding” between the City of Salix and Google, which wants to build a data center on the 900 acres of annexed land. Under the MOU, Google would pay for any independent advisors the council hires to study the data center’s impact. The MOU states the cost couldn’t exceed $150,000 and Google must pay invoices within 30 days. But if the council imposes a moratorium, Google’s payments stop immediately. First up was a vote on moratorium clarification, followed by the memorandum of understanding and updates from Google. One agenda item included “affirming and clarifying that the city council has NOT adopted a moratorium prohibiting the construction or development of data centers in the City of Salix, Iowa.” This stems from confusion during a previous city council meeting over an action where Gene Monk motioned for a moratorium, but the mayor later said it did not impose one in Salix. That vote passed 3-2. “Towards the beginning of the meeting, there was a resolution where the council voted three to two to approve a resolution saying that there is no moratorium in place, and if there was one, accidentally created, it is officially rescinded. So there is no moratorium on data centers in Salix,” the mayor said. That vote means there is no rule or ordinance in place preventing the building of a data center. The council also voted 3-2 in favor of a memorandum of understanding, an agreement between Google and the City of Salix that would see the company reimbursing the city for the cost of any unbiased research into the impact of data centers. “We take a climate-conscious approach to cooling that balances energy and water efficiency. Based on our ongoing evaluations and our commitment to protecting local resources, Google will not source any cooling water from the Dakota Aquifer,” Google representatives said. Google representatives say studies they will undertake on the site include the project’s impact on water and wastewater, on threatened and endangered species, and the impact of traffic and noise. When asked after Wednesday’s meeting if, with a moratorium failing, there are now official plans for a data center, the mayor said it is still up in the air. “Still very much up in the air. The same six or seven families that own that land last year still own that land today. They have not sold the land to Mid-American or Google or anyone else. So until they sign on the dotted line and actually buy it, then no project can proceed,” the mayor said. Google also said it is in the works for Salix residents and the city council to tour one of its already existing data centers in Iowa. artigo.texto: ComEd, Richardson Electronics to construct Illinois’ largest BESS asset Electrical utility Commonwealth Edison (ComEd) and engineering firm Richardson Electronics have partnered for a massive project, zeroing in on the Land of Lincoln. The corporate duo plans to install the largest commercial battery energy storage system (BESS) asset in the state of Illinois, officials announced Oct. 12. The companies have joined up with state and industrial leaders to announce that Richardson has expanded its local BESS manufacturing plans to install the record-breaking project on ComEd’s grid. “For generations, manufacturing has been part of northern Illinois’ identity, and Richardson’s announcement demonstrates how that sector continues to shape our region’s economic future,” says ComEd president and CEO Gil Quiniones. “ComEd is committed to supporting business growth by making the grid investments needed to deliver industry-leading reliability at rates that are well below the average commercial and industrial rates for the top 20 largest metropolitan areas.” ComEd calls the project and the manufacturing bump “a critical step toward scaling locally made battery energy storage solutions,” as the U.S. strives for grid reliability. In addition to building the largest commercial BESS system in Illinois, Richardson is installing a 5 MWh research and development demonstration project, which will go through the ComEd interconnection process. “Richardson Electronics has a long history of solving complex power and energy challenges through innovation and U.S.-based manufacturing,” says Greg Peloquin, Richardson’s EVP and general manager of power and microwave technologies, and its green energy solution groups. “Our advanced energy storage solutions will help customers manage energy more efficiently while supporting a more reliable and resilient grid. We value ComEd’s collaboration in bringing this onsite demonstration project to life.” Constructing Illinois’ energy future Increasing battery storage capabilities is a cornerstone of Illinoisan energy policy in the mid-2020s, ComEd officials say. The Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA), one of a flurry of renewable-forward bills signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker, aims to bolster both solar and storage across the Prairie State. ComEd and Richardson’s collaborative effort is part of bringing CRGA’s vision for Illinois to life, officials say. “When Kane County Commissioner Rick Williams and I first met with Richardson to discuss this project, I was immediately intrigued by both the economic and energy benefits the project could bring to the area and the state,” says Illinois State Rep. Dan Ugaste. “Energy storage will be an important part of having affordable and reliable energy going forward. Seeing the value this project could bring, I was glad to help facilitate discussions with the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity to bring this project to fruition.” The companies will also support the local community, says Illinois State Rep. Jeff Keicher. Richardson’s continued investment in its La Fox, Illinois manufacturing location serves as an example of “how Illinois businesses can lead the way in developing innovative energy solutions while creating good-paying jobs” at the local level, he says. “As Illinois works to strengthen the reliability and affordability of our electric grid, projects like this will play an important role in ensuring we meet our future needs, while strengthening our state’s position as an advanced manufacturing leader.” Battery projects across Illinois are also open to accessing ComEd’s Distributed Generation Rebate Program. With the program recently hitting the $350 million milestone, customers who install qualifying battery storage assets can receive a rebate of up to $300 per kWh of storage capacity.

artigo.texto: A heated debate is ongoing within the European Union regarding the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). In July, the European Commission presented a proposal to revise the scheme, and on 12 October this became the subject of political debates held by the Council of the EU. The Council has stated its aim to combine stronger climate ambitions with support for industrial competitiveness. This was reported by the Council of the European Union. The EU ETS is the bloc’s key climate policy instrument, which helps to reduce emissions and is the world’s first and largest carbon market. It requires companies to pay for their CO₂ emissions. Supporters of the EU ETS believe it encourages businesses to invest in the ‘green’ transition, whilst opponents see it as placing excessive financial pressure on them. "We must ensure that the EU Emissions Trading System is fit for the next decade. Our aim is to align our carbon market with our climate ambitions in a way that also ensures the competitiveness of our industry,” emphasised Dara O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, who currently holds the presidency of the Council of the EU. They added that the review of the EU ETS should align the carbon market with the EU’s climate target – to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 90 per cent by 2040. The ministerial discussions are focusing on the trajectory of the annual emissions cap after 2030, as well as the use of international carbon credits and carbon sequestration projects. The debate also assessed the proposed mechanisms for financing and allocating free allowances. Some politicians expressed the view that the EU ETS should be extended to cover aviation, shipping and the waste management sector. O’Brien noted that they would aim to reach agreements on the revision of the ETS by December 2026. At the same time, according to data from Politico, the three largest political groups in the European Parliament are set to oppose any watering down of the emissions trading scheme. It was previously reported that the European Parliament intends to make significant amendments to the European Commission’s proposal. In particular, the Member States wish to require 75 per cent of ETS revenues to be reinvested in the eco-modernisation of businesses A number of countries will call for the cancellation of the revocation of ‘excess’ quotas in the Market Stability Reserve. As a reminder, the European Commission presented its proposal to reform the EU carbon market on 17 July. It includes, in particular, an increase in funding for decarbonisation, an extension of the period for receiving free allowances, and a reduction in the level of allowances transferred to the market stability reserve. Work is continuing in Ukraine on the legislative framework for establishing a national emissions trading scheme. In addition to the draft bill from the Ministry of Economy – which was drawn up taking into account feedback from experts and stakeholders – there are three parliamentary proposals. A detailed comparison of these can be found in the article by EcoPolitika.

Connecting Scornicesti directly to the high-voltage national transmission grid, operated by Transelectrica, is a major undertaking that goes well beyond a standard project and has required extensive design works. R.Power secured a €46 million financing package for the project in June 2026. Under the terms of the deal, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) provided €44 million in investment and bridge financing, while Polish development bank Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego (BGK) issued a €2.3 million bank guarantee to secure the long-term optimisation contract in place with regional trading partner, GEN-I. The project, located in Olt County, is co-owned through a JV with France’s Eiffel Investment Group. “As a utility scale asset connected to the national transmission grid, Scornicesti BESS will actively support the stabilisation of Romania’s energy system.” said Florin Federenciuc, R.Power Country Head for Romania. “By integrating BESS at the heart of its energy transition, Romania is strengthening its grid resilience and supporting the roll-out of renewable energy generation. artigo.texto: Millington approves data center moratorium as county, Memphis weigh their own MILLINGTON, Tenn. (WMC) - Millington has approved its own data center moratorium as Shelby County and the City of Memphis weigh their own. Chris Thomas, executive director of the Millington Chamber of Commerce, confirms that the board of mayor and aldermen approved a six-month pause on development applications for non-grid power generation, accessory computing or industrial-scale computing facilities Monday. The moratorium took effect immediately and will expire April 12 unless extended. The pause gives the city time to reexamine its zoning ordinances without juggling proposals for developments that current land use regulations don’t address. “Whereas, non-grid power generation, accessory computing, and industrial-scale facilities are one of the fastest-growing land uses nationally and are not currently addressed as a distinct use in the Millington Zoning Ordinance, creating uncertainty for applicants and the city alike,” the resolution reads. In the next six months, city leaders plan to study, research, analyze and assess the impacts of any facilities of this kind, including their development, demographic trends, aesthetic qualities and burdens on the community. Applications the city has already accepted would be exempt from the development halt, but Thomas says that doesn’t apply, as Millington has yet to see a proposal for a data center. Shelby County is also considering its own data center moratorium for unincorporated parts of the county before any development applications are filed. It passed its first reading Monday by a 5-4 vote. The City of Memphis is also weighing a data center moratorium, but only after high-density computing facilities have already established a footprint in the municipality. The Memphis City Council is expected to make a final decision on its moratorium October 20. The council pushed the final vote back twice. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: Principais Pontos - As ações da Enerflex subiram 13% hoje após a empresa vencer um contrato para construir mais de um gigawatt de unidades de energia a gás natural para um data center norte-americano. - O contrato eleva o backlog de energia behind-the-meter da Enerflex para mais de 1,75 gigawatts, com entregas até 2028, e as estimativas de receita dos analistas foram definidas antes deste anúncio. - A Enerflex não divulgou o valor em dólares do contrato e está investindo cerca de US$ 100 milhões para expandir as instalações de Sistemas de Engenharia que irão construí-lo. - O CIBC elevou a recomendação da ação para Outperformer com um preço-alvo de US$ 35, e o relatório do terceiro trimestre será a próxima oportunidade para ver quanto vale o backlog em dólares. Enerflex (EFXT) As ações subiram 13% hoje após a empresa fechar um pedido de mais de um gigawatt de energia a gás para um único data center. Antes da abertura, a Enerflex anunciou que construirá unidades de energia a gás behind-the-meter para "um grande desenvolvimento de data center na América do Norte". Este novo contrato sozinho é mais que o dobro dos aproximadamente 450 megawatts anunciados em 1º de outubro. Somando esses e outros contratos, seu backlog de energia behind-the-meter agora ultrapassa 1,75 gigawatts, com entregas até 2028. O CEO Paul Mahoney atribuiu a demanda à IA e destacou o "sucesso da empresa em garantir mais de 1,75 gigawatts de backlog" (comunicado à imprensa). Às 10h, o CIBC elevou a recomendação da ação para Outperformer, de Neutral, com um preço-alvo de US$ 35. Gigawatts em um negócio de US$ 3,5 bilhões O backlog de Sistemas de Engenharia da Enerflex estava em US$ 1,5 bilhão no final de junho, acima dos US$ 1,1 bilhão no final de 2025, e a maior parte dos 1,75 gigawatts anunciados hoje foi contratada após esse período. A empresa não divulgou um valor em dólares para o novo contrato nem nomeou o cliente. O contrato chega a um negócio cuja receita tem se mantido estável, em US$ 3,52 bilhões em 2025, embora os analistas projetem US$ 4,37 bilhões até 2028... Essas estimativas são de 9 de outubro, antes do contrato de hoje. Com entregas ocorrendo até 2028, eu esperaria que os números de 2027 e 2028 sejam revisados para cima. Agora a Enerflex precisa construí-lo Para construir tudo em suas plantas norte-americanas, a Enerflex autorizou cerca de US$ 100 milhões para expandir suas instalações de Sistemas de Engenharia, e apenas US$ 15 milhões disso estão no guia de gastos de capital deste ano. A administração espera que isso aumente significativamente a capacidade de receita do negócio. É muito trabalho novo dependendo de um cronograma que se estende até 2028, então um atraso ou um custo excedente em um pedido na escala de gigawatts teria um impacto forte. A ação ainda não está esticada A Enerflex já negociava a 14x o lucro futuro no último fechamento, bem acima de sua média de cinco anos de 9,7x... Ao preço desta manhã, está próximo de 16x, ainda bem abaixo de seu pico de 23,8x em janeiro de 2022. E o preço-alvo de US$ 35 do CIBC está confortavelmente acima mesmo do preço de hoje. Eu posso ver a visão do mercado sobre a Enerflex mudando ainda mais a partir daqui. Por anos, o mercado precificou a empresa como uma fabricante de equipamentos a gás, e um pedido na escala de gigawatts é um forte sinal de que o negócio é algo mais do que isso. Os analistas também ainda não incorporaram o contrato em suas estimativas, o que deixa espaço para os números se ajustarem. Claro, ainda não sabemos quanto tudo isso vale em dólares. artigo.texto: Growth through decarbonisation: Why the EU must stand firm on emissions trading EU Climate Week began in Brussels on 12 October. The EU itself should remember that the economy can grow while emissions fall. Technology Industries of Finland does not support erratic climate policy. We support a predictable investment environment, a strong and long-term emissions trading system, electrification and clean domestic energy. Climate action is still sometimes approached with caution on the grounds that it is too expensive. Europe’s own figures tell a different story: between 1990 and 2024, the EU’s GDP grew by more than 70 percent, while net greenhouse gas emissions fell by 40 percent. Since the launch of emissions trading in 2005, emissions in the sectors covered by the system have halved. The Commission wants to support the continuation of climate policy because it links climate policy more closely to competitiveness, affordable energy and reducing strategic dependencies. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen outlined the bigger picture in her State of the Union address in September: “The transition is complex, and we have to adapt our approach and learn along the way. But Europe can, must and will stay the course on its climate goals.” The Commission has also consistently promoted the phase-out of Russian fossil energy imports, with transition periods. In Finland, security is understood broadly. Climate policy is also not seen as a separate cost item, but as part of building self-sufficiency and resilience. In Finland, the volatility of fossil fuel prices is visible in transport and logistics costs. In the marine industry and heavy transport, the transition to clean electricity and clean fuels is beginning. We need a major leap in electrification One of Finland’s strengths is that electricity is more than 95 percent emission-free and among the most competitive in Europe in terms of price. Growing electricity consumption creates demand, but networks are now starting to become a bottleneck. At the same time, the Confederation of Finnish Industries’ green investment data window, Fingrid’s assessments and the Finnish Wind Power Association’s own figures all point to strong readiness to unlock new production potential. In addition, Finland’s existing nuclear power capacity is being renewed, and readiness to produce electricity and heat with small modular reactors is being built in several locations. The Finnish economy needs a major leap in electrification, supported by hydrogen, clean fuels and other solutions. This electrification leap is the next growth step, and both society and companies must be brought on board. We cannot afford to stumble now. Emissions trading rewards the most efficient solutions Technology Industries of Finland has defended the EU Emissions Trading System as the cornerstone of climate policy because it is a market-based tool. In addition, it generates revenues that should be allocated to accelerating the transition in the sectors affected by emissions trading. It puts a price on emissions but leaves companies free to choose the means. Emissions are reduced where it makes the most sense and where it is most cost-effective. For the sake of the EU’s own competitiveness, this should not be distorted with state aid. Countries and companies that have invested early are now in a stronger position. Weakening emissions trading would punish frontrunners and would not eliminate regulation as it would simply be replaced by more detailed, less market-based and less efficient steering. Freedom from fossil fuels is also security policy Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels is both an economic and a security policy risk. Russia’s war of aggression has shown how energy can be used as an instrument of pressure and as a means to finance a war economy. Every unit of energy saved or produced cleanly in Europe reduces the need to transfer wealth outside the Union. According to Eurostat, the EU is moving in the right direction, but slowly. Energy import dependency has decreased: in 2022, net imports accounted for 63 percent of the EU’s energy, and in 2024 the figure was still 57 percent. Yet in 2025, oil, gas and solid fossil fuels worth EUR 337 billion were still imported into the EU. In other words, we remain heavily dependent on energy whose price is determined elsewhere. Fossil fuels are still needed in transport, heating and industry. But dependence — the obligation to buy — can be reduced especially through electrification, clean electricity production, a sufficient and smart grid, and energy efficiency. These are precisely the areas where Finland has solutions to offer. When carbon has a price, demand is created for clean technology. At the same time, the trade balance, security of supply and Europe’s own strategic autonomy are strengthened. Bringing the handprint into EU climate policy European solutions can also reduce emissions outside Europe. In Finland’s case, this export-driven carbon handprint is larger than the emissions of our emissions trading sector. There is therefore evidence of the positive impacts of technology exports. However, the EU has not yet strongly embraced the carbon handprint in its climate policy. Could the handprint be brought more firmly into the core of EU climate policy, alongside the carbon footprint? I am in Brussels for Climate Week — let’s discuss.

artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência do PL que faz rateio de custos de baterias elétricas Projeto ainda precisa passar pelo plenário, o que deve ficar para o período pós-eleitoral; setores argumentam que proposta traria maior segurança jurídica e previsibilidade para o setor elétrico A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira um requerimento de urgência para o projeto de lei que muda a proporção de rateio dos custos de baterias elétricas. O projeto em si, no entanto, deve ser votado no plenário da Câmara apenas após o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, marcado para 25 de outubro. Com a urgência aprovada, o texto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) se torna uma "prioridade" dos trabalhos legislativos. Na prática, o projeto altera uma revogação de uma lei de 2004, determinando que os custos das contratações de baterias sejam divididos entre os geradores e os consumidores de energia elétrica. Atualmente, uma regulamentação da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) determina a exclusividade para agentes do setor, o que produz, segundo o autor do projeto, "distorções na alocação de recursos". Ainda há a necessidade de negociar a tramitação da proposta junto ao governo federal para que vá de fato a voto. A proposta também depende de aprovação do Senado Federal para se tornar lei. Setores argumentam que a legislação atual cria um cenário de insegurança jurídica aos leilões de bateria que estão previstos para dezembro deste ano, além de acentuar a imprevisibilidade das tratativas do setor de energia. A proposta corrigiria "assimetrias" do modelo atual. As entidades Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Absolar (Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica), Apine (Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica), Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) e Abiape (Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia) emitiram uma nota em apoio ao PL. “Todas as tecnologias e soluções que prestam serviços semelhantes aos usuários devem estar sujeitas ao mesmo regime jurídico, permitindo alocação e comparação justa dos custos. Por isso, as regras de custeio da reserva de capacidade devem ser as mesmas para todas as soluções eventualmente contratadas”, diz o comunicado. O principal ponto de convergência entre as entidades é de que a manutenção do modelo atual pode elevar o custo de energia para o consumidor, tendo em vista que os custos refletem diretamente no preço da energia que chega às casas brasileiras.

Battery Storage Four-hour battery storage now beats gas peaking in 43 markets Storage LCOE falls below open-cycle gas turbines Gas shortages and scale widen the cost gap Stock video by ROMAN ODINTSOV via Pexels Oct 12, 2026 Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas Peaking on Cost in All 43 Wood Mackenzie Markets Four-hour battery storage has reached a cost milestone, with its levelized cost of electricity falling below that of open-cycle gas turbines in every one of the 43 global markets modeled by Wood Mackenzie, according to the firm's latest Levelized Cost of Electricity report. The analysis, reported by pv magazine, also finds that single-axis tracker solar is now the cheapest new-build power source in 43 of the 48 markets studied. Wood Mackenzie principal analyst Ahmed Jameel Abdullah described the economic shift as decisive and widening, noting that gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are lifting peaking costs while expanding battery manufacturing keeps pushing storage costs lower. The report attributes the change to advancing technologies and manufacturing scale that are redrawing global power market dynamics. North America as an exception North America stands apart from the global trend in long-term cost trajectories, shaped by domestic trade policies, supply chain protections, and load pressures. Unlike international markets that benefit from low-cost Chinese equipment exports, developers in the United States and Canada face near-term cost headwinds, with solar costs remaining elevated under tariffs, anti-dumping and countervailing duty actions, and Section 232 import restrictions. Utility-scale solar developers retain a buffer from 168 GW of safe-harbored capacity, but module prices are projected to rise by roughly 5 percent annually through 2030. Distributed generation faces greater pressure, with residential and commercial solar module prices forecast to increase 6 percent in 2027 and a further 14 percent in 2028. Storage incentives and load growth For energy storage, federal tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act continue to offer a competitive advantage, helping offset strict Foreign Entity of Concern sourcing restrictions and domestic supply bottlenecks. A temporary cost increase is anticipated when the Investment Tax Credit phases out in the late 2030s, but hardware commoditization, alternative cell chemistries, and localized manufacturing expansion are expected to bring long-term storage LCOE down 10 percent by 2060. At the same time, substantial load growth from data center development is prompting utilities to reassess capacity planning. Thermal capital costs remain elevated because of a supply deficit cycle in gas generation equipment through the late 2030s, which strengthens the long-term economic case for paired renewables and storage despite near-term headwinds. Faster declines abroad Outside North America, storage and solar costs are declining more quickly owing to unhindered supply chain integration. The convergence of falling storage costs and high gas turbine prices is changing how grid operators plan baseline and peaking capacity, and the underlying economics continue to favor renewable-plus-storage builds over new thermal peaking plants. Abdullah said the structural shift being tracked is no longer only about renewables becoming competitive, but about storage and solar together redefining the economics of a power system. He added that the combination of falling storage costs and strong renewable resources is closing off the economic case for new gas peaking capacity globally. artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The global failure rate for lithium-ion battery energy storage systems, on a per-GWh basis, fell 98% from 2018 to 2025 and 50% from 2024 to 2025, the Electric Power Research Institute said in a new analysis of its BESS failure incident database. - Stationary energy storage systems’ annual failure rates range from 0.04% to 0.14%, according to the analysis. That is comparable to the 0.1% annual failure rate for oil-filled electrical transformers, EPRI said in the report, Risk Factors and Failure Statistics of Lithium-Ion BESS. - Safety reviews and, in some cases, retrofits can mitigate failure risk and improve reliability in older systems, which tend to fail at higher rates than newer systems built under stricter codes and design practices, EPRI said. Dive Insight: Ninety-three percent of the BESS safety incidents EPRI reviewed worldwide resulted in no injuries or fatalities, according to the report. In the United States, no reported injuries or fatalities have occurred as a result of BESS failures since April 2019, when an explosion at an Arizona Public Service facility seriously injured four firefighters. A post-incident report by Underwriters Laboratories, the global safety science organization known as UL, noted that the APS installation was commissioned before the initial release of NFPA 855, the safety standard that governs energy storage systems today. Lakshmi Srinivasan, a senior technical leader with EPRI’s energy storage program and a principal investigator on the report, told Utility Dive that battery systems deployed over the past five years appear significantly more reliable than earlier vintages. The trend continues today. “There are things we know in 2026 that were not necessarily understood in 2019 or 2020, when the older systems were being put in place,” Srinivasan said in an interview. The most dramatic BESS failure in the U.S. involved a utility-scale installation inside a 1950s-era turbine hall at a decommissioned thermal power plant near Santa Cruz, California, known as Moss Landing. In January 2025, thermal runaway in one of the units caused fire to spread throughout the indoor facility and ultimately destroyed most of the 300-MW battery array. Thick smoke emanated from the facility for days, but no injuries were reported and subsequent soil and water monitoring found no significant threats to human health or the environment. Experts later told Utility Dive the incident was a “learning opportunity” for the energy storage industry. Indoor BESS facilities fail at higher rates and sustain more damage on average than outdoor facilities, according to EPRI’s report. Propagation-prevention measures within battery units and fire walls or similar barriers between units can mitigate fire’s spread within indoor facilities, EPRI said. Vistra commissioned Moss Landing in 2020. BESS facilities commissioned before 2021 account for just 3% of global energy storage capacity, according to the report. It’s worthwhile for owners of those older facilities to run thorough risk assessments of them and take corrective action if warranted, Srinivasan said. For example, the 2019 incident in Arizona showed a need for older BESS facilities to address explosion risk, which represents “a different risk than fire and a bigger one from a personnel and equipment standpoint,” Srinavasan said. Explosion-mitigation retrofits range from what she called “a relatively low-difficulty change,” like installing flammable gas detectors inside battery enclosures, to more significant projects like installing new ventilation systems or making structural upgrades to direct pressure waves upward and away from first responders, Srinavasan said. Those last two types of projects generally require changes to battery unit envelopes, which could void the manufacturer’s warranty or interfere with other aspects of the system’s design, Srinavasan said. In some scenarios, it could make more sense to prematurely decommission an outdated, higher-risk system, she added. Although newer battery systems appear to be safer than early-vintage systems, local permitting remains challenging in some jurisdictions due to limitations in the NFPA 855 standard that lead most developers to apply for exemptions to allow for higher energy densities or other project modifications, Srinavasan said. To assist local authorities that may lack in-house expertise, New York added a requirement to its fire code — which took effect in January — that those authorities can make energy storage developers pay for independent technical reviews of exemption applications, she added. Correction: We have updated this story to remove a reference to a new NFPA standard expected this fall. NFPA 855 will remain the key standard for battery energy storage systems.

artigo.texto: DATA CENTERS NO NORDESTE: REGIÃO PODE ATRAIR 30% DOS INVESTIMENTOS ATÉ 2036 O Nordeste poderá concentrar cerca de 30% dos novos investimentos em grandes data centers no Brasil até 2036, além de ampliar a geração de energia eólica e solar e a produção de gás natural. As projeções constam no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2036), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), sob diretrizes do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). Divulgado para consulta pública em 8 de outubro, o documento aponta que a presença de pontos de chegada de cabos internacionais de fibra óptica, a disponibilidade de energia renovável e o potencial de desenvolvimento econômico regional estão entre os fatores que favorecem a instalação de centros de dados no Nordeste. Apesar dessas condições, a maior parcela dos novos investimentos deverá se concentrar no subsistema Sudeste/Centro-Oeste, com participação superior a 65%. O Sul deverá receber os 5% restantes, segundo as estimativas do plano. Consumo de energia dos data centers A expansão dos data centers está relacionada ao avanço da digitalização da economia, à demanda por armazenamento e processamento de informações e ao uso crescente de inteligência artificial. Nesse cenário, o PDE 2036 projeta que o consumo de eletricidade dessas instalações no Brasil alcance aproximadamente 30 terawatts-hora (TWh) em 2036. Devido à dimensão dos empreendimentos previstos, o planejamento indica uma tendência de conexão direta dos novos centros de dados à rede básica de transmissão de energia elétrica. Demanda de eletricidade no Nordeste O crescimento das atividades de comércio e serviços deverá contribuir para a expansão da demanda por eletricidade no Nordeste. De acordo com o PDE 2036, a carga elétrica do subsistema deverá avançar, em média, 3,7% ao ano entre 2026 e 2036, a maior taxa projetada entre os subsistemas brasileiros. O índice supera a média estimada para o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), de 3,3% ao ano no mesmo período. Em termos absolutos, a carga global do Nordeste deverá passar de 14.209 megawatts médios (MW médios), em 2026, para 20.462 MW médios, em 2036. O indicador considera tanto o consumo final de eletricidade quanto as perdas registradas entre a geração e o fornecimento aos consumidores. O relatório também aponta uma mudança na composição do consumo nacional. A participação da classe comercial deverá aumentar de 19% para 24% entre 2026 e 2036, impulsionada, entre outros fatores, pela expansão dos data centers. No mesmo período, a parcela residencial deverá cair de 32% para 28%. Outra demanda considerada no planejamento está relacionada à produção de hidrogênio por eletrólise. Segundo o PDE, a implantação de projetos desse tipo deverá ganhar espaço no segundo quinquênio do horizonte analisado, devido ao prazo mais longo de maturação dos investimentos. Ainda assim, a participação dessas atividades deverá permanecer reduzida no período projetado. Expansão da transmissão A instalação de grandes consumidores de energia, como data centers e unidades de produção de hidrogênio, deverá exigir investimentos adicionais na infraestrutura de transmissão, segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética. O PDE destaca estudos para a integração dessas novas cargas no Nordeste e recomenda a implantação do Bipolo Nordeste II, empreendimento destinado a ampliar a capacidade de transferência de eletricidade da região para os subsistemas Sudeste e Sul. De acordo com o planejamento, o projeto e as obras complementares deverão facilitar a conexão de novos empreendimentos de geração, consumo e armazenamento de energia. A infraestrutura também deverá contribuir para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico e para a redução de cortes de geração associados a restrições de confiabilidade da rede. *Informações do site Movimento Econômico. artigo.texto: A Youdera assinala 11 anos de atividade com mais de 2.500 projetos de energia solar realizados em Portugal, Espanha e Suíça e pretende reforçar a aposta em sistemas locais que combinam produção fotovoltaica, armazenamento em baterias e gestão de energia, foi divulgado em comunicado. Segundo a mesma fonte, cinco anos depois de iniciar operações em Portugal, a empresa está a direcionar a sua atividade para soluções de energia descentralizada instaladas nas próprias instalações dos clientes, do lado do consumo, o chamado modelo behind the meter. A estratégia passa por combinar a produção solar com baterias e ferramentas digitais de gestão de energia. Segundo a empresa, a plataforma tecnológica, que recorre a inteligência artificial, permite otimizar a utilização da energia produzida localmente e a eletricidade adquirida à rede. A evolução do modelo de negócio acompanha também um reforço da capacidade de investimento. No início de 2026, a Youdera fechou uma ronda estratégica com a Amundi Energy Transition, associada a um plano de implementação de 150 milhões de euros para infraestruturas de energia distribuída. O financiamento deverá ser aplicado na instalação de novos sistemas, na incorporação de armazenamento em ativos existentes e na aquisição de projetos e portefólios já em operação nos três mercados onde a empresa está presente. “O quinto aniversário de operação da Youdera em Portugal é uma ocasião especial. Temos muito orgulho no trabalho que temos feito no país até aqui”, afirma Pedro Miranda, cofundador e CEO da Youdera. A empresa, acrescenta, começou por financiar projetos solares e evoluiu para um modelo em que constrói e opera sistemas locais de energia nas instalações dos clientes, combinando produção, armazenamento e gestão. A Youdera estabeleceu como objetivo alcançar 500 megawatts (MW) de potência instalada em Portugal, Espanha e Suíça até 2030, através da construção de novos sistemas de geração e armazenamento e da aquisição de projetos e portefólios em funcionamento. Em Portugal, a empresa mantém o foco no desenvolvimento de sistemas locais de energia destinados sobretudo ao setor empresarial, num contexto de procura por soluções que permitam reduzir custos energéticos e aumentar a previsibilidade do consumo. O modelo Energy-as-a-Service adotado pela empresa prevê que os clientes não tenham de realizar o investimento inicial nos equipamentos, ficando a Youdera responsável pelo financiamento, instalação e operação dos sistemas.

artigo.texto: Brazil’s Data Center Growth Pushes Beyond São Paulo Brazil’s data center growth is spreading beyond São Paulo to Rio, Fortaleza, and the south, but power grid delays and lengthy permitting will decide which markets actually succeed. Brazil’s data center market is beginning to expand beyond its longtime base in São Paulo as hyperscale and AI-driven projects draw attention to Rio de Janeiro, Fortaleza, and southern Brazil. The shift reflects growing demand for capacity, but it also highlights a harder question for developers: whether Brazil’s energy and connectivity advantages can be translated into sites with dependable power and workable construction timelines. São Paulo still accounts for 76% of Brazil’s live data center capacity, according to DC Byte’s August market analysis. The city continues to benefit from its concentration of customers, network density, and established operator presence. That ecosystem gives the market a depth that emerging regions cannot quickly replicate. However, São Paulo faces a shrinking supply of powered land and slow transmission upgrades. At the same time, newly enacted federal tax incentives could improve project economics in other parts of the country, even as environmental licensing and electricity infrastructure remain potential constraints. São Paulo Still Dominates Capacity Brazil’s existing market is still driven principally by hyperscale cloud demand and enterprise deployments, even as large AI projects begin to influence development plans. “Demand continues to be driven predominantly by hyperscale cloud providers, which remain the largest consumers of data center capacity in the country,” Rodrigo Gomez, senior Latin America analyst at DC Byte, told Data Center Knowledge. São Paulo’s advantage comes from more than scale alone. The market combines demand from Brazil’s largest metropolitan economy with dense fiber connectivity and access to international networks, reinforcing its position as the country’s primary cloud and interconnection hub. Operators including Ascenty, Elea, and Scala have built substantial footprints in Brazil. DC Byte also points to investments by Microsoft and Equinix as evidence of growing international interest. Gomez said the maturity of that ecosystem remains central to Brazil’s appeal. Investors can enter a market with established customers and infrastructure while also pursuing opportunities in less developed locations. “At the same time, Brazil is beginning to see greater investment in facilities designed to support AI workloads, reflecting the global shift toward high-density computing and next-generation digital infrastructure,” he said. This leaves Brazil serving two overlapping tracks of demand: continued growth in cloud and enterprise capacity, and the development of larger, higher-density facilities designed for AI and other intensive computing workloads. Power and Permitting Remain the Main Constraints Power availability remains the central variable in how quickly new capacity can be delivered. Brazil’s access to renewable electricity strengthens the country’s long-term investment case, but generation does not necessarily mean a site can be connected on schedule. Gomez identified the pace of electrical infrastructure development as the market’s main challenge. Generation, transmission, and broader grid expansion all take time, making delivery schedules for new substations and transmission capacity critical for developers. Bruno Porto, manager for industrial, logistics, and data centers in Brazil at real estate services firm JLL, told Data Center Knowledge that some locations will require transmission reinforcement before additional data center load can be supported. “Environmental licensing in Brazil is also critical, with this phase alone potentially taking up to 18 months depending on the region and the scale of the project,” Porto noted. Those factors can stretch project timelines even where land, capital, and customer demand are available. For developers looking outside São Paulo, the key question is not just whether a market looks attractive on paper, but whether permits and power delivery can align with construction schedules. Porto said he expects growth through 2027 to depend heavily on projects already negotiated during 2026. He added that the volume of facilities now under construction should allow providers to bring new capacity online within the next 12 months. That outlook applies to projects that have already advanced through the development process, not to every large campus proposal in the national pipeline. Longer-range projects still depend on securing infrastructure and approvals before they can move into execution. “Environmental licensing in Brazil is also critical, with this phase alone potentially taking up to 18 months depending on the region and the scale of the project.” – Bruno Porto, manager for industrial, logistics, and data centers in Brazil, JLL Regional Hubs Offer Different Advantages Outside São Paulo, Brazil’s emerging markets offer different combinations of customer access, connectivity, and development potential. Rio de Janeiro is positioned to support both domestic and international traffic, with Gomez describing it as an important gateway for digital services serving eastern Brazil.
