artigo.texto: Statesboro District 2 candidate Kathleen Keehner focuses on data centers, youth programs Kathleen Keehner is one of three candidates running for Statesboro City Council District 2 STATESBORO, Ga. (WTOC) - Statesboro residents will vote in just over three weeks to fill the city’s District 2 council seat, which has been vacant for nearly five months. The special election is a three-person race. Kathleen Keehner is one of the three candidates seeking the seat. Background Keehner became a homeowner in Statesboro last year when she bought a house to raise her newborn son. She said she is now looking to represent the city’s District 2. “I have a lot of ideas for the future because my son is going to be living here for the foreseeable future,” Keehner said. Data centers Keehner said her motivation for running centers on data centers. In August, Statesboro City Council approved a zoning map amendment that would allow a data center to be built within city limits. Because District 2 was unrepresented, Mayor Jonathan McCollar broke a tie to push the approval despite resident protests. Keehner said she began paying closer attention to local politics when talk of data centers began to increase in the state. She said if elected, she would vote against any data center application. “This race, it’s deeper than just surface level who’s going to win for city council, yeah the city council is made up of five people who vote on decisions, but those decisions can shape the future,” Keehner said. Budget priorities City council members are tasked with approving the city’s annual budget. Keehner said if elected, she plans to devote more taxpayer dollars to creating programs and safe spaces for the city’s youth. “Since we lost the boys and girls club in 2025, we haven’t had any major investments in young people’s programs. So, I would like to reallocate funds, I know that there was a brand new park that they spent over one million dollars on in Whitesville that is farther away from the west side,” Keehner said. Qualifications Keehner does not have experience serving as a public official. She said her qualifications come from being an active member of her community. “Because I do talk to my constituents, I am out here in the streets, I think that qualifies me more than a leader that doesn’t care about the next person, you know,” Keehner said. Keehner said voters should consider who has their best interest at heart. “It’s important to vote for somebody who you know has your best interest at heart, I think that it is important to vote for somebody who doesn’t have deep ties and deep relationships with people who are already proving not to care about you or what you’re concerned with,” Keehner said. artigo.texto: AI data centers are coming for federal land. They’re roiling the Nevada governor’s race - Click here to listen to this article - Share via - A proposed AI data center near Boulder City was moved to federal land after residents defeated it locally; a judge later halted construction over the project’s environmental review. - With more than a dozen similar projects in the works, Nevada’s vast federal holdings could become a proving ground for data centers and a tinderbox over public-land protections. - The issue is reshaping the governor’s race, as Republican Joe Lombardo and Democrat Aaron Ford spar over development, tax breaks and safeguards for electricity bills and water supplies. BOULDER CITY, Nev. — Janelle Sorenson loves the clear night skies in Boulder City, less than an hour’s drive from the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. It’s a small, quiet town, and she thinks an artificial intelligence data center would ruin the community and scar the desert landscape. So over the summer, she joined with other residents to successfully oppose plans for one of the giant computing warehouses that have popped up around the country. But their victory was short-lived. The developers withdrew their application and instead sought adjacent land owned by the federal government — and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management signed off. “Not only did we not get to decide anything or have a say,” Sorenson said, “we were just really kept in the dark.” The Townsite data center was the first in the country to be approved on federal public land, though construction is stalled after a judge ruled that the government couldn’t use an old environmental review from when the project was intended to be a solar farm. Tech companies are eager for vast tracts to build data centers that can be as large as 70 football fields, and Townsite could set a precedent for similar projects on federal property with more than a dozen others in the planning stages. President Trump has been a steadfast supporter of the AI industry, which he views as a source of economic growth and part of a global competition with China. However, data centers have been unpopular in many communities as voters worry about higher electricity bills, declining water supplies and other effects. In Nevada, where 80% of the land is owned by the federal government, Townsite and other projects have become a dominant issue in the battleground state’s closely watched governor’s race. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, one of his party’s most vulnerable incumbents, doesn’t outright oppose building data centers on public lands, as long as they have community support. He recently signed an agreement with Trump’s Republican administration to streamline infrastructure projects, which could include data centers on federal lands. Democratic nominee Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, has pledged to oppose data centers on public lands, saying affordable housing should be the priority. Both say the projects, whether on public or private land, must follow state rules, such as requiring data centers to cover their own energy costs and protecting water supplies, or they would lose eligibility for state tax abatements. Voters across the political spectrum unite against data centers Sorenson, the Boulder City resident, considers herself a liberal, but she said her conservative neighbors are on the same page as she is. “We’re all aligned on this,” she said. Autumn McGrath-Shook, who lives in the same town, said she recently left the GOP and registered with the Green Party over data centers, though she still identifies as conservative. Worried about the environmental impact on wildlife, she joined forces with “these crazy libs” to oppose the project. Data centers have quickly become a “catalyzing issue” in the midterms, catching many politicians flat-footed, said David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. Some state leaders who were previously supportive of data centers have rushed to respond. For example, Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused data center approvals until audits are completed, and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order removing data center proposals from a fast-track permitting process and requiring them to receive local approval before seeking state approval. In August, Ford announced his plan to pause new tax abatements for data centers while an audit is conducted to see whether the projects have fulfilled promises about producing tax revenue and economic benefits. In September, Lombardo, who has said data centers provide enormous economic opportunity for Nevada, signed an executive order placing more guardrails on them and requiring them to pay more taxes to support schools. The two have successfully “muddied the waters” on their data center positions, Damore said. Lombardo criticized Ford for co-sponsoring 2015 legislation that created the state’s tax abatement program for the facilities, a measure that received bipartisan support. Ford criticized Lombardo for giving more than $200 million in tax breaks to data centers, which is connected to the legislation that Ford co-sponsored. Ford told the Associated Press that he would use “every tool” at his disposal to prevent data centers from skirting state guardrails, including withholding tax abatements and pursuing litigation. Lombardo, whose campaign declined to make him available for an interview, has a similar pitch. His office said he would not hesitate to confront the federal government to advocate for Nevadans. But that’s not good enough for McGrath-Shook, who is on the fence in the governor’s race. She thinks Ford is soft on crime, but she views Lombardo as more pro-data centers. “I would much rather vote for Lombardo than Aaron Ford in a normal world,” she said. “But with the looming data centers, it really changes the landscape — and literally.” Data centers on public lands are the latest effort in AI race Last year, Trump signed an e

artigo.texto: Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID) has invited online bids for the development of a 187.5 MW / 750 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Telangana. The project aims to strengthen electricity grid stability and support the integration of renewable energy into the power network. The tender has been published through the company’s PRANIT Portal, inviting eligible firms with the necessary technical and financial capabilities to participate in the bidding process. The project is designated as Package TS-BESS-01 and carries Tender Reference Number CC/T/W-BESS/DOM/A02/26/14098. The proposed battery storage system will have a power capacity of 187.5 MW and an energy storage capacity of 750 MWh, equivalent to four hours of storage at full output. The project is expected to contribute to the development of energy storage infrastructure required to support the increasing share of renewable energy in the electricity system. The tender falls under the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) route and is classified under works related to power and energy projects. Interested bidders can access the tender documents through POWERGRID’s official tendering platform using RFX Number 5002005732. Participants are required to examine the tender conditions and pre-qualification requirements before submitting their bids. According to the tender details, the participation fee has been fixed at Rs. 25,000. The tender value and earnest money deposit (EMD) are listed as zero on the portal. Prospective bidders should refer to the official tender documents for the applicable eligibility conditions, technical specifications, commercial requirements and other instructions governing participation. The tender schedule specifies October 12, 2026, at 7:50 PM as the commencement date and time for both document sales and soft copy bid submissions. The document sale period will remain open until October 17, 2026, at 11:55 PM. The deadline for submitting bids is October 19, 2026, at 11:00 AM. The bids are scheduled to be opened on October 19, 2026, at 11:30 AM, providing a short interval between the submission deadline and the opening process. Interested companies must complete the required procedures within the prescribed schedule to ensure their participation in the tender. The tender is being managed by Satyam Gupta, Engineer (CS), at POWERGRID’s corporate office. The office is located at Saudamini, 3rd Floor, Plot No. 2, Sector 29, Gurugram, Haryana. The proposed Telangana BESS project comes amid growing requirements for flexible electricity infrastructure to accommodate variable renewable generation. Battery storage systems can store electricity when supply is available and discharge it when demand rises or renewable generation declines. Such capabilities can help balance supply and demand, improve grid flexibility and support the reliable integration of solar and wind power. Through this tender, POWERGRID is advancing the development of large-scale battery storage infrastructure. The project represents another step towards strengthening India’s electricity network and meeting the operational requirements of a power system increasingly supported by renewable energy sources. artigo.texto: Richardson Electronics, ComEd, trumpet company’s battery storage system plans Richardson Electronics, state lawmakers and ComEd officials gathered Monday to celebrate the Kane County company’s plan to build the largest commercial battery energy storage facility on ComEd’s Illinois grid. “Take it from somebody in the energy industry. This is a very big deal,” said Gil Quinones, ComEd’s chief executive officer and president. The facility, which will have containers with battery energy storage systems, or BESSes, will be built at the rear of Richardson’s headquarters in La Fox. It is intended to serve as a model for potential customers. The facility would be capable of storing up to 5 megawatt-hours of power. “We have learned that standing still is not an option,” said Edward Richardson, chief executive officer and president of Richardson Electronics. His father founded the company in 1947, selling military-surplus electronic supplies such as walkie-talkie batteries. “We’re here because we believe battery energy storage will be claiming an increasingly important role in the future of energy infrastructure,” Richardson said. “The demand for power continues to grow. The ability to store energy, improve reliability and support a more resilient grid becomes increasingly important.” Richardson said the company’s manufacturing experience, engineering expertise and customer relationships help as it grows its global power-management program, which focuses on “green” energy applications. “We believe it has significant long-term potential,” he said. In August 2025, Illinois officials announced the company would receive tax credits for the project through the state’s Re-imagining Energy and Vehicles Program. According to the state, Richardson was investing $8.5 million in the project. The agreement with the state calls for Richardson to add 54 full-time employees at the La Fox site. “The fact is, our energy future depends on having enough power to support growing communities and local economies. Battery storage helps make power available when and where it’s needed most. This is critical for grid stability,” Quinones said. He said batteries will store energy when it is cheap and abundant, to be available when power is scarce and expensive. He said using batteries also “buys valuable time needed to make infrastructure investments needed to bring excess energy onto the grid.” The company is still designing the project. The building size will depend on how many 44-ton battery energy storage systems it will contain, said Scott DuBois, the company’s director of business development. Meanwhile, it is looking to lease space in which to build BESSes, he said. Richardson Electronics sells engineered solutions, green energy products, power grid and microwave tubes and related consumables, power conversion and radio-frequency and microwave components, CT X-ray tubes, and customized display solutions. ssarkauskas@dailyherald.com

artigo.texto: More than 40 University of Michigan staff, students and Ypsilanti community members gathered in the Trotter Multicultural Center Monday evening for a data center teach-in by Stop the Data Center, an advocacy organization against the the University’s planned Ypsilanti Township data center in collaboration with Los Alamos National Laboratory. Ypsilanti Township residents organized a presentation arguing the data center is another expression of the military-industrial-academic complex, which they said only serves to advance the United States’ hegemony while ignoring local communities. The presentation then shifted to discussing new ideas to secure their collective goal: ending the development of the research computing center. At the event, assistant information professor Justine Zhang said residents opposing the center are worried about toxic chemicals and the other potential consequences of proximity to data centers. “(The project is) proceeding in spite of opposition from people in Ypsilanti and beyond, who do not want a project that will extract land, water and capacity from the community while extending the infrastructure of U.S. imperialism,” Zhang said. “Our task is to collectively analyze and strategize around these developments, so we act in solidarity with our friends, coworkers, neighbors and comrades to the data center.” Ypsilanti Township resident Robin Wylie, the School of Public Health Epidemiology staff member, said he was concerned about a recent letter from Los Alamos handed out to the community during a September town hall. The letter claimed the proposed site was only a research computing facility that would allow scientists from Los Alamos to work more closely with U-M faculty and students to explore fields like brain cancer surgery outcomes, extreme weather predicting and various other scientific and engineering challenges. “Even at the town hall meetings, we keep asking, ‘What are we going to get out of this?’” Wylie said. “They don’t have an answer for us. We’re not — Ypsilanti is not — benefiting at all from this.” Wylie also said the statement highlighted the benefits the project could provide to the University, but it did not explain how the center would affect local communities. In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Wylie expressed concerns about his community’s safety given the health complications the project may cause. “Toxic chemicals will probably be used in the cooling system, and they can leak in the data center,” Wylie said. “They’ve been known to cause serious health problems. I don’t know how they’re going to prevent that from happening. How are they going to? It’s right next to a river.” University librarian Craig Smith said he worries the project is fully in the power of the University’s Board of Regents, instead of the local community. Smith also questioned why the University is providing nearly $850 million in funds, despite Los Alamos having greater access to the facility. “In our group, we were reflecting on the fact that Los Alamos is going to have 90% access to this data center, and U-M is going to have 10%,” Smith said. “Why are we doing this? We’re paying $800 million for this thing, and we’re getting 10% out of it.” LSA freshman Katrina Hunter told the Daily she was concerned that the majority of the student population remains unaware of the University’s affiliation with Los Alamos for the data center project. She said she believes more students would get involved in anti-data center activism if they were made aware. “I think getting a collective body of students aware of it, and then we can maybe move on to protesting, handing out flyers, talking to students, getting people outside petitioning or talking to town offices, calling up and going to board meetings,” Hunter said. “We can get more involved. Once we go to board meetings we can talk to officials and try to push our way into getting the students and community of Ypsilanti involved.” Daily News Contributor Elise Maurer can be reached at elisemau@umich.edu.

artigo.texto: ComEd and Richardson Electronics, Ltd. joined state and industry leaders to announce Richardson Electronics’ expanded manufacturing of locally produced battery energy storage systems and plans to install its first onsite battery energy storage system demonstration project. This initiative is a critical step toward scaling locally made battery energy storage solutions that strengthen grid reliability, support renewable energy integration, and store energy for use during periods of high demand while helping ease supply-related energy costs. “For generations, manufacturing has been part of northern Illinois’ identity, and Richardson’s announcement demonstrates how that sector continues to shape our region’s economic future,” said ComEd President and CEO Gil Quiniones. “ComEd is committed to supporting business growth by making the grid investments needed to deliver industry-leading reliability at rates that are well below the average commercial and industrial rates for the top 20 largest metropolitan areas.” Richardson, a legacy manufacturer based in La Fox, is currently building the largest commercial battery storage system in Illinois. Its planned operational expansion will help scale the development and distribution of these products. Richardson is installing a 5-MWh research and development demonstration project, supported through the ComEd interconnection process. “Richardson Electronics has a long history of solving complex power and energy challenges through innovation and U.S.-based manufacturing,” said Greg Peloquin, Executive Vice President and General Manager of Power & Microwave Technologies and Green Energy Solutions groups. “Our advanced energy storage solutions will help customers manage energy more efficiently while supporting a more reliable and resilient grid. We value ComEd’s collaboration in bringing this onsite demonstration project to life.” The initiative is also supported by the Reimagining Energy and Vehicles in Illinois, or REV Illinois, program, which is helping Richardson Electronics strengthen its La Fox operations, advance energy technology manufacturing and support continued economic growth in Illinois. “As demand for reliable and affordable energy increases, Illinois has an opportunity not only to deploy new technologies, but to manufacture them,” said Illinois Economic Development Corporation President and CEO Christy George. “Richardson Electronics’ expansion demonstrates how Illinois’ manufacturing expertise can drive growth in emerging industries like battery storage while helping strengthen the energy infrastructure that supports our economy.” Increasing battery energy storage is a key component of Illinois’ recently enacted Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA), which seeks to strengthen grid reliability and help address forecasted energy supply shortfalls. By storing electricity for use during periods of peak demand, battery storage can support a more resilient grid, integrate additional clean energy resources, and help ensure Illinois has the energy capacity needed to power future economic growth. “Safe, reliable and affordable energy is critical to the success of Illinois’ manufacturing sector and will require new generation, transmission investment and new technologies such as battery storage,” said Mark Denzler, President & CEO of the Illinois Manufacturers’ Association. “Richardson Electronics and ComEd’s announcement of a next-generation 5 MWh commercial battery storage system is a great example of manufacturing innovation and ingenuity that will help drive growth and economic development in Illinois.” Battery energy storage systems can charge when electricity is available and discharge when it is needed, helping customers manage energy use and support a more flexible electric system. Depending on how they are configured, batteries can also provide backup capabilities, reduce demand during peak periods, and support the integration of renewable energy resources. “When Kane County Commissioner Rick Williams and I first met with Richardson to discuss this project, I was immediately intrigued by both the economic and energy benefits the project could bring to the area and the state,” said State Representative Dan Ugaste (65th District). “Energy storage will be an important part of having affordable and reliable energy going forward. This work will help to safely and reliably connect the demonstration system while maintaining service for surrounding customers. artigo.texto: By Shereen Siewert | Wausau Pilot & Review A Town of Wausau ordinance sharply restricting where and how data centers can be built goes before Marathon County supervisors Thursday, as the county considers its own rules. The board meets at 6 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15, in the Assembly Room of the Marathon County Courthouse, 500 Forest St. Thursday’s session is an educational meeting where supervisors review and discuss items; votes are scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20. Public comment is limited to items on the agenda. The Town of Wausau adopted the data center ordinance Aug. 3, following a public hearing that drew 14 residents. According to town minutes, Supervisor Steve Buntin told the audience the town attorney recommended an ordinance because the town had nothing on the books and the state exercises no control over data center siting. The ordinance is modeled on one adopted in the Town of Saratoga in Wood County and is, in Buntin’s words, “very restrictive.” Planning commission minutes note the audience “was not in favor of data centers being located in the township.” Under the ordinance, data centers could be built only in the town’s manufacturing district and only with a conditional use permit. Buildings would have to sit at least 200 feet from every property line, parking lots at least 100 feet, and no structure could exceed 35 feet in height. Noise at the property boundary could not exceed 60 decibels. The definition covers cryptocurrency mining, blockchain processing and server farms. Developers would have to submit an environmental and community impact analysis before any public hearing, including an evaluation of effects on emergency services, water supply, school district budgets and municipal revenue. Any facility relying on private wells would need a water feasibility study mapping every well within 1,000 feet and the geology within a mile. No certificate of occupancy could be issued until the utility verifies that supply lines and substations can carry the load without shortchanging other customers, and until the developer shows the cooling system “will not negatively impact the surrounding region.” Because the Town of Wausau operates under county zoning, state law requires county approval of town ordinance amendments. The county’s review is procedural; the application form signed by town officials states that the county does not assess the legality or enforceability of the language and that the town bears full legal responsibility for the ordinance. The county’s Environmental Resources Committee voted Sept. 29 to forward the ordinance to the full board. The voice vote was not unanimous. At the same meeting, the committee began laying groundwork for a countywide data center ordinance. Committee members directed staff to research state regulations, water usage, cooling systems, electricity demand, noise, lighting, traffic and utility infrastructure, and asked for an educational presentation before deciding which zoning districts might allow data centers. The ordinance itself notes that “the development of data centers is swiftly increasing across the State of Wisconsin.” Rietbrock wind and solar rules Supervisors will also review wind and solar siting ordinances from the Town of Rietbrock, in the Athens and Edgar area west of Wausau. Both cleared the Environmental Resources Committee on non-unanimous voice votes. The wind ordinance incorporates the state Public Service Commission’s wind siting rules, known as PSC 128, including noise limits of 50 decibels during the day and 45 at night and the state’s setback table. The ordinance’s findings run to 25 clauses and cite infrasound, wildlife deaths, property values, drainage, road damage and the town’s desire to “maintain the pastoral, rural nature of this region.” The solar ordinance is unchanged from a version the town board passed in 2025 but never submitted to the county. According to town minutes, the Environmental Resources Committee required a fresh public hearing, which the town held Aug. 25. The town board approved both ordinances that night. Cherokee Park expansion The board will consider buying up to 15 acres of wooded land adjoining Cherokee Park in the Town of Hull at $4,450 per acre, a cost not to exceed $66,750. The 65.5-acre park sits on the Big Eau Pleine River. According to a memo from Parks, Recreation and Forestry Director Jamie Polley, the adjacent landowner approached the county about selling the wooded portion of the property, which includes land along the river that the public cannot currently reach. Adding the acreage would open room for trails and river access, Polley wrote. The owner would be required to survey the land and split off the wooded acres as a separate parcel. Money would come from the county’s Parkland and Products account, which has a balance of about $344,400, or from state Knowles-Nelson Stewardship funds if available. Other business Supervisors will review a resolution authorizing staff to proceed with the fourth phase of construction on the county’s planned new highway facility. The resolution and supporting documents were not included in the agenda packet released Friday. As previously reported, the board will also vote on sweeping roughly $388,750 in unspent American Rescue Plan Act funds from 11 completed projects into the Regional Forensic Science Center. Federal rules require all ARPA money to be spent by Dec. 31. The largest unspent balance, $164,198, comes from medical examiner vehicle purchases. A new Solid Waste Department policy would cut landfill tipping fees for 60 days following any declared emergency. Residents, contractors, haulers and municipalities bringing certified disaster debris to the county landfill in Ringle would pay the contract hauler rate. The board directed staff to write the policy following severe weather events earlier this year. artigo.texto: Why Should Delaware Care? Local governments across Delaware have passed regulations on data centers, citing fears about their massive energy use and effects on the environment. But Dover’s data center moratorium is the first in the state, potentially marking a shift in how far municipalities will go to address these concerns. The Dover City Council on Monday unanimously approved a 18-month moratorium on the construction of data centers in Delaware’s capital city. The moratorium is the first of its kind in Delaware, and follows more than a year of discussions and debate across the state over how much the fast-growing industry could impact power bills and the local environment. Dover’s new ordinance now pauses the city’s official review of proposals for large energy-use facilities, including data centers that use more than 30 megawatts of electricity. That amount of electricity is roughly equivalent to the energy use of 24,000 homes. During the 18-month pause, city officials will research the effects data centers could have on the city; whether they should be allowed to be built; and how to regulate them if they are built. “This is not a ‘no’ to data centers. This is, we need to figure it out before we can say, ‘yes,’” Councilwoman Donyale Hall, who introduced the ordinance, said in an interview. Hall said the council will now decide the most cost-effective way to study the issue. The moratorium passed with little discussion on Monday evening, except from Councilman Brian Lewis, who said called for a ban on construction of the facilities in the city, despite potential economic benefits they could bring. “To me, the environment, people’s health and our infrastructure are more important than jobs in the city,” Lewis said. Dover officials have already been approached about potential plans for more than one data center project in the city, Hall said. She said she did not have information about the developers. And they have not yet submitted a formal application to the city, so the potential projects will not move forward at least until the moratorium is over. While Dover is the first city in Delaware to pass a data center moratorium, it is not alone. Almost every state in the country has at least one municipality that has either banned data centers or imposed a moratorium, according to the artificial intelligence research site, Programs. A boom in the construction of data centers to power the artificial intelligence industry has sparked a nationwide backlash to the facilities. Opponents say they are noisy, use too much water and cause power bills to surge. Proponents say they bring much-needed jobs and tax revenue. New Castle and Kent counties also recently approved rules limiting where a data center could be built in their unincorporated areas. Those regulations include buffer requirements, noise limits and bans on cooling systems that consume large amounts of water. When debating the regulations last summer, Kent County officials also expressed a willingness to consider an outright county-wide ban on the fast-growing industry. Adding to the county regulations are new rules state lawmakers passed in June through a slate of bills. Among those is one that would require developers to supply all of the power a data center facility would use for the first 10 years of its operations.

artigo.texto: Data centers were on tap for both the Pulaski County Quorum Court and the Little Rock Board of Directors on Tuesday night, with the city’s measure going forward for a vote next week and the county’s legislation pulled for further study. Little Rock City Director Kathy Webb tried and failed to get an 18-month moratorium passed in August – it tied on a 4-4 vote – and now has come back with a six-month pause, which was brought up at Tuesday night’s agenda meeting. There was little discussion and no vote taken. Webb said she had talked to her constituents, some of whom thought a year and a half was too long and others who thought six months wasn’t long enough. Her proposal allows for another six-month delay if more time is needed to study a data center proposal. Asked if she thinks she has the votes this time around, Webb said she hopes so. “If we were in the Legislature, lawmakers have those kinds of conversations every day,” she said. “But we can’t do that on the board so I depend on the people I’m working with to have those conversations with other board members. I can say this, there will be several co-sponsors this time.” Google has proposed a 100-megawatt, $1 billion data center that would be located on 380 acres in the Port of Little Rock area. The Board of Directors passed an ordinance in June outlining data center regulations, but it has been criticized for not going far enough. About a block and a half away from City Hall, at the county’s administration building, the Quorum Court’s own agenda was getting underway, but a proposed piece of legislation was pulled before it could be considered and placed on the full Quorum Court’s agenda. The proposed ordinance was written by Justice of the Peace Douglas House, who said he had taken his proposal off the agenda after talking with members of the county’s planning staff who had questions about some of the particulars. House, who was appointed by Gov. Sarah Sanders, is serving until the end of the year and took the place left vacated by Phil Stowers, who resigned in June. He said he has worked on the ordinance as an alternative to one proposed by Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood. Blackwood’s ordinance was passed last month on an 11-4 vote and sets out detailed conditions under which large industrial projects, like data centers, can operate. After that vote, County Judge Barry Hyde vetoed the measure because, among other objections, he thinks the county will be sued if the ordinance passes. House’s ordinance includes some of the same topics as Blackwood’s measure, but makes an exception for a large data center project being pushed by AVAIO Digital. That project, located near Wrightsville, is estimated to be worth $21 billion and need 1 gigawatt of electricity to operate. House said he also thinks the county will be sued if the Avaio project is included in any legislation that slows the construction process that is now underway. “I am 99.9% sure that will happen,” House said after the meeting. House said if the Quorum Court overrides Hyde’s veto, thereby confirming the passage of Blackwood’s ordinance — nine votes are needed — he will toss his proposal in the trash, noting that his time on the Quorum Court will end soon after. If the justices of the peace fail to override the veto, he said he will continue pursuing his proposal.

artigo.texto: Editor’s note: We are publishing a series of fact-checks of advertisements in the Pennsylvania 8th Congressional District race between incumbent Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Dallas Twp. and Democratic challenger, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti. The election is key for both major parties’ hopes of holding a House majority the next two years. The 30-second ad is paid for by Paige For PA, Cognetti’s official campaign committee. It was approved by the candidate. The scene opens with two men sitting in Adirondack chairs in a front yard outside a home. One is reading a copy of The Times-Tribune, the other a recent edition of The Citizens’ Voice. “You see this?” one man asks. “Bresnahan wants data centers all over NEPA.” It kicks off a discussion between the two men centered on Bresnahan’s views and actions on data centers. The other man complains about already-high energy costs, while the original commenter adds that data centers “use more juice than 100,000 Sheetz (gas stations).” He goes on to say that Bresnahan gave data centers a $20 billion tax break, adding that he also “bought stock in a data center company.” “Rob Bresnahan is making more money, and we’re stuck with the bill,” he says. Cognetti appears, sitting atop a fallen tree, announcing she approves the ad. She’d say more, she concludes, “but I think these guys got it covered.” Key claim Rob Bresnahan supports data center construction throughout the region and encourages them with tax breaks. Is it factual? The dialogue hits on several points scrutinizing Bresnahan’s early support for data center development in Northeast Pennsylvania. Claims that Bresnahan desires data centers be built “all over” the region is at the very least a stretch. In June, Bresnahan introduced the Local Control Protection Act in the House. He said the bill would put data center development in the hands of local communities by putting limits on a corporation’s right to sue over local zoning decisions that deny applications to build them. The bill was sent to committee in June and has not been acted upon since. “We should never let billion-dollar corporations supersede the voices of those who live in the community,” Bresnahan said in a statement introducing the bill. However, it also is true that Bresnahan expressed support for area data center development in the past. In April 2025, Bresnahan said data centers could be “catalysts for economic growth and technological innovation” throughout the region. “I look forward to these investments and encourage companies to look to Northeastern Pennsylvania as a home for economic and technological advancements,” he said then. After a joint venture between PPL Corporation and Blackstone, a leading private equity firm, to invest $25 billion in data center development in Pennsylvania was announced in July 2025, Bresnahan pointed to potential benefits in NEPA, saying the region was full of “untapped power” and was “more than ready for new growth, investments and opportunities.” It is not true that Bresnahan voted in favor of a $20 billion tax break targeted solely to data center developers. Yet, critics argue the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, for which Bresnahan was a yes vote, included language that created broader capital expensing and depreciation rules allowing companies to write off equipment costs sooner than is deemed necessary based on useful life and is especially lucrative for companies that build AI infrastructure. A study by the nonprofit Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, for example, found that five big tech giants — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle — combined to claim more than $26 billion in depreciation tax breaks in 2025. Bresnahan indeed owns stock in data center companies. According to financial disclosures filed in August, Bresnahan owns between $19,005 and $110,000 worth of stock in four companies with direct ties to the data center industry. His portfolio also includes investments worth between $804,024 and $2.04 million in companies that supply chips, networking equipment, semiconductor manufacturing tools and software that aid the development of the AI industry and data centers.

artigo.texto: SMM, October 13: Entering September, the sodium-ion battery industry chain's "advancing amid divergence" operating pattern further evolved. The electrolyte segment continued its "capacity without volume release" logic, with top-tier players' shipments highly concentrated and growth mainly flowing to undisclosed major clients. The window for scaled-up breakthroughs is expected to materialize in Q4 with GWh-level order fulfillment. In the battery cell segment, order deliveries were released intensively amid the "September-October peak season" signals, but actual project implementation pace clearly lagged plans, with regional and application-based divergence intensifying. 1. Electrolyte: Ample Capacity in Wait for GWh-Level Batch Implementation According to an SMM survey, sodium-ion battery electrolyte production rose 24% MoM and surged 115% YoY in September, sustaining high growth momentum. Production was highly concentrated, with top-tier players' shipments showing a clear breakaway lead. This round of growth likely flowed to major clients not yet publicly disclosed, and scaled shipment growth is likely delayed to Q4. September data largely reflected early stockpiling and small-batch deliveries on top of existing capacity. From an operational perspective, the number of industry players remains limited. Traditional lithium battery electrolyte leaders still attach relatively low priority to sodium-ion battery business. Apart from a few major clients, they have yet to form bulk supply to publicly disclosed entities, with only sporadic deliveries mentioned in financial reports. Downstream demand exhibited "small-batch, project-based" characteristics—some battery cell manufacturers' sodium-ion battery shipment volumes were relatively small, with cylindrical products shipped only intermittently in small batches, mainly targeting start-stop and small power applications, and no scaled energy storage application has yet formed. On the capacity side, since lithium battery electrolyte capacity is highly interchangeable with sodium-ion battery electrolyte capacity, overall industry capacity is ample with no obvious supply gap. However, it is worth noting that the current high returns in the lithium battery industry may crowd out sodium-ion battery electrolyte capacity. Enterprises' production scheduling priorities will continue to revolve around lithium battery business, leaving uncertainty in the pace of sodium-ion battery capacity release. On prices and raw materials, finished electrolyte prices remained generally stable in September, while core raw materials fluctuated slightly. NaPF6 prices were relatively stable: September production pulled back from August's unusually high level but was clearly better than the same period in previous years' normal levels. The core driver of this round of rise came from marginal improvement on the demand side. Upstream and downstream players across the industry chain generally held no additional inventory, with production strictly following produce-based-on-sales. Downstream electrolyte plants made temporary purchases as needed without advance stockpiling. Despite NaPF6's favorable storage conditions and longer shelf life than similar lithium chemical products, enterprises still scheduled production based on fixed sales, reflecting the industry's prudent judgment on the pace of demand realization. Competitive landscape-wise, the entire industry is waiting for top-tier players to deliver GWh-scale volume signals. Notably, some battery cell manufacturers have adopted low-price selling strategies right after production line commissioning and at the initial mass production stage, a commercial logic that remains to be validated over time. Looking ahead, if demand from key clients ramps up as expected in October, electrolyte and upstream NaPF6 shipments are poised for a step-change increase. SMM expects sodium-ion battery electrolyte production to rise 2% MoM and surge 146% YoY in October. II. Battery cells: Clear peak season signals, but rollout pace falls short of expectations According to SMM survey, sodium-ion battery cell production rose 1% MoM and surged 120% YoY in September, with the sodium-ion battery market showing initial signs of the "September-October peak season." Constrained by the requirement that energy storage projects generally must be connected to the grid before year-end, order deliveries are being released in a concentrated manner; however, from the perspective of project implementation, actual progress is clearly lagging behind plans, with schedule pressure and execution gaps coexisting. Regionally, utility-scale energy storage in China is concentrated in northern regions such as Hebei and Inner Mongolia, while overseas commercial and industrial storage demand is concentrated in Europe and Australia. Domestic commercial and industrial storage has yet to gain traction, presenting a three-way divergence in the demand geography: "northern storage leading, European and Australian commercial and industrial following, and domestic commercial and industrial yet to start." From an operational perspective, mainstream producers' monthly battery cell output remains at the tens of megawatt hours level. On the capacity side, some battery cell manufacturers' new bases in Sichuan will begin production and ramp up in late October, while some existing bases face clear capacity gaps that need to be filled through toll processing. Toll processing business is mostly focused on energy storage projects, with order demand expected to last until year-end. On the technology roadmap, current capacity is concentrated in the polyanion route, demand for cylindrical start-stop battery cells is steadily rising as winter approaches, and orders for prismatic energy storage battery cells remain at high levels, with route and product differentiation trends continuing. artigo.texto: Supermicro expande seu portfólio de projetos de computação aberta integrada para acelerar as implantações de data centers de IA em escala de rack AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 14 de outubro de 2026 - O portfólio integrado baseado no Open Compute Project (OCP) abrange sistemas de IA/HPC em escala de rack, racks ORv3 e ORW, alimentação de 48V CC, redes e soluções de refrigeração líquida para viabilizar a computação de maior densidade em data centers existentes e novos - O portfólio abrange desde a infraestrutura até operações inteligentes, incluindo fluidos de resfriamento DCBBS, CDUs integradas ao rack (in-rack), switches e o pacote de software de gerenciamento de sistemas da Supermicro para a gestão da infraestrutura - O Supermicro DCBBS reúne essas tecnologias baseadas em OCP em soluções integradas em escala de rack, simplificando e acelerando a implementação de recursos de computação, energia, rede e refrigeração para reduzir o tempo de entrada em operação (TTO). SAN JOSE, Califórnia, 14 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), anunciou hoje um portfólio expandido de sistemas, racks e trocadores de calor de porta traseira (RDHx) certificados como Open Compute Project Accepted(TM). Com o suporte do DCBBS, o portfólio de soluções pode ser incorporado em implantações completas de ponta a ponta, em escala de rack e cluster. “O boom da IA redefine a forma como os data centers são projetados, construídos e implementados, e a Supermicro lidera essa transformação com o DCBBS”, disse Charles Liang, presidente e CEO da Supermicro. “Ao integrar computação, redes, energia, refrigeração avançada, software e serviços em soluções validadas em escala de rack, ajudamos os clientes a simplificar a complexidade e acelerar o caminho da inovação até a produção. O DCBBS possibilita que os clientes reduzam o TTM e o TTO ao oferecer infraestrutura essencial de IA de forma mais rápida e eficiente.” As soluções OCP da Supermicro já estão disponíveis; clique aqui para saber mais. Ao aproveitar as melhores práticas da comunidade OCP e o design e serviços do DCBBS, os operadores de data centers podem aumentar a densidade de computação e a eficiência energética para cargas de trabalho de IA e HPC com base em uma infraestrutura aberta e validada em escala de rack — desde sistemas e barras de distribuição até o resfriamento em nível de rack e de data centers — para implementar soluções de alta densidade de forma mais eficiente e acelerar o tempo de lançamento no mercado (TTM) e o tempo de operação (TTO). “Os clientes precisam de uma infraestrutura aberta e flexível que possa ser dimensionada de acordo com as demandas em rápida evolução da IA, ao mesmo tempo que se adapte à realidade de seus data centers”, disse Dirk Van Slyke, vice-presidente de Marketing da OCP. “Ao reunir sistemas, racks, energia e refrigeração aceitos pelo OCP em soluções validadas em escala de rack, a Supermicro ajuda os clientes a simplificar a integração, maximizar a capacidade e a eficiência das instalações e acelerar a implantação da infraestrutura de IA de produção.” Os racks ORv3 e ORW substituem as fontes de alimentação e os cabos individuais por servidor por uma barra de distribuição CC centralizada de 48 V, permitindo que os clientes otimizem seus sistemas de CPU e GPU para racks de computação de maior densidade. Essa densidade é ainda mais reforçada pelo sistema de resfriamento líquido DLC-2 Direct-to-Chip da Supermicro, que remove o calor de forma mais eficiente de CPUs, GPUs e outros componentes críticos, enquanto o calor residual pode ser removido do rack por meio de unidades de resfriamento ORv3 RDHx especialmente desenvolvidas, sem a necessidade de adaptações adicionais nos sistemas de ar-condicionado do data center. As unidades RDHx da Supermicro podem ser montadas na parte traseira de racks ORv3 e ORW, removendo o calor residual do ar de exaustão dos servidores antes que ele entre na sala do data center. O portfólio abrange capacidades de refrigeração de 10 kW a 120 kW, oferecendo aos operadores uma maneira prática de aumentar a densidade de racks tanto em novas instalações de IA quanto em data centers existentes. Os modelos alimentados por corrente contínua conectam-se à barra de distribuição do rack para reduzir a quantidade de cabos, enquanto os designs incluem ventiladores redundantes N+1 para garantir o tempo de atividade e um sistema anticondensação inteligente para evitar danos causados pela umidade a outros componentes dentro do rack. Os operadores podem monitorar e gerenciar todo o portfólio de componentes DCBBS, por meio do SuperCloud Composer®, utilizando protocolos padrão do setor. Além disso, os softwares da Supermicro, como o SuperCloud Director, o SuperCloud Automation Assistant e o SuperCloud Developer Console, possibilitam que as empresas gerenciem e operacionalizem todos os aspectos das modernas fábricas de IA, centros de dados corporativos e infraestrutura NeoCloud, por meio de uma solução unificada de controle de software. Como parte do portfólio do DCBBS, a Supermicro também oferece um portfólio abrangente de soluções de rede para IA, que variam de switches Ethernet 800G e 1.6T com refrigeração a ar ou líquida, incluindo plataformas Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) de última geração baseadas no silício de comutação Broadcom Tomahawk 6, otimizadas para racks EIA ou ORv3. O sistema operacional de rede SONiC Advanced da Supermicro Enterprise oferece aos clientes a flexibilidade de selecionar a arquitetura de rede que melhor atenda às suas necessidades de desempenho, energia, escalabilidade e implantação, à medida que a IA e os ambientes de data center de grande escala continuam a evoluir. artigo.texto: Hanoi (VNA) - Vietnam is moving to link green credit with its carbon market, a step expected to free up additional funding for the green transition and give banks a firmer basis to assess and manage capital flows to emissions-reduction projects. The issue was among those discussed at a seminar in Hanoi on October 14, co-hosted by Tai chinh – Dau tu (Finance and Investment) newspaper and the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV). Green credit lays groundwork for carbon market In his opening speech, Pham Van Hoanh, the newspaper’s Editor-in-Chief, said Vietnam is progressively finalising policies on green growth and its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050. The domestic carbon market began a pilot on June 29, 2026, raising the need to deepen links among green credit, banking system and new financial instruments. SBV Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh said meeting the 2050 net-zero pledge will require enormous resources for technological innovation, production overhaul, energy efficiency and emissions cuts. Alongside the State budget and capital and monetary markets, the carbon market is an important mechanism to raise additional funds, he said. The Government issued Decree 29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange on January 29, setting the legal framework for the market and trading greenhouse gas emission allowances and carbon credits. The pilot market was launched with more than 511 million metric tonnes of CO₂ in allowances, allocated to facilities in three emissions-intensive sectors for 2025-2026, including thermal power, iron and steel, and cement. The pilot runs through the end of 2028, with full mandatory operation starting in 2029. Canh said green credit funds the projects, technologies and sectors that deliver emissions cuts, while the carbon market can turn those cuts into economic value. If it works well, the market can generate extra revenue and cash flow, improving credit quality and helping companies meet environmental standards for exports. Outstanding green credit across the banking system topped 856 trillion VND (32.9 billion USD) at the end of June 2026, up 9.87% from end-2025. From 2017 to 2025, green credit grew by more than 20% a year on average, focusing on agriculture, forestry, fisheries, biodiversity and green energy. Proposal to connect carbon value chain Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Agribank Training School and deputy head of its ESG team, said the issue isn’t whether banks directly trade carbon credits. What matters is how they finance the creation of emissions reductions, and when carbon value becomes reliable enough to factor into lending decisions. Agribank said financing needs emerge before any credits exist. Projects pass through preparation, investment, operation, measurement, reporting and verification (MRV), credit issuance, trading and settlement. That gap gives banks room to offer credit, bridge financing, cash flow management, guarantees and blended finance. The lender proposed drawing clear lines among emissions-reduction potential, registered projects, verified results, issued credits, carbon-credit sales contracts and proceeds already collected. Each carries a different level of certainty and can’t automatically be treated as the same source of debt repayment. Agribank identified five roles for banks in the carbon ecosystem, including financing emissions-reduction activities, linking stakeholders across the value chain, providing payment and cash-flow services, pooling climate finance, and supporting companies and individuals through the transition. As an immediate step, it proposed a framework for identifying emissions-reduction projects and a set of criteria for assessing carbon-related credit. It suggested piloting value chains where emissions can be clearly gauged, such as low-emission rice, livestock and biogas, sustainable forestry, waste treatment and biomass energy. Banks also need to build partner networks, train interdisciplinary staff and strengthen data and governance systems. Agribank plans to focus on data, capacity, partnerships and pilot models in 2026-2028, scale up in 2029-2032 as the domestic market becomes more stable, and study products based on carbon-related cash flows or receivables from 2033. To support market growth, Agribank recommended clarifying ownership, disposition rights and benefit-sharing for emissions-reduction results and carbon credits, and completing rules on receivables, collateral, accounting, taxation and foreign exchange. It also called for treating data and MRV systems as market infrastructure, cutting verification costs, developing supply and demand together, and applying blended finance and risk-sharing mechanisms. Canh said an effective carbon market lets companies convert emissions cuts into financial resources of their own, which could ease pressure on green credit. Rather than relying mainly on their own capital, State funding or bank loans to finance the transition, firms gain greater capacity to generate funds from their own emissions reductions./.

artigo.texto: Fundo para provedores de internet: proximidade com data centers (thinkstock) Editor de Invest Publicado em 15 de outubro de 2026 às 05h00. O provedor de internet de uma cidade do interior paulista tem uma receita relativamente previsível, já que milhares de clientes pagam a mensalidade todo mês. O que costuma faltar é crédito para crescer. É nesse espaço que a Möbius Capital e a Desenvolve SP querem atuar com um fundo de R$ 70 milhões dedicado a provedores regionais de internet e a data centers de pequeno porte no estado. O veículo é um FIDC (Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios), estrutura que investe em valores que as empresas têm a receber. Na prática, o fundo poderá adiantar ao provedor o dinheiro das mensalidades pagas por seus clientes, sejam pessoas físicas ou empresas. Também poderá financiar a compra de equipamentos e operações de expansão, incluindo a compra ou a fusão de empresas. Esse último ponto conversa com o momento do setor. O mercado de provedores regionais passa por um movimento de consolidação, em que empresas maiores compram concorrentes menores, e esse tipo de operação depende de capital. A Desenvolve SP é a agência de fomento do governo do Estado de São Paulo. Funciona como um banco público estadual, que empresta dinheiro a empresas paulistas, sobretudo pequenas e médias, para estimular a economia do estado. Além do crédito direto, a agência também investe em fundos administrados por gestoras privadas, selecionadas por meio de chamadas públicas. Foi assim que a Möbius chegou ao negócio. A gestora apresentou a proposta na chamada da Desenvolve SP para FIDCs e FIPs, passou por análise de elegibilidade, apresentação presencial e due diligence, e teve o investimento aprovado pelo comitê da agência. A Desenvolve SP subscreveu R$ 50 milhões em cotas seniores, que têm prioridade para receber os pagamentos. A Möbius ficou com R$ 20 milhões em cotas subordinadas, que só recebem depois das seniores e são as primeiras a absorver eventuais calotes. Se alguma operação der errado, o prejuízo bate antes no bolso da gestora. "Nossa meta é ampliar o acesso ao crédito e facilitar recursos para negócios inovadores. Por meio do blended finance, conseguimos atrair investimento privado, potencializar o impacto do recurso público e alcançar mais empreendedores", afirma Ricardo Brito, diretor-presidente da Desenvolve SP, em comunicado. O termo blended finance se refere à combinação de dinheiro público e privado num mesmo investimento. A aposta é que cidades do interior com baixa penetração de internet ganhem conectividade e acesso mais próximo a data centers, o que tende a ajudar empresas locais a ganhar produtividade. A Möbius atua há cerca de cinco anos com infraestrutura digital. "Temos um histórico de realizar financiamento para aquisições de provedores de internet, operações via mercado de capitais para fomentar o crescimento de empresas do setor, além de dar apoio no avanço da profissionalização e governança dessas companhias", diz Roberto Savaris, sócio e fundador da gestora. A Möbius foi fundada por ex-executivos do Credit Suisse e reúne cerca de R$ 1 bilhão entre capital comprometido e investido. A casa também está em captação de um novo fundo de crédito estruturado, com meta de até R$ 1 bilhão, que combina crédito privado, precatórios e compra de fazendas na mesma cota.

artigo.texto: Iowa residents raise health and environmental concerns over data center expansion Advocacy groups and residents are raising concerns about the potential health and environmental impacts of Iowa's expanding data center industry, which relies on increased fossil fuel use. Brian Campbell, executive director of Physicians for Social Responsibility, spoke during a briefing hosted by The Sierra Club, addressing the potential risks for communities near these facilities. "We know that these fossil fuel-combusting electricity-generating plants lead to and increase toxic air pollution," Campbell said. "These exacerbate the incidence of asthma, heart attacks, cognitive decline, certain cancers, adverse birth outcomes and premature death." Earlier this week, residents in Woodward learned about a proposed 600-acre data center. Many expressed concerns about the project's timeline and its potential environmental impact. The Sierra Club Iowa Chapter has stated that it seeks to provide more information about such projects to help Iowans better understand their implications.

artigo.texto: Badland Batteries has officially opened a new 80,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing facility in Fargo, North Dakota, expanding domestic production capabilities for unmanned aircraft systems, defense platforms, robotics and other autonomous technologies. The Badland Batteries manufacturing facility, which celebrated its grand opening on October 8, 2026, represents an investment in rebuilding the U.S. battery supply chain and reducing dependence on overseas manufacturers for critical energy storage technologies. The facility combines automated and operator-controlled manufacturing equipment to produce lithium-ion pouch cells, with the capacity to manufacture more than 15,000 battery cells per day as production scales. Badland Batteries Manufacturing Facility Opens in North Dakota The new Fargo facility is designed to manufacture lithium-ion pouch battery cells for defense, aerospace and autonomous systems applications. The 80,000-square-foot plant incorporates a combination of automated manufacturing processes and equipment operated by personnel. According to Badland Batteries, the facility is intended to support domestic battery production while providing greater control over materials, manufacturing quality and supply chain traceability. “Opening this facility marks an important step forward in building a secure and resilient battery supply chain here in the United States,” said Terri Zimmerman, CEO of Badland Batteries and Packet Digital. “Simply put, we believe that America should build its own batteries, and this facility represents years of work towards that goal and demonstrates our unwavering commitment to supporting our nation’s defense.” New Facility Targets Drone and Autonomous Systems Batteries The manufacturing operation is focused on producing battery cells for technologies that require reliable and domestically sourced power systems. Target applications include: - Unmanned aircraft systems - Military and defense platforms - Autonomous vehicles - Robotics - Aerospace technologies - Commercial autonomous systems Battery technology is a critical component of electric unmanned aircraft, affecting flight endurance, payload capacity and operational reliability. Badland Batteries is positioning its domestic production capabilities to support growing demand from U.S. defense and commercial customers. “These battery cells will help power today’s and tomorrow’s cutting-edge autonomous and UAS systems, which are critical to our nation’s security,” Zimmerman said. Domestic Battery Supply Chain Reduces Foreign Dependence According to Badland Batteries, more than 80% of batteries and critical materials used in autonomous systems are manufactured overseas. The company identifies this dependence as a significant supply chain vulnerability for U.S. defense and advanced technology programs. Badland Batteries describes its Fargo operation as the first UAS-specific battery manufacturing facility designed to control the complete manufacturing process, beginning with raw material sourcing and qualification. The company plans to use domestic or allied-sourced raw materials with full traceability. This approach is intended to strengthen supply chain security while giving customers greater visibility into the origins and production of critical battery components. Integrated Battery Cell and Pack Manufacturing The new facility will handle lithium-ion pouch cell production, beginning with raw material sourcing and in-house material qualification. Once cells are manufactured, they can be transported to Badland Batteries’ existing manufacturing and assembly facility located approximately one mile away. That second facility provides the capability to assemble completed cells into customer-ready battery packs. The combined operations create a manufacturing workflow covering: - Raw material sourcing - Material qualification - Lithium-ion cell production - Battery cell manufacturing - Battery pack assembly - Customer-ready power systems The company said this integrated approach is intended to provide a reliable domestic source of batteries for UAS and other autonomous platforms. Production Capacity Exceeds 15,000 Battery Cells Per Day Badland Batteries said the new facility has the ability to produce more than 15,000 lithium-ion battery cells per day. The company also designed the manufacturing operation with the flexibility to increase production as demand grows. The announced figure represents the facility’s production capacity rather than a confirmed current daily output. Actual production volumes, battery cell specifications and customer delivery schedules were not disclosed in the announcement. The manufacturing capacity is intended to support growing demand for domestically produced energy storage technologies across defense, aerospace and autonomous systems markets. Federal Investment Supports North Dakota Battery Industry The facility opening brought together federal, state, local, industry and military representatives. U.S. Senator John Hoeven highlighted the importance of domestic battery manufacturing for national security and economic competitiveness. “Building a strong domestic battery ecosystem is critical to our nation’s economic competitiveness and national security,” Hoeven said. “That’s why we’ve worked over the last six years to secure more than $50 million in federal funding to advance these efforts in North Dakota.” Hoeven said the Badland Batteries investment supports efforts to expand American manufacturing, create skilled employment opportunities and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The announcement does not specify how much of the referenced federal funding was awarded directly to Badland Batteries. artigo.texto: As data center rumors swirl, Livingston Parish President meets with battery storage company NextEra has fueled data center speculation with battery storage facility planned for parish LIVINGSTON PARISH, La. — Livingston Parish President Randy Delatte said he met with representatives from NextEra Energy as the company explores building a battery storage facility in the parish. The energy capacity of the proposed facility has fueled speculation of a possible data center development in the parish. Delatte said NextEra officials are in the parish meeting with government and business leaders. The company has filed with MISO, the Midcontinent Independent System Operator that oversees the power grid in 15 states including Louisiana, and is exploring several sites statewide. “We will be monitoring their progress in Livingston and will keep you informed,” Delatte said. No project has been finalized. Permitting records describe NextEra’s proposed 500-megawatt facility as intended to power an unnamed commercial development. That language has fueled speculation about a possible data center tied to a 690-acre site off Buddy Ellis Road, which was rezoned from residential to industrial in November 2025. Livingston Parish’s Economic Development Council (LEDC) told WAFB that plot of land is not a part of the properties it has been marketing to the state for possible large industrial developments. Delatte has previously said a facility of that size could support a data center. “I would wanna say, without starting a rumor, it would need that much power to power a data plant and more,” Delatte said. “I wanna approach this the right way, but if NextEra comes down here, then that’s smoke; where there’s smoke, there’s fire.” Delatte said he has not signed any non-disclosure agreements related to the project, citing transparency. Councilman Ricky Goff has said he did sign a confidentiality agreement tied to the rezoned site on Buddy Ellis Road. Residents near Buddy Ellis Road have raised concerns about water use, noise and property values. Delatte said any tenant would need parish approval and vowed no project will move forward with an adverse impact on residents. What is MISO and why does the filing matter? MISO — the Midcontinent Independent System Operator — manages the power grid across 15 states, including Louisiana. Energy companies like NextEra must file with MISO to connect large projects to the grid and study impacts on reliability. A MISO filing does not mean a project is approved or finalized. It is an early step in the permitting process that signals where the company is exploring development. NextEra is exploring multiple sites statewide, according to Delatte. artigo.texto: Imagine que você liga para o seu mecânico e fala: “o carro não pegou hoje de manhã, deve ser a bateria”. Em vez de concordar, ele responde com uma pergunta: “como você usa o carro durante a semana?”. Você estranha. Afinal, o que o seu trajeto até o trabalho tem a ver com um carro que não liga? Tem tudo a ver, e é isso que vamos traduzir hoje. Olá, queridos e queridas! Segunda-feira, 7h40, você gira a chave (ou aperta o botão) e o carro faz um “rrr... rrr...” sem vontade, ou nem isso. O painel acende fraco, o rádio reinicia, e vem o veredicto de sempre: “a bateria morreu do nada”. Mas ontem estava tudo certo, não estava? Bateria quase nunca morre do nada. Leia também - Troca de óleo a cada 10 mil km é regra ou é lenda? - Tudo sobre a gasolina E35: separando fato de boato antes que você acredite em qualquer coisa O que costuma acontecer é que ela vinha avisando e ninguém traduziu. E, em muitos casos, ela nem é a culpada: é só a vítima. Para entender isso, é preciso saber o que ela faz. A bateria não guarda eletricidade; ela guarda energia química, uma reação entre os componentes internos que se converte em energia elétrica na hora que o carro pede. Na partida, ela entrega muita corrente em poucos segundos para o motor de arranque. Mas o trabalho não acaba aí: com o motor desligado, é ela que mantém alarme, memórias e módulos vivos, e com o motor ligado ela ajuda a estabilizar a tensão do sistema elétrico. Quem a recarrega é o alternador. Pense na bateria como a caixa d’água da casa e no alternador como a bomba que a enche. Se a caixa estiver furada, você enche e ela esvazia. Se a bomba estiver fraca, a caixa nunca enche direito. Trocar a caixa d’água quando o problema é a bomba só garante uma caixa nova que nunca enche. E quanto tempo dura uma bateria? Não existe prazo universal, e desconfie de quem prometeu um. Trajetos curtos e frequentes não dão tempo de o carro repor a energia gasta na partida, então a conta nunca fecha. Carro parado por semanas vai se descarregando sozinho. O calor castiga a estrutura interna, e o frio exige mais dela na hora da partida. Um carro cheio de demanda elétrica (multimídia, câmeras, acessórios instalados depois) pede mais da bateria do que um carro simples. Dois veículos iguais, com donos e rotinas diferentes, podem ter vidas de bateria bem diferentes. É por isso que o mecânico perguntou do seu trajeto. Os avisos costumam aparecer antes da falha. Partida mais lenta que o normal, principalmente de manhã ou depois de alguns dias parado. Carro que “acorda cansado” depois de um período sem uso. Luzes que enfraquecem na partida, vidros mais lentos, multimídia reiniciando sozinho. Em carros com Start-Stop, o sistema deixar de atuar ou atuar de um jeito estranho também pode ser sinal, já que ele depende de condições da bateria para funcionar. Mas atenção: sintoma não é diagnóstico. Cada um desses sinais pode ter outra origem, e quem fecha a conta é o teste, não o palpite. Aliás, uma frase que ouço muito na oficina é “medi com o multímetro e a tensão está boa”. Medir só a tensão é como medir a temperatura de uma pessoa e concluir que ela está em forma para correr uma maratona. A tensão em repouso mostra quanto de carga a bateria tem naquele momento, mas não mostra se ela aguenta o esforço da partida. Uma bateria desgastada pode marcar uma tensão aceitável parada e não sustentar a corrente quando é exigida. O que revela a condição real é um teste apropriado, com equipamento próprio. E o teste não termina nela: é preciso avaliar o sistema de carga, ou seja, se o alternador está carregando como deveria com o motor funcionando. Outro engano comum é achar que bateria é tudo igual. Não é. A convencional é a mais simples e atende carros sem muita exigência. A EFB é uma evolução desse conceito, pensada para suportar melhor o ciclo de muitas partidas e paradas, comum em carros com Start-Stop mais básico. A AGM tem outra construção interna, é mais robusta em ciclos de carga e descarga e costuma ser exigida em carros com sistemas mais exigentes. Qual delas o seu carro precisa depende do projeto, e o lugar para descobrir é o manual do proprietário e a especificação do fabricante. Trocar por uma tecnologia inferior à exigida, só para economizar, é uma aposta bem ruim. E mesmo dentro da tecnologia certa, duas baterias de 60 Ah não são necessariamente iguais. O Ah indica a capacidade, ou seja, quanta energia ela armazena. Mas existem ainda a corrente de partida a frio (CCA), as dimensões, a posição dos pólos e as exigências do fabricante. É como dois tênis número 40: o número é o mesmo, mas um é de corrida e o outro é de passeio. Há ainda um detalhe que pouca gente conta: em alguns veículos, principalmente os com gerenciamento eletrônico de energia, a troca pode exigir registro da nova bateria ou algum procedimento específico. Isso não vale para todo carro, e é justamente por isso que vale perguntar antes de sair da oficina: “o meu exige algo depois da troca?”. Já a chupeta, quando bate à pressa, parece a solução óbvia. Mas improvisar pode gerar faísca, inversão de polaridade e danos a módulos eletrônicos. Muitos manuais trazem orientações próprias ou até pontos específicos para partida auxiliar. Se for fazer, faça como o fabricante prevê. E se você trocou a bateria e, meses depois, o problema voltou? Antes de culpar a bateria nova, vale investigar o resto. O alternador está carregando bem? Existe alguma fuga de corrente, algo consumindo energia com o carro desligado? E o seu jeito de usar o carro combina com a bateria que foi escolhida? Voltando à ligação para o mecânico: a pergunta dele sobre o seu trajeto não era conversa fiada, era o início do diagnóstico. Ele queria saber se a bateria está ruim, se ela é a certa para o seu carro e se o sistema que a mantém carregada está funcionando. São exatamente as três perguntas que você deve levar para a oficina. E no fim das contas, quem faz essas perguntas deixa de ser refém daquela frase “troca que resolve”. Pergunte antes de pagar.
