artigo.texto: EnOcean Pioneer in self-powered wireless standard According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Free Sensors market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Battery Free Sensors market is entering a decisive phase of commercial scale-up, moving from niche, cost-insensitive deployments toward core enablement of low-maintenance monitoring across energy storage and renewable integration systems. The central demand driver is predictive maintenance for battery energy storage systems (BESS), where conventional battery-powered sensors impose recurring replacement labor, downtime, and hazardous-waste liabilities over 20-30 year asset lives. Battery-free sensors that harvest ambient RF, thermal, kinetic, or solar energy eliminate those costs and unlock continuous condition monitoring at scale. Demand is bifurcating between high-reliability nodes for mission-critical grid and industrial assets and ultra-low-cost, high-volume nodes for distributed environmental and condition monitoring across vast renewable fleets. Adoption is not a simple sensor swap: it requires re-architecting data acquisition networks, affecting gateway placement, communication protocols, and backend analytics, which locks in system integrators and controls providers as key channel gatekeepers. Supply chain maturity is uneven, with energy harvesting components and ultra-low-power ASICs facing scale and performance constraints, while mechanical vibration harvesters remain application-specific. Project economics are dominated by total cost of ownership, where eliminated battery replacement labor, downtime, and disposal justify a significant upfront premium. Competitive advantage is shifting from component performance to system integration expertise and software analytics, as value migrates from data collection to predictive maintenance and operational optimization. Regulatory and standards bodies are beginning to formalize maintenance-free monitoring requirements in safety-critical applications, creating compliance-driven demand pull in regulated utility and industrial segments. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market through 2035, covering deployment use cases, buyer environments, upstream dependencies, qualification requirements, pricing architecture, and country capability differences. The baseline scenario for the Battery Free Sensors market through 2035 assumes continued acceleration of renewable capacity additions and grid modernization, with BESS deployments growing at a double-digit pace in most regions. Under this scenario, battery-free sensor demand is forecast to expand at a 14.2% CAGR from 2026 to 2035, lifting the market index to 380 by 2035 (2025=100). The strongest demand pull comes from predictive maintenance for BESS, where operators face mounting pressure to reduce OPEX and safety liabilities associated with battery-powered sensor replacement in hard-to-access or hazardous installations. As BESS asset fleets age, the labor and downtime costs of conventional sensor maintenance compound, making the total cost of ownership case for battery-free sensors increasingly compelling. Adoption will be fastest in utility-scale energy storage and commercial and industrial backup power, where asset criticality and maintenance access constraints are most acute. The commercial and industrial segment will also benefit from tightening functional safety standards and insurance requirements that favor maintenance-free monitoring. Supply-side constraints, particularly specialized low-power PMIC design and fabrication capacity, will moderate growth in price-sensitive, high-volume applications, but will not derail the overall trajectory. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will lead in volume terms, supported by China's dominance in BESS manufacturing and deployment, while North America and Europe will drive value growth through higher qualification and safety requirements. Latin America and the Middle East and Africa will remain smaller but fast-growing markets, underpinned by utility-scale solar and storage tenders. Key risks to the baseline include slower-than-expected BESS deployment, delays in standards formalization, and persistent cost premiums that slow adoption in cost-sensitive segments. However, the structural drivers of maintenance-free monitoring, digitalization of asset management, and the imperative to reduce hazardous waste from battery disposal are expected to keep the market on a strong upward path through 2035. Utility-scale energy storage is the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for battery-free sensors, primarily driven by predictive maintenance for battery energy storage systems (BESS). As grid operators and utilities deploy massive BESS fleets to integrate renewable energy and provide grid services, the challenge of monitoring thousands of battery modules, thermal management systems, and power conversion equipment becomes acute. Conventional battery-powered sensors require periodic replacement, which is costly and disruptive in high-voltage, hard-to-access installations. Battery-free sensors that harvest ambient RF, thermal, or kinetic energy enable continuous monitoring of cell voltage, temperature, vibration, and state of health without maintenance. Through 2035, demand will be propelled by the need to reduce OPEX, enhance safety, and extend asset life. Key demand-side indicators include BESS capacity additions, average asset age, maintenance cost per sensor, and regulatory requirements for safety monitoring. The sector will increasingly favor sensors integrated with analytics platforms that predict failures before they occur, shifting value from hardware to software and services. artigo.texto: Data Centers (KM Stock/Shutterstock) Publicado em 13 de outubro de 2026 às 21h10. A recente sanção da Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), colocou a infraestrutura digital brasileira no centro da agenda econômica no país. Mas, para além de criar um regime tributário para um setor específico, o Redata oferece a oportunidade de aproximar duas agendas que ainda são frequentemente tratadas de maneira separada: o aumento da capacidade de processamento de dados em território brasileiro e o fortalecimento de uma cadeia industrial para tornar essa expansão possível. Data centers são infraestruturas de engenharia de alta complexidade, cujos efeitos ultrapassam o setor de tecnologia, mobilizando verticais estratégicas como energia, construção civil, telecomunicações e serviços especializados. Dentro deles existem muito mais do que servidores de processamento: são utilizados sistemas elétricos, transformadores, painéis e equipamentos de distribuição, UPS, barramentos, sistemas de refrigeração de alta eficiência, automação, controle, cabos, estruturas metálicas e uma extensa cadeia de serviços especializados para instalação e manutenção desses equipamentos. Isso significa que cada novo megawatt de capacidade de data center no país representa também uma nova demanda para uma cadeia física e industrial - muito maior do que normalmente aparece quando se discute economia digital. Cada novo projeto impulsiona a procura por equipamentos, sistemas, engenharia e serviços, fomenta a criação de postos de trabalho e acelera a necessidade de habilidades verdes (green skills) e qualificações técnicas em pilares essenciais para sustentar o avanço da inteligência artificial (IA). Um estudo da FGV Projetos, utilizando a Matriz Insumo-Produto do IBGE, ajuda a dimensionar esse potencial. Para cada R$ 1 de demanda final associada ao setor de data centers é gerado R$ 1,45 em valor de produção na economia, considerando desdobramentos diretos e indiretos. Outro dado é ainda mais relevante para a discussão industrial: R$ 1,16 desse resultado ocorre por meio da ativação da cadeia de fornecedores. O mesmo encadeamento aparece na geração de empregos. Para cada R$ 1 milhão investido, a FGV estima cerca de 7,5 empregos diretos e indiretos, incluindo aqueles originados na cadeia de fornecedores. Esses números contribuem para tangibilizar o fato de que parcela expressiva do impacto econômico de um data center acontece do lado de fora e, quanto maior a participação de fornecedores instalados no país, maior tende a ser a parcela do investimento que permanece e se multiplica dentro da economia nacional. Da mesma forma, quanto maior e mais previsível for a demanda doméstica por data centers, maior será a possibilidade de ampliar a escala, a produtividade e a competitividade da nossa indústria, assegurando novas linhas de produção, investimentos em capacidade produtiva, desenvolvimento tecnológico e qualificação de fornecedores. Estamos falando, portanto, de uma relação de interdependência, na qual data centers competitivos necessitam de uma indústria forte e competitiva, e uma indústria apta a competir globalmente precisa de mercados que gerem escala e demanda tecnológica. Por isso, o debate sobre o desenvolvimento dos data centers no Brasil não pode correr o risco de ser limitado a uma escolha entre “incentivo ao investimento estrangeiro” ou “proteção da indústria nacional”. Essa é uma abordagem míope que apequena uma lógica de ecossistema a uma falsa dicotomia. O que a experiência internacional e a dinâmica dos mercados mostram é que é factível atrair capital, tecnologia e capacidade computacional e, ao mesmo tempo, tracionar nossa cadeia de fornecedores, engenharia, inovação e produção nacional. Isso não implica pressupor que todos os componentes necessários à infraestrutura digital devam ser manufaturados no país – aliás, nenhuma grande economia é autossuficiente na cadeia de infraestrutura digital. Com isso, o desafio de uma política industrial moderna é combinar o acesso competitivo às tecnologias que ainda não produzidas localmente com condições para que a indústria brasileira consolide sua participação à medida em que o mercado doméstico ganha escala. A primeira premissa para a concretização desse cenário, porém, é que novos projetos sejam viabilizados. É neste ponto que reside a importância da regulamentação do Redata e da aprovação do convênio nacional, no âmbito do Confaz, para reduzir o ICMS sobre alguns equipamentos específicos. Afinal, se a infraestrutura brasileira continuar mais cara do que a de mercados concorrentes – e atualmente o custo econômico para um data center no Brasil é 26,7% maior do que nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo – o país perde competitividade na disputa global por esses investimentos. Quando um projeto de infraestrutura digital é alocado em outro mercado, ele leva consigo a demanda que poderia alavancar a indústria local - sem mencionar as atividades econômicas habilitadas na cadeia downstream, que dependem de capacidade computacional, nuvem e IA. Por isso, desenvolvedores de data centers e fabricantes nacionais estão olhando para o mesmo horizonte. Ambos dependem de um ecossistema competitivo, capaz de atrair investimentos, estimular demanda, desenvolver tecnologia e incrementar a produção local. É nessa articulação entre políticas públicas, investimentos privados e indústria de alta eficiência que o tamanho da participação brasileira na nova economia global será definido. *Rafael Segrera é presidente da Schneider Electric para a América do Sul e líder do grupo de trabalho "Fostering Human and Social Development", da Sustainable Business COP (SB COP) *Luciano Fialho é vice-presidente Sênior de Desenvolvimento Corporativo, Energia e Imóveis da Scala Data Centers

artigo.texto: Um ataque com drones ucranianos atingiu o centro de dados principal da Yandex em Vladimir, na Rússia, na manhã de 11 de outubro, forçando a suspensão temporária das operações e interrompendo mais de 80 serviços digitais. Segundo os dados avançados pelo Vietnam.vn, a investida afetou desde aplicações de consumo e ferramentas de inteligência artificial até à infraestrutura corporativa em nuvem da empresa. Terceiro ataque à infraestrutura do gigante tecnológico Este incidente representa o terceiro ataque direcionado aos servidores da multinacional russa num intervalo de apenas quatro dias. A vaga de investidas começou a 8 de outubro com uma ação contra um centro de dados em Sasovo, na região de Ryazan, que provocou um incêndio e obrigou ao encerramento total da infraestrutura responsável por suportar serviços da rede ferroviária russa (RZhD), da operadora MegaFon e de vários órgãos de comunicação social. No dia seguinte, a 9 de outubro, outra instalação em Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscovo, foi visada, tendo a Yandex confirmado a desativação de múltiplos módulos de hardware. O complexo de Vladimir, visado na ação mais recente, foi projetado para albergar até 2.880 racks de servidores, constituindo um dos polos centrais de processamento do grupo. Serviços afetados e impacto na rede elétrica A interrupção no centro de Vladimir provocou falhas imediatas em várias aplicações de consumo, incluindo a assistente de voz Alice, o Yandex Music, a plataforma de videoconferência Telemost e os sistemas de domótica Yandex Smart Home. No setor empresarial, a plataforma Yandex Cloud registou quebras nos serviços de computação, armazenamento e bases de dados, afetando soluções como Compute Cloud, Object Storage, Managed Kubernetes, PostgreSQL e ClickHouse. As ferramentas de IA da empresa, como a API YandexGPT, o SpeechKit e o Vision OCR, também ficaram inoperacionais. O impacto estendeu-se a plataformas de comércio eletrónico, instituições bancárias, serviços de transporte por aplicação e cadeias de retalho na Rússia e em países vizinhos. Em paralelo, a autarquia de Vladimir confirmou que os ataques danificaram subestações locais e provocaram um corte geral de eletricidade, embora cerca de 80% do fornecimento tenha sido restabelecido durante a manhã. O Ministério da Defesa russo declarou ter intercetado 479 drones em 16 regiões, ao passo que analistas militares apontam que a degradação continuada destas infraestruturas visa comprometer a logística, a governação e as capacidades de comando digital do país.

artigo.texto: Open specs could cut AI data center hardware integration from a year to months As AI factories scale, hardware interoperability is becoming as important as raw performance. Accelerators, memory and storage now come from many different suppliers, and every mismatch between them slows deployment across the data center. Pressure is mounting as AI infrastructure bottlenecks shift attention from individual chips to entire systems. Open communities such as the Open Compute Project, or OCP, integrate separately developed technologies, from Peripheral Component Interconnect Express to Compute Express Link, or CXL, into complete systems that many suppliers can build, according to Siamak Tavallaei (pictured), senior principal engineer at Samsung Semiconductor, a unit of Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. “There are different companies skilled in different aspects of the problem. And you would like to, as an integrator, as an open industry … take advantage of all of that,” Tavallaei said. “Therefore, interoperability matters a lot.” Tavallaei spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at the AI Data Pipeline Forum, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why open specifications matter for hardware interoperability and how they can shorten the time it takes hyperscalers to adopt new designs. (* Disclosure below.) Why hardware interoperability depends on open integration Tavallaei’s work with OCP traces back to his time at Microsoft Corp.’s Azure cloud, where he co-led OCP’s server project. Large cloud operators kept asking suppliers to build the same hardware, but each supplier read the specification differently, so server fleets drifted apart, he explained. “Software was what Microsoft was doing well, but we wanted hardware to be common so a number of our suppliers could build the same thing,” Tavallaei said. A finished system handed to OCP as a monolithic contribution may never catch on, while one shaped in the open draws input from many companies, according to Tavallaei. That broader buy-in brings volume and more engineers working on the same problems. “If you were to work that with the community, different people will interject their own ideas, and at the end, story will be something that a number of different companies would like, and therefore adoption goes up,” Tavallaei said. “When adoption goes up, volume goes up.” Memory is the next proving ground. Samsung recently demonstrated CXL memory pooling with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. at the OCP summit, and Tavallaei is bringing the CXL specification into OCP’s Composable Memory Systems subproject. The bet is that hardware interoperability will sharply cut the time hyperscalers need to adopt new designs. “When a specific thing is built for, for example, one hyperscaler, a different hyperscaler trying to reintegrate that takes time, about nine months, 12 months of reintegrating,” Tavallaei said. “Whereas if things are crisply defined in a specification, when something is good and is recognized, integrating that into a new hyperscale data center might take three months or six months instead of a year or year and a half.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Data Pipeline Forum: (* Disclosure: ScaleFlux Inc. sponsored this segment of theCUBE. artigo.texto: Amwins Global Risks (AGR), the specialist global risk division of Amwins, has broadened the scope of its Commercial & Industrial (C&I) insurance facility to include battery energy storage systems (BESS) and electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure. The expanded facility enables developers, owners and investors to insure multiple distributed energy assets across different locations under one insurance programme. AGR said the updated offering is intended to meet the needs of businesses developing portfolios of smaller energy infrastructure projects, which may be spread across several sites but form part of a larger investment. “The expansion is designed to support the growing deployment of distributed energy infrastructure, where individual assets may be relatively small, and geographically dispersed, but collectively represent increasingly substantial portfolios for developers, owners and investors,” commented Dr Tom Harries, Director at Amwins Global Risks. “By aggregating assets within a portfolio, AGR provides a consistent underwriting approach across multiple locations while assessing and managing accumulated natural catastrophe exposure at portfolio level.” The facility will provide insurance options for the construction of EV charging infrastructure in the United States, as well as cover for assets once they are operational. AGR said protection can include Delay in Start-Up (DSU) and Business Interruption (BI), addressing risks that may affect project completion or interrupt business activities. The structure also allows deductibles to be adjusted to reflect the size and risk profile of individual installations. According to AGR, this offers an alternative to insurance arrangements developed for utility-scale projects, under which deductibles may be less suited to smaller assets. AGR said the growth of distributed energy infrastructure has created insurance requirements that do not always fit established models. While traditional cover has often focused on individual projects or large-scale energy developments, battery storage facilities and EV charging networks can comprise numerous smaller installations operating across a broad geographical area. “Individual sites can be relatively small, but developers are increasingly building portfolios comprising numerous assets across multiple locations,”added Harries. “Bringing those assets together allows us to underwrite them efficiently at portfolio scale, while still recognising the individual risk characteristics of each site.” The expanded facility builds on AGR’s existing Community Solar offering, which provides portfolio-based insurance for commercial and community-scale solar installations. By adding battery storage and EV charging infrastructure, AGR is extending its approach to cover a broader range of distributed energy assets. Harries said the inclusion of these technologies will allow AGR to assess how a portfolio’s exposure to natural catastrophes changes as further projects are incorporated. The programme is intended to accommodate portfolio growth while taking account of the risk characteristics of individual sites. “The addition of BESS and EV charging infrastructure reflects the increasing convergence of distributed energy technologies,” said Harries. “It allows us to focus on monitoring how the portfolio’s natural catastrophe exposure changes as new projects are added and gives developers the freedom to concentrate on building out their portfolios, knowing their insurance programme can adapt and grow alongside them.”

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI Leading SSB developer with precursor-free cathode focus According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Solid State Battery Precursor Free Cathodes market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global market for Solid State Battery Precursor Free Cathodes represents a pivotal enabler for the industrialization of solid-state batteries (SSBs), addressing the critical bottleneck of scalable, cost-effective electrode manufacturing. Unlike conventional cathode materials that rely on liquid or gel precursors, precursor-free cathodes are synthesized without traditional solvent-based routes, simplifying manufacturing and enhancing electrochemical performance. This market is not a materials science niche but a strategic linchpin for next-generation energy storage, fundamentally driven by automotive OEMs seeking step-change improvements in energy density and safety for electric vehicles. The value proposition shifts from chemical formulation alone to the integration of material synthesis with dry-process electrode engineering, creating a convergence point for battery materials specialists and dry-process equipment innovators. Supply chain risk is concentrated upstream in secure sourcing of high-purity metal oxides and phosphates, and downstream in multi-year qualification cycles with cell manufacturers. Pricing power will accrue to players controlling intellectual property on scalable synthesis routes and demonstrating validated performance in partner cell prototypes. The commercial model is bifurcating: a build path selling active material or coated electrodes, and a partner path centered on IP licensing and joint ventures. Geographic strategy is decoupled, with R&D and IP creation in established technology hubs and future high-volume production dictated by proximity to gigafactories and cost-competitive industrial bases. Regulatory tailwinds from enhanced battery safety and recycling directives indirectly favor SSB adoption, though precursor-free cathodes face distinct regulatory burdens in novel material handling and transportation classification. The competitive landscape is forming around distinct archetypes, with success contingent on securing a defensible position in the emerging dry-process value chain, from powder synthesis to calendaring, rather than attempting full vertical integration across the cell stack. The baseline scenario for the Solid State Battery Precursor Free Cathodes Market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust expansion, transitioning from pilot-scale qualification to commercial-scale deployment. Growth is underpinned by the accelerating adoption of solid-state batteries in electric vehicles, where precursor-free cathodes offer a pathway to higher energy density, improved safety, and simplified manufacturing. The market is expected to register a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 28.5% over the forecast period, reaching a market index of 980 by 2035 (2025=100). This trajectory assumes successful scale-up of dry-process electrode manufacturing, continued investment in gigafactory capacity, and resolution of upstream supply chain bottlenecks for high-purity metal oxides and phosphates. Early market capture will be dominated by IP licensing and joint ventures, as cell manufacturers and automotive OEMs prioritize de-risking novel material integration. Pricing power will accrue to players with validated performance data in partner cell prototypes and control over scalable synthesis routes. The commercial model will bifurcate into a build path, selling active material or coated electrodes, and a partner path, centered on IP licensing. Project economics for stationary storage applications will initially be constrained by premium cathode costs, making early adoption reliant on safety-critical or space-constrained use cases. Geographic strategy will be decoupled: R&D and IP creation concentrated in established technology hubs, while high-volume production follows proximity to gigafactories and cost-competitive industrial bases. Regulatory tailwinds from enhanced battery safety and recycling directives will indirectly favor SSB adoption, though precursor-free cathodes face distinct regulatory burdens in novel material handling and transportation classification. The competitive landscape will be shaped by distinct archetypes, with success contingent on securing a defensible position in the emerging dry-process value chain, from powder synthesis to calendaring. The electric vehicle segment is the primary demand engine for precursor-free cathodes, as automotive OEMs seek step-change improvements in energy density and safety. Currently, most EVs rely on conventional lithium-ion batteries with liquid electrolytes, but solid-state batteries promise higher energy density and improved safety. Precursor-free cathodes enable simplified, scalable manufacturing by eliminating traditional liquid or gel precursors, which is critical for cost-effective production. Through 2035, as solid-state battery technology matures and gigafactory capacity expands, demand for precursor-free cathodes will accelerate. Key demand-side indicators include EV production volumes, battery pack energy density targets, and the number of solid-state battery qualification programs at major OEMs. The shift to dry-process electrode manufacturing will further drive adoption, as precursor-free cathodes are inherently compatible with solvent-free processing. This segment will be the first to commercialize, with early adoption in premium and performance EVs, followed by mass-market models as costs decline. artigo.texto: African countries must strengthen cooperation, attract investment and ensure communities receive fair returns to turn the continent’s carbon market potential into climate and economic benefits, experts have said. The call came at the opening of the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 in Kigali on Wednesday, October 14. The two-day summit brought together around 600 policymakers, investors, project developers, corporate buyers and climate finance stakeholders. Co-organised by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment and the African Development Bank, the summit aims to strengthen African carbon markets and turn climate ambitions into investment-ready projects. ALSO READ: Inside Rwanda’s carbon credit deal with Singapore, Kuwait Rwanda’s Minister for Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, said Africa had reached a turning point in deciding how carbon markets operate and whom they benefit. "You are here because, like us, you believe that Africa’s carbon markets must be shaped by African priorities and that they must now deliver,” she told delegates. Despite progress in regulations and agreements, she said, slowing voluntary markets, concerns over credit integrity and a widening climate finance gap demanded renewed efforts. "These are not reasons to retreat. They are reasons to reset—and then build better,” Arakwiye said. From policy to investment Carbon markets generate credits from projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. When properly regulated, they can attract private investment into renewable energy, forest conservation, clean cooking and sustainable agriculture. However, Arakwiye said current market activity did not adequately reflect Africa’s development priorities. Forestry, land-use initiatives and improved cookstoves account for a significant share of African credits, while agriculture has generated barely one per cent of credits issued on voluntary markets over two decades. "The smallholder farmer, who has the most to gain and much to offer, is still standing largely outside this market,” she said. She called for greater investment in renewable energy, electric mobility, waste management, industrial decarbonisation and landscape restoration. Strengthening Africa’s bargaining power Dr Fatmata Lovetta Sesay, UNDP Resident Representative in Rwanda, said African countries needed stronger negotiating capacity despite progress in establishing carbon market regulations and institutions. Following a summit session on readiness to implement Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, she called for clear registration criteria, functional carbon registries, monitoring systems and project pipelines aligned with national priorities. "Africa is not lacking the legal framework that is required to govern how we operate in the carbon markets,” she said. "Africa is not lacking the opportunities that exist on the continent and several other places for this trading to happen.” She urged countries to negotiate from a position of strength and called for continental discussions to improve bargaining power and ensure African countries receive fair value for their climate assets. "This is not a race that is a sprint for countries in Africa. It&039;s a marathon,” she said, noting that countries were progressing at different speeds. Ensuring communities benefit Maxwell Gomera, UNDP Resident Representative in South Africa, said carbon markets must channel benefits to communities whose land and conservation efforts make projects possible. He called for stronger community rights and transparent benefit-sharing, early-stage project financing and partnerships based on measurable results. "A registry tracks a credit. It does not settle a land dispute,” he said, stressing the need for community consent and enforceable benefit-sharing arrangements. Gomera urged development banks to finance project preparation, while buyers should offer longer-term purchase agreements and advance funding. "Trust is market infrastructure, not sentiment,” he said. He also stressed the need to recognise the benefits of landscapes, from food production and water regulation to biodiversity and carbon storage, while preventing emissions reductions from being counted or sold twice. Rwanda seeks to diversify carbon credit projects beyond cookstoves Rwanda launched its National Carbon Market Framework in December 2023 to establish rules for developing, authorising, trading and monitoring credits, Arakwiye said. In May 2025, Rwanda and Singapore signed an implementation agreement under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, providing a pathway for authorised carbon credit transfers. Singapore committed to cancelling two per cent of correspondingly adjusted credits at first issuance and directing five per cent of the value of authorised credits towards adaptation measures in Rwanda. Rwanda has registered 29 carbon market projects across forestry, agriculture, land conservation, electric mobility, waste management and renewable energy. However, improved cookstove projects account for around 87 per cent of the country’s issued credits. The government has generated about $1.5 million (Rwf2.2 billion) from carbon credit sales. She called for African-suited methodologies, project-preparation facilities and long-term demand from buyers willing to pay fair prices. Rwanda is also exploring whether carbon revenue could be channelled through the Rwanda Green Fund to prepare and pre-finance projects. artigo.texto: Home › Policies & Regulations ›Finance Ministry Clarifies 10 Percent Customs Duty on Stationary and Grid-Scale BESS Finance Ministry Clarifies 10 Percent Customs Duty on Stationary and Grid-Scale BESS The Ministry of Finance has clarified that stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion BESS qualify for a concessional 10 percent Basic Customs Duty (BCD), while consumer power banks remain subject to the applicable 20 percent tariff rate. October 13, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey The Ministry of Finance has clarified that stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are eligible for a concessional Basic Customs Duty (BCD) rate of 10 percent, distinguishing them from consumer power banks, which are excluded from the concession and remain subject to the applicable 20 percent tariff rate. The clarification follows reports of divergent assessment practices among customs field formations for BESS classified under tariff item 8507 60 00. Some formations had been treating stationary, grid-scale and industrial BESS as power banks and denying them the concessional duty rate. The Ministry has clarified that the term ‘Power Bank’ applies only to lithium-ion battery devices equipped with charging and discharging ports and designed to function as external charging devices for cellular mobile phones or portable electronic devices. Consequently, stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion BESS falling under the specified tariff item are not covered by the power-bank exclusion and should not be denied the 10 percent concessional BCD rate merely on that basis. The clarification aims to address inconsistent customs assessments by establishing a clear distinction between portable consumer charging devices and stationary energy storage systems. The concessional duty provision continues to exclude battery packs used in the manufacture of electrically operated or hybrid vehicles, lithium-ion batteries or battery packs for cellular mobile phones, and power banks. artigo.texto: Os recentes ataques com drones ucranianos contra os data centers da Yandex resultaram numa queda acentuada do tráfego online de bots na Rússia. No entanto, os dados partilhados pela Cloudflare indicam que a diminuição está associada a processos automatizados da empresa e não a redes de desinformação, ao contrário do que sugerem várias publicações virais. Segundo o Tom's Hardware, um gráfico a circular nas redes sociais levou muitos utilizadores a assumirem que as quintas de trolls responsáveis por espalhar teorias da conspiração e spam tinham sido desativadas. Contudo, o investigador conhecido como antibot4navalny esclareceu na rede social X que os dados medem apenas os pedidos dos rastreadores web da Yandex, usados para indexar sites nos motores de pesquisa e fornecer suporte ao cliente. A Cloudflare confirma que a atividade geral de bots proveniente da Rússia permanece praticamente inalterada. Gráficos falsos e impacto nos serviços A confusão aumentou quando o eurodeputado Tomáš Zdechovský partilhou um gráfico sugerindo que a atividade online em torno do partido político alemão de extrema-direita AfD tinha despencado após os ataques. O informático Raphael Wimmer analisou a imagem e suspeita que esta tenha sido gerada por inteligência artificial, apontando inconsistências como a inclusão de dados referentes a uma data no futuro: 15 de outubro. Wimmer apelou ao fim da partilha de imagens não verificadas, depois de o autor original da publicação ter evitado responder a questões sobre a origem do gráfico. Entretanto, o impacto real dos ataques faz-se sentir na infraestrutura da empresa frequentemente apelidada de "Google da Rússia". A maioria dos sistemas operados pela Yandex continua offline, afetando gravemente serviços como o Yandex Pay, o que impede os utilizadores de realizar transferências, verificar saldos ou fazer compras. Dima Pirogov, responsável pela Yandex Fintech, afirmou em comunicado que a empresa ainda não consegue avançar com uma previsão exata para a recuperação, mas garantiu que a equipa não irá parar até o serviço ser restaurado.

artigo.texto: Cass County residents learn more about proposed Harmony Energy Park data center CASS COUNTY, N.D. (Valley News Live) - Cass County residents gathered in Wheatland Tuesday night to learn more about a proposed data center park, with a vote on a building moratorium just over a week away. The conversation on data centers continued as people gathered to learn about what is being called “Harmony Energy Park”. Harmony Energy Park is a proposed powered data park by Geronimo Power in Harmony Township. The property, set to be located off 32nd Street Southeast and 160th Avenue Southeast, would include two main data center buildings. Project details shared with residents Tuesday night, residents had a chance to learn about the 640-acre project, which would keep buildings at least a mile from any home. “We have noticed in our renewable energy business that the data center companies, the large tech companies have been our biggest customers for the past five or six years. When we saw what the power was going for when we were working with these different tech companies, we thought that we saw an opportunity to bring an even more big, and powerful economic opportunity,” said Blake Nixon, CEO and President of Geronimo Power. With Applied Digital building a data center in Harwood, Nixon said there are pros and cons. “When something new comes to town, change is concerning. Everybody wants to know what is this thing? Why? How is it going to impact me and my community? I think being able to see what a data center looks like is actually a really good thing because it’s just 10 miles away. I think it’s a little bit not good in the fact that, that’s a part of an industrial park and it looks like an industrial park. Which of course where we’re developing, is beautiful rural farmland,” Nixon said. Green space and community input About 80% of the space is expected to remain green space. “We’re asking the community to engage with us and tell us, ‘What do you want us to do with the other 80%? Do you want it to be trees? Grass?’ We can make it so you don’t see the data center if you don’t want to see the data center,” Nixon said. Some residents say data centers can have advantages and disadvantages. “I’m not against it coming in, it just needs to come in properly. Just like any other business, manufacturing elevator, you name it. Even farmers themselves on what they do on the land like I do. I should be cognizant of how I affect the community, too,” said Nathan Faleide, a Wheatland resident. For those who may be leaning toward not wanting a data center in the area, Nixon said: “We want to be a valued, added part of this community like we have been in the other places where we do business. We think the data center can be a big part of that story.” Moratorium vote and public forum Harmony Township has proposed a 24-month zoning moratorium on building solar and wind energy facilities as well as data centers. There is set to be a public hearing and proposed vote on October 22nd at 7 p.m. Residents will have another chance to weigh in on AI and data centers Wednesday. The Challey Institute is hosting a public forum from 5:30 to 7 p.m. in the Oceti Sakowin Ballroom at NDSU’s Memorial Union, looking at what data center growth could mean for North Dakota’s power grid, rates and local communities. The forum is free and open to anyone who wants to attend. More information can be found, here. Copyright 2026 KVLY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: ‘Yandex Pay’ partially resumes operations after Ukrainian drone strikes on data centers Dmitry Pirogov, the head of Yandex Pay’s fintech division, announced that the company has restored access to transfers and payments for some users. “Many of you can already see your money and manage it. We’re restoring access gradually so the service can handle the load. If some functionality isn’t available to you yet, please wait a little longer,” he wrote in the payment service’s Telegram channel. Pirogov stressed that the service “is still operating unstably”: some functions remain unavailable, and errors are possible during certain operations. Yandex Pay also announced special terms for users from October 11–17, covering savings accounts as well as loan payments. From the start, we built our infrastructure so that data on transactions would be replicated simultaneously across multiple data centers, because we work with literally the most valuable data our users have: data about their money. After the recent drone attacks on our data centers, our engineers had to completely rebuild the infrastructure in order to preserve this key principle and restore access to familiar functions. That’s why our service was hit especially hard, and recovery is taking longer. In recent days, Ukraine has struck three of the six data centers belonging to Yandex: facilities in the Ryazan region, Kaluga, and Vladimir. artigo.texto: This year, voters will elect the first new District 72 state representative for the first time in nearly two decades. Longtime Republican state Rep. Ed Clere, who has held the seat since 2008, is not seeking reelection. He’s focusing instead on a 2027 bid for mayor of New Albany, as an independent. Democrat Michele Henry and Republican Darrell Neeley are hoping to fill the role. Both recognize Hoosiers’ financial challenges, and they agree the state has a role in regulating data centers. Neither has held public office, though Neeley ran unsuccessfully for New Albany City Council in 2023. Meet the candidates Henry is a civil rights and worker’s rights attorney. She said she didn’t plan to run, and hadn’t previously considered running for office. But she wants to see changes. “I think that our legislature truly has just forgotten why it exists, and that is to improve the quality of life in our state,” Henry said. “And we haven't been doing that for 20 years now, and it is time to elect people who want to do that.” She said Indiana ranks poorly in some areas, such as public education. “We should be at the top of those lists,” she said. “This is a great state, and District 72 is a fantastic community.” Neeley is an associate pastor in New Albany and served more than three decades in the U.S. Navy. He said he wasn’t seeking the spot but that a lot of people reached out to him when it opened up. He said he sees it as a way to continue his track record of serving people. “This was another aspect in helping people, and being there to support those that think they don't have a voice,” Neeley said. When people asked him about running, “I finally sat down, prayed about it, thought about it, and so here we are.” Big goals Both candidates say they’ve heard from residents about how much they’re struggling to make ends meet, and Henry said focusing on affordability would be a priority. “We know that the rate of foreclosure is at…the highest in Indiana of all the 50 states, and that is largely because people are struggling to afford housing,” she said, adding that the prices of gas, groceries and utilities are also up. One way to help alleviate this, she said, is by eliminating sales tax on utilities and necessary household items, including hygiene products. She also wants to see the state minimum wage raised from its current $7.25 to at least $15. “There's nobody in the United States who could live on $7.25 an hour in any community, and certainly not in Indiana and not in District 72,” she said. She also said leaders should be responsible when bringing in new companies. “If we are going to provide incentives for companies to come to Indiana and bring jobs, we need to make sure that those jobs are quality jobs: that they offer a a salary, an hourly rate, and benefits that allow people to buy a home, to raise a family if that's what they choose to do, to not have to have a second job,” Henry said. Neeley said he wants to continue the state’s economic growth through fiscal responsibility. During his Navy career, he managed $300 million budgets, he said. “I knew how to budget, knew how to use taxpayers' money,” Neeley said. “Because it's not the government's, it wasn't the Navy's. It's the people's money.” He said he also thinks most people just want to make sure their tax money is spent wisely. He noted that 2027 is a biannual budget year for Indiana, which is a “prime opportunity to address the cost of living.” He said legislators need to increase grants and remove barriers for child care, so working families can continue to work. He wants state and local leaders to address what he calls burdensome restrictions on housing, and to see the state’s Residential Housing Infrastructure Assistance Program continue. He said he supports property tax reform, especially when it “addresses our problematic assessment system” and targets relief for seniors and people with disabilities. Getting things done Henry said she hopes Republicans won’t be in the supermajority at the statehouse after the election, which she thinks could make it easier for Democrats to be more effective, rather than continuing what she calls Republicans’ “pro-corporation legislative activity.” “I think there is a very real chance that the Democrats do get out of the superminority this year,” she said. “And once that happens, we will obviously have a lot more play at the table. We'll be able to implement proposals… We'll be able to take action that actually helps people in our communities.” She said even if the partisan gap doesn’t change, she hopes the parties can work together “to actually implement real relief and pro-Hoosier legislation.” Neeley said it’s crucial to work together, and that it’s not beneficial to reject good ideas based on party labels. “These games have to stop,” he said, adding that whether constituents support him or not, “you still have a voice in this district and at the statehouse too. We have to work together, or we're not going to get anywhere.” Both candidates said they would like to continue in the spirit Clere served with for so long. “I have a tremendous amount of respect for Ed,” Henry said. “He’s a moderate person who actually does listen to his constituents.” That’s something she’d like to continue. She also wants to make sure people in the district are represented at the state level. “Southern Indiana folks feel a lot of the time like they aren't heard, that Indianapolis doesn't remember that we are part of the state and not part of, you know, Louisville,” she said. “And so I think it's important that we listen to what the needs are in our community and bring those to the statehouse and then work on solutions that work for our community.” Neeley noted Clere’s focus on health care and legislation for people with disabilities, which he’d like to carry on. “I plan on picking his brain,” Neeley said. artigo.texto: The No Data Centers SGV Coalition and the Puente Hills Community Preservation Association (PHCPA) will hold a community fundraising rally on Sunday, October 18, to raise $90,000 for PHCPA’s legal challenge to the Marici Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facility project and potential data center developments in the City of Industry. By News Desk The rally will take place from 10:00 am to 1:00 pm at Schabarum Regional Park, 17250 E. Colima Road in Rowland Heights, across from Puente Hills Mall and near the approved Marici project site. Funds will support litigation-related costs, including legal fees, court expenses, and expert analysis. A limited portion will go toward community outreach and operational expenses related to the effort. Organizers are urging residents to support responsible development, environmental protection, and transparent public decision-making. They cite concerns about potential effects on homes, schools, parks, natural resources, and quality of life. They are calling for thorough environmental review, disclosure of project impacts, and meaningful public participation. Recent industrial and battery-related fires—including the Lineage Logistics fire in Boyle Heights, the Moss Landing battery storage fire, and a battery fire at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne—have heightened community concerns about fire hazards, emergency preparedness, toxic smoke exposure, and evacuation planning. Residents can contribute to PHCPA’s legal fund at the rally or online at this link. PHCPA will also hold a Panda Express fundraiser on October 18, from 9:30 am to 10:00 pm, at the restaurant on Colima and Azusa. Supporters can also purchase a $16 digital voucher for a dozen Original Glazed doughnuts at participating Krispy Kreme locations in the United States. Each voucher raises $8 for PHCPA.

artigo.texto: Trending Failing to regulate data centers could cost Ohioans billions of dollars in higher electricity cost and air pollution, according to a new analysis. The study by Columbus-based analytic firm Scioto Analysis estimates Ohioans would end up spending $16 billion more in electric bills and would suffer $41 billion in air pollution damage without regulations. The analysis estimates under current policies, data center growth could cost Ohio electricity customers $16 billion in higher utility costs between 2027 and 2034. Meanwhile, Ohio’s data center sales and use tax exemption cost the state an estimated $1.6 billion in revenue in 2025. "We are watching a financial crisis develop in real time, and the Ohio Statehouse is failing to respond,” said State Rep. Tristan Rader, D-Lakewood. “We have allowed some of the wealthiest corporations on Earth to receive billions in tax breaks while Ohio families face the prospect of billions more in electricity costs. At this point, our continued inaction isn’t just disappointing - it’s irresponsible.” Rader is working on legislation that he says would reconsider Ohio's "generous" tax exemptions for data centers and establish long-term financial commitments and safeguards protecting existing customers. "Ohio families should not be the venture capitalists for Silicon Valley’s expansion," the legislator said. "We don’t get a share of their profits, and we shouldn’t be handed their bills. The Statehouse needs to act before those bills come due.” According to the tracking group Data Center Map, Ohio has 240 data centers. Another study, by the Goldwater Institute, downplays the threat from data centers, "The bigger problem is an electricity system that hides scarcity from consumers until strain appears as congestion, reliability risks, or higher costs," the institute said. Higher prices would lead to higher efficiency, according to the Institute. "When millions of consumers face fixed prices, demand remains high precisely when the system is under the most pressure, the institute concluded.

artigo.texto: Amazon builds workforce pipeline alongside data center construction in Caddo, Bossier parishes Company outlines education programs, apprenticeships and tuition fund tied to new data centers SHREVEPORT, La. (KSLA) - Construction is progressing on Amazon data centers in Caddo and Bossier parishes, and the company says it is also focused on building a workforce to support the facilities. KSLA’s Marvin Andrade spoke one-on-one with Amazon Web Services Vice President of Economic Development Roger Wehner about the company’s workforce plans. Construction progress Progress is visible along Stateline Road in Caddo Parish and in Bossier Parish, about 40 minutes away. At the Resilient Parkway site in Shreveport, Amazon leaders said they are weeks away from breaking ground. Amazon said the first building is on track to go online by next summer. Education outreach Alongside construction, Amazon said one of its priorities is education. “Have you ever thought about being a fusion splicer or your really into hardware and computer do you want to be a data center technician? So that’s where we always start with educating the folks students, educators, and influencers on what those career opportunities are,” Wehner said. The company will host a program November 17 at Bossier Parish Schools’ Center for Technology and Innovative Learning, followed by sessions November 18 and 19 at North Louisiana Technical Community College. The goal is to show students the career paths a data center can open up before they apply for a job. Apprenticeship program Amazon plans to launch a four-week paid apprenticeship program designed to give students hands-on experience. “We kind of expose them to all the job skills in a data center everything from construction to operation, etc. We pay for that historically, we have had an 85% placement rate for the graduates,” Wehner said. Tuition fund Amazon said it wants to help cover community college costs for students by creating a new fund. “We’re going to create an endowment. We are going to use the current financial apparatus that already exists; we will invest in that, and then they will manage the funds back to the students when they apply,” Wehner said. Addressing skepticism Some residents remain skeptical about the data centers coming to the region. KSLA asked Wehner what he would say to critics. “We can talk and bring in folks from other communities and share them their experience of 20 years and just give us a fair opportunity to explain how we’re different and how we operate the way we do,” Wehner said. Educator workshop planned Amazon will hold an educator workshop December 3. The goal is to teach educators how to inform students about what future jobs at the data centers will look like. (KSLA) - Four of the seven candidates for Shreveport mayor took the stage Wednesday night to make their case to voters at a forum hosted by KSLA and the Greater Shreveport Chamber of Commerce. Arceneaux addresses data center concerns Incumbent Mayor Tom Arceneaux pointed to accomplishments during his time in office while also addressing concerns about data center projects. “Infrastructure is there for the data centers, will be paid for by the data centers, and will not be included in the residential rate base. So, I think that those actions have been sufficient to answer those particular questions. I also point out that all the sale of electricity also produces additional revenue to the city of Shreveport,” Arceneaux said. Gage-Watts proposes entertainment district Caddo Parish Commissioner Stormy Gage-Watts said she has her own plan for moving Shreveport forward. “I am in favor of a film and entertainment district here in Shreveport. I am open to do business with 50 Cent and any and all other public-private partnerships that will be positive and bring economic development to our area,” Gage-Watts said. Phelps calls for police pay review State Rep. Tammy Phelps focused on funding public safety and is calling for a review of police officer pay. “When we talk about recruiting, we talk about those salaries, I really would like to sit down and create a salary schedule and look at all the salaries, how we continue to move forward and how we continue to pay and raise the rates of our police department,” Phelps said. Young proposes water system audit Caddo Parish Commissioner John-Paul Young proposed an outside audit of Shreveport’s water system. “I propose to audit the system for the very first time, externally and forensically, so that we can weed out the fraud and recapture the waste to improve our system, and then put it under the management of a competent engineering firm,” Young said. artigo.texto: Future-Proofing Data Center Cooling: Designing for the Unknown Data center planners are being asked to make infrastructure decisions around workloads that can change in months. AI training, inference and traditional enterprise computing can place different demands on the same facility. Rack densities may rise unevenly, hardware roadmaps may shift, and the cooling strategy selected for one deployment may not fit the next. In that environment, future-proofing is less about choosing the winning technology and more about creating a mechanical system that can change without forcing the facility to start over. Design for a range, not a single design point A conventional design process begins with a target load, but that target ideally should be treated as part of a range. Depending on time of day, the usage may vary, requiring a varying range of cooling needs. The equipment must be able to provide necessary cooling at peak and off-peak times. Therefore, it's critical to have designed-in redundancy to maintain maximum uptime especially during peak usage. The system should account for mixed rack densities, partial buildouts and changing proportions of air- and liquid-cooled loads. A hall that supports high-density racks in one zone and lower-density equipment in another may need different supply temperatures, airflow rates and redundancy strategies at the same time. Zoning allows capacity to be directed where it is needed instead of requiring the entire room to operate for the most demanding rack. The roadmap should define day-one needs, staged additions and the physical constraints that could block growth. Space for piping, manifolds, heat exchangers, pumps, electrical distribution, controls and service access should be considered before those components are required. With capacity continuing to increase, it's important to design with that in mind. Liquid cooling does not mean water or to eliminate air The phrase “liquid cooling” can mislead important system differences. Liquid cooling is primarily tied to high-performance computing applications such as AI processing and machine learning. It's important to note that these cooling trends are not an industry wide change, but rather a modification to higher density applications where air cooling is no longer sufficient. Lower latency applications and general cloud storage will continue to be air cooled via fans. Liquid, in this case, describes how heat is transported, not necessarily tied to the water usage of the data center. Depending on the architecture, the above mentioned “liquid” may be treated water, a water-glycol mixture, a refrigerant or a dielectric fluid. Heat then moves through a coolant distribution unit, or CDU, and ultimately is rejected through dry, evaporative or hybrid equipment. Liquid cooling also does not make fans irrelevant. Direct-to-chip and immersion cooling remove heat directly from the source at the chip. Air cooling will still be required for the remaining 20-30% of the white and grey space, as heat is still produced by the remaining mechanical equipment. Rear-door heat exchangers, an air-assisted liquid cooling system, deliberately combine both media in this hybrid system. Future-proofing depends on reserving space, connections and control capacity for both air and liquid paths. That flexibility allows a facility to support higher-density or hybrid cooling without replacing the entire thermal system. The goal is not to predict which approach will dominate, but to make future transitions possible in manageable phases. Make retrofit readiness a design requirement A future-ready system should be evaluated by how it changes while the data center remains in operation. Can a new cooling zone be connected without shutting down an existing one? Can airflow be rebalanced as racks move? Can fans be replaced without reducing the required level of redundancy? Are operators able to see both air- and liquid-side performance through a coordinated control system? Can cooling capacity be increased in the existing footprint? These questions turn future retrofits from an impending construction concern into a present-day reliability requirement. Controls are especially important because installed capacity and actual demand rarely match perfectly. Temperature, pressure, flow and power data allow fans to respond to real loads rather than fixed calculations. They also give operators a baseline for identifying lost capacity, testing new configurations and verifying that a retrofit performs as intended. These critical systems can have zero downtime, even during a retrofit. It’s important to have real time and reliable controls for commissioning of these retrofit systems. Preserve choices No design can anticipate every processor, rack configuration or cooling medium that will arrive over the life of a facility. It can, however, preserve choices. A system designed around ranges, zones, modular increments, and coordinated controls can absorb change with less disruption. That is the practical meaning of future-proofing: not predicting the unknown but ensuring the next decision does not require undoing the last one. artigo.texto: Overview: A Former Navajo Nation President talks running for congress, data centers and water rights. Northern Arizona is confronting a collision of growth, drought and accelerating tech demand. Former Navajo president Jonathan Nez, now running for Arizona’s 2nd Congressional district as a Democrat, says the region’s political leadership hasn’t kept pace. Speaking to Native News Online, Nez outlines how data center proposals, shrinking Colorado River allocations and rising utility costs are reshaping daily life for Native and rural voters across the district – and how he hopes to address those issues if elected. Nez argues that transparency failures and rushed development have fueled public backlash from Tucson to Page, where residents ousted local officials over undisclosed data center negotiations. Nez ties those fights to broader questions of water security, tribal sovereignty and the future of clean energy in Indian Country. “Water is life,” Nez said. “We need to ensure water is available not just now, but for our children, grandchildren and seven generations and beyond.” This interview has been edited for clarity and length. What are your thoughts on the expansion of data centers in Indian Country and surrounding communities? Any type of economic development venture should start with local leaders being transparent with their constituents. I see time and time again, especially in Indian Country, where the public is not informed about what is going on, and the aftereffect is opposition to large-scale projects, including data centers. You have elected leaders who have good intentions for bringing in revenue and jobs, but we also have to be better stewards of the land and our resources. Data centers use a lot of water, they use a lot of energy, and there is a lot of noise from these types of facilities. Outside tribal nations, property values around these data centers lessen in value. As a person running for Congress right now, we have to have a better relationship with local leaders — and that means town leaders, city leaders, county leaders and state leaders. Technology is expanding throughout the world, and there is a need for data storage. That is why these data centers are being considered in places all across the country. But in the Southwest, we are in a drought, and water is life. I think in the Southwest, tribes are saying “no” to these data centers, and their neighbors outside tribal areas are also saying “no.” Here in Arizona, the city of Tucson in the southern part of the state has taken a position saying “no” to data centers. Recently, primary elections took place in the city of Page in northern Arizona, where local leaders, I believe, were not very transparent about what was going on. When the public found out that elected leaders were pursuing a data center, they came out in full force in opposition and even removed those council members from elected positions. So in the area, there’s a lot of pushback and opposition. The federal administration has announced that Arizona will face the largest cuts among states and tribes relying on the Colorado River amid the ongoing drought. What are you hearing from voters about water scarcity, and how are communities responding? They are upset that our current leaders, especially my opponent, are nowhere to be found and should be at the table during these water rights discussions. The federal government, as you said, made a decision to reduce water allocations from the Colorado River by 30%. That’s the largest of any state in the Upper and Lower Basins of the Colorado River. You probably have that data in front of you where it says large data centers can consume 1 million to 5 million gallons of water per day. That’s around 1.8 billion gallons per year. And that’s the concern. There’s a lot of growth in Arizona, people moving into the Southwest and into Congressional District 2 that I am running to represent. We need to make sure we get our fair share of water from tributaries that include the Colorado River and also protect our precious groundwater. There needs to be a serious discussion in the Southwest about conservation, especially when water levels are lessening. Two dams on the Colorado River right now — Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam — are at all-time lows since they were filling up. Those two dams create hydroelectricity, inexpensive power that goes to southern Arizona, California and Nevada. We’re at a point where the water that goes through the dam to spin the generators is almost below the intake valves. If that happens, they call it “dead pool,” meaning water will just sit there without going through the dam or downstream. That will increase utility rates. Electricity bills will only go up further. That’s the concern here in the Southwest. It all surrounds water security. As we say in Indian Country, water is life. We need to ensure water is available not just now, but for our children, grandchildren, and seven generations and beyond. How do you view the transition toward renewable energy in Indian Country, particularly as federal policies affect energy development and social services? As president and vice president of the Navajo Nation — the largest tribe in the country — we saw outside influence focused on shutting down coal-fired power plants in the Southwest, including the Navajo Generating Station. There were a lot of negotiations to keep that facility up because of the jobs and revenue coming in, alongside discussions of transitioning into renewable energy: natural gas, solar. But the powers that be decided it needed to be decommissioned. To this day, there is no more coal-fired power plant in that area. The coal used to fuel that station came from the Navajo Nation via Peabody Coal Company. When the plant went away, Peabody Coal had to close its doors. artigo.texto: OCP 2026: Agentic AI Drives the Data Center's Chip-to-Grid Transformation Key Highlights - OCP is extending its standards mission from servers and racks to the full AI infrastructure stack, encompassing silicon, cooling, power distribution, facilities and utility-grid integration. - AMD introduced its Helion agentic AI rack, while Arm and NVIDIA outlined new CPU architectures and infrastructure requirements for rapidly expanding autonomous workloads. - Meta detailed the engineering behind its Prometheus AI cluster in Ohio, including fabric structures, new optical networking, open-source transport software and AI-optimized concrete. - Broadcom and NVIDIA presented advances in Ethernet networking and optical interconnects designed to overcome the growing physical constraints of accelerator clusters. - New OCP data center and grid-resilience specifications, along with NVIDIA's advances in dynamic power management, signal a shift toward treating the AI factory as a coordinated, grid-aware infrastructure system. Standing before thousands of engineers and technology executives at the opening of the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, Meta's Santosh Janardhan pointed to the enormous fabric structure surrounding the audience. It was, he explained, an example of the same construction technology Meta had begun deploying to accelerate its massive AI infrastructure buildout. At the company's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio, traditional assumptions about data center construction had given way to an urgent question: What if the next generation of AI infrastructure could be built in months rather than years, using engineered fabric structures instead of conventional concrete-and-steel buildings? "We are actually also training a model while we were building it," said Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure. The presentation offered a striking illustration of the larger message emerging from Monday's opening keynotes: The AI factory is becoming a fundamentally different kind of data center. Across presentations by AMD, Meta, Arm, Broadcom and NVIDIA, a common theme emerged. The rapid expansion of AI inference and autonomous agents is forcing new approaches to computing, networking, construction, power distribution and operations. At the same time, the diversity of silicon architectures and the enormous physical scale of deployments are making common infrastructure specifications increasingly important. The result is a significant expansion of OCP's original mission. Fifteen years after the organization began applying open-source principles to hardware design, the industry's next challenge is developing interoperable infrastructure across the entire data center, from processor architecture to the utility connection. OCP's New Mandate: From Chip to Grid OCP CEO George Tchaparian opened the summit by describing an organization whose scale increasingly reflects the industry's transformation. This year's event attracted approximately 15,000 attendees, with another 3,000 on a waitlist. Tchaparian said OCP expects membership to exceed 700 organizations by year-end, while technical contributions are growing approximately 30% annually. The organization has already announced that its 2027 Global Summit will move to San Francisco's Moscone Center to accommodate further growth. More consequential than the attendance figures, however, is the widening scope of OCP's work. Originally centered on open server designs, racks and supporting hardware, the organization's roadmap now encompasses facilities infrastructure, liquid cooling, power distribution, firmware, security, networking and the increasingly complex connections between data centers and utilities. Tchaparian characterized the emerging approach as "chip-to-grid" infrastructure. This reflects a fundamental engineering problem. As hyperscalers and AI infrastructure providers deploy increasingly specialized processors, the electrical, thermal and mechanical consequences of those design decisions extend well beyond individual servers. Higher accelerator densities require new cooling strategies. New power architectures affect rack configurations and electrical distribution. Faster networks alter equipment layouts and cable requirements. Different silicon designs can introduce entirely new facility-level constraints. The traditional process of designing computing equipment and adapting data centers to accommodate it is increasingly difficult to sustain at AI scale. OCP is therefore emphasizing what Tchaparian called co-optimized data centers: infrastructure in which silicon, racks, networking, cooling and power systems are developed with common interfaces and shared design objectives. The challenge is compounded by growing silicon diversity. Hyperscalers are developing custom accelerators alongside commercial GPUs and CPUs, increasing the risk of fragmented hardware ecosystems that require repeated engineering across otherwise similar facilities. OCP also intends to extend hyperscale-derived standards into what it calls the AI computing continuum, encompassing neocloud providers, colocation operators, enterprises and geographically distributed inference infrastructure. The objective is not to eliminate architectural differentiation. It is to reduce the amount of infrastructure that must be redesigned every time the underlying computing technology changes. Agentic AI Gives the CPU a New Mission One of the most consequential themes of the opening keynotes was the renewed importance of general-purpose computing. AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su described 2026 as the year of inference, estimating that inference now represents approximately 60% of the AI computing market. She pointed to an approximately 14-fold increase in agentic AI traffic during the year, reflecting the accelerating adoption of systems that do more than respond to individual prompts. artigo.texto: Notebooks com RTX Spark terão centenas de jogos no lançamento Call of Duty em 2027! Veja teste A Nvidia e a Microsoft apresentaram o Surface Ultra, novo notebook ultrafino baseado na tecnologia RTX Spark. O modelo é um dos primeiros adotar a tecnologia, q. A Razer anunciou a chegada da nova linha de mouses topo de linha com foco gamer e ergonômico: o Basilisk V4 Pro é o destaque. O novo aparelho da geração traz melhorias no hardware, como um sensor óptico de 50 mil DPI, além de algumas revisões e adições importantes, principalmente no conjunto de botões. Em termos de design, os novos Basilisk mantêm basicamente o mesmo estilo dos seus antecessores, com aquela saliência lateral que funciona como um descanso. A parte interessante é que as opções de controle foram expandidas para 14 botões personalizáveis, ou seja, bem mais que a geração do V3. Somente na parte lateral, o novo mouse conta com quatro botões, no que a companhia diz servirem a tecnologia Hypershift, controle de IA, e dois botões livres. Como se não fosse o suficiente, a companhia também inseriu um pequeno botãozinho na borda de um dos switches para alternar perfis de configuração. Um dos pontos que a Razer retrabalhou para a linha Basilisk V4, em especial o modelo Pro, foi o anel de rolagem. O Hyperscroll de 2ª geração foi adaptado para entregar quatro modos ao usuário: modo tátil de precisão e padrão, modo de rolagem livre e um modo de rolagem inteligente. Novo sensor e 275 horas de bateria Na parte de dentro, a companhia estadunidense também trocou algumas peças do periférico, como o sensor. Agora, o Basilisk V4 Pro é equipado com o sensor óptico Razer Focus Pro de 3ª geração com sensibilidade de 50 mil DPI, velocidade de rastreamento de 930 IPS e aceleração de 90g. Junto a isso, a fabricante colocou switches ópticos de 4ª geração nos dois botões principais do periférico, projetados para suportar 100 milhões de cliques. A comunicação ocorre através do HyperSpeed Wireless, que promete uma taxa de atualização de 8.000 Hz via dongle. Por falar em conectividade, ele também funciona via Bluetooth e pode ser conectado a até cinco dispositivos. Já sobre a bateria, a Razer promete que o novo Basilisk consegue entregar uma autonomia de até 200 horas ao utilizá-lo no modo de 1.000 Hz (dongle) e 275 horas com Bluetooth. Para a recarga, ele também aceita carregadores sem fio. - Para acompanhar o mouse, a Razer também revelou a nova Mouse Dock V2 Pro para carregamento magnético sem fio; - Essa dock tem um receptor de 8.000 Hz integrado, possibilitando parear mouse e teclado compatíveis; - A companhia também anunciou o Razer HyperFlux V2, uma base de carregamento que também funciona como mousepad; - O Basilisk V4 padrão pesa somente 94g, trabalha com sensor óptico Focus X 33K, 12 botões programáveis e entrega até 140 horas de bateria. A nova geração de mouses Razer Basilisk ainda não tem data para chegar ao mercado brasileiro. No exterior, os dispositivos já estão disponíveis. Confira os preços abaixo: - Razer Basilisk V4 Pro: US$ 170 (cerca de R$ 800 em conversão direta); - Razer Basilisk V4 HyperSpeed: US$ 110 (R$ 550); - Razer Mouse Dock V2 Pro: US$ 70 (R$ 300); - Razer HyperFlux V2: US$ 119 (R$ 600). Por falar na Razer, nós já analisamos o Razer Basilisk V3 Pro e esse é um dos melhores mouses gamer disponíveis no Brasil, mas é caríssimo.
